en: The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*: A Hand-Instruction, Scroll One.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhixiang of Yunfeng, Chu and Heng.
The Buddhas of the *rajas-aṇu-kalpa* (dust-mote eons) and the Buddhas of the ten directions currently seated at the site of enlightenment—each of whom bears witness and silently concurs.
It is the wondrous Dharma. What is this wondrous Dharma? It is precisely the Buddha and sentient beings, both of whom receive it together as a numinous presence.

It is vividly distinct and solitary luminosity—without sound and without form, such that it cannot be apprehended through characteristics; it is sought through the absence of characteristics. Such is this wondrous Dharma.

Fundamentally, there is neither past nor present, nor birth nor extinction. How could all Tathāgatas possess the past and present, or the birth and extinction, of manifesting their appearance, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering parinirvāṇa?

It is simply that when the Buddhas realize this Dharma that is without past or present and without birth or extinction, they immediately vow that all people, including those of the future limit, shall together realize this. All...
If sentient beings do not realize it in a single day, the Buddhas will not be at peace for a single day.
If sentient beings do not realize it over the accumulation of kalpas, the Buddhas likewise will not be at peace over the accumulation of kalpas.

Therefore, one must inevitably manifest the birth and death of the past and present within that which is devoid of past, present, or birth and death, in order to rescue those who have not realized this state beyond past, present, or birth and death. This is precisely my original [intention].
"World-Honored One, with a heart that finds no peace, I have come to be born in this world of endurance (*sahā*).
Within that which is fundamentally devoid of past and present, or birth and cessation, I have suddenly manifested an inexhaustible succession of past, present, and the cycles of birth and cessation.
With my Buddha-eye, I behold the sentient beings of the six realms; they are impoverished, lacking in merit and wisdom, and their continuity of suffering is unceasing."
It is for the sake of these sentient beings that one gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
When a Buddha perceives that the sentient beings of the six realms are impoverished—though they truly possess merit and wisdom, yet truly lack a Buddha—he possesses spiritual power;
yet this does not exceed the capacity of a king who, by issuing a pardon, releases people from suffering. How could he possibly cause every person to attain the rank of a king?
That the Buddha felt such unease over this is no different from the worldly person who feels personal distress out of compassion for things;
it is certainly not the fundamental intent of the Buddha’s appearance in the world. One must understand that, ultimately, there is neither past nor present, and there is neither arising nor ceasing.
It must exist within the inexhaustible flow of past and present, and amidst the inexhaustible cycle of arising and ceasing.

By turning back from this past and present, arising and ceasing, until one reaches the ultimate limit of the inexhaustible, then past and present are exhausted, and arising and ceasing are exhausted; only then does it manifest before one.

Therefore, the demonstration of birth is not intended for anything other than to lead people to realize this non-arising; the demonstration of form is not intended for anything other than to lead people to realize this formlessness.
There are sentient beings whose attachment to signs is profound, and their attachment to birth is even more so.

Having become submerged within the cycle of arising and ceasing throughout past and present, they either cling to existence or cling to emptiness. To them, existence and [emptiness] seem as if they were running in opposite directions;
the further they advance, the farther apart they drift, until it seems there will be no time for them to meet again. For this reason, the Tathāgata, regarding this matter, remains far removed.

Thus, for hundreds of thousands of kalpas they have come and gone; at the very least, for over forty years they have enticed and guided others, exhausting their boundless compassion to the utmost and wearing away their infinite heart-essence until nothing remains. They take that vivid, solitary luminosity which each person possesses—

Turning left and revolving right, it molds and refines in manifold ways. When it finally employs the light of the white tuft of hair to allure and entice the eyes and mind, only then does [Shen] Lingyun revive. Thus, it causes everyone’s hearts and eyes to sway and tremble;
the ratchet-wheel seems about to turn within that empty and numinous space, such that one almost reaches out a hand to touch it, yet finds no way to do so. Therefore, it is like this:

Having arrived at this single opportunity, my original intent is finally fulfilled. Regarding the great matter for which I have come into the world, there is no cause or condition of past or present, nor of birth and death.
With open chest and sincere heart, I pour forth my teaching; provisional and ultimate truths are harmonized and fused.
I raise up the lineage that all the spiritually awakened share and entrust it to each individual in detail, so that everyone within this assembly may fully realize their own mind. Truly...
There is no past or present; in truth, there is neither arising nor ceasing. One may know with certainty that what will come in the future is precisely this ultimate attainment of Buddhahood;

that it is precisely this which shall deliver immeasurable sentient beings; that it is precisely this which returns to the source where Buddha, mind, and sentient beings are non-differentiated in their threefold identity;
and that it is precisely this which shares a single nostril with all Buddhas and World-Honored Ones, breathing together with them. Yet, for the sake of this one...
Matters. Having long been burdened by a sense of unease and inner distress, I have finally found some consolation. It is for this reason that our World-Honored One has appeared in the world;

having appeared once, he has repeatedly preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* to instruct all bodhisattvas, so that they may share in the fundamental aspiration most cherished and protected by all Buddhas.
In order to explain this sutra, I shall first divide it into four sections. △ First, a brief explanation of the title of the sutra.
As for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (The Lotus Sutra of the Sublime Dharma): "Dharma" refers to the single True Suchness Mind-Dharma (*tathatā-citta-dharma*).
It is the foremost ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), most wondrous and most profound, both mundane and supramundane. What is meant by the True Suchness Mind-Dharma?

It is because it is fully present in every single thing, fundamentally without increase or decrease. Indeed, among all living beings throughout the great earth—regardless of whether they are monastics or laypeople, male or female, old or young—[it is universally present].
Whether wise or foolish, celestial beings, immortals, gods, or ghosts, white oxen or dark-skinned slaves—all are equally endowed with the natural state; each and every one is fully manifest.
If you attempt to grope for it, investigate it, grasp at a realization of it, or try to master it, it will unfailingly respond to your mind and fulfill your wishes.
There is nothing you cannot attain, nothing you cannot realize. It is not that every single thing is individually complete, yet [it is so].

Why is this? Furthermore, all monastics and laypeople, men and women, old and young, wise and foolish, celestial beings, immortals, spirits, and ghosts, white oxen and black slaves, down to shrimp, clams, and oysters, and even blades of grass and tiny insects—all possess immeasurable wisdom yet do not employ it;
they possess immeasurable liberation yet do not realize it; they possess immeasurable samādhis yet do not enter them.
They measure their supernatural powers yet do not take [the results] for themselves. Through kalpas and successive lifetimes, they have accumulated delusions;

within the field of sounds, forms, persons, and self, they listen to and are driven by greed, anger, and jealousy. Subjected to the impulses of attachment and ignorance, they may even enter the womb of a donkey.
Whether dwelling in the belly of a horse, coming once and going once, or undergoing ten thousand deaths and ten thousand births, this very thing remains ever-present and never departs.

Is there any increase or decrease? Precisely because it is fully present in every single thing without increase or decrease, the four classes of noble beings and the six realms of ordinary beings all rely upon it as their root and foundation. Apart from this, there is nothing else that can serve as the fundamental basis.
This is why it is called the most wondrous, most profound, and supreme ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Since our World-Honored One realized this for himself through kalpas of eons past,
he has sat upon a great lotus flower within the inexhaustible ocean of fragrant water for twenty-one days and expounded the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*,
the Perfect Sūtra, having appeared in this world for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
Within that space, clouds upon clouds arise and waves upon waves emerge; these are solely Vairocana and his retinue of bodhisattvas, as numerous as atoms, acting as the principal and the attendants.
Thus, throughout an ocean of lands as numerous as atoms, there are principal and attendant figures as numerous as atoms;
even within a single most minute atom, there are such principal and attendant figures as numerous as atoms. As it is here...
These are the principal and the retinue who expound such Dharma-gates. Furthermore, how could there be any separate thing called "Dharma"?

Nevertheless, the World-Honored One, without departing from the Bodhi tree, manifests clouds of bodies throughout the Dharma-realm, sitting everywhere in the sites of enlightenment, in accordance with the nature of the Dharma-realm.
Regarding the elucidation of the Great Dharma-door of Universal, Perfectly Interfused, and Unobstructed Liberation:

it is solely because sentient beings who cling to signs have dull faculties and are obscured in both sight and hearing that [the Buddha], having no choice, manifested two aspects. Yet these two began simultaneously;
within this indivisible wondrous Dharma, he established the three categories of sudden, gradual, and secret, as well as the one vehicle and the three vehicles.
Great! To provide a detailed exposition would result in forty years of boiling tongues and cold waves.
For this Dharma, when gathered together, there is no way to discern its traces; when dispersed, there is no way to exhaust its names.
Thus, it is called the "Tathāgatagarbha-nature" in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the "Eternally Abiding True Mind," and in the *Vajracchedikā*, it is named the "Profound Prajñā."

If one names it the True Doctrine of the Real Mark (dharmatā-lakṣaṇa), it is called the Unobstructed Monastery (*anāvaraṇa-vihāra*) in the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Samantabhadra-bodhicitta-sūtra*).

In the *Laṅkāvatāra*, it is the Heart-Dharma of the Buddha’s Words. As for its presence within the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is that which is neither extinguished nor born, neither permanent nor annihilated;
it is called the "Eye of Maheśvara" and the "Poison-Coated Drum. Even down to the final act at Vulture Peak where the flower was held up, it is said: "The Real Mark is markless. Such is the teaching.
There are separate external transmissions, but in reality, they are all this very Dharma. If one adheres to it, both ordinary beings and sages are accommodated;
if one departs from it, both sages and ordinary beings are extinguished. It is profound beyond measurement and subtle beyond penetration.

It is present within its form yet lacks solidity; it unfolds within its emptiness yet lacks ostentation. It cannot be grasped through conceptual thought or deliberation. Therefore, it is called "One Wondrous [Function]."
It is designated by names. Now, that which is called "wondrous" is so because its essence remains unchanging while its function accords with conditions.
When speaking of this essence, it cannot be named, it cannot be described, it cannot be defiled, and it cannot be purified.

Furthermore, how could one point to anything such as sagehood or ordinariness, delusion or awakening? It is like clear, still water or a perfectly lustrous pearl; though profoundly still, it is luminous.
It swallows shadows and falls; it cannot be obscured. When its function is examined, the holy and the profane, delusion and awakening, revolve accordingly with it.
Even if they were not to revolve, they would certainly remain as holy and profane, deluded and awakened—what wonder would there be in that?
Furthermore, the holy do not increase, and the profane do not decrease; the wondrous is without benefit or harm. If the holy were to have even a slight increase, or the profane a small...
Wherein lies the subtle tranquility? When sentient beings attain it, all affairs are harmonized; when insentient things attain it, all phenomena flourish.
If only sentient beings were to attain it while insentient things did not, it would not be considered subtle. It is only because Heaven attains it that it is pure.
The earth thereby attains tranquility; spirits and deities thereby attain their numinous power; sages thereby open the way for those in delusion and rescue those drowning;
and the ignorant thereby attain loyalty to their sovereign and love for their kin. It is inexhaustible when drawn from and unfailing when employed.

One cannot discern its origins, nor can one fathom its novelty. How wondrous! Yet, even so, one has not yet fully grasped the subtlety of its attainment. If one were to obtain that which is immutable—
The essence: the spirit is concentrated for a thousand ages; in a single thought, ten thousand years pass. It is like the vast, azure sky; it is like the bright moon in a cold pond.
Vertically, it does not stop at the three periods of time; horizontally, how could it be limited to the ten directions? When released, it contains all the *sahasra-lokadhātus*;
when withdrawn, there is even space remaining at the tip of a hair. Examining its origin, it has no beginning; who can discern its first signs? As for its end... [it is] thoroughly examined.
It does not end; how could its vast expanse have a limit? This is likely the subtle mystery of the unchanging.

One who can employ the function of responding to conditions adapts to stimuli and accords with types, engaging with all things without fixed method—like an empty valley echoing sound, or a *maṇi* gem manifesting colors.
Within a single hair-tip appear lands as numerous as motes of dust; internally, the wheel-turning speech is both real and unreal.
It melts all phenomena into the non-dual principle. It is empty yet not empty, dispersing the one into the myriad phenomena—this is the wondrous functioning of following conditions.
The Tathāgata could not bear that this Dharma should be enjoyed by himself alone; therefore he said: "I originally established a vow."
It was because he wished to cause all sentient beings to be no different from himself that he thus emitted light and manifested auspicious omens;

he urgently desired to entrust this wondrous Dharma in its entirety, intending to reveal the principles of the ten realms, the ten suchnesses, and the provisional and real aspects of the original and the trace,
so that all people, upon beholding such a rare event, would inevitably give rise to a mind of rare wonder.
When the mind arises, the Dharma can be realized. However, the name of this sutra is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (The Lotus of the Sublime Dharma).

This name has been used by all Buddhas of the past for a long time. Long ago, at a time as distant as a kalpa of cosmic dust motes, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū accepted the request of the Brahma Kings of the ten directions and the sixteen princes, and declared that he would preach a Mahāyāna sutra named the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Furthermore, it was long ago, when the World-Honored One was a bodhisattva, that he served the immortal Asita countless, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in the past, where he heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Moreover, during the time of the Buddha Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, he heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* preached by that Buddha in its entirety from within the void. This is...
Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, how could Mañjuśrī alone have first heard it under the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa?
Furthermore, how could it be that only the present Tathāgatas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, proclaim this wondrous Lotus Sutra?
It should be understood that the same applies to the infinite Buddhas of the past and future. Thus, one knows that this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* [pervades] the three periods and the ten...
Throughout every atom and every world-system, there is nothing that is not simultaneously so.

If at any moment it were interrupted, if it did not pervade every place, if a single Buddha did not preach it, or if a single matter were incomplete, then it would not be wondrous. Therefore it is said:

"Such a wondrous Dharma is preached by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only at certain times. One must know that this word "time" (shi) pervades all atoms and world-systems without end, extending through the eternal past.
It exists eternally now; it cannot be interrupted by this time or that time, nor can it be measured or limited.

As for why the two characters "Lotus" (*padma*) are attached beneath the "Wondrous Dharma" (*Saddharma*), it is because this Dharma is subtle, wondrous, and difficult to clarify; therefore, the lotus is used as a metaphor for it. Now, a metaphor exists to manifest the Dharma.

If the metaphor is not apt, then the Dharma is not wondrous. For example: [The text continues with a series of metaphors illustrating the correspondence between the qualities of the lotus and the nature of the Dharma.]
In the creation of a portrait, the spirit lies in the divinity; in the painting of the moon, the marvel lies in the clouds. When the spirit arrives, the image comes alive of itself;

when the clouds are wondrous, the moon reveals itself. Thus, how can that which is called the "Lotus" be grasped through the forms of blue, red, crimson, or white as found in heaven or among men, and then be subjected to conceptual analysis?
If one were to grasp its form and attempt such an analysis, even if it possessed spiritual power...
This is a great auspicious treasure that blooms once every three thousand years. When it blooms, a Golden Wheel-turning King (Cakravartin) appears in the world;
he must appear as a Wheel-turning King within no more than three thousand years. How could this be merely a matter of divine arrival or the marvels of the clouds?
It is precisely what is expounded in the Great Sūtra: beneath the Fragrant Water Ocean, there is a great lotus named "Various Radiant Stamen-Fragrance Banner," which supports [the world].
Regarding the Inexhaustible Flower Treasury World (*Akṣayakusuma-garbha-lokadhātu*): although the worlds are inexhaustible and the Flower Treasury is inexhaustible, they ultimately possess limits.
When the totality of the realm is not forgotten yet its measure is limited, and when the measure is limited, the Dharma becomes obstructed and stagnant.
Furthermore, how could there not be a wondrous metaphor that is without form and without name? The reason it is now used as a metaphor for the lotus flower is as follows:

This clarifies that every person inherently possesses the wondrous Lotus Treasury. It is said that this lotus flower contains the cause within the fruit, and the fruit, in turn, encompasses the cause.
Since the present cause succeeds the fruit, the cause for the future fruit has already been planted;

because the present fruit encompasses the cause, the fruit of the prior cause was originally perfected. This precisely clarifies that within the minds of sentient beings, [the essence] has long been fully possessed.
The Buddhas are perfected within the hearts of all Buddhas; furthermore, they conceive the births of the future.
Taking the mind that cherishes the Buddha as the cause, the Buddhas are ultimately inexhaustible. Realizing the fruit through the thought of conceiving birth, how could birth ever end?

Through the Buddhas of kalpa after kalpa, they deliver the beings born from birth after birth; through the beings born from birth after birth, they perfect the Buddhas of kalpa after kalpa. It is like this:
The ceaseless flow of the celestial river resembles the solitary moon; thus it has revolved through all time, and so it is with the Buddhas of the past and present.
All sentient beings are without exception endowed with this lotus flower. To be able to awaken to this lotus flower is to attain the wondrous Dharma of one’s own self;
therefore, the title of this sutra is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (The Lotus Flower of the Wondrous Dharma). "Sutra" (*jing*) means "path" (*jing*). Thus it has been throughout the past and present.
It is the unchanging, eternal Way. In Sanskrit, it is called *sūtra*; here it is translated as "Sutra" (契經).

This means that above, it accords with the principle of all Buddhas, and below, it accords with the capacities of sentient beings. Because it accords with both principle and capacity, it is named "Sutra.

Furthermore, "sutra" (*jing*) signifies "Dharma" and "constancy. That the ten realms follow the same track is called "Dharma"; that which does not change throughout the three periods of time is called "constant."
This is the eternal dharma expounded by every Buddha throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time; therefore, it is collectively termed a "Sūtra.
This is the brief meaning of the title of this scripture. The brief explanation of the title is hereby concluded. △ Second, specifically identifying the translator.
"Kumārajīva, the Tripiṭaka Master of the Yao Qin, translated [this] by imperial decree.
Regarding "Yao Qin," there were three successive Qin dynasties; this clarifies that it was not the time of the Qin of the Ying clan (the Zhou) or the Qin of Fu Jian (the Former Qin).

"Tripiṭaka" refers to the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras, indicating that this master was proficient in all three branches of study. "Master" (*fashi*) has two meanings: first, [one who preaches the Dharma]; second, [one who upholds the Dharma]. First...
The Dharma-body is nourished and sustained entirely by means of the Dharma; therefore, one takes the Dharma as one’s own teacher.
Second, taking the Dharma realized within oneself and transmitting it from one to another so that all people may open their right eye [of wisdom], one acts as a teacher for others.
Kumārajīva is the name of the master translator; this is rendered in Chinese as "Child Longevity" (Tóngshòu). His place of origin, clan, and lineage, and—
The beginning and end of the translation are fully recorded in the *Hongchuan xu* (Preface to the Propagation). Regarding the "translator" (*yìzhě*): this refers to the act of translating.
It means to translate Indic sounds into Chinese sounds, Indic characters into Chinese characters, and Indic speech into Chinese language; all of this was due to the power of this master.
III. Separate Translation of Chapter Titles: There are twenty-eight chapter titles, each of which explains its meaning according to the specific chapter.
The titles of the sections are summarized here.
The first chapter, the "Introductory Chapter," states: "This chapter generally reveals the single, true, and equal Dharma-realm, thereby manifesting the appearance of the Tathāgata in the world."
From beginning to end, it does not depart from the Samādhi of the Momentary Boundary of Universal Radiant Wisdom.

[The Buddha] desires to cause sentient beings to realize this true reality (*dharmatā*) as the authentic cause for attaining Buddhahood. This was the original intention of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world.

Having first preached the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, he entered the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings; this precisely reveals that the Tathāgata’s speech and silence accord with [this reality].
These phenomena are all beyond the realm of mental consciousness and discursive thought.

Nevertheless, that within meditative concentration it rained four kinds of flowers and the earth shook in six ways was intended to manifest how the Tathāgata, through his effortless and wondrous power, overturns the nest of ignorance of sentient beings and removes the obstructions of the six sense faculties and the four great elements. He emitted light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows to illuminate...

Regarding the eighteen thousand worlds of the eastern direction: this directly reveals that the realms of the sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses through which sentient beings function do not depart from the Wisdom of Universal Radiance.
Within this light, the phenomena and characteristics of the *dharmadhātu*, as well as the beginning and end of birth and Buddhahood, are perfectly manifested;
this reveals the equality and non-duality of sentient beings and all Buddhas. Indeed, this true realm of ultimate reality within the light is precisely the [nature of] sentient beings.
On one's birthday, one should employ the state of direct realization; if one can simply know where to return in this very moment, realizing this constitutes the true cause for attaining Buddhahood.
It was specifically for this matter that the Tathāgata appeared in the world, yet he did not reveal it during his forty years [of teaching].
Why is this? It is because their faculties were not yet mature; they merely waited for the right time.

Furthermore, by having Maitreya raise doubts, it is shown that this realm cannot be known by mind or consciousness. His inquiry to Mañjuśrī demonstrates that it cannot be entered except through wisdom.
By citing the origins of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he corroborates the auspicious signs of the present Buddha, revealing that the Way is one and the same throughout past and present. [Forty years...]

What is discussed therein does not exhaust all matters concerning fire; therefore, this chapter is judged to be a general manifestation of the signs of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world for the sake of the one great cause and condition (*ekamahā-kṛtya-hetu-pratyaya*).
Tiantai says: "The meaning of the introduction (*nidāna*) has three aspects: *xi* (order), *you* (therefore), and *shu* (narration).
Phrases such as 'Thus have I heard' are placed at the beginning of the sutra to establish the order. The six auspicious omens of the emission of light..."
The beginning of the undertaking is the *nidāna* (introduction). The questions and answers that resolve doubts constitute the prologue to the main exposition; this is the narrative.
Because it possesses these three meanings, it is called the *nidāna*. When items of similar meaning are grouped together as a single section, it is termed a *parivarta* (chapter).
Only the "Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta" and the "Devadatta-parivarta" were personally proclaimed by the Buddha;

all others were established during the compilation or added by translators. Because this chapter stands at the beginning of all the chapters, it is called the "First. Furthermore, the introduction has two meanings:
general and specific. From "Thus have I heard" up to "sat down to one side" constitutes the general introduction, which means:
This applies to all sutras alike. From the passage "At that time, the World-Honored One" down to the end of the chapter constitutes the *pratyaya-nidāna* (introductory section).

This differs from other sutras; it serves as the specific cause for the opening of the teaching of this particular sutra. **IV. Correct Interpretation of the Textual Meaning.** The major sections are divided into three:

first, the *nidāna* (introduction); second, the *dharmadeśanā* (main body); and third, the *parīndanā* (concluding transmission). Regarding these three divisions of introduction, main body, and transmission, they were first established by Dao’an.
The Dharma Master, having personally verified this with Bodhisattva Bandhuprabha, analyzed the text by dividing it into sections according to its internal structure;

this is an established conclusion that remains unaltered through the ages. Furthermore, he divides it into two sections: first, the sixfold sequence of testimony and faith (*ṣaḍvidha-āptāgama-nidāna*).
The six factors are the sixfold accomplishment consisting of: faith, hearing, time, teacher, place, and assembly. It is said that these six are indispensable;
lacking even one is not permissible. Regarding the "testimony of faith," when the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, Ānanda requested [this formula] for the beginning of all sūtras.
What words should be placed at the beginning? The Buddha commanded that one should place: "Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was at such-and-such a place, together with a great assembly.
This is so that those of future generations throughout the world may know that the Buddhadharma has its source and origin, and is not something that can be fabricated arbitrarily by worldly people.
There are three purposes for placing this [formula] at the beginning: first, to sever doubt; second, to quell dispute; and third, to exclude the heterodox.

Regarding the dispelling of doubt: when Ānanda first ascended the seat for the First Council, his physical marks and signs were identical to those of the Buddha, and the assembly gave rise to three doubts:
first, that the Buddha had arisen again; second, that a Buddha from another world-system had come; and third, that Ānanda himself had attained Buddhahood.

Upon the proclamation of "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) and so forth, these three doubts were instantly extinguished. Regarding the settling of disputes: it would be as if one did not say "Thus."

The Dharma of our Buddha was heard from him; had it been composed by oneself, disputes would have immediately arisen. Therefore, by stating "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) and so forth, disputes do not arise.
To exclude the heterodox: the heterodox teachings of non-Buddhists all place the two characters *a-yu* at the beginning of their scriptures.
They claim that *a* means "non-existence" and *yu* means "existence," based on the false calculations of the non-Buddhists.
Although the myriad dharmas are numerous, they do not transcend existence and non-existence as the basis for auspiciousness.

Therefore, Buddhist sutras begin with phrases such as "Thus have I heard," in order to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox. This section is divided into three parts: first, the indication of faith and hearing.
"Thus have I heard. "Thus" refers to the Dharma. "I heard" clarifies the transmission from teacher to recipient; it means that such a Dharma was heard by me from the Buddha.
Among the six perfections (ṣaḍ-ākāra-sampad), these two words "thus" constitute the perfection of faith (*śraddhā-sampad*). This means that the speaker says: [I speak] with faith.

Thus it is. Those who lack faith say it is not so. According to principle, this means that when the Sage expounds the Dharma, he reveals only *tathatā* (suchness); only suchness is what is truly real.
Therefore, it is called "the perfection of faith. "I have heard" (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*) constitutes the second perfection, that of hearing.
I am indeed the compiler of the sūtras. This "self" refers to the conventional self that accords with worldly convention and the true self of the Dharma-body;
it is not the same as the self imagined by ordinary people or non-Buddhists. Regarding "I have heard," this means having seen and heard directly, rather than through hearsay from others.
As the sūtra says: "The true essence of the teaching in this land is pure within sound and hearing. It does not depend on sound.
Regarding "Hearing": how is the essence of the teaching established? Based on the principle of the true self that is non-self, one hears spontaneously without hearing;
hence it is called the "accomplishment of hearing. △ Second, the time, the principal figure, and the location.
At one time, the Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
"At one time" refers here to the fulfillment of the third period; it denotes the single occasion of teaching and listening from beginning to end when the path of teacher and disciple were in harmony.
For the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma involves a sacred realm that is difficult to equalize; how could it be fixed by mere temporal seasons? Therefore, it is simply stated: [at one time].
At one time. In terms of principle, it is the moment when mind and object, wisdom and reality, and ordinary beings and sages, as well as the fundamental and the initial, are of one suchness.

Therefore, it is called "the accomplishment of time. "Buddha" refers to the fourth [accomplishment], the accomplishment of the Lord. In the Sanskrit language, *buddha*; here it is translated as "Awakened.
This means that initial awakening and fundamental awakening have attained equal realization, thereby constituting ultimate awakening; this is spoken in terms of self-awakening. Furthermore...
It says: "Self-awakened and awakening others; the practice of awakening is perfected. This includes benefiting others. "Self-awakened" distinguishes [the Buddha] from ordinary beings;

"awakening others" distinguishes him from those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna); "perfection" distinguishes him from those still on the causal stage. This refers specifically to Śākyamuni Buddha, the Teacher of the Sahā world.
Were it not for this Great Sage, who else could have expounded this Great Dharma? Therefore, it is called the "Accomplishment of the Lord. He dwells in Rājagṛha and so forth. First...

This is the accomplishment of the five locations. As for Rājagṛha (the City of the King): King Śreṇika Bimbisāra and a thousand kings together established this city among the Five Mountains and made it their capital as a great kingdom;
this is the name of that city. Gṛdhrakūṭa is the name of a mountain; here it is translated as "Vulture Peak," so called because the shape of its summit resembles a vulture.
Within this mountain are five vihāras; the first is named Devadāru-kuñja (The Cave of the Lord of Devas).
It is also known as the Seven-Leaf Cave, the Snake-Shaped Cave, Mount Little Solitary Power, and Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak).
Both past and present Buddhas have all resided upon this mountain. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Arhats dwelt there; subsequently, Pratyekabuddhas and spirits followed in succession.
Because those who dwell there are all holy and numinous beings, it is called Lingjue (Numinous Vulture). This is explained according to principle.
As for "abiding": by means of the wisdom that abides, one dwells within the principle that is the object of abiding; without falling into either extreme, all returns to the Middle Way.
Since this wondrous scripture of the One Vehicle cannot be expounded anywhere other than this supreme land, it is therefore called the "perfection of place."
△ Third, a detailed enumeration of the audience. This constitutes the sixth accomplishment of the assembly. If there were no connoisseurs present, for whom would one speak?
Now that the selection has been completed, it is impossible not to teach. Therefore, in this enumeration of the assembly, it is roughly divided into two parts.

First, a detailed enumeration of the noble and the ordinary, which further divides into three. First, the assembly of *śrāvakas*, which divides into two. First, the *bhikṣus*, which further divides into two. First, the emergence...
The Arhats manifest through their clear brilliance. Furthermore, this is divided into four parts. First, the enumeration of the category and the number:
"Together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus.

This merely cites their outward appearance. "Together with" (yǔ) means "in common with. There are three meanings to "great" (dà): first, the large number; second, the weightiness of their names; third...
*De-lung* (Virtue-Exalted). *Bhikṣu* is a Sanskrit term; it is translated in three ways here:
first, *bhikṣu* (the mendicant), meaning that internally one begs for the Buddha-dharma to sustain the life of wisdom, and externally one begs for offerings of faith to sustain the physical body.

Second, "destroyer of evil," meaning that one is able to destroy the evils of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). Third, "terrorizer of Māra," meaning that because one has already destroyed the delusions of views and afflictions, Māra is struck with fear.
Those who are able to transcend the triple world will surely transform others; thus, the ranks of Māra’s followers will diminish, which is why [Māra] fears them.
The term *saṃgha* in the language of the Brahmans means "harmonious assembly. It possesses six meanings: harmony in precepts through collective practice;

harmony in views through collective understanding; harmony in body through collective dwelling; harmony in livelihood through equal distribution of benefits; harmony in speech through freedom from contention; and harmony in mind through mutual joy. Ten thousand...

The figure of two thousand is stated as a brief enumeration. Were it to be expanded, all those present in the assembly—whether from other quarters or this land, within the twenty-eight chapters—would constitute the multitude.

Furthermore, the twelve classes of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, as well as those who emerged from the earth in the three transformed pure lands, are likewise part of this assembly. Therefore, this is merely a brief statement; "all" refers to these.
"Complete. This refers to this great assembly, all of whom have gathered at this place. △ Second, praising their status and virtues:
"All are arhats... (up to) having exhausted all fetters of existence, they have attained mastery over their minds."
This reveals their original and manifested states. Although they appear as bhikṣus, they are in fact all great arhats. Among these holy assemblies, there are none who do not assist in transformation.
When the Tathāgata appears in the world to benefit sentient beings, how could he rely solely on those śrāvakas of actual practice?
When the Buddha says, "I am your disciple," such skillful means are used to deliver sentient beings; one should know that their distant origins are entirely inconceivable.

The Sanskrit term *arhat* contains three meanings: first, "one who is no longer subject to birth," for having attained liberation from the triple world, one is free from both *pariccheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative) death, and does not undergo further existence; thus, he is not merely capable of destroying evil. Second, "slayer of thieves."

All afflictions (*kleśa*) are exhausted without remainder. Not only is he able to terrify Māra, but as one of the three "Worthy of Offerings" (*arhat*), he possesses the merits of wisdom and abandonment, and is worthy of receiving offerings from devas and humans.
Tiantai says that the two phrases regarding the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*) praise the "slayer of thieves.

There are three kinds of outflows: first, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*); second, the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*); and third, the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). These are the causes of the three realms.

Consequences: giving rise to delusions and creating karma leads to birth and death, causing one to forget the *dharmakāya*, lose the life of wisdom, and forfeit the precious treasure—all of which carry the meaning of being "thieves.
"Afflictions" (*kleśa*) refer to turbid and vexing phenomena that disturb the mind and spirit; they consist of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Now that all outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted, afflictions are forever forgotten; this is why one is able to slay the thieves. Thus, one attains one's own benefit.

The first line praises the quality of being a Worthy One (Arhat). All causes and effects within the three realms are termed the merit of what is severed by the wisdom of others; only when this is so can it be called one’s own benefit.
Because one is fully endowed with this personal benefit, one is able to be a Worthy One. The two lines beginning with "exhausting all fetters of existence" praise the state of non-arising.
"All existences" refers to the twenty-five places of birth; "fetters" refers to the twenty-five causes of birth within those existences.

Now, when cause and effect are entirely forgotten, there is the exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*). One who has attained mastery over the mind is one for whom concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are fully perfected.
Since concentration and wisdom are both perfected, how could there be birth? This is why non-arising is attained.
△ Third, a brief enumeration of the leaders: from among the twelve thousand, twenty-one principal figures are briefly enumerated.
Their names were Ājñātakauṇḍinya (and so on) up to Subhūti, Ānanda, and Rāhula. This is the enumeration of their names. *Ājñāta* is the name;
it is translated as "one who has known. To be called "one who has known" does not mean there is nothing to be known;
rather, it means one has known that [all things] are empty. *Kauṇḍinya* is the clan name; this is translated as "Fire-Implement. He was of the Brahmin caste.

His ancestors served fire, from which his clan derived its name; he was also called Mahānāman because, upon hearing the Dharma, he attained the Way and stood foremost among all humans, devas, and arhats, such that he is called the Buddha’s eldest son. As the Āgama states:
Within my Buddha-dharma, the one foremost among those who are broad-minded, compassionate, and widely learned—those who were the first to receive the flavor of the Dharma—is the bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya.
○ Mahākāśyapa, translated here as "Great Kūrma," was of a lineage whose ancestors practiced the Way;
a divine tortoise bore the "Diagram of the Immortals" in response to their virtuous destiny, and thus the clan was named Bimbala. He was born when his parents prayed to a tree deity.
He is also called Kāśyapa, because the radiance of his body can "drink" (outshine) the light of the sun and moon. Among the disciples of the Buddha, there were many named Kāśyapa;
as he was the eldest among those of the same clan, he was called Mahākāśyapa. The term *mahā* contains three meanings: great, much, and superior.
The Tathāgata entrusted the Dharma to him, passing on to him the golden-threaded *saṃghāṭī*. He resided at Kukkuṭārāma.
Mount Pāṇḍava. He waited for Maitreya’s appearance in the world; having completed the transmission of the Dharma and the entrustment of the robe, he then entered parinirvāṇa.
The Āgamas state: "Within my Buddha-dharma, Mahākāśyapa is foremost in practicing the dhūta austerities.
Urubilvā—this means "Wooden Claw Forest"—refers to his dwelling in that forest. Gayā—this means "City"—and Nadī—this means "River"—refer to the brothers [of the Buddha].
The three men all served the fire. During the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, they together erected a sacrificial pillar; because of this karma, they were reborn as brothers.
The elder brother became the teacher of King Bimbisāra and had five hundred disciples, while each of the two younger brothers had two hundred and fifty.

They all followed their elder brother’s methods and refused to return to the Buddha. The Buddha converted them by performing ten kinds of supernatural transformations: namely, that he was not harmed by the venomous dragon;
that he was not burned by the dragon’s fire; that he was not drowned in the Ganges River; that he gathered fruit from the three directions; that he gathered non-glutinous rice from the north;

and that he took ambrosia from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. When [the brothers] felt resentment, he withdrew; when they thought of him, he appeared. When the fire was extinguished, it flared up again; when the axe was raised, it did not [fall].

[The Buddha] descended. The details are as explained in the *Śrī-mālā-sūtra* (or *Prasannārtha-sūtra*). Although they witnessed these manifold transformations, their false attachments did not lead them to return [to the truth].
He further said, "Though Gautama possesses spiritual powers, my Way is more truly real. The Buddha replied, "You are not Arhats, nor have you attained the Way.
All three men then achieved realization and together returned to the Buddha. The *Āgama* states that the bhikṣu Uruvilvākāśyapa was able to provide protection.
The fourfold assembly provided him with the four requisites, ensuring he lacked for nothing; he was foremost in this regard.
The bhikṣu Nadi had a mind that was profoundly tranquil, having subdued all fetters; he was foremost in diligence. The bhikṣu Gayā thoroughly contemplated and understood all phenomena.
He is entirely without attachment and is preeminent in his skillful ability to teach and transform others. ○ Śāriputra: "Śāri" means *śārika*, a water-bird;
"putra" means "son. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: King Bhaṭṭaraka’s wife gave birth to a daughter whose eyes resembled those of the śārika bird;
she was therefore named Śāri. Because she was born from a woman (putra), she was called Śāriputra.
He is also called Śāriputra, because his mother possessed a beautiful form and body. The Āgamas state:
"Within my Buddha-dharma, Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom, being inexhaustible and capable of resolving all doubts.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana is translated as "radish," which was the clan name of a Brahmin. His personal name was Kolita; because he was born after praying to a tree deity, he was named accordingly.
Regarding the naming: the *Āgama* states that among my disciples, Maudgalyāyana is foremost in the lightness of his supernormal powers for flying to the ten directions.
○ Mahākātyāyana: this was a Brahmin clan name; it is translated here as "Ornamentation" (*vyañjana*).
Because he was skilled in debate, the Āgamas state: "In skillfully discerning meanings and expounding the Dharma, Kātyāyana is foremost.
○ Aniruddha (also called Anuruddha; this means "Free from Poverty," or Aniruddha; this means "As One Wishes").
The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states: During the final age of the Buddha Puṣya, there was a famine.
There was a Pratyekabuddha named Liṭa who went on almsround with an empty bowl. A poor man saw him and, moved by compassion, said, "Noble one, would you be able to accept some millet?
He replied, "I can. The man then offered him what he himself was eating. After the Pratyekabuddha had eaten and manifested the eighteen transformations, he departed.
The man’s grief and devotion became even more profound; consequently, for ninety-one kalpas, he was reborn in the heavens.
A human being experiences the bliss of his desires and then joins the Buddha’s order as a renunciant. Because he fell into deep sleep, he was rebuked by the Buddha;

for seven days he did not sleep, and consequently lost both his eyes. The Buddha instructed him to cultivate the *Ratnaprabhāsa-vajra-samādhi* (Vajra Samādhi of Joyful Vision and Illumination), whereby he attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) on half his head and could see the great trichiliocosm as clearly as looking at a fruit in the palm of his hand. The Āgama states: "Within my Buddha-dharma..."
Regarding those with the divine eye who possess penetrating vision, the Bhikṣu Aniruddha is foremost; he was the second son of King Droṇodana.
○ Kapphiṇa is translated as "Lunar Mansion" (Hángxiù). His parents prayed to the lunar mansion Kṛttikā before his birth, and thus he was named accordingly.
It is further said: When he first went forth, on his way to see the Buddha, he happened to encounter rain and stayed overnight in a potter’s house, using grass as a seat.
Later, another bhikṣu also came seeking lodging; Piṇḍola immediately pushed his own grass mat aside to give it to him.
After midnight, the bhikṣu asked where he was going. He replied, "I wish to see the Buddha. The bhikṣu then preached the Dharma for him.

He suddenly attained the Way. The bhikṣu who followed later was none other than the Buddha. Because he attained the Way while staying overnight with the Buddha, his constellation is named *Bharaṇī* (the Room).
As the Āgama states: "In my Buddha-dharma, those who well know the stars, the moon, and the sun, and clearly recognize their celestial images [are here]."
The Bhikṣu Kapphiṇa was foremost. ○ Gavāmpati: this is translated as "Cow-Chewer" (Niuchi) and also as "Cow-Track" (Gyokaku).

In his previous five hundred lifetimes, he had once been a king of oxen; because he constantly made a hollow-sighing sound after eating like an ox, and that residual karmic retribution had not yet been eliminated, he would continue to chew with a constant "tsap-tsap" sound.
Therefore, people of the time called him "Cow-Chewer" (Gonichi) to avoid the derision of others.

Fearing that he might commit an offense, [Kauṇḍinya] constantly resided in the heavens. When the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa assembled one thousand arhats and dispatched a junior monk to summon Kauṇḍinya.
Kauṇḍinya asked about the Buddha, and was told that he had already passed away. Kauṇḍinya said, "When the Buddha appeared, I appeared; when the Buddha remained, I remained.
Since the Buddha has now entered nirvāṇa, I too shall pass away. He then entered parinirvāṇa. The Āgamas state:
He delights in the heavens and does not delight in the human realm; he is the foremost among the *goṣṭhika* bhikṣus.
○ Revata, also named Revata, is here translated as "Constellation. His parents prayed to the stars for his birth, and thus he received this name.
Although he had left the household life, he still followed his original name. The *Āgama* states: "Revata sits in meditation and enters samādhi, his mind neither falling nor becoming confused."
The foremost among bhikṣus was Piliṅgavatsa (Pi-ling-jiabochuo). This name means "residual habit.
Having been a brāhmaṇa for five hundred lifetimes, although he had attained the fruits of the Path, his residual habits still caused him to be haughty.

When crossing the Ganges River, he shouted at the river deity, "You little slave! Stop your flow! The river deity split into two branches. Having been thus rebuked, the deity went to complain to the Buddha.
The Buddha ordered him to repent and apologize. He immediately joined his palms before the assembly and said, "Little maid, do not be angry.
The great assembly laughed at him. The River Deity said, "He repents yet still reviles me. The Buddha said, "His habitual nature is such; truly, he has no prideful heart. The *Āgama* says:
"Sitting in austerity beneath trees, avoiding neither wind nor rain—Bakkula is foremost among bhikṣus. *Bakula* (Baku-ra).

This person is named Shanrong (Good Appearance), so called because his countenance is upright and handsome. He is one hundred and sixty years of age, yet he remains free from illness and untimely death;
this is due to his observance of the precept against killing in the past. For ninety-one kalpas, his life has never been cut short prematurely.

During the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, there was a bhikṣu suffering from a headache; [Shanrong] gave him an āmalaka fruit as an offering, and the illness was cured. Consequently, he has experienced the benefits of this merit for kalpa after kalpa.
In every lifetime he was always free from illness. The *Āgama* states that his lifespan was the longest;
he delighted in solitude and quietude, and was foremost among those named Bakula. ○ Mahākauṣṭhila means "Great Thigh" in Chinese; he was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra.
In the past, when debating with his elder sister, he always prevailed; however, once she became pregnant, he could no longer defeat her.

Realizing that she harbored a man of wisdom within her womb, he understood that even the entrustment of eloquence was already superior in this way, let alone the birth of such a person. He then left home and traveled to South India, where he studied eighteen scriptures.

At that time, the crowd mocked him, saying, "What was difficult to master over many lifetimes—how can you hope to achieve it in a single lifetime? Thereupon, he sighed deeply and said, "I have acted as a brother to my sister while remaining at home."
He was defeated [in debate] and, upon going outside, was held in contempt by others. His vow never ceased; he had no leisure even to trim his nails.
Thus, people of the time called him the Brahmin Dīrghanakha (Long-Nail). Later, he joined the Buddha and left the household life, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye (*dharmanetra-viśuddhi*).

According to the Āgamas, he attained the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidah*) and was foremost among those who could answer difficult challenges. ○ Nanda, also known as Gopāla-nanda (Cowherd Nanda).
*Śubhāṅkara*. This is translated as "Excellent Joy. *Miaole* (妙樂) says: He was named from his initial aspiration for the Way;
because he excels among those who experience joy, he is called "Excellent" (*śubha*). He is one of the hundred thousand Śākyas whom King Śuddhodana compelled to leave the household life.
○ *Sundarananda*. *Sundara* means "lovely" or "beloved"; this is the name of his wife. *Nanda* means "joy."
"Joy" (*Nanda*) is his own name. To distinguish him from others who share the name Nanda, his wife's name is specified to differentiate him.

He was the Buddha’s own younger brother, born on the ninth day of the fourth month. He was four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha, yet his appearance and demeanor were exceptionally distinguished and extraordinary compared to those of the world.
Later, the Buddha led him to leave the household life, where he realized the fruit of Arhatship. *Pūrṇa-maitrāyaṇīputra* (Fu-lou-na-mi-duo-luo).
Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra: *Pūrṇa* means "Full" (or "Abundant") in this language; his father’s name was Maitra, meaning "Compassion.
In the Western Regions, sons are called *nara* and daughters are called *nārī*; he received his name from his parents, hence he is named Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. The Āgamas state:
"He is most capable of extensively expounding and discerning the principles of meaning; Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra is foremost [in this]. ○ Subhūti. This...

He was named Kūṭadanta (Empty-born). On the day of his birth, all the storehouses in his home became empty; therefore, he was called Empty-born. His parents were struck with wonder and sought a divination.

A physiognomist declared, "Auspicious. He was also named Śreṇika (Good Fortune). When he left the household life, he perceived emptiness and attained the Way, while simultaneously cultivating a mind of loving-kindness.
He attained the Saṃjñā-vivāda-samādhi (the Samādhi of Non-contention) and was skilled in expounding the Dharma of Emptiness. The Buddha [descended] from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven...
He brought benefit to all under heaven. People from across the land flocked together like spokes converging on a hub, vying with one another to pay him homage.
Only Subhūti sat upright in his stone chamber, contemplating the emptiness of all dharmas; he attained sudden and perfect enlightenment, and thus became foremost among those who understand emptiness.
Ānanda—here translated as "Joy," or "Celebratory Joy," or "Untainted"—was born on the day the Buddha attained enlightenment. The entire nation rejoiced and celebrated.
For this reason, he obtained his name. Whenever he accompanied the Buddha into the palaces of devas, humans, or nāgas, and beheld the throngs of women, his mind remained free from defilement;

thus he was named "The Undefiled" (Vimala). He served as the Buddha’s attendant for twenty-five years, memorizing all eight thousand *gāthās* he heard without omission, never asking about a single verse twice.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the great assembly requested the compilation of the various sūtras, he ascended...
He sat upon a lion throne, his physical marks and signs being identical to those of the Buddha. Kāśyapa praised him, saying: "Your face is like the pure, full moon;
your eyes are like blue lotuses. The great waters of the Buddha’s Dharma flow into Ānanda’s heart.
That the Tathāgata’s precious treasury now circulates throughout the heavens and the human world is entirely due to the power of the Venerable One. When he entered parinirvāṇa, at the Ganges River...
In the middle, he entered the *Vāyu-vikrīḍita* (Wind-Display) Samādhi and divided his body into four parts:

one he gave to the heavens, one to the dragon palace, one to the kingdom of Vaiśālī, and one to King Ajātaśatru. As the Āgama states: "Knowing the proper time and clearly discerning things, he is without hesitation wherever he goes;
what he remembers he does not forget; he is widely learned and profoundly adept, capable of receiving and upholding [the teachings]."—Ānanda.
First among those who have attained the *dharanis*. ○ Rāhula. This is translated as "Obstruction" (*āvṛti*). He was the Buddha’s own son.
Because in a former life he blocked a mouse hole, and furthermore because he did not attend to a Brahmin for six days, he remained in the womb for six years; thus he was named "Obstruction.
When the Buddha was a prince and desired to leave home to become a renunciant, his father the King would not permit it. Thereupon [the Prince] said: "If you..."
"My son, I grant you permission to leave the household life. The Prince then pointed his finger at the Queen's belly and said, "Six years from now, you shall conceive.
Once he had left the household life, Yaśodharā became pregnant. All the Śākyas were indignant, suspecting that she was unchaste.
Yaśodharā then prepared a fire pit and made a vow, saying: "If I have committed any wrong, may mother and son perish together;

if this is truly my offspring, let the heavens bear witness. She then embraced her child and threw herself into the pit. The pit was transformed into a pond, and a lotus flower emerged, cradling the body.
Thereupon, the King, her father, rejoiced; though he had lost his son, he had gained a grandson. This grandson shall become a Golden-Wheel-turning Monarch, and I too—
"What is there to regret? Later, when she had grown up, the Buddha sought her ordination, but the King-Father would not permit it.
Yaśodharā was about to ascend to the high tower when Maudgalyāyana flew through the air and took her away. The Buddha ordained her, and she became a disciple of Śāriputra.
Among the great assembly, she was foremost in secret conduct. △ Fourth, the summary of the gathering of the multitude.
"Such great arhats, well-known to the multitude," etc.—this phrase subsumes the remaining assembly.

The two characters "such as" (rúshì) refer to the twenty-one ranks mentioned above. As for the remainder of the twelve thousand who have not yet been specifically named, they are encompassed by the character "etc.
(děng). This is the general structure of the text. To hear their names is called "knowing" (zhī); to see them is [called] "seeing" (jiàn).
"Form" is called consciousness (*vijñāna*). Furthermore, seeing form is "knowledge" (*jñāna*), while seeing the mind is "consciousness.
Regarding the phrase "known by all," this refers to those who are commonly seen and known by the great assemblies of humans and devas—namely, the Great Arhats. 2.
Designating those in training (*śaikṣa*) to encompass the broad range. "Broad" means that by mentioning those in training, the persons of the first and second fruits are included.
There were none who did not reach full realization.
Furthermore, there were two thousand persons, both those still in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*);
these comprised the entirety of the assembly of those in training. The previous twelve thousand, however, were those who had truly exhausted all delusions and were beyond training.
These two thousand learners (*śaikṣa*) are about to investigate the truth and sever their afflictions, hoping to realize the four fruits of the path.

They are those who are training toward the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Here, only the number of their ranks is mentioned without praising their virtues, because they are equal in status to the aforementioned spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Once they have realized and entered the four fruits, their virtues and deeds will be no different from theirs; therefore, they are not praised again here.
△ Second, the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs.
The bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī was present together with her retinue of six thousand.
This further specifies the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, as it is certain that such an assembly must exist within the dharma-gathering. *Prajāpatī* means "Great Love" (*Mahāprema*).

The name "Dau" (Dao) is derived from her wisdom. She is also called Gautamī, which means "Leader of the Nuns"; she was the Buddha’s maternal aunt. Fourteen years after the Buddha attained enlightenment, his mother requested to leave the household life, but the Buddha did not grant permission. Ānanda made three requests on her behalf, and the Buddha instructed Ānanda to convey the Eight Rules of Respect (*gurudharma*): if she could practice them, he would allow her to go forth. First: 1. A nun who has been ordained for a hundred years must pay homage to a monk ordained but that very day. 2. A nun must never criticize or find fault with a monk. 3. A nun must not spend the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) in a place where there is no community of monks. 4. At the conclusion of the rainy season retreat, a nun must perform the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) before both communities [of monks and nuns]. 5. When a nun commits an offense, she must undergo penance before both communities. 6.

A nun who has completed her probationary period (*parivāsa*) must seek reconciliation before both communities. 7. A nun may not ordain anyone under the age of twelve. 8. A nun may not ordain anyone unless they have been trained for at least twelve years in the six rules of conduct. If she could observe these eight rules, she would be permitted to go forth. First.
1. A bhikṣuṇī who is one hundred years old must rise to greet, bow to, and invite a newly ordained bhikṣu to sit when she sees him.
2. She must not revile a bhikṣu. 3. She must not expose the faults of a bhikṣu; whereas a bhikṣu may speak of a bhikṣuṇī’s faults. 4.
Within the Saṃgha, she must seek to receive the full ordination (upasaṃpadā). 5. If she commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, she must perform the mānatva penance before the Saṃgha for half a month.
Sixth, one should seek a preceptor within the Saṃgha. Seventh, one should not observe the summer retreat (varṣā) in a place where there are no bhikṣus.
Eighth, when the summer retreat has concluded, one should go before the Saṃgha and seek those who will grant the invitation for self-examination (pravāraṇā).
Following these instructions one by one, she was finally ordained and left the household life; together with her kinsmen, the number reached six thousand.
The bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, mother of Rāhula, was also present together with her retinue.
Yaśodharā is here translated as Huase (Flower-Color) and also as Mingwen (Fame). While at home, she was the wife of the Bodhisattva.

A celestial being and human sage, she left the household life to become the leader of the community of nuns; her rank was that of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and she was renowned by the name Miaomen (Fame-Audition).

She was also accompanied by her retinue. Zhizhi says: "The three types of *śrāvakas* mentioned above correspond to the *Āgama*, *Vaipulya*, and *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras, which are the sheep, deer, and ox carts [of the Parable of the Burning House].
This should be understood as referring to those who received predictions [of Buddhahood] during the latter three weeks [of the Lotus Sūtra]. This is a summary of their application.
One should understand this according to human rights. △ Second, the assembly of bodhisattvas. This is divided into four parts. First, the enumeration of their types and numbers:
"Eighty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
This indicates those of high rank, clarifying that they serve as assistants to the Dharma assembly. "Bodhisattva" is a Sanskrit term; [it is] complete [in meaning].
One should say *bodhisattva*. This translates as "enlightened sentient being" (*jue youqing*): one who has already attained self-enlightenment and now enlightens others.
*Mahāsattva* translates as "great," "many," and "excellent"—three meanings. It is also called "sentient beings with the mind of the Great Way."
This means that because he possesses great compassion, has attained great wisdom, has cultivated great causes, and has realized the great fruit, he receives this name.
This assembly constantly follows him, numbering eighty thousand. △ Second, the clarification of his rank and virtue.
All have attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
*An* translates as "none" (or "without"); *uttara* translates as "above"; *samyak* translates as "right" (or "correct"); *saṃbodhi* translates as "awakening.
Taken together, this is called "Unsurpassed Perfect Complete Awakening. In Sanskrit it is *abhibhūti*, which here means "non-retrogression. There are three [types].

Non-retrogression consists of three aspects: first, the stage; second, the practice; and third, the mindfulness. From the initial stage of abiding, one possesses these three virtues in their entirety.

Attaining *prajñā* (wisdom) constitutes non-retrogression in terms of the stage, because one is free from the two types of death. Attaining *vimukti* (liberation) constitutes non-retrogression in terms of practice, because all practices are fully perfected.
They attain the Dharma-body; this is non-retrogression in mindfulness because they have realized the realm of truth.
This single phrase is a general praise of the primary cause of the eighty thousand great beings. The subsequent twelve phrases specifically praise the various gates of merit they have cultivated.
Although their cultivation comprises myriad practices, they do not exceed the ten *pāramitās*; these should therefore be correlated with the ten perfections.
All attained dhāraṇīs.
"Upward" refers to the people; according to the dharma, the people and the dharma are one, hence it says "all therein.

Here, by means of the category of dharma, the people and the multitude of dharmas are ten, hence it says "all attained. This runs through the following twelve phrases, meaning that these eighty thousand people all—
Having attained the ten perfections, one’s name becomes universally renowned, and one is able to deliver and liberate countless sentient beings.
*Dhāraṇī* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "total retention" (*zongchi*). This means to encompass all phenomena and to maintain immeasurable meanings.

I [the author] say that this is precisely the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). Ethical discipline has two aspects: cessation and cultivation. Regarding cessation: it means not committing any evil. Since one is already able to cease...

Within the cessation of the multitude, ten thousand delusions are forever stilled. Once delusion has ceased, all spiritual beings are fully present; is this not the subsumption of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*)?
All phenomena consist of the causes and effects of defilement and purity, as well as mundane and supramundane dharmas. As for the "agent," it is the practice of all virtues.
Being able to perform what is to be done, there is no practice that is not cultivated. Once these practices have been cultivated, all wisdoms are ever-present.

To preserve [this]—is this not precisely to uphold the meaning of the immeasurable? The "immeasurable meaning" refers to the principles of the ten realms, the ten suchnesses, the provisional and the real, and the fundamental and the trace.

Thus, regarding the causes and effects of both ordinary beings and sages, it is only through the *śīla-pāramitā* (perfection of ethical discipline) that one maintains these in their entirety without loss;
only then is it called the supreme, unsurpassed Great *Dhāraṇī*. Therefore, by means of this, one encompasses ethical discipline.

The eloquence of joyful exposition (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) is precisely the vow of deliverance. There are four types of eloquence: first, unimpededness regarding phenomena (*dharma*); second, unimpededness regarding expression (*nirukti*); third, unimpededness regarding meaning (*artha*);

and fourth, unimpededness regarding joyful exposition (*pratibhāna*). Upon reaching the ninth stage (*bhūmi*), the Bodhisattva eliminates one hindrance and two delusions, and is then able to realize it.
This "delight in preaching" (*pratibhāna*) synthesizes the preceding three [perfections] and achieves them. One preaches constantly day and night, fervently and without interruption.

It makes no distinction between those of sharp or dull faculties; it does not differentiate between suffering or joy. It pervades all lands within the dust motes of the universe, and its duration through kalpas is inexhaustible.
If one’s great vow were not profound, how could one endure to this extent? Therefore, this is used to encompass the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*).

To turn the non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma is itself the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*). Having realized this Dharma within the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one is able to universally manifest form-bodies to enter all lands and realms, extensively guiding the twelve classes of sentient beings so that they all ascend to the precious destination. The wheel never stagnates; thus...

It reaches the point where not even a single thought arises that is satisfied with realization; that is to say, as long as the realm of space endures and the realm of sentient beings endures, this practice of mine shall ultimately be inexhaustible.
How could this wheel of diligence ever come to an end? Therefore, it is used to encompass and advance progress.

Making offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas is the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). For one who is able to make such offerings must necessarily give rise to a mind of joyful relinquishment;
because of this joyful relinquishment, they are not only able to renounce external treasures, wealth, wives, children, and retinues, but even their own bodies, heads, eyes, and hands.
There is nothing that is not offered with a joyful heart; how much more so when what is being offered is not from just one or two Buddhas?

When expressed in countless hundreds of thousands of words, how could there be any limit to the precious jewels provided for the Buddhas' offerings, as well as the various parts of one's own and others' bodies?
According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the offerings presented by Bodhisattvas consist of immeasurable clouds of clothing.
The canopies of clouds are immeasurable, and even the songs and hymns of praise are each said to be immeasurable;
yet all of these are merely the giving of material wealth. As the *Pratimokṣa-saṃvara-vinaya* states: "Among all forms of offering, the Dharma-offering is supreme.

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas seek the higher path above and transform those below, practicing what is difficult to practice, they manifest the body of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-kāya*) to respond to lands as numerous as motes of dust—how much more so is this [the case for] the Dharma-offering?
Because it exerts the power of giving, it is subsumed under the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).

"Planting the roots of all virtues in the presence of the Buddhas" refers to the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*). "The presence of the Buddhas" refers to the buddha-fields as numerous as motes of dust; "planting the roots of all virtues" refers to one's own purification.
This is the Buddha-field. To desire to purify the Buddha-field, there is nothing that surpasses meditative concentration (*samādhi*). When concentration is deep, the roots of virtue are established.
Now, if a Bodhisattva wishes to bring to perfection the fruits of the two benefits for self and others and to plant the true cause, only the Buddha can be relied upon.

Only when adorned with both merit and wisdom and when great functions arise in abundance is one capable of saving sentient beings. Thus, the cultivation of concentration and wisdom is precisely what purifies the Buddha-field for oneself.
It is the earth-element. Vimalakīrti said, "When the mind is pure, the buddha-field is pure. Therefore, this is used to encompass dhyāna.
It is constantly praised by all the Buddhas.
This is precisely the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Whether a bodhisattva seeks the higher for themselves or transforms those below, all that benefits oneself and others is wisdom.
For example, a bodhisattva of the ninth stage establishes various distinct gateways of mundane and supramundane arts and crafts.
He thoroughly penetrates all gateways of liberation, up to and including immeasurable supernormal powers and samādhis;
he is praised by all Buddhas, and thus he is said to encompass wisdom.

To cultivate the person through loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is precisely the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). Loving-kindness is the universal salvation of all sentient beings. That it is called "cultivating the person" must be understood as follows:

if the measure of loving-kindness is not yet full, then there is a deficiency in the cultivation of the person. Therefore, when loving-kindness is profound, patience is likewise profound, like that which never ceases.
For the sake of even a single sentient being, a bodhisattva will not abandon them even while remaining in the most extreme hells for immeasurable eons.
How vast, then, must be the power of their compassionate patience! It is for this reason that they embrace patience.

Skillfully entering the Buddha’s wisdom is precisely the perfection of expedient means (*upāya-pāramitā*). This Buddha-wisdom is the reality-mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), which is profoundly deep, immeasurable, difficult to understand, and difficult to enter.
With the exception of one Buddha and another Buddha, there is no one capable of entering it. Now, this is the fundamental greatness of the Bodhisattvas...
Once wisdom has been planted, one can, through the wisdom of skillful means, penetrate the profound source and reach the limit of true suchness (*tathatā*),
attaining millions of *asaṃkhyeya* supernormal powers and being endowed with millions of *asaṃkhyeya* samādhis, thereby beholding such worlds.
To perform such offerings, to emit such radiance, and to expound such meanings of the Dharma—is this not indeed to have skillfully entered the Buddha’s wisdom?
Therefore, these are subsumed under skillful means (*upāya*).
To penetrate and realize great wisdom is precisely the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Great wisdom is the wisdom of unexcelled *bodhi* that perfectly illumines the *dharmadhātu*.

To extend this and put it into practice is called "penetration" (*tong*); to reach both this shore and the other shore is called "realization" (*da*). Once the Bodhisattva has arrived at this state...
The stage of non-retrogression enables one to place the single mind within all phenomena and to dissolve all phenomena into the single mind.
This is what is meant by the myriad phenomena of the universe radiating light from the Ocean Seal, wherein the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated in the three.
Since its wisdom-seal is how perfectly complete, it is used to encompass all wisdom.
To reach the other shore is the power of strength. That "other shore" is the city of Nirvana; one cannot reach it without great strength.
The reason one does not reach it is that one is bound to this shore by immeasurable causes of birth and death and immeasurable fruits of affliction. Now...
The Bodhisattva, by means of adamantine sublime wisdom, severs [all bonds] simultaneously; thus, the cause is forgotten and the fruit is lost.

Consequently, the five stages of dwelling are exhausted and the two types of death are forgotten. Thereupon, one mounts this precious vehicle and proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment. How sharp is its power!
Therefore, it is called the "Power of Gathering."
"Their fame is heard throughout immeasurable worlds.
This summarizes the ten perfections mentioned above. "Name" is the manifestation of reality.

When a Bodhisattva’s internal wisdom is fully perfected and external conduct is completely fulfilled, upon reaching this stage, their name is heard throughout immeasurable worlds; this is naturally so.
As for the term "稱" (cheng), it means "equal to. An immeasurable world is thus all-pervasive and inexhaustible;
since its name is heard so far away across such worlds, how could its reality possibly be easily measured?
He is able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.
The preceding sections all clarified self-benefit; this section now raises the topic of benefiting others. Generally, where there is the practice, there must be the capacity.

Now, the Bodhisattva’s myriad practices are without omission, and his provisional and ultimate teachings are fully complete; he is thus personally able to manifest bodies as numerous as motes of dust.
Buddha-fields. According to the capacities and numbers of beings, he manifests each individual form and preaches each individual Dharma; therefore, it is said that he "is able to deliver.
The phrase "countless hundreds of thousands" is a term that encompasses the inexhaustible. △ Third, a brief indication of the names.
Their names are Mañjuśrī (up to) Ratnakūṭa Bodhisattva and Nāyaka Bodhisattva.
These eighteen positions, according to principle, are all names for the Tathāgata himself who possesses expedient wisdom;
they may be understood through the mind and need not be described at length. Mañjuśrī means "Wondrous Virtue" (*Miaode*) in this language, and is also called Mañjuśrī.
This one is called Mañjuśrī. In the past, he became a Buddha named Nāgottararāja. According to the account in this very sūtra, he was the Dharma Master Prabhāketu;
having previously served as the fundamental great wisdom, he concealed his excellence and manifested inferiority to assist in propagating the Dharma and its transformation.
Thus, together with the Tathāgata, he serves as a model for sentient beings. Therefore, in this chapter, the Tathāgata [emits] light...
Thus it is said. Yet Mañjuśrī manifests this through words, like a seal and its impression; there is never any distinction between master and subordinate. Regarding Avalokiteśvara:
the Sanskrit is *Bhagavad-avalokita-īśvara*, which is translated here as "Avalokiteśvara.

Here, "contemplation" (*guan*) is the subjective wisdom, while "worldly sounds" (*shiyin*) are the objective realm. This will be explained in detail in the subsequent chapter. The Bodhisattva, by means of great compassion...
