Tiantai says: "Profound wisdom" means that their insight exhausts the fundamental principle. "Firm resolve" means that their vows are vast and great.
This constitutes the two kinds of adornment: being able to inquire and being able to uphold. △ Question: That he is able to receive [the teaching] clearly demonstrates the depth of his wisdom.
That he receives it and is able to uphold it is due to the firmness of his resolve. This further reveals that Maitreya’s vision is clear and his understanding is profound.
Furthermore, one sees the sons of the Buddha endowed with both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), (up to) shattering the hosts of Māra and beating the Dharma drum.
These two—concentration and wisdom—are only fully perfected upon reaching the stages of the Separate (*byō*) and Perfect (*en*) teachings.

Through immeasurable analogies, that is, by employing various skillful means (*upāya*) within the various teachings, countless parables are cited to assist in revealing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). [They] transform all...

The Bodhisattva transforms others through successive stages. As for Māra, this is translated as "the Killer. There are the Māra of afflictions, the Māra of the five aggregates, the celestial Māra, and the Māra of death;
yet the Bodhisattva, with the sharp sword of wisdom, is able to destroy each of these Māras and cause them to retreat.
Furthermore, the discourse on the Dharma can be turned [toward others]; thus it is said that he "beats the drum of the Dharma.

Moreover, when a Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma using the Brahma-voice to awaken all beings, there is the significance of "beating a drum. The former [refers to] self-benefit; this belongs to the benefit of others.

Profound wisdom and firm resolve are the causes and conditions for preaching the Dharma. To hear it and receive it with full retention is precisely faith and understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*). It is the beating of the drum that shatters Māra.
This is the description of their appearance. In the "Chapter on Upholding," the various bodhisattvas make vows to propagate the sutra, saying:

"We, out of reverence and faith in the Buddha, shall don the armor of patience for the sake of preaching this sutra. Based on this, [the section ends]. △ Third, the miscellaneous questions, divided into seven parts.
First, the question regarding meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Furthermore, I saw a Bodhisattva who remained in profound silence; though devas and nāgas paid him homage, he did not consider this a cause for joy.
Previously, they had questioned him in succession regarding the six perfections, yet he was unable to exhaustively express what he perceived.

I have also seen various kinds of people performing various deeds; for instance, there were those who entered silent meditative absorption, and while devas and nāgas paid them respect, [he did not...]
Regarding "being joyful": at this very moment, he does not yet perceive a self; how then could he know that devas and nāgas are paying him homage?
He does not even conform to reality; how then could he feel joy because others are honoring him?
Such profound meditative concentration may truly serve as the sublime abode of the wondrous Dharma.
Furthermore, I see Bodhisattvas dwelling in forests, emitting light to relieve the sufferings of those in the hells and causing them to enter the Buddha-way.

This further demonstrates profound meditation saving the world. "Dwelling in the forest" clarifies the locus of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). "Emitting light" signifies the deep fusion and overflow of that concentration.
"Saving those in hell" refers to the refinement of the mind and the dissolution of objective realms, whereby compassion responds to the movement of suffering.
"Causing them to enter the Buddha-way" means transforming suffering and pleasure within the *Avīci* hell, gathering them back to the truth. This, along with the preceding section, belongs to—
Dhyāna-samādhi. The former refers to the essence of concentration; this refers to the wondrous responsiveness within concentration. △ Second, the question on diligence:
Furthermore, one sees sons of the Buddha who never indulge in drowsiness or sleep, but practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) in the forest, diligently seeking the Buddha-way.
That which one desires while sleeping is different from that which one maintains when not sleeping. Walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*) is not merely for dispelling sleep;
its intent lies in the Buddha-way, and it may be called diligent and tireless effort. When the mind and spirit are dark and obscured, it is "sleep";
when the six consciousnesses are blocked and dull, it is "slumber. To practice walking meditation without sleeping is identical to the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi* of mindfulness of the Buddha. △
Third, he asks about pure precepts.
Furthermore, he sees those who possess the precepts with unimpaired majestic deportment, as pure as a precious gem, seeking the path to Buddhahood.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies ten types of precepts: first, not deficient; second, not broken; third, not pierced; fourth, not mixed; fifth, following...
1. The Path; 2. The six types of non-attachment; 3. Praised by wisdom; 4. Sovereignty; 5. Accordance with meditative concentration; 6. Fulfillment—this is the ultimate.
Now, "not deficient" refers to the primary precept; "pure as a precious jewel" refers to the tenth. By citing the beginning and the end, all others are subsumed.
A Bodhisattva uses these to solemnly guard their deportment while seeking the Buddha-way. △ Fourth Question.
Patience (*kṣānti*).
Furthermore, one sees the sons of the Buddha abiding in the power of patience (up to) being able to endure all things in order to seek the Buddha-way.
Tiantai says: "Because the inner mind can remain at peace, enduring external insults, it is called patience. There are two kinds. First,"

This refers to the patience of endurance (*kṣānti*). Furthermore, there are two types: first, being able to endure without attachment amidst respect and offerings, so that arrogance and negligence do not arise;
second, being able to endure anger, physical assault, verbal abuse, as well as [the stinging of] mosquitoes and gadflies, so that resentment and affliction do not arise.
The second is the patience toward phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*). This also has two aspects: first, non-mental phenomena, namely cold, heat, wind, rain, hunger, thirst, old age, sickness, and so forth;

second, mental phenomena, namely anger, desire, pride, various false views, and so forth. To be able to endure these two types of phenomena without being moved is called the patience toward phenomena.
Regarding the term "power of patience," "power" here means measure; it does not refer to a broad or expansive capacity.
Those whose resolve is firm and whose power is sharp find it difficult to endure. The first phrase refers to the person capable of endurance; what follows refers to the objects of that endurance.
This is illustrated by the case of Sadāparibhūta. △ Fifth, a further inquiry regarding dhyāna.
Furthermore, one sees bodhisattvas who, for billions of years, remain free from all frivolous laughter while seeking the Buddha-way.

Tiantai says: "Being free from frivolity" means setting aside the hindrance of restlessness and remorse; being free from delusion removes the hindrance of ill-will; drawing near to wisdom removes the hindrance of doubt;
removing distraction sets aside the hindrance of sensual desire; and collecting the mind removes the hindrance of torpor. These constitute the removal of the five hindrances. [Billions...]
"Ten thousand years! Mingding (明定) is profound. By means of this profound concentration (*samādhi*), he seeks the Buddha-way; how courageous and sharp is his resolve and power! Question:
"Maitreya perceived the auspicious omen through the light and saw it as occurring in a single moment. Why, then, do you say 'hundreds of millions of years'? Answer:
"These various manifestations are all the old paths traversed by Maitreya. A single vision penetrates them all; why harbor any doubt?"
The existence of obstructions. △ Sixth, the question regarding the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*):
Or, seeing a bodhisattva [offering] delicacies and food (up to) with joy and without satiety, seeking the unsurpassed path.
Furthermore, regarding those who practice giving, they perform various kinds of deeds. First, they give food, drink, and medicinal decoctions;

since these are said to be "of a hundred kinds," it means there is nothing that is not provided. It is said that even famous garments have a price, yet there are even those that are priceless, which are likewise used to make offerings to the Buddha and bestow upon the Sangha.
Second, as for dwellings, numbering in the thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions daily, they may truly be called vast.
All were adorned with sandalwood and various precious gems; they may truly be called the height of beauty.
Within each and every dwelling, there were many exquisite beds and furnishings; these may truly be called the ultimate in sufficiency.
Furthermore, there were flower and fruit gardens, groves, flowing springs, and bathing pools; thus, in all their movements, nothing was contrary to their wishes. These four matters were all...

Subtle yet not coarse; wondrous yet untainted. With single-minded joy and without weariness, they bestow [these gifts], none of which is not intended to pray for the fulfillment of the path to Bodhi. △ Seventh: Inquiry on Prajñā.
There may be bodhisattvas who preach the Dharma of quiescence and instruct countless sentient beings through various teachings.
Furthermore, they see those who practice prajñā and seek the Buddha-way through various skillful means within the midst of the Dharma of quiescence.
The path of language is cut off; what further can be said? Now, it is said that there are various teachings and instructions, and that there are "innumerable sentient beings.

Thus, by means of the wisdom of skillful means, one speaks without speaking and demonstrates without demonstrating, skillfully accommodating the diverse capacities of all beings. This may be called being skilled in expounding the essentials of the Dharma.
Alternatively, one may see the Bodhisattva contemplating the nature of all phenomena as being without dual characteristics, just like empty space.
The nature of all phenomena is precisely the wondrous nature; the absence of dual characteristics is precisely the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Contemplating this mark by means of this nature can be called the fusion of the two truths within true emptiness; therefore, it is said to be "like empty space."
Furthermore, one sees the sons of the Buddha whose minds are without attachment, seeking the unsurpassed path through this wondrous wisdom.
To be "without attachment" means to be free from both emptiness and existence. Since they do not cling to either emptiness or existence, their minds abide nowhere.
A mind that abides nowhere is precisely what constitutes wondrous wisdom. Seeking the Buddha’s sublime knowledge with this wisdom may be likened to water.
He cast himself into the water. △ Sixth, the verse on the Buddha’s entry into *nirvāṇa*. This section is divided into two parts. First, clarifying the construction of stupas and offerings.
Mañjuśrī, furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, make offerings to his *śarīra* (relics).
I have come here to see those bodhisattvas who, despite various causes and conditions, extensively practice the six perfections and the myriad deeds;
who, during the Buddha’s lifetime, followed his transformative rites and cultivated with fierce vigor in their quest for the Unsurpassed Way;
and who, furthermore, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, mindful of repaying the Buddha’s kindness, perform yet another round of practice in order to make offerings to the *śarīra*.
Because this is the direct path, he calls Mañjuśrī by name once more and questions him.
Furthermore, he sees the sons of the Buddha constructing various stupas and temples (up to) constantly making offerings of incense, flowers, and music.
Stūpas are for the purpose of enshrining śarīra relics, while temples are for enshrining physical images.

Since [the Buddha] has bestowed predictions upon beings as numerous as the sands of countless Ganges Rivers, the śarīra relics of the Buddhas within those eighteen thousand lands must likewise be countless. As for the adornment of these realms:
Because the stūpas were so numerous, the land was naturally adorned, and their dimensions—both length and breadth—could be known.

Each stūpa had a thousand banners and streamers, all strung with pearls to form canopies; those "exposed canopies" refer to those spread and displayed outside the stūpas. As for the "harmonious chiming of bells":
since the stūpas were countless, it is evident that the bells were many. When moved by the wind, they sounded in unison; hence, they are called "harmoniously chiming. This...
All clearly manifest the adornment of the stūpas and shrines, serving as offerings made by bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, it is revealed that the various devas and the eight classes of beings likewise make such offerings. △ Second, the manifestation of the stūpa’s adornment of the national realm.
Mañjuśrī and the sons of the Buddha [proceeded] until they reached the site, which was like the king of celestial trees with its flowers in full bloom.

They adorned the stūpas and temples, originally for the purpose of making offerings to the śarīra. Because the stūpas and temples were so magnificent and beautiful, the realm became exceptionally sublime;
this is "adornment through non-adornment. The celestial tree is named Pārijātaka, which in this language means "Round."
It grew to a height of five hundred yojanas, with branches and leaves spreading fifty yojanas, and its floral fragrance likewise pervading fifty yojanas.
When its roots, stems, flowers, and fruits all came forth together, it was like all the trees of Jambudvīpa growing simultaneously;
therefore, it is called the "King of Trees. Now, it is said that the land is adorned by the stūpa, just as the blossoming of a tree’s flowers is most pervasive and all-encompassing.
It is extraordinary and sublime. The verse inquiry is now complete. △ Second, the request for an answer, divided into two parts: first, raising a matter of doubt to state the request.
"The Buddha emitted a single ray of light, and I, along with the great assembly, beheld this land with its various wonders and excellences."
This verse refers to having doubts based on what has been seen. Before the Buddha emitted light, all that we saw was ordinary;
now, because of this light, everything we see is extraordinary, marvelous, and sublime, such that various doubts cannot help but arise.
This realm is the native land itself, replete with all manner of wonders and excellences—namely, the six auspicious omens of the native land.
"The spiritual power and wisdom of all Buddhas are rare and marvelous... (up to) we have seen this and attained what we have never experienced before.
This verse—referring to the two lines concerning seeing the spiritual powers of the Buddhas in other lands—is subsumed under the phrase "we have seen this."

Regarding "shines above," one should say: "It emits a single pure light that illuminates immeasurable lands. I and the assembly behold those buddha-fields and the inconceivable power and wisdom of the various Buddhas;

their significance is thus self-evident. As for the eighteen thousand [rays] mentioned previously, these are reckoned according to the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of sentient beings and do not exceed the scope of the eighteen realms (*dhātu*).
This occurs through the supernatural power (*ṛddhi-bala*) of the Buddhas; therefore, it is called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*).
As for the measure: within this light, I behold the characteristics of the ten dharma realms;
I also see all the bodhisattvas performing their various practices, as well as the spiritual powers and rare wisdom of all the Buddhas—all of which I have never seen before.
"O Son of the Buddha, Mañjuśrī, please resolve the doubts of the assembly.
The preceding section consisted of the intent of their questions; this section requests the answer. That which has been seen above—the characteristics of the two lands—is truly inconceivable.
It cannot be answered except through the power of Your Honor. We only pray that You will speak swiftly to resolve the doubts of the assembly. △
The second section explains the underlying intent by addressing anticipated objections. Regarding these "anticipated objections," Tiantai states:
Although Mañjuśrī dwells in great wisdom, Maitreya is the Honored One who is next in line for succession; how could it be appropriate for Mañjuśrī to provide an answer so abruptly?

Furthermore, there are many within the assembly who understand this matter. Therefore, four objections were proposed to express deference, thereby perfecting the etiquette between guest and host. Moreover, Mañjuśrī...
He hesitated and did not respond; this was because he wished to express the sincere request of the assembled multitude.

First, the objection raised by Maitreya: he said that he wished to resolve the doubts of the assembly. Mañjuśrī’s intention was that if there were any doubts in the assembly, they should naturally pose questions themselves;
since the assembly now does not ask anything, what would he have to resolve? Maitreya secretly understood that Mañjuśrī held such an intention, and therefore...
They requested with a verse, saying:
"The fourfold assembly looks up to you with joy; why, O World-Honored One, do you emit this radiance?
That the fourfold assembly does not now ask is because they look up to you and me alone with joyful intent. The thought in that assembly was: [Why do we not ask?]
“World-Honored One, for what reason do you now emit a great radiance from between your eyebrows, illuminating eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction?
This was Maitreya’s way of inquiring on behalf of the assembly, as he knew their thoughts. Mañjuśrī then countered him, saying:
“Since the entire assembly shares this same doubt, how could I possibly answer? Wait until the Buddha emerges from his meditative absorption; then the matter will be clear of itself.”
Maitreya requested again, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha, by answering at the proper time to resolve doubts and bring joy, what benefit is there in manifesting this radiance?

To answer "at the proper time" means to respond when the moment is right; that is to say, when the assembly is precisely in a state of profound doubt and seeks resolution, it is truly appropriate [to speak].
"Administer the medicine; pray do not delay and lose this opportune moment. This is the point where Maitreya most urgently wishes to reveal for the sake of others.
Now, the assembly thinks: 'Since the light has already been emitted, there must surely be something to be expounded.
However, we do not know what benefit we shall obtain when he expounds during this time of radiance. Mañjuśrī then asked: "I and you, O worthy one, dwell together..."
"O Noble One, as one still on the stage of training, it would not be improper for you to deliberate upon this matter together with me; why do you alone defer to me?
Please, try to explain what this means. Thus, Maitreya spoke again.
The Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) to attain the sublime Dharma; was he about to preach this, or was he about to bestow a prophecy?
"Sitting at the site of enlightenment" means attaining supreme perfect awakening beneath the Bodhi tree. Maitreya said: "My mind was indeed hesitating and deliberating:
could it be that he wishes to speak of the Dharma attained at the site of enlightenment? Or could it be that he is transforming those with the karmic capacity?"
"It has already been accomplished. You have been entrusted with the wondrous Dharma and granted a prophecy. Because of this, Mañjuśrī again raised an objection, saying:
"Based on what you have said, the intention of the Tathāgata is now clearly understood, and the doubts of the assembly may be dispelled.
Why then is it necessary to elaborate further with redundant words? Maitreya requested once more, saying:
To reveal the various Buddha-lands adorned with myriad jewels and pure splendor, and to allow one to behold the Buddhas, is no small cause or condition.
Yet, that the Tathāgata now emits this light and displays this sign is entirely an inconceivable realm.

Not only does one behold these wondrously adorned lands, but one also beholds the Buddhas and hears the Dharma; how could this possibly be due to minor causes and conditions? How could it be otherwise?
With my hesitant mind, I have resolved this great matter; Mañjuśrī concealed his intent, while Maitreya manifested it.
This may be called the distinction between guest and host being perfectly clear.
“Mañjuśrī, you should know that the fourfold assembly, the nāgas, and the spirits are all gazing upon you, wondering what you will say.
This constitutes the formal expression of their request. You need not offer further refusals; you should know that the great assembly here is now present.”

That which is to be observed is none other than benevolence (*maitrī*). Benevolence, you should truly explain whether it concerns the causes and conditions for the Tathāgata’s deeds, or the preaching of the sublime Dharma, or the bestowing of a prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*). Therefore, it is asked: "What is being taught? [△@△] Question:

In Maitreya’s verses, why is the fruit of Buddhahood among the six classes of ordinary beings treated so extremely briefly? And for what reason is there such [extensiveness] regarding the ten thousand practices of a Bodhisattva?
The details are as follows. [The Buddha] replied: "This present assembly is fundamentally intended to urge the followers of the Two Vehicles forward toward the Precious Abode.

Moreover, the followers of the Two Vehicles have long been weary and indolent, taking pleasure in the three samādhis; fearing that the practices of the Path are difficult to perform, they ultimately cannot reach the true realm of the One Vehicle.
Furthermore, even the six realms of ordinary beings are things already loathed and abandoned by those of the Two Vehicles—how much more so the fruit of Buddhahood?"

It is still far off; why need it be explained in detail? One should simply clarify and reveal, one by one, the signs seen within the light, saying "Son of the Buddha" and "Bodhisattva," and "seeking the Buddha-way" and "seeking the unsurpassed way.

All of these are indirect strikes and direct blows intended to inspire those of the Two Vehicles to aspire toward the Great Vehicle. Therefore, as soon as the Tathāgata emerged from samādhi, he spoke.
Śāriputra said: "The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable; it is something that no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas can know.
This means that while Maitreya is a peripheral guide, the Tathāgata is the primary leader; the teacher and disciple share a single, secret mechanism of realization—this is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, one must understand that the manifestations appearing within the light are none other than Śākyamuni himself.
The Muni. Within the three realms of hell and the intermediate states, he is Śākyamuni. Among the eight classes of gods and humans, he is Śākyamuni.
Among the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and those practicing the six perfections, those of all various appearances are all Śākyamuni.
If there were even a single thing or a single person who was not Śākyamuni, this light would not [shine].
It can be manifested. This shows that the Tathāgata, in one place in the eastern direction, personally approached and made offerings to all Buddhas while practicing the bodhisattva path;
if this is so for one place, then it is likewise for all nine other directions.
Therefore, it is said that within the Sahā world, there is not even a space the size of a mustard seed where I have not sacrificed my body and life. Thus, from the World-Honored One—
It is clear that from cause to fruit, the beginning and the end are both manifested within the white curl (ūrṇā-kośa).
△ Fifth, Mañjuśrī emulates the ancients to provide the answer to the question, divided into two parts. First, the prose section, divided into four. First, the direct contemplative response.
At that time, Mañjuśrī (up to) blew the great Dharma conch, struck the great Dharma drum, and expounded the great Dharma meaning.
This was Mañjuśrī’s way of comparing the past with the present to demonstrate that he would certainly preach the Great Dharma and certainly receive the holy prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
He reflected, deliberated, and pondered, thinking: "In the past, the Buddha once preached this sūtra, once entered this samādhi, and also once emitted..."
When such light appeared and such auspicious omens were manifested, he immediately preached the Great Dharma, revealing the ultimate truth and opening up the provisional teachings.
Comparing the past with the present, there can certainly be no duality between them; therefore, he spoke forth and declared clearly:

"As I contemplate it, the Tathāgata today will certainly not be as when he previously preached the Dharma of the Three Vehicles. He must surely intend to preach the Great Dharma and rain down the great rain."

...and so forth. Regarding the "rain of Dharma": for forty years prior, he irrigated [beings] according to their respective needs; now he must surely rain down the single flavor of equality. This is as stated later:
"The rain of a single flavor that issues from those clouds. Regarding the "Dharma conch": it is used to summon and command devas and humans.
Previously, he used various metaphors to entice and guide them; now he must surely use a single voice to [pervade all].
It is announced as stated later: "I am the Tathāgata, the Arhat," and so forth. As for the "Dharma Drum," it carries the sense of a warning or admonition.
Previously, by striking the drum, one was alerted to enter the City of Expedient Means and destroy the afflictions of outflows (*āsrava*);

now, one must certainly be alerted to enter the Precious Abode and shatter ignorance (*avidyā*). This is as it says: "Now, for your sake, I shall speak of the most ultimate reality. This is the Dharma.
"Meaning" refers to the teachings previously expounded, which were not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Now, he will certainly proclaim the Great Dharma, as it is said:
"This alone is the one true reality; the other two are not real. [△@△] Question: Mañjuśrī fundamentally belongs to Great Wisdom (*mahāprajñā*).
"However, since wisdom is beyond deliberation, how could there be any reflection? [The opponent] replies: "This too is the humble speech of host and guest.
Since these two Great Beings are the foremost leaders of the assembly, all their discourse must fully express their respective capacities; otherwise," [it would not be fitting].
Otherwise, the formal structure of the dialogue would not be established. If one discusses the clarity of his wisdom, please observe that it is self-evident from the subsequent answer.
△ Second, a brief response regarding what was previously seen:
"O sons of good family, because I [preached] this dharma which is difficult to believe (up to 'difficult to believe'), I have manifested these auspicious signs."
Previously, I deliberated based on my own wisdom; now, I answer based on what I have briefly witnessed.

That "all may hear and know" means that hearing is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), while knowing is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). That which is difficult to believe is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) being cultivated.

This refers to the Tathāgata’s desire to cause all people to perfect the three types of wisdom; therefore, he manifested this auspicious sign. △ Third, the extensive account of what was previously seen.
Answer: It is divided into three parts. First, citing the same account as one Buddha. This further has three sections. First, clarifying the time:
"O sons of good family, as in the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas ago..."
This correctly cites the ancient to corroborate what is seen in the present; it must be a discourse on the Great Dharma.

The Sanskrit term *asaṃkhyeya* translates here as "incalculable," meaning immeasurable and boundless; that is, distant and vast eons. This clarifies that the duration of time is extremely remote, yet when observed with great wisdom, it is like a single day.
The *Yāoyào jiě* (Essential Explanation) states: "If one seeks the origin of the radiant auspicious signs, one must trace them back to the non-existent."
Regarding "inconceivable kalpas": this light and this Dharma have, in truth, existed from the beginningless beginning, transcending all calculation and measure.

△ Previously, it was said that he had seen [the Buddhas] in the past; this was a general statement. Now, it specifically points to the actuality of what was seen during the time of Candrasūryapradīpa.
Thus, one knows that what Mañjuśrī and Maitreya have accumulated has likewise passed through such [an incalculable duration].
It has been countless eons since then. △ Second, the designation of the name:
At that time there was a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp), [up to] the Teacher of Gods and Men, the World-Honored One.

This passage introduces the ritual sequence of the *Dīpaṃkara* [Sūtra], which first employs provisional means and subsequently reveals the ultimate reality. "Sun, Moon, and Lamp" (*Sūryacandradīpa*) is a specific epithet: "Sun" refers to correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*);
"Moon" refers to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) that universally provides shade; "Lamp" refers to the dispelling of delusions according to the capacities of beings.
"Tathāgata" and the other nine titles are general epithets possessed by every Buddha. Now, they shall be briefly explained in summary. Regarding "Tathāgata": there is no place where he is deluded.

Therefore, following the titles of former virtuous masters: "Arhat" (Worthy of Offerings), because he is a truly excellent field of merit; "Bhagavat" (Possessor of the Title of Field of Merit), because he is worthy of being a field of merit;

"Samyaksaṃbuddha" (Perfectly Awakened One), because he knows the dharma-realm; "Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna" (Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct), because he possesses the three types of supernormal knowledge—this title reveals the causal virtues through the manifestation of the fruit;
"Sugata" (Well-Gone), because he does not return again—this title refers to his wondrous abiding in Bodhi; "Lokavid" (Knower of the World), because he knows the three [realms].

Because he is of the world, yet penetrates the conventional while attaining the ultimate, he is named the Unsurpassed One (*Anuttara*). Because there is none equal to him, he is the Great Man Who Tames Others (*Puruṣa-damya-sārathi*).

Because he gathers and transforms others to follow the Path, he is the Teacher of Gods and Humans (*Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*). Because he acts as the eye for sentient beings, he is the One Who Responds to Capacities by Bestowing the Dharma.

Because his three types of awakening are perfected, he is the Buddha (*Buddha*). Because he awakens others to the return to Truth, he is the World-Honored One (*Bhagavat*). He is endowed with these ten [titles].
Because of his virtue, he is called a Pratyekabuddha of the Three Realms. △ Third, the preaching of the Dharma, which also has three parts. First, the teaching of the Sudden Vehicle is the same:
he expounds the True Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, and which possesses the characteristics of the pure and white Brahma-conduct.
The above refers to the identity of names; this refers to the identity of the teaching of the Dharma. "Expounding the True Dharma" is the general heading.

That the beginning, middle, and end are all called "excellent" (kuśala) refers to the meaning of what is described below as "profound, far-reaching, skillful, and so forth. "Excellent" means sublime and beautiful.
To say that phenomena contain principle is called "profound penetration"; to say that characteristics accord with nature is called "skillfulness. Principle transcends right and wrong.
It is called "pure unity" because it is fully equipped with both the provisional and the ultimate. It is called "complete" because it does not involve subject or object.

It is called "pure and white" because cultivation and realization are untainted. It is called "Brahma-conduct. Thus, throughout the beginning, middle, and end, every single dharma possesses these three aspects.

Whenever one matter is raised, it necessarily involves these three periods; therefore, among the Buddha’s teachings given during his five periods, each individual teaching likewise possesses these three periods. This is precisely...

When the Tathāgata preached the *Avataṃsaka*, he expounded it all at once over three weeks. In each of its three parts—the beginning, middle, and end—every teaching proclaimed the true and wondrous nature.
Whether according to principle or according to capacity, everything was integrated into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge); therefore, all is called "good.
Consequently, in meaning, it is profound and far-reaching, difficult to fathom and difficult to know; in expression, it is exquisite and skillful, difficult to hear and difficult to believe.
...and so forth. △ Second, the opening of the gradual teaching is the same.
For those seeking to become śrāvakas (up to) for the sake of all bodhisattvas, he teaches the six pāramitās.

This is the provisional teaching of the non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*) spoken for the three vehicles. As for "śrāvaka," they are those who hear the Buddha’s voice-teaching and thereby attain [realization].

The Path is such. The Four Truths—namely suffering (*duḥkha*), accumulation (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*)—are all non-illusory; therefore, they are called "truths" (*satya*). Suffering has oppression as its nature;

throughout the upper and lower realms of the three worlds, there is nothing that is not suffering. There are the three types of suffering and the eight types of suffering, which constitute the fruits of the world.
Accumulation has the induction [of future existence] as its nature; it consists of the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the collection of root and derivative afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Accumulation" refers to that which can induce the fruit of suffering; it is the cause of the mundane world. "Cessation" refers to *nirvāṇa* with remainder, which can be realized as its nature;
having transcended the three realms and departed from birth-and-death through successive stages, it is the supramundane fruit.

"Path" refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), which can be cultivated as its nature; being able to accomplish the fruit of the Truth of Cessation, it is supramundane.

The intermediate cause is [the path]. "Crossing over birth and death" and so forth refers to liberation from suffering. "Ultimate equality" refers to the attainment of bliss. Nirvāṇa consists of the three samādhis.
*Sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (Nirvāṇa with remainder) pertains to the *Pratyekabuddha*—here translated as "Conditionally Awakened One" (*yuanjue*).

Because they contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination and awaken to the principle of the True Dharma, they receive this name. As for the twelve links of dependent origination: first is ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the very beginning.

1. Ignorance (*moha*): because there is no clear understanding. 2. Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*): "formations" refers to the act of conditioning; this is the aforementioned aggregate (*skandha*).

This constitutes the cause for the two factors of the past. 3. Consciousness (*vijñāna*): this refers to the eight consciousnesses at the moment of entering the womb, which is the stage of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

4. Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*): this refers to the five aggregates while in the womb. "Name" consists of feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness; "form" is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). 5. [Contact]... (The fifth factor follows).

Sixth is the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). This refers to the six faculties immediately upon emerging from the womb; it is the manifestation of the aggregates (*skandha*). Seventh is contact (*sparśa*).

This is the stage when the six faculties first come into contact with their objects, before feelings of attraction or aversion have arisen. Eighth is feeling (*vedanā*). This is the stage when attraction or aversion arises in response to those objects.

From consciousness up to this point, these are called the five present factors of the fruit. Ninth is craving (*tṛṣṇā*). This refers to the various objects of desire, before [grasping] has yet arisen.
The ninth is *upādāna* (clinging), which refers to the time of pursuing the objects of desire. The tenth is *bhava* (existence), which refers to having already obtained what was sought.
From *tṛṣṇā* (craving) up to this point constitutes the causes for the three links of the future.

The eleventh is *jāti* (birth), which refers to the emergence of the subsequent aggregates from the womb as birth. The twelfth is *jarāmaraṇa* (old age and death); thus, birth and death pertain to the future.
The two branches of the fruit—sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction—collectively constitute the characteristic of suffering within birth and death;

this is the twelvefold dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). This is the gate of cyclic flow (*pravṛtti-mukha*). From the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction is called the gate of reversal (*nivṛtti-mukha*);
this is the dharma practiced by the *pratyekabuddhas*. The Bodhisattvas practice the dharma of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); in the Sanskrit language, these are called *pāramitā*.
*Madhu* (honey). This is translated here as "Reaching the Other Shore" (*pāramitā*). First, generosity (*dāna*), which has three types: namely, material wealth, the Dharma, and fearlessness.

Second, ethical discipline (*śīla*), which also has three types: namely, the vows of restraint (*saṃvara*), wholesome dharmas, and [the welfare of] sentient beings. Third, patience (*kṣānti*), which has six types. The first is the patience of power (*balakṣānti*).

First, one cannot forget anger, yet simply refrains from retaliating. Second, one forgets anger through a refined capacity for patience that accommodates all things, remaining as if unaffected when encountering insult.
Third, one practices "counter-patience," reflecting upon oneself and reproaching oneself rather than blaming others. These three methods do not necessarily accord with the ultimate principle.

1. Patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*). 2. Patience through contemplation (*anupaśyanākṣānti*): realizing that both external objects and one's own body are like a dream. 3. Patience of joy (*prāmodyakṣānti*):
rejoicing when one is insulted, as it perfects one’s own power of patience, just as a strong man rejoices when testing his strength. 4. Patience of loving-kindness (*maitrīkṣānti*):
feeling compassion for those who insult one, seeing them as shrouded by ignorance, and making a vow to deliver them. The final three belong to patience regarding principles (*yuktikṣānti*).

Fourth is diligence (*vīrya*). "Diligence" (*jing*) means being focused and unmixed; "advancement" (*jin*) means being courageous and unyielding. Fifth is meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), here translated as *zhenglü* (静虑).

There are various types of dhyāna, such as the Great and Small, the Expedient and the Real, the Partial and the Perfect; these will not be cited in detail here. Sixth is wisdom (*prajñā*), which is threefold:

wisdom of words and letters, wisdom of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*). These six constitute the practices that lead toward [enlightenment]. [These are] the *pāramitās*.
Honey represents the principle toward which one proceeds. The Bodhisattva presides over this and extensively practices the myriad deeds.
△ Third, returning to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), it causes one to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and achieve the All-Knowledge (Sarvajñā).
Tiantai says: "To be able to know and understand the various modes of activity within the single mark of quiescence is called the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*);
this is precisely the Buddha-wisdom. Regarding the so-called "ten causes" mentioned by the ancients:

from "At that time there was a Buddha" up to this point constitutes the first cause, the "Cause of Identical Dharma-Characteristics," which demonstrates the descent of his birth and traces. Second is the "Cause of Two Myriads of Buddhas Being Identical."
Next, there was another Buddha also named Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp Brightness), [up to] the Dharma he preached, which was good in the beginning, middle, and end.

First, one Buddha is cited to fully illustrate both the sudden and gradual teachings; his preaching of the Dharma is the same as that of the present [Buddha]. In the interim, twenty thousand Buddhas are cited.

This passage merely cites the sudden teaching; thus it says, "the Dharma that can be preached. Later, it cites a single Buddha, citing only the opening of the gradual teaching, which is the same as the present case;
thus it says, "preaching the immeasurable meanings," and so forth. This is Mañjuśrī’s skillful exposition, avoiding prolixity.
One must understand that the models established by each Buddha are non-dual and without distinction. Pūrṇa—this means "sharp faculties"—is directly pointed out.
It is said: In terms of principle, "twenty thousand" refers to the fact that both the fundamental substance of the sages and ordinary beings each possesses ten thousand dharmas.
Now, by encompassing both the true and the deluded, this constitutes the essence of the *dharmatā* (real mark) of this sutra; hence it is called "twenty thousand.

If one views this from the perspective of the past, then the three capacities receiving their predictions will appear in the future. If one views it from the perspective of the future, then the characteristics of the three periods of time remain perfectly distinct. Why?
[The interlocutor] takes this to be the characteristic of the One Vehicle. Mañjuśrī, fearing that people would regard it as an assembly of past Buddhas, hurriedly called out:
"Maitreya, you should know that the first Buddha and the subsequent Buddhas all share the same name and the same clan."

To say in general that those of sharp faculties [attain Buddhahood] implies that it is not through dull faculties that one attains Buddhahood; there is profound significance in this. This is the second point:
the shared intent of the Buddhas regarding the path to Buddhahood is not accidental. △ Third, the final point: the identity of the last Buddha. This is divided into three parts.
First, the identity of their renunciation.

Regarding the final Buddha mentioned, prior to his renunciation of the household life (up to the point where he possessed sovereign majesty and ruled over four continents), he cited only one Buddha—neither more than once seen nor once heard—and there was never a time when he did not discuss him. Now, however, he cites twenty thousand Buddhas.
The teachings revealed are shown to be no different. Therefore, one knows that the teachings revealed by the present Buddha are likewise no different.
Furthermore, it is cited that the final Buddha had eight sons, whereas the present Buddha has but one son; thus, while their names differ, their essence is non-dual.
Now, that which is called "home" refers to the three realms and the six paths of existence; it is also the five aggregates, the eighteen elements, and all afflictions.
To say one has not yet left home means that one has not yet transcended these various defilements.

The eight sons represent the eight consciousnesses, and their being named after the "mind" (manas) indicates they are not separate from consciousness. Zhizhi says: "The myriad phenomena of the world all arise from..."
The *ālaya-vijñāna* is established as containing all seeds without exception; therefore, it is called the "intentional mind" (*manas*).

The seven consciousnesses skillfully grasp and maintain [objects], and are thus called the "virtuous intention. The mental consciousness discriminates between good and evil, being indeterminate from moment to moment;

thus, it is called the "immeasurable intention. The body-consciousness consists of the objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) cherished by those in the six realms of existence; thus, it is called the "precious intention. Furthermore, the tongue-consciousness perceives flavors...

That which is able to skillfully expound the essentials of the Dharma is called the Mind of Increase. That which enables the olfactory consciousness to distinguish between fragrances and stenches is called the Mind that Dispels Doubt.

That which enables the auditory consciousness to respond to sounds according to their resonance is called the Resonant Mind. That which enables the visual consciousness to clarify the characteristics of all phenomena is called the Mind of Dharma.
Each stage possesses its own functional capacity; hence it is called "majestic power" (vaibhava). Each is able to give rise to function from its essence;
hence it is called "sovereignty" (vibhu). Each stage has its own four marks, such as self and person; hence it is said that each governs the four continents.

These princes, having heard that their father had left the household life (up to the point where he had) already planted various roots of goodness under ten million buddhas—this further clarifies that these princes were all practitioners of past learning.

As for "leaving the household life," it means that a person, by means of non-active merit (*anabhisaṃskāra*), attains correspondence in a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta*) and accords with the principle of suchness (*tathatā-nyāya*); they suddenly shatter ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, it is called "leaving the household life. Having heard this...
When the father leaves the household life, he immediately realizes that phenomena are fused with principle; as one thing turns, all things turn.

When one abandons the royal throne to follow him into the homeless life, one abandons the mundane and enters the Real, whereby the entire body is fully revealed. Therefore, it is said that "one gives rise to the Mahāyāna mind. The Direct Pointing says:
"From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the eighth stage, all belong to the cultivation of meritorious achievement"; therefore, it is said that "one gives rise to the Mahāyāna."
The meaning is as follows: from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the ninth stage, one does not cling to a state of silent stillness, yet does not lose the practice of cultivation;
therefore, it is said that "one constantly practices the Brahma-faring. At the tenth stage, one serves as a bridge across the Dharma-realm; therefore, it is said that "all are Dharma-teachers.

In every thought-moment, the light of the mind is uniquely revealed, such that the ultimate and the conventional are of one taste; therefore, it is said that "one has already planted all roots of goodness under millions of Buddhas. If we discuss this...
The "One Son of the Buddha" here represents the single eighth consciousness (*aṣṭhavijñāna*), because the eighth consciousness is able to encompass those seven [consciousnesses].
The name *Rāhula*, meaning "obscuration" or "veiling," refers to the state of the karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*) prior to its transformation. This constitutes the third stage:
the similarity between the cause and the effect of abandoning worldly life for ordination and attaining the fruit.
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa [appeared]... [as] the various Buddha-lands seen now.

This clarifies that the six auspicious omens manifested by the former Buddha in his own land were identical to those of the present. Tiantai says: "Mañjuśrī cites the account of what was seen in the past:

the preaching of the sutra is the same, the entry into meditative concentration is the same, the falling of flowers is the same, the earthquake is the same, and the assembly attaining realization of the meaning is the same."
The same applies to the Tathāgata’s emission of light; the underlying intent is all consistent with what preceded and may be understood accordingly.

The two phrases regarding what is now seen encompass the six auspicious omens in other lands; thus, they are summarized in a single statement. Since these are the omens perceived within the present assembly, they are not described in detail.
This constitutes the fourth reason: the manifestation of auspicious signs prior to preaching the Sublime Dharma.

Maitreya, you should know that at that time, within the assembly—[down to] those who wished to know the causes and conditions for which this light appeared—the doubts and reflections of this assembly were identical to those of the present.
Furthermore, it teaches people here that the twenty billion bodhisattvas are precisely what humans call "wondrous wisdom accordant with nature" (*dharmatā-jñāna*);
however, they have not yet attained the universal integration of the three periods of time, and thus they do not equal the [Buddha’s] realization.

Because he is the Samyaksaṃbuddha, it is said: "If one wishes to know the causes and conditions for which this light was manifested. Fifth, seeing the signs gives rise to doubt; one desires to know the cause for which they were manifested.
△ Second, the identity of the teaching. This is divided into two parts. First, the name of the sutra is no different.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Wonderful Light (*Prabhāketu*)... [who] taught the Dharma to the bodhisattvas and was protected by the mindfulness of the Buddhas.
This clearly demonstrates that the ancient and the present are not two. Tiantai says:

"In the past, when the Buddha arose from meditation, he told Wonderful Light to take the eight sons as his teachers and entrusted the Dharma to him. Now, when the Buddha arises from meditation, he tells Śāriputra to take Rāhula..."
The Master of Clouds (Nanquan) transmitted it to him and likewise entrusted the Dharma to him; this is the non-dual path throughout all time. Zhizhi says:
"Miaoguang was the previous incarnation of Mañjuśrī. In terms of its meaning, it encompasses the Sun, Moon, and Lamp; therefore, it is called 'Wondrous' (Miao).
As for the eight hundred disciples, they were referred to as the 'Eight Princes' based on their causal state in terms of the Mind-King; now, they are designated by their fruition. [He] transformed...
Because there are various mental factors (*caitasika*), it is said there are eight hundred. Regarding the phrase "preaching the wondrous Dharma by means of Wondrous Light":

this shows that the Dharma has causes upon which it depends. One must pay close attention to the character "cause" (*yin*). If the Sun, Moon, and Lamp-Light did not rely on Wondrous Light, then even though the wondrous Dharma existed, from where could it have been preached?
Therefore, it is rightly observed that the meaning [of the title] subsumes the Sun, Moon, and Lamp-Light. This insight is indeed profound.
Regarding the title *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*: this sutra has already borne this name for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas prior to the present;
thus, its current name is already an established term. Nevertheless, one must further understand this.
The sun, moon, and lamps still have a source from which they derive their light.
If a student can investigate the place from which the sun, moon, and lamps derive their light, only then may they be said to be a fellow-student of the ancient Buddhas;
one will then know that this is the Dharma for instructing Bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas. II. The time and season are no different.
For sixty minor kalpas he did not rise from his seat, nor did his body or mind experience weariness or fatigue.
This clarifies the duration of the preaching of the sutra: for sixty kalpas he did not rise from his seat. It is not difficult for the speaker to preach, but it is difficult for the listener to hear.
Now, because it is said that his body and mind were unmoving and that no weariness arose, we know that he had already attained the Dharma.
He is sovereign. Therefore it is said that it was "as long as a meal. Otherwise, how could he remain with body and mind unmoving for sixty kalpas?
And how could sixty kalpas be as brief as a meal? Question: The World-Honored One taught the *Avataṃsaka* in only twenty-one days.
Yet in the past, the Buddha spoke this sutra for sixty kalpas; and now, the present Buddha has also already passed fifty kalpas. Why is this?
Regarding the claim that the *Avataṃsaka* is brief while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is extensive, the answer is as follows:

The spiritual capacities (*indriya*) addressed by the *Avataṃsaka* are all those who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*) up to the level of Equal Enlightenment (*samāpatti-jñāna*). Their wisdom is in profound accord with reality, such that the speaker and the listener are of one essence.
Thus, even twenty-one days may still be considered long. This sutra intends to overturn and dismantle the old habitual tendencies of the three vehicles.

Here, "sixty kalpas" refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*), while "fifty kalpas" refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). The five aggregates and the six sense faculties are merely names for the opening and closing of form and mind.
Because sentient beings have long been enveloped by the five skandhas, they falsely perceive length and brevity. Therefore...

The two Buddhas first moved [the world] through meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and subsequently uprooted it through wisdom (*jñāna*), causing those seated there to perceive sixty kalpas as a mere meal-time and fifty kalpas as half a day;
all of this was due to the miraculous power of the Buddha. This constitutes the sixth cause for arising from samādhi:

preaching the sublime Dharma according to the capacities of sentient beings. △ Third, the commonality of proclaiming extinction (*parinirvāṇa*). This is divided into two parts. First, the proclamation...
The prediction regarding his parinirvāṇa is no different [from that of other Buddhas].

When the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa had completed sixty intermediate kalpas [and] it was said in the sūtra that he was about to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, his worldly activities were finished; he then proclaimed his extinction before the assembly of devas and humans.
This serves to awaken one to impermanence. *Brahmā* is the lord of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). *Māra* is the lord of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
*Śramaṇa* means "one who is diligent and at rest. *Brāhmaṇa* means "one of pure conduct," referring here to those among the non-Buddhist outsiders who have left the household life.

"Midnight" takes the middle portion [of the night] to symbolize that worldly affairs have ended and one returns to the ultimate principle; it also symbolizes the Middle Way. This is what the Tathāgata performed.

All [teachings] accord with the Middle Way and do not abide in the two extremes. That which is called "ultimate" in *nirvāṇa without remainder* refers to the exhaustion of the five abodes, the forgetting of the two types of death, and the full possession of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; this is precisely the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings.
When first preaching the sutra, he emerges from this samādhi—this is the emergence of the immeasurable from the one. When the sutra concludes, he returns to this samādhi. This is...
This is to subsume the immeasurable into the one. Therefore, it is said that entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* is no different from the present proclamation of extinction.
That is, once the seventh task is completed, he immediately proclaims *nirvāṇa*.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Guṇakośa (up to) who entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* during the middle watch of the night.

This is the formal exposition of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). "Bestowing" (*śāsana*) refers to the holy word being given; "prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*) refers to the fruit being granted in accordance with one's mental aspiration.
To state it directly: since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has already completed its teaching on the three vehicles, the matter of bestowing predictions then arises. Now, the Buddha speaks [of this].
The Dharma-cycle is complete. First, Śāriputra was predicted; this refers to the transformation of the *manovijñāna* (consciousness). That Buddha, however, predicted only Guṇakara;
this refers to the transformation of the *ālayavijñāna* (store-consciousness). Therefore, upon reaching the state of fruition, he is called "Pure Body" (*śuddhakāya*).
*Tathāgata*, here translated as "Thus-Come One"; *Arhat*, here translated as "Worthy of Offerings"; *Samyaksaṃbuddha*, here translated as "Perfectly All-Knowing. These are the ten titles.
Third. Question: Those who were previously granted predictions were bodhisattvas; those now granted predictions are all śrāvakas. Why is it said there is no distinction? Answer:
What Mañjuśrī has recounted today concerns past events. Looking back from the present to the past, they were called "bodhisattvas.
Since this sutra has now granted them the prediction of Buddhahood, how could they not be called "bodhisattvas" in future assemblies? This is precisely...

The eighth [point] concerns the cause for bestowing a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) through the harmonious convergence of the faculties and the teaching. As for the statement "he immediately enters nirvāṇa":
once the Dharma has been taught and the prediction has been bestowed, the light of the Sun-Moon-Lamp has already continued; to then enter the principle without remainder is the meaning of nirvāṇa.
This is the ninth cause for entering nirvāṇa at night once the conditions for transformation have concluded. △ Second, after his passing.
The general exposition does not distinguish [the specific periods]; it is divided into three parts. The first clarifies the time periods for upholding the sutra:
from "after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa" until "the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light (Prabhāpāla) preached it for others for a full eighty minor kalpas."

This clarifies that after the ancient Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there were those who could propagate [the teaching]. Regarding the statement that "after the Buddha’s extinction, Wondrous Light (Prabhāpāla) upheld the Dharma," the character "upheld" (chí) should be understood in its deeper sense.
The Buddha is the principle of suchness (*tathatā*); Wondrous Light is the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*).

Furthermore, since the Dharma was spoken by the Buddha, once the Dharma remains while the Buddha has become hidden, there is the meaning of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; it is necessarily through Wondrous Light upholding the Dharma [that the lineage continues].
When the Buddha has entered extinction, the principle is integrated; when the principle is integrated, wisdom is inexhaustible.
To maintain this Dharma with this wisdom is to maintain it perpetually throughout ten thousand ages. The "full eighty minor kalpas" refers to the duration for which the Dharma is maintained.
Thus, one fulfills the wisdom of self-benefit. Endowed with the eight sublime tones and manifesting the eight sublime knowledges, one may then begin to expound the teaching for others;

only then are the merits of the two benefits fully realized. Question: Why was the prophecy not granted to Miaoguang (Sublime Light), and why is Dezang (Virtue Treasury) not mentioned in the context of upholding the Dharma? Answer: There is a specific principle underlying this. In the preceding [section],...

This refers to Wondrous Light (Prabhāsa), who expounded the wondrous Dharma based on the Sun, Moon, and Lamp. Since the principle is fundamentally undivided, how could there be a formal prediction (vyākaraṇa) to bestow?
Because the Dharma was expounded based on that cause, its upholding must reside with him; therefore, the Dharma cannot be upheld by Wondrous Light alone.

Although Virtue-Treasury (Guṇagañja) has already received a prediction, his treasury and virtues have not yet been fully integrated; he is thus only capable of self-benefit. Therefore, [the task of] circulating [the teaching]—
For now, I shall not address this further. △ Second, clarifying that the Dharma will be transmitted to worthy recipients:
From "The eight sons of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa" (up to) "making offerings, honoring, respecting, and praising [him]."
That all eight sons took Miaoguang as their teacher means that Mañjuśrī is the fundamental, ultimate wisdom; this is also clear.

Without fundamental wisdom, there would be no means to serve as a model for later students. Since the eight sons have received the instruction and transformation of Miaoguang and are thus firmly established in Bodhi, once they have received such instruction and are firmly established in Bodhi, one ought not to continue addressing them by [their former names].

Prince, it is simply that conventional truth has not yet been fully integrated. Only when one has made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas and attained the perfection of merit and wisdom does one first receive the title of Buddha.
The practitioner, in every thought-moment, reveres and cherishes the sacred embryo;
this is making offerings to all Buddhas with the intent to realize the Way of the Buddha, which is precisely the fulfillment of the single true mind. Finally, one attains Buddhahood.

The name "Dīpaṃkara" (The Lamp-Maker) represents the *ālaya-vijñāna*, which only functions upon reaching the stage of fruition; thus, being called Dīpaṃkara signifies the great wisdom that continues the lamp-light of Subhūti.
Among the eight hundred disciples, there was one named Yaśaskāma (Seeker of Fame), who represents the six consciousnesses. *Zhízhǐ* says:

"Benefit (*lì*) refers to the dharma-attachment of benefiting sentient beings during the three stages of worthiness (*triyānika-pudgala*); nourishment (*yǎng*) refers to [the practice] within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*)."

This is realized within the realm of principle; therefore, it is called "clinging. To read various sutras without awakening to the Lotus Sutra is like striking water to produce fire—how could one ever achieve mastery?
Since these teachings have been brought in from the outside, much is forgotten and lost.
