these constitute the main body (*samyak-siddhānta*) of the Trace Gate. Now, focusing on the main body of the Trace Gate, it is further divided into two parts. First is the revelation and manifestation (*vivaraṇa-prakāśana*) of the Trace Gate, which is further divided into two.

First is the brief revelation of the three to manifest the one (*saṃkṣipta-traya-vivaraṇa-eka-prakāśana*), which is divided into two. First is the brief presentation of the revelation and manifestation (*saṃkṣipta-nirdeśa-vivaraṇa-prakāśana*), which is divided into two.

First, a double eulogy of the two wisdoms. This section further divides into two: first, the prose exposition; this further divides into two: first, a eulogy expressed through words. This further divides into two:
first, clarifying the provisional and the real of all Buddhas, which is divided into three parts. First, a double eulogy; this further divides into two: first, the introduction by the sūtra compiler.
At that time, the World-Honored One arose calmly from samādhi and addressed Śāriputra.
"At that time" refers to the moment when the dialogue between the host and guest, Mañjuśrī and Maitreya, had concluded. "Calmly" means:
"Xixu" means slowly and gently; "qi" means to arise and emerge. This is spoken in contrast to the word "ru" (to enter).

Previously, when entering samādhi, the Tathāgata caused a portion of his own internal enjoyment of the true realm to be revealed, thereby demonstrating the principle of suchness to the people. At that time, the assembly...
Beholding this land and other lands, all are inconceivable; thus, within the breast of every person, there is a segment of luminous reality that cannot be fully articulated.
Recalling the Tathāgata’s emergence from meditative absorption, one must expect the heavens to shake, the earth to tremble, the oceans to surge, and the mountains to soar.
Now, as he emerges from absorption, he gives rise to unconditioned great compassion and manifests suchness-wisdom, yet remains without uttering a sound.

When Śāriputra peacefully arose from samādhi and addressed him without waiting for a question, it was precisely because he wished for people to realize that this wondrous Dharma is of a single flavor and ordinary—neither marvelous nor strange.
Therefore, the use of the two characters "peaceful and composed" (ān-śāng) is most profound. Question: There were limitless people in the assembly; why did he address Śāriputra alone?

What does this mean? The answer is: The Tathāgata originally established the discourse on opening, showing, awakening, and entering as a manifestation of skillful means for those who do not know and do not believe.
Thus, while he was previously in meditative concentration, Mañjuśrī, representing ultimate wisdom, provided the responses that elucidated this truth.

Now, emerging from meditative absorption, he must again rely on Śāriputra to manifest his provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), thereby merging the two types of wisdom into the single reality of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Moreover, since Śāriputra was originally a manifestation of great skillful means, appearing as the foremost in wisdom among those of the Hīnayāna, [the Buddha] first addressed him in order to shatter the Lesser Vehicle and reveal the Great Vehicle, thereby stirring the multitude. Furthermore, it was asked: "The Tathāgata is eternal..."

[The Buddha] was in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). How can it be said that he arose? If there were entering and emerging [from concentration], it would not be called "correct concentration" (*samyak-samādhi*).

Answer: Do you not know that this is a skillful means (*upāya*)? Since it belongs to skillful means, when has the Tathāgata ever emerged from concentration? △ Second, the formal praise of the two wisdoms.
The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable.
Since they are called "all Buddhas," this includes those of the ten directions and the three periods of time; in reality, they are but a single Buddha.
This "wisdom" is what this sutra calls the "wonderful Dharma" (Saddharma), the "true aspect" (bhūtalakṣaṇa), and the "one vehicle" (ekayāna)—that which all Buddhas have realized as the unsurpassed.
The suchness of bodhi is true wisdom. That which emitted light during meditative concentration previously was also this very same real wisdom.
This wisdom cannot be named by names, nor can it be seen by seeing. What is called "profound" is unfathomable;
what is "immeasurable" is beyond comparison. Observe, for instance, Sudhana within a single pore of Samantabhadra.
In the midst [of this], taking a single step, one passes through worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields.
Proceeding in this manner until the end of the future, one would still be unable to know the sequential order of the oceans of lands within even a single pore, let alone the realm of the Buddhas.
Thus, the wisdom of all Buddhas is truly unfathomable; therefore, it is called "profoundly deep and without limit."

[The section on] Measure. Tiantai says: This praises true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). As for the mention of "all Buddhas," it does not refer to the provisional and real [teachings] used by the Three Vehicles to transform others;
rather, it refers to the provisional and real [wisdom] of the Buddhas' own practice.
This gateway of wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter; it is something that cannot be known by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
A "gateway" (mukha) carries the sense of being opened and the sense of entering and exiting.

What is called the "gateway of wisdom" refers to the provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), which, by means of ultimate wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), opens up, reveals, and provides a differentiated exposition. It does not exist separately outside of the ultimate; it is neither separate from nor apart from it.

"Harmonization" refers to skillful means (*upāya*). It is when the Buddha, while in meditative concentration, emits light and manifests auspicious signs to fully reveal the distinctions between the defiled and pure states of the ten dharma realms, causing every person who sees them to exclaim that they have encountered something unprecedented.
Regarding "difficult to understand and enter": because the assembly beheld these manifestations of light, each gave rise to doubt, saying, "We do not know the source of this light."
Regarding the causes and conditions for this: Maitreya likewise used them to question Mañjuśrī. Although Mañjuśrī answered by drawing upon ancient precedents, he still required careful reflection;

how could this be easily understood or entered? As for the claim that the śrāvakas did not understand it, this is truly because when the World-Honored One manifested his traces in the human realm, he pointed his finger at heaven and earth, and throughout forty years, he continued to manipulate that finger.
Every point serves to clearly manifest this wisdom, demonstrating that it is inherently possessed by all people.

Yet the followers of the Two Vehicles conversely claim that it is not within the scope of their own wisdom. Throughout this, they employ various expressions and indirect approaches to open wide this gateway;
yet the followers of the Two Vehicles conversely claim these are merely "teachings for Bodhisattvas. Thus, all Śrāvakas—
They do not have confidence in knowing that such wisdom exists, nor do they comprehend the gateway of the Tathāgata’s such wisdom;
therefore it is said, "that which cannot be known. Tiantai says: This praises the provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
It is because the Buddhas realize the principle through ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) and teach the Dharma through provisional wisdom. △ Second, the dual explanation.
Why is this? Because the Buddha has personally attended upon [the Buddhas] (up to) fully practicing all the immeasurable path-dharmas of the Buddhas.
What was explained above is difficult to understand and difficult to enter; this serves to alert those who have not yet awakened.

Now, in order to present the models of what the Buddhas have cultivated so that the assembled multitude may have something to take as a standard for their practice, he poses the question and provides the explanation. Thus, the phrase "Why is this? [is used].
This pair of questions probes the two types of wisdom. The following section provides a singular explanation of the wisdom of reality (*bhūta-jñāna*).

It asks: "For what reason is the wisdom of all Buddhas so profoundly deep and immeasurable? It replies: "During their causal stages, the Buddhas were not like you, who are indolent and merely follow those with whom they are personally intimate;
rather, there have been hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of countless Buddhas. For each and every one of these Buddhas..."
There is the Way and its Dharma; there is nothing that is not fully practiced, and nothing that is not thoroughly mastered.

It is said that if water does not accumulate to a great depth, it lacks the power to support a large ship. Because the application of its power is profound and far-reaching, the wisdom attained is likewise thus exceedingly deep and immeasurable.

"His valorous diligence is renowned everywhere"—this refers to the provisional wisdom of Śākyamuni. As for the gateway of wisdom, why is it also difficult to understand and difficult to enter? It is said:
one must know that this is the practice performed by all Buddhas during their causal stages; because of their valorous diligence, they were able to enter what is otherwise difficult to enter.
This is the gateway. Once one enters this gateway, their application of wisdom becomes profound and vast, their eloquence becomes unimpeded, and their fame quickly spreads everywhere.
Consequently, all that they say should logically be difficult to understand and difficult to enter.
The reason why the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot understand or enter it is none other than a lack of courageous and diligent effort. You followers of the Two Vehicles, as soon as...
Having attained a *nirvāṇa* with remainder, one deems what has been gained to be vast; yet how could there be the vow to draw near to countless Buddhas?
Moreover, with a mind harboring such dull and inferior resolve, how could there be the cause for courageous diligence whose fame is heard everywhere?
Regarding the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas, if one’s heart finds no joy, how can there be the accomplishment of the profound and unprecedented?
Is there a fruit of dharmas? Therefore, I say that this is what you are unable to know. △ Third, the double conclusion:
the accomplishment of the profound and unprecedented dharma.
Tiantai says: This constitutes the perfection of true wisdom; because it accords with reality and is ultimate, it is called "accomplishment" (*siddhi*).
Because it reaches the very bottom of the other shore, it is called "profound. Because it was never previously taught, it is called "unprecedented."
The underlying intent of what is taught according to what is appropriate is difficult to understand.

This concludes the section on provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). To accord with capacities and meet [the needs of beings] is called "according to what is appropriate. It is not something known by those on the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*).

It is said that this is difficult to understand. [△@△] Because the Tathāgatas have in the past attended many Buddhas, practiced with courageous diligence, and performed manifold wholesome deeds, what they have attained is profound and what they know is vast.
When it comes to responding to capacities and engaging with beings—whether through provisional or ultimate means—they exhaust their entire treasury of realization.
Like a bright pearl rolling across a tray, moving freely in all directions without obstruction; it is only fitting, therefore, that they should cause people to find them difficult to comprehend.
"Understanding the difficult entry. This introduces the various Buddhas; they possess such practices and studies, and the evidence is thus clear.
△ Second, clarifying the provisional and the real of Śākyamuni, divided into three parts. First, a double eulogy.
Śāriputra, since my attainment of Buddhahood until now, I have guided sentient beings to cause them to leave behind all attachments.
The Tathāgata now intends to reveal this section of light, so that those of the Two Vehicles will surely know that there exists this great causal condition of one great matter.
Therefore, he first cites the testimony of countless Buddhas to prove the ultimate nature of this path; there has never been anyone who did not follow it.
It comes from being close to [the teaching]. There has never been anything attained that did not arise from diligence.
First, he uses the example of other Buddhas to clarify it, and only then does he speak of himself, so that all people will surely awaken to and enter [the truth]. Tiantai said:
"Since my attaining Buddhahood, I have first praised true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). Since it is called "attaining Buddhahood," one must have first obtained true wisdom.
The foundation of this [teaching]. Having fulfilled self-benefit, the passage beginning with "through various causes and conditions" below praises expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
Regarding "causes and conditions": distantly, it refers to the causal conditions from the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū as a prince;

proximately, it refers to the forty years during which [the Buddha] turned his belly and emptied his entrails—nothing but these served as causes and conditions for this matter. Regarding "parables": in the Hīnayāna, [it is like] the plantain tree...
The analogy of water bubbles; in the Mahāyāna, there are the analogies of the city of the gandharvas, mirrors, and illusions, as found throughout this sutra—all of which are various metaphors.

As for "extensive exposition," it means opening up immeasurable dharmas from a single dharma, teaching them according to the three vehicles and the ninefold division of scriptures, skillfully adapting to the various faculties of sentient beings;
hence, it is called "innumerable skillful means. Regarding "being free from all attachments," it refers to preaching the ten wholesome actions in their dispersed form.

To eliminate attachment to the three miserable realms, he taught the ten pure wholesome deeds; to eliminate attachment to the desire realm, he taught the Tripitaka; to eliminate attachment to views and afflictions, he taught the Bodhisattva Dharma;
to eliminate attachment to Nirvana, he taught the Tathāgata’s path-dharmas; and to eliminate attachment to the craving for dharmas that accord with the Path, [he taught the Mahayana].
Therefore, it is said that these are all attachments. Yet, since the World-Honored One has already realized this for himself, how could he bear to sit idly by and fail to reveal it to others?
Alas, all people claim to be "perfectly enlightened" (*yuanjue*) throughout their lives, yet they are unable to realize and enter it;
thus, he now reveals it to them. To those followers of the Two Vehicles, it is as if a ball were blocking their ears or leaves were covering their eyes; the Tathāgata beholds them thus...

Being thus bewildered and as if in darkness, one can do nothing but humbly employ skillful means, creating various causes, conditions, parables, and metaphors to explain them extensively through detailed analysis.
This, too, does not go beyond guiding people to depart from all attachments. △ Second, the dual explanation.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has fully perfected the *pāramitās* of skillful means, knowledge, and vision.
This pair explains the two types of wisdom. It asks: For what reason is the Tathāgata able to guide sentient beings so that they are free from all attachments?

Because the Tathāgata is fully endowed with the perfection of skillful means, knowledge, and vision (*upāya-jñāna-darśana-pāramitā*), his knowledge and vision are themselves the reality, while skillful means are the provisional.
Since the two characters "Tathāgata" precede the terms "knowledge and vision," this is not merely ordinary knowledge and vision.
When the Tathāgata realizes this inconceivable and wondrous Dharma, there is nothing he does not know and nothing he does not see. Truly...
The ocean of wondrous adornments realized by all Buddhas is inconceivable and immeasurable;
it is the most profound and the most secret—this is what was previously called "profound," yet there is nothing that the Tathāgata does not know. It is ineffable and boundless;
it is the most vast and the most sublime—this is what was previously called "immeasurable," yet there is nothing that the Tathāgata does not see.
This is precisely the Tathāgata’s perfection of knowledge and vision regarding unsurpassed bodhi. The Tathāgata has reached the ultimate limit of this;
he nevertheless reveals that which he knows and sees to all sentient beings, enabling all people to awaken and enter into it.
Thus, while the revelation is indeed the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, those who awaken and enter it will necessarily realize the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
It is seen that when sentient beings reach this state, they are no different from the Buddha; all are led in by the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Tathāgata.
Thus, each and every one of the two wisdoms penetrates to the very bottom of the Dharma. Therefore, it is said in general that the *pāramitās* are all fully perfected.
△ Third, the double conclusion.
"Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are vast and profound (extending to: ...he has accomplished all unprecedented dharmas). This passage now sets forth the exposition.
In the previous section praising the Buddhas, it spoke of "the wisdom of the Buddhas"; therefore, here it speaks of the "Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision.
Previously it was said to be "profound and immeasurable," whereas here it is said to be "vast and profound. This is what each Buddha possesses.
This realizes the principle of non-duality. This concludes the section on true wisdom (*samyagjñāna*).
As previously stated, the wisdom attained by all Buddhas is acquired through practicing immeasurable deeds under immeasurable Buddhas with courageous diligence;
thus, these dharmas—the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and so forth—each penetrate deeply and are boundless. Is this not indeed the result of courageous diligence?
One advances toward all wholesome dharmas practiced by the Buddhas and thereby attains them. Therefore, the preceding conclusion states:
"One accomplishes the profound and unprecedented dharma. This means that one accomplishes all unprecedented dharmas;

however, while "profound" clarifies the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), "all" reveals the provisional skillful means (*upāya*). The World-Honored One himself explains and concludes this, saying: "As for what the Tathāgata..."
The knower is vast, and what is seen is profound and far-reaching. That which is accomplished consists entirely of unprecedented dharmas;

it is certainly not something that your shallow knowledge and inferior views can understand or enter. There are four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), namely: loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Because those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) do not deliver sentient beings, they do not attain these. There are also four kinds of non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇa*); the first is...

1. Non-obstruction regarding phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*): because one can expound immeasurable phenomena through a single phenomenon. 2. Non-obstruction regarding meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*): because one can expound immeasurable meanings through a single meaning.
3. Non-obstruction regarding expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*): because one can expound immeasurable sounds through a single sound. 4. Non-obstruction regarding eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*).
He teaches the Dharma according to the capacities [of beings] because he is free from weariness. His powers (*bala*) are tenfold:

first, the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (knowing who can be saved and who cannot); second, the power of knowing the retribution of karma throughout the three periods of time (meaning knowing whether there are obstructions or no obstructions);

third, the power of knowing the superiority and inferiority of the faculties (knowing that the faculties such as faith are of weak, middling, or superior degree); fourth, the power of knowing the various elements (*dhātu*) (referring to the three vehicles, the five natures, etc.; *dhātu* here means "nature"); fifth, the power of knowing the various...

1. The power of knowledge regarding the resolution of others' faculties (or the power of desire, which refers to attachment to wealth, profit, fame, and so forth). 2. The power of knowledge regarding the paths leading to all destinations (knowing the various practices of sentient beings—whether they are paths of transcendence or non-transcendence—and that each can reach its respective fruit).
3. The power of knowledge regarding the meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and their purity (such as those with outflows and those without outflows, etc.).

4. The power of knowledge regarding the recollection of past abodes (knowing one's former names, clans, sufferings, joys, and so forth). 5. The power of knowledge regarding the divine eye (referring to death...)

[He knows] rebirth in this life or that, falling into good or evil realms, and [the details of] size, beauty, and ugliness, etc. Tenth is the power of knowledge that eradicates all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), which is the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*).
Because those of the Lesser Vehicle do not seek the Buddha-way and do not train in the ten powers, they do not know this.

There are four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*): first, the fearlessness of omniscience. [Regarding this,] suppose someone were to challenge: "If the Buddha is omniscient, there are bhikṣus who have come from other regions whom he ought to know; why did he ask whether they were dwelling in peace and happiness? To this, the Buddha [responds...]

1. Fearlessness regarding being challenged [on the path]: [The Buddha remains] secure and fearless when challenged. He replied: "I am an omniscient one; however, it was merely for the sake of receiving those who came to me that I conformed to the worldly sentiments of teacher and disciple, and spoke thus.

2. Fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-vaiśāradya*): Suppose someone were to challenge: "If the Buddha has indeed exhausted all outflows, why did he speak kindly to Rāhula yet revile Devadatta? Regarding this challenge, the Buddha remains secure and fearless, saying to him: "I have truly exhausted all outflows;

it was only to subdue them according to their respective faculties (*indriya*) that I acted as I did. 3. Fearlessness regarding the proclamation of obstacles to the path (*antarāyika-dharma-deśanā-vaiśāradya*): Suppose someone were to challenge: "The Buddha said that sensual desire truly obstructs the path; why then [did he allow it for] a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*)..."

The Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) still gives rise to desire and attachment toward wife and children. Regarding this objection, the Buddha remains secure and fearless, saying to them: "I declare that the obstacle of sensual desire prevents one from attaining the three higher fruits and Arhatship; it cannot be abandoned at the first two fruits.

Fourth is the fearlessness regarding the path to the exhaustion of suffering (*duḥkhakṣayagāminīpratipad-vaiśāradya*). Suppose an objection is raised: "The Buddha says the Noble Path can exhaust all suffering.

Why then does an Arhat experience the suffering of open sores or being bitten by snakes? Regarding this objection, the Buddha remains secure and fearless, saying to them: "I say that the Noble Path truly can exhaust suffering, but I speak of the future, not because of what is observed in the present. Among these four [fearlessnesses], the first is the abandonment of what is to be known (*jñeya*). The second...

[The first three] are the separation from afflictions (*kleśa*). The third is the obstacle to renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa-āvaraṇa*). The fourth is the path of renunciation. [This is because] the followers of the Hīnayāna do not exhaust all obstacles and possess timidity; therefore, they do not know this.
As for "liberation" (*vimukti*), it refers to the inconceivable liberation, the unobstructed liberation, the pure observation liberation, up to the liberation of the limit of no-remainder.
With these ten as the foremost, there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of doors of liberation. Because the Hīnayāna [only]...
They have attained the three gates of liberation; therefore, they do not know this.

As for the samādhis, there are the Samādhi of Universal Radiance, the Samādhi of the Square Net, the Samādhi of the Ocean Seal, and even the Samādhi of the Unobstructed Wheel, as well as immeasurable hundreds of thousands of other samādhis, all of which the Tathāgatas have fully accomplished, as described extensively in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Due to the attachment of the followers of the Hīnayāna...
Because it is the samādhi of quiescent extinction, he does not know this. "Dhyāna" refers to the Dhyāna of the Unsurpassed Vehicle; "samādhi" refers to the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
As described above, the Tathāgata has deeply entered each and every one of these to their boundless limits; it is not that he merely attains them alone.
Having finished the eulogy of his virtues through words, △ second, the eulogy of the two wisdoms beyond words, divided into two parts. First, citing the ineffable...
Regarding the reasons for this praise:
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is able to distinguish various [teachings] (up to: his speech is gentle and pleasing to the hearts of the multitude.
From the beginning, he has vigorously extolled the two types of wisdom—the provisional and the ultimate—realized by himself and others. Such is their profound depth.
Such is the difficulty of understanding; such are these dhyānas and samādhis; such are these unprecedented dharmas.
All of these are what is known and seen by those of unsurpassed, great wisdom; they are not within the capacity of people like you to emulate. It is as the saying goes:

"The trampling of a dragon-elephant is not something a donkey can endure. The intent is to rouse the indignation of those of the two vehicles and inspire their aspiration for the Great [Vehicle], thus speaking to the ultimate point.
In this regard, it may be said that he has drawn a crossbow bolt weighing a thousand jin. Next, when he wishes to transcend words, it is to manifest that which words cannot reach;
yet, not knowing the point where words are cut off, he speaks with all his might. Therefore, he again addresses Śāriputra, saying:
"The Tathāgata is able to make various distinctions. This word "able" directly contrasts with the "inability" of those of the Two Vehicles.
It is like a great wealthy man who brings forth immeasurable rare treasures and shows them to a poor son,
observing what kind of actions he performs and how he is able to make various distinctions and skillfully explain all phenomena.
The words of his distinctions and skillful explanations are not without being individually gentle and supple, causing the hearts of those who hear them to be without exception joyful and at ease.
Furthermore, the phrase "to gladden the hearts of the multitude" is a statement intended to strike the assembly with a cold, sobering blow. One might ask:

can those who hear it truly be gladdened or filled with joy? This is merely, following the sequence of stimulating them with the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate truth, to summarize that there is nothing they possess that will not be accomplished.
Śāriputra, to speak in brief, the Buddha has fully accomplished immeasurable, boundless, and unprecedented dharmas.
If I were to explain each of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision for you one by one, it would be difficult to exhaust them even at the end of an eon.
For now, I shall summarize and state only the essentials: these are immeasurable, boundless, and unprecedented dharmas never before heard or seen.
There is nothing I have not accomplished. However, since the Dharma I have attained is boundless and immeasurable, how could it ever be exhausted in a mere moment, or expressed in a few words?
This is the reason for this utter amazement. II. The actual expression of amazement beyond words.
This has two parts: 1. The expression of amazement beyond words.
"Stop, Śāriputra; there is no need to speak further.

Since it has already been stated that he has fully accomplished immeasurable and unprecedented dharmas, this is his desire to entrust these dharmas entirely to others, so that all people may realize them. Yet, alas, these dharmas are such that words cannot reach them."

One can do nothing but cease speech to offer praise. Here, the character "zhǐ" (cease) is employed; it is not that one does not wish to speak, but rather a regret that the wisdom of the assembled multitude is not easily prepared to hear this.
Moreover, as this is the supreme practice of the Tathāgata, those who hear it truly find it difficult to comprehend.
Though one wishes to remain silent and say nothing, the heart finds it hard to bear such restraint; thus, one can only praise oneself and offer self-eulogy.
Now, let us examine the Tathāgata’s inner intent here. How urgent it is!
That he repeatedly restrains himself and repeatedly sighs thereafter, yet does not explicitly reveal it, sufficiently demonstrates how earnest his compassionate heart is. II. Explaining the Intent.
This has two parts. First, the supreme practice cannot be described.
Why is this? From "that which the Buddha has accomplished" up to "only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully exhaust [it]," the meaning is explained as follows:
it is as if one were to ask, "For what reason do you, the Tathāgata, stop and not speak?
[The answer is: "That which I have accomplished is the foremost Dharma; it is neither second nor third. How much more so for this rare Dharma, which is indeed the ninth.
Regarding the sentient beings of the realms: that which cannot be attained—that which is unattainable—is so because it is profoundly deep and difficult to understand;
this is why I have desisted and not spoken of it. Only I and the Buddhas can exhaustively fathom this;
beyond this, none can know it. 2. The Profound Realm is Inexpressible.

"The true reality of all phenomena (dharmas), namely that all phenomena have such-and-such characteristics... [up to] such-and-such beginning, end, and ultimate equality. This follows from what was stated above.
What is it that the Buddhas alone are able to exhaustively fathom? It is precisely the true reality of all phenomena.
"All phenomena" refers to all mundane and supramundane phenomena, both sentient and insentient; these are the provisional and the phenomenal. The Real...
"Phenomena" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) among all dharmas; it is reality and principle.
The essential point here is to lead people to realize that worldly phenomena are themselves the supramundane Dharma—that they are the provisional and the real, and the principle and the event.

Without destroying worldly appearances, one accomplishes the true mark (*dharmatā*). If one insists on clarifying the principle by departing from events, this is like discarding the waves to seek the water.

It is like water. To depart from the provisional (權) to clarify the real (實) is to forget the form while seeking the reflection. These [approaches] all fail to reach the meaning of the perfect reality (圓實).
Therefore, the single phrase "the true mark of all phenomena" (諸法實相) serves as the foundational basis for opening up the provisional and revealing the real for those of the Two Vehicles.
Tiantai, reading the text according to its underlying meaning, provides three interpretations. First, it says:
"This is the suchness of characteristics; this is the suchness of nature; even this is the suchness of retribution. The second [interpretation] says:

"Such characteristics, such nature," and so forth. The third says: "Characteristics are thus; nature is thus," and so forth. Furthermore, the first, "the suchness of characteristics," is the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The second, "such characteristics," is the meaning of the provisional (*prajñapti*). The third, "characteristics are thus," is the meaning of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).
The three and the one are perfectly interfused; they are neither vertical nor horizontal. One realm contains ten, ten realms contain a hundred, and a hundred realms contain a thousand.
As they unfold and multiply in this manner, they are inexhaustible. Furthermore, the nine realms are provisional while the Buddha-realm is real;
thus, the Buddha-realm perfectly encompasses the nine realms, yet the nine realms do not depart from the Buddha-realm. This alone constitutes the reality of all Buddhas.

This is the meaning of "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*). Zhizhi says: "In principle, one should take the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) of the ten dharma-realms as 'characteristics,' the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the ten realms as 'nature' (*prakṛti*), the inherent presence of the ten realms as 'substance' (*tattva*), the karmic activity of the ten realms as 'power' (*bala*), the functional capacity of the ten realms as 'action' (*kriyā*), the actualization of the ten realms as 'cause' (*hetu*), the supportive factors that trigger the ten realms as 'condition' (*pratyaya*), and the ten realms following their respective karma..."
The discovery of the fruit of the sun: the ten realms of retribution being unfailing is called *vipāka* (recompense). The dense array of phenomena arising from the single mind is called the "root.

The myriad objects, remaining as they are (*tathatā*), ultimately returning to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is called the "branch. From cause to fruit, it is clearly manifest without obscuration;

the three periods of time are equal, and the ten directions are decisively severed—this is called "ultimate consummation" (*niṣṭhā*). With fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), one faces the present directly.

A single illumination: the entirety of the ten realms being empty is called "Thus" (Tathatā). By means of discerning wisdom, proceeding through the differentiated array without obstruction, the ten realms remain undestroyed;
this is called "Is. The complete conventional is the ultimate; this is the non-obstruction of principle. The complete ultimate is the conventional; this is the non-obstruction of phenomena.

The mutual integration of the ultimate and the conventional is the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai*). The simultaneous transcendence of both the ultimate and the conventional is the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shi-shi wu-ai*).
This interpretation is extremely precise and substantial. However, the meaning of the word "equal" (*deng*) remains uncertain; it is not clear what phenomena are being equated.

According to the *Lengqie jing* (Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra), it states: "The Buddhas have four kinds of equality: namely, equality of letters (*akṣara*), equality of speech (*vāk*), equality of dharmas (*dharma*), and equality of bodies (*kāya*). If this is the case...

This means that it is the equality of all Buddhas, not merely the equality of all phenomena. How much more so when this text explicitly states that the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is suchness (*tathatā*).
Since one phenomenon is suchness, all phenomena are suchness; since one phenomenon is real, all phenomena are real.
This is what is meant by True Suchness pervading all places; how could there be a single phenomenon that is not suchness, or a single phenomenon that is not real?
"Ya. As for "equal," it means equal to all dharmas. △ Second, the verse summary, divided into two parts.
First, the verse expressing praise through words, which further divides into two. First, a combined verse for the two Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Hero of the World is immeasurable; among all classes of beings—gods and humans alike—none are able to know the Buddha."
Regarding the term "World Hero" (Shixiong): "World" refers to the three periods of time; by mentioning the three periods, the ten directions are thereby included. "Hero" means heroic and fierce.
This refers to all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and three periods of time, for they all possess the great, majestic, and courageous wisdom of heroism.

Thus, wisdom is subsumed within the syllable *Vīra* (the Hero). It is immeasurable; this corresponds to the preceding verse on profound immeasurability, which refers to the true wisdom (*jñāna*) of all Buddhas.
The following three lines praise the expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) of all Buddhas. "None can know it" means that it is difficult to understand and difficult to enter.
The Buddha’s powers, fearlessnesses, liberations, various samādhis, and all other Buddha-dharmas cannot be measured by anyone.
This verse explains the two types of wisdom of Śākyamuni. The word "Buddha" (佛) in the verse corresponds to the aforementioned "I attained Buddhahood"; this is true wisdom (*jñāna*).
The "powers," "fearlessnesses," and so forth, correspond to his various merits; these are expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). As for "all other dharmas," they are immeasurable and boundless.
This is a phenomenon never before seen. Because the Buddha’s wisdom is profoundly deep, none can fathom it; because the Buddha’s wisdom is boundless, it cannot be measured.
△ Second, the combined explanation and concluding praise.
"From the beginning, following countless Buddhas, I have fully practiced all paths" (up to) "I have already known and seen them all.
The first two lines of this verse praise how the Buddha has personally attended hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and perfected the practice of the Dharma.

The phrase "profound" praises his accomplishment of profound and unprecedented dharmas. The phrases "difficult to see," and so forth, praise the fact that his underlying intent (*abhiprāya*) is difficult to comprehend.
The two lines beginning with "Throughout immeasurable kalpas" eulogize the perfection of knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana-pāramitā*), which are already fully complete.
These clarify the fulfillment of the causes; only when [enlightenment] is attained at the site of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*) is there the fulfillment of the fruit.

"I have known and seen" eulogizes the vastness and profundity of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision. As for the "site of awakening," according to principle, it is the union of suchness-wisdom (*tathatā-jñāna*) with suchness (*tathatā*).

In principle, the wisdom of the principle and the principle itself are non-dual; this is the site of true, quiescent extinction. In terms of phenomena, it is the site beneath the Bodhi tree where the Way was attained.

Having practiced these various paths—the character "yi" (已) signifies that one's merit is perfected and practice is fulfilled—at the moment of sudden awakening to one’s own mind in a single thought, one understands all through understanding one. Therefore, it is said: "I have fully known. △ Second.
The verse concludes with words of praise. It is divided into five parts; the first verse concerns the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*).
Regarding the phrase "such great fruits of retribution, with their various natures and characteristics" (*evaṃrūpaṃ mahāvipākaṃ nānā-dharmatā-lakṣaṇārtha*), Tiantai says:
"This verse refers to the 'Ten Suchnesses' (*daśa-tathatā*); 'great' (*mahā*) means 'wondrous' (*miao*). Because the ten realms (*daśa-dhātu*) are distinct, it is said they are 'various' (*nānā*)."

[The text] enumerates only the beginning and the end; the middle may be understood by implication. This meaning also encompasses the verse on "ultimate" (*niṣṭhā*) and so forth. "Meaning" (*artha*) refers to principle (*yukti*);

it is because this single term "ultimate" contains the principles of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the middle (*madhyama*). △ Second, the verse following up on the realm beyond words.
"I and the Buddhas of the ten directions alone can know this matter.

To summarize the preceding verse, it means that the Buddha has fully accomplished all things. "This matter" refers precisely to the inconceivable Dharma that is difficult to understand and difficult to enter.
△ Third, the subsequent verse concludes the discourse on the ineffable.
This Dharma cannot be demonstrated; its verbal signs are quiescent.
Verses have ceased, and there is no need for further explanation. The true mark is markless; fundamentally it has no location or direction, and therefore it cannot be demonstrated.
The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) transcends speech; it cannot be reached by words. Therefore, it is said that "the characteristics of speech are quiescent.

The preceding lines merely mention this matter, and these lines identify it as the Dharma. Ultimately, this refers to the four characters: "the true mark of all dharmas" (*sarvadharma-bhūtala-kṣaṇa*).
4. Verse on the failure to know the person. This section has eight parts. First: a general exclusion of those who do not understand.
"No other classes of sentient beings are able to understand this" refers to those who have attained the seven stages of expedient means (*upāya*).

That is to say, humans, devas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and those of the Tripitaka, Shared, and Distinct Teachings—these seven types are all brought to this state through the Tathāgata’s expedient means;
this is the general selection. As for the specific selections that follow, they likewise do not go beyond these.
This. △ Second, the specific selection of those capable of entry:
"Excluding those among the assembly of bodhisattvas whose power of faith is firm.
"The bodhisattvas" here should be understood as referring to those within the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao). "Firm power of faith" refers to those from the stage of the Ten Faiths (shixin) onwards.
These are the three types of worthy ones (*śaikṣa*) as well as the bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*). △ Third, distinguishing them from those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*):
"The assembly of disciples of all Buddhas who have made offerings to all Buddhas" (up to) "...is incapable of its power."

This distinguishes [the Bodhisattvas] from those of the Two Vehicles who are unable to understand. *Zhizhi* says: "The Buddhas" refers to the fact that every Buddha has a community of disciples of the Two Vehicles;

this points to those who have attained the four fruits [of the śramaṇa]. Because their two delusions—viewing and thinking (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-heya*)—have been exhausted, they are called "those in their final bodies free from outflows" (*anāsrava-paścima-deha*).
They are said to "abide" because the bonds of the fruit have not yet been severed. "These people" refers to those from the first fruit up to the fourth fruit.

They remain confined in a one-sided emptiness and lack the aspiration for the Great [Vehicle]. Therefore, it is said that they are "unable to bear the power [of this teaching]. △ Fourth, citing Śāriputra alone:
Even if the entire world were filled with those like Śāriputra, and they were to exhaust their thoughts to measure it together, they could not fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.
Previously, the śrāvakas were mentioned in general; here, the members of the assembly are specifically identified. He points directly at them, saying:

"Śāriputra, you are the most eminent among the śrāvakas. Suppose the people filling the entire world were each as wise as Śāriputra, and they exhausted their mental faculties to measure it together—they could never fathom the wondrous wisdom of the Tathāgata. Why is this? [Because...]
The Dharma cannot be understood through deliberation or discrimination. △ Fifth, regarding the assembly of disciples:
even if those filling the ten directions were all like Śāriputra (up to), they likewise would be unable to know it.
This excludes all śrāvakas throughout the ten directions. Zhizhi says: "The previous statement 'even if' was still merely approximate;
this statement 'precisely even if' is a definitive expression. The previous spoke of filling the world; this speaks of filling the ten directions."

To speak more broadly: not only was there one such as Śāriputra, but even disciples such as Maudgalyāyana and Kāśyapa were all fully present; thus, the *śrāvakas* of the ten directions are immeasurable and boundless.
Even if they were to exhaust their mental faculties and collectively attempt to measure it, how could they ever know the Buddha’s wisdom? It is utterly impossible.
[The character] *du* (pronounced *duò*). △ Sixth, the assembly of Pratyekabuddhas.
The Pratyekabuddhas possess sharp wisdom and are free from the pride of being supreme; [from their final body... none are able to know even a small portion [of their realization].
This excludes all *pratyekabuddhas* throughout the ten directions. Zhizhi says: "To discern in a single thought that dependent origination is like an illusion is called 'keen wisdom.
These are those who have realized the untainted state in their final body.

Although the first four fruits [of the *śrāvaka* path] may fill the worlds of the ten directions, their number is still sparse; now, filling them as densely as a bamboo grove, the multitude is vast indeed.

Yet their minds are unified as one. Even with such a multitude of single-mindedness, contemplating the Buddha’s wisdom together for immeasurable kalpas, they still cannot know even a small fraction of it. △ 7. Bodhisattvas Who Have Resolved Their Minds.
"A bodhisattva who has newly resolved to attain awakening (navayānasamprasthita-bodhisattva), though they have made offerings to countless buddhas, is unable to know the wisdom of a buddha.

This passage distinguishes those at the initial stage of the three stages of worthiness (trikalyāṇa) within the Separate Teaching (bhedavyavasthāna). *Zhizhi* states: "Because they enter the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) from the Separate Teaching, they are called 'those who have newly resolved.
Furthermore, the first abode (prathamavihāra) of the Perfect Teaching is also called 'one who has newly resolved. Nevertheless, since they have already drawn near to countless buddhas..."

It is not merely a matter of making offerings; rather, the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) are cultivated together as the cause. Thoroughly comprehending all meanings constitutes wisdom (*prajñā*), which also encompasses merit (*puṇya*).

Thus, the fulfillment of the two benefits—self and others—constitutes the fruit. By means of the wisdom of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), one illuminates both the ultimate and conventional truths;
hence, it is called "thorough comprehension. With a mind that is clear and lucid, one dedicates oneself to benefiting others; hence, one is skilled in preaching the Dharma. This...
The number of such Bodhisattvas does not stop at being merely like a grove of bamboo; if they were as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, or reeds, their number would still be inexhaustible.
Filling the lands of the ten directions, they are all of one mind, and together they attempt to fathom the Buddha’s wisdom with their subtle intelligence (*miào zhì*).
Even after passing through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they cannot know the Buddha’s wisdom. "Subtle intelligence" is precisely the Middle Way.
The wisdom of contemplation is like a reed (pronounced *wei*).

△ As for the non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas—those Bodhisattvas who do not regress are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; even if they were to contemplate and seek with a single mind together, they still could not know it.

This distinguishes between the general and specific types of those who do not regress. In the General Teaching (*pāṭha*), from the third stage, the Stage of the Eight Persons (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*), up to the seventh stage, the Stage of the Accomplished (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*), one abandons the afflictions within the realm; this is called "non-regression in position.

In the Specific Teaching (*viśeṣa-pāṭha*), from the first *vihāra* through the seventh *vihāra*, one also abandons the afflictions within the realm, which is likewise called "non-regression in position. Upon entering the eighth *vihāra* through the tenth *pariṇāmana*, it is called "non-regression in practice. Thus it is said.
Even if Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were to seek with single-minded intent, they would still be unable to know it. Question:
From the preceding layers of analysis, the number of people has increased, the eons have become longer, and wisdom has grown deeper; yet, why is it that one ultimately cannot know it? Answer:
This wisdom does not fall within the scope of the mind of consciousness (*vijñāna-citta*) for measurement. To attempt to fathom the Buddha’s wisdom with the mind of consciousness is like...
One who intends to go to Yue but goes north instead, travels further and further away from his destination.

Not seeing the Way, yet attempting to know it through thought and contemplating it through conceptualization—all this is the livelihood of ghosts; how could it ever culminate in Buddha-wisdom? Question:
Your previous statement that sentient beings and śrāvakas do not know is certainly correct. However, your claim that pratyekabuddhas do not know even a small portion [of it]—

It appears that [the Śrāvakas] possess some degree of knowledge. As for the Bodhisattvas, they have already been able to draw near to countless Buddhas and have mastered the various meanings and intentions [of the teachings].
Since they contemplate with such wondrous wisdom, how could it be that they lack all knowledge?
Moreover, to say that even non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas do not know—what kind of statement is this? Answer: Although Bodhisattvas are said to possess wondrous wisdom, it is simply that...

If [the wisdom] that surpasses the two vehicles were indeed the realized, sublime wisdom of truth, then regarding what the Tathāgata has taught, it would be like Zhongni seeing Wenbo Xuezi—[a state beyond words].
Why then does the Tathāgata further say that "all must together contemplate and seek"? Thus, the two characters "contemplate and seek" (sīqiú) are precisely the grounds for selection.
For those who have newly resolved their intent and do not yet understand, this is provided as an instruction for the future.
Regarding the cases among those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) where it might seem that Ānanda should not have received his prediction:

this refers to the instance in the "Devadatta" chapter where Zhizhi did not believe the dragon girl would attain Buddhahood, and the instance in the "Life Span" chapter where Maitreya did not believe in the assembly of beings who emerged from the earth in later ages. △ Fifth, "Only Buddhas and Buddhas Know," divided into two parts. First:
This reveals the Buddha’s knowledge. Furthermore, he told Śāriputra: "The untainted and inconceivable [wisdom]... (up to) the Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise so. Tiantai says:
"Untainted" refers to both the provisional and the real wisdoms; both are free from leakage and loss. Thus, the provisional and the real—

Non-dual. Each and every one is difficult to fathom and difficult to know; thus it is called "inconceivable. This is the phrase of profound depth, which praises the first rare and difficult-to-understand Dharma.
"I have now fully attained the three phrases" praises the fact that only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively penetrate it.
△ Second, clarifying the Buddha’s manifestation, which has two parts. First, all Buddhas manifesting the reality.
"Śāriputra, you should know that the words of all Buddhas do not differ... (omitted)... they must speak the truth.

This passage explains the meaning of why [the Buddha] speaks of cessation while not speaking of it; it is precisely for the purpose of manifesting the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and exerting every effort to uplift [beings].
Therefore, he repeatedly calls out to Śāriputra and instructs him to "know," desiring to bring about his definitive resolution.
This is firm faith: knowing that one is originally a Buddha. This is what is meant by "shouldering this burden alone.

When it says, "The words of all Buddhas are not different," it means there is no second or third; they are fundamentally non-different. You should give rise to great power of faith in the words of the Buddhas.
To speak no other words is definitive teaching; to possess great power of faith is definitive belief.
Now, the reason I teach you to have faith in all Buddhas is precisely to teach you to have faith in me. Thus, from this point forward, I shall certainly not follow my previous indications;
I will resolutely expound for you the path of the One Vehicle, and you, in turn, must resolutely give rise to definitive faith.
In this regard, one may know that returning [to the source] is appropriate. Thus, the two characters "true reality" (zhēnshí) are precisely that which is quiescent and beyond verbalization.
II. Śākyamuni opens the three vehicles.
He addresses the assembly of śrāvakas and those seeking the vehicle of pratyekabuddhas: "I have caused you to be liberated from the bonds of suffering and to attain nirvāṇa."
These [passages], together with the two subsequent sections, are words intended to preemptively sever provisional doubts. Tiantai says:

"The preceding section spoke of all Buddhas manifesting the reality (the One Vehicle), while this section speaks of Śākyamuni opening up the three [vehicles]. It is not that each possesses only one side;

one must know that the opening of the three necessarily manifests the one, and the manifestation of the one necessarily opens the three. These aspects clarify one another to demonstrate that the Way of every Buddha is identical. Suppose...
There are those who harbor doubts, asking: "Since the Tathāgata possesses the true Dharma, why does he not teach it swiftly, but instead insists on waiting to teach it later?

[The answer is: It is simply because their capacities (*indriya*) are unequal. When sentient beings are tormented by suffering and distress, they urgently desire to leave suffering behind and obtain happiness;
therefore, [the Buddha] tells those seeking the vehicles of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas: "I wish to cause you..."
To say that one is liberated from all bonds of suffering and that there is nirvāṇa is, in reality, not true. Hereafter, you must certainly be taught the True Dharma.
The "bonds of suffering" refers to the three types of suffering and the eight types of suffering within the Truth of Suffering;
because suffering can bind a person, it is called a "bond. "Nirvāṇa" refers here to the nirvāṇa of the three samādhis.

The Buddha, through the power of skillful means, manifests the teachings of the three vehicles to lead sentient beings who are attached in various places and draw them out so that they may attain liberation.
Even if one were to say that all that has been heard during the forty years [of his ministry] constitutes the Dharma of the three vehicles, this is what the Buddhas have taught.
The Dharma of the Three Vehicles likewise exists; thus, the designation of the "Three Vehicles" has been established from antiquity to the present.
How could it be that the Three Vehicles are unreal dharmas? [The opponent] replies: "All of these are merely manifestations shown through my skillful means; how could they be real dharmas?
If that is so, since the Three Vehicles are unreal, it would be appropriate not to proclaim them. Why, then, do every Buddha preach the Three Vehicles?"

It is said: "For the sake of all people, those who hear of existence become attached to existence; those who hear of emptiness become attached to emptiness. This is much like avoiding drowning only to throw oneself into fire.
It is merely by means of these three vehicles that they are led out of their attachments; how could there truly be such [fixed] assertions?
Furthermore, these provisional attachments are precisely the doubts that must arise for followers of the Two Vehicles who are unable to recognize the true mark (dharmatā). Thus it is said.
The Tathāgata has first refuted each point individually so as not to allow any lingering doubt; thus, one may aspire to reach the Mahāyāna.
The brief exposition on the revelation is hereby concluded. △ Second, the raising of doubts and the request for further instruction, divided into two parts.
First, the narration of the doubt. This further has two parts. First, the narration by the sūtra compiler:
"At that time, among the great assembly... [up to] Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the other twelve hundred people."
This compiler of the sutra records the various doubts [of the assembly]. There are some śrāvakas who speak in terms of the cause, referring to arhats whose outflows are exhausted;

and there are those who speak in terms of the fruit. Among the twelve hundred followers, Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya alone is singled out because he was the first among those of the Hīnayāna to be called "one who has attained understanding.
Since previously it was stated that there were both those with understanding and those who had entered [the path], the Buddha now generally excludes [those who] do not know.
How could they not harbor attachments and give rise to doubts? Therefore, [the Buddha] first mentions them;
this includes those who have resolved to become śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.

These are all those who are in the stages of training (*śaikṣa*) and beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); therefore, it is called "arousing the mind. However, in the section discussing doubts, only one class of practitioners—the followers of the two vehicles—is mentioned.
This is because the intent of this sutra is fundamentally to extol the wondrous wisdom for their sake, thereby stimulating their aspiration toward the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).
Consequently, because the two vehicles cling tenaciously and harbor deep doubts, they are singled out for mention. As previously analyzed in the section on preliminary investigation:

It is said that even the non-retrogressive bodhisattvas do not know this. Although it is not explicitly stated here, when we reach the section on the expression of doubts later on, it will be evident that there were eighty thousand great numbers of bodhisattvas who sought Buddhahood. Part Two: The Assembly’s Reflections.
This is divided into two sections: First, doubting the Buddha; Second, doubting the two types of wisdom.
Each formed this thought: "Now, that which the World-Honored One has attained (up to) is beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Since the World-Honored One emerged from samādhi, he has expended such great mental effort only for his disciples of the two vehicles to form such thoughts and give rise to such doubts;
thus we know that hereafter there is much more to be expected. Each formed [this thought].
As for "recollection": having heard the Buddha most earnestly extol the wisdom of the Buddha, the śrāvakas—whether teachers or disciples—could not fail to reflect:

"What kind of causal conditions are these, that the World-Honored One so fervently and diligently extols and praises, saying that the Dharma attained by the Buddha is thus profound and thus difficult [to realize]?"
"Is it understood? This refers to the doubt regarding ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*), which possesses verbal expression yet its underlying intent is difficult to comprehend.
This refers to the doubt regarding expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). Within these, whether expedient or ultimate, all are said to be beyond what we can know.
If we truly did not know them, we should not have previously been granted the attainment of *nirvāṇa*. If we do truly know them, for what reason does he further say "one"?
"This is something that no śrāvaka can know. How could it be that the Buddha possesses some other dharma-gate that we do not know or have not realized?
This is doubting the Buddha's wisdom. △ Second, doubting what one has attained oneself.
The Buddha spoke of the meaning of the single liberation (ekāyano mārgaḥ), yet now we do not know where this meaning leads.
This is a doubt regarding what one has realized oneself; it is a failure resulting from [mis]apprehension. The "single liberation" is precisely the liberation spoken of forty years ago;
it was an *neyārtha* (provisional) teaching. To claim that one has attained this dharma now is likewise *neyārtha*.
This is the Dharma of meaning. Those who realize *nirvāṇa* have merely halted at the conjured city; it is a place of temporary rest, not the ultimate treasure-place.
Yet they harbor doubts, thinking: "If what I have attained is not the truth, then I have already realized the meaning of liberation and reached *nirvāṇa*.
If this were indeed the truth, why would it be said that all classes of *śrāvakas* [have not yet attained it]?"
There is no one capable of fathoming the Buddha. Thus, as he circled about reflecting within himself, he did not know where this meaning would lead.

This "meaning" (yi) is precisely the meaning extolled by the Buddha; "tending toward" (qu) means "returning to. II. The Formal Request. Divided into three parts. A. The Initial Request. Further divided into two. 1.
The Appropriate Audience Presents the Request. Further divided into two. 1. The Prose Exposition. Further divided into two. 1. Stating the Doubts.
At that time, Śāriputra knew that the fourfold assembly harbored doubts regarding this most profound, subtle, and wondrous Dharma so difficult to understand.
He perceived that the members of the assembly were thinking within their minds but did not dare express it in words because their wisdom fell short of the response provided by the Great Man.
Since Śāriputra’s wisdom surpassed that of his peers, he had already grasped the thoughts of the assembly; thus, he was able to voice what was in the minds of others.
This is doubt. Below this, there are three requests, yet the Tathāgata only twice stops him; together with the previous instance, there are three instances of stopping.

This is because the Buddha observed that among the various capacities of the assembly, there were those who would gain benefit through three cycles of teaching; he stopped at different points because of these differing circumstances.
As for Śāriputra’s doubt regarding the causes and conditions, the Tathāgata’s answer treats them as a single matter. Thus it is said:
One must speak of the truth. The foremost skillful means of all Buddhas consists in [addressing] doubts regarding provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), the profound [Dharma], and so forth;

that is to say, one addresses doubts regarding ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*). Now, Śāriputra’s doubt was resolved immediately after the teaching on the Dharma, and he received his prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).

When each of the others, such as Ājñātakauṇḍinya, had their respective doubts, they each received their predictions during the teaching by way of parables. As for those who have newly resolved their minds [to seek awakening], their doubts...
After the cycle of causes and conditions was complete, each received a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). This is what is meant by "neither doubting nor awakening":
because their doubts were of varying degrees of depth, they obtained different predictions regarding the duration until their liberation. △ Second, the formal request.
Since I first followed the Buddha, I have never [heard] such a profound, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma.
For many decades since I began following the Buddha, I have never heard of such an exalted expression of the Buddha’s wisdom.
Just as I was about to proclaim it, he stopped and did not speak; this is precisely why a multitude of doubts arise in competition. How much more so, then, [in the present case]?
Those present in this assembly—who among them does not harbor doubts in their hearts? For this reason, I venture to request that the Tathāgata expound upon this matter:
what are the ultimate causes and conditions for such praise? What dharma is so profound, so difficult to understand, and so difficult to enter?
II. Verses in Praise (divided into four parts). A. Verses on the Doubts Concerning the Two Wisdoms of Expedient Means and Reality.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

This verse expresses doubt regarding the Buddha’s true wisdom. As for "Wisdom-Sun," the sun is able to dispel darkness; all worldly beings rely upon it for their daily activities.
As for the power of the sun’s radiance, so too does the Buddha transform sentient beings through wisdom.
Among the activities of living beings throughout the nine realms, there is none that does not rely upon the illumination of the Buddha’s wisdom; therefore, he is called the Great Holy Honored One.
Regarding the phrase "after a long time he spoke," it means that he endured and refrained from speaking for several decades, and only now has he finally spoken.
He himself declares that he has attained such powers, fearlessnesses, and samādhis (up to) those which all Buddhas have attained.

This verse clarifies that his provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) is unfathomable and cannot be questioned. Each of the powers, fearlessnesses, and so forth, can be understood by referring to their respective prose explanations.
The "site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*) is the locus of true, quiescent cessation; it is also the place beneath the Bodhi tree. That is to say:
Regarding the Dharma attained by the World-Honored One at the site of enlightenment—that which is most profound and called unsurpassed—who could possibly question it?
As the Buddha said, even if all the people filling the world were like me, Śāriputra, they still could not fathom it;
how then could I alone fathom it? Among those such as myself within the ranks of the śrāvakas, [who would dare to inquire]?"
Furthermore, how could there even be anyone capable of posing a question? Because there was no one to ask, the Buddha emerged from samādhi and had to speak on his own.
That which he spoke of consists entirely of realms difficult for us to enter—what is known as that which only a Buddha and a Buddha can know.
△ Second: The doubts of the followers of the Three Vehicles and the Fourfold Assembly.
"May the Buddha explain for us those who are free from outflows—namely, the various Arhats—and those who seek nirvana.
Those "free from outflows" are persons who have already realized the three samādhis; those "seeking nirvana" are those who have not yet realized them.
Those who have already attained realization and those who have not both fall into the net of doubt, because they do not comprehend the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, among those seeking the state of a *pratyekabuddha*—namely, certain members of the community of *bhikṣus* and *bhikṣuṇīs*, as well as the eight classes of gods and humans—they likewise look upon one another with hesitation.
This is because they have heard what they had never heard before; thus, their doubt regarding the non-duality [of the teachings] persists. They remain in a state of indecision.
This means they could not resolve their doubts. [The text] says: "All have fallen into the net of doubt"; "They gaze at one another in hesitation";

"For what reason do you speak thus?"; "What is the nature of this matter? From these words, one can grasp the essence of their earnest desire for clarification and the sincerity of their longing for an explanation. △ Third, the individual presentation of Śāriputra’s doubt.
"Among all the disciples, the Buddha has declared me to be the foremost"—this was Śāriputra’s own statement.
He said that during his ordinary days, the World-Honored One had praised him as the first among the śrāvakas;
yet now, hearing of the wisdom of the Buddhas extolled by the Tathāgata, he remains utterly bewildered and does not understand it. How can this be considered wisdom?
I simply do not know whether that which you have praised is the wondrous Dharma of ultimate emptiness within the fruit of the Tathāgata, or the wondrous path practiced within the cause.

Next, I request the Buddha to provide clarification. Although I possess but a slight measure of wisdom, it is entirely due to the power of the Tathāgata’s grace in preaching the Dharma; thus, I am one born from the mouth of the Buddha.
"You have become my son. Now, with palms joined, wait for the Buddha to speak according to the time and according to the capacity, as it truly is.
This is appropriate. Observing the moment Śāriputra joined his palms and waited in expectation, one can say that he has fully pressed himself into [the Dharma];
it will not be long before he enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. △ Fourth, a general clarification of the doubts of the assembly.
"The various devas, nāgas, spirits, and others, their number like the sands of the Ganges" (up to) "desiring to hear the complete path.

This generally clarifies the assembly; since it already encompasses the devas and others from this world and other directions, numbering like the sands of the Ganges, one knows they do not belong to the original assembly.
As for the bodhisattvas, they were not previously mentioned in the section on the formal request; the text is abbreviated.
Therefore, it is said that there are eighty thousand [teachings], all for the sake of those seeking the fruit of Buddhahood; this further reveals that they belong to the profound stages.
That the Wheel-Turning King speaks using the languages of ten billion nations is due to the resonance of the Buddha’s perfect voice and his reception of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
Having come to this Dharma assembly, they now all join their palms in the utmost reverence, wishing to hear the Tathāgata fully elucidate the inconceivable Way.
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s refusal to answer.
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra (up to): "The devas and humans will all be struck with alarm and doubt.
That the Tathāgata remains here and does not speak is because the Dharma is difficult to conceive; were he to speak of it, they would fear being alarmed."

"At that time, they were permitted [to listen]. This is why I spoke with such gravity and did not explain [it further]. Question: "In the section enumerating the assembly, you mention only those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Why is it that those currently residing with the Buddha are referred to exclusively as 'devas and humans who are struck with wonder and doubt'? Answer: "If we discuss the *śrāvakas*..."

In the preceding section on cessation, having already given rise to doubt, he requested instruction with a resolute intent to hear it—namely, "With palms joined, gazing up in reverence, he awaited [the teaching].
How could he now again be startled by doubt and unwilling to hear? This second cessation is intended to inspire faith in those who have not yet believed.
△ Second, the request for instruction, which has two parts: first, the formal request presented by the disciple.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying: “...upon hearing what the Buddha has spoken, they will be able to revere and believe it.
This refers to Śāriputra acting as the requester on behalf of humans and devas.

His two-fold exclamation, “I only pray that you will speak,” expresses his earnest desire to hear the wondrous Dharma and his absolute lack of doubt. However, although the assembly at this gathering is immeasurable, it is not—
All these various [beings] have deeply planted the roots of goodness; those whose faculties are sharp and wisdom profound will certainly be able to believe with reverence.
I only wish that you would speak of it. Yet, how could the Tathāgata not know that the assembly possesses sharp faculties and profound wisdom?
Why must he wait for Śāriputra’s request before speaking? It is not so. That the Tathāgata does not speak is precisely what most clearly manifests the wondrousness [of the teaching].
The Dharma is difficult to proclaim. Śāriputra’s request was intended to inspire the assembly’s desire to hear it.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
O Dharma King, Unsurpassed Honored One, please speak; do not hesitate, for among this immeasurable assembly there are those capable of respectful faith.
"King" carries the sense of sovereignty; the Tathāgata has attained mastery over the Dharma, and is thus called the Dharma King.

The Buddha abides above all who have attained equal enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), with none surpassing him; hence he is called the Unsurpassed Honored One. The following three lines constitute a most earnest entreaty.
...these words. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s cessation of speaking:
The Buddha again stopped Śāriputra (up to) the bhikṣus of overweening pride who were about to fall into a great pit.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Cease, cease! There is no need to speak; my Dharma is subtle and inconceivable. Those with overweening pride will surely not respect or believe it upon hearing it."
Now, within this third cessation, he further identifies those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*); thus, it may be said that his intention is fully exhausted with nothing remaining.
He says: "If I were to preach this sublime Dharma, there would be a class of people with overweening pride who, lacking faith, would give rise to slander."
Because of this slander of the Mahāyāna, one will inevitably fall into suffering; therefore, it is better not to speak of it at all.
If those who truly possess overweening pride hear such words, they should naturally change their disposition and alter their tone. There are seven kinds of pride.

To rely on oneself and oppress others is called *asmimāna* (self-conceit). To be arrogant toward those of equal virtue is called *māna* (conceit). To contend for superiority over equals is called *adhimāna* (excessive conceit).
To contend for superiority over those who are superior is called *mānātimāna* (conceit beyond conceit). To claim attainment of what has not been attained is called *abhimāna* (overweening conceit).

To settle for being superior to those who are inferior is called *ūnamāna* (inferiority conceit). To fail to pay homage to the Triple Gem is called *mithyāmāna* (false conceit). However, the World-Honored One ceased [the teaching]...
Furthermore, his repeated refusal to preach was not out of stinginess with words. It was because the wondrous Dharma is difficult to express;

it is neither existence nor emptiness, transcending names and forms. It is to abide within all forms while remaining detached from them, even reaching the point where both "abiding" and "detachment" are negated.
Fearing that śrāvakas who cling to appearances would fail to develop faith upon hearing it, he therefore refused to speak up to three times. △ Third, the repeated request.
This section is divided into two parts. First, the request made by the recipient of the teaching:
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying... [up to] "...for a long night, they shall be at peace and greatly benefited."
When the Buddha had thus again paused, the one who was ready for the teaching (Śāriputra) addressed him once more. This may be called drawing upon [the Buddha’s power] with success;
the Great Dharma can now be imparted. Because Śāriputra had been firmly stopped by the Buddha and remained silent, he therefore requested again, saying: "In this assembly today..."
There are hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, and millions of others like me, all of whom have long been transformed by the Buddha’s teachings;
they will surely be able to respect and believe [in them]. "Peaceful stability" is spoken in contrast to "fear"; it signifies the true state of the one reality throughout the long night.
This means that all are able to abide securely in the ground where the ultimate and conventional truths are non-dual; therefore, it is said that "there is much benefit.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The Unsurpassed Honored One among Two-legged Beings vowed to teach the foremost Dharma (up to the point where) they gave rise to great joy.
Those who, according to their capacity, declared themselves to be the eldest sons did so because the wisdom of skillful means arises from fundamental wisdom;

thus, there is the sense of being "sons. Because they heard the Buddha’s words regarding the attainment of this foremost, rare, and difficult-to-understand Dharma, they necessarily requested that he preach it.
This is the foremost dharma. By observing that the Buddha had already taught [this] in two phrases, the distant cause of the Prince Mahābhijñājñāna is revealed.
How could it be intended that Śāriputra was meant to be a literal śrāvaka? Throughout this interval, his requests were diligent and earnest;
they were nothing other than a desire to clarify this difficult-to-understand dharma. Therefore, at the conclusion of his request, he said: "I shall give birth to the Great..."

They were filled with joy. After the Tathāgata granted his permission for them to speak, until the conclusion of this chapter, it is said that they were once again free from all doubts and their hearts gave rise to great joy.

Thus we know that the intention of both teacher and disciple was nothing other than to ensure that all people would surely reach the fulfillment of the benefits of the Dharma and attain great joy before finally coming to rest. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s Permission.
[The Buddha] said:
"At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra: 'Since you have already made your earnest request three times, how could I not speak?

Because of the former circumstances of the occasion's readiness for firm entreaty, as well as the sincere seeking of the assembled multitude, it is known that the faculty of faith has already been planted; there is no further [need for hesitation].'"

Doubt and uncertainty. Faith is established as the true cause for attaining the fruit of Buddhahood; because one who is free from doubt can receive inconceivable instruction, he spoke these words to grant permission for the teaching.
The brief exposition on "opening the three to reveal the one" is complete. II. The extensive exposition on "opening the three to reveal the one.

As for what is meant by "extensive," it refers to the expansion of the aforementioned brief terminology. Throughout seven fascicles and a half of the sutra, all passages open the three and reveal the one.

First. Furthermore, it is divided into three sections. The first is the comprehensive exposition for those of superior faculties, which is divided into five parts. The first is the Tathāgata’s formal discourse, which is divided into two parts.
The first is the prose section, which is divided into three parts. The first is the admonition to listen and the selection of the audience.
