"Listen attentively now and reflect upon it well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Since the Tathāgata has already granted permission to speak, he further exhorts the listener to listen carefully, for this is not an ordinary discourse on the Dharma of today.
By saying "listen attentively" and "reflect well," he intends for the listener to attain immediate realization. Thus, he analyzes and explains.
These four characters constitute the great thesis regarding the provisional and the real, the original and the trace of this sutra.

Had the Tathāgata merely entered into meditative concentration and emitted light, there would have been no means for this wondrous Dharma to be revealed; had he emerged from concentration only to praise its virtues and then ceased speaking, [the truth would likewise remain hidden].
How could this wondrous Dharma otherwise be made known to the multitude? Fortunately, because those present have earnestly requested it, we have reached this point and are permitted to analyze it.
Thus, the gate that was difficult to enter shall now be entered; since its exposition has been granted, the Dharma that was difficult to understand will surely be understood.
As for "analysis," it means to distinguish the causes of the provisional traces.
"Opening and revealing" (*kaishō*) means to explain. "Explaining" (*kaishaku*) means to resolve the conditions of its fundamental reality; this is precisely "entering through awakening" (*wonyū*).

Thus, it is clear that the categories of provisional and real, origin and trace, opening and revealing, and awakening and entering are all subsumed within the four characters: "discernment" (*funbetsu*) and "explanation" (*kaishaku*).
This is evident.
When these words were spoken, there were bhikṣus in the assembly (up to the point where they) rose from their seats, prostrated to the Buddha, and withdrew.
Even before the Tathāgata had opened his mouth, five thousand people who were sitting there withdrew.
This clearly demonstrates that their arrogance was rooted in deeply grave offenses. For this reason, the Tathāgata did not speak [of it] four times over.
The assembly heard this. As for those who assist the Tathāgata in appearing in the world to benefit sentient beings, there is yet another explanation to be given.

According to the manifest traces, there were in fact a class of people within the assembly who harbored overweening pride; they took no pleasure in the Mahāyāna and were deeply attached to the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle.
Therefore, these five thousand members of the assembly were now temporarily made to withdraw from their seats, so that the Tathāgata might censure the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle.
Although their offenses are profound and their defilements heavy, those who praise those who embrace the path of reality will surely be able to advance toward the Buddha-vehicle.
If this causes those śrāvakas of actual practice to feel resentment toward the Mahāyāna, the benefit to others remains no small matter. This is the fundamental thesis of the treatise.

These were all of the lineage that possesses the True Eye of the Crown (uṣṇīṣa-cakṣus). Upon seeing the Tathāgata merely grant permission for a detailed explanation, they immediately brushed their sleeves and departed.
Their intention was to make those śrāvakas of fixed nature within the assembly realize that there is a wondrous truth beyond the upward path that is not transmitted;
how could it be something to be found at the corners of people's mouths, like leftover snot? This is what is meant by "As soon as the blue falcon sees [the prey]..."
To capture [him] alive—how can this be compared to the lack of spiritual intelligence in a hunting dog that merely guards a withered post?
Otherwise, even though the Great Dharma had not yet been proclaimed and the imperial decree had not yet been issued, these fellows already made such calculations of gain and loss.
One must know that what those who assist in the transformation of beings ought to do does not stop at this alone. The Buddha said: "To manifest..."
The multitude possesses the three poisons and manifests the signs of false views; my disciples act thus as skillful means to deliver sentient beings.
The four characters "prostrating before the Buddha and then withdrawing" (禮佛而退) are seen to be of great significance. What is called "prostrating before the Buddha" has its source;
"withdrawing from one's seat" has its destination. This is by no means comparable to those who have lost their way in youth and do not know where to return.
Why is this so? Because these types of people have deeply rooted and heavy [afflictions] (extending up to) such faults; for this reason, they do not abide [in the truth]. Tiantai says:
"The five turbidities are thick and chaotic, which is called 'heavy sin. To cling to the small while obscuring the great is called 'deep ignorance.
To claim one has attained the three fruits when one has not, or to claim one has realized the four fruits when one has not, is called 'arrogance' (*adhimāna*). Those who possess such faults..."
This refers to the three faults of obstruction, attachment, and pride; because of these, one does not abide [in the Way]. [△@△] There shall be a separate discussion on this point:
in a lion’s den, there are originally no other beasts; how could there still be those who lack practice hidden within the assembly on Vulture Peak?
Even if there were such persons who had already undergone forty years of refinement, they certainly would not be as extreme as this. Based on...
In Śāriputra’s request, he mentions those whom the Buddha has already taught and transformed throughout successive lifetimes.

If [the assembly] were to withdraw from their seats due to lack of faith, then Śāriputra would not have fully recognized people; or perhaps it was said out of concern for those who had only temporarily arrived at this assembly.
It may well be so. Even those who arrive for a brief moment must have been moved by the Tathāgata’s perfect voice and must possess profound roots of goodness.
Should there truly be those with overweening pride who withdraw from their seats and depart, the Dharma would not be complete;
how then could it be called "wondrous"? Furthermore, how could it be said to function in severing doubt and engendering faith? One must know that this is a self-admonition regarding listening.
The section beginning with "Selecting the Capable" (*jian ji*) is a narrative by the compiler of the sutra. It describes how, at that time, there were those who withdrew from their seats;
seeing them withdraw as soon as they heard [the teaching], the text therefore reproaches them for the depth of their transgressions and so forth.

However, observing the subsequent passage, it merely states, "Their withdrawal is also excellent," and does not severely censure them. This is sufficient to recognize that this serves as the introductory context for the primary assembly.
Furthermore, as the Tathāgata stated in the third *śamatha* [section]: "Those who are conceited will certainly not show respect or faith upon hearing this.
How is it that he experienced such a response? Let those with the eye of wisdom examine this clearly.
The World-Honored One remained silent and did not stop him. Tiantai says:
"Above, he heard a brief exposition on 'opening the three to reveal the one. Because the words were brief, the meaning was obscure; thus, he had not yet given rise to slander.

This was sufficient to serve as the causal condition for the 'tying of the jewel' (the parable of the lost pearl), and his departure would have been beneficial. Had he heard the extensive exposition on 'opening the three to reveal the one,' he would certainly have been at odds [with the teaching]."
If one gives rise to slander out of emotion, there will surely be harm. For this reason, [the Tathāgata] does not intervene.

Furthermore, one must understand that even where the Tathāgata remains silent and does not intervene, it is still conceivable; this sufficiently demonstrates that he is the father and they are his children.
As the saying goes: "The embroidered mandarin ducks are for you to behold; I do not hand over the golden needle to others."
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra: "In this assembly of mine now, there are no longer any branches or leaves; it consists purely of those who are real. Tiantai says:
"Branches and leaves are mere trifles, unfit for use as vessels. Those who cling to the provisional [teachings] are not vessels for the Great [Vehicle].
Now, 'having no branches or leaves' means they have already become complete timber, capable of serving as vessels for the Mahāyāna Dharma. (△@△) This is based on the context.
In principle, apart from the root, how could there be anything else called branches and leaves? Thus, the branches and leaves clarify what is delusory, while the root is precisely the Real.
If delusion persists and mingles with wisdom, the Dharma will not be sublime.

Now, to say that there are no branches and leaves but only the true reality—this can be called taking the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as the essence. Based on this, one may [eliminate] the five thousand [words].

The term "person" (*pudgala*) signifies the complete exhaustion of the five consciousnesses. That is to say: the eye does not see forms; the ear does not hear sounds; the nose does not perceive odors;
the tongue does not discern tastes; and the body does not experience tangibles. These are the exhaustion of the branches and leaves. There remains only the single intention directed forward.
This serves as the fundamental basis; it is purely the meaning of ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*). To speak in this manner ensures that one does not fall into partiality or deficiency.
Śāriputra, such persons of overweening pride—[listen attentively] until [the end], for I shall now explain it to you.

Tiantai said: "One should know that those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) are not entirely devoid of the Dharma; it is simply that, from their own shallow stage, they consider themselves superior and thus become arrogant toward others.
As for those who regard falling back as excellent, this is because they obscure themselves with the small while simultaneously obstructing the great in others."

Now that you have withdrawn, you are free from the fault of slandering the Dharma, nor do you incur the transgression of obstructing others; therefore, it is said, "Excellent. [△@△] "Excellent" means beautiful.

The Tathāgata praises the fact that its branches and leaves have fallen away entirely, leaving only the single reality. This is what is meant by the exhaustion of the false and the preservation of the true;
thus, there will be no difficulty in bestowing the Great Dharma. Therefore, the instruction below says: "Listen well now, as the Teacher..."
The milk of a child can only be contained in a lapis lazuli vessel. △ Second, receiving the command with sincere attention:
Śāriputra said, "So be it, World-Honored One; I wish most earnestly to hear it."
Tiantai says: "Weiyran" (唯然) refers to the urgency of responding to a call; it is an immediate assent.
The sound of "wei" (唯) is swift and plain, while the word "nuo" (諾) is slow and refined. "Yuànlè" (願樂) expresses an intention of pure sincerity and utmost reverence.
It is as if to say: "How could anyone not wish to hear [this], given our extreme earnestness? Part Three: The Actual Bestowal and Revelation, divided into two sections.
First, the extensive exposition of the provisional and the real of all Buddhas. This section has two parts. First, a general clarification concerning all Buddhas, which is divided into four sections.
The first is the praise of the rarity of the Dharma: The Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "Such a wondrous Dharma... (omitted)... is like the udumbara flower, appearing but once in an age."
This section constitutes a major case for the entire sutra. It is precisely intended for those who are ready to receive the teaching (*āśraya-yogya*).

It provides a detailed explanation of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, which cannot be known by any *śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*, but can only be fully exhausted by a Buddha and a Buddha alone.
The "Knowledge of the Sound" (*Yinzhi*) states: "The two characters 'thus' (*evam*) refer to what was previously called the 'suchness-mark' (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena."
The ten "thusnesses" (tathatā). The two characters "wondrous Dharma" (myōhō) refer to the various dharmas previously mentioned as nature, characteristics, root, and branch.
While the previous section spoke of "all dharmas," this section speaks of the "wondrous Dharma. This is because, previously, the assembly had not yet resolved their minds toward the Great Vehicle;

thus, the three vehicles could not be conflated with the One Vehicle, nature and characteristics were not yet harmonized, and the root and the branches were not yet unified, such that ultimate perfection could not be achieved.
Because they share a single characteristic and a single essence, they are called "all dharmas"; this is because the characteristics of dharmas have not yet been forgotten.

For this reason, those of the Two Vehicles do not receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood. Now that you have requested a revelation according to reality, and the Tathāgata has further granted permission to analyze and explain it, all dharmas—whether regarding nature or characteristics, the fundamental or the derivative—will ultimately converge in the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This being so...

All distinctions—whether defiled or pure, pertaining to the three vehicles or the two vehicles—are fused into a single dharma. It encompasses immeasurable meanings while constituting a single meaning;

therefore, it is called the "Wondrous Dharma" (Saddharma). As for those of the two vehicles, they only now begin to have their portion of receiving a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), as well as their share in the adornment of the kalpa and the land.
Thus, when the Tathāgata arrives at this point, he specifically identifies the preceding text, saying: "Such is the Wondrous Dharma."

Regarding the phrase "only then did he speak it," the word "time" (時) is the most important. If the time has not yet arrived, even if the Great Sage were to stand before us, there would be nothing he could do about it.
Why? Because for forty years, although he harbored such a wondrous Dharma within him, he had no opening through which to speak it.
Once the time arrived, however, the hundred plants burst forth with fragrance, each sprouting its own buds. Thus, after Śāriputra made his three requests, [the Buddha finally spoke].

This opens the fragrance of a hundred generations beyond the kalpa. Therefore, all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time who wish to fulfill their original aspiration must wait for the proper time so that the assembled multitude may hear such a proclamation;
this is truly a rare encounter in a thousand lifetimes, just like the appearance of the udumbara flower, which cannot be forced by human effort, yet now we are about to joyfully encounter it.
That you have suddenly been able to meet him is truly a rare and auspicious encounter; it should not be regarded as an ordinary matter.
The *udumbara* is the great, auspicious, precious blue lotus. When this flower appears, a Cakravartin King will certainly manifest in the world.
The land is naturally majestic and beautiful, and the lifespan of its inhabitants all increases to eighty-four thousand years.
Thus, rare and wondrous jewels of the mundane world are borrowed as metaphors for the rare and wondrous Dharma that transcends the world.
△ Second, the teaching is without falsehood.
Śāriputra, you all should believe what the Buddha has spoken; his words are not false. The time for the aforementioned teaching has now arrived;
these words are without falsehood. Although various paths are taught, their reality is but the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
The instruction is intended solely to ensure that believers have no other [goal] than this: it is nothing but the single Great Matter of the causal conditions.
△ Third, the opening of the gate of skillful means (*upāya-mukha*).
Śāriputra, the Buddhas preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate [up to] expounding all dharmas through parables and verbal expressions.

This correctly explains the preceding gate of wisdom (*prajñā-mukha*) as being difficult to understand and difficult to enter. "According to what is appropriate" means that the Buddhas open the gate of skillful means.
This is an expedient gateway; it is the provisional teaching according to the faculties, faith, and inclinations of sentient beings.
For what reason is the intent of these skillful, provisional explanations likewise difficult to understand and difficult to enter?
It is said that although the Buddhas employ various causes, analogies, and verbal expressions, in reality, they are all but a single Dharma. All the dharmas they expound are the One Vehicle.
It is not that, apart from this, another One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is separately expounded; this is why it is difficult to understand and enter.
△ Fourth, showing the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa), divided into five parts. First, indicating the excellence of the person and the dharma.
This Dharma cannot be understood through conceptualization or discrimination; only the Buddhas can know it.
This explains that the aforementioned wisdom is profoundly deep. "This Dharma" refers to the various dharmas explained above, which are the wondrous Dharma of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding "conceptualization" and so forth: the six consciousnesses inherently possess the function of discrimination, as does the seventh consciousness.
They cling to a self that possesses the capacity for deliberation, thinking: "Though I employ various skillful means, what is expounded is but a single Dharma.

This Dharma can certainly not be understood through deliberation or discrimination; therefore, you followers of the Two Vehicles, though you constantly employ thought and reflection, are unable to reach its ultimate depth.
Yet this is precisely the Dharma that is both provisional and real, which belongs only to the Buddhas.
Only then can one truly know it. △ Second, the discussion of the original intent for appearing in the world.
Why is this so? It is because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition.
This further follows from what was stated above: since the Dharma is so exceptionally sublime that only a Buddha can know it, no other person is capable of knowing it.
Therefore, this is discussed once more: the Buddhas take this Dharma of non-duality between the provisional and the real as their foundation;
because people are unable to know it, they appear in the world to point it out for them. Thus it is said that the Buddhas act solely for the sake of this one great matter.
It transcends the world. It unifies the wills of all phenomena into one; it exhausts the capacities of both the holy and the ordinary to become great.

The functioning of subject and object is called "phenomenon" (*shì*); the possession of the nature of both origin and manifestation is the "cause" (*yīn*); the fulfillment of virtue for oneself and others is the "condition" (*yuán*).
The Tathāgata’s original purpose was to cause people to manifest and realize the profoundly deep wisdom that each inherently possesses;

therefore, it is called the "one great causal condition" (*ekamahākaruṇā-hetu-pratyaya*). Furthermore, it is said that there is only this matter and no other. △ Third, the inquiry into the causes and conditions for appearing in the world.
Śāriputra, what is meant by [the Buddhas appearing in the world] for the sake of one great cause and condition?

The preceding section clarified that all Buddhas appear in the world based upon this; this question asks for what reason and by what cause and condition the Buddhas appear in the world based upon this.
Therefore, it is said below: "It is fundamentally because they wish to open up and reveal this Dharma to sentient beings, so that each and every person may attain awakening."
Entering this Dharma, one thus transcends the world. △ Fourth, the correct analysis of the four gates has four parts.
First, clarifying the oneness of principle, which further has two parts. First, the direct explanation.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world because they desire to lead sentient beings (up to) into the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

These Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—encompassing all Buddhas of the lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time—appear in the world by means of this Great Matter.
They are the ones who can open, can demonstrate, can awaken, and can cause others to enter; they are the presiding masters of the single principle.

"Desire" (*yu*) means "to seek. "To cause" (*ling*) means "to command. "Sentient beings" (*zhòngshēng*) collectively encompasses all sentient entities within the nine realms. "To open" (*kāi*) means to dispel their ignorance and confinement.

The two characters "knowledge and vision" (*zhījiàn*) comprehensively subsume the six sense faculties. By adding the single character "Buddha" (*fó*), one refers to the wondrous Dharma inherently possessed by sentient beings;
this is precisely the *Tathāgatagarbha-kāya-samādhi*. Therefore, it is called "the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."

This pertains to the knowledge and vision within the causal stage. Furthermore, by adding the process of purification, it sufficiently demonstrates that the essence while in delusion is not necessarily pure unless it undergoes development.

Nevertheless, the primary purpose for all Tathāgatas appearing in the world is to cause the sentient beings of the nine realms to each develop their own inherently existing Buddha-knowledge and vision, thereby [purifying] their six sense faculties.

Both attain purity. Thus, once this is opened, one will forever be free from the delusions of the six sense objects and will no longer be confined by the attachments and doubts of those who cling to expedient means.
"To show" means to clearly announce something to the sentient beings of the nine realms;
thus, these three characters—Buddha’s knowledge and vision—are that which all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have realized and attained. They belong to...

Regarding "the knowledge and vision on the level of fruition": although sentient beings inherently possess the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and do not need to rely on cultivation, how can they realize it?
Therefore, the Buddhas first demonstrate what they have themselves realized, emerging from meditative absorption to proclaim their virtues.

Thus, the emission of light and the manifestation of auspicious signs mentioned previously were all demonstrations of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; as for "opening and showing," this pertains to the teaching, which is that which is opened by the Buddha.
"Revealing and pointing out" means to manifest and indicate. "Awakening" means to suddenly become alert and aware.

Following the Tathāgata’s revelation and indication of the wondrous, luminous true nature inherent within the six sense faculties, when one reaches the point where effort is exhausted and power is spent, there comes a moment of sudden clarity—as if waking from a dream—whereby one finally awakens to the Buddha-knowledge and vision of one's own nature. "Entering" means to personally...
This is "Approaching" (*ābhimukha*). Furthermore, it is said that "knowing the path of vision" (*darśanamārga*) refers to the place reached;
after the Buddha has revealed it, one initiates the practice and reaches the ground of ultimate realization through cultivation. Therefore, it is called "knowing the path of vision.

This entry into awakening belongs to the capacity of the practitioner (*yogin*), while [the first and third] belong to the inherent nature (*dharmatā*), and [the second and fourth] belong to that accomplished through cultivation. [The text] previously questioned why the Buddhas...
This appears for the purpose of revealing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; it is for the purpose of causing sentient beings to awaken to and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Thus, this knowledge and vision of the Buddha constitutes a single great matter (*ekamahā-kṛtya*), and this great matter is precisely the cause.
"Opening, showing, awakening, and entering" collectively belong to the conditions that give rise to cultivation and realization; this constitutes the causal condition of a single principle.
△ Second, the conclusion:
Śāriputra, it is for the sake of this one great causal condition that all Buddhas appear in the world.

This section concludes the formation [of the chapter]. The Buddha originally appeared in the world for the purpose of revealing his Buddha-knowledge and vision, and thereby enabling others to enter into awakening and enter into that Buddha-knowledge and vision. Part Two: Clarifying the Person (1).
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "All Buddhas, Tathāgatas, teach and transform only bodhisattvas.
Tiantai says: "Regarding the provisional means of the past—namely, teaching and transforming the three vehicles—the underlying intention was fundamentally to transform bodhisattvas.
It is like that impoverished son who considered himself a lowly laborer, yet in the eyes of the elder, he was truly his own child."
My son, the person who performs this task is not one of two or three. Therefore it is said: "To teach and transform bodhisattvas. Third, regarding the single practice:
whatever they do is always for a single purpose—namely, to use the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to reveal and awaken sentient beings.
The various practices of the three vehicles are called "all that is done. They are manifold because they aim for perfection;
yet, in essence, they constitute a single matter. All that is practiced and performed is solely through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; there is no other path leading there.
△ Section Four: The One Teaching.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata [teaches] only [the One Vehicle], up to [the point where it is said that] there are no remaining vehicles, whether two or three.
This Single Buddha Vehicle is precisely the One Great Matter; it is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The "remaining vehicles" refer to the two and the three.
Tiantai says: "If this is so, then within the *Prajñā* [period] there is the inclusion of the two, and within the *Vaipulya* [period] there is the inclusion of the three."
All these were teachings of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). Up to the present day, however, the teaching is solely that of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
△ Fifth, concluding that all Buddhas are thus: Śāriputra, the Dharma of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions is likewise.

This refers back to the fact that the appearance of all Buddhas in the world is likewise so. Furthermore, the mention of "all ten directions" expresses the sense of a comprehensive totality without exception;
this is what is meant by "the Way of every Buddha is the same. △ Second, a specific clarification of the three periods of time.
This is divided into three parts. First, clarifying the past, which is further divided into two. First, revealing the provisional:
"Śāriputra, all Buddhas of the past... [and so forth]... expounded various dharmas for the sake of sentient beings."
○ This extensively cites how the Buddhas of the past appeared in the world for the sake of the one great matter.
All their teachings, principles, practices, and fruits are non-dual. Their expounding of all dharmas constitutes the non-duality of the teaching. △ Second, revealing the reality.
These teachings are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle (ekabuddhayāna), until finally all attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
For the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle—this principle is non-dual—it causes sentient beings to hear the Dharma and attain the knowledge of all modes.

This practice and its fruit are non-dual; this is the Dharma. It refers precisely to that which is the Dharma among all dharmas. It is not that there is a "Dharma" spoken of separately outside of all dharmas.
Therefore, it is said that by opening up the provisional (kaiquan) to reveal the real (xianshi), the real is the reality within the provisional;
they are definitively non-dual. II. Explaining the Future. This also has two parts. First, opening up the provisional.
Śāriputra, future Buddhas (up to) shall expound all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings.
△ Second, revealing the reality:
These dharmas are all for the sake of the One Buddha Vehicle (up to) ultimately attaining all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
○ This extensively enumerates the appearance of all future Buddhas in the world for the sake of sentient beings;
their entire teaching, principle, practice, and fruit are likewise so. △ Third, the explanation of the present, divided into three parts. First, indicating the intent of appearing in the world.
"Śāriputra, [the Buddhas] currently existing throughout the ten directions... bring great benefit and peace and happiness to sentient beings.

This refers to the present, encompassing all ten directions; furthermore, it mentions "immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of lands," clarifying that the supporting environment is pervasive in its horizontal extent.

As for the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, this includes their primary retributions (the bodies of the Buddhas) exhaustively and without exception. Although many Buddhas appear, [they are all included].
In this world, there is nothing that is not revealed through the causal conditions of the One Great Matter. This must bring great benefit, causing all sentient beings to awaken and enter [the Way];
it must bring great peace and happiness. This is the fundamental intention of the Buddhas appearing in the world.
2. The Expedient Means for Revealing the Provisional.
These Buddhas likewise, by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful expedients (up to), expound all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings.
△ Third, manifesting the reality for the assembly. This is divided into two parts. First, specifically clarifying the current teachings and practices.
"These dharmas are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle (ekabuddhayāna), until finally all attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
These three preceding turns all state that whenever a Buddha appears in the world, although he teaches by means of the Three Vehicles, in the ultimate sense there is only one.
Although those who hear the Dharma from the Buddha have distinctions of small and great [capacities], in the final analysis they all return to all-knowledge.
Wisdom. The World-Honored One has thus raised this theme in order to cause those in the assembly to each attain realization for themselves;
therefore, he previously exhorted them, saying, "Listen attentively and contemplate it well. △ Second, a general explanation of the human principle throughout the three periods of time.

Śāriputra, although the Buddhas’ teachings may appear to be of two kinds, in reality they all instruct the bodhisattva-dharma. That which is revealed is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and that which you have realized and entered is likewise the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
You should not, therefore, limit or disparage yourselves. This is appropriate.
Zhizhi says: This passage summarizes how the Buddhas of the ten directions appear in the world in succession; all their teachings, principles, practices, and fruits are entirely non-dual.
This serves to conclude the purport of the four gates—opening, showing, awakening, and entering—as taught by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, at the beginning of this chapter.

By relying on these four gates, one sweeps away the turbid attachments of the Great and Small Vehicles, as well as the confusion between the holy and the ordinary, and between delusion and awakening. Thus...
To see the ultimate and the conventional as one, the ordinary and the sage as one body, and the past and the present as one color—this is called the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
△ Second, the extensive exposition of Śākyamuni’s provisional and real teachings, divided into four parts. First, clarifying the revelation and manifestation.
"Śāriputra, I now do exactly the same... through the power of skillful means I preach the Dharma.
Having already cited and clarified [the case of] the Buddhas of the three periods of time above, this passage now reveals the reason for his own [action].

That is to say, it is not only the Buddhas of the ten directions throughout the three periods of time who appear in the world for the sake of the One Great Matter—opening up the provisional and manifesting the real—but I, too, on this very day, do the same.
It is so. The reason I did not previously speak of the One Vehicle was that I knew deeply that you all possess various inclinations.

"Various" means that, like those of provisional capacity in the Three Realms, each has different desires; it is not merely a matter of desire alone, but is further deepened by what the mind is attached to.
Thus, I could not help but follow the inherent nature of attachment of these sentient beings. Therefore, I had no choice but to do so.
This refers to the application of skillful means (*upāya*). As stated previously: "Sentient beings are attached everywhere; I lead them so that they may emerge.
Therefore, through various causes and conditions and so forth, he provides provisional teachings. This specifically pertains to the revelation of the provisional (*kaiquan*).
Śāriputra, all of this is for the sake of attaining the Single Buddha Vehicle and the Knowledge of All Modes (sarvākārajñatā).
These two phrases point back to the meaning explained above regarding the provisional opening [of the three vehicles];

ultimately, it is not for any other purpose, but is entirely intended so that all people may attain the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and accomplish the Knowledge of All Modes. For this reason, by means of countless methods...
"Conveniently" means to entice and lead them [toward the truth]. This passage reveals the reality: "all-aspect wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is precisely the Buddha’s "seed-wisdom.
△ Second, the clarification of the five turbidities (*pañcakaṣāya*). This is divided into two parts. First, the statement of the intent.
Śāriputra, in the worlds of the ten directions, there are not even two vehicles, let alone three.
If one considers this Dharma as fundamentally pure, profoundly still and uniform like space, then since even "two" do not exist, how much less could there be "three"?
Yet, one does not yet understand why the Buddhas do not immediately reveal the reality (*tattva*), but must necessarily open up the provisional (*upāya*). △ Two.
Clarifying the turbidities:

Śāriputra, the Buddhas appear in the world of the five turbidities—namely, the turbidity of the kalpa, the turbidity of views, the turbidity of afflictions, the turbidity of sentient beings, and the turbidity of lifespan.
In this context, it is clarified that [the teachings] were spoken out of necessity as either two or three [categories]. Tiantai says: "Kalpa" refers to a division of time.
"Turbidity" means being muddy and unclear. Furthermore, the water of the sentient beings' minds is originally pure;
it is only because the five kinds of disordered thoughts have entered into it that it suddenly becomes turbid. However, the kalpa-turbidity has no separate self-substance of its own.

It is simply because of the presence of the latter four defilements that they receive the designation "turbidity"; hence, they are called the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), and the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
The turbidity of views has the five sharp fetters as its essence; when expanded, it comprises sixty-two views. The turbidity of afflictions has the five dull fetters as its essence.
The five [defilements] all cause the body and mind to be clouded, afflicted, and distressed; this is the *sattva-kaṣāya* (the defilement of sentient beings). It likewise has no intrinsic substance;

it is established as a provisional designation by gathering together the three defilements of views, pride, and karmic retribution (*vipāka*). The *āyus-kaṣāya* (the defilement of lifespan) takes the continuous connection of form and mind as its essence.

Regarding the characteristics of the five defilements: when the four defilements intensify and converge at one time, it is called the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (the defilement of the eon). [This includes] hatred...
As violence increases, warfare breaks out; as greed increases, famine breaks out; and as delusion increases, epidemics break out.

Because these three calamities arise, afflictions flourish twofold, which is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). As various views become increasingly intense, it is called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).

Coarse and debased form and mind, along with evil reputations and foul appellations, are called the *sattva-kaṣāya* (degeneration of sentient beings). The shortening of years and the reduction of lifespan are called the *āyuḥ-kaṣāya* (degeneration of life).

○ Furthermore, speaking from a proximate perspective, it is when the human lifespan reaches one hundred years that one first enters the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (degeneration of the eon). However, tracing back through the flow of time...

Sentient beings have been without beginning. Since the time they were shrouded in darkness and became the void, they have entered the kalpa-turbidity (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), which encompasses the four great elements, mountains, rivers, and so forth, as well as the kalpas of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness. As for the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*):

because the four great elements are fundamentally insentient, yet due to the weaving of delusion, even the point of a needle or the prick of a blade of grass becomes a sensation of pain; yet sentient beings stubbornly give rise to [this perception].
The view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is the sovereign of all views. Regarding the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*): it means being vexed and troubled; it means weariness and toil.

As sensory objects (*viṣaya*) fill the mind, there is no moment when one is not weary and disturbed. Regarding the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*): it arises from transmigrating through the various realms of existence (*gati*).
This is because it manifests the various forms of all sentient beings. As for the turbidity of life (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*): it arises from the entanglement of the six sense faculties.
Life is entrusted to that which lies between them; when the faculties and their objects coalesce, life exists, and when the faculties and their objects disperse, life perishes.
Thus, Śāriputra, during the period of the defilement of the kalpa... [up to] "distinguishing and preaching three within the single Buddha-vehicle.

This collectively encompasses the five corruptions (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*): stinginess and greed are the corruption of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*); jealousy is the corruption of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*); and the unwholesome roots are the corruption of life-force (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*).

Because these five turbidities are turbid and deep, and the obstructions of sentient beings are heavy, the Buddhas can only open the gate of expedient means and conceal the ultimate reality to manifest provisional teachings.
△ Third, clarifying the true and the false, divided into two parts. First, distinguishing the false.

"Śāriputra, as for my disciples—[from 'who are not Arhats' to] 'who are not Pratyekabuddhas'—the preceding passage has already explained the provisional opening [of the three vehicles]. Since it was originally unavoidable, all that was taught is in fact one.
If my disciples claim for themselves that they have already realized Arhatship or attained Pratyekabuddhahood, the Tathāgata must now manifest the One Vehicle. You..."
Furthermore, they have neither heard it nor do they know it, yet they conversely claim that this is the matter of teaching bodhisattvas.
Thus, taking skillful means as the reality is not the truth. Therefore, it is said: "They are not disciples of the Buddha," and so forth.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, it is impossible for these bhikṣus (and so forth) not to believe this Dharma;

yet, to claim for themselves that they have attained the Way is not what the Buddha permits. Although they may have exhausted their *pariccheda-bhava* (segmented existence), they have not yet forgotten *pariṇāma-bhava* (transformative existence);
how then could they truly be in their final body? To no longer aspire [to enlightenment] means that they have not turned their minds back [toward it]. If...

If one merely attains a small fruit and becomes complacent, realizing it and yet not turning the mind toward the Great Vehicle, this is precisely "claiming to have attained what one has not attained" and "claiming to have realized what one has not realized.
Such a person belongs to the class of those with *adhimāna* (arrogance); their roots of transgression are deep and heavy, and they certainly cannot be my disciples.
Why? If there were truly such realization, how could they not believe in the *nirvāṇa* that lies above it?
△ Second, clarifying the true [nature].
Excluding the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa when no Buddha is present before one (up to): “Those who understand the meaning are difficult to find.

The former refers to those who have attained the state of an Arhat or Pratyekabuddha but do not believe [in the Mahāyāna], being characterized by overweening pride (*adhimāna*). This is because [the Buddha] is currently present.
They claim there are teachings to be shown, yet they take no pleasure in hearing them; they believe for themselves that they have attained something and realized something.

If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they emerge in a world without a Buddha, there will be no one to provide such instruction. Consequently, although they do not give rise to faith or acceptance toward this sutra, [they still harbor these views].
It may still be permitted that they do not belong to the ranks of those who are conceited. Why is this?

Although this sutra exists after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, because it is exceedingly profound and difficult to understand, those who seek to read and recite it are hard to find. If one can understand its meaning, this is already even more difficult to find.
As for those who seek to realize the unsurpassed path, they are ultimately as rare as the udumbara flower. I.
All [beings] love and delight in it; this is why it is permitted to be considered authentic.
If one encounters another Buddha, one will attain definitive understanding within this Dharma.
Tiantai said: "I fear there may be those who harbor doubts, thinking that after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, one cannot comprehend this profound [teaching]."
If this were the case, then people in future ages would never have the opportunity to realize the Truth. To this, [the author] replies: Not so.
If, in another land, they encounter a Buddha appearing in the world, that Buddha will certainly preach this sutra. If they hear it even once, they will immediately attain definitive understanding.
Thus, when the Buddha said, "I shall become a Buddha in other lands under different names and preach the wondrous Dharma," this was his intended meaning. △
The four clarifications are without falsehood.
Śāriputra, you and the others should be single-minded (until: there is no other vehicle, but only the Single Buddha Vehicle).
From my own disciples, to those who have attained decisive understanding within this Dharma—each and every one of them is exhorted and admonished.
Commentary: At this point, it is clearly revealed to the assembly that they must certainly give rise to faith, which is non-dual and non-triple.
Since the Buddha emerged from his samādhi, he has repeatedly brushed aside the traces of the Three Vehicles and repeatedly manifested the wondrousness of the One Vehicle.
Here, once again, he raises up the sole Buddha-vehicle and swears by his own vow that it is not false, thereby exhorting the assembly to believe and understand with a single mind.
There is no difference between them; it simply requires that each person have self-confidence and self-awareness.

Each and every one possesses a segment of radiant light between the eyebrows, within which the marks of the ten dharma-realms are perfectly complete. You must by no means push this responsibility onto the shoulders of the Buddhas.
Yet they bury their own spirits. Therefore, the concluding verse of the later section says: "Knowing for oneself that one shall become a Buddha, there is no doubt whatsoever.

This is also reiterated four times from this point onward: to believe with a single mind that one’s own nature is inherently endowed [with Buddhahood], and to understand that the Original Buddha’s words are not false.
△ Second, the Verse Recitation. Divided into two parts. First, the verse corresponding to the preceding promise.

Answer: Furthermore, there are two [points]. First, regarding those who have already regressed and are incapable [of receiving this teaching], at that time the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who harbor overweening pride... are incapable of receiving this Dharma.”
This verse refers to five thousand [monks] withdrawing from their seats; the prose section mentions only these five thousand. This passage divides them into four assemblies. Zhizhi states:
"In terms of principle, these are the four assemblies who collectively transform the five consciousnesses along with their associated mental factors (*caitta*).

The two monastic assemblies mistakenly claim to have attained the Way, and thus the afflictions they are driven by belong to overweening pride (*abhimāna*). The lay assembly relies on its own nobility, and thus the afflictions they are driven by [belong to that]."
These belong to the conceit of "I. As for women, their power of faith is particularly feeble; thus, that which they are driven by belongs to lack of faith.

Those who do not recognize their own faults do so because their minds are shrouded by the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). Those whose precepts have gaps and leaks do so because their minds are scattered and unsettled.
A flaw (*khaṇḍa*) is like a blemish on fine jade; that which drives them is a blemish upon True Suchness (*tathatā*). So it is said.
"Guarding and cherishing" means that one does not wish for others to know the evils committed by the mind. The cleverness of the mind is called "limited wisdom.
The frivolity and hypocrisy of the mind are called "dregs and husks. When True Suchness is about to turn [toward enlightenment], it is said that they depart due to the majestic power of the Buddha.
That the mental factors (*caitta*) are false is called "meager merit" (*alpa-puṇya*). That the mental factors have no substantial essence is called "incapable of receiving the Dharma.

When one first perceives that the false is exhausted and the true is fully realized, there is a sudden shedding [of attachments]; this is the meaning of "retiring from one's seat" (*niṣadyā-vyāvṛtti*).

In terms of the Dharma, this refers to Śāriputra and others who do not cling to the branches and leaves of provisional teachings but are about to approach the single reality (*eka-tattva*); therefore, he grants permission for them to speak. *Xiá* (pronounced *xiá*) and *xiǎn* (pronounced *xiǎn*).
△ Second, having recited the two verses, he exhorts the assembly to listen:
"In this assembly there are no 'branch-abandoners' (śākhā-tyāgī), but only the true Śāriputras; listen well.
The word "all" (sarva) does not mean "many"; it is a term used to form a verse. It refers to those for whom the profuse branches have fallen away entirely.

"There is only one true reality. This further admonishes those who listen well; it is a repeated exhortation to awaken. △ Second, the verse summary of the preceding "Direct Answer" section, divided into two parts.
First, the verse summary of the chapter on the Four Buddhas, which is further divided into four. First, the verse summary of all Buddhas, which is further divided into five.
The first verse concerns the Buddhas’ bestowal of skillful means (*upāya*). It further consists of two parts: first, the verse itself on the bestowal of skillful means:
"The Dharma attained by the Buddhas, through immeasurable powers of skillful means... causes all to rejoice."
The first three phrases clarify that all Buddhas have realized this Dharma and further transformed it through skillful means—what is called "the wondrous manifestation in every instance.
That which the Buddhas have attained is the actual wisdom of self-realization; the prose refers to this as "such a wondrous Dharma.
The two phrases concerning "immeasurable skillful means" refer to provisional wisdom; the extended text states that the Buddhas act according to what is appropriate.
This refers to the preaching of the Dharma. "The mental conceptions of sentient beings" refers to the thoughts of sentient beings within the nine realms;

it denotes the formation of mental images prior to the actual execution of an action. "Various practices" refers to the numerous matters contained within those thoughts, which are so many as to be difficult to enumerate.
The three characters "path of practice" (*shōdō*) refer to the road upon which one proceeds to carry out these activities. "Some" (*sukana*).
This is an inexhaustible statement. Regarding those of various desires and dispositions, the nine realms of sentient beings have differing inclinations; hence they are called "various desires.
Nevertheless, that which each desire privately possesses—whether defiled or pure—is entirely derived from the causal karma of good and evil from previous lives.
The Buddha, knowing that the root-natures of sentient beings differ in this way, guides them through skillful means.
He causes all people to attain joy according to their respective natures,
whether by preaching the Sūtras, Gāthās, Itivṛttakas, or even Upadeśas.
Tiantai says: *Sūtra* is here translated as "Scripture of Accordance" (*qijing*). There are two kinds: the general and the specific.

Generally, it is the common name for the holy teachings; specifically, among the twelve divisions of the canon, it refers to those that directly explain the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). *Gāthā*.
This is called "isolated" (gūqǐ), meaning it does not follow the prose (chángxíng) but rather stands alone and arises independently.
"Past Events" (běnshì) refers to accounts of deeds performed in the past, such as the giving away of one's head, eyes, marrow, brain, kingdom, city, wife, and children.
"Birth Stories" (běnshēng) refers to accounts of taking birth within the nine realms in the past. "Unprecedented Events" (wéicéngyǒu) refers to...
The Buddha manifests various supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*); this refers to the "causes and conditions" (*nidāna*) that cause sentient beings to marvel at what has never occurred before.

There is a distinction between the internal and external, and the great and the small; for example, as described in the "Chapter on the Phantom City" regarding matters of past-life causes and conditions.

"Parables" (*avadāna*) include those in this sutra such as the *udumbara* flower and the parable of the burning house. "Verses" (*geya*), which are stanzas of repetition, and "Explanations" (*upadeśa*).

This is called "discourse" (*upadeśa*). It refers, for example, to the debates between non-Buddhists and the Buddha regarding the causes and effects of humans and devas, and whether worldly and world-transcending phenomena are existent or non-existent, true or false, and so forth.

These teachings on the nature and characteristics, the root and the branches of all phenomena, which the Buddha preached as appropriate during the first forty years of his ministry, are recorded in the nine divisions of scripture (*navāṅga*).
If one adds the Vaipulya, the *Aparipṛcchita-svayaṃbhāṣita* (Unasked Spontaneous Discourses), and the *Vyākaraṇa* (Prophecies), [they constitute the twelve divisions].
[This] forms the twelve divisions [of the canon]. △ Second, the conclusion regarding the intention behind the provisional teachings:
"Those of dull faculties who delight in the Lesser Dharma and are greedily attached to birth and death... for their sake, he speaks of *nirvāṇa*."
This establishes the intent of employing skillful means (*upāya*). Those who understand the Way say: these teachings of the nine divisions of scripture were not the Buddha’s original intention;

rather, they were taught out of necessity for sentient beings of dull faculties who delight in the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), do not believe in the Mahāyāna, and are attached to the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Because in the past, under immeasurable Buddhas, they did not practice the profound and wondrous path, [the Buddha] acted thus for their sake.
Disturbance by suffering and affliction. Because of such people, one can only speak of *nirvāṇa with remainder* as a state of cessation.
△ Second, the verse clarifying the reality. This is divided into four parts. First, the verse on the oneness of principle.
I have established these skillful means to enable them to enter the Buddha’s wisdom; for this reason, I preach this sutra.

As for "establishing skillful means," it refers precisely to the fact that this Dharma, as expressed in the long prose sections, cannot be understood through mere intellectual calculation or conceptual discrimination.

Originally, because this Dharma is inconceivable and difficult to understand, I could only speak of the ninefold teachings as a provisional means to guide people and lead them into the Buddha’s wisdom.

Since these are called "expedient means," how could they be the ultimate reality? This is why I did not say that you possess the potential for Buddhahood, nor why I did not bestow the prediction of enlightenment upon you.
It was not out of stinginess that I withheld this; rather, it was because I spoke of this [provisional teaching].

The time for the Great Dharma has not yet arrived; however, now that the faculties of you followers of the Two Vehicles have fully matured, it is surely the time to bestow the prediction [of enlightenment].

How could this be like the previous instances where there were two or three different teachings? This is the definitive manifestation of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and it is merely the preaching of the Mahāyāna.
It was precisely when the long prose section was being delivered that it should have been taught; one must understand that what is being spoken today is essential.
This is true. Thus, the ninefold teachings of the forty years past were merely expedient means in accordance with circumstances.
Examining their original intent, they were nothing other than provisional teachings used to lead [beings] into the Mahāyāna as the fundamental goal.
For this reason, today I have finally preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for you all. △ Second, the verse on persons, part one.
"There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure, supple, and also sharp" (up to) "all will undoubtedly attain Buddhahood.
This verse clarifies that while all Buddhas and Tathāgatas teach only Bodhisattvas, it is specifically for the sake of Bodhisattvas that the Mahāyāna is expounded.

"Pure mind" means that the delusions of ignorance and the states of awakening have both been forgotten. "Supple" means that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) are unified. "Sharp" [refers to their faculties].
As for the "roots": when principle and phenomena reach together in the profound and wondrous Way, one simultaneously cultivates both merit and wisdom.

How much more so for such people! Since they are able to practice the profound and wondrous Way, their minds are like those of a Buddha; since they have attained pliancy and freedom from anger, their forms are like those of a Buddha.
When they are like a Buddha both internally and externally, will they not surely attain Buddhahood in a future life? These are all the most supreme.
Regarding the roots of the Supreme Vehicle: from "With a deep mind, they recollect the Buddha" onwards, it further clarifies a certain class of persons who have given rise to the Mahāyāna mind.
Although they have not yet practiced the profound and wondrous path under immeasurable Buddhas, they now likewise recollect the Buddha with a deep mind and strictly maintain the pure precepts.
Upon hearing that there is a time when one attains the Buddha-way, they give rise to great joy. Therefore, I know them.
They possess resolute faith and orientation; their minds and conduct are both adorned. For this reason, the Mahāyāna is taught for them.
Throughout this assembly, there are both śrāvakas and bodhisattvas; upon hearing even a single verse of this Great Sūtra, they may likewise plant the cause for attaining Buddhahood in the future.
Thus, one knows that the people in this assembly, whether great or small, all share a single capacity. These śrāvakas...
"Bodhisattva" here refers to those among the three vehicles who possess both the general and specific [aspects]. △ Third, the teaching of the One:
"In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma" (up to) "...because he preaches the Buddha’s wisdom."
This verse states that the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for sentient beings using only the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*), and there is no other vehicle, whether dual or triple.
Tiantai says: "There is no duality" means there is no duality of the "half" and "full" teachings within the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇayāna*).
"There is no triad" means there is no three-vehicle system within the Tripitaka Teaching (*piṭakatriyāna*). Such instances of duality and triad are all... [omitted].
"Using provisional names to guide sentient beings" refers precisely to the teaching of skillful means (*upāya*).

As for the previous statement that śrāvakas and bodhisattvas who hear even a single verse will undoubtedly attain Buddhahood, this is because what is being taught today is the wisdom of the Buddha itself.
△ Fourth, one verse on practice.
"The Buddhas appear in the world; this alone is the one true reality" (up to) "this matter is not possible.
The first three lines of the verse praise the aforementioned fact that all actions performed always serve a single purpose.
The final two lines clarify the intent of always serving a single purpose: "The Buddha himself abides in the Great Vehicle" up to "by means of this he delivers the multitudes."
"Arising. The preceding verse indicates that the Buddha’s wisdom and insight alone are used to reveal and awaken sentient beings.
The sole reason all Buddhas appear in the world is to demonstrate this single matter of the Buddha’s wisdom and insight; this is the true teaching.

The vehicles of the Two and Three Vehicles are not their original vows, yet the Tathāgata ultimately does not transform or deliver people through the Lesser Vehicle. This will be explained and established below.

Why does he not transform people through the Lesser Vehicle? Since the Buddha himself abides in and upholds the Mahāyāna, the dharmas he has attained are all adorned with concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*);
it is solely by means of these dharmas adorned with concentration and wisdom that he delivers sentient beings.

The text further explains below: "If the Buddha had personally realized the supreme Mahāyāna Dharma of equality, yet still used the Hīnayāna to transform others, it would mean the Buddha harbored a partiality for himself and would inevitably fall into the fault of stinginess.
This would be utterly contradictory to his appearance in the world for the sake of the Great Matter (ekakṛtya). Therefore, it is said: 'This matter...'"

It cannot be done. △ Third, the verse exhorting faith. This is divided into two parts. First, the exhortation to faith by citing the fruit. This is further divided into two. First, citing the internal mind:
"If a person has faith and takes refuge in the Buddha, the Tathāgata does not deceive [them]... (until) he alone possesses no fear."
This passage establishes the intention of the Buddhas to transform people through great means. "If a person" refers to one who is capable of faith and capable of taking refuge.
Since a person has already taken refuge and placed their faith in me, how could I deceive that person? The Tathāgata does not deceive; thus, his actions are true and real.
This body is pure and fit for people to take as a refuge. The Tathāgata does not mislead; thus, what he speaks is... [not false].
Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is purity of speech; one becomes trustworthy to others. Freedom from greed and envy is purity of mind;
one becomes worthy of others' veneration. When the three karmas are thus purified, all evils within all phenomena have already been severed and eliminated.
As for "all phenomena," this refers to the impurity of the three karmas of sentient beings, which give rise to various types of karma upon the objects of the sensory realms. Now...
Regarding "cutting off": because the Tathāgata’s three karmas are pure, all evils are forever severed. Thus, throughout the ten directions, he benefits sentient beings by transcending the world;
acting freely within the nine realms, he moves both vertically and horizontally without fear. △ Second, citing external forms.
I have adorned my body with marks and my radiance illuminates the world; thus honored by immeasurable multitudes, I preach for them the Seal of the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇamudrā*).
Because the three karmas mentioned above are pure, such adornments are thus induced.

If the Tathāgata were to harbor views of high and low, self and other, or were to speak of the Great and the Small, he would be committing deception. How, then, could his body be adorned with the marks and signs and possess such radiance?
His brilliance illuminates everywhere, and he is revered by immeasurable humans and devas.
Furthermore, how could he not be able to expound the Dharma-seal of the true aspect for immeasurable humans and devas? This is intended to cause people to resolutely believe in this non-duality.
As for the seal of the true aspect, the Buddha takes the wondrous Dharma as his seal; it certifies that all sentient beings of the nine realms shall all become Buddhas.
If, in the ultimate sense, the true reality of the One Vehicle were not taught, it would not be the authentic seal;
it would then be a provisional teaching and a false transmission of its essential meaning. △ Second, citing reasons to encourage faith.
Śāriputra, you should know that I originally established a vow desiring to cause all sentient beings to be no different from myself.
This is the vow held by the Tathāgata while in the causal stage; it is precisely the Four Great Vows.
"Desiring to cause all sentient beings to be no different from myself" is the vow to save all beings. Saving beings is not possible for one who has not fully mastered the Dharma gates.
I am able; therefore, I vow to study the Dharma-gates that encompass all phenomena.
As I have vowed in the past, my aspiration is now fulfilled: I shall transform all sentient beings and cause them all to enter the Buddha-way.
The vow has been fulfilled; thus, the Buddha-way has already been realized. As for one who has attained Buddhahood, how could it be that afflictions have not been severed?

Therefore, the preaching of the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle now constitutes the repayment of causes and the answering of results. Question: The Buddha’s vow states, "I vow to deliver infinite sentient beings.
This implies a vow to deliver all beings. Since sentient beings have not yet been exhausted, why do you say the vow is fulfilled?
Answer: When the Buddha attained equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), all sentient beings likewise attained equal and perfect enlightenment.

How could there be any sentient beings remaining outside of the Buddha who were not saved? According to this assembly, at the point when his period of responding to conditions was nearing its end, he caused those of the three vehicles to all receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of attaining Buddhahood; this is called the fulfillment of his vows. Therefore, it is said: "But..."

There are those who hear the Dharma; there is not one among them who does not attain Buddhahood. △ Fourth, the verse on the five turbidities, divided into three parts. First, a general explanation of the heavy obstacles of the five turbidities:
"If I were to encounter sentient beings and teach them all the Buddha-way, those without wisdom would become confused and deluded, and would not accept the teaching."
Sentient beings undergo suffering, and the Buddhas give rise to compassion. Because compassion and suffering meet one another, it is called "meeting.

Furthermore, "meeting" means that when sentient beings have a resonance, the Buddha immediately responds; this subtle and hidden communication between stimulus and response is therefore termed "meeting.
As it is said: "If sentient beings do not meet me, that is that; but if they do meet me, I must surely preach the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," regardless of the four [types of beings].
They are born into the six realms of existence, yet all are taught to attain Buddhahood. Alas, sentient beings lack wisdom; they practice in a confused and disorderly manner.
Not only do they fail to attain Buddhahood, but they instead become śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, non-Buddhists, celestial māras, or the retinues of māras.
All of these are cases of hearing [the teachings] without understanding; those who do not relinquish the consciousness-mind naturally fall into confusion.

Furthermore, there are those of meager wisdom who delight in inferior dharmas; they stubbornly cling to their own attachments and sit and realize a partial emptiness, falsely claiming to have attained realization.
They do not believe in attaining Buddhahood, they do not give rise to the Mahāyāna mind, and they do not practice the profound and wondrous path. This, moreover, is a case of neither hearing nor...

To see those who do not relinquish their attachment to provisional means as being themselves devoid of wisdom is itself a lack of wisdom. Thus, the four characters "lack of wisdom" (*mūḍha*) and "confusion" (*saṃbhrānta*) encompass two types of people who do not accept the teaching:
those whose practice is confused and those whose practice is characterized by a lack of wisdom. Those who are confused do not accept it because they are deluded;
those whose practice lacks wisdom do not accept it because they are bewildered. Furthermore, the deluded are like one who has lost their way, having no knowledge at all of which direction to take.

As for those who are deluded: although they know the general direction, they take south for north; thus, while the two characters "delusion" (*mo*) and "confusion" (*huo*) differ in their degree of severity, both together signify a failure to accept the teachings.
△ Second, the detailed explanation of the profound source of the five turbidities, divided into five parts. First, the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).
"I know that these sentient beings have never cultivated the roots of goodness (up to) fully experiencing all manner of bitter poisons.
Tiantai says: "The roots of goodness are the true suchness (tathatā) and the real mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa). The five desires are form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch."
Delusion is ignorance; craving is greed. These sentient beings are those previously mentioned who were deluded and did not accept the teaching.
I know that such people, throughout past kalpas, have not heard of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
therefore, they have not cultivated the root of sublime goodness. The reason they lack roots of goodness is precisely because they are stubbornly attached to the five desires. Because...
Delusion and ignorance give rise to all forms of craving and attachment; because of this craving and attachment, various sufferings and afflictions arise.

Regarding the conditions of desire: ignorance and craving act as the cause, while the five objects of desire act as the condition. Furthermore, the five things—wealth, beauty, fame, food, and sleep—are all that humans desire.
Due to these conditions of desire, one is led to fall into the three evil realms. Three.
The "evil paths" (durgati) refer to the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals; as these three are all lands inhabited by those of extreme wickedness, they are called evil paths.

Not only are there these three evil paths, but due to these causes and conditions, sentient beings transmigrate through the six realms of existence, experiencing all manner of the three sufferings, the eight sufferings, and the various poisons of the three poisons. Thus, these sentient beings may be described as being turbid.
It has reached its extreme. Therefore, it is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). △ Second, the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣ-kaṣāya*):
those with meager virtue and little merit, whose subtle forms at conception constantly increase through successive lives, are oppressed by manifold sufferings.
"Life" (命) is named for its continuous sustenance of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*); thus, the character for "form" (*xing*, *rūpa*) already fully encompasses both form and mind.
"Subtle form" (*weixing*, *sūkṣma-rūpa*) is spoken of in contrast to the vast Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

This refers to the Dharma-body possessed by sentient beings, which fundamentally pervades the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and is never confined or entangled by the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). It is solely due to a single moment of non-awakening that it suddenly becomes [conditioned].
Deluded and inverted, they revolve without ceasing due to the causes and conditions of various desires, passing from birth to birth with no way out.
Thus they receive this subtle form; because delusion and karma draw one another along, it increases life after life.

In this way, they enter suffering after suffering, all because their virtue is meager, their defilements heavy, their merit small, and their karma deep. For these reasons, they undergo birth, old age, sickness, and death.
When one is oppressed by manifold sufferings, the life of wisdom perishes, and the defilement of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*) is formed. △ Third is the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).
Entering the dense forest of false views—such as "existence" or "non-existence"—one relies upon these various views, which comprise the sixty-two [types].

This arises because sentient beings, oppressed by suffering, falsely seek liberation from it and erroneously enter into various views; these all belong to wrong understanding and are therefore called "wrong view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
It is called a "dense forest" because these various views are as thick and impenetrable as a forest. "Existence and non-existence" refers to the two views of nihilism and eternalism.
The term "and so forth" includes the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), extreme views, false views, views regarding precepts and vows, and the sixty-two views. Because of these...
All views are turbid, and because right view does not arise, this constitutes the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).
Tiantai says: For example, the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) postulate a self (*ātman*) through four propositions: first, form (*rūpa*) is the self; second, the self is apart from form;

third, the self is large and form is small, with the self dwelling within form; fourth, the self is large and form is small, with form dwelling within the self. Regarding each of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), [the same applies].
There are four types [of views], which constitute twenty views. Furthermore, when categorized according to the three periods of time, each period possesses twenty views, resulting in sixty views.
Adding the two fundamental views of annihilationism and eternalism, they total sixty-two. (Chóu, pronounced *chóu*). △ Fourth, the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kāṣāya*).
Deeply attached to false and illusory phenomena, they stubbornly cling to them and cannot relinquish them; with self-conceit and arrogance, their minds are crooked and insincere.
"Illusory phenomena" refers to the various views previously grasped. Because their attachment is profound, they accept these views so firmly that they are unable to abandon them.
Since they have taken what is wrong for what is right, they conversely claim that the truth is unattainable. Thus...
One gives rise to great *asmimāna* (self-conceit), looking down upon all others; this is to be self-exalting and self-admiring. As for "flattery and crookedness":
using one's own erroneous interpretations to flatter others in hopes that they will bend to one’s will—all of these are insincere states of mind.

Because of these, the field of the mind is agitated, becoming clouded by affliction and distress, thereby forming the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). "Self-admiring" (*jing*)—the pronunciation is *jing*; it means being haughty and self-important.
△ Fifth, the defilement of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).
For thousands of millions of billions of eons, such persons do not hear the name of the Buddha nor do they hear the True Dharma; thus they are difficult to deliver.

Because of the aforementioned four defilements, their original truth is disturbed and agitated, causing them to sink and wallow for long eons and undergo all manner of extreme suffering. Having thus become deluded—
Regarding the one true and wondrous nature, they do not know it is inherently natural; this is what is meant by "not having heard the name of the Buddha.
Since they cling to false views and deluded principles, they do not hear the wondrous Dharma that exists from the beginning; this is what is meant by "not hearing the True Dharma.

For those who thus cling to the delusive and are confused about the truth, such that the True Cause remains unmanifest—how could they be easily delivered? △ Third, the conclusion on preaching the Lesser Vehicle.
This is the reason for it.
Therefore, Śāriputra, I have established skillful means to teach the path that exhausts all suffering and point them toward Nirvāṇa.
This clearly explains that, for the sake of sentient beings in the five turbidities, I preach the Dharma of the Four Truths through the three vehicles. Suffering is simply suffering.

The Truths: by subsuming the cause within the fruit, the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya) is included; the path that exhausts suffering is the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya), namely the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
and the demonstration of nirvana is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya).
Although I speak of *nirvāṇa*, this too is not the true extinction (up to: "one shall attain Buddhahood in a future life").
What I call and demonstrate as *nirvāṇa* refers to the three samādhis—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—and the *nirvāṇa with remainder*.
All of these are reached through meritorious effort. Since they belong to meritorious effort, they are termed "with remainder"; how could they be the ultimate truth?
Is this the Tathāgata’s great ocean of quiescent extinction, the ultimate *nirvāṇa*—like gold extracted from ore or wood reduced to ash?

Therefore it is said: "This too is not true extinction. Regarding the phrase "all phenomena are equal from the very beginning," this means that all various phenomena of the mundane and supramundane worlds are none other than the Tathāgata’s wondrously luminous, perfect mind; that is to say, the original *tathāgatagarbha*.
The nature of form is true emptiness; it does not depend on effort or achievement, and has been quiescent from the beginning.
Within it, one cannot find even a hair’s breadth of the marks of coming and going, birth and extinction. Therefore, it is said that it has been eternally quiescent from the very beginning.
Now, if you wish to realize this mark of eternal quiescence, you, my sons of the Buddha, must practice this path and thereby attain merit.
Only when wisdom is perfected does one finally attain Buddhahood. This is what is meant by: "Matters are not eliminated all at once; they are exhausted through successive stages.
5. Verse on Non-emptiness:
"I possess the power of skillful means, To reveal the teachings of the three vehicles, Until there is but the One Vehicle, And no second vehicle exists."
The first two lines clarify that Śākyamuni opened [the teaching] into three; the next two lines clarify that all Buddhas manifest the reality.

The final four lines collectively clarify that what all Buddhas teach and what I have spoken are ultimately non-dual. One must know that my teaching of the Three Vehicles was originally intended to manifest the One;
the Buddhas' teaching of the One is a skillful means to open it into three, all for the sake of the single Great Matter. Thus it is said.
Manifested in the world. This verse summarizes the long prose passage. You all should have faith and understanding in the Buddha’s words; they are not false. There is no other vehicle;
there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle. II. Verses on the Buddhas of the Past. Divided into two parts: 1. A verse on the opening of the three [vehicles].
Throughout incalculable kalpas of the past, immeasurable Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa (up to the point where they) expounded the characteristics of all dharmas.
[This] praises the immeasurable Buddhas of the past who appeared in the world for one great cause: to open up the provisional and teach the three vehicles.

There was none among them who did not use skillful means to explain the characteristics of all dharmas. These "characteristics of all dharmas" refer to what was previously mentioned: the ten realms and the ten suchnesses.
This is the section on the characteristics of the Dharma. △ Second, the verse that reveals the oneness [of the vehicle]. This is divided into two parts. First, the general verse:
"All these World-Honored Ones equally preach the Single Vehicle Dharma, transforming immeasurable sentient beings and causing them to enter the Buddha-way."
To speak of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is the oneness of the teaching; to transform immeasurable sentient beings is the oneness of the person;

to cause them to enter the Buddha-way is the oneness of principle, which also encompasses the oneness of practice. II. The Separate Verses are divided into two parts. First, a general summary of the five vehicles to reveal the One.
Furthermore, the Great Holy Lords know all worlds... [and so forth] ...to assist in manifesting the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This clarifies that the Buddhas of the past, observing that sentient beings' faculties were dull, established provisional means based upon the reality;
