this proves that the present revelation of the provisional to manifest the real is not in vain. The character "know" (*zhī*) refers to the Buddha’s observation of capacities, whereby he knows all worlds. If...

Whether gods or humans, or indeed all classes of sentient beings, each has what they desire according to their deep-seated inclinations. These "deep-seated inclinations" refer to the minds of humans and gods that are attached to sensory objects;
they are firm and cannot be uprooted. What they "desire" refers specifically to the pleasure-seeking of the five sense-objects (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
Because these habitual desires are difficult to eliminate, the Buddha employs various skillful means (*upāya*) to gradually entice and lead them, inevitably...

Because one attains the Buddha-wisdom, it is called "aiding manifestation. As for "different skillful means," these refer to the conditioned activities performed by humans and devas, ranging from a single flower or a single incense offering to a single sound or a single form; thus they are called "different.

Since there is nothing that does not lead people back to the primary meaning (paramārtha), they are called "skillful means. II. Specifically explaining the One by means of the five vehicles, divided into three parts. First, regarding... [text fragment]
"Bodhisattva.
If there are classes of sentient beings who encounter the various Buddhas of the past (up to) all having already attained the Buddha-way.
Tiantai says: "If one explains this according to the five vehicles, it refers only to the Bodhisattva vehicle of the six perfections. If one explains it according to the seven [vehicles]..."

The explanation by way of skillful means (*upāya*) encompasses both the general and specific Bodhisattva vehicles. Why is it that although the Mahāyāna of the three teachings all practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), there is a distinction in their application of the mind?
Practicing the six perfections with a mind characterized by marks (*nimitta*) is the Bodhisattva of the Tripiṭaka teaching.

Practicing them with a markless mind (*animitta*) is the Bodhisattva of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika*). Practicing them through the sequence of a mind that is neither with nor without marks is... [the Bodhisattva of the Distinct Teaching].
Regarding the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), only the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) are listed here; it is not yet clear to which teaching they belong.

According to what was stated above regarding "different skillful means," these refer to the skillful means of the Bodhisattvas of the three teachings. Of the six perfections, the first five belong to the gate of merit (*puṇyamukha*), while the last one belongs to wisdom (*prajñā*).

Therefore, it is said that they practice "various kinds of cultivation. Although the Buddha has provisionally opened up these skillful means, their true purpose is to lead [beings] toward [enlightenment].
They entered the Buddha-way; therefore it is said that they have all already attained the Way. Question:

Since the topical outline states that "one [vehicle] is revealed," the Six Perfections ought to be the primary expedient means (*upāya*) of the Mahāyāna. How can they be equally called "different expedient means"? Answer:
Although the expedient means differ, the Buddha-way into which they are led is one and the same. Moreover, these are instances where the Buddha cites his own past cultivation of practice.
To this day, it has become the cause for attaining the Way. It is not that people lack detailed understanding;

△ Third, the verses on future Buddhas, divided into two parts. First, the verses opening the three [assemblies].
"The future World-Honored Ones shall be immeasurable in number" (up to) "by means of immeasurable skillful expedients.

This refers to various causes, conditions, and so forth. △ Second, the verse clarifies the oneness [of the Buddha-nature]. This is divided into four parts. First, one verse clarifies the person:

The untainted (*anāsrava*) is precisely true wisdom. The Buddha, with a single voice, preaches the Dharma of the One Vehicle;
that is to say, all are of one characteristic and one kind. Since what is preached is one, it causes those who hear it to enter the Buddha’s untainted state, whereby they all become Bodhisattvas.

If this single True Suchness, the mental dharma, were not constant, it would result in annihilationism; how then could there be the Three Vehicles or the Five [Nikāyas]?

Regarding its nature: if this dharma were fixed as fivefold, then śrāvakas would remain merely śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas would remain merely pratyekabuddhas, and even those of the six realms—including humans and devas—would remain merely humans and devas, forever without the time to achieve Buddhahood.
This is determined and unchanging. Because one knows that this Dharma is truly eternal yet lacks a fixed nature, it forms seeds according to conditioning:
when conditioned by ordinary dharmas, it becomes ordinary; when conditioned by holy dharmas, it becomes holy.

This is what is meant by "the essence remains immutable while its function follows conditions. That the essence remains immutable is its permanence; that the function follows conditions is its lack of fixed nature.

Therefore, because all Buddhas are fully endowed with merit and wisdom, they know that all sentient beings inherently possess this indeterminate nature.
Consequently, they perfume them with the Great Dharma of the One Vehicle. Through the induction of these conditions, [sentient beings] will inevitably attain realization.
The Buddha said: "Therefore, it is said that there is but one vehicle (ekayāna). Since the one vehicle is taught, the teaching is likewise one.

4. Verse on the Unity of Principle: "This Dharma abides in its own place; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant. Having realized this at the site of enlightenment, the Guide speaks through skillful means."
This Dharma is precisely the single mind of True Suchness (*tathatā*). It is also what is called the "Sublime Dharma" (*saddharma*) in this very sutra.
This word "Dharma" is the great root and the great source of both the mundane and the supramundane. Regarding "the station of Dharma" (*dharmasthiti*):

It has never for even a moment been separated from it. The characteristics of the world encompass both the sentient and the insentient;
that which is eternally abiding is both the conventional and the ultimate. Fundamentally, there are no signs of birth, death, formation, or decay;

thus, every single phenomenon is none other than the sign of universal, equal, and singular quiescence. As it is said: "This wondrous Dharma of True Suchness sustains and maintains both the sentient and the inanimate worlds."
In the two worlds, within the positions of the myriad dharmas, there is fundamentally no arising or ceasing; what dharma, then, is not eternally abiding?

Those who know this at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) realize that although these dharmas are of one equal mark, inherently possessed by both sentient beings and Buddhas, they must nonetheless sit and realize the site of enlightenment, awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision before they can truly realize and know them. He can serve as a guide for the four modes of birth and employs skillful means to preach this Dharma.

Although they appear in the world in numbers as vast as the sands of the Ganges River, each does so for the sake of the great causal conditions, employing the Dharma of the Three Vehicles to provide peace within the burning house until the attainment of Buddhahood.
Therefore, he speaks of such a Dharma. Such a Dharma is precisely the Dharma known at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). II.
The verse reveals the reality:
Knowing the supreme tranquility, by the power of skillful means, although various paths are shown, their reality is the Buddha-vehicle.
"Knowing the letters" refers to that which is known only by Buddha after Buddha; this is the single principle of supreme quiescence, which encompasses persons.

For what reason does the Buddha invariably employ skillful means? It is because sentient beings possess immeasurable karmic actions that differ from one another;
each has different attachments and mental preoccupations in their deep-seated minds; their desires and natures differ in terms of diligence or indolence;
their habitual practices differ in depth or shallowness; and their faculties differ in sharpness or dullness. The Buddha fully understands all these things, and therefore he creates various causes.

This is divided into two parts. First, a brief verse on the provisional and the real, serving as the general analogy for the foundation.

The preceding reveals the reality; the following clarifies the disclosure of the provisional.

This is the observation with the Buddha-eye (buddhacakṣus). Question: If one speaks in terms of observing form, it should be the divine eye (divyacakṣus); if one distinguishes according to the capacities of sentient beings, it should be the Dharma-eye (dharmacakṣus).
Why, then, is it said in all cases that it is the Buddha-eye? Answer: The Buddha-eye is perfectly pervasive (paripūrṇa-vyāpin). By citing the supreme, it encompasses the inferior.
Furthermore, when the four eyes enter into the Buddha-eye, there is no difference between them. II. Clarifying the object of observation.

To see the sentient beings of the six realms as impoverished and lacking in merit and wisdom—this is the turbidity of the living beings (*sattva-kāṣāya*). Because they have not cultivated merit over immeasurable kalpas, they lack merit due to their poverty;
because their will is exhausted, they lack wisdom. Hence it is said: "impoverished and lacking in merit and wisdom."
To enter the perilous path of birth and death, where the continuity of suffering is never severed—this is the turbidity of life-span (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*).

The character "enter" (*ru*) signifies turning one's back on awakening and uniting with the sensory dust; it is to go from darkness into further darkness. There is only the perilous path of birth and death;
once one enters it, one loses the Dharma-body and forfeits the life of wisdom. Therefore, the *Pariṇāmanā-parivarta* (Chapter on the Transformation City) says: "It is utterly remote and cut off..."
It is a place abounding in many venomous beasts, devoid of water and grass, and a source of terror for all people.
It is here that they are deeply attached to the five desires, like a yak that loves its tail; blinded by their own craving and attachment, they are as if sightless and see nothing.
This is the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kāṣāya*). Having become deeply attached to the five sensory desires, one is then pulled along by the objects of desire;
afflictions persist and extend, never ceasing for even a moment. Both body and mind are entirely unsettled, yet sentient beings ultimately do not regard this as suffering.
To love that which one loves is truly pitiable. As for the yak (*gaur*), there is a beast among the southwestern tribes that resembles an ox;
its tail is long and five-colored. The ox loves its tail and constantly uses its body to protect it, and thus it is eventually killed by people.
This is a metaphor for how those who covet various desires likewise bring harm upon themselves; because of the mind of greedy attachment, they are obscured.
Their wisdom is like that of one born blind who cannot see; they will inevitably fall into pits and ditches. Therefore it is said:
"One is obscured by one's own craving," and so forth. (The character *máo* is pronounced as *máo*.)
Not seeking the Buddha of Great Power nor the Dharma that cuts off suffering, they deeply enter into various false views, desiring to abandon suffering through further suffering.

The first two phrases refer to the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (the defilement of the age); the subsequent phrase refers to the *dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya* (the defilement of views). This is indicated by the words "not seeking" and so forth; they are precisely obscured by these defilements.

The Buddha possesses great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), which can extract one from the suffering of the two deaths; He possesses great kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), which can bestow the two adornments (*dvividha-saṃbhāra*).
This joy connects with those in the nine realms and enables them to emerge from the ocean of birth and death; it may be said to possess great power.
Yet sentient beings do not seek the truths, conditions, and other dharmas that liberate them from the bonds of suffering, nor do they practice them.
The reason they neither seek nor practice these is that they are attached to various false views. To abandon suffering by means of suffering is, fundamentally, [the case].
When wisdom does not arise within oneself, one falsely gives rise to views such as permanence, annihilation, existence, or non-existence;

one regards what is not a cause as a cause, and what is not an effect as an effect, just like the various non-Buddhists who observe the vows of cattle or dogs, worship fire or follow water, sleep on thorns or swallow charcoal, and falsely claim that suffering is exhausted and bliss is produced, thereby attaining nirvana—all of these are defiled by false views. Furthermore,
The Buddha of Great Power is none other than our own one True Suchness Mind (*tathatā-citta*). Its power is inconceivable.
If the true mind of a single thought-moment were to manifest perfectly, then how could birth and death not be severed? How could the Buddha-way not be accomplished?
What is called seeking a Buddha with external forms is not compatible with you. △ Third, clarifying the arising of compassion in response.
For the sake of these sentient beings, he gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
"For the sake of these sentient beings" refers specifically to sentient beings in the five turbidities who are extremely wicked. He contemplates them with the perfect vision of the Buddha-eye.

Regarding all sentient beings as one’s own children, it is only for the sake of those suffering in extreme misery that the Buddha can first move his profound heart of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), necessarily employing skillful means (*upāya*) to rescue and deliver them. If he were to abandon even a single sentient being without transforming them, he would not be called "Greatly Compassionate.
△ Second, the verse on the application of skillful means, divided into two parts. First, the attempt to employ the Mahāyāna was unsuccessful; this further has three sections. First:
The Dharma is vast and difficult to apply.
When I first sat at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), observing the trees and also walking in meditation, [I attained that which is] subtle, wondrous, and supreme.
"First sitting" refers to the moment of initial attainment of perfect enlightenment; it is the time when, seated at the great *bodhimaṇḍa* of Bodhi, I preached the *Avataṃsaka*.

When the Tathāgata was practicing walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) under the tree, he did not depart from any of the Bodhi trees, yet he ascended to places such as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to practice walking meditation there.

During the three weeks of contemplation, when he was about to suddenly expound the *Avataṃsaka*, because those of the Two Vehicles were present in the assembly and neither saw nor heard him, the Tathāgata reflected that his Dharma would not be able to bring universal benefit. He then desired to employ skillful means to accommodate their capacities.
He then engaged in reflection. This was not something separate from the contemplation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* performed while walking and observing the trees for twenty-one days;
rather, it was the very reflection upon this matter, which is one of the great undertakings of a Buddha’s appearance in the world to deliver sentient beings.
Regarding the two lines, "The wisdom I have attained," he meant that if he were to bestow the Great Dharma upon them in its entirety, then what he had attained—
This wisdom is subtle and wondrous, beyond the reach of measurement or knowledge; it is supreme and cannot be swiftly realized.

Furthermore, that which is "subtle" is not what the followers of the Two Vehicles perceive; that which is "wondrous" is not what the followers of the Two Vehicles know; and that which is "supreme" is not what the followers of the Two Vehicles study.
Therefore, it is called the unsurpassed path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Through this contemplation, there first arose the gesture of removing the precious ornaments and unveiling the two hanging marks. II. The Request of Brahmā due to Heavy Obstructions.
Sentient beings have dull faculties; blinded by attachment to pleasure and ignorance, how can such as these be delivered?
He thought to himself that the Dharma he had realized was sublime, yet these beings of dull faculties were difficult to transform.

To apply the subtle and wondrous Dharma to such dull and ignorant capacities was much like trying to fit a square block into a round hole—how could it possibly be of benefit? Thus he considered those whose faculties were dull.
They do not see, hear, understand, or believe in [the truth of] attachment to pleasure and so forth;
that is to say, they all cling to the five desires as being pleasure. Being shrouded by the delusions of ignorance and folly, how could such people be easily delivered?
This was my first week of contemplation, reflecting upon and evaluating myself.
At that time, the various Brahma kings and the various Śakras, lords of the devas, [up to] requested me to turn the wheel of Dharma.
If one considers a single set of four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*), there is but one Brahmā King.

Since the Tathāgata governs a great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*) consisting of ten billion sets of four continents, there are likewise ten billion Brahmā Kings; hence the term "various" (*zhū*).
Nevertheless, these various devas merely requested [the teaching]; they themselves had not yet determined whether the Dharma to be requested was Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna. How is this known?
Contemplate the Tathāgata’s application of mindfulness: it can be seen that if he were to preach the Great Dharma, sentient beings would suffer;

yet if he were to bestow only the Lesser Teachings, it would not be his original intention. Why is it that within this [passage], there is no mention of Bodhisattvas or Śrāvakas requesting the Dharma?

It is said: Since the various devas possess urgent practice regarding the vehicle but laxity regarding the precepts, how much more so for those who serve as external protectors? Even they ought to request the Dharma;

when Bodhisattvas are correctly hearing the Great Teaching of the Avataṃsaka, how could they possibly request the Lesser Vehicle? As for the Śrāvakas and those of the Two Vehicles, they have no aspiration to seek it.
How could there be any occasion for requesting the Dharma? Furthermore, one must know that this assembly of devas are all manifestations of Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages (bhūmi).
Thus, they may be said to be in perfect harmony with the Tathāgata, like a lead singer and his accompanying musicians.

This passage generally refers to the request from all the devas of the three realms to turn the wheel of Dharma. At this point, the old man Gautama’s city walls and moats are not secure; on the contrary—
Having been glimpsed by the various devas, he immediately stepped forward among the assembly to act as the master who requests the Dharma.
Had he not opened this path at that time, how much more stable and convenient it would have been for every single person to date, with each one’s nostrils reaching toward the heavens!
Nevertheless: "Were it not for the wild geese arriving last night, how could one see the autumn at the sea-gate? △ Third, contemplating the lack of conditions.
[The fire] was extinguished.
I then reflected to myself: "If I were to praise only the Buddha Vehicle [up to the point where they] quickly enter nirvana.
This describes the second seven-day period. Having already accepted the invitation from the Heavenly King, I further reflected: "If I were to praise only..."
Regarding the Buddha Vehicle, sentient beings are submerged in the five desires;

they not only lack faith, but fear that it might instead become a cause for destroying the Dharma, leading them to fall into suffering. Thus, it is not only of no benefit, but actually harms them. Such is the case.
"I would rather not speak; it is better simply to enter nirvana quickly. △ Second, the thought that one may [speak] only after becoming equal to all Buddhas.
This is divided into two parts. First, the thought of the skillful means of all Buddhas. This is divided into three parts. First, clarifying the provisional suitability for the Three Vehicles.
Reflecting upon the power of the skillful means practiced by the Buddhas of the past, [he thought: "The path I have now attained should likewise be taught as the Three Vehicles.
This describes the third set of seven contemplations. He gives rise to a mind of great joy and first deduces and reveals the underlying pattern:
"Since the path I have attained is identical to that of all Buddhas, my saving of sentient beings should also be like theirs; thus, it is appropriate to teach the Three Vehicles."
△ Second, the explanation of the various Buddhas’ praise and consolation. This is divided into two parts. First, the formal praise of Śākyamuni:
"When he was reflecting in this way, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared... and employ the power of skillful means."
The Buddhas of the ten directions appear; this means they arrive immediately upon being called to mind. The *Yinzhi* (Record of Sounds) says:
"During the first seven days, one dwells solely upon oneself, and because the wondrous Dharma is difficult to encounter, the teachings of the Buddhas do not yet manifest before one.

During the second seven days, one dwells upon the capacities and afflictions of others, and because it is difficult to believe, the teachings of the Buddhas likewise do not manifest before one. Now, reaching the third seven days, both self and other are forgotten."
Above, they follow the principle of all Buddhas; below, they accord with the capacities of sentient beings. Thus, the Buddhas of the ten directions appear simultaneously.
This is the case of the sixteen princes from the Parable of the Phantom City, who are currently attaining Buddhahood throughout the ten directions.
These Buddhas, moreover, are not Buddhas existing separately outside of this [reality]; rather, they are the fruit of thirty-seven days of practice.
It is accomplished, manifesting all at once and in equal measure. "Brahmic voice" means that in preaching the Dharma, one is untainted. "Consolation" means peace;
"metaphor" means exhortation. The Buddhas, by means of their untainted voices, provide consolation, exhortation, and accomplishment, thereby praising [beings].
"Excellent" (śobhana) has two meanings: first, it is a praise for opening the gate of skillful means; second, it expresses the joy of being instructed by the same teaching.
Śākyamuni is translated here as "The Able Benevolent One" (Nengren); this is the clan name of the Tathāgata. "Wen" (文) carries the meaning of "Confucian" (Rú);
thus, he is both "Able Benevolent" and "Able Confucian. Because the Dharma he has attained is unsurpassed, it is called "the foremost" (prathama). It accords with all things.
The Buddha, employing the power of skillful means, then brings forth the meaning of what he has praised. Below, he begins by citing himself as testimony.
△ Second, he sets forth his own account.
"We have all likewise attained the most wondrous and foremost Dharma" (up to this point).
The following four lines clarify the intention of the various Buddhas to conceal their ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) and employ provisional means (*upāya*).

The next four lines, beginning with "those of little wisdom," explain exclusively the employment of provisional means. The final two lines, beginning with "although," clarify exclusively the manifestation of ultimate reality. Previously, it was said that only between Buddhas...
This concludes the discourse on the exhaustive investigation; here it is also clarified. △ Third, Śākyamuni’s response to Ānanda, which is further divided into three parts.
First, the direct response to Ānanda:
"Śāriputra, you should know that when I heard the profound, pure, subtle, and wonderful voice of the Holy Lion, I cried out, 'Namo to all Buddhas.'"

This is the proper response to all Buddhas; it restores the relationship between guest and host. To speak of the unsurpassed Dharma is called "Profound" (Shen); to speak of the undefiled Dharma is called "Pure" (Jing).

Possessing these two meanings of profundity and purity is called "Sublime Sound" (Miaoyin). As for the two characters "Namo": [Note: The provided text fragment ends with "Namo," which is a transliteration of the Sanskrit *namas* (homage). In the context of Buddhist liturgy, this phrase typically precedes the name of the Buddha or Bodhisattva being invoked.]
This is the meaning of respectfully following and obeying the command; it is not the words of requesting the Buddhas to deliver me as my refuge.
Furthermore, one should think: "I have emerged from this defiled and evil world; just as all the Buddhas have taught, I shall likewise act in accordance with their instructions."
This is the teaching that provides consolation. Previously, when the Brahma King requested the Dharma, the Tathāgata hesitated as he deliberated on what was appropriate;
it appeared as though he was unwilling to preach the Hīnayāna, because it was not his own aspiration. Now, however, he has accepted the exhortations of the Buddhas.
Therefore, having no other choice, he opened the way of skillful means (*upāya*). He further reflected: "I am now encountering this age of turbidity and evil;
if I do not employ the three [vehicles], it will be difficult indeed to fulfill my vow. I must simply follow the words of all the Buddhas and accord with them by applying provisional means.
Furthermore, when the World-Honored One appeared in the world, the human lifespan was one hundred years, precisely at a time when the five turbidities were raging.
At that time. △ Second, explaining the manifestation of transformation.
Having contemplated this matter, he immediately proceeded to Vārāṇasī (until) he spoke for the sake of the five bhikṣus.
This clearly demonstrates that the Tathāgata employs skillful means in his teaching. "This matter" refers to contemplating how the Buddhas exercise provisional expedients (*upāya*).
This refers to that matter. Vārāṇasī is a region within Central India, also known as the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva);
it was a royal park where ancient kings raised deer. It was here that the five bhikṣus resided to practice after they had separated from the Buddha.
It was at this site that the World-Honored One spent twelve years teaching the Hinayana doctrines of the Āgamas. The *Yinzhi* (Sound-Knowledge) commentary states: "All dharmas are quiescent..."
The mark of cessation is the principle realized by the Buddha himself; it transcends the marks of mental objects.
This Dharma is truly ineffable, yet through the power of skillful means, it is divided into the Three Vehicles and taught to the five bhikṣus.

The Buddha thought that these five would be the first to attain liberation, and thus he went to the Deer Park. During one summer retreat, he disciplined their faculties and first taught the Four [Noble Truths] to Ājñātakauṇḍinya.
He attained liberation through the Dharma of the Truths. Next, for Bimbisāra, he preached on the blessings and joys of heaven resulting from generosity;
both men simultaneously realized the fruit [of the path]. Thirdly, for the two, Kāśyapa and Kauṇḍinya, he spoke as before, and they all attained the noble fruit.
Some say that these five bhikṣus were those who followed and attended the Buddha when he first left the household life at the command of his father while still a prince.
There were three men: the first was named Abhi, which in this language means Ma-sheng (Horse-Victorious); the second was Bāṭi, which means Xiao-xian (Little Virtuous);
and the third was Kūli, whose meaning in Chinese is not detailed, though it is also said to be Mahānāman. There were two others from maternal kinship: the first was Ājñāta.
This "Jiebenji" (解本寂) is Dharmapāla, who is Cennana (陳那). The second is Kāśyapa, which means "Drinking Light.
These five men had all long served as his close attendants; therefore, they were ordained first. △ Third, the benefits received.
This is called the turning of the wheel of Dharma, whereby there arise the sounds of *nirvāṇa* and the distinct names of the *arhat*, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha.
"Turning" possesses the characteristic of flowing without stagnation; the "wheel" possesses the function of pushing, crushing, and moving.

The turning of the wheel of Dharma refers to the method of the four truths in three turnings, which, through their progression, constitute the twelve aspects. First is the turning that demonstrates the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
1. The Turning of Declaration: "This is the nature of suffering as oppression; this is the nature of origination as that which invites [suffering];

this is the nature of cessation as that which is realizable; this is the nature of the path as that which is cultivatable. 2. The Turning of Exhortation: "This is suffering; you should know it. This is origination;
you should abandon it. This is cessation; you should realize it. This is the path; you should cultivate it. 3. The Turning of Realization.
He turned [the wheel] and said: "This is suffering; I have known it, and you should know it as well. This is the origin [of suffering];
I have abandoned it, and you should abandon it as well. This is cessation; I have realized it, and you should realize it as well. This is the path; I have cultivated it."

You, too, should practice this. Regarding the "sound of nirvāṇa": this refers to Dignāga and others who, upon hearing the Dharma, attained the fruit, severed the delusions of views, and partially realized *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. It was from this point that the proclamation of the sound of nirvāṇa first began.
An Arhat is the fruit realized by the Saṅgha; through this, the names of the Three Jewels—Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha—became manifest.
Within the world, it is therefore said: "The names 'Dharma' and 'Saṃgha' are distinct. △ Second, explaining the constant manifestation over a long duration:
"From kalpas long ago, I have praised and revealed the Dharma of Nirvāṇa, wherein the suffering of birth and death is forever exhausted; I have always spoken thus."

Tiantai says: Fearing that there may be those who harbor doubts—claiming that at the very beginning the Buddha was not yet able to discern their capacities, and that it was only after seeking out the thoughts of all Buddhas and receiving their consolation that he finally came to know their root-natures and proceeded to teach with differentiation—the Buddha therefore explains this with the following verse:
"It is not that I did not know how to employ skillful means; rather, I specifically desired to lead [them]..."

This clarifies that the Way of all Buddhas is the same. How could one fail to recognize that from the time of kalpas long ago, I have always praised and constantly demonstrated this Dharma of Nirvana, and have always spoken of the Sangha who has exhausted the suffering of birth and death?
It is not only today that these names of the Three Jewels exist. Therefore, it is said: "He always speaks thus. △ Third, the verse manifesting the One Vehicle, divided into four parts. First:
Having attained the capacity to manifest the reality, Śāriputra,
you should know that I see these sons of the Buddha [and others]— this refers to the teachings spoken through skillful means.
Furthermore, from the distant kalpas of antiquity, I have constantly taught the Dharma and transformed beings, so that the single vehicle of the Mahāyāna has been awakened within them.

It is because he must necessarily expound the Mahāyāna path for them. Furthermore, when it was said, "Śāriputra, you should know that today I shall certainly expound the Mahāyāna," this was solely due to the resonance of their spiritual capacity (*indriya*).

When I say "I see," it is with the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*) that I behold those of perfect capacity seated here, declaring their aspiration to seek the Buddha-way and so forth; that is to say, there is a class of true sons of the Buddha whose original vow...
Seeking unsurpassed bodhi, there were hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of beings who all gave rise to a heart of profound and respectful veneration.
They came to where the Buddha was. That they "came" means it was not through hearsay passed down from one to another, but that they personally saw the Buddha and personally heard the Dharma.
That they were "respectful" means they must have deeply conceived a love for the Dharma; thus, they had something seen and something known.
Such persons as these have not planted roots of goodness under only one or two Buddhas;
they have already heard the teachings spoken through skillful means under hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. Tiantai said: "There are four such types."
There are those whose obstacles have been removed but whose capacity has not yet been aroused, such as the various Arhats.

There are those whose capacity has been aroused but whose obstacles have not yet been removed, such as the humans and devas in this assembly. There are those whose capacity has been aroused and whose obstacles have been removed, such as the sons of the Buddhas.

There are those whose capacity is not aroused and whose obstacles have not been removed, such as those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Those spoken of here belong to the latter category—those whose capacity has been aroused and whose obstacles have been removed. △
Second, regarding the time for the actual manifestation of the Great [Vehicle]:
I then had this thought: "The reason the Tathāgata has appeared is to preach the Buddha-wisdom; now is precisely that time.
Previously it was said that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, preach it only at such times; therefore, now is indeed that very time. Thus the Tathāgata acted.
I reflect: "It was for the sake of one great causal matter that I appeared in the world; originally, it was to reveal and demonstrate the Buddha’s wisdom.
Now, since the capacity [of beings] has been stirred and the time is right for its proclamation. △ Third, bestowing the teaching of the One Vehicle.
Śāriputra, you should know that for those of dull faculties and small wisdom—up until now—I have spoken only of the Unsurpassed Way.

It is not that I did not speak of the Great [Vehicle] during the forty years prior; rather, it was because the faculties of the assembly were dull and their wisdom shallow, and they were full of many forms of pride.
They are attached to various false views; hearing this, they would not understand it, and I feared it would become a cause for them to slander the Dharma and fall into suffering.
Now there is one of great capacity, whose disposition accords with my original intention; therefore, I have given rise to great joy and deliver this teaching of fearlessness. As for "fearlessness":
It is not that there is anything else to fear; rather, it is that [the Buddha] does not fear that those who hear the Dharma will fall into suffering.
He is upright and speaks with directness, unlike the skillful and expedient discourse used for inducement mentioned previously. Now, he shall speak only of the Unsurpassed Way.
△ Fourth, clarifying the benefit of entering the principle.
Upon hearing this Dharma, the Bodhisattva’s net of doubts has been entirely removed, and the twelve hundred Arhats shall all likewise become Buddhas.
This Bodhisattva refers to those who, forty years ago, harbored the great seed [of enlightenment] but had not yet matured;
they are precisely the ones capable of hearing this Dharma and may all receive the name of Bodhisattva. Regarding the "net of doubts," among the three types of doubt:

This pertains to the category of those characterized by doubt. That is to say, although these individuals of bodhisattva lineage believe and know that they will attain buddhahood, all that they have heard thus far has been taught as provisional means (*upāya*).
Furthermore, they cannot yet avoid doubting whether the fruit of the Great Dharma truly exists or not.
Now, hearing that the Tathāgata has completely relinquished provisional means to preach the Unsurpassed Way, the net of their doubts is entirely cast off. Now, having heard...

The practice of the Dharma. It was not for the sake of the Bodhisattvas gaining benefit that you twelve hundred people—who previously were not permitted to attain Buddhahood—are now granted full permission;
it is certain that you shall all become Buddhas in the future, and this will not be in vain.
Hearing such words is what is meant by the "clashing of the capacity and the teaching. IV. Verses on the Rarity of the Dharma. This section has two parts. First, verses on the Tathāgata...
This is the sublime Dharma.
Just as the Buddhas of the three periods of time have the ritual for preaching the Dharma, so do I now likewise preach this non-discriminative Dharma.
All the rituals for preaching the Dharma used by the Buddhas of the three periods of time consist of provisional means first and ultimate reality last; such too is my present [teaching].

The coming [of this teaching] and its returning are likewise so; this was previously explained through expedient means. Now, definitively revealing and clarifying the One Vehicle, he teaches the Dharma of non-discrimination.
△ Second, the verse on the time when it is taught, divided into two parts. First, citing those who find it difficult to encounter:
"The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is remote and difficult to encounter; likewise, it is difficult for such a person [to arise].
The first two lines clarify the difficulty of encountering the Buddhas. Furthermore, within the world of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), sentient beings lack merit;

thus, even though the Buddhas constantly dwell in the world, they may not meet them even when they are present, and they may not see them even when they are visible. Therefore, there is the account of the Brahmā King requesting the Buddha [to teach].
It is said: "One hundred and eighty kalpas passed in vain without a Buddha appearing; therefore, it is called 'remote. Since the Buddha is so remote, how could he be encountered easily?

Thus, this constitutes a difficulty. The two phrases regarding his appearance in the world mean that although a Buddha appears in the world, if he wishes to preach this dharma that is difficult to believe and difficult to understand for the sake of sentient beings, he must wait for the proper time; it is not otherwise.
If it were not spoken at that time, one would know that even to preach this wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle is not easy.

As for the statement that "it is difficult to hear the Dharma throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas," it means that sentient beings must pass through immeasurable kalpas before they finally encounter a Buddha;
yet even when they do encounter a Buddha, some have eyes but cannot see, and some have ears but cannot hear. For example, among the ten trillion people in the city of Rājagṛha, there were three...
Ten trillion people saw the Buddha and heard the Dharma; thirty trillion people saw the Buddha but did not hear the Dharma; and thirty trillion people neither saw the Buddha nor heard the Dharma.
Thus one knows that even seeing the Buddha and being able to hear this wondrous Dharma of the Mahāyāna is still difficult.
Those who are able to listen to this Dharma are like the hundreds of thousands of humans and devas in this assembly—there are none among them who do not hear it.
Furthermore, how many are there who can penetrate the principle and uphold it? Such individuals as those who believe, understand, and uphold it are not easily found.
Because this Buddha-dharma is difficult to hear and difficult to encounter, the *udumbara* flower is cited as a metaphor to clarify this point.
△ Second, the illustration of its extreme rarity:
"For example, like the udumbara flower, which all cherish and delight in... (up to) "...it is even rarer than the udumbara flower.
This flower blooms but once every three thousand years; thus, it is truly a rare occurrence in both the heavens and the human realm. If...
Upon seeing these flowers, there is none who does not find them delightful. As for their appearing "from time to time," this means that these flowers do not manifest at improper times;
they appear only when it is the proper time. This serves as a general metaphor for the Buddhas encountered previously, the teachings they expounded, and the Dharma that was heard.
Those who hear [this teaching] are all as rare and difficult to encounter as this flower.

Furthermore, it clarifies that those who hear the Dharma with joy—even those who merely utter a single word of praise—are not among the ranks of those who hear the Dharma in a casual or superficial manner;
even they are the most difficult to find among the difficult to find. How much more so for those who, with a single-minded heart, believe, understand, accept, and uphold it!
Yes. If one is already able to believe and accept it and is able to praise it, then there is no need for extensive offerings;

one has thereby already made offerings to the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time. Why is this? Furthermore, that which the Buddhas of the three periods have realized is this Dharma, and that which they appeared in the world to reveal is also this Dharma.
Now, since one is able to believe in this Dharma and give rise to praise, [one has already made offerings].
Such a person attains perfect enlightenment together with the Tathāgata, is thus delighted by the Tathāgata, and receives his Dharma-offering.
How could such a person be easily found? Therefore it is said: "rarer than the udumbara flower.
△ Fifth, the verse on "not being in vain," divided into two parts: first, the person is not in vain.
"You all must not harbor doubts that I am the King of All Dharmas... [and] that I have no śrāvaka disciples.
Regarding "you all must not doubt," this was an entrustment intended to ensure that you go forth from here without further hesitation. I am the Great Dharma King;
what I have spoken is entirely truthful. How much more so now, as I sit upon the throne of devas and humans, addressing not just one person—what I have said is not false.
"It is not two, nor three; it is the path of the One Vehicle. Those taught are not śrāvaka disciples, but followers of the Bodhisattva Vehicle.
How could you still harbor further doubts? △ Second, the Dharma is not in vain.
"Śāriputra, you śrāvakas and bodhisattvas should know that this wondrous Dharma is the secret essence of all Buddhas.
That which cannot be fathomed by those of the two vehicles is called 'secret' (mi); that which summarizes the wondrousness of the ten dharma-realms is called 'essence' (yào).
Since all Buddhas regard this Dharma as both secret and essential, it is indeed worthy of trust. This was the preceding entrustment."
"Do not harbor doubts regarding the Buddha. This is an exhortation not to harbor doubts regarding the Dharma. △ Sixth, the verse on encouraging faith, divided into two parts.
First, the selection of the assembly:
in this world of the five turbidities, beings who merely delight in and cling to various desires will ultimately never seek the Buddha-way.
Sentient beings in the five turbidities are attached only to various desires, like a yak that loves its tail; how could they have a mind that delights in the Dharma?
Therefore, they must be excluded. Moreover, those who are attached even to *nirvāṇa* are still excluded as not being vessels for the Mahāyāna, let alone those attached to desire.
It is known that such people certainly do not seek the Buddha-way, and I likewise do not [entrust them with] the secret essentials.
He preaches the Dharma for their sake.
However, in future ages, wicked people, hearing the Buddha preach the One Vehicle, will become confused and fail to believe or accept it; they will destroy the Dharma and fall into evil realms.
It is clear from this that this is the time when he entrusts Śāriputra to preach the Dharma. As for "future ages," the times will grow ever more degenerate.
As for evil people, their faith becomes increasingly meager; at such a time of extreme degradation, how easy could it be to explain this difficult-to-believe Dharma to those who are so wicked?
Thus, when such ignorant, deluded, and confused individuals hear it and do not believe, they will inevitably destroy the Dharma and fall into suffering—of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, those who preach this Dharma must be cautious; one must know this secret and essential point.
This is the meaning. It must not be bestowed upon those who are not fit vessels.
For those who possess a sense of shame and modesty and whose pure resolve seeks the Buddha-way, one should extensively praise the path of the One Vehicle for such individuals as these.
This further entrusts the duty of preaching; one must not miss the opportunity or the proper time. Those with a sense of shame and modesty do not become deluded.
Those who are pure are not deluded. Regarding those whose resolve seeks the Buddha-way, this is said in contrast to those who do not believe or accept the teaching.
For such persons, one should extensively praise the unsurpassed, wondrous path of the One Vehicle; this may be called preaching the Dharma according to their capacity.
From "Do not harbor any doubt" up to this point, the meaning of these several passages is that although the World-Honored One had not yet [bestowed it] upon Śāriputra...
Although Śāriputra was granted the prophecy of his future Buddhahood, there was already an implicit entrustment within that intent. The reality of benefiting oneself and others is as follows:
the previous instruction not to doubt the Buddha-dharma was intended to comfort his mind regarding self-benefit;

this current instruction to select the person for whom he should preach is the transmission of the teaching for the sake of transforming others. Thus, the Tathāgata’s words were spoken with bitter earnestness and a heart of fervent compassion.
He instructed him repeatedly and earnestly, intending that in the future he would become an eye for gods and humans and serve as a master of transformation and instruction.
This itself constitutes the completion of Śāriputra’s attainment of the prediction at the end of his life. △ Second, Encouraging Faith.
"Śāriputra, you should know that the Dharma of all Buddhas is thus" (up to) "they cannot clearly understand this.
This is a general conclusion and exhortation. It means that the Buddhas appear in the world for one great matter;

the ritual of their preaching the Dharma to awaken sentient beings—beginning with the small and ending with the great—is entirely like this. Those who do not study and learn this [will remain as they are].
This shows that [others] were unable to understand it, whereas by contrast, it reveals that Śāriputra was able to study and understand this sublime Dharma.
This passage constitutes the World-Honored One’s statement that he knew Śāriputra had already attained realization and entry.
"Since you have already known that the Buddhas, the Teachers of the World... [up to] ...you yourselves shall become Buddhas"—this refers to Śāriputra and the others.
Regarding Kāśyapa, Maudgalyāyana, Subhūti, and Kātyāyana, they are cited as examples of those who received their predictions within the *Parivarta*;
furthermore, the twelve hundred others are cited as the causal conditions within the *Parivarta*.
Having already understood those who have received the prediction, he then proceeded to provide various detailed explanations according to the supreme Dharma:
"You all now know that the Buddhas are the Teachers and World-Controllers; you also know the Dharma taught by the Buddhas."
Regarding the provisional and the ultimate, the Great and the Small, these are matters of skillful means applied according to suitability.
Once one understands the Buddha-dharma, all previous doubts will be eliminated without remainder. As long as doubt has not been removed, how can a joyful mind arise?
Now, however, there is immeasurable joy. The reason for this joy is that a human body is difficult to obtain, and now, fortunately—
It has been attained! Faith is difficult to produce; now, fortunately, it has arisen. The Buddhas are difficult to encounter; fortunately, you have encountered them.
The Buddha-Dharma is difficult to hear; fortunately, you have heard it. Even this should not be considered great joy, for this is the treasury of the Great Dharma-Jewel.

"Since the kalpa as numerous as motes of dust, that which you had not yet attained—that is, the permission for Śrāvakas to attain Buddhahood within forty years—has now been heard by you in the words of me, the Tathāgata.
Your heart knows with compassion that in a future age you will certainly attain Buddhahood;
would this not cause you to give rise to great joy? Since the Tathāgata emerged from samādhi, he has twice uttered these praises."

From the perspective of the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate truth, he extensively cites therein the historical manifestations of the Buddhas of the three periods appearing in the world, as well as his own forty years of diligent effort in skillfully employing expedient means, revealing them one by one;

all of this is nothing other than an elucidation of the provisional and ultimate characteristics of the four classes of sages and the six realms of ordinary beings contained within the light between his eyebrows. And...
This was the Tathāgata returning to his original intention for appearing in the world for the sake of all people:
to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, which is the single great cause and condition.

Taking this Dharma of provisional and ultimate wisdom, he expounded it from beginning to end in its entirety, speaking it for Śāriputra; yet Śāriputra had no many questions or doubts therein, but only one.
Taste this silence and listen attentively. When the teaching reaches its conclusion, he says: "Since you have already understood, your hearts give rise to great joy.
From this, one can see that the student attained immediate and clear awakening; their provisional doubts were instantly extinguished.
This is what is meant by saying that only a father truly knows his son. Thus, the Tathāgata’s correct teaching was completed.
The *Miaofa Lianhua Jing Shou* (Hand-Instruction on the Lotus Sutra),
Fascicle Two; *Miaofa Lianhua Jing Shou*, Fascicle Three,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhixiang of Yunfeng, Chu Province.

The third chapter, the "Parable Chapter" (Upamā-parivarta), states in its section summary: The general purport of this chapter is as follows. Because the World-Honored One had directly expressed his fundamental intention in the preceding chapter, Śāriputra—being the foremost among those of wisdom—was the first to realize it.
Through that realization, he attained the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and thus for the first time recognized his former ignorance.

He repented his transgressions and reproached himself, whereupon he was granted the prediction of attaining Buddhahood. Now, as for those who are śrāvakas, they have long been stalled within the provisional vehicle;

that they now, upon hearing this once, immediately believe and receive the prediction of becoming Buddhas, is because they have realized that all phenomena are the very nature of the mind itself, thereby accomplishing the body of wisdom through their own awakening rather than through another. Since it has been granted that they shall become Buddhas, it must also necessarily follow that...

Regarding those who pass through many kalpas: because ignorance has not yet been exhausted, they must proceed directly for a vast duration, serving many Buddhas and refining themselves until it is completely purified before attaining actual realization. Such is the general meaning of the bestowal of predictions (vyākaraṇa).

As for the fourfold assembly, because their attachment to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) was so deep and heavy, they harbored doubts and lacked faith, each thinking to themselves that they would certainly never attain Buddhahood.
He likewise had no aspiration [for enlightenment]. Now, seeing that Śāriputra has received his prediction, the entire assembly has given rise to joy;
therefore, he disrobed to make an offering to the Buddha, thereby expressing his intent toward liberation.

While Śāriputra’s wisdom is preeminent and he has already attained faith and entry, there are still many in the great assembly whose faith has not yet reached such a level. For this reason, he specifically requested the World-Honored One to explain the causes for this.

This serves as a condition to cause them to abandon doubt and regret. Now, the World-Honored One has expounded the Parable of the Burning House to describe the state of birth and death within the triple world and to clarify the Tathāgata’s compassionate mind of salvation.
By first promising the three vehicles and subsequently bestowing them equally, he precisely reveals his intention today of abolishing the provisional to establish the real.
Although the śrāvakas may still harbor attachment and parsimony toward *nirvāṇa*, [he now grants it to them].

As for "Abandonment" (Śāradvatīputra), having now heard this teaching, he has also attained resolute faith and inclination toward it; therefore, it is followed by the title "Chapter on Faith and Understanding.

"Parable" (*dṛṣṭānta*) means comparison; "analogy" (*upamā*) means instruction through elucidation. By borrowing worldly matters to provide comparisons, one clarifies the intent of the Dharma-exposition;
hence, it is called the "Chapter on Parables. II. Śāriputra’s Account of Receiving the Teaching and Attaining Understanding. This section is divided into two parts. First:
The sūtra author describes the scene:
At that time, Śāriputra leaped for joy and, rising immediately, joined his palms and gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance.

"At that time" refers to having received the aforementioned teaching on the Dharma, which elucidates the single great cause and condition (*ekamahākaruṇāhetu*), whereby he has already awakened to the Buddha's knowledge.
This was at the time of his seeing [the Buddha]. He leaped for joy and rejoiced greatly. This resulted from the understanding he had attained through hearing the Dharma previously;
now that the wondrous Dharma had been obtained, his sublime realization was fully manifested—how could he not be joyful?

As for "joining his palms and gazing upon the countenance," the author of the sutra, intending to relate his own account, first describes his physical appearance to demonstrate the utmost reverence of his three karmas (body, speech, and mind). *Yue* (pronounced *yuē*). Section Two.
Śāriputra speaks for himself. This is divided into two parts. First, the prose section, which is further divided into three. First, expressing his joy, he says to the Buddha:
"Now, having heard this Dharma-sound from the World-Honored One, my heart leaps with joy; I have attained what I have never experienced before."

The "Dharma-sound" refers to the aforementioned teaching that opens the three [vehicles] to reveal the one, as well as the various causes and conditions, including the sounds of the Dharma concerning the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) for śrāvakas to attain Buddhahood. Indeed, this Dharma-sound was previously unheard, but is now heard for the first time.
Therefore, he attained such exultation as had never been experienced before. [△@△] One must understand that this joy of Śāriputra was not obtained today, but was obtained yesterday.

In the preceding chapter, the Tathāgata said: "Since you have already understood the expedient means of all Buddhas and no longer harbor any doubts, your hearts give rise to great joy; you know for yourselves that you shall become Buddhas. Thus, it was joy.
The sentiments of his joy have already been set forth by the Tathāgata in advance.

As for Śāriputra, having gone to such lengths to bare his heart and reveal his innermost thoughts, exhausting the account of his deluded states over several decades, he truly demonstrates today how deeply he has attained right view and how extreme is his remorse.
II. Specific Explanation, divided into three parts: 1. Explanation of his former grief and lamentation.
Why is this? From the time I followed the Buddha [until] I lost the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision—"of the past" refers to the period of the Vaipulya sūtras.
The meaning is: why is it that today I leap for joy and say that I have attained what I never had before?
It is because regarding such a great Dharma, during the period of the Vaipulya, when did I ever...
I have not heard it. Furthermore, how could I have failed to see the Tathāgata bestowing the prediction of Buddhahood upon the various Bodhisattvas?
Yet, although I was present in this assembly, it seemed as though I had no part in it; that I ultimately could not participate in such a matter is truly a source of profound sorrow.
To dwell together, to reside together, to see together, and to hear together, yet alone not receive a prediction—this is to lose oneself before the Tathāgata.
"Immeasurable knowledge and vision. This is likely an account of his self-reproach and self-blame.
That he now experiences such joy is entirely due to the sorrow he felt in the past. "Yu" (預) means to reach; it means to participate and enter.
△ Second, explaining the remembrance of former sentiments.
“World-Honored One, we have always dwelt alone in mountain forests and beneath trees... (omitted)... this is our own fault, not the World-Honored One’s.
This clarifies the reason for their sorrow at not having been included [in the assembly]. It describes the mind they habitually applied themselves to.
“Always dwelling alone” does not mean dwelling there by mere chance; rather, mountain forests and the shade of trees are places that depart from clamor and avoid distraction. Thus they practiced.
"Sitting" refers to the time when one engages in contemplation. "Whenever one forms this thought" does not mean that it is merely a single instance of reflection.

"Dharmatā" (the nature of phenomena) refers to the true nature of this wondrous Dharma. "Entering together" means that one considers oneself to be entering the dharmatā in common with all the bodhisattvas.
It means: "In the past, when I dwelt in solitude—whether sitting or walking—I constantly reflected upon myself and the bodhisattvas."
“Sā. We have equally realized this nature; it is fitting that we should all receive the prediction [of enlightenment] together.

Why does the Tathāgata alone deliver me by means of the Hīnayāna? Furthermore, I reflect: this must surely be because my mind has not yet expanded, my strength is insufficient, and my resolve is inadequate.
It is the fault of my failure to seek diligently; truly, this is my own error, and not that the World-Honored One holds a dual mind.”
...Thus it is. △ Third, explaining why [the Buddha] did not wait in the past.
Why is this? If we had waited for him to preach [until] the end of the night, we would have reproached ourselves every day.

This clarifies the reason for his self-reproach. Regarding the character *dai* (await): it refers to the moment when one’s power and skill have reached maturity and the conditions for the transformation of the vital energy (*qi*) have arrived.

Regarding the character *yin* (due to): this means that because the time had not yet come for the Buddha or the followers of the Two Vehicles, he did not swiftly bestow upon them the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
That which the Tathāgata endured and did not speak for twenty years was because our spiritual power was not yet pure and the time had not yet arrived.

If we had maintained this same patient attitude toward ourselves, cultivating with sharp resolve and diligent effort, and been able to forget our former inferiority, the Buddha would surely have delivered us by means of the Mahāyāna. Yet, we ultimately failed to realize this.
The Tathāgata employs skillful means to reveal the provisional teachings. Hearing what was first spoken, they immediately accepted it with superficiality;
engaging in contemplation, they immediately grasped realization with superficiality. For this reason, throughout the past, day and night, there was no time or place where I did not reproach myself.
[△@△] To meet [the teaching] and immediately accept it describes the cause of insubstantiality. Contemplating—
"Merely seeking realization" describes the fruit that is not yet real. He constantly reproaches himself;

although this is the resolve to turn from the small toward the great, his sincerity in diligent study and courageous effort is no less than the Tathāgata’s acts of gouging out his own flesh for lamps and cutting off his flesh during his causal stage.
How could he truly be characterized by the term "Small Vehicle"? (The character *kè* [pronounced *kè*] means "to reproach"). △ Third, the conclusion.
It is accomplished.

Now, having heard from the Buddha what has never been heard before (up to) being born through transformation by the Dharma and attaining a portion of the Buddha-Dharma—this precisely clarifies that today one has attained true knowledge and realized the truth. This unprecedented phenomenon is precisely the provisional and the ultimate.

This is the wisdom of the ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*). Regarding the severing of doubt and regret: once one knows that the provisional (*upāya*) is identical to the ultimate, one no longer doubts oneself or others.
Generally, there are three kinds of doubt: first, doubt regarding the Dharma;

that is, thinking, "If all the dharmas possessed by the Tathāgata are non-dual, and I have now already realized them, why does he alone bestow predictions upon the bodhisattvas? Could it be that my realization is not true?"
First, doubt regarding the Dharma: "Is this not the True Dharma? Second, doubt regarding the person: "The Buddha never fails to save all his children with an impartial mind;
why does he now record such distinctions? Why does he alone fail to think of us? Third, doubt regarding oneself:

"The task of sitting at the site of enlightenment and turning the wheel of the Dharma is no light matter; perhaps it is not something we are capable of bearing. There are two kinds of regret: first, regret... [text ends]
Transgressions cannot be rectified; second, remorse for past goodness cannot be transformed. Such doubts and regrets are now all forever severed; hence it is said, "severing all doubts and regrets.
"Serene" (*taiyan*) clarifies that body and mind are pervaded by joy. If doubts and regrets were not eliminated, one would ultimately be beset by long sighs;
how could body and mind be made universally joyful? Now, with joy and the exhaustion of doubt, one begins to believe in the Truth.
Suddenly liberated from anxiety, one attains peace and stability. Once faith is true, one realizes that there has never been any difference between oneself and the Buddha;
therefore, I am truly a son of the Buddha. The Dharma arises from the mouth, for it is that from which the Dharmakāya is born.
Thus we know that the Buddha-dharma is precisely our own dharma; therefore, one attains its proper portion. [△@△] Śāriputra said, "Today I have come to know it.
This is not a superficial or ordinary knowledge; it is the very point of thorough penetration from beginning to end, the place of actual awakening and realization.

It is what is called the "correct eye at the crown of the head," crossing over the profound barrier of the ultimate. How could this not be called "something never before encountered" as one attains the Dharma?
Section on the Divisions. △ Second, the Verses in Praise. This is divided into three parts. First, the verse that marks the joy.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"I have heard this sound of the Dharma and attained what I have never had before" (up to the point where it says) "hearing it also removes sorrow and affliction.

This verse describes the present attainment and expresses joy and fortune. As for "the sound of the Dharma," it refers to hearing the aforementioned revealed sound of the Dharma concerning the provisional and the real, wherein Buddha and Buddha are non-dual.
"Attaining what has never been had before" means that for forty years [since the beginning of his teaching], [this has not occurred].
Having now just heard this, my heart is filled with great joy; all the nets of doubt that have long entangled me are completely cleared away.
Although the Buddha’s teaching I previously received was called "Hīnayāna," the Mahāyāna was already contained within it.
Thus we know that the Buddha’s voice is perfect and wondrous, manifesting both the provisional and the ultimate. Therefore, it is truly rare for those who hear it to each find what they need.
Explanation: When the burdens of worldly dust are cast off, it is said that "all suffering and affliction are eliminated.

As for myself today, having heard this sound of the Dharma, all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted and all sorrows have been released; such is the manifest proof. II. Specific Explanation, divided into three parts.
One verse expresses lamentation:
"Whether I dwell in mountain valleys or beneath forest trees" (up to) "all these I have lost.
This verse further clarifies the lamentation. The two lines beginning with "I dwell" indicate the places of lamentation; the lines beginning with "walking and sitting" indicate...
At the time of lamentation, the phrase "contemplating" indicates the cause of the lamentation. "Alas! is a sound of sorrowful sighing. "Self-reproach" is the reality of the lamentation, meaning:
"I was not permitted to participate in this matter. "Truly regretting not having attained Buddhahood" is a term of self-interrogation.
"Self-deception" means: "I did not receive the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa). This refers to being truly self-deceived and self-obscured, refusing to be courageous.
"Fierce diligence" refers to the heart that is moved by a sense of poignant grief. Why is it that one feels such grief?
It is because [one thinks]: "I too am a son of the Buddha. The meaning of liberation is something I have also attained.

Since I have entered the state of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*) together with all these bodhisattvas, why do they alone receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), while I alone am unable to expound the Unsurpassed Way in the future? Thus, [the mind is filled with] anguish.
Is it adorned with the marks [of a Great Man] and endowed with the ten powers and other such merits? This is the reality of that which evokes compassion.
It is the "Nirvana with remainder" attained through the aforementioned contemplative realization; it is not the ultimate Nirvana without outflows.
"Sharing the same single Dharma" means that I and the Bodhisattva have both entered together into the single nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
"I alone have not attained it" means that the Bodhisattva has attained it alone.
These two phrases conclude all the aforementioned merits, which I have entirely lost. ○ "Golden-colored" refers to the entire body of the Buddha. All...

The color of purple-gold light. The thirty-two marks are: first, the soles of the feet are level and even like the bottom of a casket; second, the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of the feet;

continuing thus up to the thirty-first, the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows; and the thirty-second, the cranial protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) on the crown of the head. The ten powers (*daśabala*) are:
beginning from the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna-bala*), up to the tenth, the power of knowing the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-jñāna-bala*).

Exerting all effort, there are the various liberations, namely the eight liberations; the eighty minor marks, beginning from the mark of the invisible crown of the head and ending with the mark of excellence on the hands and feet;
and the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), beginning from the non-failure of bodily action.
Ultimately reaching wisdom, one knows the three periods of time without obstruction; this is entirely not shared with those of the two vehicles.
△ Second, the verse on remembrance, which has two parts. First, the remembrance of not yet attaining Buddhahood.
"When I was walking alone in meditation, I saw the Buddha amidst the great assembly... as to whether he had lost [his way] or not.

The former refers to his own reflection that he had lost the merit of the Buddha’s self-realization; this refers to his own reflection that he had lost the merit of the Buddha’s benefit for sentient beings.
That is to say, whenever he saw the Tathāgata dwelling amidst the ocean-like assembly and extensively proclaiming the Way and the Dharma, he was alone.
I am unable to speak of it. I see that the Buddha’s name and fame pervade the ten directions, whereas I alone lack such renown.

I see that the Buddha is able to bring vast benefit to all living beings, whereas I alone lack such efficacy. Yet whenever I reflect upon this, there is no occasion when I do not strike my breast in pain and feel deep shame.
Retreating into contemplation, I consider what the Tathāgata has realized, what he has proclaimed, what he harbors in his mind, and what he has revealed. I—
All possess [this potential]. Yet, that you are currently unable to realize it or practice it is self-deception.
To falsely claim that there is something to be attained or realized in *nirvāṇa-with-remainder*, while failing to seek the Unsurpassed Vehicle (*anuttarayāna*), is self-delusion.
In the past, I constantly contemplated this throughout day and night for many cycles; unable to resolve this matter myself, I was about to seek instruction from the Tathāgata for my own benefit.
"This is a wondrous application for the benefit of others; have I indeed lost it, or have I not? This was my concern twenty years ago.
[△@△] Consider the words of Śāriputra when he said that he saw the Buddha while walking alone:

this does not merely mean seeing the present Buddha, but rather personally beholding the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) in such a majestic and sublime form, and the wondrous qualities inherent within that Dharma-body.
To employ [this] in such a vast manner while previously refusing to take it upon oneself is to deceive and delude oneself.
Desiring to seek the Buddha’s seal of approval, he therefore questioned the World-Honored One.
I have constantly observed the World-Honored One praising all bodhisattvas (up to) leading the multitudes to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

"Constantly observing" means that within the assemblies of the Vaipulya sūtras, I have seen the Tathāgata disparage the Hīnayāna while extolling the perfect and subtle [Dharma], and most highly praising all bodhisattvas. For this reason, day and night, I have constantly deliberated upon this Mahāyāna.
How could I be excluded from this wondrous realm? Could it be that the Tathāgata has shown partiality toward me by withholding the Mahāyāna to save me?

Now, hearing the sound of the Dharma which reveals that provisional means return to the ultimate reality, I finally understand that what was previously taught was a wondrous response suited to the occasion.
Although it was called "Small," its essence is actually the inconceivable One Vehicle (Ekayāna) free from outflows. Such is my realization.
"It has already been established, yet it must cause us to reach the place of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).

[△@△] Previously, it was said that constantly contemplating this matter day and night, yet not attaining Buddhahood—this matter is precisely the work of bringing benefit to sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
This 'deliberating day and night' refers to not attaining the Dharma; this matter is precisely..."

Regarding the matter of being praised by the Buddha and entrusted with the affairs of the Buddha-dharma, the two phrases concerning the "outflow-free" (anāsrava) state clarify that these are now all attained.

Thus, the phrase "outflow-free" refers to the attainment of the Dharma; it is only upon reaching the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) that one becomes a Buddha. △ Second, the contemplation of realizing the minor fruit.
"I was originally one who clung to false views and served as a teacher to various brahmins" (up to) "attained entry into nirvāṇa.
This verse reflects upon his past realization of the Lesser Vehicle; it bears witness to the profound compassion with which the Tathāgata rescued him.

It means that in my former life, I was fundamentally a person clinging to heterodoxy; not only did I myself cling to it, but I also served as a teacher for those who clung to heterodoxy, preaching to them.
Adhering to false teachings, how could I have known of this right knowledge and right view?
With his Buddha-eye, the World-Honored One perceived that I would certainly become a Buddha in the future; at present, I was merely attached to delusive falsehoods.

Therefore, he taught me the various dharmas of emptiness to uproot the source of my error. I immediately attained realization through emptiness and gave rise to a sense of peace and security. How extraordinary!

I did not realize that the Tathāgata taught this Dharma of emptiness as a medicine precisely suited to the disease, a skillful and expedient means intended to cause one to leave behind all attachments.
Yet I proceeded to claim that I had attained nirvāṇa; was I not thereby betraying this profound resolve?
"Brahmacārin" refers here to the non-Buddhist practitioners of the Brahmin tradition. III. Verses on the Present Attainment (divided into four parts). 1. Verse.
"Self-awakening.
Now, for the first time, he awakens to the fact that [what he previously thought] was not true extinction (nirvāṇa)—that it was not the eternal cessation where nothing remains.
This verse describes his present awakening in order to clarify that his previous state was mistaken. Previously, he had considered himself to have attained extinction; this was because he did not...
I have awakened to this. Now that I have received the Buddha’s seal of approval, I finally know that [the marks] are not real. Only nirvana is not real.
As long as I am in this world, I certainly cannot possess all the various marks and signs; and as long as others are present, they will certainly not be sincere and respectful in their faith.

If I were to attain the perfection of merit and wisdom with my body adorned by the marks and signs, and be revered by devas and humans, only then could it be said that I have entered final extinction without remainder.
This is merely the ultimate Great Parinirvāṇa. When Śāriputra reached this point, his provisional attachments were severed. 2. Verse on the Elimination of Doubts:
"The Buddha, in the midst of the great assembly, said: 'I shall become a Buddha'... (until) 'having heard this, my net of doubts is severed.'"
This verse describes the removal of present doubts, thereby illustrating the many doubts that existed on that day. It means:
"In the past, I requested the Buddha to proclaim this matter. Before the assembly of humans and devas, the Buddha declared that we were certain to become Buddhas.
Having heard such a teaching, I examined myself and reproached myself; it has accumulated until this day, and only now have my doubts and regrets been entirely removed, just as at the beginning."
Hearing these words, his heart was greatly startled and filled with doubt. Within his mind, he reflected:
"Could this not be a demon manifesting as a Buddha to vex my heart and disturb my concentration? Otherwise, why would he so lightly claim that the Buddha-way can be accomplished by anyone?
Furthermore, the Buddha does not begrudge his compassionate heart; through various causes and conditions, he skillfully explains all dharmas."
"Having been guided by you, we have deeply reproached ourselves, and our diligence has become even firmer.
Only now have the clouds dispersed and the mist cleared; thus this mind is as tranquil as the ocean, and no further doubts shall arise.
Śāriputra, having reached this point, his provisional doubts were finally severed. △ Third, the verse on knowing the skillful means.
The Buddha spoke of the immeasurable Buddhas of the past who have attained parinirvāṇa (up to the point where it was said that these were the deeds of Māra).
This verse clarifies that the mind is as calm as the ocean because one realizes that skillful means (*upāya*) are identical with reality (*tattva*).
Previously, there was still great terror and great doubt; why is it that all at once the mind becomes as calm as the ocean? It is because our Buddha has extensively cited [scriptural evidence].
The Buddhas reveal the provisional to manifest the ultimate; through various skillful means (*upāya*), they guide and receive sentient beings.

Furthermore, as in the case of the World-Honored One today, from his manifestation of birth, renunciation, attainment of the Way, and preaching of the Dharma, throughout the intervals of movement and stillness, speech and silence, everything is nothing other than the use of skillful means to entice and advance them, so that every person may become like himself. Thus we know that the World-Honored One...

At that time, the sons of the gods, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"In the past, at Vārāṇasī, you turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths... [until] there were few who were able to believe."

The first four lines of the verse commemorate the former provisional teachings. "Vārāṇasī" refers to the place where the Hīnayāna was taught; "the five groups" refers to those who attained the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle;
and "arising and ceasing" refers to the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing, which differ from the Four Noble Truths of non-arising and non-action.
The final four lines of the verse praise the present reality. Because the Dharma is profound and subtle, it is difficult to understand and difficult to enter;
therefore, those who are able to believe in it are few. △ Second, the personal statement of dedication.
"Since ancient times, we have frequently heard the World-Honored One teach [up to] that which is most honored and unsurpassed.
This describes how, from the time we began following the World-Honored One, we have constantly heard the Dharma; yet never before has it been as profound and difficult to understand as it is now.
However, today the World-Honored One has preached this wondrous Dharma, and we are fortunate to have heard it and rejoice in it."

There must surely come a time when one attains Buddhahood. How much more so since the World-Honored One has clearly declared: "Among all who hear the Dharma, there are none who shall not become Buddhas.
