Furthermore, seeing now that the Venerable One has received this sublime prediction, we know that we too shall certainly become Buddhas.
Among all the worlds of devas and humans, I too shall surely become the most honored, unsurpassed being. (1)
"All worlds" refers to three types of worlds: first, the receptacle world; second, the world of sentient beings;
and third, the world of those reaching perfect enlightenment.
"The Buddha-way is inconceivable; expedient means are taught according to what is appropriate" (up to) "all are dedicated toward the Buddha-way.
The two lines following "Buddha-way" clarify that the provisional and ultimate aspects of the *Lotus Sūtra* are unfathomable, thereby concluding the meaning of its profound and subtle nature.
The final four lines indicate that one does not dwell in the karmic merit of the three periods of time, nor does one dwell in the karmic wisdom of the present. This is because...
Bestowing both merit and wisdom, and turning those of small capacity toward the Great Vehicle, the meaning of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*) is thus established.

This concludes the first cycle of the Dharma-exposition for those of superior faculties. II. For those of middling faculties, the exposition by way of parables is divided into four parts. First: The Opening Revelation through Parable.

Furthermore, there are two parts. First, the World-Honored One provides an illustration to reveal the teaching. Furthermore, there are two parts. First, the request made by those present. This is divided into three sections.
First, expressing one's own lack of doubt.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha [up to the words] “the prediction of *samyaksambodhi*.

The commentary states: This was because Śāriputra wished for his colleagues to likewise attain the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*), just as he himself had resolved his doubts and received his prediction;
therefore, he requested on their behalf to initiate the sequence of various parables. Furthermore—
Regarding the passage in the "Chapter on Expedient Means" which states that [the Buddha] knew the doubts in the minds of the fourfold assembly and that he himself had not yet fully understood them:

since the Buddha has now bestowed the prediction upon him, his own doubts are already resolved. He now makes this request in order to completely resolve the doubts in the minds of the fourfold assembly.
△ Second, there is a response from those of equal standing.
These twelve hundred who have attained mastery over their minds (up to the point mentioned) have all fallen into doubt upon hearing what they have never heard before.

As for myself, having fortunately already received my prediction, I dare not ask further; however, for the sake of this assembly, my hidden doubts are profound and sincere, and thus I cannot help but inquire.
Those who have attained mastery over their minds are those whose reality is fully realized and whose delusions are exhausted. They abide in the stage of learning (*śaikṣa*).
"Ground" (*bhūmi*) refers distantly to the past and proximately to the periods of the *Āgamas* and the *Vaipulya* (Mahāyāna) sūtras; therefore, it is said to be "of old.
"To teach" means that the Buddha taught the Dharma by which one exhausts delusions through the realization of truth and attains the fruit. "Birth and death" (*saṃsāra*) is the suffering of the world;
"nirvāṇa" is the bliss of the supramundane. Since the Tathāgata teaches others to leave suffering and attain bliss, he says, "I..."

Through the Dharma’s ability to bring about detachment and so forth, those practitioners who study it immediately receive the teachings and attain understanding, thereby beginning to leave behind all views.

The view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is the cause of suffering in the three realms; it is the root, namely the view of a real body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*). "Existence" and "non-existence" refer to the views of eternalism and nihilism.
The word "etc. (*ādi*) encompasses all such views. To say they are "left behind" means that all views have been forgotten. [This applies to] the two vehicles.
As soon as people depart from various views, they claim to have already attained *nirvāṇa* and no longer seek further progress;
this describes the characteristics of their prior provisional attachments. Now, with the passage "Hearing [the teaching] below," the author finally describes the presence of doubt.

Because they have not yet reached the ultimate, when they hear the words that reveal the provisional to manifest the real—proclaiming that all shall universally attain Buddhahood—they do not understand what kind of causes and conditions these are, and thus [doubt arises].
He gave rise to doubt and wished to request [an explanation]. △ Third, for the sake of the fourfold assembly:
"Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly, so that they may be freed from doubt and regret."
"Excellent! This is the earnest sincerity with which Śāriputra requests on behalf of others. He says: "We have already received your compassionate salvation;
regarding all the skillful means of the Tathāgata—the causal conditions of provisional teachings preceding the ultimate truth—we have already come to know them."
And thus the net of doubt has been severed. Yet, how is it that those gathered here today among the fourfold assembly find it difficult to attain realization?
Therefore, I must again entreat you to bestow your compassion and expound upon this once more, so that their doubts and regrets may be eliminated and they may realize the True Path.
Only then will the great purpose and causal conditions for which the Tathāgata appeared in the world not be in vain. This is intended to bring the matter to a complete conclusion.
Regarding the case of what was referred to as "the reason and the condition for which he earnestly praised [the Buddha]" within the *Bianpin* (Chapter on Expedients):

it is for this reason that [Śāriputra] now raises the cause and condition with great gravity to make his request. Having thus completed the formal request by the one who is ready to receive the teaching (*dengji*), △ second, the Tathāgata’s detailed response, divided into three parts.
First, the arousal [of the mind]. Furthermore, there are two [aspects]: first, suppressing [them] to incite their indignation and valor.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra (up to): "All these teachings are for the sake of transforming bodhisattvas."
I have already stated this previously; I cite it now to awaken you from your current doubt. You should not harbor such doubts again.

I have previously said that the horizontal and vertical teachings of all Buddhas are nothing other than expedient means to lead toward this single reality. Within these, there may be instances of permission or of censure.
There is nothing other than to lead people to realize this one great matter. This has already been fully disclosed in the "Expedient Means" chapter;
what further doubt or regret could there be? Why, then, would it be necessary for the Tathāgata to speak of it again? △ Second, urging them to advance swiftly.
However, Śāriputra, you should now listen further (until: "Those with wisdom attain understanding through parables.

Since Śāriputra, out of his compassionate heart for the assembly, requested again, the Buddha had no choice but to lower his hand for the sake of the assembly and speak once more of the causes and conditions.
Arriving at this point, the reality is revealed; there are no further distinct causes and conditions to be spoken of. The parable borrows from mundane affairs.
What prevents the manifestation of the principle? Furthermore, let us employ metaphors to clarify this meaning. The sages of antiquity did not eschew analogies;

it was precisely because beings attain understanding by means of one thing to reach another that the truth becomes easy to illuminate. △ Second, the section on Parables, which is divided into two parts. First, the prose section.
From here onwards, the extended prose and the subsequent one hundred lines of verse present parables. The latter consists of six [parts].

The fifteen verses of the gāthās exhort faith. This is further divided into two parts. First, the introduction of the analogy, which is itself divided into two. First, the general analogy, which is further divided into six.
First, the analogy of the great elder, which is further divided into two. First, the presentation of his name and status.
Śāriputra, suppose there were a great elder in a kingdom, city, town, or village.
This following section provides a single parable in its entirety to clarify that the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is fundamentally for the sake of one great cause and condition.
Because sentient beings of the three realms are attached to various objects of desire and shrouded by delusion, they do not seek the essential means of deliverance;

thus, one can only open up provisional means to rescue and receive them. As the subsequent text states: "If I were to rely solely on my supernatural powers and wisdom while abandoning skillful means, sentient beings would be unable to attain liberation through these.
Therefore, now, due to the earnest entreaty of those who are ready to receive the teaching, I shall once again provide the intermediate instruction.

"Root" (*mūla*) refers to the explanation of the causal conditions of skillful means (*upāya*). Within this, the various schools each have their own strengths regarding the coordination of phenomena and characteristics;
however, one should follow that which accords with the meaning of the text. "If" (*jā*) signifies "as if," "supposing," or "let us assume"; it is the basis for establishing metaphors.
"Kingdoms," "cities," and "villages" all proceed from the broad to the narrow, each being capable of encompassing [the others]. Kingdom...
A village (*nigama*) can contain a town (*grāma*), and a town contains a settlement (*janapada*). In this treatise, the house of the elder is treated as one among many houses within a settlement.
Now, first we clarify the master who is capable of delivering [beings], presenting both the primary and secondary retributions (*vipāka*) together.

This implicitly contains the meaning of concealing the superior and manifesting the inferior, and of bestowing provisional means based upon the ultimate reality. Since the single burning house has already been used as a metaphor for the three realms (*tridhātu*), [the following continues].
Thus, the country should be understood as a metaphor for the one true dharma-realm; the town as a metaphor for the adornment of the land of real fruition;

and the village as a metaphor for the dwelling place where ordinary beings and sages coexist. Within that village, a single house represents the three realms of existence at their inception; and the five hundred people within the house represent [the various classes of sentient beings].
It is only by using the five destinies as an analogy that the comparison becomes truly appropriate.

This is because the Land of Quiescent Light subsumes the Land of Real Reward, and the Land of Real Reward subsumes the Land of Shared Residence, just as the territories of a nation—whether large or small—are unified under a single administration; thus, the principle is clear and the correspondence between fact and reason is evident.

This constitutes the "land" which serves as the support for those who dwell therein. Next, the "master" who performs the transformation is presented: the term "elder" (gṛhapati) is used here as a general designation.
He is named the Master of a Single Dwelling. This is a metaphor for the Buddha’s transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), who acts as a guiding teacher within the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka*).
Tiantai says: "It is like a worldly elder who possesses ten virtues: first, noble lineage, being a descendant of the Three August Ones and Five Emperors;
second, high rank, serving as a prime minister like Yan-mei or A-heng; third, great wealth, possessing copper hills..."

1. His wealth is like that of the Jin Valley: abundant and inexhaustible. 2. His fourfold majestic presence is like the weight of severe frost: imposing and awe-inspiring without the need for sternness. 3. His wisdom is profound;
his breast is like a military arsenal, yet he is extraordinary and transcendent. 4. At sixty years of age, he is hoary and imposing, such that all things submit to his dignified demeanor.
5. His conduct is pure, like a flawless white jade disk. 6. His etiquette is complete; one observes his disciplined propriety.
He is serene and composed. Ninth, he is honored above as the object of supreme veneration. Tenth, he is relied upon below, providing all within the four seas with a place of refuge.
Because he is fully endowed with these ten virtues, he is called "Great. The World-transcending Elder is none other than the Tathāgata.
His lineage is born from the *tathatā* (suchness) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). His station encompasses the sentient beings of the nine realms, being unsurpassed.

He is enriched by the adornment of myriad virtues; his majesty is endowed with heroic ferocity, invincible. His wisdom is the fusion of the three types of knowledge, perfectly, universally, and exhaustively complete.
His age spans the past and present, beyond the reckoning of dust motes and sands. His conduct employs the three karmas through the movement of wisdom.

There is no fault in this. His rites are governed by the Way, as vast as the sands of the Ganges; he serves as a model and a paradigm. Above, he is praised by the wise and awakened ones of the ten directions;
below, he is venerated by all sentient beings throughout the myriad realms. Thus, he is called the Great Leader who has transcended the world.
II. Discourse on His Virtuous Deeds.
As for the phrase "advanced in years," its interpretations vary; moreover, this parable was spoken forty years later.

Furthermore, since he had proclaimed his passing at this assembly, it should be understood as a metaphor for the conclusion of his transformative activities and the arrival of the time for *nirvāṇa*, rather than requiring a separate interpretation.
This is a metaphor for manifoldness. His wealth being immeasurable serves as a general metaphor for his myriad virtues, as it is said:

"He is fully endowed with immeasurable knowledge and vision (jñāna-darśana-pāramitā). Regarding the fields, houses, and servants being described as "many," this specifically brings forth the meaning of his immeasurable superior wealth.
That the fields and houses cannot be moved represents true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), namely, the Dharma.
Emptiness is the chamber. The servants are the persons who exercise function; they are a metaphor for skillful means and wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*).
That is to say, skillful means is able to perform tasks. *Mai* (pronounced *mai*), *tóng* (same pronunciation), *pú* (pronounced *pǔ*). △ This is the analogy of the vast house.
That family is vast and extensive.

Since the elder was previously used as a metaphor for the Buddha’s transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), it is certain that this great household serves as a metaphor for the Land of Common Dwelling (*sahā-loka-dhātu*).
As for describing the household as "vast and extensive," it is because the triple world broadly encompasses all phenomena, containing everything without exception.
Thus, the twenty-five states of existence all rely upon it to sustain their bodies and lives. △ Third, the analogy of the single gate:

There is but one gate. This "one gate" is the gate through which both ordinary beings and sages travel together; it is a metaphor for the true mind. Although there are distinctions between the sacred and the ordinary among those who pass through it, [the gate itself remains one].
Apart from the mind, there is nothing else that enters or exits. It is only because sentient beings are deluded regarding this that birth and death arise;

it is because the sages have awakened to this that it is True Suchness (Tathatā). Although the delusion and awakening regarding entering and exiting differ, both the holy and the ordinary are fundamentally derived from the one mind.
Therefore, it is said that there is only a single gate. △ Fourth, the analogy of the five hundred people.
"Many people, numbering one hundred, two hundred, or even five hundred, dwell therein.
This is a general reference to the twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*). *Zhizhi* says: "The 'many people' is a metaphor for the twelve classes of sentient beings;
'five hundred' is a metaphor for the sentient beings of the five destinies, who cohabit within the triple world and reside therein."
This is a metaphor for sentient beings who each cling to the two attachments of self and dharmas, yearning for and remaining within the triple world, refusing to abandon it.
The "knower of sounds" explains that this follows the parable of the conjured city (*nirmita-nagara*). First, five hundred *yojanas* are used as a simile;
this is a general metaphor for the sentient beings of the triple world, as their number totals five hundred. Later, after they have traveled three hundred *yojanas*, a city is conjured. This is...
A separate analogy illustrates how the two vehicles transcend the triple world and attain nirvana. △ Fifth, the Parable of the Great Fire Breaking Out, divided into two parts.
First, explaining the characteristics of the burning house:
the halls and pavilions are dilapidated, the walls have crumbled, the bases of the pillars are rotten, and the beams and rafters are tilted and precariously unstable.
The hall represents the lower level, which metaphorically signifies the stages from one’s own realm up to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). The upper stories represent the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
That they are "decayed" indicates that they belong to the outflows (*āsrava*) and are impermanent (*anitya*).

The walls and fences represent the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—illustrating how all three realms depend upon the support of these four elements, yet are nonetheless destroyed by them. "Ruinous" refers to the four... [text fragment ends]

This is a great diminution. The base of the pillars is a metaphor for the conditioned existence of the three realms (*traidhātuka*). That the roots of merit and goodness have rotted away signifies that the roots of virtue are feeble.

The beams are a metaphor for the beams of preceptual goodness and merit in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); the ridgepole is a metaphor for the ridgepole of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

That it is leaning and precariously unstable is a metaphor for the weakness of the power of merit and wisdom, such that they cannot provide support. Thus one knows all that exists within the three realms.
All are illusory transformations. They collapse (tāi) and crumble (bài). △ Second, the emergence of the realm of the consuming fire:
all around, at the same time, fire suddenly erupts, burning down the houses and dwellings.

This metaphor illustrates the general characteristics of the three realms being tormented by the eight sufferings and the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*). These are explained in detail within the verses.
It is said that the eight sufferings and five turbidities pervade all four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*) and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), hence the term "all-encompassing" (*parikṣipta*).

Because they manifest identically through shared karma, they are said to occur "simultaneously. The word "suddenly" (*kṣaṇāt*) indicates that what was originally non-existent now exists. [It] burns down houses and dwellings.
This is the sign of the world’s destruction. However, the ancient [commentators] used the analogy of halls, pavilions, and so forth to represent the skin, flesh, hair, and beard of a single body;
this seems to be in significant discordance with the various preceding and succeeding passages.

Moreover, since it is clearly stated that the burning house represents the triple world as a whole, one would hardly dare to record many of these individual analogies here. (The character *xū* is pronounced like *xū*. △ Sixth: The Analogy of the Thirty Sons.
"The elder’s sons, whether ten, twenty, or even thirty, are within this house.
This indicates that the noble and the ordinary share one location. Zhizhi says: "The previous mention of 'many people' referred to the five destinies;
the present mention of 'the elder’s sons' specifically singles out those of the Three Vehicles who receive a portion of the Buddha-dharma. Therefore, there is [this distinction].
The meaning of the "Sons" (Subhūti): ten illustrate the Bodhisattvas; twenty illustrate the Pratyekabuddhas; thirty illustrate the Śrāvakas.

Those of the three vehicles all dwell together within the triple world; because their subtle afflictions have not yet been eliminated and their fundamental ignorance has not yet been shattered, they collectively receive this retribution.
They differ from ordinary beings of the lower realms only in the degree of coarseness or subtlety. Where others speak in hundreds of words, the Son speaks in ten; thus it is seen.
Among the sentient beings of the three realms and five destinies, those who have received the Buddha’s transformation to become his children are but ten.
This is sufficient to know that those who attain this Way and escape the three realms are few indeed. This concludes the general analogy. II. The Specific Analogy, divided into four parts: 1.
The Analogy of the Elder Seeing the Fire.
When the elder saw this great fire arising from all four sides, he was immediately seized with great alarm and fear.

By mentioning the elder’s vision, the text identifies the person capable of such insight; it demonstrates that one who gives rise to the great compassion of identifying with the suffering of others manifests birth within the three realms.
This corresponds to my previous statement, "I observe with the Buddha-eye. The phrase "a great fire breaks out" indicates the realm that is perceived;

it corresponds to my previous observation of sentient beings in the six realms. The "great fire" refers to the five turbidities and the eight sufferings, which possess the sense of scorching and oppression.

Regarding "from the four sides": the text below clarifies that birth, old age, sickness, and death constitute the four sides; however, this does not precisely accord with the meaning of the fire’s ignition.

Furthermore, since birth, death, and so forth are the fruits of suffering, which are accumulated by the fourfold afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, and so on, it is more appropriate to interpret the meaning as the fire arising from these four factors of greed and the rest. "Greatly terrified" indicates...
With a heart that extends compassion and uproots suffering, the Tathāgata has, for kalpas long past, taught these sentient beings the Mahāyāna.

That they have now, all at once, abandoned and forgotten it causes him to look upon them with alarm. Not only have they fallen away from their former resolve, but they have instead given rise to various grave evils; therefore, it is called "great terror."
And he forms this thought: "Although I am able [to dwell] in this [state], my mind does not feel weary or distressed, nor do I have the intention to seek liberation.
One who forms such a thought should first contemplate during the three preceding weeks, intending to conceal what is superior and manifest what is inferior.
The door that is burned is precisely the one mind shared by both the holy and the ordinary; even the Buddha, from the stage of an ordinary person, knew of arising and ceasing.
It is suffering. By cultivating the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, one realizes this mind and thereby attains Buddhahood. Contemplate these two characters, "I" and "though":
they signify that the Tathāgata could not bear to abandon all sentient beings in order to seek his own peace and happiness.
This means that although I, by the power of illuminating wisdom, shall reach the state of Bodhi in safety from within this burning gate.
"Attaining non-arising and non-ceasing. The passage beginning with "And all these children... is precisely where the mind of compassionate rescue arises.
As the later text states: "All sentient beings of the triple world are my children; those who take pleasure and attachment in playing within the burning house," Tiantai says:

Attachment to views is called "sporting"; attachment to craving is called "play. This refers to sentient beings who, through their greedy attachment to the five desires and their adherence to various false views, fail to abandon them;
that is to say, they enter the perilous path of birth and death, where the continuity of suffering remains unbroken.

Those who do not realize this lose the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; unaware of the five aggregates and the eight sufferings, their minds are intoxicated as they toil in the weariness of worldly defilements.

Those who do not feel alarm or fear are like the devas and humans who, although they possess the divine eye and see all sufferings, and though they constantly hear the Dharma-sound from the celestial drums and know them all to be suffering, do not seek the essential means of deliverance.

This is because they are deeply attached to the five desires and are shrouded by their own craving and love. Regarding the four phrases beginning with "oppressed by fire," this refers to those within the three realms who, [driven] by desire...

Below the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), one is oppressed by the fires of the three poisons and the eight types of suffering; this is the coarse aspect. For example, there are the fires of karmic retribution and the fires of karma.
Above the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), one is oppressed by the blazing intensity of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and the fires of subtle delusions and afflictions (*kleśa*).
When suffering and delusion confront one, they are extremely difficult to endure and truly strike at the very core of one's being; yet, within this...
Sentient beings ultimately do not give rise to even a single thought of weariness or aversion, nor do they seek out the intention [to escape].
That is to say, they do not seek the Buddha of Great Power, nor the Dharma that severs suffering. △ Second, the analogy of discarding the small table and using the carriage.
This is divided into two parts. First, the analogy of first discarding the small table. This is further divided into two. First, the exhortation regarding the provisional suitability.
Śāriputra, when this elder thought thus (up to) "if I carry him out of the house on a small table," he should then ascend to observe the trees while walking in meditation.
At the time he first formed this thought, his body was like supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), by which he is able to bear the burden;
his hands were like wisdom (*prajñā*), by which he is able to perform actions. That he possesses strength is due to his being fully endowed with both wisdom and supernatural power.
This has the meaning of "possessing power. *Yījì* (衣裓) is a foreign vessel for holding flowers; it is also said to be a garment worn on the chest to protect one's clothes.
*Jǐ* (几) refers to an incense stand, and *àn* (案) refers to a desk or writing tablet. To take an analogy from the subsequent text:
"If I were to use only the power of my spiritual transformations and the power of my wisdom to praise the Tathāgata’s powers of knowledge and vision, as well as his fearlessnesses, the assembly..."

Those born [in this world] cannot attain deliverance by these means alone. Since the Superior One has already taken the power of spiritual faculties (*ṛddhi-bala*) as his body and the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*) as his hands, the robe and lap-sack should be understood as a metaphor for the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
the small table as a metaphor for the ten powers (*daśabala*); and the desk as a metaphor for the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). This means:
"I now have the robe and lap-sack upon my person and the table and desk in my hands; by my own power, I can likewise carry all the children out from the house."
He brought it forth. This was when the Tathāgata first attained enlightenment; he intended to use the Great Dharma to save sentient beings, as in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
(The character *gèi* is pronounced *gé*.)
He further reflected that this house had but a single door (up to) it might collapse and be consumed by fire.
"Furthermore" refers to the time when he accepted the King’s invitation and again engaged in reflection.

As stated previously, if one were to praise only the Buddha Vehicle while sentient beings are submerged in suffering, the phrase "this house has but a single door" refers to the cycle of birth and death within the three realms.
Suffering and pleasure, rise and fall—all that enters and exits is this single mind. Because the power of faith is slight and wisdom is not vast, it is said to be "narrow and small.
The "infantile" refers to those whose roots of goodness are weak and who lack the aspiration for the Mahāyāna.
Those who "have no awareness" refer to those whose ignorance is dense and thick, lacking the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This is due to the weakness of their goodness.

Next, the strength of evil is explained. Those who are attached to places of play are those who are deeply clinging to various views and are deludedly infatuated with the objects of desire, taking suffering to be pleasure.
This refers to sentient beings whose faculties are dull, who are attached to pleasure and shrouded by ignorance. They may fall;
because they previously destroyed the Dharma and lacked faith, they will plummet into the three evil realms. The phrase "may fall" (or "might fall") indicates a possibility.
Indeed there is. I thought that although I possess strength in my hands and body, and am further equipped with the means for victory, alas, the gate is large while the opening is small;

and the child is young and lacks understanding. To send a child who is ignorant yet fond of play through a narrow and cramped gate in such a state of panic—this would not only be of no benefit, but I fear he will be burned by the fire. As it was said previously: "In this manner..."
[They are] of such a kind. How can they be delivered? [The word] *zhì* (pronounced *zhì*) means "infant. △ Second, the section on admonishing and preparing the way:
"I shall now speak of things to be feared" ... [up to] "... fully inform all my children: 'You must quickly come forth!'"

This correctly expresses the intention behind the contemplation of "I shall speak for them" and so forth; that is to say, the Blessed One speaks of the various afflictions and hardships for the sake of all sentient beings.
The four lines beginning with "This house is already burning" demonstrate the extreme earnestness of his concern, fearing that a mistake might cause him to lose his footing and his life.
From the passage beginning with "Having formed this thought," it is only then that [the teaching] is about to proceed.
Having completed his contemplation, he manifested it to others and informed his sons, saying, "There is great urgency;
there is no time for even a moment’s delay. Thus he said, "All of you, come out quickly! These very words were decisive and unyielding, like spring thunder awakening hibernating creatures.
Linji says: "Observe how at first it is said that 'suddenly a fire breaks out,' and then..."

It is said that fire breaks out on all four sides; it is further said that the fire comes to press against one's body; and it is said that this house is already burning. How urgent is the meaning of these words!
Furthermore, they do not merely describe a state of weeping and shedding tears; as it is said:
"Once one loses this human body, ten thousand kalpas will pass before it can be regained. Below it says: "You should quickly depart at once; do not let yourself be burned by the fire."
It was harmful; moreover, it went beyond mere beating one's breast and stamping one's feet.
Although the father compassionately enticed him with kind words, [the son] merely ran back and forth playing, looking at his father.
This metaphor describes, at first glance, the state of being deluded regarding principle and pursuing the false. Zhizhi says:

"Although the Tathāgata has repeatedly extended his guidance, the sentient beings of the triple world are utterly unwilling to believe him. Furthermore, they do not take birth and death as a cause for alarm, nor do they regard the five aggregates with dread.
Their karmic consciousness is vast and indistinct, entirely lacking the thought of transcendence; they do not realize that the three poisons are fire."
They do not realize that the three realms are a great prison, nor do they know how to lose their respective inherent Buddha-nature;
they merely allow themselves to drift from kalpa to kalpa, passing from death here to birth there within the wombs of horses and donkeys.
Without rest, they transmigrate through the six realms of existence, taking suffering for pleasure; thus it is said that they "run and play to the east and west.
As in the *Avataṃsaka*, though they have eyes, they do not see, missing the opportunity right before them and failing to obtain the enjoyment of the Great Dharma;
thus it is said that they "only look at their father. △ Second, the analogy of the chariots, divided into four parts. First, the provisional application of the three chariots.
At that time, the elder had this thought: [omitted] "I shall cause my sons to escape this calamity.
He then looked back upon the various skillful means practiced by the Buddhas of the past, following the intention of establishing the Three Vehicles based on the One Vehicle.
Previously, he spoke of the pain as being "cutting to the core," which was still merely the proximity of death; now, saying they "will certainly be burned," it carries the full sense of death itself.
One must employ skillful means; this is the teaching of the Three Vehicles, wherein the superior is concealed and the inferior is manifested.

My words and those of my sons are metaphorical teachings, whereas the Dharma-teachings appear difficult to reconcile. One must understand that the Buddha speaks in accordance with the capacities of his audience.
The Tathāgata regards all beings with a compassionate heart as if they were his own children; the sickness of sentient beings is the sickness of the Buddha.

If we speak solely from the perspective of the sentient beings' own portion, although they are situated amidst the greatest delusion and suffering, this luminous and unobscured Buddha-nature has never for a moment been abandoned; this is the meaning of "I" and "my children. 2.
The Father Knows the Child's Mind.
The father knows that the former inclinations of his sons—up to their attachment to extraordinary and marvelous things—indicate that they will surely delight in them.

Tiantai clarifies that there are those with the capacity for deliverance through the Hīnayāna; that their former inclinations each have their own preferences is because these are seeds perfumed over distant kalpas.
Thus, while the Great and Small Vehicles differ, their dispositions and desires are each distinct. Furthermore, [Zhiyi] had previously practiced...
It is great; hence it is called the "prior mind. In the middle, one feels weary of old age and death. These [beings] each have their own preferences.

Using rare treasures, curiosities, and wonders as metaphors and proofs, one illustrates the principles of partial emptiness and so forth. By observing their past causes, one offers what they prefer. Thus, one knows that their minds will surely find pleasure and attachment therein.
This is what is called "conforming skillful means. △ Third, praising the rarity of the chariot, he addressed them, saying:
"Those things which you hold dear as playthings... (until)... if you do not take them now, you will surely later feel sorrow and regret."
This praises the rarity of the vehicle, which is analogous to the aforementioned correct bestowal of the three vehicles.

Having reflected upon these matters, he proceeded immediately to Vārāṇasī to demonstrate the characteristics of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; this was the initial turning of the wheel of demonstration.
These various goat-carts, deer-carts, and ox-carts are now outside the gate, available for play.
Śrāvakas who hear the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and thereby transcend the triple world are likened to the goat-carts.

Pratyekabuddhas who contemplate the emptiness of the nature of the twelve links of dependent origination and thereby transcend the triple world are likened to the deer-carts. As for Bodhisattvas of the Middle Vehicle, they cultivate the six perfections...
"Setting out" means departing from the triple world. The ox-cart serves as a metaphor; the cart represents the principle realized, while the beast represents the wisdom that realizes it.

Although the three carts refer to what is already present, in reality they require one to practice according to the Dharma, sever the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhava-kleśa*), transcend birth and death, and depart from the burning house before one can individually enjoy them. Therefore, it says: "Now at the gate."
"Outside. It can be used for recreation. This is the second turning of realization. The *Yaojie* (Essential Explanation) states:

"The chariot symbolizes the fruit-dharma, which does not belong to the three realms; hence it is said to be 'outside the gate. That 'it can be used for recreation' is a metaphor for delighting oneself in the joy of the Dharma.
The ox is that which possesses the power to draw and ride; it precisely illustrates the great root (*mahāmūla*) capable of bearing the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). The sheep and deer..."
They are not fit for riding or drawing; they are merely oxen in form, serving as toys for the young. By this provisional analogy, those of small capacity are entrusted with the Small Vehicle.

Knowing that sheep and deer are not fit for riding or drawing, but are merely objects of play, one understands that the Two Vehicles are insufficient for attaining the Way and are nothing more than the dharmas of frivolous discourse.
"You all should quickly come out from this burning house; whatever you desire, I shall give it all to you.
"Quickly come out" is a word of exhortation. The final two phrases contain the meaning of the great white ox-cart.
This is the third exhortation to practice the transformation. Zhidui says: "There are no carts outside the gate, yet it is said that the three carts are all present;
not a single cart exists, yet it is said, 'I shall give you whatever you desire. All of this is shown through the wisdom of skillful means."
Therefore, what follows serves as proof that [the teaching] is not false. △ Fourth, fulfilling the sons' wishes:
At that time, having heard what their father said, the sons vied with one another to run and scramble to escape from the burning house.

Tiantai says: "One whose wishes are fulfilled" refers to the correspondence between the capacity [of the practitioner] and the teaching; this is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). "One whose mind is courageous and sharp" refers to the movement of thought and deliberation;

this is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). "Mutually pushing and displacing" refers to investigating the principle of the Four Noble Truths and displacing or subduing the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).

Because right and wrong have not yet been determined, it is called "mutual. This enters the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) and belongs to the stages of *uṣmagata* (Heat) and *mūrdhan* (Summit).

"Competing" (*kṣānti*) refers to competing for the principle that is to be won. Initially, one universally contemplates the eight truths across the upper and lower realms, traversing the sixteen aspects, competing to advance toward the Truth of Reality (*satya*).
Subsequently, the contemplation is contracted until one reaches the "patience regarding the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) within the Truth of Suffering of the desire realm;

this is called the stage of patience (*kṣānti-dharma-avasthā*). "Common" (*sāmānya*) refers to the stage of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukika-agra-dharma*), which likewise contemplates the Truth of Suffering of the desire realm, being identical to patience.

Their stages are not distinct; therefore, they are said to be "shared. "Rushing forward" refers to entering the fifteen moments of mind of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), wherein one swiftly perceives the principle.
Having severed the delusions of seeing (*dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa*), one partially attains *nirvāṇa*; this corresponds to the sound "nirvāṇa" mentioned above.

"Competing to emerge" refers to the stage of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), wherein one competes to emerge from the three realms, achieves the fruit of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*), and exhaustively severs the delusions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*). This corresponds to [the sound] above.
This also includes the distinct names for the Arhats, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha. The *Yinzhi* (Sound-Knowledge) commentary states:

"Although the scriptural text may seem plain when read, the structural progression of the narrative naturally possesses its own emphasis and hierarchy. For instance, it begins by saying: 'Suddenly, fire broke out.'"
Next it says: "Or they may fall [into hell] and be burned by fire. Although there is the sudden calamity of being burned, it merely says "arises" or "or.
How can one speak so indifferently? When it comes to this point, it says, "They have already been burned by the great fire," yet it adds, "I and my children will surely be consumed by it.
How utterly despondent and terrified this is! Previously, it said there was absolutely none...
The children emerged from their minds and ran about playing to the east and west, merely looking at their father. How indolent and obstinate they were!

Yet now, it is said that each mind is brave and sharp, pushing one another to compete to escape the burning house. How diligent and energetic they have become! One can thus see the power and function of skillful means (*upāya*);
however, the true nature (*dharmatā*) is easy to describe but difficult to express. (The character *ruì* is pronounced *wèi*). △ Third, the bestowing of gifts upon the sons.
This is divided into four parts. First, the children are spared from disaster:
"At that time, the elder saw his sons... (up to) "...his mind was composed, and he leaped for joy with delight.

This precisely serves as a metaphor for opening the provisional to reveal the real. *Zhizhi* says: "Since the afflictions of views and thought are exhausted, and the stages of partial severance have already been transcended..."
Being oppressed by the three poisons and the five desires, it is said: "He emerges safely. This corresponds to the previous statement: "I am able to emerge safely from the burning gate.
Upon reaching this point, the Four Noble Truths are all truly eternal; hence it is called "the crossroads. The *Erya* states:
"That which leads to four directions is called a *qu* (crossroads). Partial emptiness is what is maintained therein.

Therefore, one sits in the open air. As for "open air," it means that one is no longer shrouded by various afflictions (*kleśa*), and the fences of the eighteen realms (*dhātu*) have already been dismantled;
thus, there is no obstruction. Because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the *ālayavijñāna* are exhausted, it is called "serene.
Because one has attained mastery over the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), one leaps with joy. Furthermore, this serenity of mind refers to returning to the Father.
"Previously, seeing the fire break out on all four sides, I was greatly terrified; now, fortunately, I have escaped in safety, and thus I am at ease.
Previously, it was said: 'If you do not emerge at once, you will surely be consumed by the flames'—how painful and regrettable that would have been!
Seeing my children running and playing here and there, how sorrowful I was! Now, seeing them sitting in the open space, I am filled with joy."
This clearly demonstrates that the natural affinity between father and son is such that their physical bodies (*rūpakāya*) and Dharma-bodies (*dharmakāya*) are both non-dual.
Qú (pronounced qú). △ Second, the sons request vehicles.
At that time, the sons each addressed their father, saying: "[... (up to) "We pray that you will grant us the goat carts, deer carts, and ox carts at this time.

Tiantai says: This corresponds to the previous passage: "I see these sons of the Buddha, those who are determined to seek the Buddha-way, all of whom with reverent hearts have come to the place of the Buddha.
Although the word "sought" (*suǒ*) does not appear in the text, based on this context, it clarifies that they are seeking the carts.

Regarding "intention" (*yì*): according to the perspective of the Two Vehicles, there are three types of intention. First, the "intention of the stimulus" (*jī-suo*). This refers to the period after they realized the Lesser Vehicle at the Deer Park;

when they reached the Vaipulya (Vaipulya) teachings, they were secretly benefited in a profound way. Although they were repeatedly rebuked, they did not slander [the Mahāyāna], and thus their underlying intention was indeed present.

Second, the "intention of the disposition" (*qíng-suo*). During the Prajñāpāramitā period, they came to comprehend the Great Dharma, and although the aspiration for the Great Mind had not yet fully arisen, even so—
The statement is clear, yet the pursuit of its meaning is also urgent. Third, regarding "seeking": this refers to the three requests made during the assembly when the father spoke.

Indeed, the desire to beg for the three carts outside the gate was originally established as a provisional device. While the sons had not yet emerged, it was intended that they would surely obtain the carts outside the gate.
Once they have stepped out of the gate, the father’s skillful means (*upāya*) will be understood without being explicitly taught.
Once he had stepped outside the gate, his father indeed possessed the three chariots and gave them to his sons, yet they were of no further use.
Thus we know that seeking the chariots in this place was precisely what won the father’s heart. Therefore it is said: "In the dream, the six realms of existence are vividly clear;
upon awakening, all is empty, and not even a great chiliocosm remains. As for the statement that each spoke of their own whiteness, it arose from their realization.
There are degrees of depth. The wise know that fundamentally there was no chariot, yet they nonetheless seek it from their father;
this is like a lion cub leaving tracks of its backward leaps. Or, for those who are hindered by traces and wish to investigate the ultimate depths, such a seeking intention may also be permitted.
△ Third, the equal bestowal is non-dual. This is divided into three parts. First, the formal indication of the equal bestowal.
"Śāriputra, at that time the elder gave each of his sons an identical great carriage.
This corresponds to the teaching in the *Lotus Sūtra*: "The former [teachings] were upright and direct; he abandoned expedient means and spoke only of the Unsurpassed Way. Tiantai says:

"Since it is said that he 'gave to his sons,' he views his children without distinction. This is an analogy for observing that all sentient beings equally possess Buddha-nature. Regarding the carriages as well..."

The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) indicates that these are all of one characteristic and one kind; they are the Dharma praised by the Sages and taught for the sake of Bodhisattvas. Directly pointing [to the truth], it says:
This is the underlying principle of the three cycles of universal prediction, which remains hidden. This inherently present reality is like the sky, which universally covers all;

therefore, it is likened to the Great Vehicle. Because the sons were deluded, they sought three [vehicles]; because the compassionate father opened [the way], he made them equal and one. Thus we know that the preceding...
The three vehicles are categorized, yet their origin lies in the One Vehicle. Within this context, the three carts originally constitute a single cart.

Because the Dharma is equal and the persons are equal, and because they have attained Right and Perfect Enlightenment, it is said that they are "equally bestowed. △ Second, a detailed explanation of the characteristics of the carts, which has two parts.
First, describing the body of the carts.
The chariot is high and wide, adorned with various jewels, [extending] to its layered, elegant cushions where a crimson pillow is placed.
This is a direct metaphor for the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings; it is named according to its underlying principle. Only the Principle (li) can carry all things;

therefore, it is likened to a chariot. *Zhizhi* says: "Because it sustains both the ultimate and the conventional truths, it is called a 'Great Chariot. Vertically, it exhausts the three periods of time."
Its name is "High. It extends horizontally throughout the ten directions, which is called "vast. Adorned with the cultivation of the myriad practices, it is like being decorated with various jewels;
the surrounding balustrades are a metaphor for *dhāraṇī*, which maintains all that is good and wards off all that is evil.

Bells suspended on all four sides are a metaphor for the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence, by which one transforms sentient beings below. The canopy is a metaphor for compassion universally covering all. It is further embellished with various precious gems.

This metaphor represents the myriad virtues used to adorn compassion. The Great Sūtra states: "If compassion is fully endowed with the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and so forth, it is called the Tathāgata’s compassion.
The interlacing of precious cords is a metaphor for the Four Great Vows, representing the firm and steadfast mind of great compassion.

The hanging of various flower garlands is a metaphor for the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), supernatural powers, and so forth, which gladden and move sentient beings. As for the layering of elegant mats:

The fifty-seven stages are like the objective realm of the principle of *tathatā* (suchness). The red pillow placed there is a metaphor for the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), representing the state of perfect repose beyond all dependence.
Tiantai said: "A pillow is that which brings rest to the body and head; it is a metaphor for the *ekavyūha-samādhi* (the samādhi of one practice)."
It brings to rest all-encompassing wisdom and all practices. The above provides a general explanation of the adornments upon the carriage, which serves as a metaphor for the Tathatā (Suchness):
quiescent yet ever-illuminating, arising from its essence as function; the one becoming the infinite, thereby perfecting the unimpeded Dharma-realm.
*Xiǎn* (the sound of 幰); *wǎn* (the sound of 婉).
The carriage is drawn by white oxen whose coats are pure and clean, and it is further attended by a multitude of servants and guards.
This precisely illustrates the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, which derives its name from fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). *Zhizhi* says: "Wisdom acts as the vanguard;
therefore, it is called 'carrying' (*jia*). This wisdom does not admit a single speck of dust, hence it is called the 'white ox. Its essence is endowed with myriad virtues. As it is said:

The skin is full: because it is unstained by afflictions, its color is pure. Furthermore, because true wisdom (*jñāna*) can give rise to all differentiated wisdoms, it is said that "the skin and color are full and pure.
Because the two wisdoms of skillful means (*upāya*) and reality (*tattva*) do not depart from its essence, it is said that "the physical form is beautiful.
Because it possesses these ten kinds of great meanings, it is said to have "great strength. Because the whole body is function, and the whole conventional is...
"True. Cause and effect are as one; this is called "walking with even and upright steps. Wisdom has no interior or exterior across the three periods of time in each instant;
this is called "as swift as the wind. Furthermore, having many attendants is a metaphor for the *upāya-pāramitā* (perfection of skillful means), which is applied according to circumstances.
That is to say, the minor practices of the two vehicles and all demons and non-Buddhists all follow the functional application of expedient wisdom.

Furthermore, the supernatural powers that operate at the stage of fruition also carry the sense of being servants. (The character *shū* is pronounced *shū*. △ Second, explaining the origin of the chariot.
Why is this so? Because this great elder possesses immeasurable wealth, and all his various treasuries are completely overflowing.
This is a metaphor for the Buddha himself abiding in the Mahāyāna, never teaching others by means of the Hīnayāna.

It is pointedly stated that "immeasurable wealth" refers to the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate, as well as the perfection of meditative concentration, liberation, powers, and fearlessness. All these are fully possessed.
Furthermore, as for the various treasuries, these are the treasury of practice, the treasury of principle, and the treasury of emptiness and non-emptiness.
To be self-perfected is called "fullness"; to transform others through this is called "overflowing."
He then formed this thought: "My wealth and possessions are inexhaustible; it is not fitting that I should give to each differently. Tiantai says:
This clearly explains that he gives with an impartial mind. Because his wealth is inexhaustible, he has no partiality toward his sons;
how could he help but give them all equally the great chariots? That "the seven treasures are immeasurable" is a metaphor for the revelation and clarification of the present sutra.
Whether in teaching or in practice, all are the Mahāyāna Dharma. That "the young children are all my sons" refers to the non-differentiation of the three [vehicles].
That "they are equally granted the great chariots" refers to the non-differentiation of this Dharma.
The reason for this is that even if I were to distribute these goods throughout an entire kingdom, they would still not be exhausted; how much less so for my sons.
This explains the meaning of his immeasurable wealth. These "goods" are a metaphor for the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—that which the Tathāgata universally opens up and reveals to humans and devas.
"Distributing them throughout" means they encompass all beings, both good and evil, those who believe and those who do not.

If they can deliver even those who lack the karmic conditions, how much more so those whose faculties are mature, who possess the karmic conditions, and who have previously been perfumed by the Great Dharma?
△ Fourth, the joy of obtaining the vehicle.
At that time, the sons each mounted a great carriage, obtaining what they had never experienced before and which was not what they had originally expected.
This is like the bodhisattvas above who, upon hearing this Dharma, have all had the net of doubt removed. Tiantai says:

"The people of the three vehicles originally sought the sheep, deer, and ox carts, hoping to transcend the realm of birth and death (*bhavāgra*). Now they obtain the great white ox cart, exhausting [the cycle of]..."
It has been transformed beyond what was originally expected; how could one not be joyful? △ Fourth, the analogy of being without falsehood, divided into three parts.
First, the question:
"Śāriputra, what do you think? (up to: Could there be any falsehood in these precious great chariots?"
"This great carriage has been bestowed equally upon us from above. Zhizhi said: "Previously, it was promised that there were three carriages outside the gate;
thus, the matter seemed like a falsehood. Now, what is bestowed is an equal great carriage, which was not previously promised, yet is now given;
thus, its reality seems like a fabrication. You should examine this: is such a thing truly false and deceptive, or is it not?"
This correctly illustrates the establishment of the Three Vehicles, which serves merely as a means to transcend the triple world; ultimately, they are not real.
Therefore, they exist first and then cease to be. Although the principle of the single reality was not previously expounded, it now opens up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
It is indeed real; therefore, it was previously non-existent and subsequently came into being.

By means of these two characters, "empty" and "false," the critical junctures between the preceding and following sections are opened up, arising from the phrase "not what was originally expected. △ Second, the answer. This is divided into two parts. First, avoiding the difficulty that [the response] is not empty.
Śāriputra said, "No, World-Honored One" (up to the point where it says) "...and rescue them from that burning house.
Śāriputra then asked this in order to understand the meaning of the non-falsity [of the Buddha's words], referring to what was previously stated: "The skillful means devised by the elder."
To cause his sons to escape this harm, the provision of the three carts was merely a skillful means (*upāya*).

Now that the sons are vying to exit the burning house with their minds set upon the carts, while the elder’s original intention was solely to free them from suffering, the efficacy of that skillful means is now clearly manifest once they have escaped the calamity of suffering.
How could he, on the contrary, accept something that is empty, false, and unreal?

"How regrettable! Why? To have escaped the fire with one's whole body and already obtained playthings—this is like a person who has attained the Small Vehicle’s fivefold Dharma-body and the life-force of the wisdom of self-emptiness; they have already obtained what their hearts desired.
How much more so this, which was originally the Tathāgata’s heart of expedient means for deliverance; how could it be false? △ Second, "Not False Beyond Expectation."

"World-Honored One, if this elder [from the previous passage]... wishes to benefit his children by giving them great chariots," this clarifies that the bestowal of the great chariots was not what they originally expected.

Even if the elder had reached the exterior of the burning house and not given a single chariot, it would still not have been false. Why? Because the chariots served as the means for escaping the calamity; now...
After they were saved from the peril, not only did he give them carts, but he gave them great carts—those which the sons had not even expected.

How could one instead accuse the father of the sin of falsehood? This parable illustrates that although the World-Honored One spoke of the three vehicles, his intention was actually fixed upon the Great Vehicle;
thus, there is absolutely no sense of falsehood. Śāriputra has here provided proof for this.

"Vast. Having already established the precedent for the four great disciples and the twelve hundred followers to sever their doubts and give rise to faith, the chapter concludes with the Master himself expressing his own faith and understanding. △ Third, the Praise.
The Buddha told Śāriputra, "Excellent, excellent! It is just as you have said.

The Tathāgata wishes to personally declare his intention of bestowing the chariots according to the capacities of those present. Thus, by means of both the false and the non-false, he brings forth what each perceives.
Fortunately, Śāriputra’s voice resonates in harmony with this; therefore, the Buddha immediately commends him, saying 'Excellent'."
“As you have truly said. By this single phrase, one knows that Śāriputra’s claim—that he was born from the Buddha’s own mouth and has obtained a portion of the Buddha-dharma—is indeed not false.
The first section, the illustration of the parable, is concluded. △ Second, the application of the parable. This is divided into two parts.
First, the application of the general parable. This is divided into five sections. First, the application of the great elder.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is likewise thus; he is the father of all the world.
Tiantai says: Because it was difficult to clarify [the meaning] in the preceding chapter by explaining it solely through the Dharma, he permitted its understanding to be attained through parables.
The subsequent application of the Dharma to the analogy is intended to provide an explanation for those of middling faculties;

it also demonstrates that the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma reaches both principle and phenomena. Regarding the mention of "all worlds," this defines their names and positions according to their locations.
While previously it was said "countries, cities, towns, and villages," the current application of the analogy speaks directly of "all worlds," thereby encompassing everything.
The three lands are all places that are the retribution of the wondrous form and mind. Because the Tathāgata’s blessings and responses pervade these three lands, he is the father of all worlds.
Amidst all fears, decays, afflictions, and anxieties, he constantly seeks out wholesome matters to benefit all beings.
This statement means that the Tathāgata alone has attained true permanence, thereby giving rise to the compassionate wisdom that benefits sentient beings.

The three phrases beginning with "fear" all refer to the realms of suffering in the mundane world. Because the Tathāgata, while still in the causal stage, had exhausted the five abodes of ignorance and forgotten the two types of death, there was no evil he did not sever;
hence it is said, "forever exhausted without remainder. Furthermore, the phrases beginning with "and fully accomplished" all refer to the sublime bliss of the supramundane.
In the fruit of enlightenment, the Tathāgata fuses the provisional and the real, mobilizes wisdom and compassion, and is fully endowed with all virtues; thus it is said that he "benefits all.
This precisely accords with the aforementioned "immeasurable wealth," as he responds in secret to the various capacities of sentient beings.

As for the term "immeasurable knowledge and vision," this refers to the various provisional and real wisdoms, as well as the immeasurable powers and fearlessnesses that correspond to them—all of which are subsumed within the virtue of wisdom.
This is clearly consistent with the aforementioned wealth. The "Great Supernatural Power" (mahā-ṛddhi) should likewise be understood as having two aspects: the immeasurable and the manifest.

As in this very sūtra, the snapping of fingers, the clearing of the throat, the threefold transformation of the pure land, the emission of light, and the manifestation of auspicious omens—all of these are but minor portions of that supernatural power.
The union of means (upāya) and wisdom (prajñā) is the power of wisdom; wisdom is that which serves as the locus for all things. This corresponds to the meaning of the "house.
Being fully endowed with skillful means and so forth refers to the ten perfections (pāramitās) and various forms of knowledge.
This corresponds to the meaning of the "various servants. Compassion is the very foundation of transformative teaching (nirmāṇa); being without indolence refers to [the absence of]...
The mind of exhaustion. These merits are all fully accomplished. This clarifies self-realization. From below, the mind that benefits sentient beings emerges;

one comes to be born within the triple world. Constantly seeking virtuous deeds means responding to the capacities of others to rescue them and benefiting all, which is the vow to deliver sentient beings. △ Second, the house.
Thus one is born into the three realms, this dilapidated and ancient fire-dwelling.
Tiantai says: "The 'three realms' refer to those from the hells up to the human realm, which are called the 'five destinies of mixed habitation.

From the human realm up to the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), it is called the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). In the four dhyānas and the eighteen Brahma heavens, all possess form and color."

The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) consists of the four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpya*). Abiding in the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) is called the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Because these three locations each have their own distinct boundaries and lineages, they are called the "Three Realms. Those born into the Three Realms do so by virtue of the aforementioned tireless resolve for the sake of benefiting others;
it is not that they are born as a result of karmic retribution. "Decayed" refers to the characteristics of the kalpa of destruction (*saṃvartakalpa*).

Therefore, this is the characteristic of the *sthāna-kalpa* (the kalpa of abiding). The triple world is the field where the Tathāgata practices his transformative teachings; thus it is called "his own dwelling.
This corresponds to the previous statement that "his house is vast. △ Third, the assembly of five hundred people.
It is for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
Sentient beings are the very foundation of all sages. If the Buddha did not deliver beings, from what source would the sages arise?

Therefore, whenever a Buddha attains enlightenment, he vows to deliver sentient beings; this is the meaning of an uninterrupted succession of transformation after transformation. The nature of sentient beings is fundamentally...

This "coming" refers to the Buddha. Because the spiritual mind is shrouded by various defilements and afflictions, the Tathāgata delivers and liberates beings according to their respective capacities and natures.
Thus, the three vehicles and five natures are collectively termed "sentient beings. Therefore, the five hundred people and the thirty sons are included herein.
△ Fourth, the confluence with the great fire arising.
Birth, old age, sickness, and death; sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction;

the darkness of ignorance and the fire of the three poisons—birth, old age, sickness, and death are that which no one in the world can avoid. Between gods and humans, there is only a distinction of coarseness and subtlety;
these constitute the fundamental suffering. The four characters "sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction" collectively refer to all forms of suffering, yet when discussed individually:

Sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is the meeting with what is disliked; grief (*parideva*) is separation from what is loved; suffering (*duḥkha*) is the burning intensity of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*);

and affliction (*upāyāsa*) is the failure to obtain what one seeks. As for taking the obscuration of ignorance (*avidyā*) as suffering: all sentient beings fundamentally possess the virtues and functions of the Tathāgata.
Due to the darkness of ignorance, they lose the vision of the Buddha; due to the obscuration of ignorance, they lose the knowledge of the Buddha. Because of this...
They lose the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and for this reason they undergo the cycle of rebirth in vain.

Thus we know that the bitter fruit of birth and death, as well as the bitter causes of the three poisons, are all established from ignorance; therefore, ignorance is the greatest of sufferings. As for the three poisons:
That is to say, when a deluded mind encounters all objects that accord with its desires and draws them in without satiety, it is called greed (*rāga*).
When a deluded mind encounters all objects that oppose its desires and gives rise to resentment and anger, it is called hatred (*dveṣa*).

To be deluded regarding all phenomena of principle and fact, failing to understand through ignorance and giving rise to various wrong practices, is called delusion (*moha*). These three are all called "poisons" because they are able to—
Because they destroy the supramundane roots of goodness, this combines with the above to cause fire to suddenly break out. △ Fifth, combining [the previous points] into a single gate:
he teaches and transforms them so that they may attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The path of Bodhi-realization seems difficult to unify into a single gate; yet that which all sages have realized and all ordinary deluded beings are confused about does not lie outside of this.

Now, the Tathāgata has appeared in the world, taking what he himself has realized to awaken others from their delusions, skillfully demonstrating it through manifold means so that all sentient beings may cultivate and practice it in every thought-moment, transforming birth-and-death into the one True Suchness. Out...
To depart from birth and death and realize nirvana—there is only this single gate. Thus, it is combined with the preceding single gate.

△ Second, combining the individual metaphors. This is divided into four parts. First, combining [the metaphor of] the elder seeing the fire. This is divided into three parts. First, combining the seer and the seen.
"Seeing all sentient beings [subjected to] birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth—these various kinds of suffering.
The word "seeing" (*jian*) refers to the wisdom that contemplates; "all sentient beings" below it refers to the objects of contemplation.
This corresponds to the great fire rising from the four directions; since the fire is vast, the calamities gathered therein must be many.
Therefore, with the Buddha-eye, the Tathāgata beholds all sentient beings being scorched and boiled by various afflictions;

these constitute the fires of the three sufferings and the eight sufferings. As for the eight sufferings: birth, aging, sickness, and death constitute four; attachment and the like constitute the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;
and taking birth in the hells or the heavens constitutes the suffering of the blazing five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), further compounded by encountering those who cause resentment.

Separation from what is loved constitutes the eighth [suffering]. Regarding the three types of suffering: sorrow, lamentation, burning, and boiling, as well as the three miserable realms such as hell, constitute *duḥkha-duḥkhatā* (the suffering of suffering).

To be separated from and parted from beloved objects constitutes *vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā* (the suffering of change). The incessant instability of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) constitutes *saṃskāra-duḥkhatā* (the suffering of conditioned formations).
All these various sufferings arise from the four inversions; therefore, they are combined with the aforementioned fire rising on the four sides. △ Second, combining the extensive [explanation].
[He] sees sentient beings submerged therein (up to) not regarding even great suffering as a calamity. Zhizhi says:
"The Tathāgata sees the sons of the three vehicles within the three realms and five destinies, who are constantly afflicted by the eight sufferings."

"Scorching" serves as the general designation for the root of suffering. Those with even a modicum of merit become intoxicated by the five desires—wealth, beauty, fame, food, and sleep—and thereby undergo various forms of suffering.
Those without merit pursue the causes of these five desires and subsequently receive the retribution of the three miserable realms.
Once the retribution of the three realms is exhausted, they may be born among humans or in the heavens; yet even then, they cannot escape poverty and hardship.

Among parents, wives, and children, there is the suffering of separation from those one loves; with water, fire, thieves, creditors, and enemies, there is the suffering of encountering those one hates.
Furthermore, there is birth, old age, sickness, and death, as one transmigrates through the six realms of existence in a cycle of suffering that is inexhaustible.
Yet these children, on the contrary, regard this as pleasure, sporting within the four modes of birth, unaware of the Buddha-nature inherently possessed within them.
By nature, they are neither aware nor cognizant of the perils of birth and death; they are neither startled nor terrified by them.
Though they clearly know this is suffering, they do not give rise to revulsion or renunciation; though they clearly know there is a Buddha, they do not seek liberation.
They take pleasure in this fire-hall of the triple world, receiving retribution according to their karma, running hither and thither. Although they encounter such great suffering, they do not—

This is indeed a source of affliction; such a person is truly to be pitied. This precisely accords with the aforementioned state where suffering cuts one to the core, yet the mind feels no aversion toward it and lacks the intent to seek liberation. △ Third, the appropriate arousal of alarm and fear.
Śāriputra, having seen this, [the Buddha]—up to—"causes them to sport in the joy of the Buddha’s wisdom.
He joins his entire body and hands into a single powerful joint.

Yet sentient beings, shrouded by their own ignorance, are incessantly tormented by the fires of the three poisons and the like. Since I am their father, ought I not to provide for their rescue and relief?

How can one truly extract them from their suffering and distress? By means of the power of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he transforms all sentient beings and extracts them from the sufferings of the five turbidities (*pañcakaṣāya*).
If he were merely to extract their suffering without causing them to attain supreme bliss, then his role as a father would be deficient.
Therefore, he further bestows the bliss of Buddha-wisdom (*buddhajñāna*) so that they may sport within it; thus, by the power of great kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), he causes all sentient beings—
One attains the joy of the two adornments. The children within the burning house take delight in playing with the pleasures of the five desires;
they have brought these upon themselves. Here, by means of the joy of the Buddha’s wisdom, one causes them to play; this is what the Buddha bestows upon them.
Although the realms of suffering and joy differ, it is merely a single turning of the mind. II. Combined Abandonment.
The Use of the Couch. This is divided into two parts. First, the relinquishing of the couch. This is further divided into two. First, the consideration of what is appropriate.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata again had this thought: (up to) sentient beings cannot be delivered by means of this.
Tiantai says: "The preceding [passage] provides two gates—exhortation and admonition—as provisional models.

Now, we only combine the gate of exhortation, for exhortation constitutes the primary cultivation, whereas admonition serves merely as an auxiliary support. Within this provisional model, the supernatural power corresponds to the body;
wisdom corresponds to the hands; the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision correspond to the robe and lap; and the powers and fearlessnesses correspond to the table and desk. Sentient beings..."
Those who could have been delivered by this [teaching] were such that the Dharma was great while their faculties were small, and thus they did not harmonize.
Why is this? Because these sentient beings [from here until] for what reason could they understand the Buddha’s wisdom?
This explains the reason why they could not be delivered. It corresponds to the preceding section concerning how the sons were immature and ignorant, clinging to their playgrounds.
The reason they were unable to attain deliverance was that the obstructions of the five turbidities were deep;
being pressed by the various fires, how could they have understood the subtle, wondrous, and inconceivable Dharma of the Mahāyāna?
△ Second, explaining the cessation of activity.
"Śāriputra, like that elder... (up to) "...and then gave each of them a precious great chariot.

This is a reiteration of the preceding text to clarify the intention of employing skillful means (*upāya*) to manifest the ultimate reality (*bhūta-artha*). △ Second, the combined application of the chariots. Section.
Fourth: The single [vehicle] is intended to correspond to the three carts.

The Tathāgata is likewise; from [the passage] "in this same way" up to "rescuing sentient beings from the burning house of the triple world," each point can be seen through the correspondence between the Dharma and the parable.
Therefore, one knows that the Tathāgata conceals his excellence and manifests inferiority, teaching by means of the One.

3. Regarding the burning house of the triple world, how could the employment of skillful means be anything other than necessary? △ Second, the father, knowing his sons' inclinations, speaks of the three vehicles:
the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the buddhayāna.

This clarifies that the Buddha taught the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*). "Vehicle" (*yāna*) takes the sense of transporting or conveying. Tiantai says: "The *śrāvaka* takes the Four Noble Truths as their vehicle;
the *pratyekabuddha* takes the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination as their vehicle; and the *bodhisattva* takes the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) as their vehicle.
They transport themselves out of the triple world and return to *nirvāṇa*. Within their respective teachings, the *bodhisattvas* of the Six Perfections likewise..."

It is called the Mahāyāna. It is now also called the Buddha-vehicle because the Bodhisattva, through thirty-four moments of mind, suddenly severs the afflictions of view and thought along with their habitual tendencies and thereby attains Buddhahood;
for this reason, it is also named the Buddha-vehicle. △ Third, a combined praise of the rarity of the vehicle.
And he spoke these words: "You must not take pleasure in dwelling [in the realms]... [down to] the vehicles of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or the Buddha-vehicle.
This clarifies that the Buddha exhorts them to abandon greed and grasp for true happiness. Tiantai says: "The burning house of the three realms" refers to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
"Form, sound, fragrance," and so forth, refer to the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), as they all arise from the accumulation and increase of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
The burning house represents all manner of sufferings. Among the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), there are both those that are "intimate" and those that are "distant.

Regarding form (*rūpa*), the intimate is the beautiful appearance of men and women; the distant refers to the various worldly colors such as black, yellow, red, and white. Regarding sound (*śabda*), the intimate is the singing and chanting of men and women;
the distant includes the sounds of stringed and wind instruments, jade ornaments, and various other noises. Regarding fragrance (*gandha*), the intimate is that of men and women...

The fragrance of the body: as for its direct [perception], it is like various worldly perfumes such as agallochum, sandalwood, dragon’s blood, and musk; as for its indirect [perception], it is like medicinal herbs, fruits, and foods. The flavor:
