as for its direct [perception], it is like various delicious tastes such as delicacies and fine foods; as for its indirect [perception], it is like [the taste of] medicinal herbs, fruits, and foods. The touch:

as for its direct [perception], it refers to the soft and supple touches of the male and female bodies; as for its indirect [perception], it refers to coldness, warmth, roughness, and smoothness. These are called the five objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), and they are also called...
The five desires are the cause of all sufferings; therefore, they constitute the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

To swiftly emerge from the triple world (*tridhātu*), he points out the two truths of Cessation (*nirodha*) and the Path (*mārga*), showing that beyond the triple world there exist the fruits of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) resulting from wisdom and abandonment.

Thus, he causes them to emerge swiftly so that they may attain the three vehicles, which correspond to the aforementioned three carts now standing outside the gate. Within the context of the fourfold turning of the Four Truths, this is—
This indicates the turning [of the wheel] through manifestation.
"I now guarantee this matter for you" (up to the point where it says) "the Tathāgata uses these skillful means to entice and advance sentient beings.
To "guarantee" means to take responsibility so as not to lose [the path]. By means of this course of action, both [the teacher and the student] traverse the same path already traveled by themselves.

"Now I cause you all to diligently practice therein. All essential matters whatsoever, I shall take responsibility for and bear upon myself for you, until you have certainly attained this vehicle of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, or Buddha, and only then shall it end.
How could there ever be any error regarding you? Sons, you should simply focus your resolve and proceed forward; do not give rise to regression or fall away."
Such is the meaning of these words. How urgent and how essential they are! This is the second turning for the sake of realization.
Again, he spoke thus: "You should know... (until)... you shall thereby obtain immeasurable peace and happiness."
This combines with the preceding section on "those things you may cherish, which are rare and difficult to obtain. Tiantai says:

These three vehicles are the ritual methods by which all Buddhas employ skillful means to guide sentient beings; therefore, they are called "praised by the sages. To attain the wisdom of non-arising is called "sovereignty";
to attain inexhaustible wisdom is called "non-attachment. [The realization that] "my births are exhausted and I shall not receive further existence" [is the fruit].
"Having nothing further," is called "having no basis. "Having accomplished what was to be done" and "the holy life having been established" are called "having nothing further to seek.
These all sequence the merit of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). Following these three vehicles, one then sequences actual wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).

By means of the two characters "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*), all subsequent qualities such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) are subsumed; they are all outflow-free, not the outflow-tainted wisdom of the provisional vehicles.

The five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the four dhyānas, the eight concentrations, the eight liberations, as well as right concentration and so forth, all belong to true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). Consequently, one attains immeasurable peace and happiness.
This is the third exhortation to practice and transform. IV. Meeting the Aspirations of the Disciples. This is divided into three parts. First, meeting those who desire the sheep-cart.
"Śāriputra, if there are sentient beings... (up to) "...they leave the burning house seeking the goat-drawn carriage.
This clarifies that the sons, through transformation, realize the fruits of the Way. First, the Śrāvaka-yāna is clarified. *Zhizhi* says:

"If there are sentient beings" refers generally to those within the six realms of existence. Because they possess the seeds of the Three Vehicles from past habituation, it is said that "they have the nature of wisdom within.
Now, upon hearing the holy teachings of the Three Vehicles from the Buddha, they immediately accept them with faith; this is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

"Diligently and energetically" refers to the practice of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmas*). [This leads to the overcoming of] the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-heya-kleśas*).

When [the afflictions] are exhausted, one finally emerges from the triple world; this is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). Those who seek *nirvāṇa* for themselves attain the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-prajñā*) and realize *nirvāṇa* with remainder;
this is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Because their understanding arises from following the teachings, they are called the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
Their power is weak, and they are able only to benefit themselves, like the children who sought the goat-drawn carts to escape the burning house. △ Second, the combined [explanation].
The deer cart:
if there are sentient beings who, for the sake of seeking the deer cart, emerge from the burning house by means of the Buddha, the World-Honored One—this clarifies the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
In Sanskrit it is called *pratyekabuddha*, which is translated here as "Pratyekabuddha" (Solitary Realizer); it is also termed "Duo-jue" (Solitary Enlightened).

Appearing in an age without a Buddha, by virtue of the seeds of wisdom cultivated in past lives, they personally recognize that birth and death are suffering and spontaneously give rise to the wisdom that severs suffering.

Now, hearing the twelve links of dependent origination from a Buddha, their seeds of wisdom increase profoundly as they repeatedly investigate and exhaustively analyze the principle of the twelve links.
Furthermore, this principle of dependent origination exists inherently; it was not created by a Buddha or a deity. Therefore, it is said:

Possessing natural wisdom, he delights in dwelling alone. Directly and immediately he illuminates and realizes that all conditions are like illusions, thereby realizing the state of partial quiescence;
hence he is called "well-quiescent. One who deeply understands the causes and conditions of all phenomena is able [to master] both the gates of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Contemplating the principle of causes and conditions refers to all phenomena, which are precisely the twelvefold chain of dependent origination.
The *pratyekabuddha* hears little of the Dharma from others but extensively infers its meaning for themselves; they take as their metaphor the deer that does not rely on humans.

Furthermore, their nature encompasses both the common teachings and the specific doctrine, possessing a compassion that looks back, just as a deer looks back toward its herd. △ Third, the inclusion of the ox-cart.
"If there are sentient beings who, from the Buddha, the World-Honored One... [up to] seeking the ox-cart, exit the burning house.
This clarifies the Bodhisattva Vehicle of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*). *Zhizhi* says:

"In terms of the delusions to be destroyed, it begins from the three categories of aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), up to the seven great similarities and transformations. In terms of the wisdom that destroys them, it begins from the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*)..."

Because one desires to thoroughly comprehend all stages—namely, the stages of abiding, practice, direction, and the grounds, as well as the two types of sublime awakening—one is said to "seek all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*).
Contemplating both the ultimate and the conventional is called "Buddha-wisdom. The simultaneous integration of the provisional and the real is called "spontaneity" (*svayambhū*).

Responding to objects with fundamental, wondrous clarity is called "teacherless. The Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, the ten powers, and so forth, are the Prajñā of the Dharma-body; they belong to the ultimate reality.

Wisdom—such as compassionate mindfulness, peace, and bliss—belongs to expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). Because it is the simultaneous integration of the expedient and the real, it is called the Mahāyāna.
One is termed a *mahāsattva* because they benefit both themselves and others; thus, this Bodhisattva’s essence and function are in perfect accord.

Being sovereign, heroic, and courageous, and possessing the virtue of universal support, they are metaphorically likened to an ox-cart. If judged according to time, [the other vehicles are] the sheep and deer carts.
The two carts refer to events from the twenty years prior to the *Vaipulya Āgama*. The ox carts refer to events from the twenty years following the assembly on the *Prajñāpāramitā* [Sūtra].
If judged according to the capacities of the disciples (*yogya*), then the preceding and succeeding accounts mutually clarify one another.
△ Third, the equal bestowal of the great carts, divided into two parts. First, the simultaneous citation of the two metaphors.
Śāriputra, it is like that elder (up to) bestowing great chariots equally upon his sons.

This clarifies that the equal bestowal is free from dualistic thought. In the previous parable, there were four sections: escaping the peril, requesting the chariots, the granting [of the chariots], and the joy [thereof].
Now, these are condensed into only two: because reaching the place of fearlessness encompasses the intent of requesting the chariots, and because of this equality.
"Bestowed upon the center" also implies joy. △ Second, the combined application of the two parables, divided into two parts. First, the application regarding the avoidance of calamity:
"The Tathāgata is also like this" (up to) "...attaining the bliss of nirvāṇa from the perilous path of fear."
This means that the Tathāgata is likewise so; it is the principle that he should equally bestow the great chariots. Tiantai says:
"The Tathāgata takes the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle as the great chariot; thus its substance encompasses all virtues, maintaining both emptiness and existence."

This is simply because the ultimate truth and conventional truth proceed side by side. As for the "gateways of the Buddha's teaching," these refer to the dharmas such as the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the Six Perfections.

"Those who are terrified" refers to the burning house of the three realms. "The perilous path" refers to the six destinies of rising and sinking—the most extremely dangerous and evil paths. II. Bestowing [the teachings] equally.
At that time, the Tathāgata thought: (up to) "I shall bring them all to nirvāṇa by means of the nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
This corresponds to the section where the carriage is high and wide, adorned with various jewels, and filled to overflowing with all kinds of treasuries.
The Tathāgata thought: "This is precisely the Lotus Sūtra. He then gathered all the kings together and entrusted his family estate to them.
"At this time," "immeasurable power of wisdom, fearlessness, and so forth" refers precisely to these dharmas; they are the Tathāgata’s great treasury of the Dharma-treasure and the like.
"To those of the Mahāyāna" means that he entrusts the secret treasury of the three virtues—immeasurable wisdom and so forth—to his sons.
"Not allowing anyone to enter parinirvāṇa alone" refers to the three cycles of universal [teaching].

Record: To cause all people to universally attain Buddhahood—just as arriving at this assembly, gathering the three vehicles into one and subsuming the provisional and small into the real—means that persons are not different from persons, and dharmas are not different from dharmas. Birth and Buddhahood are non-dual;
sages and ordinary beings are of one essence. This is called "extinguishing them by means of the Tathāgata’s extinction."
"These sentient beings who have escaped the triple world... [up to] ...are able to give rise to the supreme, pure, and wondrous joy.
This corresponds to the section: "This accords with my infinite wealth and property; furthermore, each rides upon a great vehicle, which was not what they originally expected.
*Zhizhi* says: First, it cites how sentient beings of the three vehicles rely on provisional wisdom to exit the triple world, as when the sons...
He sat in the open air. This is equal to the meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) of all Buddhas; it is the intention of bestowing with an impartial mind.

The *dhyāna* of the Buddhas is the unity of the ultimate and the conventional, belonging to the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā*). The meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the Buddhas is the suchness of emptiness and existence.
The Dharma-body virtue belongs to the liberation of all Buddhas; the simultaneous operation of the provisional and the real belongs to the liberation virtue.
These three virtues are inherently complete, and the four wisdoms are perfectly luminous; these constitute the instruments for the Buddha’s enjoyment.

He bestows them all upon the children of the Three Vehicles, entrusting them with the family inheritance. All such dharmas as those entrusted above are of a single characteristic and a single flavor; they are definitively not otherwise.

Although it may be attained through provisional means, those who uphold this single characteristic and single vehicle realize that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated in their threefold equality, thus forming the one true Dharma-realm;
hence it is called "one characteristic. When sought with sincerity throughout the ten directions, no other vehicle exists;
hence it is called "one vehicle. Furthermore, these dharmas are all collectively guarded by the various sages until the attainment of eternal bliss.
Because I purify the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), it is said that I can produce the pure, wondrous, and supreme bliss.
△ Fourth, the union with non-falsity:
"Śāriputra, just as that elder... [until] ...and only then deliver them by means of the Mahāyāna."
This clarifies that the provisional and the real are without falsehood. The application of the analogy can be understood accordingly.

That "the Tathāgata is without falsehood" is a general conclusion that both the provisional and the real are not false. First, the provisional teaching of the three vehicles was expounded to lead sentient beings out of the triple world.

Thus, the Tathāgata’s employment of skillful means is not in vain; he later delivers them by means of the Mahāyāna, universally enabling those of the three faculties to equally achieve perfect enlightenment.
This is his non-falsity regarding the ultimate reality.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable wisdom (up to: ...), he distinguishes and teaches three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle.
Why is this? It is because there is no falsehood in his purpose; that is to say, why must the Tathāgata necessarily employ provisional means first and reveal the ultimate reality later?
It is because the treasury of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, meditative concentrations, and all dharmas is fundamentally inexhaustible.
As for why the provisional teachings were taught first: it was because their capacities were small and they were unable to receive [the ultimate truth].
Now, the Tathāgata bestows the Mahāyāna Dharma upon all of them without exception; yet, although the Tathāgata bestows it completely, sentient beings are unable to receive it entirely.

Therefore, within the single Buddha-vehicle, he speaks of two and three vehicles. Śāriputra previously asked: "I pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly."

Therefore, it is said now that this is for such causes and conditions. As for what you previously said—that these twelve hundred people have fallen into doubt upon hearing what they have never heard before—you should know today that all of this is the power of the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Buddhas.

In reality, there is fundamentally only the One Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*); it is merely distinguished and taught as three. The Tathāgata has thus compassionately and exhaustively bestowed [this teaching].

Through compassion, the minds of those who doubt shall be resolved as clearly as ice melting away. The prose section of parables is now concluded. II. Verses in Praise (Gāthā). This is divided into two parts.

First, one hundred verses praising the preceding section. This is further divided into two. First, verses praising the opening parable. This is further divided into two. First, verses praising the general parable.
This is divided into four parts. First, one verse praising the Great Elder.
The Buddha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"For example, there was an elder.
This stanza clarifies the person capable of rescuing others; he is the master of a single house. Tiantai says: "This verse indicates the title of the superior position."
He is also renowned for his conduct; his virtuous deeds are honored by the kingdoms, cities, and villages.
Thus, he is an elder of advanced age and virtue, who serves as an analogy for Śākyamuni Tathāgata, the Great Dharma-King of the three lands. △ Second, the verse on the extensive dwelling.
There was a great house that was ancient and dilapidated (extending until) its surrounding walls were winding and crooked, filled everywhere with filth and impurity.

This "great house" is a metaphor for the general characteristics of the triple world (*tridhātu*). Its being "ancient and dilapidated" signifies that since beginningless kalpas, sentient beings have been deluded regarding the truth and have pursued the false, thereby illusorily forming these delusive realms of the triple world.
Its being "suddenly decrepit" is a metaphor for the imminent arrival of the kalpa of destruction (*saṃvarta-kalpa*).

This collectively indicates the characteristic of the three realms as being unstable. From "the hall and house" down to "filled everywhere with filth," this collectively clarifies the four phases of the burning house of the three realms:
formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness. The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is the hall; the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) is the house.
Since one cannot avoid falling [from them], they are said to be "high and perilous. The "base of the pillars" refers to the life-root of karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*). By means of...
The consciousness of karmic destiny is called "crumbling decay. When the beams and rafters collapse and become perilous, this signifies that one's wholesome merit is diminishing.
The foundation and steps represent the ignorance that drives the movement of birth and karma; their ruin signifies long-standing, deep-seated [afflictions].

The crumbling and splitting of the walls signifies the deterioration of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). The plaster represents the defiled mind within the four great elements. *Dha*... [text fragment]
"Fallen" refers to the entanglement of defilements (*saṃkleśa*). "Roofing and thatching" refers to the use of these to shield against the wind and rain from the four directions;
it is a metaphor for the arising and ceasing of the four marks of self and person (*ātman-pudgala*) from moment to moment, hence the term "chaotically falling.

All scattered wholesome virtues and the dharmas of precepts are the rafters and eaves that protect the three realms. "Lapses and omissions" refer to neglecting and failing to practice them. "Complete enclosure" is...
The six consciousnesses revolve in mutual obstruction and separation. "Crookedness" refers to the bending and non-convergence of the six sense organs.

Because consciousness relies upon the organs to grasp various sensory objects, it is said that "impurity pervades everywhere. This is because although the three realms are vast, they are formed by the delusive afflictions of all sentient beings;
as it is said: "Due to delusive ignorance there is empty space; depending on space, the world is established."
The realms (*dhātu*)—all these metaphors, without exception, illustrate how sentient beings achieve their existence through delusion.

While using them to represent a single person may be quite appropriate in terms of their essential nature, they are not as pertinent as using them to illustrate the characteristics of the three realms.
This world is a continuous succession; it crumbles (*pi*), splits (*che*), decays (*chi*), leaks (*shan*), and its rafters (*chuan*) fall apart.
Lǚ (pronounced lǚ). Cī (pronounced cī). △ Three verses on five hundred people.
There are five hundred people dwelling therein.
The three realms are divided into twenty-five locations; because the locations upon which they rely differ, so too do the classes of beings who rely upon them.

These are also of various kinds. Taken collectively, they all constitute the sentient beings of the five destinies; thus, the thirty sons are also included therein. This is the continuity of sentient beings.
△ Four: Verses on the Arising of the Great Fire. Divided into four parts. One: Explaining the analogy of the fire upon the earth as representing the desire realm. Further divided into four. One:
Explaining the types of things burned as representing the ten fetters (*daśa-ānuśaya*). Further divided into two. One: The actual [explanation].

This clarifies that which is burned. Furthermore, the section on "crookedness" is divided into two parts. First, it clarifies how birds and beasts are burned, serving as a metaphor for the five dull afflictions (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*).

Moreover, the physical forms of sentient beings within the three realms are produced by the retribution of karma; karma arises from delusion. Within this process, there is the ascent and descent of good and evil.

Whether horizontal or vertical, large or small, although the retributions they receive differ in myriad ways, their successive cycles of saṃsāra are all driven by ignorance, the three poisons, the five turbidities, and the ten fetters; thus, the continuity of karmic fruits is established.
The Tathāgata now wishes to explain in detail all the various defiled and evil characteristics within the triple world, so as to...
People know that all of this is produced by the delusions of sentient beings. If, in a single thought-moment, one suddenly gives rise to wondrous wisdom, one overturns defilement to achieve purity;
only then does one believe that within this state which is fundamentally pure, it is due to sentient beings' failure to maintain their own true nature.
Thus, the conditioned phenomena of mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all sentient beings suddenly arise.

Therefore, from this point downward, the text provides a detailed explanation of the sentient beings in the three realms who undergo the most extreme suffering, revealing their conditions as they receive the retributive sufferings of the three miserable paths.
First, the retribution of animals is presented; it is that which is summoned and induced by the five dull afflictions: greed, anger, ignorance, pride, and doubt.
The following sections largely follow the Tiantai interpretation; however, they are indicated here by circles. The analysis is divided into two parts.
First, the five dull afflictions (*mūḍha-kleśa*) are separately opened up and divided into five. The first is the latent tendency of pride (*māna-anuśaya*).
The hawk, the owl, the eagle, the vulture, the crow, the magpie, the pigeon, and the dove. As for "pride" (*māna*):
it is to exalt oneself and disparage others, like a bird soaring high and looking down from above. Thus, these eight birds are used as metaphors.

To look down upon others constitutes pride (*māna*), while to hold oneself in high esteem constitutes arrogance (*mada*). According to the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, there are eight types of pride. [The first is] the pride of youth (*taruṇa-māna*).

Arrogance regarding prosperity is like that of an owl; arrogance regarding nature is like that of an *xiāo* (owl); arrogance regarding wealth is like that of a hawk; arrogance regarding power is like that of a vulture;

arrogance regarding longevity is like that of a crow; arrogance regarding intelligence is like that of a magpie; arrogance regarding the performance of good deeds is like that of a pigeon; and arrogance regarding physical beauty is like that of a dove.
These eight types are all driven by pride. [Owl] (pronounced *tái*); [Xiāo] (pronounced *jiāo*); [Hawk] (pronounced *diāo*); [Vulture] (pronounced *xiù*).
Pigeon (pronounced gé). △ Second, the affliction of anger (*dveṣa*).
Vipers, snakes, vipers, scorpions, centipedes, and millipedes.
○ Regarding "anger": it is the inability to endure various evils. There are three types. First, irrational anger: not considering whether something is appropriate or not.
It arises suddenly. Second is anger that accords with reason (*yoniśo-dveṣa*), which arises when another person actually harms me.
Third is anger of contention (*vivāda-dveṣa*), which means regarding oneself as right and others as wrong. A viper (*vṛścika*) is most large and poisonous;
it stings without being touched, like anger that does not accord with reason. A *vṛścika* (also meaning "retribution") stings when touched; when one is enraged, its venom is present.
Regarding the head: it is also called the *fùshé* (viper). Its snout is turned upward, and there are needles upon it; this species is born only from a womb (*jarāyu-jā*).
At birth, it immediately tears open its mother’s belly. When touched, its venom is unbearable. This is a metaphor for harboring anger while clinging to one's own principles.

As for the centipede: another name is *jíqū*. Upon seeing a large snake, it climbs up and eats it, causing distress. That which is mentioned in the *Zhuangzi* as "the *jíqū* delights in the *dài*" refers to this very creature.
The *yòuyán* belongs to the class of centipedes. Those with red necks are *wúgōng*; those whose necks are not red are called *yòuyán*.
They have a hundred legs; they are also called *mǎxián* and *shāngjù*. This is what the *Zhuāngzǐ* refers to as the "shāngjù galloping across the river.
It serves as a metaphor for frivolous argumentation (*prapañca*) and anger (*dveṣa*). Furthermore, among people in the world who harbor the poison of anger, although their physical forms differ...

It is no different from anger; upon hearing this, one must recognize it and repent. [The venomous snakes] are the *vān* (pronounced yuan), the *fù* (pronounced fu), the *xié* (pronounced xie), the *wú* (pronounced wu), the *sōng* (pronounced gong), the *yóu* (pronounced you), and the *yán* (pronounced yan). △ Third, the latent tendency of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*).
Geckos, centipedes, weasels, badgers, mice (up to) dung beetles and various other insects gather upon it.
"Ignorance" refers to the lack of understanding regarding objects; it is precisely nescience (*avidyā*). It is of two kinds: first, independent (*kevala*); second, associated (*saṃprayukta*).
The "gecko" is the lizard, also called the *maṇḍūka*. If one feeds it with vermilion, its body becomes entirely red.

Red. Pound it ten thousand times with a pestle and apply it to a woman’s body; it will remain for her entire life and not fade away. When she engages in sexual intercourse with a man, it becomes hidden.

In common parlance, this is called the "scorpion-tiger" (*xièhǔ*); it is adept at climbing fences and walls. This is a metaphor for the "isolated ignorance" (*mūla-avidyā*). The "weasel" (*yòu*) is simply the wild rat.
The reddish-yellow animal is the wildcat (*mārjāra*), which is skilled at devouring swarms of mice; it is also a skilled diviner. When it moves, it stops to deliberate and measure its path.
The *kṣīra-mūṣika* (the "dwarf mouse") is the smallest of mice; it is also called the "sweet-mouthed mouse. It inflicts injury on people without them knowing the pain.

This is a metaphor for the ignorance (*avidyā*) that corresponds [to the conditions]. As for the various evil insects, they arise from the root of delusion (*moha*), fully manifesting all the fetters (*saṃyojana*). They intermingle...

Horizontal phrase: This clarifies how the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) condition one another, or how they condition the three realms, arising with such rapidity as if crossing over one another.
The phrase "running toward excrement and urine" clarifies that the objects to which the deluded mind clings are all impure.
*Śālāṅka* is also called *gōngqiāng*. According to the *Chuān*, the *śālāṅka* has no nose yet can smell fragrances; it frequents foul places.
Therefore it is said: "The wisdom of the dung beetle lies in its rolling of balls.

The worldly people who are attached to various objects of desire and whose deluded minds persist for a long time are not much different from this. *Shǔ* (pronounced yòu), *lí* (pronounced lí), *xī* (pronounced xī), *qiāng* (pronounced qiāng), and *láng* (pronounced liáng). △ Fourth: The Latency of Greed.
Foxes, wolves, and jackals gnaw and trample [the corpses] until they become emaciated and weak; terrified and frantic, they seek food everywhere. Regarding "greed" (*tṛṣṇā*):
it is the state of being deluded by attachment and unable to let go. There are two kinds: first, those with power; second, those without power.
The fox is a beast of seductive charm that attains spiritual efficacy by worshipping the Big Dipper and is skilled in transformations. The wolf is as large as a dog.
The *śṛgāla* (jackal) is a species of dog that howls at night as an omen of ill fortune; it is among beasts one who is possessed by demons and malevolent spirits.
To "chew roughly" is called *cuǒ*, and to "chew finely" is called *jiáo*. To *cì* means to devour the flesh; to *niè* means to gnaw the bones.
This is an analogy for powerful greed, which seizes things through force and intimidation, like foxes and wolves. As for powerless greed, it can only follow...
He begs for coarse and wretched things, like a jackal or similar beast; how much more so when the greedy mind seizes upon objects.
Whether they are useful or not, if useful, it takes them as if chewing; if useless, it takes them as if trampling.

Furthermore, the greedy mind seizes upon objects either by taking one thing or many, like gnawing and biting, until bones and flesh are left in a chaotic mess—this is the accumulation of the five [aggregates].
"Dust" refers to not knowing where to stop. "A pack of dogs pouncing and seizing" is a metaphor for the manner in which those with strength plunder those who are weak.

"Pouncing" (*tuan*) means to spring up and search with both feet; "seizing" (*cuo*) means to gather [the prey] into one place. It refers to the remains left over after the foxes and wolves have eaten.

"Dogs come to snatch and seize" means that a pack of dogs arrives together; "they compete to come" describes those who, lacking strength, vainly strive to take [what is not theirs]—this is enough to provoke a laugh.
"Greed knows no satisfaction" is like hunger; "seeking but unable to obtain" is like emaciation; "in terror and alarm" refers to various kinds of searching and seeking.
"Seeking food everywhere" means rushing after the realms of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). Furthermore, "terror and alarm" [refers to their state of mind].
Those who are fearful and unsettled, and those who are excessively greedy, are poor despite their wealth; thus it is said they "panic and seek everywhere.

*Gān* (pronounced *àn*), *jǔ* (first tone of *jū*), *jiào* (second tone of *qiáng*), *tà* (pronounced *tà*), *cì* (pronounced *qí*), *niè* (pronounced *niè*), *tuó* (pronounced *tuán*), *cuō* (second tone of *zuàn*), *léi* (pronounced *léi*), *zhāng* (pronounced *zhāng*), *huáng* (pronounced *huáng*). △ Five.
The proclivity of doubt.
They fight, struggle, seize, drag, snap at, howl, and bark.
Regarding "doubt": it is hesitation between two extremes. To snatch from the front is called *ca* (seizing); to pull back from behind is called *che* (dragging).

"Chè" (pulling/tugging) represents the state of quarreling. To snap at an object while struggling over it to death is called "jiānzhī" (snarling). To lose an object and cry out wildly is called "háo wèi" (howling and barking).

These are the sounds of contention and strife; they serve as a metaphor for worldly people who harbor doubts and fail to reach a decision, manifesting the aspect of verbal disputes over self and other, right and wrong—such instances exist.
The separate exposition of the five dull afflictions (*pañca-nivaraṇa*) is now complete. "Zhā" (pronounced zhā). "Chè."
(The sounds penetrate). Jǎi (pronounced yái). Chī (pronounced chái). Háo (pronounced háo). △ Second, a summary of the transformed states.
Such are the terrifying transformations within that house;
this summarizes the aforementioned five *anuśayas* (latent tendencies). This house is a metaphor for the triple world (*tridhātu*).

It is said that the minds of those in the triple world possess these [afflictions] of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt, and are thus fearful and terrifying. These transformations are like the birds, beasts, insects, and snakes upon the *tathatā* (suchness).
None can fathom it. △ Second, the analogy of ghosts and spirits being burned, representing the five *pañca-dṛṣṭi* (five views). This is divided into two parts.
First, a general explanation of the sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇa-indriya*). Everywhere there are *ch’i-mei* and *wang-liang* (goblins and specters).
This uses the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*) within the three realms as an analogy for sentient beings who possess five sharp mental states; their form is like this.
The preceding five—greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt—are still merely what makes one an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), and thus they are called "dull.
Only these five—the view of a self, the view of extremes, wrong view, attachment to precepts and rituals, and doubt—no ordinary person can escape them, even regarding the Four Truths.

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are present wherever one comes into contact with them. For example, if I wish to study the Buddha’s teachings and the path of the sages, he [the Māra] will, within that very process of studying the Buddha and the sages, cause one to unknowingly and imperceptibly go astray. Therefore, it is said: "everywhere."
This is because they are advantageous for the five aforementioned emissaries. *Chī-mèi* (goblins) are the essences of things, the monsters of mountains and marshes.
The *Xijing fu* states: "The mountain deity with a tiger’s form is called a *chī*; the house-deity with a pig’s head and human body is called a *mèi*.
*Wǎnglǎng* (sprites) are transformations of wood and stone. These four can hide or manifest; they may seem to exist or not exist. They are skillful...

There are a hundred kinds of monsters, their transformations manifold and inconsistent; therefore, this is used as a metaphor for the mind of sentient beings’ views concerning the self and its possessions, and their attachment to heterodox precepts.
△ Second, the separate opening of the five benefits, divided into five parts. First, wrong view.
The yakṣas and evil spirits devour human flesh... (up to) the sounds of their quarreling are most terrifying.
This is a metaphor for wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Because one calculates [existence] in terms of annihilationism or eternalism and does not believe in cause and effect, it is called wrong view.
"Yakṣa" here is translated as "swift ghost"; this serves as a metaphor for those with wrong view who deny cause and effect. "Human" refers to a wholesome retribution; this serves as a metaphor for...
Regarding the causes and effects of the supramundane: those with false views deny the existence of good retribution, which is like eating human flesh.

Venomous insects represent evil retribution; this is analogous to the causes and effects of the mundane world. Those with false views deny the existence of evil retribution, which is like devouring venomous insects.
Regarding the phrase "incubating and suckling," the *Guangya* states: "Incubating (*fu*) also means to give birth; suckling (*ru*) means to nourish. This refers to the category of oviparous beings.
That which is produced from the *nakhāvaraṇa* (claw-guard) is called *pho*. That which is produced from the *garbha-kośa* (womb-receptacle) is called *nu*.
Generally, according to the laws of the world, good and evil each follow their own kind; from causes of a similar nature, fruits of a similar nature arise.

As for the "receptacle-guard" (*kośāvaraṇa*), it is called a "receptacle" (*kośa*) because the cause possesses the fruit, and it is called a "guard" (*āvaraṇa*) because that which is obtained will certainly not be lost. This refers to how, in the world, good and evil each have [their respective categories].
It is that which is stored and protected. As for the yakṣas vying to eat, this is a metaphor for those with false views who deny the causality of good and evil;
this is what it means to "vyingly seize food. That they have eaten their fill refers to the fulfillment of the mind of false views.

"Malicious intent becoming more intense" refers to the further expansion of a mind of false views. "The sound of contention" means that what was accomplished within the inner mind is manifested outwardly through verbal instruction;
by proclaiming a doctrine that denies cause and effect, it causes those who hear it to fall into the three miserable realms.
Therefore, it is said to be most terrifying. △ Second, the view of clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
The *kumbhāṇḍa* spirits crouch upon earthen mounds (until) they wander back and forth, acting wantonly and sporting in play.

This is an analogy for the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). To grasp what is false as the path is called "reckoning that which is not a cause to be a cause," such as when non-Buddhists observe the precepts of cows, dogs, and so forth.
*Kumbhāṇḍa*—translated here as "jar-shaped"—is also called "the Terrifying"; it refers to the ghost of impermanence that kills.

This serves as an analogy for practicing tainted (*sāsrava*) goodness, which can overcome various insects. To sit with the legs tucked under one is called "crouching" (*khuṅ*); to sit with the legs outstretched is called "squatting" (*ju*).

"Earth mound" (tǔchuí) refers to a raised embankment. This is an analogy for how non-Buddhists who cultivate the ten wholesome precepts can be reborn in the high realms of the six heavens of the desire realm, just like an earthen mound.
When such a mound rises one or two feet above the ground, it is analogous to those who further cultivate the various dhyānas and attain the meditative absorptions of the form realm.

As with the first foot, one attains the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*). As with the second foot, one attains the ascent to the higher realms as "going" and the falling back into the lower realms as "returning.
To falsely give rise to the view of attachment to precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is like indulging in wanton play, crouching, squatting, or sitting on a mound.
He seizes the dog by its two hind legs and throws it down until it cries out, then places his foot upon its neck, taking pleasure in terrifying the dog.
The dog is the fruit of suffering; the legs are a metaphor for the cause of suffering. False precepts are fundamentally not causes, yet through deluded conceptualization they are taken to be causes;
to hold fast to them and refuse to relinquish them is like seizing the dog by its two hind legs. Furthermore, he slanders the world by claiming that there is no suffering.
Regarding cause and effect: this is like striking someone until they lose their voice, yet turning to false precepts as if they were right practice.

It is like using suffering to abandon suffering—like placing one's foot upon one's own neck—or taking suffering to be pleasure, maintaining and preaching with instability, much like a dog that delights itself while fearing others.
Question: The Buddha causes people to uphold the ten wholesome precepts (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*) as a cause for rebirth in heaven; this too is a skillful means (*upāya*). Why is this so?

Therefore, I have answered with the analogy of the *kumbhāṇḍa*, for the underlying causes are different. The true cause of the Buddha’s teaching has long been made to progress, and one will certainly attain the correct fruit.
Now, the heterodox precepts held by outsiders further slander the world by claiming that there is no causality between suffering and its results.
This analogy is made because of the discrepancy between cause and effect. *Ging* (pronounced jǐng). △ Third, the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, there are various hungry ghosts whose bodies are tall and large... [up to] ...emitting great, evil cries as they wail and seek food.
This is an analogy for the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Within the aggregates, bases, and elements, falsely conceptualizing them as a self is called the "view of a self-body.
To project a self vertically throughout the three periods of time is called "long"; to project a self horizontally across the five aggregates is called "great.

To conceive of the self as autonomous and failing to cultivate wholesome dharmas—thereby lacking shame and remorse—is called "nakedness. Because one is adorned with evil, one is "black," being devoid of merit.
Because it relies on [the body], it is emaciated. One who conceives of a self does not transcend the three realms; therefore, it is said that they are always "within" them.

When one conceives of a self as being in the mind and speaks words proclaiming the characteristics of a self, it is said that they "utter a great evil sound. It is hoped that by means of this teaching [they may be transformed].

Because they hope to attain the fruits of the Path, it is said that they "cry out seeking food. [The characters] 躶 (pronounced luǒ) and 瘦 (pronounced chù) [indicate their state]. △ Fourth, the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Furthermore, there are various hungry ghosts whose throats are like needles. This is a metaphor for the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

That is to say, because of these false views, one reaches as far as the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); this is called the grasping at views. Although the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception is impermanent, one reckons it to be *nirvāṇa*.
It is like having a narrow throat and a precarious life, yet claiming to preserve one’s longevity; therefore, it is said that their throats are [like needles].
Like a needle. △ Fifth, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, there are various ghosts whose heads are like those of oxen (extending to) being driven by hunger and thirst, crying out and running about.

○ This is a metaphor for the view of extremes; based upon the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one further calculates [the self] as either annihilated or eternal, clinging to eternity rather than annihilation.

To cling to annihilation or permanence, following one extreme, is called the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). The two extremes of annihilation and permanence are like the two horns on a cow’s head;
based on the view of self (*ātman*), one gives rise to the view of extremes, such as "the body is the self" or "the self is the body," which is like the two horns on a head.
The fault of calculating annihilation or permanence can sever the roots of supramundane goodness (*lokottara-kuśalamūla*), just as eating human flesh can sever worldly [virtue].
These roots of goodness are like devouring dogs; they may be reckoned as eternal or reckoned as annihilated, revolving back and forth like disheveled hair.
To reckon them as eternal is to destroy annihilationism; to reckon them as annihilated is to destroy eternalism—like a cruel and violent slaughter.
Lacking wisdom and concentration, they sustain themselves with food and drink as if driven by hunger and thirst; each expresses their own view like one crying out and running in haste.

This clearly concludes the explanation of those who are being burned. [The character for "bōng" (pronounced péng) indicates a disheveled appearance. △ Second, a summary of the sharp and dull faculties.
Yakṣas, hungry ghosts, and various evil birds and beasts—[up to] such immeasurable perils and terrors as these.

The first two phrases summarize the characteristics of afflictions in the desire realm: the upper phrase summarizes the sharp-facultied afflictions (tīkṣṇa-mārga), and the lower phrase summarizes the dull-facultied afflictions (mṛdu-mārga).
The subsequent two phrases collectively summarize both the sharp and the dull; all are out-flowing minds (sāsrava-citta) that lack the flavor of the Path (mārga-rasa).
To eat until full is called "satiety"; to be swift in birth and death is called "urgency.

As for the "four directions," although the delusions of view are numerous, they do not exceed the four propositions of severance, permanence, existence, and non-existence. To "peep through a window" means to look through a small opening;
this clarifies that although one may observe the principle of emptiness through erroneous contemplation, it is not right view, and therefore one cannot attain the vast, true emptiness.
The object [of perception] is thus like looking through a window and seeing the void. The final two lines summarize the extensive discussion as a conclusion.
Because sentient beings do not cultivate the True Dharma, their false understandings become erroneous, leading them to fall into suffering; hence, the fears are immeasurable.

This concludes the analogy for the types of things being burned, which represents the ten *anuśayas* (latent afflictions). [Note: *kuī* (音奎) means "to peer"; *yǒu* (音有) means "window. △ Second, explaining the fire.
The origin of this [parable] is illustrated by the five turbidities.
It is like an old, dilapidated house belonging to a single person who left it not long ago.
The three realms are the place where the Buddha manifests his transformations; having come and gone eight thousand times, how could they not be ancient and worn?
Dàkuǎ says: This is like when the Tathāgata was in the world teaching and transforming sentient beings, causing them to subdue their afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because he had to respond to and transform others in other directions, he was temporarily absent; this caused the fire of the afflictions to arise among sentient beings. Question:

Above, it was just said that [the afflictions] "belong" [to the beings], yet here it is said they "emerge. If they belong, they do not emerge; if they emerge, they do not belong. What is the meaning of this?
As for the answer: if it were not said that [the fire] "belongs" to the upper part, then it would have no connection to oneself; how could there be any sentiment of rescue?
If it were not said that [the fire] "emerges" from the lower part, then one would be burned along with it; how could there be any merit of rescue? Thus, both "belonging" and "emerging" are relevant.
△ Third, the momentum of the fire’s arising is used as an analogy for the turbid marks.
Thereafter, a fire suddenly breaks out within the residence (continuing until) the structures collapse and the walls crumble.

This clearly illustrates the signs of the destruction of the three realms (*traidhātuka*) during the kalpa of dissolution. Furthermore, the preceding passage described the realms of the two paths: animals and ghosts.
It is already thus. This resembles the realm of the Hell of Manifestation; how much more so the various sufferings of hell, where fire alone is paramount.
Furthermore, hell is a place of imprisonment; how much more so for the sentient beings of the nine stages within the three realms, who are never liberated.
How could this not become a field for the prison of *liṅyǔ*? Thus we know that wherever there is binding, the meaning of "prison" (*yù*) is present.

Tiantai said: "The three realms are the dwelling; the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are the house; the four sides are the locations—namely, body, sensation, mind, and phenomena (*kāya-vedanā-citta-dharma*).

Within these four dharmas, if one gives rise to the four inverted views (*catur-viparyāsa*), then the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) and the eight sufferings (*aṣṭa-duḥkha*) will all arise. Therefore, it is said: "One..."
At that time, as the continuity gradually increases, it is called "blazing together. As for the subsequent destruction of the house, this refers to the arrival of the kalpa of dissolution.

Because the ignorance of sentient beings is thick and the five turbidities are deep and murky, the four great elements and the four marks of existence, along with the notions of self and person, become intensely active.
Consequently, all the conditioned merit and goodness of the triple world are utterly destroyed; this is like the shaking of the rafters and beams.
This is the sign of being torn asunder. *Bào* (pronounced *bào*). △ Fourth, the signs of being burned. This is a metaphor for the various sufferings.
Various ghosts and spirits raise their voices and cry out loudly (until) they are overwhelmed with panic and terror, unable to escape on their own.
When the kalpa of destruction arrives, the merit of sentient beings is exhausted, and they give rise to various evil karmas and heterodox views;
all of these are driven by the fires of karma. Above, spirits and deities were used as a metaphor for the faculty of gain;

now, the mention of "raising one's voice and crying out" refers to those who cling to the notion of permanence, asserting that dharmas are eternally fixed, and thus [fearing] that existence returns to non-existence, where non-existence is [nothingness].

This is what they conceive as permanence. As for those who calculate [existence] as annihilation, they mean that the dharma is definitively severed; there is only this one death, with no further continuation.
Each adheres to their own view and proclaims it as a definitive teaching; thus it is said they "raise their voices and cry out. [They are like] vultures and eagles.
This is like the dull afflictions (āśrava). The kumbhāṇḍas represent the sharp affliction of clinging to precepts and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa), which originally did not conceive of cessation;
now, seeing impermanence, they merely give rise to doubt and fear. Thus, both the sharp and dull afflictions are attached [to existence] and do not know the method for transcendence;
hence it is said that they are "terrified and unable to escape. The explanation of the fire rising on the ground concludes the section on the desire realm. II. Explanation of the Form Realm.
Fire within a hole is a metaphor for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Wild beasts, venomous insects, and *piśāca* demons hide and lurk within these holes and also dwell therein.
The meditative concentration of the fourth dhyāna is like a hole that is not deep; although it has emerged from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it does not reach outside the gate.
Vast and open, one may still escape the coarse and fierce flames of the desire realm. By benefiting sentient beings, one also attains meditative concentration;
thus it is said that the Vaiśravaṇa (Pi-she) dwells in the center. Vaiśravaṇa refers to the spirits who consume vital essence.

The first two phrases refer to the dull afflictions (*mṛdu-kleśa*), and the latter two phrases refer to the sharp afflictions (*tīkṣṇa-kleśa*). The high and low [stages] are distinguished according to the coarseness or subtlety of the ten afflictions (*daśa-kleśa*). To flee...
(Sound of cooking). Because their merit and fortune are meager, they are oppressed by fire.
This passage explains the reason why they are burned; that is to say, the reason they are burned is due to their meager merit and fortune.
Evil karma increases and blazes intensely. Tiantai says: "Within the cavities, although there is no fierce flame, there is still the torment of heat;
it is like those in the fourth dhyāna who are likewise tormented and oppressed by the subtle marks of craving for joy and bliss."
They mutually harm one another, drinking blood and devouring flesh, until foul smoke and flames billow and fill the four directions.
○ Whether sentient beings are of sharp or dull faculties, they are alike in attaining dhyāna, yet their calculations differ; they contend with one another as right and wrong.
This is what is meant by "mutually harming one another. Since they give rise to various views within meditative concentration, they are unable to produce the outflow-free (anāsrava) samādhi.
Wisdom. Being addicted to the flavor of dhyāna is like drinking blood; being attached to the five factors such as *vipaśyanā* is like eating meat.

The jackal is a metaphor for the craving of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Having already severed this craving by cultivating the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) within the desire realm, it is said that "it dies first.

The craving for meditative absorption (*dhyāna-rāga*) is like a great predatory beast, capable of swallowing all the cravings of the desire realm; therefore, it is said that "they come vying to devour [it]."

The four inversions and eight sufferings of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are like fierce flames; the four inversions and eight sufferings of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are like foul-smelling smoke.

They are distinguished as lower and upper based on their relative gravity. Furthermore, because they pervade the body, sensation, mind, and phenomena (*dharmas*), as well as the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), it is said that they "fill and obstruct the four directions" (the character *pò* [pronounced *bài*] is used here). △ Third, the fire within the void is a metaphor for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Centipedes, millipedes, venomous snakes, and the like, scorched by fire, scramble to flee from their burrows.

Previously, within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), centipedes were used as a metaphor for anger (*dveṣa*); now, within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), centipedes are likewise used as a metaphor for anger.
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), "venomous insects" refers specifically to the class of centipedes. Thus, one knows that anger pervades all three realms. Regarding "poison":
Snakes and the like [represent] the aversion to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the craving that leads toward the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

The aversion to the coarse objects of form and the contemplation of formless phenomena likewise involve the migration and flux of karma; this is the meaning of being driven out of a hole by fire. Question:

Since anger (*dveṣa*) does not function in the two upper realms, how can it be said that there are also centipedes and the like in the formless realm? Answer: It is merely stated that these do not function in those two realms; it does not mean...
In the two realms [of the form and formless], there is absolutely no anger. That it is now said they "rush out of their holes" is because they are still being driven by the fires of karma;
their loathing for existence and their movement toward emptiness is precisely the sign of severing anger.
The kumbhāṇḍa ghosts seize whatever they encounter and eat it; (until) they run about in confusion, obstructed by the burning afflictions of hunger and thirst.
○ If one attains the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), one eliminates the conditions of the lower realms; therefore, it is said that they "seize whatever they encounter and eat.

Even those dwelling at the summit, the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), cannot escape the various sufferings of perversion, which are like a fire burning upon the head. The Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception is likewise [subject to this].
There are eight kinds of suffering. When the mind gives rise to divergent thoughts, it is called the suffering of birth. When every moment does not abide, it is called the suffering of aging.

When the active mind is restless and obstructs meditative concentration, it is called the suffering of illness. To regress from concentration is the suffering of death. To seek concentration and fail to attain it is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.

That one fails to obtain concentration due to various obstructions is the suffering of association with the disliked. The moment one loses concentration is called the suffering of separation from the beloved.
Separation. The four aggregates are the mind; this is the flourishing of the five aggregates. Lacking the sustenance of untainted food and drink, they are thus afflicted by hunger and thirst.
Being still within saṃsāra, they therefore run about in terror and distress. △ Fourth, a summary concluding that the various hardships are not one.
That dwelling is thus extremely terrifying, with manifold perils such as poison, harm, and fires.
This summarizes the realms of the three worlds, from the coarse to the subtle; none are exempt from being oppressed by the afflictions of the three poisons.
All this arises from the myriad transformations of sentient beings' mental states, which in turn evoke these poisons, harms, and fires.
Calamities are not of a single kind. Among the various schools here, their analogies and applications are particularly novel;

however, only the interpretation of the Tiantai school does not contradict the scripture regarding principle and phenomena. Since the burning house is used as a metaphor for the triple world, the calamities of fire involving hungry ghosts and animals are all matters existing within that house.
If one were to interpret this according to personal sentiment by equating it with the three miserable realms or specific phenomenal characteristics, then—
One can exhaustively describe the similarities among those dwelling in the five realms of rebirth within the human world, yet one cannot fully exhaust the explanation of the three realms.
Therefore, I followed the teachings of Tiantai and investigated them through the continuity of the three phases and the characteristics of the three miserable paths;
thus, I was able to complete the account of all beings within the burning house and perceive the entire scene of the three realms as if it were a painting.
The general analogy has concluded. △ Second, the verse on the specific analogies, divided into three parts. First, the verse on the elder seeing the fire:
"At that time, the master of the house stood outside the gate... having heard this, the elder was startled and entered the burning house."
The "owner of the house" is the person capable of seeing [the truth]. Those "standing outside the gate" are the Tathāgatas on the ground of the Dharmakāya;

they constantly harbor great compassion and desire to save sentient beings, yet they do not occupy the Dharma-seat of the ultimate emptiness (paramārtha-śūnyatā), which is why it is said they are "standing.
Those who "hear people speak" and so forth are the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages (daśabhūmi), who manifest as Brahmā Kings and Śakra Devendra to request the turning of the Dharma wheel.
[This refers to] the wheel. Furthermore, the *Wenju* (Commentary on the Text) quotes a sūtra which says: "The Buddhas of the ten directions said to Śākyamuni Buddha:
'Your karmically connected children are within the triple world; their roots of goodness are about to perish. You must go and save them.
All of this is the meaning of hearing someone speak. The phrases such as 'because of playing' and so forth are precisely the words heard from that person. (3)
The sons who ride [the vehicle] have fundamentally not yet emerged from the triple world; why, then, do you say they have come in? It is said:
perhaps during the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, they once gave rise to the great resolve and were about to emerge, but they soon forgot it and thus entered again.

This is like a person leaving a door who, having only just reached the side of the gate, turns back; this is called "leaving and then re-entering. According to principle, the self-nature is fundamentally pure.

They cannot be constrained by the three realms. Because they do not awaken due to ignorance (*avidyā*), they give rise to various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*), thereby forming birth and death.
Thus it is said that they "enter through play. In the past, their karmic connections were shallow and great goodness had not yet taken root;

this is called being "young and small. After regressing from the Great Vehicle, they transmigrate through the three realms; being shrouded by ignorance, this is called being "unaware. They remain attached to the conditioned virtues of the three realms.
"Dharma and the pleasures of the five desires" is called "delighting in and attachment to joy. Regarding the phrase "the elder hears it and enters in alarm":

the former refers to the fire arising on the four sides, which is "seeing"; the latter refers to this [hearing], which is "hearing. This embodies the full meaning of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*).

"Entering in alarm" signifies the simultaneous integration of wisdom and compassion (*prajñā-karuṇā-yuganaddha*). △ Second, the verse on abandoning the bench and using the chariot, divided into two parts. First, abandoning the bench.
"One should appropriately provide relief so that there is no burning harm" (up to) "in this place of suffering and difficulty, how much more so with a great fire.
"Appropriately" means to apply the Great Teaching as is fitting; this is the simultaneous practice of the provisional and the real.

"To inform and exhort" means to explain the various calamities and hardships and thereby instruct and admonish them. In the prose section, it simply states that the fire comes to press upon the body, causing suffering.

Having concluded the section on the intensity of suffering, the following verses now extensively describe the characteristics of the fire. The first four lines clarify that the Tathāgata intends to rescue [beings];

"evil ghosts and venomous insects" collectively represent the delusions of both sharp and dull *dṛṣṭi* (views) and *kleśa* (afflictions). "The calamitous fire spreads across the floor" describes the extent of what is being consumed.
"Spreads across the floor" means it continues in an unbroken succession. From "venomous snakes, vipers, and adders" onwards, the burning is explained in detail.
The characteristics [of the realms] are presented in this text in a miscellaneous manner, without further sequential order;

they all collectively describe the causes and effects of suffering within the three realms, causing people to develop an extreme sense of weary detachment and to seek deliverance from the three realms. (Màn, pronounced wàn).
The sons, being ignorant, although they heard their father’s instruction, still took pleasure in their play and would not cease.
(Verse above: "The sons were unwilling to believe and accept. The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states: "Not accepting [the teaching] means they are ignorant;
this also refers to their being young and small. The text on 'ignorance' is merely abbreviated. As for "still taking pleasure in their play and not ceasing," this refers to their indulgence.
They are attached to views and afflictions, yet do not seek the essential way out. Lacking the aspiration for the Mahāyāna mind, the Tathāgata can only bestow the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle.
△ Second, the verse on the employment of the carts, divided into three parts. First, the proposal to employ the three carts.
At that time, the elder had this thought (up to) he then contemplated and devised various skillful means.

The first four lines clarify the intention of his preparatory plan. "His distress increased" means that when sentient beings do not accept the teaching, the Tathāgata’s compassionate heart becomes even more intense.
"The house has no joy" clarifies that among the causes and effects of the triple world, there is not a single dharma that brings true happiness.
It is indeed pleasurable. As for those who indulge in and become addicted to games and amusements, this arises from the application of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

This is truly because sentient beings are deeply attached to the five desires, like a yak that loves its tail; due to the profound weight of their views and afflictions (*kleśa*), they can only be reached through the One Buddha Vehicle, which is taught as three for the sake of differentiation.
If the Lesser Vehicle were not employed, then both the Great and the Small would perish together, and they would surely be harmed by the fires [of saṃsāra]. And...
Their bodies and lives were all lost. (Dān) [pinyin: dān]; (Mǎn) [pinyin: miǎn]. △ Second, praising the rarity of the chariot.
He addressed his sons: "I have various kinds of [chariots] (up to) for you to play with as you please."
The "wondrous jewel" refers to the reality contained within the provisional; it is the wondrous jewel among skillful means.

"Standing outside the gate" is like the manifestation of the Four Noble Truths to cause one to know the transcendence of the world; this is the initial showing of the sign. "Come forth, you all" is the exhortation to practice.
"I [shall give it to you]" and so on constitutes the providing of testimony. Since it is said to be "constructed," it refers to the carriage outside the gate.

This clarifies his skillful means. However, the Tathāgata, through countless expedient means, accords with the inclinations and desires of sentient beings, bestowing teachings according to their capacities;
thus we see that what he has spoken is not erroneous, and it is proven that what he has bestowed is not in vain.
△ Third, fulfilling the wishes of his sons.

When the sons heard it said that such chariots had arrived at the open space, free from all suffering and hardship—this corresponds to the prose section describing how the sons, upon hearing this, became courageous and impetuous, racing and running forward;

this is a metaphor for the two vehicles’ vision of the Truth and their cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), which has already been explained above. "Open space" refers to the [partial] truth.
Emptiness. Suffering and hardship refers to the various sufferings of the five destinies. △ Third, the verses on bestowing the great chariots equally, divided into four parts.
First, one verse on the joy of escaping danger:
The elder sees his children have emerged from the burning house and are sitting upon lion thrones at the crossroads.
Regarding what was said earlier about standing outside the gate: it was because the Son had not yet emerged. Now that the Son has emerged, he is permitted to sit at ease.

Furthermore, because the great capacity [of the audience] had not yet been met, it was said they were standing; because the small capacity [of the audience] was already fully engaged, it is said they are sitting at ease.
Thus, "standing" represents hidden benefit (*mínglì*), while "sitting" represents manifest benefit (*xiǎnyì*). The Four Noble Truths all pertain to the true, eternal, world-transcending Great Way.
It is said: "The four crossroads. Because they are greedily attached to the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), they do not advance toward the place of treasure;

therefore, it is called "staying. [△@△] The lion symbolizes fearlessness. Seeing that his children have escaped danger, he can now exercise his transformative teaching; thus it is said: "Now I rejoice in fearlessness.
This means he does not fear that his children will fall into suffering.
And he spoke in self-congratulation, saying, "I am now happy" (up to) "therefore, O people, I am now happy. Regarding "self-congratulation":
it means congratulating himself on having obtained the receptive capacity (*bhājana*) for conversion. For twenty *koṭi* of Buddhas, the Buddha...

Having previously taught the Mahāyāna causes and seeds, this constitutes "birth. During the intervening period, they constantly infuse [the mind] with the fruits of the Hīnayāna until these reach maturity;
this constitutes "nurturing. To undergo instruction on the Path for many kalpas is "rearing," which is extremely difficult because the great seeds are weak and subtle;

hence, they are called "foolish and small. Because they falsely give rise to the five turbidities, they are called "ignorant. Because the cause elicits the fruit, they are said to have "entered a perilous house," which is fraught with many dualities.
The first two phrases describe the fire of the views and afflictions that have arisen; the latter two phrases describe the intensity of being consumed by that fire.
These two sets of phrases precisely correspond to the mind characterized by these two delusions. From "I have already" onwards, the text clarifies the reason for his joy.
Therefore, [the text] below concludes the expression of joy. △ Second, the sons request the vehicles.
At that time, the sons knew their father was sitting at ease... (until) "Now is precisely the right time; please deign to grant them."
This passage reveals the harmonious rapport between that father and son. The father said, "I shall grant you whatever you desire.
The son replied, "Please bestow upon me only the arising [of phenomena]. In this manner, one grants and the other requests; how earnest and substantial it is! Zhizhi says:

From the perspective of principle, the sons have already departed from the boundary and awakened to the essence of nature; therefore, they are said to "know their father. They thoroughly understand that nature is devoid of coming and going.
It is said: "Sitting at ease. By means of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons, one turns toward the principle of true emptiness. It is said: "All go to the father's place.
Without seeking the provisional, there is no way to open the real. This is precisely the wondrous realm of this father and son’s mutual suppression and encouragement, their withholding and granting.
One must by no means read this as a dead word. △ Third, the bestowal of the great carriage.
Just as a wealthy elder possesses many treasuries filled with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, and agate, so too within the Tathāgatagarbha all things are universally contained;
that which has not yet manifested is therefore called a "garbha" (treasury), while that which has already manifested is...
Stored within the treasury. As previously stated—in brief—there are immeasurable, boundless, and unprecedented dharmas;
these are merely the minor items within the treasury and do not represent the vast abundance found within the Tathāgata-garbha.
Because it now encompasses all that is contained within the treasury as a whole, it is called "great wealth. The subsequent mention of gold, silver, and so forth refers to the sevenfold dharma.
It was fully replete with wealth and provisions. "House" refers to what is abundant within, while "storehouse" refers to what is abundant on the ground.
It was constructed with various precious objects for great chariots, with bells suspended on all four sides and entwined with golden cords.
The dharma of cause and effect is collectively termed "various jewels. According to the teachings, there is the sense of "creation" in terms of cultivation and attainment;

because the practices are manifold and numerous, the vehicles are not one. Thus, various vehicles are created, and they are moreover great. Furthermore, one must point them out so that they may be known.
The practice of initiating and cultivating is called "constructing" (*zào*). By means of the nature that dissolves cultivation, this construction returns to the principle of original existence;
this is precisely the meaning of the various great vehicles. All other points are explained as previously stated.
A net of pearls is spread over it (extending to) being surrounded on all sides by various colorful ornaments.
○ Regarding "pearls" and so forth: this brings out the characteristics of the canopy and parasol, serving as a metaphor for the manifold gates of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Just as there is a single pearl within each mesh of the net, so too do the various gates of loving-kindness all accord with reality. The preceding text merely stated:

"Hanging down flower garlands" merely means causing those who see them to rejoice. Now, by saying they "hang down everywhere," it clarifies that all capacities [of sentient beings] are universally gladdened.
"Adorned with various colors" is a metaphor for the different manifestations established in the various places where transformations are displayed.
It was surrounded on all sides. This is an analogy for the appropriateness of gathering things together, such that nothing is lacking.
With soft silks and cotton wadding used as carpets and mattresses... [up to] ...he bestowed these wonderful chariots and other items upon his sons.
The preceding text spoke of "double-layered mats. Now, the addition of "soft and supple" serves as a metaphor for mastery over the various *dhyānas*.

Furthermore, covering them with fine woolen cloth represents the further enhancement of the most excellent and wondrous *dhyānas*; thus, the sublime surpasses the coarse. Regarding the term *yīn* (mattress/pad):

the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it refers to double-layered seats within a carriage. This serves as a metaphor for the *dhyāna* of complete practice (*sambhāra-dhyāna*), which differs from the various minor divisions; hence it is described as "white and pure like moss."
"Clean. The rest are all explained as before. *Zēng* (pronounced zēng), *huàng* (pronounced kuàng), *yīn* (pronounced yīn), *rù* (pronounced rù), *dié* (pronounced dié).
△ Fourth, the joy upon obtaining the chariot.
At that time, the sons of the Buddha were filled with joy and leaped for gladness; they played and sported with ease, freedom, and unimpededness. Regarding "joy":
it is because they have obtained the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), which they did not previously expect, that they rejoice. Regarding "wandering in the four directions":

this means that by means of the wisdom of the Middle Way, they traverse horizontally through the four types of four gates and the four types of Four Noble Truths; and vertically, they traverse the forty-one stages.
The four virtues of ultimate permanence, bliss, self, and purity allow him to attend the Buddhas wherever they may be and to deliver sentient beings wherever they may be;

therefore, it is said that he is sovereign and unimpeded. The verse on the analogy has concluded. △ Second, the verse on the application of the analogy, divided into two parts: first, the application of the general analogy.
I tell you, Śāriputra: I am likewise the most honored among the assembly of sages and the father of the world.
(The first two phrases correspond to his title and rank; the latter two phrases correspond to his name and conduct, while together they express the meaning of praising his virtues.
The Tathāgata is the most honored among the seven kinds of expedient means and the sages, and the father of the nine kinds of worldly beings. [The seven expedient means...]
Regarding this: among the nine realms, excluding the four evil destinies, one opens up the Bodhisattvas of the Three Teachings—Tripitaka, Shared, and Distinct—together as seven.

Because the meaning of "son" applies universally to all, they constitute the fathers of the nine realms. However, because those with whom he has established a karmic connection are not numerous, the provisional teaching speaks only of the seven locations.
"All sentient beings are my children; yet they are deeply attached to worldly pleasures and lack the mind of wisdom.
With the Buddha-eye, I view all sentient beings as having the status of my children. Because they are deeply attached to worldly pleasures, their minds of wisdom do not arise;
this is why they do not resemble the Buddha. This encompasses the sentient beings of the five destinies, including the thirty [sub-classes].
My son, furthermore, when one universally examines the three vehicles and the five natures, none possess any reality; therefore, it is said that there is no heart of wisdom.
The three realms offer no peace, being like a house on fire.
"In sum, although their households may be vast, try observing the three realms: what therein can be truly enjoyed? They are like a burning house;
one must not remain attached to them."
"Filled with manifold sufferings and most terrifying" (up to) "such fires blaze forth without ceasing.

The first two phrases provide a general indication of all forms of suffering; the next two phrases explain the three types of suffering (*triduḥkha*) and the eight types of suffering (*aṣṭa-duḥkha*), which constitute the characteristics of the great fire arising.
The final two phrases conclude the description. "Blazing forth" means increasing and intensifying from moment to moment; "without ceasing" means it never stops.

This means that [the afflictions] grow and increase from moment to moment. △ Second, the verse on the synthesis of the individual parables, divided into four parts. First, the verse synthesizing the elder’s seeing of the fire:
The Tathāgata has already departed from the burning house of the triple world; he dwells in tranquil seclusion, peacefully abiding in the forest wilderness.
Having thus united with the Tathāgata, one emerges in peace and security. Quiescence means being without attachment; the causes of suffering are thereby eliminated.

Abiding securely in the unborn means forgetting the fruits of suffering. This is why the five stages of dwelling are brought to exhaustion; it is precisely because of this profound stillness and absence of affairs.
Only upon seeing the sons of the five turbidities oppressed by fire does one give rise to the mind of rescue and relief;
those who dwell in the forest and wilderness reside in the *paranirmita-vaśavartin* (other-enjoyment) land, the place where compassion is exercised with loving-kindness.
"Now these three realms are all mine" (up to) "and now this place has many afflictions and perils.
This corresponds to the preceding analogy of seeing fire. The first four lines clarify that this place and these people are all subject to me.
Since they have already become my own, can I not employ skillful means to rescue and succor them? The latter two phrases are as before.
The text says: "He sees all sentient beings being scorched and boiled by birth, old age, sickness, and death."
"Only I alone am able to provide rescue and protection.
When the Buddha saw this, he thought to himself: "I am the father of all sentient beings; I ought to extract them from their suffering and distress. [End of section] II.
Verses on the Abandonment of the Stool and the Use of the Chariot. This also has two parts: first, the abandonment of the stool.
Although they are instructed and exhorted, they do not believe or accept [the teaching] because their attachment to the defilements of various desires is profound.
