Consequently, as mentioned above, they cannot yet escape birth, old age, death, and so forth. That they do not believe the instruction means that the Dharma is great while their capacity is small;
that their attachment is profound refers to their emotional longing for various desires. It is because of this longing for various desires that they do not believe the instruction. △
The second is the combined use of vehicles.
By means of this expedient, he speaks of the three vehicles (up to) revealing and expounding the supramundane path.

This single phrase regarding the expedient is precisely intended to correspond to the expedient of using the vehicles. It corresponds to the preceding [passage] which says, "But by means of wisdom..."

If one employs the skillful means of wisdom and relinquishment, sentient beings cannot attain liberation. That which is shown as the supramundane path refers to the provisional, lesser nirvana with remainder of the Three Vehicles.
Among these sons, if their minds are resolved, they shall attain the stage of a pratyekabuddha or become non-regressive bodhisattvas.
○ If the mind is determined, from the stage of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) upward, this is true determination.

This single line summarizes the stages of the three vehicles’ galloping forth. Taken together with the following four lines, each verse summarizes the stages of the three vehicles’ vying for emergence.

Regarding the "three knowledges" (*trividyā*), the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) quotes the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, which says: "The knowledge of past lives [knows] the suffering of the past; [the knowledge of the death and rebirth of beings knows] birth..."

One feels great revulsion. Through the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), one knows future suffering and gives rise to great revulsion. With the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), one is able to practice correct contemplation and sever all afflictions (*kleśa*). These three are called "clear knowledges" (*vidyā*). The supernormal power of the basis (*ṛddhividhi*) is merely a skillful artifice. The supernormal power of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*)— [The remainder of the passage continues: ...is merely the hearing of sounds; it does not involve knowing the meaning of those sounds. The supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is merely the perception of the mental states of others; it does not involve knowing their past or future destinies. If one were to forcefully preach the Dharma to them, it would be a false proclamation. This refers to those who calculate a self and grasp at realization.
It cannot be spoken. Next, it is explained that ordinary persons know only to cling to desire as pleasure;
how much more so for those who are deeply attached? Their delusion is even greater, and they certainly do not wish to hear. Even if they were to hear it, they would have no intention to understand.

For such people, what benefit would there be in speaking? This is why it cannot be spoken to those ordinary persons who lack wisdom. Furthermore, as for the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) of the wondrous Dharma—
Being protected and remembered by all Buddhas, how could one dare to proclaim this recklessly?

Therefore, by contrasting these two kinds of people who neither hear nor believe with the previous three kinds who are able to hear and believe, the distinction between sin and merit is as clear as the light above.

As stated in the preceding text, those who are merely able to rejoice and receive it upon their heads will, in this very life, abide in the stage of non-retrogression and continue the Buddha’s wisdom-life; thus, one should know that—

Those who draw near to the Buddhas will certainly become sons of the Buddha. If even those who merely rejoice for a moment and accept this with faith receive such vast benefit as this, how much more so for those who have long practiced and attained realization? As for those who now do not believe or accept it—
They will inevitably give rise to slander; because of this slander, they suffer. Therefore, the following passage sets forth the sin of lack of faith, which is likewise extremely painful and grave.
One must understand that the power of the Sublime Dharma is inconceivable, such that it brings about the merit of those who believe.
The offenses of those who lack faith are all beyond the power of thought or calculation.
If there are people who do not believe and slander this sutra—listen now as I explain the retribution for the offenses of such persons.
These words—slandering the sutras and severing the lineage of the Buddha—are a great evil; they are no less grave than shedding the blood of a Buddha.

Those who do not believe thereby sever their own roots of goodness. Although the Tathāgata is inherently endowed with vast knowledge and vision, wisdom, supernormal powers, various samādhis, and immeasurable skillful means, because of this lack of faith, he loses them all.

Because of this, they lose their joy and will inevitably fall into suffering. Those who slander [this teaching] destroy its cause for attaining Buddhahood in the future and malign its fruit of appearing in the world in the future.
When both cause and fruit are negated, this constitutes the meaning of annihilationism.
Regarding "all worlds," this sutra is the fundamental basis for the nine realms. Since it has been slandered...
This sutra is precisely the cause for severing the nine realms to achieve Buddhahood; therefore, it is said that it "severs the Buddha-seed of all worlds.
"Frowning" refers to knitting the brows and furrowing the forehead, indicating a refusal to hear [the teaching]. The two characters "disbelief" (不信) serve as the general term;
"slandering" is the expression of disbelief, while "frowning" is the physical manifestation of disbelief. "Doubt" is the state of disbelief.
Because they have transgressed through all three types of action, the retribution they receive shall not be light. Their brows will be knit and their faces contorted.
Whether the Buddha is in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa—[listen now again] to the retribution for this person’s offenses.
The previous section clarified that severing the Buddha-seed in the world makes it difficult to escape retribution; this present case further involves slandering the Triple Gem.

Therefore, we shall collectively set forth the characteristics of these offenses. If one utters even a single word while the Buddha is in the world, it constitutes both slandering the Buddha and slandering the Dharma he taught.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it constitutes merely slandering the sūtras he preached. This applies to those who are seen reading, reciting, copying, or upholding the sūtras.
Whether they treat them with contempt, harbor hatred and envy, or cherish resentment—these are all slanders against disciples who uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Therefore, it is said: "Listen further to the retribution for these sins. Below, the aforementioned offenses of slandering the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha are summarized and presented together so as not to make the text overly prolix. (Fěi, pronounced *fēi*; Jí, pronounced *jí*).
When such a person’s life ends, they enter the Avīci Hell, continuing thus in succession for incalculable kalpas.
Yet those who slander the sutras and lack faith are mostly those who merely assume the name of the Dharma while acting as impostors—what are known as "the worms within the lion's body.
It is not the ignorant among the laity who can create the causes and conditions for slandering the Dharma.
Furthermore, within this section on retribution, based on the *Direct Pointing*, it is divided into ten parts. The first clarifies the retribution for those who slander the sutras:
they are first born in hell because, during their present life, they did not believe in the sublime Dharma and slandered the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Since these acts constitute the disparagement of the most supreme and most venerable fruits, they fall into hell at death and descend into the lowest and most painful of paths. Because...
When one gives rise to slander, being deluded regarding oneself and others, one consequently experiences retribution for kalpas, which increases as it passes from one to another. Question:
Why are the specific conditions of suffering in the hells not described? Answer: Because the offenses committed are manifold, the hells are likewise manifold;
moreover, the kalpas are so long that it would be impossible to describe them all exhaustively through slander.
Upon emerging from hell, one shall fall among the animals (up to: because they sever the lineage of the Buddhas, they receive this retribution for their sins).

Second, it clarifies that those who slander the sutras will further enter the retribution of the animal realm. According to the *Changlun* (Treatise on the Lengthening [of Life]), those who slander Mahāyāna sutras emerge from hell and fall into the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Although the realm of ghosts is not explicitly mentioned here, it should logically exist; perhaps the text is abbreviated.
Furthermore, regarding the retribution received in the realm of ghosts, no one has knowledge of it; thus, its painful retributions are not described in detail, just as those of the hells are not.
Moreover, while ghosts merely undergo suffering, animals must also repay their debts.

Therefore, I shall now speak based on what is commonly known and seen by people, so that they may certainly respect and believe the Mahāyāna sūtras and refrain from slandering them. However, as for...

As for those who have fallen into the realm of animals: because in a previous life, during a time of arrogance, they donned the skin of a lion while making the cry of a jackal, they now receive such retribution.

Precisely because at the time of their deceptive and false preaching they did not know the orthodox teaching of the three virtues and the single mind, they are thus moved to a haggard and emaciated form; because they failed to distinguish between the provisional and the real, they are retributively dark and sallow.

One adorns oneself with vulgar speech; therefore, one is repaid with scabies and leprosy. One feigns the Dharma through falsehood; because this damages right faith, it provokes the resentment and harassment of others.
Relying on the Dharma, one treats the virtuous with contempt; consequently, one is reborn as one who is despised by others. One accepts offerings and gains beyond what is due;

therefore, one is repaid with hunger and thirst. One causes others to lose their right wisdom; therefore, one is repaid with the wasting away of one's own flesh and bones. During one's lifetime, [one acts] thus...
There is no real benefit; therefore, one undergoes bitter suffering. After death, the filth is transferred to others, and thus one is pelted with tiles and stones.
This is the first retribution for the animal realm incurred by slandering the sutras. [Qiē] (pronounced kuò).
Lí (pronounced lí). Tàn (pronounced tǎn). Ráo (pronounced ráo).
If one is reborn as a camel or among donkeys (up to the point stated), it is because they slandered this sutra and thus incurred such retribution.
Third is the retribution of being a beast of burden: camels and donkeys exist solely for the purpose of carrying heavy loads;

these are the rewards for those who slandered the Dharma, returning to them the retribution of their own arrogance and self-importance. It was due to the words of defamation they added to others during their causal stage that they now receive this result.
In the state of fruition, one is subjected to the suffering of being beaten with staves; in the causal state, there were many erroneous interpretations that deluded and confused others.
In the state of fruition, one thinks only of water and grass, having no other knowledge. (The character for "luò" is pronounced *luò*.)
There are those who become jackals (*śṛgāla*) and enter villages, where they undergo various sufferings and sometimes even die.

This fourth [category] clarifies the suffering of illness as a karmic retribution for animals. Because in a previous life they falsely claimed superiority within a village and received the veneration of others, they now return here to act as wild fox spirits.
This is because they did not understand the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) in the past.
He suffered from scabies and sores. Because in the past he had not harmonized provisional and ultimate truth, he was reborn with only one eye.

Because in the past he had played with the demonic and deluded, gathering together a motley crowd of followers who brought no Dharma benefit to others, he was reborn as a child struck and pelted by those ignorant of him.
In the past, deluded people did not know when to cease [their misconduct], and thus they experienced suffering and met their deaths.
Having died there, they further received the body of a python; because they slandered this sutra, they incurred such retribution as this.

The fifth [consequence] is that the poison of anger leads to rebirth as an animal. Because one harbored resentment upon seeing a holder of the sutras during the causal stage, one is thus moved to receive the body of a python.
How much more so for the Sublime Dharma, which possesses the fivefold Dharma-body; because the True Path was slandered, one is thus moved to receive a body measuring five hundred *yojanas*.
Because one frowned and took no pleasure upon hearing the Great Dharma, one is thus moved to receive the state of being deaf, foolish, and footless, crawling on the belly.
One employs various arts to repay [the debt], and consumes food to compensate for greed;

yet through the provisional dharmas within the causal stage, one enjoys pleasure throughout one's life, while in the resultant stage, one must suffer without respite. (Mǎng, pronounced *mǎng*; Āi, with the first tone).
If one obtains a human birth, the faculties will be dull and obscured (extending to: whatever is acquired is immediately forgotten).

This is the sixth retribution for being born in the human realm due to the lack of wisdom regarding the clear principles. There are three types of such retributions: first, the six sense organs are incomplete;
second, medical treatment goes awry and increases the illness; third, one suffers calamities inflicted by others. Because the Dharma-eye was not clear during the causal stage, these results follow.

Because their faculties are dull and obtuse, they are retributively manifested as being unable to distinguish the three bodies. Because they do not clarify the provisional and the real, they are retributively manifested as having stunted and deformed limbs.
Because right faith is not established, they are retributively manifested as having crippled and broken feet. Because they lack the eye of the Dharma that discerns without choice, they are blind.
Because they loathe hearing the wondrous Dharma, they are deaf. Because they do not believe in the eternally abiding Dharmakāya, they are hunchbacked.

Because one was crooked and used false speech to delude others in the interim, one is met with a lack of faith from others. Because one preached what is not the Dharma as being the Dharma, one has a foul breath.
Because one’s teachings deluded the foolish, one is possessed by *chi* and *mei* spirits. Because one received honor and respect in vain, one is poor and lowly.

Because both principle and practice were deficient, one suffers from many illnesses and emaciation. Because both wisdom and principle were lost, one has no one to rely upon. One harbors hatred and resentment.
Those who uphold this sutra may consequently cause others to feel resentment and disregard for it; because they do not cherish the Dharma in their hearts, they soon forget and lose it.
This is because, in failing to understand the Great Dharma, they recklessly discourse upon Prajñā. Due to such slander of the Dharma, they receive such retribution.

Dwarfish (pronounced zhuó, level tone). Ugly (pronounced lòu, with the sound of lù). Hunchbacked (pronounced lián, with the sound of lián). Lame (pronounced bì, with the sound of bì). Crooked-backed (pronounced wǔ, upper tone).
Consumptive (pronounced xiāo, with the sound of xiāo).

If one practices the way of medicine and treats illness according to the prescriptions—up to the point where, even after taking excellent medicine, the condition worsens again—this seventh section clarifies the false explanations given out of greed for profit.
The Buddha is the King of Physicians for the three realms; he is able to cure the illnesses of birth and death within the five destinies and the three vehicles.
The medicine for curing these illnesses is entirely contained within this sutra. When an ordinary person first receives instruction from a teacher, they immediately...
Upon attaining the realization of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, the ailments of body and mind are completely exhausted, and one suddenly emerges from saṃsāra.

Sentient beings with false views do not believe in the Buddha’s Mahāyāna True Dharma; for the sake of profit and sustenance, they propagate it erroneously and falsely, thereby deluding themselves and others.

Consequently, their karmic retribution is to serve as physicians who merely know how to treat diseases by following prescriptions, yet fail to grasp the principles of medicine and do not recognize the underlying causes of illness.

On the contrary, it increases the illness of others. For example, while sentient beings originally seek the sublime fruit, those who crave profit falsely preach the characteristics of emptiness, causing listeners to practice in a confused manner, thereby losing their Dharma-body and severing their life-force of wisdom. Consequently, they are punished by being reported as physicians who have caused death;
though they have not actually attained realization themselves, they refuse to receive the teachings of others, and thus, being ill themselves, they remain without anyone to save them.
If one attempts to guide them with the True Dharma, they immediately give rise to anger and vexation; thus, by administering wholesome medicine, one only increases the illness of others.
If others are rebellious, plundering, robbing, or stealing, [they will suffer] up to being born deaf, mute, or lacking physical faculties.

Eighth, it is clear that these reports have been transmitted through successive errors. Those who came before made false claims for the sake of profit, and those who followed subsequently adopted and practiced them in turn;
thus, it is only natural that they should experience such calamitous retributions. The following serves as a summary:

As for those who slander the sutras through the three aforementioned types of offenses and fall into suffering, because they slandered the Buddha during their causal stage, they shall never see him; because they slandered the Dharma, they shall never hear it; and because of their resentment...

Because they harbor resentment toward the Saṃgha, they are constantly reborn in difficult places and lose the seed of the Triple Gem; thus they become deranged and remain far removed from the True Dharma, suffering for long kalpas.
Sentient beings with false views, lacking the eye of wisdom, willingly refuse to listen and give rise to the causes and conditions for slandering the Dharma;
therefore, at birth they are immediately deaf and mute, [and their speech is] suddenly stammering (pronounced *zhè*).
Constantly dwelling in hell as if visiting a pleasure garden—up to this point—it is because of slandering this sutra that one incurs such punishment.
Ninth, it clarifies further dwelling in the retribution of hell to repay the transgression of turning one's back on the Dharma for one’s own convenience.

Because one does not turn toward the correct principle, one constantly resides in hell; because one treats the True Dharma as a plaything, it is like visiting a pleasure garden. This refers to playing with the Dharma.
Because they did not abandon such thoughts, they are repaid with [rebirth in] their own dwellings; because of their impure deeds, they dwell together with animals.
If one obtains a human form yet is deaf, blind, mute, or [so forth], it is because they have slandered this sutra that they incur such offenses.
Tenth, it clarifies rebirth in the human realm as a retribution for the remaining karma. The phrase "if one attains" is an indefinite expression;
it means that if the transgression is heavy, one will certainly be reborn in hell. However, if the suffering of the transgression is somewhat light, one may attain human status;

yet, even so, the six sense organs will remain incomplete and the four necessities of life will all decline. Through the provisional dharmas within the causal stage, one may obtain wealth, pleasure, and adornment.
Adornment. Those who have attained the fruits [of the path] are adorned with poverty, suffering, and various illnesses.

Wise people who propagate the Dharma take the three bodies, the four wisdoms, and the myriad practices of the six perfections as their clothing. Those who slander the Dharma among the heterodox adorn themselves with dropsy and consumption.
The one who propagates the Dharma breathes forth fragrant flowers from the mouth, with body and mind pure and bright; whereas the one who slanders the Dharma—[their body...]

Constantly dwelling in foul places, defiled and impure, the wise person awakens to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*); the four marks are suddenly empty, and the three poisons are forever stilled.

Those who are heterodox are deluded regarding the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; they are deeply attached to the notions of self and person (*ātman-pudgala*), whereby the three poisons increase and they cling to birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

Consequently, their lustful desires blaze forth and their wise nature becomes obscured and confused, leading them to make no distinction between humans and beasts. Thus ends the ten preceding sections.
All these belong to the retribution for slandering the sutras. Therefore, each case concludes by stating: "The offense incurred is such as this. How tragic!

Should those who slander the Dharma not stand in awe? [The afflictions include] scabies (pronounced *jiè*), leprosy (*lài*, pronounced *làì*), carbuncles (*yōng*, pronounced *yōng*), and abscesses (*jū*, pronounced *jū*).
He addressed Śāriputra: "To those who slander this sutra... do not preach this sutra among people who lack wisdom.
This concludes the previous section on those who slander and prohibits preaching to them; it now initiates the subsequent section for those who have faith, for whom one should preach.

Having presented each of the characteristics of these transgressions in the preceding ten sections, he causes people to know that slandering the sutra is the root of all evils. Therefore, he addresses [Śāriputra].
The recipient of the teaching understood the intent and said: "This is but a brief exposition.
If I were to explain it in full, though an eon might come to an end, the manifestations of such offenses would never be exhausted. The final four lines correspond to the beginning of the chapter:

"This Dharma-seal of mine, wherever you may travel, must not be recklessly transmitted to those lacking wisdom. Miaole asked: "If slandering the sutra gives rise to sin, then [the text says] the sutra..."
[Objection: "On the contrary, this becomes a cause for committing sins. What benefit does it bring to people? [Response: "Both sin and merit arise from the mind itself.
The Buddha’s intention was fundamentally to provide succor to sentient beings so that they might emerge from the sea of birth and death.

For those who hear the sutras, if they have even a single moment of true faith, they will immediately and wondrously accord with their own fundamental mind; this is precisely the condition for attaining Buddhahood. As for those who do not believe, on the contrary, [sin arises]..."
To slander and revile [this teaching] is to lack faith that one’s own mind is the Buddha; it is to lose its very root and transform immeasurable sublime bliss into extreme suffering.
This is brought about solely by what the self-mind grasps; what does it have to do with the sutras? It is like one who has lost their way:
this is the fault of the confused person, not the fault of the village. △ Second, according to the gate of great compassion, the virtuous should...
The explanation is divided into two parts. The first part provides an interpretation through five pairs [of categories]:
"If there is one of sharp faculties whose wisdom is clear and lucid... (until)... for such a person as this, one may then preach it."

This constitutes a pairing of the past and present. Although five pairs are designated, they do not exceed the ten *pāramitās*. This can only be explained for those who practice the dharma of the ten *pāramitās*.

The first six phrases clarify the capacities of the present; it is directly stated that the *prajñā-pāramitā* constitutes its essence. Therefore, it is said at the outset that the faculties are sharp.
Because nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are mutually fused, it is called "clearly understanding. This refers to clearly understanding their distinctions.
Having fully realized all practices with perfect clarity, one is said to be "widely learned and of strong memory. This constitutes the conditions for seeking the sutras.

The passage beginning with "If a person has previously seen... clarifies the past causes; taking the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) as its essence, the merit planted and the goodness cultivated under billions of Buddhas make that giving so preeminent that it is beyond comparison.
The state where both subject and object are forgotten is called the "profound mind" (*gambhīracitta*).

"Generosity that does not regress is called 'firm. The commentary states: when one plants merit through giving without seeking the minor fruits of humans or devas, it is said that the 'deep mind is firm.
Because such causal conditions are fully present, one should preach for them."
"If a person is diligent and constantly cultivates a mind of loving-kindness (up to...)—to such a person one may preach this.

This is explained through the pairing of the upper and lower [levels]. Diligently cultivating loving-kindness is the act of having compassion for those below; it takes the faculty of diligence as its essence.
The知音 (Zhiyin) says: Constantly cultivating a mind of compassion is to diligently bestow happiness; not sparing one’s own body or life is to diligently extract suffering.
To be respectful without distinction is to be venerable and superior. Taking the perfection of dhyāna as its essence and having no divergent mind is mental concentration.

To dwell apart from the mountain of folly is the concentration of this body; furthermore, to have no divergent thoughts is for the inhalation not to abide within the aggregates or realms—this is the reverence of the single principle.
To dwell apart from the mountain of folly is for the exhalation not to involve manifold conditions—this is the reverence of non-attachment.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, if you see someone [up to] such a person, only for them may you preach this.
This constitutes a contrast between the internal and the external: abandoning evil and approaching good is seeking externally; it takes skillful means as its essence.

Abandoning evil is the expedient means for distancing oneself from the mundane; it brings one near to provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). Approaching the good is the expedient means for advancing toward the ultimate; it brings one near to true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*).
Pure observance of the precepts is internal protection, having the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) as its essence. Master Yin says: [as follows].

Maintaining the precepts is like holding a precious jewel; it becomes the cause for the purification of the six sense faculties. Seeking the Mahāyāna sūtras provides the condition for attaining the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
If there is a person who is free from anger, upright, and gentle—only to such a person as this may you preach.

This contrasts the self with others. To have compassion for sentient beings and reverence for the Buddha constitutes one’s own practice; it takes the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) as its essence.
A commentary states: "Being upright and gentle, one is not humiliated by others. Having compassion for sentient beings and reverence for the Buddha means not being humiliated by others.
As for "upright," the mind is like a straight bowstring; all things are true and real. Because they are true and real, [one is not humiliated].
When others are angry, because one is gentle and soft, one remains free from anger oneself.
Having personally realized the samādhi of pliant patience (*kṣānti*), one constantly feels compassion for all sentient beings whose anger and resentment are false and illusory.

Since one has personally known that this is the very samādhi realized by all Buddhas, one constantly gives rise to reverence. To preach the Dharma with a pure mind is precisely what constitutes transformation.
He takes the perfection of wisdom as his essence and attains purity of mind within the assembly; thus, he benefits himself through wisdom.

By employing parables and preaching the Dharma, he benefits others through wisdom. Question: Since this person is already able to preach the Dharma with a pure mind amidst the great assembly, he may be said to possess true wisdom.
How much more so when he can further employ various causes, conditions, and parables?
Regarding the words: "He expounds the Dharma without obstruction; it seems as though for his own benefit. Having already attained [enlightenment], what more need he say?
Only for such a person may one preach. Answer: Have you not heard that the Buddhas open up the provisional means (*upāya*), saying merely, "By means of various causes and conditions," and so forth?

He preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate. Although this is called preaching with unimpeded eloquence through the use of parables and words, it merely attains the provisional vehicle and has not yet reached the ultimate truth;
therefore, one must necessarily preach this wondrous Dharma for them.
"If there is a bhikṣu who [seeks] for omniscience (up to) such a person as this, then one may preach it to him.
This serves as a contrast to the beginning and end of the following section. "Seeking the Dharma in the four directions" marks the commencement of making inquiries.

It takes the power of diligence (*vīrya-bala*) as its essence. Master Yin says: "To seek the Dharma for the sake of wisdom means that the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*) is profoundly deep. One delights in the Great [Vehicle].
"Not small" means that the power of wisdom is exceedingly great. "The Omniscient One": true wisdom is indeed the foundation of omniscience.
"That which is now sought" refers to seeking the wondrous wisdom of the Tathāgata. "Seeking in the four directions" means extensively seeking merit and wisdom.

"Joining palms and receiving upon the crown of the head" indicates the urgency with which one upholds and maintains [the teaching]. "Seeking the Mahāyāna sūtras" signifies the desire to advance toward [enlightenment].

Regarding the fruit of Buddhahood: those who do not rely on other sutras desire to initiate practices for the benefit of others; therefore, they do not study the Hīnayāna to seek their own liberation alone.
As it is said, "If a person seeks the Buddha's *śarīra* with a sincere heart"—to such a person as this, one may then preach [this teaching].

To receive [the teaching] with the highest reverence and practice it single-mindedly is the ultimate form of reliance. Taking the vow of deliverance as its essence, the "Commentary on Sounds" (Yinzhiyun) states:

"Not seeking other sutras means that one’s vow does not desire the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Never consulting external texts means that one’s vow remains far removed from all heterodoxies. Śāriputra.

This is indeed a portion of the Buddha’s own body; one must seek it with the utmost earnestness. Thus, it is said that one should apply the sincere heart—that is, the mind seeking the sutra—just as one would when seeking śarīra relics and the like.

If one seeks it with such utmost sincerity and receives it upon the crown of the head with single-minded devotion, as if obtaining a supreme treasure, and having already attained deep faith in the Mahāyāna, how could one ever again harbor the intent to pursue the Hīnayāna? Furthermore, one would not...
"Are these the scriptures of the non-Buddhists? △ Second, the summary of what should be taught:
[The Buddha] addressed Śāriputra: "I have explained these characteristics... you should preach for them the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*."
These signs refer to the ten kinds of virtuous signs mentioned above; however, they have been stated here only in brief.

If one were to explain at length the benefits gained from upholding this sutra, they would not be exhausted even after the end of an eon. As for the previous instruction not to speak recklessly, it was because those who lack faith and understanding will, on the contrary, create the conditions for falling into suffering.
Therefore, the ten kinds of sinful characteristics of those who slander [the Dharma] are enumerated in detail so that they may be heard.
Even if they do not believe or understand, do not give rise to slander; for in the future, this will serve as a condition for their gradual entry into the Buddha’s wisdom.
These ten types of believers and those with understanding will surely achieve the realization of noble wisdom and succeed to the wondrous fruit of the Buddha;
for them, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* must be preached. However, the World-Honored One [distinguishes] between these two types: those who believe and those who slander.

The retributions for good and evil are clearly set forth here, so that people may know how to distinguish between faith and doubt, and understand how good and evil lead to reversals of fortune—success or failure—precisely as they do.
This may be called the ultimate in analytical exposition. These sixty-five lines.
Having concluded the exhortation through [the discussion of] sins and merits, [the text] states directly:

"In this chapter, because the twelve hundred [disciples] did not awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, the World-Honored One was again troubled to enter the mud and the water to establish these parables. Through these parables, one knows that the triple world is like flowers in the sky;
one knows that sentient beings are like dreams; one knows that fixed karma is difficult to escape; and one knows that evil habits must be severed."
One knows that the provisional and the real are non-dual; one knows that the ultimate and the conventional are of one suchness; one knows that the mind and the Buddha are equal.

One knows that the Buddha appears in the world for the sake of the single great cause and condition; one knows that those with deep faith and resolve will certainly enter the Buddha-vehicle, while those who slander it will certainly fall into ruin;

and one knows that those with faith and understanding will surely receive a prediction of enlightenment. This single category alone encompasses the skillful means of the preceding [stages] and subsumes the causes of the subsequent [stages].
The conditions [of] the two gates of black and white are as clear as the sun and moon. How excellent is this analogy! It is truly beyond the reach of thought or conception.
*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Volume Three: "Handing Over."
The Lotus Sutra: A Manual for Instruction, Scroll Four, Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhixiang of Yunfeng, Hengzhou, Chu Province.
Chapter Four: The Attainment of Faith and Understanding.

The *Pinjie* (Section on Chapters) states: Regarding the intent behind the arrival of this chapter, it is because the four great disciples, upon hearing the parables of the Tathāgata and seeing Śāriputra attain realization, finally came to believe that their former fruits were but expedient means.

Regretting their past delusions, they used the story of the impoverished son to express their original intention, fully depicting the state of paternal compassion and filial obstinacy; hence it is called "Belief and Understanding" (*śraddhā-adhimukti*). —Tiantai.
It is said: Indeed, faculties vary in sharpness or dullness; delusions vary in thickness or thinness; teachings vary in their use of principles or metaphors; and awakenings vary in their sequence.

The ranks of various noble families and those of pure conduct surround [the Buddha] with reverence;
since they are said to "surround him with reverence," they are not merely those gazing from outside the palace walls, but represent the *dharmakāya* Mahāsattvas on this earth.
The pearl necklaces are the adornments upon the body of the elder, representing the ten *pāramitās*, which are sufficient to adorn the *dharmakāya*. As for the term "price" (*mūlya*)...
A single [white whisk] is worth ten million [pieces of gold]. Thus, ten times over, it is able to open the Dharma-gates of the myriad practices (*sahasra-caryā*).

The officials, citizens, and servants are those who serve internally and labor externally; yet here they hold white whisks and stand at the left and right, which is fittingly intended to represent skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
The white whisk is the function of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), while "left and right" is a name for the two extremes. This represents the Buddha’s employment of skillful means.

Skillful means and wisdom function inexhaustibly within the two extremes of emptiness and existence. Furthermore, one obtains the precious canopy of compassion, from which hang the flowered banners of the myriad practices;
with the water of wisdom, one sprinkles the mental ground of sentient beings and scatters famous flowers.
This manifests the causal cultivation of the five assemblies and arrays the true merits of the various stages (*bhūmi*).

It brings forth the boundless, wondrous meanings of both self and others, revealing in their entirety that the three bodies (*trikāya*) are fully endowed, the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*) are equally perfected, and the myriad virtues are majestic and awe-inspiring, such that their spiritual power is unfathomable;
thus it is called "the manifold adornments of especially sublime majesty. *Zhizhi* says: "Arising from the essence..."
To "give forth" is to manifest function from essence; to "take within" is to gather function back into essence. This clarifies the principles of the body and its function, of gathering and releasing.
(The character "nei" is pronounced "na.
The impoverished son saw that his father possessed great power and influence [up to the point where he realized], "This is not a place where I can obtain goods through hired labor."
This explains that when the impoverished son sees his father, fear arises in his heart;
it serves as a metaphor for those of the three vehicles who have not yet had the Buddha’s knowledge and vision opened to them, and thus experience terror upon encountering the Mahāyāna. Tiantai says:

"Great power" refers to wisdom as "great strength" and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) as "great influence," in the sense of having physical strength in one's hands and body. "Terror" refers to those of inferior capacity (*hīnayāna* faculties).

"Inferior and weak" means they are timid and fearful of the Great Way. "Those who regret having come" refers to those who, upon seeing the Buddha manifesting the Great Dharma for them, refuse to believe and accept it;
they secretly harbor thoughts of withdrawing from the Great Vehicle—this likely refers to King Ajātaśatru and others. The Direct Pointing says:

"The followers of the Small Vehicle know only the illusory city as their home and take the *zhànglù* (the sixteen-foot form) as their master; yet they behold the *zūntè shēnà* (the sublime, transcendent *sambhogakāya*)."

The body is the sovereign of the Flower Treasury World and a Buddha of other realms. This clearly elucidates how one is deluded regarding the fundamental and pursues only the derivative, turning one's back on the Great and heading toward the Small, contenting oneself with inferiority; hence it is said, "I am not a hired laborer," and so forth.
"It is better to go to a poor neighborhood and exert one's strength there. Having formed this thought, he ran off quickly.

"The poor neighborhood" refers simply to the realization of partial emptiness (*ekāṃśa-śūnyatā*). Zhiyi says: "Because one cuts off delusions and realizes the Truth, it is called 'the ground for exerting strength.
Since there is cultivation and realization, it is said that food and clothing are easy to obtain. If one dwells there for a long time," etc. Tiantai says:
To cultivate the Mahāyāna path necessarily requires passing through immeasurable kalpas; hence it is said that one must "dwell for a long time.

Those of the Two Vehicles fundamentally fear birth and death, yet those who cultivate the Mahāyāna must enter into birth and death; this is truly not their original vow, and thus it is said they are "compelled to act against their will."

Abandoning the great and taking the small, it is said that he "ran away swiftly. [△@△] The former refers to turning one's back on original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) and hastening toward the five realms of existence;
thus it is called "fleeing. This refers to fearing the Mahāyāna while being attached to partial emptiness (*pradeśa-śūnyatā*); thus it is called "running swiftly.
This correctly captures the meaning of the previous passage regarding "running east and west to look for his father. 2. The Parable of the Father Seeing His Son.
At that time, the wealthy elder [from the Lion Throne passage]... "Although I am old, I still cherish [this treasure].
This clarifies that the elder rejoices upon seeing his son; it is a metaphor for the Buddha’s joy at finding the *tathāgatagarbha* (the spiritual capacity). Tiantai says:

"The Buddha abides in the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) and discerns the capacities through great perfect wisdom (*mahā-pūrṇa-jñāna*). 'Upon seeing the son, he immediately recognizes him' means he knows [the son's nature]."
These were disciples with whom I had formed karmic connections in the past; fortunately, their faculties and my teachings struck one another, giving rise to joy.

Within this reception of the Dharma, he gave rise to a mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). In the analogy, this corresponds to the sense of being greatly startled and terrified. He then used that great compassion to uproot suffering.

Therefore, it is said that they were struck with alarm and fear. This statement refers to bestowing happiness through great compassion; hence, it is called "joy. One who forms such a thought is about to receive the Great Teaching.
Now, seeing that the great capacity [of sentient beings] has been activated in accordance with his own compassionate mind, the Mahāyāna finds its point of entrustment.
Therefore it is said that while one’s wealth and storehouses may have a trustee, for a single day one cannot obtain the benefit of this One Vehicle and remains adrift in the cycle of wandering.
Yet for a single day the Tathāgata holds one in his compassionate thought without forgetting; thus it is said, "I am constantly mindful.
Though he desires to save you, your capacity has not yet responded, and so there has been no way to see him. Now, however, there is a capacity ready to be saved, and thus he has suddenly appeared.

"Meaning" (*yi*) refers to being in accord with a compassionate mind; this is the meaning of "being in accord with one's vows. The following two lines explain the reason why being in accord with one's vows is difficult to accomplish immediately:
although the conditions for conversion are nearing their end, the great capacity [of the beings] has not yet been struck by resonance, and one remains in a state of careful deliberation;
hence it is said, "still cherishing and begrudging [the departure]. △ Third, the analogy of luring those nearby. This is divided into two parts. First:
He sent an attendant to pursue him.
He immediately sent an attendant to chase him back quickly, saying: "I have committed no offense against you; why have you seized me?

This refers to the time when he was leading [the assembly] through the *Avataṃsaka*. The Buddha wished to bestow the Great Teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) all at once upon those of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*), yet he did not...

In the *Self-Explanatory* (Zishuo), he then commanded fifty-five Dharma-body Great Beings (*dharmakāya-mahāsattva*) to each expound the principle of the equality of birth and Buddhahood within the single true Dharma-realm (*ekadharmadhātu*).
This is precisely what is meant by "sending out the attendants. As for "hastily pursuing them to bring them back," Tiantai says:
To speak directly of the Great Teaching: it is like urgently pursuing a messenger of the Small Vehicle to quickly cause them to remember the fundamental vows of the Mahāyāna;

thus it is said, "about to bring him back. Those who run swiftly to seize him do so because they desire to lead every person directly toward Bodhi through the Mahāyāna’s *tathatā* (suchness) and the wisdom of principle and phenomena, just as the great white ox-cart is as swift as the wind. This is the manner in which the Bodhisattva expounds the Dharma.
To explain: the Bodhisattva possesses his own supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and has also received the Buddha’s empowerment;

thus, he is able to cause sentient beings to swiftly attain *bodhi*. As for the "poor son who was startled": although he had once resolved upon the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), he had long since abandoned it and no longer remembered it.
Now, suddenly hearing this Great Teaching, he is startled; because he does not recognize this realm, he is struck with amazement. For the Hīnayāna practitioner, [this is] due to the afflictions...
Afflictions are the enemy; birth and death are suffering; the triple world is a great prison.

Now, hearing that afflictions are themselves bodhi and birth and death are themselves nirvāṇa, one returns to enter the triple world to teach and transform sentient beings—this is what is called "the great wailing of the wronged.
One does not find joy in accomplishing sentient beings within pure buddha-lands; therefore, it is said: "I..."
"I have committed no offense; why are you seizing me? This passage from the introductory section on exhortation is intended for those who lack the karmic capacity [to understand].
Startled, the messenger held him even more tightly and forcibly dragged him back. As they went, he became increasingly terrified, fainted, and collapsed to the ground.

The more they are restrained, the more they strive; these Bodhisattvas discuss the wondrous meaning of *tathatā* (suchness) at every stage, asserting that the initial resolve is equal to the ultimate fruition, and thus they ardently desire to achieve *bodhi*.
As for the statement that "the two vehicles originally have no inclination toward this, and are forcibly drawn back," Tiantai says: "Sin" (*zuì*) refers to compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*).
Sentient beings enter the prison of birth and death because of their transgressions. Bodhisattvas, out of compassion, likewise enter that prison with them as if they were guilty.
Those of the Two Vehicles lack the resolve to benefit living beings and are thus termed "guiltless"; yet they wish for others to enter the prison of birth and death as if they were being imprisoned.
Without the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Mahāyāna, if one enters birth and death, one will inevitably and forever lose the wisdom of the Three Vehicles.
Because life is thus [fleeting], it is said that death is certain. When one contemplates the various matters mentioned above, one becomes increasingly terrified;

therefore, the Great Dharma is forcibly cast upon them. Yet those of small wisdom do not understand this, and thus it is said they "faint away. They give rise to slander and fall into the three miserable realms—this refers to collapsing to the ground.
This summarizes the preceding section on the gate of admonition regarding the suitability of the teaching for those who lack the capacity.
The father saw him from afar and told his messenger: "[... so that he may attain awakening; do not speak with him again.

This, together with the two preceding gates of exhortation, constitutes the provisional method for ceasing the transformation through the Mahāyāna. Tiantai says: "He saw him from afar" because the Great and Small Vehicles are vastly separated;
since this is a child with whom [the father] has established a karmic connection, it is said he "saw him from afar. Regarding "he told his messenger," and so forth:
The Tathāgata then said to the various bodhisattvas: "There is no need to manifest your sublime and wondrous bodies so that those of the two vehicles may see them.
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Withdraw the fragrance of your bodies so that those sentient beings do not give rise to deluded attachment."

Furthermore, when Samantabhadra enters the Sahā world, he contracts his body to make it small; all such instances carry this same meaning. As for the instruction not to force [the teaching] upon those who have not yet come:

since they lack the great capacity (*mahā-indriya*), if one were to manifest a superior body and preach the Mahāyāna Dharma, it would not only be of no benefit, but there is even fear that it might instead damage their roots of goodness.

"Cold water" refers to the water of principle (*tattva*)—namely, the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*) and the cessation through incineration—which removes the feverish afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). "Face" refers to...
To turn away from suffering is the "back"; to advance toward principle is the "face.

"The awakened one" refers to the opening of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings to suit the capacities of beings, enabling them to escape the distress of afflictions and realize the Four Noble Truths. "Do not speak further" means that one should definitively cease the Mahāyāna teachings.
Why is this so? It is because the father knows his son [and so forth], yet he does not speak to others, saying, "This is my son.

Those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) weary of suffering and delight in emptiness; they fear and find the Great Dharma difficult. Thus, for the time being, allowing them to practice the Lesser Vehicle is a suppression of the Buddha’s original intent.
Tiantai says: "As for 'knowing thoroughly,' it means that the Tathāgata already knew [this] while under twenty thousand Buddhas, where he had previously resolved upon the Great [Vehicle]."

The mind possesses the meaning of "having a child. However, through skillful means and the like, within the former teachings of the Hīnayāna, he followed the intent of others' words and used skillful means to conceal [the truth], referring to himself as a śrāvaka; he did not say that, according to his own intent, he was a bodhisattva.
The messenger said to him, "I now release you [to go] to the poor quarters to seek food and clothing.
By saying "I release you," he knew that his great potential was weak; by saying "as you wish," he knew that his minor goodness was strong. It was because of these two conditions.
This is the great transformation of the breath. Tiantai says: Because they were not oppressed by the Great Teaching, they rejoice;

because they have no sin of slandering the Great [Vehicle], they are spared from the three miserable realms, and thus it is as if they have risen from the earth. Since small roots of goodness have arisen, it is said that they "arise.

Furthermore, previously, when the Great Dharma was presented to them, they were bewildered and unable to understand, lying upon the ground of ignorance; now, as the teaching has been adapted to their capacity with the Small [Vehicle], they are able to awaken.

He attained awakening; therefore, it is said that he rose from the ground. Within the Four Noble Truths, because he sought the Dharma of the Path, it is said that he went to the poor quarters to seek food and clothing.
II. Sending two people to entice him. This is divided into two parts. First, the simultaneous instruction and guidance.

At that time, the elder was about to entice his son [to the Deer Park]. The phrase "his appearance was haggard and he lacked majesty" marks the period when [the Buddha] led [the five bhikṣus] to the Deer Park.
Regarding the phrase "was about to entice," Tiantai says: "Since the great transformation had ceased..."
Unable to leave him alone and abandoned, he immediately established skillful means; thus it is said, "intending to. Regarding "secretly dispatching," etc.:

here it is clarified that concealing the ultimate reality constitutes "secrecy," while pointing toward the partial truth constitutes "dispatching. As the Direct Pointing says: "Now, this refers to the inferior response-body manifesting provisional power to meet the capacities of beings;
the time belongs to the *Āgama* period, hence it is said 'he established skillful means. First, he commanded the bodhisattvas of the stages above to transform [beings]."

Acting as *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, they are born together within the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*). Internally concealing [their true nature] while externally manifesting [a different form], they do not pursue [beings] with haste;

hence it is said, "secretly dispatching two persons. The Bodhisattvas of the Grounds (*bhūmi*) conceal both their wisdom and their principle (*jñāna* and *tattva*), appearing together as ignorant and small-minded;

hence it is said, "withered and haggard. They do not employ various supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and such matters; hence it is said, "lacking majestic power. The two characters "secretly dispatching" (密遣) are precisely...
This is the skillful means (upāya) that has been established. As for these two types of persons, because they employ the provisional wisdom of skillful means, they depart from the Middle Way;
thus, they use the dual dharmas of emptiness and existence to transform those of limited capacity.

Their "haggard appearance and so forth" result from the application of provisional wisdom, as they are unable to manifest fully in accordance with the true nature (dharmatā) and extensively display its wondrous function.
"You may go to him and speak gently to that impoverished son, saying: 'We two shall also work together with you.
This is an approach through the practice of *samānārthatā* (common purpose) to gather him in. Zhizhi says: 'Go to the place of true emptiness;
study Prajñāpāramitā together. Therefore, he commands: 'You may go to him and speak gently,' and so forth. As for 'the place of work,' Tiantai says it is..."
The path of seeing and the path of cultivation are the places where views and afflictions are severed. To give you double the price:

by practicing the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions, one merely stops rebirth in the three miserable realms; however, through the Four Noble Truths and the twelve links of dependent origination, one can transcend the triple world—this constitutes the "double."

Furthermore, the six practices of the non-Buddhists can only suppress afflictions; now, by cultivating the Four Truths, one can sever afflictions and attain nirvana—this constitutes the second "doubling.
If the impoverished son consents, the teaching is established according to his capacity; it merely requires the removal of the dung of views, thoughts, and conceptual proliferation.
As for the two persons acting together, in terms of principle, this refers to the mutual support between wisdom and the Truths.
Regarding "the person": this refers to the provisional person practicing together with the real person. The two characters for "removing filth" are exceptionally striking;
the metaphor is perfectly apt.
At that time, the two messengers immediately sought out the impoverished son (until) they first took his wages and then gave him the task of removing filth.

All the bodhisattvas, in accordance with the Buddha’s command, manifest bodies that accord with various types of beings within lands of skillful means and preach teachings that accord with those types of beings;

thus they provide instruction according to the capacities of their audiences. Since these serve as the foundation for the Mahāyāna and constitute the teaching of the bodhisattva-dharma, it is said that they are "complete."
This refers to the aforementioned matter. Those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) aspire to the fruit and practice the cause; therefore, it is said that they first take its price.
△ Second, taking the meaning for understanding:
the father, seeing his son, felt pity and was struck with wonder.
He takes pity on those who do not resolve their minds toward the Great Vehicle and laments that they selectively seek only the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle.

This is precisely where the Buddha feels profound compassion: he perceives that what they lose is vast, while what they gain is meager, and thus they are unable to partake in the same enjoyment as the Buddha.
Wu-ling asked: "If he is to be pitied or rebuked, one should simply save him by means of the Great Dharma.
Why, then, did you secretly send someone to instruct him to take up the Lesser Vehicle? The answer was: "Since he would not come when pursued openly, it was necessary to send someone in secret.
Although instructing him to remove filth was not the father’s original intention, because [the father] wished to entrust [the legacy] through explicit words, he cherished [the son] for this reason."
Furthermore, on another day, [the Buddha] looked through the window and saw that it was defiled by excrement, soil, dust, and impurities.

This clarifies the concealment of the superior and the manifestation of the inferior, serving as a metaphor for the moment when the two aspects of the *Avataṃsaka* are simultaneously suspended—the two beginnings occurring at once.
*Zhizhi* says: "Another day" refers to the day when skillful means use wisdom to examine the capacities [of beings]. "Window" is a metaphor...
The wisdom of wondrous observation shines upon those of small capacity; since the distance between the small and the great is vast, it is said they are "seen from afar.
Those of the Two Vehicles are shrouded by the two attachments to self and phenomena, which obscure the Dharma-body; thus they are described as being covered by "filth and dust.
Because the seeds of wisdom are enveloped by the fetters of the five desires, they are called "defiled and impure. Tiantai says: "The power of their cultivated causal wisdom is weak and feeble."
He becomes emaciated; his merit from cultivating causes is shallow and thin, so he grows gaunt day by day. The four abidings are like dung and soil, and ignorance is like dust and grime.
He immediately casts off his necklaces and fine, soft garments, appearing as though he were filled with dread.

The Tathāgata conceals the realm of his true reward-adornment; this is like casting off jeweled necklaces. Employing skillful means according to the capacities of beings, he manifests a body sixteen feet tall, as if wearing tattered and soiled garments.
He shows birth in the household of King Śuddhodana and appears to fulfill the eight phases of enlightenment through the five desires;
hence it is said that "dust and dirt smear his body. Relying on reality to manifest expedient means, he extensively expounds the Three Vehicles; hence it is said:
In his right hand he holds a vessel for removing filth, which also demonstrates the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death; therefore, it is said that his appearance is fearsome.
Tiantai says: "Dust and dirt covering the body" represents the manifest existence of afflictions (*kleśa*), conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), and outflows (*āsrava*).

The right hand is a metaphor for skillful means (*upāya*); by means of these provisional teachings, he severs the fetters and attains Buddhahood, and he likewise uses them to transform others—hence, it is said he "holds" [the vessel].
The dung-removal vessel: its appearance is that of something fearsome, demonstrating that [the Buddha] shares with the two vehicles the dread of birth and death.

Furthermore, there were retributions such as the cold wind and the horse-barley. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha had nine afflictions (nirvṛti), namely: the six years of ascetic practice;

the slander by Sundarī; the iron spear; the horse-barley; the slaughter of the Śākya clan by Virūḍhaka; the empty bowl when begging for alms; the slander by Ciñcā-mānavikā; and the [plot involving] Devadatta."
He reached Mount Tāḍa, where the cold wind made him long for clothing; this, along with the pain in his back from the twin trees, makes ten.
He said to the laborers, "Work diligently and do not be indolent; by such skillful means, you shall draw near to his son."

Regarding the phrase "addressing all people," Tiantai says this refers to the teaching of the Tripiṭaka. It indicates the four foundations of mindfulness as the vessel for removing filth and the realm for severing the fetters.
This corresponds to the "readiness and vigor" within the Burning House parable; it is the stage of the ordinary person (bāhyapṛthagjana) characterized by the wisdom derived from hearing.
"Work diligently and do not be lax" means to cause them to practice the four foundations of mindfulness with diligence; this is right effort (samyakpradhāna).
Regarding skillful means: if one gives rise to indolence, one will be unable to extinguish the two evils (namely, those already arisen and those yet to arise) and produce the two virtues.

By means of the two types of diligence, one can kindle the fire of "warmth" (*ūṣmagata*), pushing and shoving against others within the burning house to enter the stage of the warmth of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

Regarding "attaining proximity through skillful means": by employing the skillful means of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*), one first attains proximity with those of lesser capacity.
Thereafter, he further addresses them, saying: "Ho, man! (and so forth)... I also have aged and infirm servants; if you need them, I shall provide them to you."

This explains the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). Tiantai says: "The exclamation 'Du' (Tut! signifies a sense of startled awakening. Within the preceding [stage of] right effort (*samyakpradhāna*), there was agitation;

this is the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), like a man who possesses a yang-nature. Now, the bases of psychic power are the nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), like a woman who possesses a yin-nature.
This is because, through the stimulating exertion of right effort, one cannot yet be in resonance with true emptiness (*śūnyatā*)."

This means to cause them to abandon distraction and enter into tranquility. "If you always act in this way, there shall be no further wandering" refers to the previous applications of mindfulness and right efforts, where movement was not yet one-pointed;
now, by entering into the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), concentration is free from divergent objects.
Because it definitively severs all outflows (*āsrava*) through one-pointed concentration, it is said thus. This still remains within the process of mutual exclusion and displacement.

This is the stage of the Dharma of the Summit (*mūrdha-dharma*). Regarding the phrase "I shall increase your price": while one was unable to give rise to the Truth during the practice of Right Effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*), one now begins to give rise to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state within this practice of the Wish-Fulfilling Contemplation (*yathābhilaṣita-vipaśyanā*); hence it is called "increasing the price.

As for "whatever is required," this refers to both outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) and outflow-free wholesome qualities—both the auxiliary path (*sambhāra-mārga*) and the direct path (*pratipad-mārga*)—all of which are sought from within this Wish-Fulfilling Contemplation; whatever one desires, one obtains immediately.

Furthermore, the essence of the four dhyānas contains a forest of constituent factors (*aṅga*), like a basin or vessel. The wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) is coarse, like rice; the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is subtle, like flour.

This is the Right Path (*samyak-mārga*). The sixteen aspects of contemplation (*ākāra*) within the Four Noble Truths—impermanence being like salt and the truth of suffering like vinegar—are the Aids to the Path (*sambhāra-mārga*).
Just as rice and flour are difficult to eat and must be seasoned with salt and vinegar, so it is by means of the Right [Path].

The Way is difficult to manifest; it must be brought forth through the assistance of the Path (pratyaya-mārga). Do not harbor self-doubt or difficulty. This concludes the discussion on the primary and auxiliary practices.

Since [the goal] is clearly present within the Contemplation of Accomplishing One’s Wishes, one is told not to doubt; it can certainly be accomplished. One should regard it as one's own property, and thus it is said: "do not find it difficult.
If you wish to directly attain supernormal powers (abhijñā) to serve as hands and feet, like employing servants for labor, it is as follows:
Within the contemplation of the mind, one can give rise to these supernormal powers (abhijñā), though their manifestation is weak and inferior, similar to being worn out by old age.
Although the powers are subtle and deficient, they can still be employed; therefore, it is said that those who require them shall be provided with them.
"Set your mind at ease; I am like your father, so do not worry further.

This clarifies the characteristics of the powers of the five faculties (*pañcendriya-bala*). Regarding "set your mind at ease," Tiantai says: it means attaining the five faculties, such as faith (*śraddhā*) and the rest.
"Secure and firm, it is difficult to destroy. "I am like your father" means that I have already attained a semblance of understanding and am close to realizing the truth;

because this semblance is not yet the reality itself, I say I am "like your father. "Do not worry or be anxious" is intended to set their minds at ease and to shatter their views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi* and *kleśa*).
"Why is this? My years are advanced... from now on, you shall be as a son born to me.
Regarding "I am old and you are young," Tiantai says: The Buddha abides at the end of the Path; since his wisdom and severance are already complete, he is called "old.

The son is at the beginning of the Path, in the stage of causes; since his wisdom and severance are only now being cultivated, he is called "young and vigorous. This refers to the stage of *kṣānti* (patience).

Furthermore, by attaining these five powers (*pañcabala*), one leaves behind the five unwholesome qualities (*pañcakuśaladharma*). That is to say: because one attains the power of faith (*śraddhābala*), one does not deceive;

because one attains the power of diligence (*vīryabala*), one does not become indolent; because one attains the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*), one does not become angry; because one attains the power of concentration (*samādhibala*), one does not harbor resentment;

and because one attains the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*), one does not bear grudges. As for the phrase "other laborers," this refers distantly to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); those who seek the truth through false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are termed "others."
"Those who act" refers proximately to the four stages of Heat, Summits, and so forth; as they have not yet escaped the five destinies, they are also called "remaining actors.

From this point onward, the sixteen moments of the lower patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*) still involve a long duration of time. Although the middle patience (*madhya-kṣānti*) contracts the contemplation, it is still not yet a single moment.
As for the supreme patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) and the highest mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), these constitute the final single moment of mind.
Because it is adjacent to the ultimate truth and close to the state of the Sage, this stage is named after it, just as one names a newborn child.
Immediately thereafter, the elder further bestows a name upon him, calling him "son.
This clarifies that the Eightfold Noble Path and the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) are not far from the ultimate truth; hence it is called "immediately. — Tiantai.
