"Grown old and advanced" is a metaphor for when the Buddha had long since attained the fruit of enlightenment. As for the "one thousand two hundred people," they have not yet attained [the goal].
"Ji" (記) means "early. "Ye" (夜) means "evening. "The time of death" is a metaphor for the arrival of the time of *nirvāṇa*.

"The foolish son" is a phrase expressing the father’s heartache for his child. Having abandoned me for over fifty years—this refers to the long lingering within the five realms of existence (*pañcagati*).
Since one has long been submerged in birth and death (*saṃsāra*), the bonds of suffering have not yet been severed; how, then, could one be capable of shouldering the Great Dharma?
Therefore it is said: "As for how one should deal with the various items stored in the treasury.
At that time, the impoverished son sought food and clothing (until), gradually traveling on his way, he arrived at the city where his father resided.
This verse describes the suffering of the impoverished son from the *Sūtra of the Poor Son* as he wanders about without any support; this is the reason for his travels. Tiantai says:
the mutual interpenetration of the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) is like going from one village to another. The eighteen realms (*dhātu*) are like nations.

Cultivating the contaminated (*sāsrava*) virtues of the three realms is like having something gained. Cultivating the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) virtues of the two vehicles is like having nothing gained—nothing can be attained.
The Mahāyāna Dharma-food is like one who is starving; lacking the great function of the Mahāyāna, they are weak. Lacking great merit, they are emaciated.
Regarding existence and non-existence, they give rise to the afflictions of views and thoughts, which are like sores and scabs.

The Tathāgata, through his observation, knows that after sentient beings have regressed from the Mahāyāna since the time of twenty thousand Buddhas, they are driven by various sufferings and falsely seek to restore their original truth.
The Way. It is like seeking food and clothing; when the village is small and the kingdom is large, it refers to all sentient beings seeking the path to liberation.
From shallow to deep, from small to great, whether there is attainment or non-attainment, it is appropriate to rely on the previous explanation.

That which has been gradually opened up and explained over the course of forty years is called "gradual" (*ānupūrva*). Next, "passing through and arriving at the father’s city" refers to reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
It is understood. *Xiǎn* (pronounced xiǎn). *Luó* (pronounced léi). △ Second, the verse on the meeting of father and son:
Having traveled from place to place by means of hired labor, he eventually arrives at his father’s house... [up to] ...the recording of assets and liabilities and the drafting of deeds and documents.

Tiantai says: "The former refers to the side of the gate; this refers to the interior of the gate. That is, within the one true dharma-realm, it is the place where both the seeing and the seen are attained.
The mention of 'spreading great jeweled canopies' and so forth precisely clarifies the characteristics of what is seen. Zhanran says:
The extensive exposition of the concise is the commentary (*ṭīkā*); the bestowal of the prediction of enlightenment is the record (*vyākaraṇa*); the four great vows are the bond (*paṇya*);
and spiritual practice is the sub-commentary (*ṭippaṇī*). [Note: *Paṇya* is pronounced *quàn*; *antaḥ* is pronounced *nà*.]
The impoverished son sees his father’s wealth, nobility, and majestic dignity... [he] asks about a poor neighborhood, wishing to go there to work for hire.

This clarifies how those of the Two Vehicles, upon beholding the realm of the Flower Treasury (*Avataṃsaka*) and seeing the Body of Exalted Distinction (*vairocana-kāya*), give rise to alarm and fear.
The two characters "spontaneously" (*zì*) and "strange" (*guài*) describe the state of their own former years, when they were content to remain inferior. "Reflecting again" refers to their own minds.
He deliberated within himself, fearing the Mahāyāna; because he had not abandoned his old habits, he returned once more to the poor quarters.
Out of craving for the lesser fruits, it is said that he "wished to go out to seek work."
At that time, the elder was upon his lion throne; seeing his son from afar, he recognized him silently.
This clearly illustrates that within the site of enlightenment, one observes and knows the inferior and weak faculties of sentient beings and does not teach the Great Dharma;
hence it is said, "recognized silently. For this reason, he manifested a body sixteen feet tall to meet their capacity. △ Third, the verse on the manner of pursuing and inducing.
Approaching. This is divided into two parts. First, a verse dispatches bystanders to pursue him;
that is, he commands the messengers to seize and bring him back [until] he does not believe my words and does not believe that this is his father.

This general verse exhorts that there are two gates for ceasing transformation due to a lack of receptive capacity (*anādhimukti*). Seeing [the man] being killed is identical in meaning to the aforementioned "inevitable death.
The imperial decree to pursue and capture him represents the Tathāgata’s universal compassion, which desires to cause all sentient beings to likewise attain this Path.

The passage beginning with "The impoverished son, startled and crying out," illustrates the failure to receive the teaching due to a lack of receptive capacity. The following four sections concern those who cling to a self (*ātman*).

This passage describes the deluded attachments of the impoverished son. It means that because he clung so desperately to the notion of a self, he felt as though being forced to work against his will, as if it were of no benefit to him and would surely lead to his death.
He thought, "If they were merely providing me with food and clothing, how could they urge me on so urgently? This clarifies how, in the past, he lacked faith in the Buddha.
The intention that there is no distinction among the three types of sentient beings. △ Second, the verse on the two persons who entice:
"He immediately uses skillful means to dispatch other people [to say]: 'Go and remove all the filth and excrement, and I shall give you double the wage.'"
Since the Great Transformation had already ceased, he employed skillful means to preach the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle in order to entice and guide them. Tiantai said:
"The 'blind eye' is a metaphor for partial emptiness, as that which is seen is not upright. The 'dwarf' is short in height; the 'ugly' is narrow in breadth.
Those who perceive partial emptiness cannot vertically exhaust the source of true reality (*dharmatā*), nor do they possess horizontally the adornments of the myriad virtues of the Mahāyāna."

Thus, being like one who is short and ugly, he lacks the four fearlessnesses; this is called "lacking majesty. Being different from the [true] permanence, bliss, self, and purity, it is called "lacking virtue.

He dispatches bodhisattvas of the stages above, secretly concealing his inner state while manifesting outwardly, to demonstrate the gathering through "sameness of purpose" (*sādharmya-saṃgraha*). He says, "I can speak with you," thereby leading them to practice the Lesser Teaching.
He says, "I will hire you to remove dung," which means entering from the mere emptiness (*tathatā-śūnyatā*) into the true emptiness (*bhūta-śūnyatā*); this is called "doubling the payment."
The "miao" (pronounced miao) refers to the impoverished son who, upon hearing of this, comes with joy to remove filth and purify the various rooms.
"Coming with joy" means that his capacity (*ji*) accords with the teaching (*jiao*); it is to provide what he desires. To purify the various rooms...

Abandoning [them] is like the first fruit [of the path]: one does not enter into form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas, and simultaneously attains the pure abode of the five aggregates of insight and contemplation.
The metaphorical meaning of the phrase "pure abode" is exceedingly profound.
The elder constantly saw his son from the window, observing that the son was foolish and inferior, delighting in base matters.
"Window" refers here to a hole or aperture in the wall. It means that the Tathāgata did not manifest his sublime and extraordinary body for public viewing.
Fearing that they might again give rise to alarm and terror, he does not abandon his compassionate heart and constantly keeps them in mind; thus it is said, "he sees them constantly.
Knowing that they lack the aspiration for the Great [Vehicle], it is said, "he pities their ignorance and inferiority."
Thereupon, the elder put on worn and soiled clothes (and so forth), and further addressed him with gentle words, saying, "You are like my own son.

He then gave the elder instructions for work, which consist of seven categories. What is now called "associating with and speaking to him" corresponds to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

Tiantai says that "diligent labor" corresponds to the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*). The single line beginning with "I shall increase your wages" corresponds to the four [bases of psychic power].
The *ṛddhipāda* (bases of psychic power): applying oil to the feet enables one to walk upon deep water, which is an analogy for supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Furthermore, that oil can dispel wind, which is an analogy for meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Abundant food and drink refers to the aforementioned rice and flour. Thick and warm mats and bedding refer to the four types of dhyāna—the cultivation through refinement and perfuming.
Because one cultivates these concentrations, one is able to eliminate distraction and movement; thus, it is called "as one wishes" (*yathāruci*).
This is the conclusion. Thus, the two lines concerning harsh speech correspond to the fourth [section], consolation, which refers to the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).

The fifth, freedom from fault, refers to the five powers (*pañcabala*). Once the faculties and powers are perfected, one is then capable of enduring harsh speech. Furthermore, the two lines concerning gentle speech [correspond to the sixth section].
The sixth character added above the verse refers to the Eightfold Noble Path. The seventh, "to cause to be constantly practiced," refers to the Seven Factors of Enlightenment;

both constitute the stage of the "son. Regarding these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), according to conventional discourse, the Seven Factors of Enlightenment precede the Eightfold Noble Path.
However, here they are arranged according to their sequential positions, and thus they have been placed out of order. If it were like my son, it would be the character "if" (*ruo*).
This refers to your name. In the *Zhuangzi*, this usage occurs frequently. △ Fourth, the verse on thoroughly knowing the family business, divided into two parts.
First, the verse on taking charge of knowledge:
"The elder, possessing wisdom, gradually causes him to enter and exit... [until] he makes him know all the goods that come in and go out."

The elder possessed wisdom; he employed skillful means, which is precisely expedient wisdom (*upāya-kauśalya*). To cause those who enter and exit gradually is to use skillful means to entice and lead them, so that they may gradually enter the profound realm of the Mahāyāna.

His twenty years of managing household affairs correspond to the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, during which the World-Honored One extensively expounded the Mahāyāna for twenty-two years, teaching the characteristics of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*) and causing those of the Two Vehicles to propagate the teachings.
"Xuan" means to grasp and act. Within the Prajñā, having been refined through twenty years, it immediately reveals its golden treasure;
it expounds the Dharma that benefits both oneself and others, thereby causing one to know how to enter and exit.
It is like staying overnight in a thatched hut outside the gate, thinking to oneself regarding one's poverty, "I have no such thing.

This verse speaks of settling for the small. Daokuang says: "Though one knows that the true emptiness of Prajñā can transform the Great Teaching, if one is unwilling to take it up and shoulder its responsibility, one will ultimately remain separated by a single door; such a person is but a lowly hired laborer. This refers to thinking of oneself [in this way].
Regarding the matter of poverty: "I do not possess this thing" is due to the failure to abandon the inferior mind. Question:

Since those of the Lesser Vehicle have already transcended the three realms, why do they still dwell in grass huts? Answer: Although they have emptied themselves of afflictions (*kleśa*), they have not yet exhausted what is to be known (*jñeya*);
therefore, although they have exited the gate of the burning house, they still dwell in grass huts and have not yet entered the gate of the Tathāgata. 2. [The second section]
The verse concerns the entrustment of the task.
"The father knew his son’s mind had gradually become expansive" (up to) "...he traveled everywhere seeking him and finally arrived here.
"The father knew his son’s mind" means that only a Buddha can know the faculties and natures of sentient beings. "Expansive" means it was no longer as it was before.
They were deludedly attached to a narrow and inferior mind. Since the mind is now vast, the fruit of Buddhahood can be attained; therefore, he proclaims this before the assembly.
He spoke these words, "He is my son," and so forth, as previously described. Addressing Śāriputra, he said:

"In the presence of twenty thousand Buddhas, I constantly taught you to aspire to the Buddha-way, yet you have now completely forgotten it. This was because in the interim you regressed from the Mahāyāna and gave rise to delusions."
Thus, he traversed the five paths; that is to say, having abandoned me to practice elsewhere for fifty years.
As for the statement, "It has been twenty years since I last saw my son," this refers to the two vehicles within the *prajñāpāramitā*:

when they first develop a mind of aspiration and aversion, they become close to the wondrous principle of the Tathāgata’s Mahāyāna. This is the meaning of father and son meeting. Formerly, in a certain city...

"Lost" means that the false arises depending on the true; it has no fixed location. "Pervading everywhere until reaching this point" summarizes the gradual cultivation and refinement over forty years until completion.
"Whatever I possess—my houses, my people, and so forth—[up to] they were filled with great joy, having attained what they had never experienced before.

"Whatever I possess" refers to the Tathāgata’s possession of immeasurable knowledge, vision, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), powers (*bala*), and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*);
he gives all of these to them. Therefore, it is said that they may "use them as they please. The section beginning with "My son, you should reflect... follows below.
Chen Deye was filled with joy and said, "From the past until now, I have fundamentally sought only the small fruits of the Śrāvaka vehicle;

for a long time I have held this thought, believing that I was forever excluded from the Mahāyāna. Now, all at once, I hear that those of the two vehicles can attain Buddhahood, and that all the Tathāgata’s majestic adornments and myriad virtues are now mine to possess.
This is truly something I have rarely, if ever, encountered before. How could I not [rejoice]?"

How joyful and fortunate! The verse on the analogy has concluded. △ Second, the verse on the application of the analogy, divided into three parts. First, the verse on the application of the loss of the [true] nature and the seeing of the [false] nature:
"The Buddha likewise knows that I delight in the Small [Vehicle]."
The first line combines with the aspect of loss; the second line combines with the aspect of seeing. The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states:

"If one relies solely on the first line to combine with the aspect of loss, its meaning is not yet manifest; if one relies solely on the second line to combine with the aspect of seeing, the meaning is likewise not clarified. Why is this so?"
The preceding line is completed by means of the following line: because their joy was small, they consequently fell away. The following line is likewise manifested by means of the preceding line:
because the Buddha knew that they were content with little and had regressed from the Great Mind, this is why He came to meet them.
△ Second, the verse on the combined pursuit and enticement toward proximity.
"I have never said to you, 'You shall become Buddhas' (up to) 'you shall achieve the status of disciples of the Lesser Vehicle Śrāvakas.

The first two lines are combined with the bystanders' retrospective reflection: "Because we lacked the aspiration for the Great [Vehicle], He did not say that there would be a time when we would attain Buddhahood.
As for the following four lines regarding "me," they are combined with the two types of people to entice them; thus, one attains all...

"Anāsrava (the untainted) is precisely *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder). Zhizhi says: "This refers to the time when the Four Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination were taught in the Āgamas;
having accomplished the six kinds of understanding, the untainted state is the ultimate. Although the verse text is brief, its meaning is exhaustive.
Generally, because the preceding [prose] was detailed, the verse summarizes it. This is the skillful arrangement and transformation of the Dharma-preacher."
Excellent. △ Third, the verse on entrusting the knowledge of the family business. This is divided into two parts. First, the verse on the entrustment:
The Buddha commands us to expound the supreme path, stating that those who practice it shall attain Buddhahood.
This verse refers to the time when the Prajñāpāramitā was transmitted and proclaimed, expounding the most supreme path. Tiantai says:
"This is precisely the wisdom of emptiness (śūnyatā-prajñā); there is nothing superior to it. This means that whenever one cultivates this Mahāyāna wisdom of emptiness, [it is the ultimate].
"You shall certainly become a Buddha.
Having received the Buddha’s teaching, I [act as] a great bodhisattva... "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood.
Having received the Buddha’s teaching, I—namely, one who follows the Lesser Vehicle—accept the command and preach the Unsurpassed Way. It is the Buddha’s intention that he himself...

Knowing how to become a Buddha, one realizes and enters the perfect principle. How could it be known that those of the Lesser Vehicle do not understand this meaning, but merely act as messengers, contenting themselves with being excluded from the path and remaining like wanderers outside the gate?

To speak of the Unsurpassed Way is to uphold the mandate and expound the Way of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Those who hear this Dharma, through diligent reflection and cultivation, shall receive the prediction of their future enlightenment.
Yet the one who preaches the Dharma still occupies a subordinate position; how is this not to be lamented? Regarding the mention of the Buddhas' bestowal of predictions and the phrase "at this time":
it refers either to receiving a prediction at the conclusion of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, or to obtaining a prediction before the Buddhas of other directions;
in all cases, it occurs within a short period of time, and thus it is called "this time."
Regarding the secret treasury of the Dharma of all Buddhas... [up to] ...you have not spoken this essential truth for my sake.
Those of the Two Vehicles, having themselves failed to awaken to the perfect meaning of the One Vehicle, instead give rise to doubt within themselves, thinking:
"If the World-Honored One has commanded me to expound it for the sake of the Bodhisattvas, then this must be the Unsurpassed Dharma; since it is indeed this Dharma, why..."
"Therefore, while we who preach the Dharma still linger in the Lesser Vehicle, those who hear the Dharma from us all receive predictions of enlightenment.
How could it be that the Buddha expounds the ultimate reality only for the sake of the Bodhisattvas, yet does not explain its essential truth to us?"
Just as that impoverished son, upon approaching his father, knew of all the goods but had no desire to take them, this cites the previous parable;
the application of the analogy is clear.
Although we speak of the Buddha’s Dharma-treasury (up to the point of) teaching and transforming sentient beings, we have no joy or delight whatsoever in it.

Tiantai says: "Internal extinction" refers to the internal essence of delusion; it means internally extinguishing the three poisons and exhausting the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*).
This clarifies the fault of adhering to the Hinayana. If we were to hear these three phrases, only then would the error of lacking joy in the Mahayana be raised.
Why is this? Because when one contemplates all phenomena [up to] in this manner, joy and bliss do not arise.

This clarifies that it is due to a lack of aspiration for the Great Dharma. To point directly: by internally contemplating the body and mind and externally contemplating the world, both are found to be entirely empty and quiescent.
The perceiving aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses dissolves, leaving only the principle of universal emptiness; therefore, it is said:

There is neither arising nor ceasing. Furthermore, when observing the objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses, there is only the wisdom of universal emptiness; hence it is said that there is "neither large nor small.
Since both the seeing-nature (*darśana-bhāga*) and the objective-aspect are extinguished, it is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*) and "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).

While contemplating in this way the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, one erroneously calculates that even the Dharma of the Mahāyāna is empty and quiescent; therefore, no joy or delight arises.
"For a long night we [have been] regarding our own understanding of the Dharma as ultimate" (up to this point).
This verse clarifies that within this long night of biased emptiness, there was no attachment to the Buddha’s wisdom.
This refers to the previous statement, "I have not committed such an offense," and so forth; it was a mistaken calculation that regarded biased emptiness as the ultimate.
"We have long practiced the dharma of emptiness (up to) dwelling in the nirvāṇa with remainder of our final existence.

This verse clarifies the exclusive emptiness. Having practiced the three types of emptiness throughout the long night, one attains liberation from the burning house of the triple world and dwells in the final existence;
this is to be celebrated as a source of joy. "Final existence" refers to the arhat. It is...
This final body of an ordinary person is called the "bondage of the fruit.
Since the Buddha’s teaching has led me to attain the Way without fail, I have already repaid the Buddha’s kindness.
This verse describes the state of no longer seeking further progress; it means that the Tathāgata taught me, desiring that I emerge from the three realms, and I am fortunate...
I have attained realization upon the path of renunciation; thus, the fruit is not in vain.
Since I have already realized nirvana, I have not failed the holy transformation and may be said to have repaid the Buddha’s kindness. What else, then, could I further seek?
Although we are the sons of the Buddhas, [from the beginning] you did not exhort us or speak of the actual benefits.

This verse reiterates that, despite being commanded to turn the teaching and having explained it thoroughly from beginning to end, we ultimately did not give rise to even a single thought of aspiration or joy.
Consequently, the Tathāgata did not utter a single word to clearly manifest an exhortation for us.
This explains that there is the true benefit of my śrāvakas attaining Buddhahood. △ Second, the verse on the shared karma:
"Just as a wealthy elder, knowing his son’s inferior disposition... [until] having tamed his mind, he then teaches him great wisdom."

This verse summarizes the section on entrusting the family estate. Only now does one realize that the elder’s countless skillful means to entice and lead [the son] near were originally intended for the purpose of entrusting him with the family estate. For forty years, the Buddha exerted every ounce of his strength.
He subdued our own minds. His original intention was to reveal to us the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; that is to say, he manifested rare and wondrous events.

Because we did not hear or understand this and instead delighted in and clung to the Lesser Dharma, the Buddha used skillful means to entice and lead us forward, waiting until this day before finally clarifying that we possess the capacity for Buddhahood. How can such benevolence and virtue be surpassed?
How profound are these words! We deeply feel the grace of this salvation.
Today we have attained what we have never before experienced—just as that impoverished son obtained immeasurable treasures.
This verse clarifies that throughout forty years of successive and gradual unfolding, the wondrous meaning of the One Vehicle has now been revealed up to this day.
The immeasurable treasuries of provisional and ultimate truth are bestowed all at once; these were not within the expectations of the impoverished son during his earlier time.
Therefore, it is reiterated that the impoverished son did not seek them, yet they came to him of their own accord. Such a narration is deeply moving and worthy of being recorded.
My words are insufficient, for they cannot be fully exhausted. It is only upon reaching this point that I am able to clearly express my gratitude.
World-Honored One, having now attained the Way and its fruits, I shall everywhere receive offerings therein.
From the beginning, since the presentation of parables, all [the teachings] have collectively elucidated the faults of past ignorance and attachment to the Hinayana.
Only now, at this point, is it clarified that today there is new realization and new attainment, and the reasons for this awakening are set forth;

this alone is the definitive conclusion regarding the subsequent bestowal of the prediction (vyākaraṇa). Observe the two characters "my present" (觀我今); they do not speak of matters from the past, but rather declare the attainment of the Way.

...is to hear the aforementioned teaching on the Buddha-wisdom of all Buddhas—the ten realms and the ten suchnesses—which is the mark of quiescence realized at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Furthermore, regarding the parable of the great white ox-cart, it is the wondrous path of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) guaranteed by the Tathāgata as being not in vain;
this I have now fortunately attained. As for "attaining the fruit," it is that which all Buddhas of the three periods of time [share].
Although one has not yet attained the supreme and wondrous fruit known as "realization through shared knowledge," one knows for oneself that it will certainly be realized in the future;
this is equivalent to having an attainment today. This is precisely what it means to receive and realize the Buddha’s knowledge.

Regarding the attainment of the pure eye within the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas: the "untainted" here does not refer to the untainted state obtained by the two previous vehicles, which belongs to the wisdom of partial emptiness.
What is attained now is the untainted dharma in which the provisional and the real are merged.

By means of this subtle untainted wisdom, one illuminates and exhaustively penetrates the principle of the three types of enlightenment (*trividha-bodhi*); thus, ignorance is completely purified, and both phenomena and principle are [fully realized].
When both [eyes] are opened, it is first called "attaining the eye of purity"; this is precisely to realize that this is the Buddha's vision.
Having maintained the precepts through the long night, one now attains the fruit; thus, one realizes that provisional power (*upāya*) is itself reality (*tattva*).
Although it was a provisional means in former days, it is now all brought to ultimate fulfillment. This refers to the Dharma of the Dharma-King practiced throughout forty years—all of it...
It was not in vain; it was also the result of long-cultivated pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). As the saying goes, "when the water reaches, the channel is formed.
Thus, one has now attained the stainless, unsurpassed, and great fruit. This can be trusted as a definitive self-knowledge that one will attain Buddhahood without error.

"Truly a śrāvaka. This is spoken by means of the real in contrast to the false. Although he previously attained the name of "śrāvaka," it was merely because he heard the sound of the Four Truths and entered into the small fruit; thus, his hearing was not true hearing, and his sound was not true sound.
Today, by means of the sound of the Buddha-way, he causes all to hear; thus, there is no place where the sound does not reach, and no one who does not hear.
Only when [defilements] are exhausted can one be called a true śrāvaka. Even the title "Arhat" is an old name held by us;
moreover, it is not truly authentic. Formerly it was called "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat), which merely meant being worthy of offerings from the heavens and the human realm.
Now, to say that one is universally worthy of offerings among all worlds implies that, like a Buddha, one should exhaustively transcend the nine realms. This is the truth.

He is worthy of offerings. Formerly he was called "One Who Is Unborn" (Anutpāda), which merely meant that he had exhausted the *pariccheda* (segmented) existence and was no longer born within the three realms.

Now that he has received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) to become a Holy Honored One among two-legged beings, he is one for whom even *pariṇāma-vipariṇāma* (transformative change) does not arise; this is the true attainment of non-arising.

Formerly he was called "Slayer of Thieves" (Arhat), which merely meant that he had severed the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhava-kleśa*) and exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*). Now it is said...
When the darkness of ignorance is forever extinguished without remainder, one truly becomes a slayer of the thief [of afflictions].
Here, regarding the Arhat, because the term "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat) is used to state the actual fact, the other two names can be understood without being explicitly mentioned.
The explanation of the verses is now complete. △ Second, praising the Buddha’s benevolent virtue.
The Great Benevolence of the World-Honored One is such a rare occurrence that it could not be repaid even throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Until now, I have been one who has failed to repay his kindness, failing to recognize the Tathāgata’s heart of diligent toil and rescue over successive kalpas.

Although I have heard the preaching of the Dharma and possess a vague understanding of it, it was only through the detailed exposition of the Burning House that I first realized how deeply a father pities and grieves for his children.

The depth of this [gratitude] is such that a child, having reached the extreme of folly and obstinacy, only upon attaining something for themselves begins to know the debt of gratitude and how to repay it.
The four lines beginning with "The World-Honored One’s great kindness" contain inexhaustible implicit meaning; therefore, Zhangan [Zhiyi] elucidated them by dividing them into ten layers.

First, the Buddha, through the compassion of the Four Great Vows, universally covers all beings and uproots the suffering of the six realms of existence, bestowing upon them the... [four... (of the noble fruits).
This is the sublime joy. It is the great kindness of the World-Honored One that, through this rare occurrence, has benefited us and allowed us to enter the Tathāgata’s chamber and dwell in peace.
Second, when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, he constantly taught and transformed me;

though I may have forgotten it in the interim, his wisdom and vows have not been lost. This is the great kindness of the World-Honored One, who out of compassion and pity has taught and transformed me with great loving-kindness.
1. He bestows happiness upon them. 2. We, having regressed from the Great Vehicle, have encountered suffering;

yet the Buddha, amidst this, observed the awakening of their capacity and skillfully guided us—this is the great kindness of the World-Honored One, who teaches out of compassion and draws us forth with great pity to uproot our suffering. 3.

The various trees, according to their superior, middling, or inferior [capacities], attain growth and develop flowers, fruits, blossoms, and seeds.

The preceding section clarified the reception of moisture; this is termed "growth. Tiantai states that there are two causes for the seven types of sentient beings: the cause of wisdom (*jñāna-hetu*) and the cause of retribution (*vipāka-hetu*).
Once wholesome dharmas have been moistened by the rain of the Dharma, both the fruits of cultivation (*bhāvanā-phala*) and retribution (*vipāka-phala*) will each attain growth.

"In accordance with their spiritual capacities" clarifies that the employment of skillful means accords with the faculties of beings: for those of lesser capacity, there is no excess; for those of greater capacity, there is no deficiency.

This refers to the two causes: the seven kinds of *vāsanā* (habitual tendencies) and *vipāka* (maturation). "The blossoming and ripening of flowers and fruits" refers to the two fruits: the seven kinds of *vāsanā-phala* and *vipāka-phala*.
Miaole states: "The flower is like the *vāsanā-phala*; the fruit is like the *vipāka-phala*. This is a case of using separated characters for contrast;
it should properly be read as "the blossoming of flowers and the ripening of fruits. △ Second, the analogy of non-differentiation.
Although they are all produced from the same earth and moistened by the same rain, each type of grass and tree has its own distinctions.
The earth is a metaphor for the mind that serves as the basis. That which is subsumed within this foundational mind is vast:

beginning from the wholesome causal mind of the ordinary person on the broad ground, through the fifty stages of practice in the interim, up to the final stage of Equal Enlightenment—all are collectively considered Buddhas.
The fruit is caused by the mind. Hence it is called "one ground. As for "one rain," this is a metaphor for the Buddha’s single voice preaching the Dharma;
fundamentally, there is no distinction between the three vehicles or five natures, for the Buddha’s teaching is equal and non-dual.
Yet, the various grasses and trees each have their differences; this is how they initially benefit according to their individual capacities. Regarding "the various grasses and trees," Tiantai says:
The small grasses are likened to humans and devas; the medium grasses are likened to those of the Two Vehicles; the superior grasses are likened to Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka Teaching;
the small trees are likened to the Shared Teaching; and the large trees are likened to the Distinct Teaching.

Just as these three types of grasses and two types of trees receive the moisture of a single rain and each attains growth according to its own capacity, yet none are aware of it themselves. △ Second, the application of the parable, which is divided into two parts. First, the application of the differences.
Another analogy. This is divided into two parts. First, the actual application of the dharma. This is further divided into three. First, the application of the "dense clouds and single rain.
Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is also like this... [omitted] ...pervading and covering the trichiliocosm.

Tiantai says: This corresponds to the analogy of the dense clouds. It means that the Tathāgata’s great compassion manifests in form to cover and nourish all beings, just as a great cloud covers everywhere. By means of his great voice, it corresponds to the fact that clouds possess sound.

As for "devas, humans, and so forth," these specifically list the three good realms of existence who receive the benefit of the Buddha’s secret of speech (*vāk-guhyaka*). That is to say, the Tathāgata universally responds to them through the mechanism of his secret of speech.

"Truly! Like a great cloud covering the trichiliocosm," [△@△] "appearing in the world"—these two lines signify that the Tathāgata manifests birth within the unborn and manifests form within the formless, just as a cloud arises suddenly and without intention.
From the phrase "with a great voice" onwards, it begins to correspond with the preceding description of "dense clouds spreading everywhere."
...and so forth.
Within the great assembly, he proclaimed these words (up to): "May those who have not yet attained nirvāṇa attain nirvāṇa.

Tiantai cites the *Bie xing xuán* (The Profound Meaning of the Separate Practice), Part II, which says: "The great vows fundamentally constitute compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Since compassion and loving-kindness take suffering as their object..."

Joy. The great vows are also based upon the Four Noble Truths. If one perceives the oppression, agony, bitterness, and pain of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), one gives rise to a vow on this basis;

thus it is said: "May those who have not crossed over be made to cross over. If one perceives that the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) involves inverted, revolving transmigration and the fetters of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) that are vast and boundless, which is truly pitiable, one gives rise to a vow on this basis; thus it is said: "May those who have not been liberated..."
To cause understanding of the path of purity. Sentient beings do not recognize it; those who practice this path are able to transcend birth and death and reach the ground of peace and bliss.

Desiring to show sentient beings and establish them upon this path, it is said: "I shall bring to peace those who are not yet at peace. The place where afflictions are extinguished is called *nirvāṇa*.
By means of the uninterrupted succession of cause and fruit, one attains the two types of *nirvāṇa*; it is with reference to this that the vow is made.
Therefore it is said: "To cause those who have not attained to attain;
to know, as they truly are, this world and the world beyond. (Up to: "All should come here for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
This is the Tathāgata’s own explanation of his appearance in the world to reveal, awaken, and lead all sentient beings into the knowledge of the Buddha.

"Seeing this is the way. Regarding the two phrases "this world and future worlds," Tiantai says: "This clarifies the three knowledges (*trividyā*): the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) clearly knows the past;
the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) clearly knows the future; and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*) clearly knows the present.
Although the past is not explicitly mentioned here, it is already fully contained within the intended meaning. "I am the all-knowing one" means that a single mind possesses [all things].

He possesses the three types of knowledge (*trividya*). Furthermore, he should possess the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*); because he has attained complete penetration of all things, he is called the "All-Knowing One" (*sarvajña*).
"One who sees" means he is fully endowed with the five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*). "One who knows the path" refers to non-restraint of the mind.

"One who opens the path" refers to non-restraint of the body. "One who speaks the path" refers to non-restraint of speech; that is to say, the Tathāgata’s three karmas are always [in accordance with the path].

Because it is conjoined with wisdom, it is not [subject to] protection. [△@△] This refers to the knower of the three periods of time; it should be understood as having the intention that his words are without falsehood.
This is the vertical discourse. The two characters "I" (吾) and "am" (我) first point to and present oneself.

The term "all" (一切) generally refers to all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane, including both defiled and pure causes and effects; this is the horizontal discourse. The two characters "knowledge" (知) and "vision" (見) collectively clarify the Buddha.
This wisdom and vision does not fail to illuminate the three periods of time vertically and penetrate all things horizontally.

The characters "knowing" (知), "opening" (開), and "expounding" (說) refer to the path of provisional and ultimate truth; they are also the path of the Buddha’s wisdom and vision. "Opening the path" means opening the Buddha’s wisdom and vision;
"expounding the path" means revealing the Buddha’s wisdom and vision; and "knowing the path" means awakening to and entering the Buddha’s wisdom and vision. Therefore...
The conclusion states: "You, all you hosts of devas and humans and all the various spirits, should all listen to and receive this Dharma with a resolute mind.
The fifth is the character 'person' (人), which carries the meaning of the character 'I' (我). All [the phrases] should be read by connecting them with the two characters 'I am' (我是).
For example: 'I am the person who knows all'; 'I am the person who sees all'; 'I am the one who reveals, awakens, and leads others into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.'"
Those who follow the Way should carefully examine the meaning of this passage.
Furthermore, since you—this assembly of devas, humans, and asuras—all ought to listen to the Dharma, it appears that the parable of the medicinal herbs was taught for those of inferior capacity.
As for those of middling capacity, they had already awakened to the Tathāgata’s intent in employing skillful means to clarify the ultimate truth while within the burning house.
This passage merely serves to extend the explanation for those of middling capacity, intending to bestow upon them the prediction of attaining Buddhahood.

Its true purpose is to cause those of inferior capacity to clearly recognize that the Tathāgata is without distinction—just as a single rain universally moistens all things, yet the three types of grasses and two types of trees each receive the moisture differently. △ Second, the Synthesis.
Regarding the land, grasses, and trees:
at that time, countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings came to the Buddha’s presence to hear the Dharma.
Tiantai says: "The phrase 'thousands of myriads of koṭis' encompasses the nine dharma-realms; here, it specifically refers to the sentient beings of the seven stages of expedient means."

This is merely a distinction. Regarding the combination of this with the preceding "land" (*bhūmi*): the term "land" carries the sense of supporting and bearing, as well as the sense of growth and development.
Now, it is said that innumerable sentient beings come to the Buddha’s presence; this means that the seeds of the Three Vehicles are about to sprout.
As for those who listen to the Dharma, the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is like rain; yet those who listen receive and uphold it without loss, thereby being able to bear it.
At that time, the Tathāgata observes whether the faculties of these sentient beings are sharp or dull, and whether they are diligent or indolent.
In the previous analogy, there were distinctions among the grasses and trees, such as differences in size;

here, in the application, it is clarified that roots have sharpness or dullness and practice has progress or indolence—this precisely refers to the depth or shallowness of the causes for cultivation, which corresponds in meaning to the grasses and trees.

Tiantai says: "Regarding 'at that time,' if one discusses the beginning of the gradual [teaching], it refers to the time when the Three Vehicles were first preached at the Deer Park. If one discusses...

Regarding the intermediate period, one may discuss this at various points. As for those of dull or sharp faculties: if judged collectively, those in the three miserable realms—who possess evil causes and experience suffering as their fruit and are thus unable to receive the Way—are called "dull.
Those who hear the teaching and gain benefit through the seven stages of expedient means are called "sharp. If judged individually:
Humans and devas merely receive karmic retribution; their unwillingness to accept the Way is termed "dull. Those of the three vehicles who sever delusions and transcend the realms are termed "sharp.
Furthermore, śrāvakas who contemplate arising and ceasing are termed "dull," while bodhisattvas who contemplate non-arising and non-ceasing are termed "sharp."

The three teachings—*tong* (Shared), *bie* (Distinct), and *yuan* (Perfect)—can be understood by discussing their respective degrees of sharpness and dullness. Regarding diligence and indolence: negligence within the three miserable realms is called indolence;
the precepts and wholesome deeds of humans and devas are called diligence. Furthermore, failing to feel weary of suffering as a human or deva is indolence;
fearing impermanence as a follower of the Two Vehicles is diligence. The greed of the Two Vehicles for realization, without seeking to become a Buddha, is indolence; the resolve of a Bodhisattva...
Seeking the Buddha-way is progress. When the capacity [of the student] and the teaching correspond, their value lies in being simultaneous.

Thus, regarding the two characters for "time" (*shi*), it is the beginning of the convergence of the provisional and the real, and the fusion of the trace and the source; one might say it is like the meeting of wind and clouds.

It is precisely when the teaching is imparted that the subtlety lies in the character "contemplation" (*guan*). If one were to preach without taking its timing into account, all such words would be mere idle chatter; therefore, one must ride upon this [timing].
According to their progress, indolence, acuity, or dullness, they each receive benefit according to their capacity and what is bestowed upon them.

This is just as a single rain universally nourishes all things, yet the three types of grasses and two types of trees each attain growth accordingly. △ Third, the harmonious reception of moisture and subsequent growth.
He preaches the Dharma according to their respective capacities, in ways that are manifold and immeasurable, causing them all to rejoice and swiftly obtain wholesome benefits.
"According to their respective capacities" means, as Tiantai says, that it accords with and meets their spiritual needs (*jīyí*), free from the error of adding or subtracting.
"Rejoicing and obtaining wholesome benefits" means that each receives the nourishment of the Dharma and attains benefit. Miaole says: "There is no adding or subtracting."

As for these apparent discrepancies, they are designated according to the capacities of the five vehicles; therefore, there is neither increase nor decrease. For instance, when the capacity of a human is addressed, the ten wholesome actions are taught as an "increase," while for the capacity of a deva, the five precepts are taught as a "decrease.
This continues in such a manner up to the bodhisattvas, with each stage being viewed in relation to the one preceding it.
It is likewise so.
When these sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they shall gradually enter the Path according to their individual capacities and abilities.

Having heard this Dharma, it accords with the causes for growth mentioned above; they will attain peace and security in the present life, which perfectly accords with growth, and [will continue] hereafter.
"Being born in a good realm" is a sign of increasing merit. Tiantai said: "The Buddha is like a great cloud that universally covers all things;

even the three miserable paths receive the nourishment and moisture [of his compassion]. As it is taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the Vaipulya sutras, it is also clarified that those in hell gain benefit—such as the extinguishing of fires and the cooling of boiling water—which constitutes peace and security in the present life, or rebirth in the heavens or among humans."
Thereafter, one is born in a good destination, practicing the Path among gods and humans; thus, through the Path, one experiences happiness.
If humans or gods hear the Dharma and uphold the precepts, their merit supports their bodies so that ghosts and dragons do not harm them; this is peace and security in the present life.
Whether a god is reborn as a god, a human as a human, or gods and humans are reborn interchangeably, this constitutes being born in a good destination. One is born...
They are able to awaken to and understand it; thus, they receive joy through the Way. When those of the Two Vehicles hear the Dharma, they attain *nirvāṇa* with remainder;
this is peace and security in the present life. Being born in a land of skillful means is a good rebirth for future lives; there they hear the sutras, and thus receive joy through the Way.
As for Bodhisattvas by birth, when they hear the Dharma preached by Vairocana Buddha, they attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). This is...
Peace and security in the present life, and birth in the Land of True Reward—this is subsequent rebirth in a favorable realm where one attains various forms of excellence;
thus, one experiences happiness through the Path and is freed from all obstacles. This constitutes peace and security in the present life.

Exercising one's capacity as far as it permits, one gradually enters the Path, whereby one subsequently experiences happiness through the Path in future lives. Miaole (妙樂) says: "In the sutras, it is simply referred to as 'a favorable realm.'"

Now, regarding those who take the evil paths: first, it is because the ten realms are subsumed within desire; second, it is because the three evil existences possess the potential for the seven good realms.
△ Second, citing the analogy and applying it to the case at hand.
"Just as that great cloud rains upon all [beings]... until they are fully moistened and each attains growth," this further serves as a metaphor to clarify the Dharma.
The phrase "just as that great cloud" corresponds to the preceding section:

"Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is also like this," up to the passage "pervading and covering the three thousandfold world system. "Raining upon all" corresponds to the preceding section.

Within the great assembly, he uttered these words: "All should come here for the sake of hearing the Dharma. This section corresponds to the preceding passage concerning the Tathāgata’s arrival at the time [of teaching].
"The grasses, trees, and forests" correspond to the preceding four lines regarding those who are diligent and those who are indolent.

"According to their respective natures, they fully receive the moistening [of the rain]" corresponds to the preceding five lines from "according to what each is capable of" up to "swiftly obtaining excellent benefit."
Each attains growth. This concludes the preceding section on how these various sentient beings gradually enter the Path, which comprised the analogy of differentiation.
△ Second, the analogy of non-differentiation, divided into three parts. First, the direct application of the analogy of non-differentiation.
The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is of a single characteristic and a single flavor, culminating ultimately in all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).

This follows from the preceding text: although in the past he taught the dharmas of the Three Vehicles—small, intermediate, and great—according to their respective capacities, this was not an impediment;
it is precisely this very dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor that the Tathāgata teaches today.

The *Yinzhi* (Record of the Sound-Knower) says: "The 'one mark' refers to the true reality-mark (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*) of the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa, which both sentient beings and Buddhas share in common.
This corresponds to what was previously stated in the discourse on the Dharma: that the Tathāgata perceives and knows the ultimate destination to which all phenomena converge."

In this combined analogy, although [the plants] grow from the same ground, it is because, within the great trichiliocosm, although mountains, rivers, streams, and valleys differ in form and color, they all share the same earth.

As for the "single flavor": although the Buddha’s teachings—the three vehicles and nine divisions—differ in their verbal expressions, they are of one and the same nectar-like flavor. This corresponds further to the preceding explanation of the Dharma. Regarding...

He thoroughly investigates and clearly elucidates all dharmas, revealing all-encompassing wisdom to all sentient beings. Within this teaching of analogies, it is like the moisture provided by a single rain:
although the grasses and trees of the great trichiliocosm differ in their bitterness, sourness, saltiness, or pungency, the cloud-rain they receive is of a single flavor.
This refers to the "inferior" [teaching], which employs the three gates of liberation as previously explained for the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

Section: Explaining the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*) of the present Supreme Vehicle (*agrayāna*). This means that what is now called the "single characteristic" taught by the Tathāgata is none other than the three characteristics previously mentioned—namely, liberation (*vimukti*) and so forth;
it is not a separate characteristic existing apart from those three previous characteristics.

These two vehicles contemplate emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), yet they do not [attain] the playful supernatural powers (*vikrīḍita-ṛddhi*) of the Bodhisattvas.
Because the mind finds no joy [in conditioned things], it now clarifies emptiness, signlessness, and so forth; this is precisely the exercise of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-vikrīḍita*).
This is truly because liberation is itself detachment, and detachment is itself quiescence (*śānti*); although there are three names, their meaning is in fact a single characteristic.

"Ultimately" (*atyanta*) below explains the attainment of a single flavor by means of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). "Ultimate" refers to the final stage, which is identical to the beginning.

This constitutes a correspondence. It means that initially, because sentient beings had limited capacities and were unable to bear the Great Dharma, the One Vehicle was taught according to their appearances and suitability as the three phases and three flavors.

Now that their capacities and conditions have increased and matured, and the Buddha’s time for ultimate *nirvāṇa* has arrived, he must surely act in accordance with his original intention by subsuming the provisional teachings of the preceding forty years.
The characteristics of the three marks and the three samādhis ultimately return to the single flavor of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Therefore, the "Expedient Means" chapter states: "After a long time, O World-Honored One, you must preach the truth. This "single mark" is precisely the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the One Vehicle;
this "single flavor" is the supreme flavor of *amṛta* (nectar); and the "mark of liberation" is unconditioned liberation (*anabhisaṃskāra-vimukti*), which is the mark of detachment.

This is the liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣa*). The cessation of signs is the liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*). △ Second, clarifying the intent of the distinctions, divided into five parts.
First, sentient beings do not know [this].
There are sentient beings who, upon hearing the Dharma of the Tathāgata, do not realize for themselves the merit they have attained.
This clarifies that sentient beings fail to penetrate the single, unified Dharma, and thus, according to their respective understandings, distinctions arise.
"Sentient beings" refers here to those who lack such knowledge; "Dharma" refers to the Dharma of the single voice. As for those who uphold and expound it, [it is] precisely...
This clarifies that they do not know. Tiantai said: "Holding [the precepts] and explaining them differ; their practice is likewise different.

Therefore, those of the human and celestial realms understand them as precepts and wholesome deeds, while those of the Three Vehicles understand them as the Truths, Conditions, and Liberations. This is the difference between holding and practicing them. As for the fact that one does not know one's own merit:
it is because these five types of people each have different understandings, resulting in differences in the magnitude of what they achieve, yet in the end, they do not know it as it truly is.
Originally, [the Dharma] was of a single characteristic and a single flavor, without distinction; this is precisely the One Reality.

Furthermore, not knowing that the seven stages of expedient means possess distinctions is itself the nature of the provisional. Yet, in the end, each clings to their own understanding, taking it to be the realization of reality.
Therefore, it is said that they do not self-awaken to this knowledge. △ Second, the Tathāgata alone knows.
Why is this? Because only the Tathāgata knows the seeds, characteristics, and essential nature of these sentient beings.
This section investigates and explains the meaning of sentient beings being unaware while the Tathāgata alone knows. The investigation asks:
"If sentient beings are able to practice according to the teaching, why do they not personally realize the merits they have attained? The explanation states:
Although it is said that one attains merit, in reality, one has not yet attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Only the Tathāgata, who possesses all-knowledge (*sarvajña*), is able to know the seeds, characteristics, and essential natures (*svabhāva*) of these sentient beings. "Sentient beings" refers here to the beings of the three vehicles and five natures.
"Seeds" refers to their causal potential; collectively, there is only the single Buddha-seed, while individually, there are distinctions such as wholesome, unwholesome, and sharp.
"Dullness of wisdom" refers to the differences in the depth of ignorance. "Phenomena" (xiàng) refers to the essential nature (tǐxiàng).
Generally speaking, all sentient beings inherently possess one true mark; specifically, however, the three vehicles and five natures each have their own distinctions of sharp and dull faculties.
"Body" (*ti*) refers to the essence of nature (*xingti*). In its general sense, it is the essence of the true mark of *tathatā* (suchness) shared by all;

in its specific sense, it refers to the physical forms and appearances—whether beautiful or ugly—that constitute the retributive bodies of the three vehicles and five natures. "Nature" (*xing*) refers to the emotional-nature (*qingxing*).

In its general sense, it is the nature of universal enlightenment shared by all; in its specific sense, it refers to the distinctions between good and evil possessed by each of the three vehicles and five vehicles.
These are the various natures. This is known and seen by the Tathāgata exactly as it is. Since it is said that he "knows," he must necessarily also possess vision.
This refers to the Tathāgata’s actual knowledge and vision of the past events of all sentient beings.
"What do they contemplate, what do they reflect upon, and what do they cultivate?

This clarifies that the Tathāgata not only knows the various characteristics and essential natures of all sentient beings, but also knows the dharmas that all sentient beings contemplate, reflect upon, and cultivate, understanding them all without exception. Contemplation and reflection.

Regarding "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*): the initial movement [of the mind] is called mindfulness (*smṛti*); its continuity is called reflection (*manasikāra*); and its active engagement is called cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Regarding "what matters":

these are the various matters such as the truths, objects of focus, and the perfections (*pāramitā*) of the five vehicles, both small and great. For example, sentient beings of inferior faculties cultivate the matters of humans and devas through mindfulness, reflection, and cultivation;

those of middling faculties cultivate the matters of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas through mindfulness, reflection, and cultivation; and those of superior faculties cultivate... [the matters of the Great Vehicle].
Regarding the affairs of a bodhisattva, because they vary according to their magnitude and are not fixed, one asks: "What are these affairs? How does one recollect them?
How does one contemplate them? How does one cultivate them?"—extending to: "By what dharma does one contemplate? By what dharma does one cultivate?"
The Tathāgata further knows that for all sentient beings, there are various causes and conditions by which their mindfulness, reflection, and cultivation differ from one another.

The two characters "how" (*yǒu hé*) are terms used for precise determination; they mean, for instance, that when one contemplates the matters of the celestial and human vehicles, there is the cause and condition of meritorious retribution.
When one contemplates the matters of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), there is the cause and condition of fearing suffering and seeking happiness.
One should contemplate the affairs of a Bodhisattva; therein lie the causes and conditions for both self-benefit and the benefit of others.
By means of these two characters, the Tathāgata clearly knows which dharmas he should cause these sentient beings to contemplate, to reflect upon, and to cultivate.
This is precisely the skillful means of "prescribing medicine according to the illness. What was previously contemplated, and as it is said:
Regarding the phrases such as "what mindfulness" and so forth: this refers to the Tathāgata’s contemplative knowledge that sentient beings possess such capacities (*indriya*).

These phrases concerning the mindfulness of specific dharmas constitute the observation of capacity and the subsequent teaching. This is precisely the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision of all sentient beings' present circumstances exactly as they are.
By what dharma does one obtain what dharma?

By what dharma serves as the cause, and what dharma is obtained as the fruit? For example, taking the goodness of ethical discipline (*śīla*) as the cause results in obtaining the fruits of human or celestial rebirth.
Taking the conditions of the Truths (*satya-pratyaya*) as the cause results in obtaining the fruits of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha. [Likewise,] by means of the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*)...

This serves as the cause, which immediately brings about the attainment of the fruit of a bodhisattva. This is precisely the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision of all future events concerning sentient beings.
Sentient beings abide in various stages, yet only the Tathāgata perceives them truly, clearly, and without obstruction.
The seven stages of expedient means abide in seven positions; therefore, they are called "various grounds.
This constitutes their differentiation. Tiantai says: The Tathāgata perceives them as they truly are with his Buddha-eye.

Just as when various rivers flow into the sea, they lose their original flavors and there is no longer any distinction, so too does he speak according to the intentions of others, expounding through the skillful means of wisdom. Thus...

The Tathāgata is able to know distinctions; yet, as for the Dharma he teaches, it all reaches the stage of omniscience, whereby the Tathāgata is also able to know non-distinction. △ Third, the illustration and its application.
Just as those flowers, trees, forests, and various medicinal herbs do not themselves know their superior, middling, or inferior natures—this is the illustration.
This concludes the preceding section on the passage beginning with "If there are sentient beings who hear the Dharma of the Tathāgata," etc.

It should be understood that this refers to sentient beings of the five vehicles who, while dwelling in their respective stages, each remain unaware that they have received the merit of the Tathāgata’s One Vehicle.
It is just as various plants and trees do not each know for themselves that they are being moistened by the single flavor of the clouds and rain from heaven.
△ Fourth, restating the preceding and concluding the explanation:
The Tathāgata knows this to be a dharma of one characteristic and one flavor (up to) the characteristic of eternal quiescence, which ultimately returns to emptiness.
This is the method of citation. It refers back to the preceding passage: "Only the Tathāgata knows the seeds, characteristics, essence, and nature of these sentient beings.

To understand this: although sentient beings—like various grasses and trees—are each unaware of the merits they have attained according to their superior, middling, or inferior natures, the Buddha knows that from the very beginning there is no such distinction of superior, middling, or inferior; it is simply direct [realization].
This is the Dharma of the single vehicle’s true reality, the ambrosia of a single flavor.
That which was previously called "inferior" when the one characteristic was explained by means of the three characteristics clarifies the meritorious virtue of the fruit of bodhi;

therefore, it is spoken of in terms of ultimate *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect omniscience), because *sarvākārajñatā* is itself bodhi. This [present section], in turn, explains the one characteristic by means of the three characteristics to clarify *nirvāṇa*.

To "know the outflow-free" means to know the dharma of realizing suffering and abandoning its origin (*samudaya*). This distinguishes them from gods and humans, including Śakra and Brahmā, whom they surpass.

"Knowing" refers to that which can attain *nirvāṇa*—that which neither devas, humans, Śakra, nor Brahmā can attain; this is *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. Within this lies the intent to cultivate the path with a longing for cessation (*nirodha*).
