The Prophecy for Humans. This is divided into two parts. First, the request for prophecy by three individuals. This is divided into four sections. First, the formal request.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, [and others]... (up to) they then spoke these verses in unison.
"The Great Hero, the World-Honored One, the Dharma King of all Śākyas" (up to) "seeing [them] and bestowing upon them the prediction.
This clarifies that these three persons were terrified because they did not receive a prediction.

Indeed, as the four individuals heard and understood together, they were all equally likened to impoverished sons. Thus, Kāśyapa described it, saying: "We occupy the foremost rank among the Saṃgha; our years..."
They were all aged and decrepit. As for the phrase "all [of them] together," it refers to these four people.
Now, seeing Kāśyapa receive the prediction of supreme enlightenment before the assembly of devas and humans, the other three were all struck with awe and trembling; they spoke a verse in unison.
Having reached such a state, their own conviction was already keen, and their longing for realization became even more intense than before.
This means that when body and mind are weary and one contemplates the three samādhis, the single word "contemplation" (guan) is not merely a request for oneself;
it also carries the sense of a representative petition, such as that made by Śāriputra. As for the "Great Hero and Mighty One":
"Great" means that the Tathāgata’s wisdom and majestic spiritual power surpass all others.

"Valiant" means possessing great intellectual power capable of shattering the various realms of existence (*bhava*) of all sentient beings, and possessing great majestic power capable of uplifting those in the nine realms to return together to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Possessing such greatness and such great strength, he is the Dharma King among all Śākyas. This is...
He praises the Buddha’s wisdom and virtue; below this, he requests a prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*). He says:

"Out of compassion for us, we pray that before the assembly of devas and humans, you will grant us your wondrous voice, proclaim our names, and bestow upon us a prophecy, so that our fear and trepidation may be instantly stilled. This too is a prayer.
If the Tathāgata, out of pity for my sincere heart today in requesting a prophecy, were to grant me one, it would be even more so.
This is the prayer. [The characters] sǒng (pronounced as sǒng) and lì (pronounced as lì). △ Second, the request by means of a simile:
"It is like sprinkling nectar to remove heat and attain coolness... (until) only then does one dare to eat."

This metaphor illustrates that each of us feels uneasy at the sight of one another. Now, seeing Śāriputra and Kāśyapa, both of whom have already received their predictions, we feel no more than a slight feverish distress here.
If we were also granted our predictions, it would be exactly like being sprinkled with nectar;
our feverish distress would be removed, and we would attain cool clarity. How much more so for those who have heard these words and witnessed these events!
This is clearly trustworthy. All that we śrāvakas have previously realized was not ultimately real; hereafter, we shall certainly become Buddhas.
Do we not, therefore, place our full trust in this? Yet, having not personally received a prophecy from your own lips, we cannot help but harbor a sense of longing like that of hunger and thirst.
It is just as if someone had come from a land of famine and, fortunately, encountered a great [feast].
At a royal banquet, although rare delicacies fill the tables and precious foods are laid out in rows, one dares not eat immediately unless the King has called them by name.
Only after receiving an imperial decree may they then feel at ease to accept the rewards.
(The character *sǎ* is pronounced as *jiǔ*, meaning "wine"). △ Third, the combined analogy.
"We, too, are likewise; whenever we contemplate the faults of the Hīnayāna [until] we finally attain joyful peace and security.
This passage clearly articulates the reason for his lack of inner tranquility. "To contemplate" means that he had no intention of turning toward the Mahāyāna.

This is precisely the fault of the Hīnayāna. That is to say, when we were settled in the Hīnayāna, we constantly contemplated the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed and profound wisdom, wondering how we might ever come to attain it.

Now, although we have heard the Buddha declare that we shall become Buddhas, we do not yet personally know the reason why we shall achieve Buddhahood; thus, our minds cannot help but feel [uncertainty].
I harbor anxiety and fear; if the Tathāgata would clearly grant us a prediction [of our future enlightenment], this mind would finally find relief and be free from worry.
△ Fourth, the conclusion of the request:

O Great Hero, O Fierce World-Honored One, you who constantly desire to bring peace to the world, we pray that you grant us a prediction, just as one who suffers from hunger must be taught what to eat.
This was a firm request, certain that they would receive a prophecy. The Tathāgata manifested his appearance in the human realm like the rising of a great cloud;
he originally came into the world desiring to bring peace and security to all the world.
Now we ourselves are in a state of insecurity—how could the Tathāgata not speak clearly so as to let us be like those who obtain food when hungry? Thus spoke the three men.

The request for the prediction has been completed. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s bestowing of the prediction, divided into three parts. First, the bestowing of the prediction upon Subhūti, further divided into two.
First, the prose section, divided into five. First, the causal basis of the practice.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the great disciples [from the preceding passage] up to those who constantly practiced the pure conduct and were fully endowed with the path of a bodhisattva, bestowed upon each of them a prediction of enlightenment in response to their request. Within that request, it was said: "If you would know my profound intention."
This phrase, "knowing the thoughts in the minds of the great disciples," refers to the two characters "deep mind" (shenxin) and these two characters "what is being thought" (suonian).
It does not merely mean that [the Buddha] seeks to bestow predictions of enlightenment upon himself; rather, he acts as the petitioner on behalf of the twelve hundred people.
Thus, when the disciples think in this way and the World-Honored One records it in this way, it is a matter of the mind sealing the mind.
This is the time of receiving the true prediction (vyākaraṇa) of the mind. One constantly cultivates the pure conduct (brahmacarya) and fulfills the path of a bodhisattva;
this constitutes the extensive practice of the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) and myriad practices, reaching the time when merit and wisdom are perfected. △ Second, attaining the fruit.
In his final existence, he attained Buddhahood, becoming the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
This World-Honored One personally realized [this truth], Subhūti. As for the name "Fruit" (the result), it is spoken in relation to the "Cause.
While Subhūti was still in his mother’s womb, he already understood emptiness and quiescence; thus, when he became an Arhat, he was named Kūṭadanta (Empty-Womb-born). This was due to the cause.
The middle [section] concerns self-benefit. That is to say, when practicing at this critical juncture, one must ensure that not even a speck of dust remains established.
If there were even a single dharma that was not empty, one could not realize unsurpassed *bodhi*. Now, although the fruit is designated by names and marks, one must prioritize benefiting others.
When manifesting these manifold and great functions, one must necessarily display all manner of marks within the realm of formlessness.

At the outset, he did not fail in his single act of responding to the destiny of the age. Thus, while within the cause what is most esteemed is the empty void (*śūnyatā*), within the fruit what is most honored is wondrous existence (*prabhāsvara*). △ Third, the kalpa and the land.
The kalpa is named Possessing Jewels (Yǒubǎo), and the land is named Jewel-Born (Bǎoshēng). [This continues] up to incalculable thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas.
This is based on their primary names. Subhūti is also named Śobhita; therefore, he receives the name of the kalpa, "Possessing Jewels.
He is also named Sudarśana; therefore, he receives the name of the land, "Jewel-Born. That realm is level and even, extending to the limit of...
Regarding those who have "convenience and so forth": because they realize all things are empty and quiescent, they do not establish even a single speck of dust.

As for the fact that "the people all obtain residence in jeweled terraces and dwell in wondrous pavilions," it is because sentient beings, by their own nature, partially attain the samādhi of emptiness.

This is the nature of the cause of non-forgetfulness. That both Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas are boundless and innumerable is because the wondrous nature of true emptiness gathers in all things without exception. △ Fourth, the lifespan.
The Buddha’s lifespan was twelve small kalpas.
Having already dwelt in the samādhi of emptiness, he attained liberation from the internal sense-faculties and liberation from external objects;
thus, not being disturbed by the faculties or their objects, he was able to maintain a lifespan of twelve small kalpas. △ Five: The True and Semblance [Dharmas].
The True Dharma shall remain in the world for twenty minor kalpas, delivering and liberating immeasurable bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas.

This clarifies that the Buddha preached the Dharma to deliver sentient beings. That Buddha constantly dwells in the emptiness of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) and teaches the truth of the ultimate meaning;
it is for this reason that he delivers and liberates the various bodhisattvas. Furthermore, the mention of "and the assembly of śrāvakas" indicates...
The Tathāgata Renown (Nāman) likewise taught the Dharma of the Three Vehicles through skillful means. Thus, the "Chapter on Skillful Means" states:
"Future Buddhas will also, by means of various causes, conditions, parables, and expressions, expound upon all dharmas," and so forth.
Furthermore, how could there be any Buddhas outside of these? II. The Verse Recitation, divided into six parts: 1. The Exhortation to Listen.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"O assembly of bhikṣus, I now address you all: you should all listen with a single mind to what I shall say."
This verse serves as an admonition to listen, praying that one may properly receive and uphold [the teaching].

One who is able to receive and uphold it possesses the true cause for attaining Buddhahood in the future. Otherwise, what is the meaning of "listening with a single mind"? △ Second, the verse on causal practice.
My great disciple Subhūti (up to) follows the conduct of the Buddha and gradually perfects the Great Way (*mahāyāna*).
To follow the conduct of the Buddha is to not deviate from the Buddha at all. The "Great Way" refers to the ocean of fruition wherein merit and wisdom are perfected.
"Gradually perfecting" means that one correctly perceives how this has come about through serving many Buddhas over the course of many kalpas.
...Thus. △ Third, the verse on attaining the fruit:
"In his final body, he attains the thirty-two marks, upright and exquisite like a mountain of jewels.
This verse clarifies the primary retribution (vipāka). Since there is no mention of the thirty-two marks in the preceding or following sections, this is provided here for mutual clarification.
These are mutual omissions. As for the "Jewel Mountain," it carries the meaning of radiance; since all Buddha-bodies are of the color of purple-gold light, this serves as a metaphor for them.
△ Fourth, the verse on the purity of the land.
That Buddha-land is foremost in its majestic purity... (up to) they all join their palms together to listen to and receive the Buddha’s words.

This verse describes the land as the *niśraya-pratigraha* (the supported environment). Compared to the prose (*gadya*), it further clarifies the virtues of the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, as well as the Buddha’s manifestation of supernatural powers and transformations, and the matter of humans and devas receiving the Dharma with a sincere mind. [The eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*)...]

These are the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because one turns one's back on these pure pleasures of the five desires and abandons all attached minds, they are called 'liberations' (*vimokṣa*).
Tiantai says: "If one gives rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and exhausts the fetters and karma of the three realms, this is termed 'liberation.
Regarding the eight liberations: first, having internal perception of form, one perceives external forms. [Internal perception of form...]

Regarding "signs" (*nimitta*): it refers to not destroying internal form and not extinguishing the signs of internal form. This is the stage of the first liberation (*prathama vimokṣa*), which resides in the first dhyāna;

for it is able to relinquish all attachments to oneself, others, and the lower stages. Second, "having no internal signs of form, one perceives external forms. Regarding "having no internal signs of form":

this refers to destroying internal form and extinguishing the signs of internal form. Regarding "perceiving external forms": [it refers to perceiving external forms while being free from internal signs].

One does not destroy external forms, nor does one extinguish the marks of external forms. Because the practitioner enters the third dhyāna, the state of meditative concentration gradually deepens and internal forms have already ceased;
however, as the fetters and latent tendencies of the desire realm are difficult to sever, one continues to contemplate the marks of external impurity.
Regarding the "third pure liberation realized through the body": the practitioner eliminates the marks of external impurity and dwells only in the concentration.
Within this state, one cultivates the eightfold radiant light, which is pure and brilliant like the color of exquisite jewels; therefore, it is called "purity.
Because one experiences the sublime bliss pervading the entire body within the third dhyāna with a mind free from craving and attachment, it is said that "the body is realized."

4. The liberation of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-vimokṣa*): If one eliminates the form (*rūpa*) of the fundamental fourth dhyāna, one enters meditative absorption by focusing the single mind on infinite space, without undergoing attachment.

5. The liberation of the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-vimokṣa*): If one relinquishes space, one enters meditative absorption by focusing the single mind on consciousness, without undergoing attachment.
6. The liberation of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-vimokṣa*): If one relinquishes consciousness...

With single-minded focus, one takes the sphere of nothingness as an object and enters meditative absorption, yet remains free from attachment. Seventh is the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception:

having relinquished the sphere of nothingness, one takes the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as an object with single-minded focus and enters meditative absorption, yet remains free from attachment.
Eighth is the liberation of the cessation of sensation and perception: one turns away from and ceases all mental states of sensation and perception.
The mental factors: this is the liberation through the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-vimokṣa*). △ Fifth, the verse on the lifespan:
that Buddha’s lifespan shall be twelve small kalpas.
△ Sixth, the verse on the True and Semblance Dharma periods.
The True Dharma shall remain in the world for twenty minor kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain for twenty minor kalpas.

All that precedes this consists of verses summarizing the prose sections. Regarding matters therein—such as the serving of Buddhas, the erection of stupas, up to the transmission of the Dharma by the original Buddha’s disciples, and the distribution of relics—the details are already provided throughout the preceding and following sections; thus, they will not be elaborated upon here.

At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the assembly of bhikṣus... [until] "fully possessing the bodhisattva path."
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: Kātyāyana was skilled in debate. There was a non-Buddhist who held the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), asserting that there is no future world.
Kātyāyana asked him: "Are the sun and moon of today this world, or another world? If there truly were no other world, there would certainly be no tomorrow.
He further said: "I observe that when people die, they do not return; it seems as though there is no other world."
Shi Yan said: "It is like a criminal who has been imprisoned; how could he possibly return? Furthermore, those born in the heavens are free from all constraints and attachments;
why then do we not see anyone returning? Yan said: "It is like a person who has fallen into a latrine;
once they have emerged, would they willingly enter it again? Moreover, one day in heaven is equivalent to a hundred years in the human realm. [He continued: "As for those three..."

On the fifth day, he had not yet had the leisure to plan his return. He further remarked, "If there were those who do return, what would become of you? Moreover, it is said that when sinners are boiled in cauldrons, their tops are covered with a lid; one observes them and sees no spirit emerge. Therefore, we know there is no other world. Yan replied: [The remainder of the text follows: "Your argument is not so. It is like a person who has been struck by a poisoned arrow. If they do not receive medical treatment, they will surely die. Yet, after some time, they regain their senses and feel as if they have been reborn. This is because the poison has already spread throughout their body; it is simply that the pain was not yet manifest. If the poison had not spread, the pain would not arise even if the wound were cut open. "When you sleep during the day, or when you dream of traveling far away, does a spirit emerge from you that others can see?
Yan replied, "I have flayed dead people from their feet to their heads, dissecting their bones and flesh in minute detail, yet I could find no spirit. Therefore, I know there is no other world.
Yan said, "Fire is produced from wood; if one were to dissect the wood into its finest parts, where would the fire remain? Yan further said, "I..."
When weighing a dead person, they were found heavier than when alive. If the spirit had departed, the person should have been lighter; therefore, one knows that there is no other world.
Yan said: "It is like fire and iron: while the fire is present, the iron is light; once the fire has subsided, it becomes heavy again.
When a person dies and the spirit departs, their heaviness is likewise. He further said: "I have seen people who, upon death, searched for their spirits in every direction, yet could not find them."
"Therefore, we know that there is no future life. Yan said: "It is like a person blowing a horn; the sound comes from the horn.

If one were to search back for the sound, could one ever find it? He further said: "Though you employ all manner of arguments to refute me, I shall certainly not abandon the characteristics to which I am attached.
Yan said: "It is like a person seeing hemp; they take its substance. Having obtained the hemp, they take the bark; having obtained the bark, they take [the fibers]."
"Sinews [are inferior]; one obtains sinews and takes cloth. One obtains cloth and takes silver. One obtains silver and takes gold.
To discard the inferior and take the superior is the common sentiment of humanity. Why do you persist so stubbornly? Furthermore, you say:
'As for what I maintain, that person is exceedingly profound; how could I alone hold such a view? Yan replied: 'It is like two merchants traveling on a road who encounter a ghost. The ghost said...'"
A human form appeared and said to the merchants, "The road ahead has abundant grain and sufficient fodder; why do you carry these?
One merchant discarded everything he was carrying, and both man and ox became hungry. The ghost took advantage of this situation. Then another merchant said, "If we obtain new supplies..."
"You may discard the old items; thus, both the people and the oxen will not suffer from hunger, while the ghosts will receive no food.
The people spoke falsely, as the ghosts had deceived them: "If you do not accept my words, you will surely be devoured by ghosts. Now that you have obtained these new ones..."
"Why do you not discard what is old? The man’s arguments could not prevail, so he spoke with anger and abuse, saying: "Ignorant fool! Why do you trouble yourself to urge me? Yan replied:
"It is like a man who raises fish and picks up various scraps of filth by the roadside, carrying them upon his head.
When he encounters a heavy rain on the road, the liquid filth soils his body. A bystander urges him to discard it, but he instead blames the other, saying: 'You, you fool... [The text ends here.]
There is no difference between the two. Consequently, the non-Buddhists were humbled by his eloquence; thus, at the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, he was praised as being foremost in debate.
Regarding Kātyāyana’s offerings to the Buddha and the construction of stūpas during his causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*), the textual meaning is quite clear.

However, while it is stated earlier that he made offerings to eight thousand *koṭi* of Buddhas, it is later stated that he made offerings to twenty-two thousand *koṭi* of Buddhas. This seems to exclude the two categories of self and dharmas.
The merit of this practice lies in the principle of progressing from the shallow to the profound. *Yojana* is translated here as "measured limit" (*liàngxiàn*).
There are three different types: the large is eighty *li*, the medium is sixty *li*, and the small is forty *li*. △ Second, attaining the fruit.
He shall attain Buddhahood with the name Jambūnada-prabhāsa (Golden Light of the Jambu-river), [up to] Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.

This clarifies the primary retribution (*vipāka*). Because he diligently swept the grounds of the Buddhas during his causal stage, completely removing all dust and impurities, he was moved to inspire eloquence upon reaching the stage of Arhatship.
As for why his sharpness of speech is like an arrow and his fluent eloquence is like a river, it is because...

The mind-ground is pure and free from defilement. That he now experiences the fruit of being named Jambūnada-prabhāsa (Golden Light of Jambū) is because his bodily radiance resembles the color of Jambūnada gold;
thus we know that the merit of removing dust and eliminating defilement will be of great benefit for the future.
△ Third, the purity of the land.
That land is level and even, with crystal for its ground (extending until) immeasurable billions of adornments embellish that country.
This clarifies the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment as retribution). Generally, because people do not cultivate wholesome dharmas, the evil realms increase while humans and devas diminish.
Now, it is stated that there are no four evil realms; thus one knows that the people of that country all practice the teachings of Jambudvīpa.

They come to teach and transform others, deeply cultivating the goodness of the precepts; thus, devas and humans flourish, and it is said that the śrāvakas are numerous and the bodhisattvas are immeasurable.
One sees even more clearly that their adornment with wholesome dharmas is inconceivable. △ Fourth, [the section on] lifespan.
The Buddha’s lifespan is twelve minor kalpas.

The commentary states: Regarding the intent of this chapter’s introduction, since the five individuals previously mentioned have all received their predictions, [the Buddha] now intends to bestow predictions upon the twelve hundred people as well.

The "White Ox. The purport of this chapter lies in the transformation city and the treasure place. One enters the transformation city from the burning house and, riding the white ox, returns to the treasure place;

Question: This chapter contains extensive text on causes and conditions (*nidāna*), while the analogies (*dṛṣṭānta*) are but a small portion.

Although the causes and conditions are long-standing, they all pertain to the meaning of "forming a karmic connection" (kṣetra-bandha) and none are ultimate.

The reason for establishing the name "illusory city" (nirmāṇa-pura) is precisely to complete and restore what were previously called those causes and conditions. Furthermore, the title at the beginning of this sutra uses the metaphor of the lotus flower.

This is the Dharma; therefore, this chapter is also established by means of a parable. Although it does not speak of the "Jeweled Place," it specifically refers to the "Transformation City" (the illusory city) because one truly desires people to realize the Real through the Provisional, and to clarify the True by means of the False. Once one knows that the city is a transformation, one will know that the Jeweled Place must be real.
This is precisely the great purport of this sutra for opening up the provisional and revealing the real. It should be understood as follows:

This is the knowledge. △ Third, explaining the causes and conditions for those of inferior faculties. This is divided into two parts. First, the main section of this chapter correctly explains the causes and conditions.

The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: “...that Buddha passed into parinirvāṇa an exceedingly long time ago.
This Tathāgata wishes to bestow a prediction (vyākaraṇa) upon those who have not yet received one, so that they may know this prediction is not false.

"Complete. From "The Buddha told [the assembly]" below, he marks the beginning of the remote past, specifically to clarify the vast number of kalpas.
From "At that time" below, he cites the Buddha Jñānābhibhū as the father-teacher of Śākyamuni; this demonstrates that without Jñānābhibhū, Śākyamuni could not have been brought into being.
As for the name of the Buddha, Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū: "Great" (*mahā*) encompasses all phenomena, signifying the great perfection of the circle.
The ten realms are called "pervasive" (*tong*). That which can shatter all delusions is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*). That which transcends all things is called "supreme" (*śreṣṭha*).

Furthermore, "great" refers to the principle of suchness (*tathatā*), while "pervasive" refers to the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*). Because the wisdom and the principle are perfectly interfused, it is called "supreme wisdom.
Thus, the ten titles that follow are all nothing other than what is possessed by this supreme wisdom. As for the name of the land being "Good City," it is because of this wisdom.

The "Victorious" (Jiǎngshèng) is the ultimate; it dwells in a wondrous and excellent reliance. This may be called the land of tranquil light (*sukhāvatī*), wherein reliance and the ultimate are one, and essence and function are identical.

The eon is named "Great Characteristics" (*mahālakṣaṇa*); these are the infinite characteristics of the "ten realms and thousand suchnesses," which are also what the Victorious Wisdom inherently possesses.
Apart from this Victorious Wisdom, how could there be any other so-called "Exquisite City"?
"How magnificent is the adornment of these great marks! Following the parinirvāṇa of that Buddha, this is spoken in reference to the *nirvāṇa* of his supreme wisdom;
thus, an inconceivable analogy is established. For this reason, it is first designated as 'extremely great' and 'long distant. The *Yaojie* (Essential Explanation) states:
'Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū' is the very essence of awakening that is the source of all sentient beings. The essence of awakening within sentient beings has always been like this."

It is only because one is deluded within form and mind that they are small rather than great; because one is confined and stagnant within the shell of ignorance that they are obstructed rather than penetrating;
and because one lies hidden in the meanness of false consciousness that they are inferior rather than victorious.

If one can comprehend this delusion and stagnation of form and mind and shatter the confining shell of ignorance, then superior wisdom will manifest before one, and one will be no different from a Buddha.
It is distinct. The statement that it spans immeasurable and inconceivable kalpas clarifies that the essence of this wisdom has no beginning;
it is not something that can be reached by the calculations of sentient beings or the dust of phenomena. △ Second, the metaphor clarifying its long duration.
For example, [from] the trichiliocosm [up to] hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
This following analogy clarifies that the parinirvāṇa of that Buddha was exceedingly long ago; it employs what is not an analogy as an analogy.

Within this, there are three successive comparisons, all of which are inconceivable. First, if one were to take the element of earth as ink and make dots like motes of dust, the number of ink-drops would be immeasurable.

The number of these lands is immeasurable. Suppose one were to take all the lands—both those with sentient beings and those without—and reduce them entirely to atoms, with each atom representing one kalpa;

As for the element of earth, it refers to the earth of the great trichiliocosm, which is capable of producing and sustaining both sentient and insentient things.
It is a sentient object; therefore, it is called the "earth element. The phrase "suppose that" is a term used for illustration.
Suppose there were a person who took the earth of a great trichiliocosm and ground it into a single pool of ink.

What do you think? Why did he ask this? It was because he wished for people to know that the number of lands thus pointed out is immeasurable and boundless, beyond what can be known by mathematicians or their disciples. This refers to the lands passed over by that person below.
Furthermore, take the countries already marked and the nine hundred and ninety-nine unmarked countries;
likewise, by this successive process, exhaust them all. Grind both the marked and unmarked countries into fine dust, and then use a single grain of dust to represent one *kalpa*.
Since the parinirvāṇa of that Buddha Jñānavijaya, more time has passed than the number of these grains of dust.

The measure [of time] spans boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; thus, one knows that the number of kalpas is utterly inconceivable, and that such a long duration has passed.
The Essential Explanation (*Yāojiàn*) states: "The Victorious Wisdom is neither ancient nor modern; it has never entered parinirvāṇa."
As for the statement that "that Buddha entered parinirvāṇa such a long time ago," this is merely said in reference to the deluded perceptions of those with inferior faculties.
If we speak of us ordinary people, as to how long it has been since we lost our wisdom and have been submerged in the cycle of delusion, we do not know if it has passed through several kalpas;
truly, it cannot be reckoned by the measure of dust or ink. △ Third, seeing the past as the present.
By means of the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, I observe that distant past as if it were today.

Thus, those who rely solely on outward traces and cling to appearances will be startled, doubtful, and disbelieve upon hearing this. Therefore—
The World-Honored One further said: "By the power of my Buddha-eye and mind, I see and know that although his parinirvāṇa was so long ago, it is just as if it were today.
One must understand that the ten periods of past and present do not depart from the present moment.
Thus, the incalculable *kalpas* of motes of dust mentioned above and this present thought of mine are fundamentally without interior or exterior. It may also be said:
To see the realms of infinite lands without being separated by even a single hair-tip—this very non-separation of self and other is *tathatā-jñāna* (suchness-wisdom).

That it is not separated from the past or present is *tathatā-artha* (suchness-principle). By inferring these two kinds of vast realms, one reveals in their entirety the measure of the Great Universal Wisdom-Victory (*Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū*).
The *Direct Pointing* says: "In the 'Expedient Means' chapter, it is said that the Buddha once drew near to..."

This constitutes a single thought-moment throughout past and present. Thus, the verse says: "The Buddha’s wisdom is pure and subtle, untainted and..."

they are not partitioned. The Essential Explanation says: "Because sentient beings' cognitions and views are mired in delusion and involve false conceptualization, their wisdom is separated [from the truth] by kalpas as numerous as motes of dust."

If the dimensions of past and present, or self and other, were not extinguished, there would be obstruction; how, then, could there be the wondrous realization that the past is like the present?

it is just like this. Section Twenty: The Invitation by the Brahmās of the Ten Directions. This is divided into two parts. Part One: The Nine Directions. This is divided into four sections. First, the Eastern Direction.
Divided into seven parts. First, witnessing the auspicious omen of light.
At that time, five hundred myriads of koṭis [of suns] in the eastern direction (up to) the radiance shining forth was twice as bright as the usual light.

This describes the sign of the movement of the auspicious omen of the light illuminating the ten directions of the Brahma heavens when the Buddha Jñāna first attained perfect enlightenment. Because...
When the Buddha’s light of middle-way wisdom shone forth once, the palaces were suddenly illuminated with a brilliance twice that of their usual radiance.
Yet, the Brahma Heaven already does not rely on the light of the sun and moon; the various devas possess their own bodily radiance, and both their palaces and gardens are naturally luminous.
Now, because the Buddha’s light surpassed theirs by ten million times, each was struck with wonder, doubt, and astonishment.
Question. △ Second, the thought of alarm and doubt:
Each of the Brahmā devas had this thought (up to): "By what causes and conditions does this sign appear?
△ Third, their mutual questioning.
At that time, the Brahma Kings (up to) spoke these verses for the assembly of Brahmas:
"The radiance of our palaces has never existed before; it now shines everywhere throughout the ten directions."
Thus, each of these Brahmās perceived the radiance differently, and doubts arose among them as they deliberated together in one place:
"What, ultimately, is the cause and condition for this light? Among the Brahmās was one named Sarvatra-trāyī (Savior of All).
This clearly reveals that it was manifested for the Bodhisattvas on the stages (bhūmi) as a sign of their arrival. Each of the various devas harbored doubts;
before they had even spoken to discuss the matter, only the Heavenly King Sarvaśūra raised his voice and addressed the assembly, saying:
"Could it be that a Great Virtuous Deva has been reborn here? Or could it be that a Buddha has appeared in the world, resulting in this occurrence?"
"Does the Great Light shine everywhere? Brahmā cultivates meditative concentration and concurrently practices the four immeasurable minds;
therefore, he is called the "Virtuous Deity. This lord of devas, wishing to govern all the heavens, sought the light and beheld the Buddha, who is the guide and teacher among all the devas.
That is to say, for those who are to be delivered through a celestial body, he manifests a celestial body to preach the Dharma.
If the Tathāgata did not emit this light, by what cause would the devas behold the Buddha? It is precisely because of the emission of this light that his compassionate salvation is inexhaustible.
Although the Buddha may enter meditative absorption for ten kalpas through his wisdom, wherever this light shines, all humans and devas therein give rise to infinite, supreme resolve.
In such cases, how could it be said that the Tathāgata has ever failed to preach the Dharma? At this place...
The subtlety lies in the doubts of the Brahmā deities. If they did not doubt, how could there have been the act of seeking the light?

If they had not sought the light, how could there have been the opportunity to see the Buddha? If they had not seen the Buddha, how could they have attained the function of the great, wondrous, and sublime wisdom?
△ Fourth, seeking the radiance.
At that time, from five million billion lands (up to) the sixteen princes requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma—
this describes the arrival of five million billion Brahma kings from the eastern quarter.

That they were accompanied by their palaces is because the Brahma heavens possess such profound and deep-rooted merit that the palaces manifest and follow them at will, just as in the world, where even secular kings may possess inexhaustible [treasures].
How much more so for the Heavenly King! They filled their robes with flowers to prepare for making offerings.
In the world, gold and jewels are considered precious; in the celestial palaces, flowers are considered precious. Therefore, all offerings presented consist of celestial flowers.
Those who traveled together toward the West were following the direction of the light, just as people from the ten directions each follow where their respective lights lead them.
As for this method: follow it directly and straight ahead, and you will surely behold the Buddha. This also demonstrates that this light is all-pervasive and reaches everywhere.
To see the Buddha seated upon his throne is to arrive at him personally and see him face-to-face; it is not a matter of knowing or hearing of him through mere resemblance.
Not only do you see the Buddha, but you also see the assembly who protect and request the Dharma, and you shall likewise hear them.
He turned the Wheel of Dharma. By virtue of this illumination, he immediately enabled the Brahmā to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
how swift and how simple it was! △ Fifth, the offering of worship.
Immediately, the Brahma Kings prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet (until: with one mind and in unison, they praised him in verse, saying:
"The World-Honored One is most rare and difficult to encounter (until: we only pray that you will compassionately accept [our offerings]."
When the Brahmā devas and others have personally beheld the Tathāgata, their offerings are without exception characterized by profound sincerity.
Prostrating with their heads at his feet is the ultimate reverence of the body; chanting verses in unison is the ultimate reverence of the mouth;
scattering flowers and honoring the hall with a single-minded focus is the ultimate reverence of the mind. Mount Sumeru is originally eighty-four thousand yojanas high, yet each [of them]...

The flowers from their robes were scattered, which immediately became equal [in quantity] to those already there; this clearly shows that the number of those who had come was vast. Furthermore, as for the offering to the tree:
the tree is that upon which Jñānavijaya relies, and it is also that which ought to be honored. The tree was ten *yojanas* high, symbolizing that his wisdom transcends the ten realms.
As for each person offering a palace, it was because the previous offerings of flowers were insufficient to fully express their sincerity. Therefore...

Furthermore, he offered him a palace; how much more so the palaces of devas and humans! Never for even a moment has there been a separation, yet now, in abandoning them all at once, he manifests that his attachment to a self (*ātman*) has already been liberated.
He prays that the Buddha remain therein, signifying the transformation from a reliance on the mundane (*pṛthagjana-āśraya*) into a reliance on wisdom (*jñāna-āśraya*).
The character "chu" (處) means "to remain. In the verse, he first praises the Buddha’s two types of wisdom—expedient (*upāya*) and ultimate (*tattva*): "The World-Honored One is most rare!"

The first two lines praise the Real (the *dharmakāya*); the following two lines praise the Expedient (the *upāyakauśalya*). Together they clarify that Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) uproots suffering; thus it is said, "capable of rescuing and protecting.
The four lines beginning with "all devas and humans" praise the Buddha’s vastness of benefit. Together they clarify that Great Benevolence (*mahāmaitrī*) bestows happiness;
thus it is said, "all universally receive his benefit. Next, the arrival of the assembly is described, meaning those of us who have come.
This method has already traversed five million billion lands. Having abandoned the profound meditative bliss of the Brahma palaces, they have come from afar;

there is not one among them who has not come for the sake of seeing the Buddha. According to principle, one must pass through fifty stages of causal practice, fully perfected, before one can personally reach the realm of the Buddha.
To abandon deep meditative concentration is precisely to arouse the resolve for enlightenment.

Turning the mind toward it means to suddenly aspire to the wondrous bliss of the fruit of Buddhahood. Question: When the rain of flowers falls like mountains and the trees and thrones continue to descend, what is the nature of these phenomena?
Answer: These are inconceivable matters; they do not obstruct one another. 6. Requesting the Preaching of the Dharma.
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha with verses, they spoke these verses with one mind and in a single voice:
"O Hero among Men, Honored One among the Two-legged, we pray that you will expound the Dharma; by means of the power of great compassion, deliver sentient beings from suffering and affliction."

"The two-footed" refers to the dual adornment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Tiantai says: "Since it speaks of 'delivering sentient beings from suffering and affliction,' this is precisely the request for the turning [of the wheel].
The 'half-words' are like the present, when the Buddha, in the Deer Park, preached the Tripiṭaka teachings to deliver sentient beings from the five turbidities and the eight sufferings.
The prose section says "opening the path to *nirvāṇa*," while the verse says "I only pray that you will expound it."

As for the Dharma, how could one know that he specifically requested only the "half-words" (the provisional teachings)? Moreover, those who are transformation-bodies on the stages of the bodhisattva grounds have made the vow to seek the Buddha-way;

thus it is said that they do so by the power of great compassion. Furthermore, kindness (*maitrī*) can bestow the bliss of the four noble beings, while pity (*karuṇā*) can extract the suffering of the six classes of ordinary beings.
From this, the general intent of his request may be clearly seen. △ The Seven Buddhas silently grant their consent.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent.
His silent consent was due to the intention of the Brahmā who had come; it accorded with the Buddha’s own mind that the time had come to emit light and preach the Dharma.
Therefore, he did not speak, yet his heart gave its approval. As the *Ziyin* (Record of Knowledge) says, citing the *Shishuo*: "The World-Honored One used silence..."
Nevertheless, he granted permission. When the Original Buddha first sat at the site of enlightenment and had already attained Buddhahood,
he held fast to the Great Seal of the True Mark of the One Vehicle with such firmness that not only did the various Buddhas fail to appear,
but even his own sixteen princes born of his own body were unable to approach him, let alone the Brahma Kings from the five hundred million lands throughout the ten directions.
Thus they all come; this is why it is said that he is "about to attain Bodhi.

When, after ten intermediate kalpas of contemplation have passed, he releases a single thread—using the Real to open the Provisional—and thereby attains the skillful means of the Buddhas for delivering sentient beings, then the Prince comes and Brahmā also comes;
only then is it said that he has attained the realization of Bodhi. It can thus be seen that [Bodhi] is attained.
The word "bodhi" (enlightenment) merely causes sentient beings to perceive the signs and become Buddhas. Expedient and provisional wisdom possesses such marvelous efficacy;
therefore, when the Buddhas attain the Way, they invariably first preach the Three Vehicles. This is because the essence of the teaching in the Sahā world is thus:
sentient beings find benefit in the faculty of hearing and enter through it. For this reason, below—
After the Buddha Mañjuśrī-jñāna had accepted the invitations from the Brahmās of the ten directions, he first turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths and Dependent Origination;
only thereafter did he preach the reality-mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of the One Vehicle for the sixteen princes.

Although this passage describes the events following the Buddha Jñāna’s attainment of enlightenment and his reception of the Brahmās from the ten directions, it actually elucidates the beginning of my Śākyamuni’s own sitting [in meditation] as described in the "Expedient Means" chapter.

The ritual for the Brahma Kings of the various directions requesting the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, as described in the *Daochang guanshu jingxing* (Sutra on Observing Trees and Walking at the Site of Enlightenment).
Although there are variations in the texts of the nine directions below, they do not deviate from this; they may be understood by analogy. △ Second, the Southeastern Direction.
This is divided into seven parts. First, beholding the auspicious light.
Furthermore, the bhikṣus of the southeastern direction (and so on) each saw their own palaces illuminated by a brilliant light.
△ Second, they were struck with wonder and doubt;
having never experienced such a thing before, they leaped for joy and gave rise to a sense of rare wonder.
△ Third, the mutual inquiry:
they each went to one another’s place and deliberated on this matter (until) they spoke these verses for the sake of the assembly of Brahmās:
"By what causes and conditions has such a sign appeared (until) to deliver sentient beings from suffering?"
Among the various Brahmās, there is one called Mahākāruṇika (Great Compassion). This is also a designation for one who manifests traces by taking up a provisional station.
Observing his speech, it consists entirely of the words of one who possesses certain knowledge; that is to say, he says we should together seek with a single mind.
He further states, "It is mostly when a Buddha appears in the world that he delivers sentient beings from suffering and distress. The meaning of this is evident. △ Fourth, seeking the light.
[The Buddha] said, "At that time, five million billion Brahma Kings... [down to] the sixteen princes requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Whether people of the southeast face the west or the north, it is never impermissible; yet they must always say 'west.'"
"The north" means to go straight ahead. If there is even the slightest deviation, one will not reach the mark.
To "seek and investigate" these two words refers to the effort of diligent and uninterrupted practice.

Even if one seeks until reaching beyond thousands of millions of billions of lands and beholds the Tathāgata Jñānavijaya, in reality, this light is none other than that which was present within each respective palace before one had even stepped out the door.
To see [the Buddha] is to perceive his light. Nevertheless, if one does not seek that light, how could one be able to see the Buddha?
This is what is meant by "knowing and thereby attaining. △ Fifth, making offerings.
Then the Brahma kings prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet (and so forth), and with one mind and a single voice, they praised him in verse:
“O Holy Lord, King among Gods, with a voice like the kalaviṅka bird... having now encountered the World-Honored One.”
The Sage among Sages is called the Lord; the Heaven among Heavens is called the King. Kan Ze said:

"The teachings of Confucius and Laozi are practiced in accordance with Heaven, not daring to disobey Heaven. The teachings of Śākyamuni are followed by all the heavens, not daring to disobey the Buddha.
Therefore, he is called the King among Heavens. *Kalingapinga* means "Wondrous-Sound Bird" in this language. *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*.
The Sūtra says: "There is a mountain named Vana-vyūha (The Forested Wilderness). Within it dwell many kalaviṅka birds that produce wondrous sounds.
Such beautiful voices cannot be matched by anyone—whether devas, humans, or kinnaras—with the sole exception of the Buddha’s voice."
This also borrows from that [example] to illustrate excellence. It is not that the Buddha’s voice resembles it; rather, as Zhizhi says:
"The 'one hundred and eighty kalpas' symbolize the one hundred and eight afflictions that serve as obstacles for sentient beings. When these obstacles are heavy, evil increases;
when evil increases, the heavens diminish—this is what the heavens lament. Now, fortunately, the Buddha has appeared to act as the Eye for humans and devas, for the sake of the nine realms."

He is the true Great Compassionate Father to whom all turn for refuge. For those who have already entered the evil realms, the Tathāgata employs various skillful means to rescue them and cause them to emerge;
for those who have not yet entered, he likewise uses various skillful means to protect them so that they do not enter.
Therefore, he possesses great compassion and benefits sentient beings. To have now encountered the Buddha is certainly no small cause;
it is due to the merit planted in past lives that such auspicious fortune exists. △ Sixth, requesting the preaching of the Dharma.
At that time, after the Brahma kings had praised the Buddha with verses, they spoke these verses with one mind and in unison:
"The Great Sage turns the wheel of Dharma, revealing the characteristics of all phenomena... [omitted] ...those who possess patience and goodness shall increase."
Having already attained the sight of the Buddha, one must surely hope to hear the Dharma. If one were to see him alone without hearing his teaching, what benefit would there be?

Therefore, one must certainly request that he preach the Dharma. "The characteristics of all phenomena" refers to the three categories of aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), as well as the characteristics of the truths, the factors of enlightenment, the perfections, and so forth.
"Suffering and affliction" refers to the sentient beings within the six realms of existence in the burning house. "Patience and goodness" refers to...

This refers to those at the stage of the seven expedient means who have attained the forbearance of all dharmas; as their wholesome paths increase, they will certainly reach the point where unwholesome dharmas are diminished.
△ The Seven Buddhas silently consented.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent.
△ Third, the Southern Quarter. Divided into seven parts. First, witnessing the auspicious omen of light:
Furthermore, the bhikṣus in the southern direction (up to) each saw their own palaces illuminated by a brilliant radiance.
△ 2. Arousing Surprise and Doubt:
They felt unprecedented joy and exultation, giving rise to a sense of wonder.
△ 3. Mutual Inquiry.
Thereupon, they each went to one another and deliberated on this matter (up to: and spoke these verses for the sake of the assembly of Brahmās:
"The radiance of our various palaces is exceedingly majestic and brilliant (up to: it is because a Buddha has appeared in the world."
The name of the Brahma Lord, "Wondrous Dharma" (Miaofa), seems to be the name of one who has already attained great pervasive wisdom;
thus he is able to lead the multitude in seeking the light. This implies that it is not without cause or condition that he desires to seek it.
Furthermore, when he says that he has never seen this sign for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, we know that he must have seen it before those hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Thus, one further knows that this is a manifestation of the traces of responsive transformation. △ Fourth, seeking the light.
At that time, five million billion Brahma Kings (up to) entreated the Buddha to turn the wheel of the Dharma.
△ Fifth, the Offering.
At that time, the Brahma Kings prostrated themselves before the Buddha’s feet (and so forth), and with one mind and in unison, they praised him in verse, saying:
“The World-Honored One is most difficult to behold, he who has shattered all afflictions... (and so forth)... We only pray that you will graciously accept [this offering].”
In this verse, the Buddha’s virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) is first praised. "All afflictions" refers to the exhaustion of the ignorance of the five stages of dwelling.
"One hundred and thirty kalpas" indicates the emergence of a rare and difficult-to-perceive realization. "The hungry and thirsty" refers to sentient beings of the six realms;

it means that if the Buddha did not appear in the world, there would be no nectar of the joy of Dharma, the delight of dhyāna, and liberation to provide them with relief. Now that he has appeared in the world...
May the sentient beings of the six realms all receive the rain of Dharma to their full satisfaction, so that their feverish afflictions may be cooled.

The phrase "what was never seen before" and following praises the Buddha’s wisdom and virtue; his wisdom is rare and difficult to encounter, just like the udumbara flower, which all love and delight in.
As for the statement that the palaces were adorned and embellished by the light, each point follows accordingly.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that there are inconceivable adornments of various jewels, with which these subtle and exquisite palaces are offered as worship to the Tathāgata.
From this, one knows that their devotion is ultimate. △ Sixth, the request for the preaching of the Dharma.
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha with verses, they spoke with one mind and in unison, reciting these verses:
"We pray that the Honored One among Gods and Humans will turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma... [until] he shall proclaim his profound and far-reaching voice."
The Brahma King’s mind in requesting the Dharma was not for his own sake; he said, "all the worlds," which encompasses the six realms of existence in general.
To specifically mention Māra and Brahmā is to pair them as the worldly opposites of evil and good. As for śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas...

This constitutes a pair of opposites in the world: the heterodox and the orthodox. The subsequent conclusion, stating that "all obtain peace and security," means that when the Buddha turns the wheel of Dharma, there are none among those in the world—whether good or evil, heterodox or orthodox, defiled or pure, wise or foolish—who do not attain peace and stability.
By beating the drum, he warns them all to reach the precious destination together; by blowing the conch, he urges them to never retreat from moment to moment. He rains down...
It rains, moistening the withered and parched states of the six realms. This request seeks to open the three [vehicles], yet it must unfold the profound and far-reaching sound;

this request seeks to reveal the One, thereby manifesting the discourse of the ultimate. The initial restoration of the Brahma Lord’s original name was surely for the purpose of requesting the teaching of his own wondrous Dharma.
△ The Seven Buddhas silently granted their consent.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent.
△ Fourth, a general explanation of the six directions:
from the southwest to the nadir, it was likewise so.
"Up to and including" refers to the six directions—omitting the west, northwest, north, northeast, southwest, and downward directions—which are likewise treated in this same manner.
"Is also likewise" means that in each of these directions there are five hundred million *brahmā* heavens.

Upon the illumination of their light, they gave rise to doubt and deliberated together; then, following the light, they saw the Buddha seated, as well as the kings of the eight classes of supernatural beings.
The disciple requests the Dharma, performs offerings, and so forth; all are according to the previous format, so there is no need for prolixity—they are generally the same.
The above concludes the explanation of the power of the directions. △ Second, the explanation of the upper direction, divided into six parts. First, beholding the auspicious omen of light.
At that time, the palaces where [the Buddhas] of the upper direction resided—five million billion in number—were filled with radiant and majestic light.
△ Second, the thought of wonder and doubt:
they experienced unprecedented joy and leaped for gladness, giving rise to a sense of rare wonder.
△ Third, the mutual inquiry:
They each went to one another’s abodes and deliberated upon this matter (until) they spoke these verses for the sake of the assembly of Brahmās:
"By what cause and condition have all our palaces [appeared]... (until) it is because a Buddha has appeared in the world."
In the introductory section of the various chapters, there was once Śikhin, who served as the lord of the Sahā world; this is translated here as "Crest" (Dingji).
It is now said that he traveled five hundred million *koṭi* of lands toward the nadir, where he followed a light and beheld a Buddha. Perhaps he is indeed this very lord of the Sahā world.
This is like the twenty tiers of worlds within the lotuses of the Fragrant Water Sea of the Flower Treasury Adornment (*Kusumatalavyūha*).

World: This Sahā world is located within the thirteenth layer. From that first layer, ascending to the second layer, there is a world called Various Fragrant Lotuses, situated beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field.
Its Buddha is named Lion Light, and it is surrounded by worlds as numerous as the atoms in two buddha-fields. Reaching the Sahā...
Vipaśyin then said, "If one passes through as many worlds as there are atoms in thirteen Buddha-fields, then five hundred trillion lands will be near. 4. Seeking the Light.
At that time, five million billion Brahma Kings (up to) requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of the Dharma.
△ Fifth, the offering of worship:
At that time, the Brahma Kings bowed their heads to the ground in homage to the Buddha (up to) chanting together with one mind in a single voice, speaking in verse:
"Excellent! To behold all the Buddhas, the Holy Honored Ones who save the world... (until)... all together attain the Buddha-way.
Excellent! This is a joyful and fortunate thought. Regarding "to behold all the Buddhas," this reveals that the Buddha and the Buddha-way are identical; to behold one Buddha is to behold all Buddhas.
Regarding "saviors of the world," the Buddha is the Great King of Physicians, for he heals the body and mind of sentient beings.
"Sickness" refers to those who regard the three realms as a prison; they are like people within a burning house, imprisoned by the various fetters of affliction (*kleśa*).
Only the Tathāgata can exert himself to cause them to emerge from the three realms. These four lines praise the Buddha’s compassionate heart.
The four lines beginning with "Universal Wisdom" (Puzhi) praise the Tathāgata’s merit of wisdom. This means that the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable wisdom and is honored by devas and humans;
through various skillful means, he compassionately regards all beings. "Qunmeng" (multitudes of sprouts) refers to the multitudes of living beings.
The initial sprouting of grass is called "míng" (the bud). This signifies that all sentient beings possess the seeds of goodness, which sprout within their hearts;

it is simply that they lack the conditions to bring them forth. Now, fortunately, the Tathāgata has opened the gate of ambrosia to universally nourish all budding beings, causing the path of goodness to emerge.
The following verse concerns not meeting a Buddha for a long time and thus the failure of the roots of goodness to sprout; this refers to how, from time immemorial in this land...
For immeasurable kalpas, time has passed in vain without a Buddha; we have not received the holy transformation for a long time.
Until the appearance of Tathāgata Jñānavijaya, sentient beings in the ten directions did not behold the Buddha’s light;

they all remained upon the ground of the darkness of ignorance, giving rise to delusions and creating karma. Because their evil karma increased and blazed, the evil realms were prolonged, and they were unable to cultivate goodness. Therefore...
When devas and humans pass away, there are those who are reborn among the heavens and the human realm;

yet because their power of merit is slight, their physical strength, vitality, and wisdom all diminish. This is the bitter fruit brought about by those of meager fortune. Below follows the cause of suffering:
because they do not see the Buddha and do not hear the Dharma, they constantly practice the ten non-virtuous actions, and their ignorance becomes ever more heavy.
Thus, both pleasure and the perception of pleasure are lost. One’s wisdom is left unadorned; because the cause is forgotten, the fruit is lost.
Lacking right knowledge and vision, one maintains false views and abandons suffering with further suffering, failing to recognize proper conduct.
There is no doubt that upon death, such a person will surely fall into the evil realms. These eight lines, beginning with "The Buddha is the eye of the world," celebrate the appearance of the Buddha.
"O World, you have opened the true eye for humans and devas, transcending all sentient beings and emerging from the triple world; we are truly filled with profound joy and gratitude.
The first four lines describe the offering of the hall and the request for acceptance; the final four lines express the arousal of the bodhicitta and its dedication.
This is not for one's own sake—what is called 'one who has not yet crossed over themselves first seeks to cross others' is the arousal of the mind of a Bodhisattva. △
Sixth, the request to preach the Dharma.
At that time, five million billion Brahma Kings (up to) then the Brahma Kings spoke these verses:
"World-Honored One, turn the wheel of Dharma; beat the drum of the nectar-like Dharma... [up to] having practiced the Dharma for immeasurable kalpas."

This describes the Brahmās’ formal request for the Dharma. It brings great peace and security; whereas previously, before the Buddha had appeared in the world, the ten directions were shrouded in darkness and the evil realms flourished, resulting in extreme instability.
It brings about great liberation and deliverance; whereas previously, [beings] had not transcended [suffering], now he has attained Perfect Enlightenment.
One should rejoice and marvel at this unprecedented event, which causes all sentient beings to universally attain Buddhahood. May it be so!

This refers to the great number of those who are liberated and delivered. The first four lines of the verse state that when a Tathāgata appears in the world, he inevitably preaches the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, saying, "I reveal and demonstrate the path to Nirvāṇa";
this seems to clarify the provisional (upāya). The final four lines constitute the request to manifest the ultimate reality (paramārtha).
Therefore it is said: "Out of compassion, he expounds the Dharma practiced throughout immeasurable kalpas. Zhizhi says:
From what was previously described, although the arrival of the Brahmā kings from the ten directions follows a sequence, in reality they all arrive simultaneously;
they all see the light together, deliberate together, and at the same time follow the light from their respective directions to reach the center, where they all see it together.
The Buddhas simultaneously presented offerings and simultaneously requested the Dharma; thus one knows that their radiant light shines universally, and their realm is truly inconceivable.
This concludes the section on the distant causes for establishing karmic connections. △ Second, the proximate causes for establishing karmic connections, divided into two parts.
First, he first turned the wheel of the half-letters; furthermore, there are three [stages]: first, the Tathāgata accepted the invitation.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū [was invited] by the sixteen princes.

This precisely clarifies the immediate cause for establishing karmic connections. Because the Buddha accepted the invitation to preach the Dharma, the sixteen princes were subsequently able to lecture upon it;
this is why it serves as the primary means for establishing karmic connections. △ Second, the actual turning of the wheel of Dharma.
"Immediately, he turned the Dharma wheel of twelve aspects in three revolutions.

This describes the Buddha of Wisdom’s initial attainment of perfect enlightenment; having accepted the invitation, he emerged from meditative absorption and first turned the Dharma wheel of the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination for the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Zhizhi says: "This first indicates the characteristics of the Dharma; as it accords with the capacities of beings without contradiction, it is so called."
At that moment, by means of preaching the Dharma, he transformed afflictions (*kleśa*) into Bodhi and transformed birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) into Nirvāṇa;

thus it is called "turning. Because it was revealed three times, it is termed the "three turnings. As for the "Dharma-wheel" (*dharmacakra*), it refers to the Tathāgata taking the Dharma as a wheel to transport sentient beings out of birth-and-death.

This is called the practice of realization (*phala-sākṣātkriyā-caryā*). Each Truth undergoes three turnings, collectively constituting the twelve aspects of the Wheel of Dharma.
"If it cannot be overturned by śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māras, Brahmās, or anyone else in the world"—this is the analysis of that which cannot be overturned.

Neither of us dares speak of "turning"; only a Buddha and a Buddha can turn it. That is to say:

greed, anger, ignorance, pride, and so forth, with the views and afflictions (*kleśa*) serving as the cause. This means that once suffering is known, one should sever its origin. This...

The eight knowledges and thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are of a nature that can be cultivated.

"Craving" refers to the arising of craving and attachment by seeking out various excellent and wonderful requisites, as well as objects such as forms and sensual desires; therefore, it is said that "feeling conditions craving."

*Upādāna* (clinging) means that once a mind of craving and attachment has arisen toward various objects, one necessarily seeks and grasps them; therefore, it is said that "craving conditions clinging.

*Bhava* (existence) means that once clinging and attachment have been produced, afflictions and karma form heavy bonds, and as a result of good and evil causes and effects, one must undergo future existence;

therefore, it is said that "clinging conditions existence. Furthermore, these constitute the causes for the three links of the present life, all of which belong to the category of afflictions (*kleśa*). And...
The past [links], ignorance conditioned by which there are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), are the same as birth (*jāti*). This refers to taking birth within the six realms of existence.
Because these present causes and effects—good and evil—exist, one will inevitably take birth within the three realms in the future; hence it is said that "existence conditions birth.
Aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) refer to the maturation and decay of the body that has taken birth. These, in turn, constitute the two resultant links for the future.

Sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction constitute the state of suffering within old age and death. The above sequence of conditions arising from one another is called the gate of transmigration (*pravṛtti-mukha*).
Specifically, the three afflictions—ignorance, craving, and grasping—and the two factors of volitional formations and existence belong to the path of karma.
From consciousness through feeling, together with birth and death—these seven factors are collectively termed the single path of suffering; that is, affliction, karma, and suffering.
When ignorance ceases, then volitional formations cease (and so on, until): when birth ceases, then old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair cease.
This is the gate of cessation (*nirodha-mukha*). Daoku states: "Take the single dharma of ignorance (*avidyā*) as an example.

The Buddha, amidst the great assembly of devas and humans... [up to] immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable.

Because this concentration is profound, the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are manifested—namely, the three knowledges (*vidyā*) and the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*). Their meaning and characteristics are as explained previously.
The above summarizes the assembly that benefited from the teaching at the first assembly. For the second, third, and fourth assemblies, the text again describes multiple assemblies of teachings.

The subsequent sections are similar. The commentator notes: "Although this passage describes the Buddha’s act of teaching the Dharma through wisdom, its true purpose is to clarify the text from the verses in the 'Expedient Means' chapter which states:

This clarifies that the sixteen princes, having heard the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, renounced secular life to become monks.

*Śrāmaṇera* means "one who quiets [evil] and practices kindness," signifying the cessation of unwholesome conduct and the cultivation of compassion. Regarding "the various faculties": because the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) were pure, they are said to be "penetrating and sharp.

The eighty trillion people he leads symbolize the transformation of the eight consciousnesses and their mental factors (caitta). His "leaving home" (pravrajyā) symbolizes departing from the household of the eighteen realms (dhātu).
This is also a major pivotal point in the single assembly of the Wisdom Buddha. △ Fourth, the Tathāgata Accepts the Invitation.
At that time, that Buddha accepted the śrāmaṇera’s invitation (up to the point where they all together received, upheld, recited, and mastered it).

The Vaipulya [sūtras] extensively clarify matters of inconceivable supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Furthermore, the verse states:

This is indeed so. To summarize the principle: twenty years prior [to his parinirvāṇa], Śākyamuni preached the Hīnayāna teachings to clarify the transcendence of the mundane and entry into the ultimate truth.

By means of non-explanation, he clearly explains the Prajñāpāramitā. For the sake of the sixteen princes, he eradicates all attachments to both the ultimate and the conventional until they are exhausted;

For this reason, he again allowed the sixteen princes to listen to the re-exposition of the lecture, thereby establishing the distant cause for their future karmic connection. △ Sixth, the timing of the preaching of the sutra.

This is to obliterate all previously mentioned characteristics of speech, desiring that the sixteen novices forget both subject and object.

How much more so for the ten great disciples, all of whom possessed superior faculties; their realization and receipt of predictions were originally without priority or sequence.
Rather, each specialized in a single virtue, yet collectively they responded to various capacities. Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra was foremost in preaching the Dharma;

he constantly preached the unsurpassed path for the five hundred arhats, and was thus titled "Universal Radiance" (Puming). He was precisely the one suited to the capacity for this preaching of the Dharma.

Therefore, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra was appointed to preside over them. Just as Ānanda and Rāhula were also great disciples, each was assigned to lead a specific group of students for their respective reasons. Question:

After the text has finished bestowing the prediction upon Pūrṇa, it immediately states that at that time, the twelve hundred arhats had this thought. Why is it that only five hundred are specifically named? Answer: The scripture explicitly states: [△@△] "At that time, the twelve hundred arhats had this thought. It does not say "five hundred arhats. The text clearly specifies the total number as twelve hundred. Furthermore, the term "arhat" (羅漢) is used here as a general designation for those who have attained the fruit of arhatship; it is not intended to exclude others. Thus, there is no contradiction. Moreover, the Buddha’s teaching is vast and profound, and the assembly of those present is immeasurable. While the text mentions the twelve hundred, this serves as a representative figure for the entire multitude. This is similar to how the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* mentions the four assemblies—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—yet the actual number of beings present is far greater than that. Therefore, one should understand that the mention of twelve hundred is merely a conventional way of referring to the entire assembly. As for the specific mention of five hundred, this likely refers to a distinct subgroup within the larger community, perhaps those who were particularly prominent or whose spiritual progress required specific encouragement. In any case, the primary intent of the passage is to record the thoughts of the arhats regarding the Buddha’s predictions, and the numerical details are secondary. Thus, the text remains consistent and complete.
As for the five hundred arhats such as Uruvilvā and the others—let alone the five hundred [other] people—they were constantly at the seat, following the Buddha like a shadow follows a form.
As for the remaining seven hundred members of the assembly, they were not at their original seats when the prophecy was given;
therefore, he later entrusted them to Kāśyapa, saying: "O Kāśyapa, you already know these five hundred who possess mastery; this is what is being manifested here."
Regarding the words spoken during the bestowal of the prophecy, it further states: "The remaining assembly of śrāvakas shall likewise be so;
you should proclaim this for those who are not present in this gathering. The meaning of this is clearly evident: namely, that the task of bestowing the prophecy is a great one.

Why are the names not listed individually? Answer: The Buddha’s words are perfect and subtle; they are already complete within the phrasing itself. By mentioning a few, the rest is encompassed, thus avoiding prolixity.
