"If it were not for the wondrous fundamental essence of the Dharmakāya, there would be no way to manifest this foremost and supreme trace. Hitherto, people have only spoken of him as being foremost in preaching the Dharma among the traces."
"Now, he manifests the unsurpassed Dharma and has long since attained the foremost [state]. This cites the traces to reveal the fundamental.
The next two phrases indicate that the merit and wisdom of the fundamental stage are fully manifested.
Since the fundamental stage already possesses various merits, why would the traces consist of nothing more than the Two Vehicles? This cites the fundamental to clarify the traces.
"Exerting diligence to protect, maintain, and assist in proclaiming my Dharma" (up to) "no one can exhaust the eloquence of their discourse.
This indicates that within the preaching of the Dharma there are various merits. To be single-mindedly mindful of the One Vehicle is called "diligence" (*jīng*);

to practice with valor and without indolence is called "exertion" (*qín*); to remain unharmed in every thought-moment is called "protection" (*hù*); to encourage and restrain without fail is called "maintaining" (*chí*). To provide support and assistance is called... [the text continues].
"Assist. To expound extensively is called "proclaiming. Diligently protecting and upholding these four characters means that one assists in proclaiming the Buddha-dharma and benefits all people.
By virtue of these merits of twofold benefit, one is able to provide instruction according to the capacities of the fourfold assembly, ensuring that all obtain benefit and give rise to joy.
Within the traces of this treatise, the provisional means (*upāya*) are fully employed in the following four [sections].
This passage clarifies the reality of practice within the fundamental [truth]. "The True Dharma" refers precisely to the unsurpassed path of the One Vehicle.
Being able both to fully embody it and to explain it constitutes the merit of the two benefits (self-benefit and benefit for others).

Consequently, among fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life, one brings great benefit to those who are companions in both internal secrecy and external manifestation. This constitutes the two modes of teaching: the fundamental and the manifested.
As for their spiritual power, with the exception of the Tathāgata, no others are able to fully fathom their discourse and their unimpeded eloquence.
Therefore, I have always praised him as the foremost in preaching the Dharma, and I have also constantly extolled him for being endowed with all meritorious virtues.
△ Second, citing past Buddhas to reveal his original nature.
"Do not say of Pūrṇa... [up to] "...he constantly performs the Buddha-work to transform and teach sentient beings.

The preceding section has elucidated his present *honji* (original ground) and *saku* (traces), thereby allowing for a discussion of the reasons for his past internal secrecy and external manifestation.
The phrase "Do not say" and what follows reveals his profound mind (*shinjin*). Regarding "do not say," it is intended to instruct the assembly.
It is known. If one merely assists in proclaiming the Buddha-dharma within this assembly and is called the foremost, how could the mind alone suffice to perceive its depth?
In truth, among the teachings of ninety billion Buddhas of the past, he was likewise the foremost in assisting in their proclamation.
Although ninety billion is cited, it is still a proximate reckoning; yet his fundamental connection to the distant past is profound and obscure.
It is difficult to find those who are truly faithful and good; therefore, I have made this selection. Furthermore, following the passage on "all Buddhas," he reveals their original vows.
If one were to seek only upward within my own Dharma and transform others only downward, how could such a vow suffice to reveal its origin?

In reality, there is nothing among the teachings of all Buddhas that they do not thoroughly penetrate and clearly understand. The "Dharma of Emptiness" refers to that which transcends both the ultimate and the conventional truths simultaneously.
The emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). To see with refinement is called "clarity" (*míng*); to penetrate thoroughly is called "comprehension" (*liǎo*);

to be unimpeded is called "pervasion" (*tōng*); to reach profound depths is called "attainment" (*dá*). These terms describe how the Dharma of the single characteristic and single flavor of all Buddhas is seen with nothing but refinement and penetration.
This vision reveals the source from which the Way is realized; it is the merit of seeking self-benefit through the highest aspiration.

The four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) below all clarify the activities of downward transformation and benefiting others. According to the scriptural interpretation: if one is always able to examine with discernment, then one perceives the phenomena with clarity and precision;
this is the unhindered knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*). If one preaches the Dharma with purity, then one is free from all faults and defilements.

This is the unimpededness of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*). Being free from doubt, one necessarily achieves the integration of principle and phenomenon; this is the unimpededness of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).
Since these three are all present, there will inevitably be joyful eloquence (*pratibhāna*); thus, the unimpededness of joyful eloquence is fully contained therein.

The supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of a Bodhisattva cannot be matched by those of the Two Vehicles. Since it is said they are "fully endowed," they must have attained mastery in the Samādhi of Play (*vikrīḍita-samādhi*) and all [other samādhis].
Being unimpeded, such a person at the stage of the "one who is next to be seated" (the *upapadya-parivarta*) is able to extensively manifest great functions. Therefore, it is said below:

"According to their lifespan, they manifest bodies that accord with each type [of being] and harmonize with the multitude; thus, they manifest the appearance of nirvana in accordance with all sentient beings."
From "He himself attained the four analytical knowledges" up to "according to the duration of his lifespan," all these phrases concern matters of benefiting others.
Although he was submerged in mud and water throughout his entire body, he did not abandon his fundamental practice; therefore, it is said that he "constantly cultivated the pure life.

Regarding the passage "those people of that Buddha's world," this refers to those under the ninety billion Buddhas of the past, none of whom were able to know the original nature of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra.
These bodhisattvas all manifest traces that lead others to believe they are actually śrāvakas.

This skillful means—pointing toward the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), and longevity—is such that they all display the "lesser" within their traces in order to deliver so many people of lesser faculties.
Furthermore, they transform those in the lower realms, clarifying the Mahāyāna within their fundamental nature and delivering immeasurable asaṃkhyeya of sentient beings.
"Truly so. The final three phrases mean that Pūrṇa’s such skillful means of provisional and ultimate truth are not solely for the purpose of transforming sentient beings;
they are also the means by which he accomplishes his own merit and adorns and purifies his own Buddha-land.
Thus, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: "A bodhisattva takes up a Buddha-land according to the sentient beings he transforms. △ Third, [the section] concerning the three...
The causes cultivated by the Buddhas of the world:
the bhikṣu Pūrṇa (up to... constantly and diligently applied himself with vigor to transform sentient beings.
This extensively extols the profound mind and original vows of the three periods of time; he was truly the foremost person among them. The *Yinzhi* (Sound-Knower) says:
Regarding the seven Buddhas: the traditional names are Vipaśyin, Śikhin, and Viśvabhū; these belong to the final three Buddhas among the thousand Buddhas of the past *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa* (Adornment Eon).
Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni belong to the first four Buddhas among the thousand Buddhas of the present *Bhadrakalpa* (Fortunate Eon).
Now, observing the text of this sutra, since it mentions "seven Buddhas," and furthermore...
The phrases "now before me" and so forth, as well as "in this Bhadrakalpa" and so forth, indicate that Śākyamuni alone is assigned to the present, while the others belong to the past.
Furthermore, regarding the future mentioned below, one should understand that this refers to the future after the Bhadrakalpa;
for instance, when the twelve hundred arhats attain Buddhahood, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra likewise [does so].
To protect, uphold, and propagate the immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharma, one becomes a disciple;
thus, how could the depth of such a mind and the breadth of such a vow be measured? This is because it is nothing other than seeking the supreme above and transforming those below.
Purifying the Buddha-lands completes the aspiration for the supreme, while transforming sentient beings completes the transformation of those below; these together constitute the ultimate goal.

Describing his causal practices, the text below grants him the prediction of his fruition. △ Second, the bestowing of the prediction, divided into four parts. First, clarifying the perfection of causes and the fulfillment of the fruit:
gradually fulfilling the Bodhisattva path (up to) the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
This clarifies the fruit accomplished through the fundamental vows of the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*).

"Gradually becoming fully endowed" refers to the totality of practices performed over immeasurable *kalpas* throughout the three periods of time while serving many Buddhas; once these practices are perfected, the Way is complete.
Furthermore, the statement "passing immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*" is made in reference to the Tathāgata bestowing the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) upon [the Bodhisattva] today.
It does not mean that one must first gradually complete the bodhisattva path and then subsequently pass through such many kalpas.
As for "in this land," it refers specifically to the present Sahā world. Furthermore, this land is, first, the source from which the Way is received and initiated;
there are such causes here that lead to the realization of such fruits. Second, it is due to the power of original vows, as seen in the subsequent passages on making vows and upholding the sutra.
As for why we do not see Śāriputra and Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra [attain this state], it is because they still maintain their original vows.

These three [bodhisattvas] have realized the principle of original enlightenment through the wisdom of initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*), thereby adorning their own nature and becoming buddhas of self-nature. Thus, one knows that this has been so for immeasurable kalpas.
Without departing from this land, one practices all deeds; without departing from this land, one serves all Buddhas;
without departing from this land, one secretly maintains the inner truth while manifesting outwardly to assist in proclaiming the Buddha-dharma—altogether, one never departs from this land.
If there were even a single moment or a single event occurring outside of this land, it would constitute the work of Māra. Therefore, one must attain Bodhi within this very land.
As for the title of the fruition being "Dharma-Illumination," it is because one clearly understands the dharma of emptiness taught by all Buddhas, and thus expounds the Dharma without hindrance;
this fruition is brought about in accordance with its cause. △ Second, explaining the adornment and purity of the land.
That Buddha [possesses lands] as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River (up to... all of whom are born by transformation and are free from sexual desire.
He unites great trichiliocosms as numerous as the sands of the Ganges into a single land. Furthermore, it is not only the Tathāgata who transforms the Sahā world into three;
how much more so for the Tathāgata Dharmaprabhāsa, who is unhindered regarding all phenomena—how could his supporting land be otherwise?
It is also unobstructed. "Luminous" means that the ancient mirror is one zhang wide; the world is likewise one zhang wide.

Regarding "the ground is made of the seven treasures," the ground is the *prakṛti-bhūmi* (intrinsic nature of the ground), which is adorned by the seven types of pure wealth. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "level as the palm of a hand":
if a palm were not level, it would not serve as the analogy. This refers to a stone at the bottom of the ocean named "Palm," which is perfectly level. It does not mean an ordinary human hand.
"Even a speck of dust's worth of unevenness. Furthermore, the *Bhadrapāla-kalpika-sūtra* directly clarifies that it is like the palm of a Buddha’s hand.
Viśvabhū Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara: "When you level the mind-ground, then all the lands of the world will be level.
This is what is meant by being "level as a palm," from which it follows that there are no mountains or forests; this establishes the reality of the earth being level. Although...
He said: "This land is not like the present one, which is uneven with high and low elevations. There were towers and pavilions for the people to ascend and enjoy themselves;
that it was said to be 'filled' allows us to know that the people there suffered no bitterness from seeking gain or vying for position.
As for the celestial palaces, they are places unseen by the masses. That it is now said they 'interconnect' implies that people have not [yet seen them]."
Originally, it was not [a realm of] devas; yet humans and devas are of one accord. One observes that in this land there is no person who does not practice.

The above is a brief discussion on the adornment of the *pariṇāmanā-vipāka* (the environment as a result of collective karma). Next, we discuss how the land is free from evil filth. "The various evil paths" refers to the three miserable realms (*triyāṇī*).

Because the land lacks the causes for such states, their effects are not summoned. Not only do beings of different species not dwell there, but even among those of the same species, there are no women...
Humans likewise do not dwell there. Since humans are born through transformation (*upapāduka*), their lust has already been severed.
As the cause of lust no longer exists, the fruit of lust is also forgotten; thus, it is fitting that there are no women in that land.

All of this was taught by the Tathāgata Dharmaprabhāsa while he was still in the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*), as a means of instruction to lead people to transform their ignorance into wisdom, so that there are no evil realms, and to transform existence...
Having realized the true emptiness that is free from outflows, one attains transformation-birth (*upapāduka*). Not only is there no suffering, but sentient beings are also born together with merit.

One attains great supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and the body emits radiance; [among the foods,] first is the food of Dharma-joy (*dharmaprītyāhāra*), and second is the food of dhyāna-delight (*dhyānaprītāhāra*).
In this land, the primary retribution and adornments of all sentient beings do not transcend the two categories of form and mind.

For instance, such qualities as supernormal powers, resolve, mindfulness, and diligence belong to the mind; whereas radiance, flight, golden complexion, and the marks and signs of excellence belong to form—these are precisely what is meant by the purification of the six sense faculties.
Since the people of this land possess such merit and wisdom, [the environment is likewise adorned].
Adorned and possessing sovereign power of flight, how would they differ from the devas?
One must know that all the deva-multitudes, as well as the followers of the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas in that land, become successively more excellent; this can generally be seen.

Regarding the "two kinds of food," Tiantai cites the ninth fascicle of the *Candragarbha-sūtra*, which clarifies the food of Dharma (*dharma-āhāra*), the food of joy (*prīti-āhāra*), and the food of dhyāna (*dhyāna-āhāra*). The sūtra text states in general terms: "Dharma-joy..."

Regarding the "joy of dhyāna" (*dhyāna-prīti*), there should be a distinct classification into three types of differences. *Miaole* states: "The 'food of Dharma' (*dharma-āhāra*) refers to hearing the Dharma.
For example, those born in the lower grade in the Land of Ultimate Bliss constantly hear Amitābha and Avalokiteśvara preaching the Dharma while within their lotus flowers."

Regarding "joy in the Dharma": it is to rejoice upon hearing the Dharma. Hearing the Dharma correctly serves as the food of the Dharma; having heard it, one belongs to joy. Regarding "food of dhyāna":
it is to sustain oneself through the methods of dhyāna, without requiring material food.
There are immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya, thousands of myriads of koṭis (up to) those who are well-able to teach and transform the various classes of sentient beings.
Those mentioned previously were the people; this clarifies the dharma-heirs. Because the Tathāgata has taught the Dharma for a long time, those who have benefited from it are numerous.
To point directly: because he unifies the provisional and the ultimate, he attains great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); because his four wisdoms are perfectly luminous, he attains...
They are unimpeded. Because their teachers are eminent and their resources are abundant, they are able to teach and transform sentient beings;

all of the above is what is brought forth by true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). The two characters "of this class" (*zhī lèi*) belong to the side of the Bodhisattvas in the statement, meaning that these Bodhisattvas are all Great Beings of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-mahāsattva*), a group well-able to practice transformation and teaching, and are not to be compared with Bodhisattvas of expedient or gradual stages.

As for the assembly of śrāvakas, their number—calculated and reckoned—reaches those possessing the six superknowledges (ṣaḍabhijñā), the three types of clear knowledge (trividyā), and the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa).
Among the bodhisattvas, they are said to be immeasurable; all are great bodhisattvas. Thus, the assembly of the three stages of worthiness (trikalyāṇamitra) is vast, and it cannot be fully perceived.
Now, if it is said that even the śrāvakas cannot be calculated, then the vastness of the pratyekabuddhas can likewise be seen.
This collectively clarifies the number of persons in the three vehicles, all of whom have attained full completion and so forth; this collectively clarifies their virtues.
All of these are transformed by the expedient wisdom of the Tathāgata.
That Buddha-land is thus accomplished with such immeasurable meritorious adornments.
This summarizes the aforementioned adornments of both the environment and the inhabitants; hence it says "such as these" regarding the immeasurable merits.

It cannot be fully described. Regarding what are called "adornments" and "accomplishments," as clarified in the fifth chapter of the *Candragarbha-sūtra*, each of the ten wholesome paths of action possesses ten kinds of merit. First, by refraining from killing, one attains ten merits:
(1) one attains fearlessness toward all sentient beings; (2) one attains a mind of great compassion toward sentient beings; (3) one severs evil habits.
1. One’s karma [is purified]; 2. one has little illness; 3. one has a long life; 4. one is protected by non-human beings; 5. one has no bad dreams; 6. one has no enemies; 7.
one does not fear the evil realms; 8. at the end of life, one is reborn in a good realm;

and later, when one becomes a Buddha, there will be no instruments of killing in the land, and the people will have long lives—up to the tenth point, being free from wrong views, one likewise attains these ten kinds of merit.
The nature of their single mind is gentle and virtuous; they have already reached the tenth stage of the wholesome path of birth and death.

When they become Buddhas, the people of their lands will possess correct faith. Such as these are all the result of the Tathāgata’s accomplishment of causal practices; therefore, they are called "immeasurable merits.
△ Third, the explanation of the kalpa, the land, and the lifespan.
The kalpa is named Ratnaprabhā and the land is named Suviśuddha; the lifespan of that Buddha is immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Even in kalpas where no Buddha dwells, such periods are many. Now that the Tathāgata Dharmaprabhāsa dwells in this world during this kalpa, the Buddha is indeed its treasure.
Since the Buddha has preached the Dharma, extensively dispelling ignorance, his illumination is bright and inexhaustible; therefore, he is so called.

The kalpa is called Jewel Radiance (Ratnaprabhāsa). As for "Delighting in Purity," it is because the people possess wisdom and diligence, take the dharma of meditation as their sustenance, and are free from evil and defilement;

thus they receive this name. Regarding the Buddha’s long life span: while in the causal stage he was already able to accord with the lifespans [of beings] to teach and transform sentient beings, and having realized the fruit of the Dharma-body, it neither exists nor does not exist.
One is accomplished through the power of vows; the other arises from the response of karmic conditions. △ Fourth, clarifying the propagation of the Dharma and its transformation:
the Dharma shall abide for a very long time, and after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, stupas made of the seven treasures will arise and fill his land.
It does not specify the duration of the True and Semblance Dharma eons, but merely states that "the Dharma will abide for a very long time.

This too is spoken in brief by way of abbreviation, referring to the power of that Buddha’s original vow to maintain [the teaching] firmly. Since he abides in the world for such a long time, those he transforms become increasingly numerous;

thus, stupas arise until they fill the land, which serves to repay his kindness and benefit the masses. △ Second, the section on the verses in gāthā, divided into two parts. First, the verse summarizing the preceding account of the manifestation of his origins.
Furthermore, there are two [sections]. The first verse provides a general exposition on the path of the śrāvakas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Listen attentively, O bhikṣus! The path traversed by the sons of the Buddha, because they have skillfully studied expedient means, is inconceivable."
Therefore, the commentary states: "These twenty-eight lines following [the previous section] collectively eulogize the profound minds and original vows of the twelve hundred followers.

They were introduced by Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra as an opening for their manifestation. Although there is a sequence in the recording, all these individuals belong to the Mahāyāna; they are categorized according to the three turnings of the wheel and the three faculties."

There is no sequential arrangement for the simultaneous establishment of the non-dharma gate; fundamentally, there is neither high nor low. [△@△] The World-Honored One exhorted the bhikṣus to listen attentively:

"It is simply that you must know that all the śrāvakas present in this assembly, including those who serve as leaders, are all great bodhisattvas who conceal their inner reality while manifesting externally. Therefore, they are called 'Sons of the Buddha,' they are said to 'practice the Way,' and they are said to..."
Skillfully learning expedient means is called "inconceivable. These all involve the simultaneous application of the provisional and the ultimate of the Mahāyāna;
blending with the multitudes without being recognized, entering into worldly toil without being defiled—this is truly inconceivable.
Practicing the Way is the upward seeking [of enlightenment], while learning expedient means is the downward transformation [of sentient beings].
Knowing that the multitude delights in inferior teachings and fears great wisdom, the Bodhisattvas manifest as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
The following five sections all clarify the reason for skillfully practicing inconceivable means. This is known as the "Knowledge of Sounds."
O Sons of the Buddha, the reason why they manifest the Great as Small is that they know the capacities and natures of sentient beings:
that they crave minor fruits and fear the Great Vehicle. Therefore, for the sake of such individuals, they specifically manifest as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
this is their skillful mastery of means, the first point which is inconceivable.
"By means of countless skillful means, he transforms all classes of sentient beings (until) they all achieve fulfillment.
This clarifies that one leads others by means of oneself, establishing the standard for employing skillful means.
When Mahākātyāyana heard the teaching of the Bodhisattva’s inconceivable Dharma-door of Great Liberation, he said to Śāriputra: "It is, for example, as if..."
It is like showing forms and appearances before a blind person; they cannot see them.

In this same way, all the śrāvakas, upon hearing this dharma-gate of liberation, are unable to comprehend it. When the wise hear this, who would not resolve to attain the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment?
Why have we severed its very roots? Regarding this Mahāyāna, we are already as [if dead].
"Like rotten seeds, all śrāvakas who hear this dharma-gate of liberation should all wail and weep, their voices shaking the trichiliocosm.
Furthermore, it says: "Today we are no longer capable of generating the bodhicitta.
These are all instances where Bodhisattvas manifest as followers of the Hīnayāna, mingling among their peers to provide indirect and thorough access to the Mahāyāna.
This is the Dharma by which immeasurable multitudes are delivered; this is the second instance where the great is designated by the small, such that it cannot be conceived by thought.
Although they may be small and prone to indolence, one should gradually cause them to become Buddhas.

This uses indolence as a means to cultivate diligence, serving as a condition for skillful expedients. Although it appears to show the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) by manifesting physical exhaustion and weariness, in reality, it is diligence within that very indolence.
By leading those of similar standing, it encourages them to exert themselves with vigor so that they do not ultimately abandon their path halfway;
it ensures they fulfill their great aspirations and gradually enter the Buddha-way. This must be done.
Third, those who attain [this state] yet still engage in conceptualization:
they secretly practice the conduct of a bodhisattva within, while outwardly manifesting as śrāvakas with few desires, weary of birth and death, while in reality purifying their own buddha-fields.
This shows the external traces and internal root of the skillful means of their practice. The *Dàkuǎn* states:

"These bodhisattvas internally conceal their great practices and do not reveal their miraculous displays; externally, they manifest limited wisdom and delight in practicing the dharma that the poor enjoy—the conduct of contentment.
Although they weary of the suffering of birth and death and seek the bliss of nirvana, in reality..."
Fourth, it is inconceivable that one purifies one’s own buddha-field while regarding it as unattainable.
Furthermore, manifesting the three poisons to the assembly and appearing with the marks of false views, my disciples employ such skillful means to deliver sentient beings.
This is using the perverse to lead toward the correct; it is an expedient means (*upāya*). The *Yinzhi* says:

"The preceding sections all demonstrated expedients in accordance with [the truth], whereas this demonstrates the three poisons (*triviṣa*) in an inverse manner. Thus, both accordance and inversion are expedients.

The three poisons are the three fundamental delusions of greed, anger, and ignorance. Their activity causes people to fall into the three miserable realms; therefore, they are called "poisons" (*viṣa*). Perverse.
The "view" (dṛṣṭi) is one of the five afflictive views (*pañca-kudṛṣṭi*). It refers to the false view of those who venerate fire and water, sacrifice to heaven, and seek blessings through such means.
For example, Sundarī demonstrated lust to Ānanda, while Śāriputra and Rādha demonstrated anger in their dispute for victory.

Devadatta’s attempt to harm the Buddha, the display of ignorance by Cūḍapanthaka, the arrogance of Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja, and the three Kāśyapas’ veneration of fire and water were all manifestations of great skillful means.
Their sole purpose was to cause all people to take refuge in the Buddha-way; therefore it is said, "My disciples are like this. This is inconceivable.
This is the fifth point of deliberation.
If I were to fully explain the various matters of manifested transformations, sentient beings who hear this would harbor doubt and confusion in their minds.
This concludes the preceding [discussion on] the reality of the inconceivable skillful means of well-trained practice; that is to say, if I were to fully...
To speak of the various skillful means manifested by the sons of the Buddha involves immeasurable varieties;
this would surely cause those who hear it to give rise to doubt and lack faith. The *Yinzhi* (Sound-Knower) says:
"Before praising Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, he first praises the various disciples because among the five hundred arhats there are the group of six bhikṣus. Thus, the group of six...
The deeds performed are also various skillful means of manifestation. △ Second, the verse on the original and trace manifestations of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra:
"This Pūrṇa, under thousands of billions of Buddhas in the past... [until] he purified his own Buddha-field."
These twenty phrases specifically versify the past causal practices of the responsive capacity [of the audience]. Their wording subsumes the present.

The intent of the verses does not transcend the simultaneous operation of provisional and ultimate [truths], the concurrent practice of wisdom and compassion, and the benefiting of self and others, for the sake of purifying the Buddha-field; this pertains to the principle of suchness (*tathatā*).
The extensive proclamation of the Great Dharma constitutes the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*).
In the future, they shall also make offerings to immeasurable and incalculable Buddhas (until) they achieve all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
These eight lines of verse correspond to the capacities of the audience. Regarding the various Buddhas of the future, they seek the higher [enlightenment] and transform those below;

the merits of these two benefits may be explained according to the text. △ Second, the verses on the bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), divided into three parts. First, the verse on the perfection of cause and fruit.
By making offerings to all Tathāgatas and upholding the treasury of the Dharma-jewel, one subsequently attains Buddhahood, named Dharmaprabhāsa (Dharma-Illumination).

Making offerings to the Tathāgatas constitutes the fulfillment of merit cultivated throughout the three periods of time. Upholding the treasury of the Dharma constitutes the fulfillment of wisdom, as it entails the complete knowledge of all dharma-gates.
This section generally clarifies the perfection of the causes; the following two lines clarify the fulfillment of the fruits.
The two verses concern the names of the lands and eons.
That land is named "Excellent Purity" (*Suviśuddha*), composed of the seven treasures, and its eon is named "Jewel Radiance" (*Ratnaprabhāsa*).
Since it is named "Excellent Purity" and is further composed of the seven treasures, it is certainly a land of true retribution (*vipākabhūmi*); therefore, [it is] the land.
The people within it all fly through the air with complete mastery; this is why the kalpa is named "Jewel Radiance. △ Third, a verse on the adornment and purity of the land:
"The assembly of bodhisattvas is exceedingly numerous, their count being immeasurable billions... (omitted)... I now speak of them only briefly."
The preceding seventeen lines of verse praise the adornment and purity of the buddha-field; each may be explained according to the text.
The six lines beginning with "Pūrṇa" summarize the venerable one’s great case from beginning to end, pointing directly to it by saying:

"The venerable one’s great cause and great fruit emphasize that the foundation lies in the teaching of the Dharma. All sutras compare the path to the two types of giving—material wealth and the Dharma—and certainly [establish] this as the definitive [criterion].
The gift of Dharma is supreme; how much more so when the Dharma can cause people to transcend birth and death, realize the Dharma-body, and continue the life of wisdom.
Now, based on the efficacy of the gift of Dharma, its causes and fruits are shown to be particularly sublime. The initial bestowal of the prediction upon Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra is hereby concluded.
△ Second, the bestowal of predictions upon the remaining assembly. This is divided into three parts. First, the request made by those present in the assembly:
At that time, the twelve hundred arhats... (up to) "would it not also be a joy for us to be like the other great disciples?"
This also records the thoughts of those [Arhats] as described by the compiler of the sutra. Zhizhi says:
"At the beginning of the 'Teaching through Dharma,' the twelve hundred Arhats still claimed they did not know where this meaning was heading.

By the time of the 'Teaching through Parable,' although they knew that the three vehicles were provisional and the One Vehicle was the reality, they remained attached to their minor fruits and did not give rise to a single thought of aspiration."

With such a mind, how could one hope for the prediction of attaining Buddhahood? The Buddha, knowing that they were still attached to the "transformed city," therefore spoke of the causes and conditions of his own accord without being asked.
For the sake of the assembly, he drew back to recount distant past events, whereupon the twelve hundred disciples were like those returning from a midday dream;
they finally believed that the jewel within their robes had never been lost. Now, seeing Pūrṇa receive his prediction, they believe that they themselves shall become Buddhas. Therefore...

Each [of them] thought to themselves, "We hope for such a prediction. Tiantai says: "Because they are not afflicted by the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*), it is said that their minds are sovereign.
The *Zhīyīn* says: "Our joy is such that, reflecting upon the 'Expedient Means' chapter, we must experience great rapture;
we know for ourselves that we shall become Buddhas. Ah! This single cycle of causes and conditions has exerted a profound power over these twelve hundred people. It may be said: [so it is].
One sees that the sequential order of the three cycles in the scriptural text is not established in vain. △ Second, the Tathāgata bestows predictions.
This is divided into two parts. First, the prose section. This is divided into three parts. First, the general prediction for the twelve hundred [disciples].

The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in the minds of these [people] (up to the point of their receiving the prediction of *samyak-saṃbodhi*), granted the prediction for all one thousand two hundred people whose thoughts and aspirations were identical.

That he immediately bestowed the prediction upon them was because he placed primary emphasis on the power of faith. Zhizhi says: "From the three assemblies onwards, the seeds [of awakening] that have been heard..."
The various expositions regarding the view have already been made clear; by means of a single faith, one enters and abides in the stage of realization.
Therefore, the reason for summoning Mahākāśyapa and bestowing upon him a prophetic declaration was that there was a specific intention to be entrusted.

Moreover, this also serves to conclude the case from the "Expedient Means" chapter, wherein it was stated that all twelve hundred arhats shall likewise become Buddhas. 2. The Separate Prophecy of Kauṇḍinya.

Among this assembly, my great disciple, the bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya—[up to] the Buddha, the World-Honored One, Teacher of Gods and Men—was the first to realize the Way and dwells as the foremost among the multitude; therefore, he is given a special prediction.
After receiving this prediction, the Venerable One still made offerings to sixty-two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, which was precisely his profound original vow. He desired...
Having fulfilled the merits of the two benefits, the fruit is named "Universal Radiance" (Puming). The essential explanation states:
it is because one uses the light of wisdom to shatter the darkness of all delusions, universally causing sentient beings to clearly understand the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Miaole asks:

"If he was recorded separately at the very beginning, why was he not recorded during the first cycle [of teaching]? Answer: "If we consider actual practice, there are distinct conditions for the Great and Small Vehicles."

The two initial stages differ. Śāriputra first established a great connection; therefore, he attained awakening during the first cycle [of the wheel of Dharma]. Ājñātakauṇḍinya first established a minor connection;
therefore, he attained awakening at the Deer Park. If one considers their expedient practices for guiding sentient beings, the intentions of these two are each distinct.
The methods of manifesting traces cannot be standardized in a single way. △ Third, the postscript concerning the five hundred [disciples]:
those five hundred arhats (up to) all share the same name, called Puming (Universal Radiance).

Kālodāyin—this is translated as "Black Radiance" (Heiguang) or "Coarse Black" (Cūhe). His complexion was black yet luminous. Cūḍapanthaka—or Cūḍali—is translated as "Born by the Side of the Great Road.
According to the *Buddha-benxing-jing* (Sutra on the Original Deeds of the Buddha): His mother followed her husband to another country;
after a long time she became pregnant. As her delivery neared, she longed to return home. While traveling halfway there, she gave birth.
Son, in this manner he gave birth twice, producing two sons in total; they were distinguished by their seniority and juniority.
The younger was Śāgata, also called Pāṇḍaka, or Pānta; this means "born by the side of a small path.

All other matters are as explained in the Introduction Chapter (Nidāna-parivarta). Question: The World-Honored One previously granted permission, saying, "These are the twelve hundred; I shall now [act for them]."

Regarding the sequential prediction and the bestowal of the prophecy upon Dignāga, why is it that [the Buddha] singled out the five hundred [Arhats], and within those five hundred, further singled out the three Kāśyapas, Kāludāyin, and others? How can this be reconciled?
Answer: The principle of expansion and abbreviation has already been clarified in the titles of the chapters. It is simply that while the five hundred were present, [others were not].

Honored Seat. As for the three Kāśyapas and the ten great disciples, during the period of the Āgamas, they were the leaders among the assembly and had previously served as teachers to twelve hundred followers;

this is why they are mentioned separately. If one speaks of "granting" [the prediction], since the Tathāgata has already said they will receive it "in succession," and has also said that "all shall attain it," and further that they "shall all have the same name," then these twelve hundred...
There is nothing that this does not exhaustively encompass. They share the same name, "Universal Radiance" (Puming), because they have equally realized the wisdom of universal radiance.
△ Second, the verse summary, divided into two parts. First, a preliminary verse summarizing the bestowal of predictions upon Cienru and the five hundred [disciples].
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya shall behold immeasurable Buddhas... [omitted] ...therefore he is named Samantaprabhāsa."

The first four lines of the verse describe the perfection of causes. While the prose commentary merely states that one "shall make offerings to sixty-two billion [Buddhas]," the present text says that one "shall see immeasurable Buddhas.

It should be understood that "making offerings" refers to events following the attainment of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) from this day forward, whereas "seeing immeasurable Buddhas" is spoken in terms of the three periods of time; it comprehensively discusses the causal practices throughout the three periods.
There are those who exceed an *asaṃkhyeya* [kalpa]. The following six phrases clarify the fulfillment of the fruit.

This explains the virtues of the fruit, which are fivefold: first, radiance; second, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); third, renown; fourth, the respect of the multitude; and fifth, the preaching of the Dharma.
Because these various real virtues exist, one perceives this excellent reputation.
That land is pure, and its bodhisattvas are all courageous, possessing such supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
This verse concerns the purity of the *adhiṣṭhāna* (the environment). "Dharma" belongs to the category of courage.

As for "ascending the pavilions to travel through various lands," this means that without even leaving the threshold of one's chamber, there is nowhere they do not pervade. As for "making unsurpassed offerings to the Buddhas," it refers to...

This is the offering made by directing the mind. To offer to the Buddha with joy and return to one's country in an instant means that although myriad functions arise together, they do not depart from their proper place.
When those in the land of Amitābha Buddha offer to the ten directions, it is done precisely at the time of eating.

He then returned to his own country. All of this was due to the bodhisattva’s supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) being such as this; therefore it is said that he possesses this supernatural power. The Buddha’s lifespan was sixty thousand *kalpas*;

the period of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) remained for twice that duration, and the period of the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*) remained for twice that again. When this Dharma perished, devas and humans were filled with grief.
The *Zhīyīn* (Record of Knowledge) states: "This record has four parts: first, a record of the Buddha’s full lifespan; second, a record of the True Dharma (*saddharma*);

third, a record of the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*); and fourth, a record of the Final Dharma (*paścima-dharma*). The fact that gods and humans grieve over the extinction of the Dharma pertains entirely to the affairs of the Final Dharma.
These all supplement what was not previously present in the prose section. The verse concerning the single individual, Ājñātakauṇḍinya, is likewise."
Those five hundred bhikṣus shall successively become Buddhas, as described above for each case.
These fourteen phrases follow the pattern of the single instance of Cunda, yet they collectively eulogize the causes and effects of all five hundred persons.
The term "a certain person" (amuka) is used as a designation for the successive bestowal of predictions upon the five hundred. Just as when Cunda entered parinirvāṇa, [the Buddha] said: "I..."
"After my parinirvāṇa, Upatiṣya, you shall become a Buddha. Your adornments of the primary and secondary realms, as well as the world you shall convert, will be no different from mine.
The supernatural powers, majestic virtue, True Dharma, and Semblance Dharma of that Buddha and his disciples shall likewise be so."
The number of kalpas for their lifespans need not be stated further; they are all likewise non-dual, as previously described.
This concludes the five hundred [disciples]. △ Second, a general verse summarizing the bestowal of predictions upon all the śrāvakas.
"Kāśyapa, you already know [the account] from 'the five hundred masters' (up to) 'you should proclaim it for them.
This was the entrustment to Mahākāśyapa. As for the remaining seven hundred, their predictions are complete.

Regarding their physical and spiritual causes and effects, the adornments of their kalpas and lands, and the lifespans of their True and Semblance Dharma periods—all are identical and without distinction. Although you have not yet received this direct oral instruction face-to-face, you..."
One may explain each of these in detail. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "One receives the prediction of enlightenment in one's presence;
one also receives the prediction of enlightenment in one's absence. How marvelous is the scriptural text! Its essential summary is thus.
△ Third, the assembly’s realization and understanding. This is divided into two parts. First, the prose section, which is further divided into two. First, the narrator describes their joy.
At that time, the five hundred arhats [from "approached" until] prostrated their heads at his feet, repenting and reproaching themselves.
This summarizes the meaning of the causal conditions from past lives between myself and you all mentioned previously, and completes the text of the chapter on the Parable of the Phantom City.
At the previously marked point, the World-Honored One granted universal predictions to the twelve hundred people; this now recounts that.
Xiezi said only "five hundred," referring specifically to those present at the assembly who were recorded as having received the prediction.

Thus, he stated that they had received their predictions before the Buddha, thereby excluding the seven hundred members who were not part of that specific assembly. As for "rejoicing and leaping for joy," this refers to the inner celebration of their good fortune;
it follows from the previous hope for a prediction: "If the World-Honored One would grant us each a prediction, would that not be most delightful?"
Ah! Now that things have occurred exactly as originally wished, one ought to feel immeasurable joy.
This is why I have risen from my seat to pay homage and confess my transgressions. Herein, the emphasis lies in the phrase "confessing and reproaching oneself":

failing to believe that one's own mind becomes a Buddha, failing to practice the great deeds of a Bodhisattva, and forgetting the causes and conditions of long ago—this constitutes a betrayal of the Tathāgata’s compassion.
"Rescue! All of this stems from my past transgressions. Because I have now attained new awakening, I feel remorse and reproach myself.

The two characters for 'self-reproach' carry a weight that exceeds even the state of sacrificing one's physical form or losing one's life. In the past, though I repeatedly received reprimands from the Buddha, I still did not recognize my faults.
Now that I have awakened to and clarified this Way and have received the sublime prediction [of enlightenment], I therefore reproach myself for the stubbornness of my former delusions."
Yet we did not realize the true emptiness early on; our regret is boundless. △ Second, the personal confession of understanding, divided into two parts. First, the explanation by way of Dharma:
"World-Honored One, we have constantly harbored this thought, believing ourselves to have already attained ultimate *nirvāṇa*; now we know it for what it is."
In this passage, the place where the metaphors are explained refers to the World-Honored One (Bhagavān) as being most intimate. It is not that he is so called because he is invisible or unattainable;

rather, the word "I" refers to Ājñātakauṇḍinya. The phrase "and others" includes the five hundred [disciples]. "Constantly harboring thoughts" refers to the fault of persistent delusion, which has not been present for a single day.
From the words "considering oneself... onwards, it is the expression of repentance; that is, to be satisfied with a mere small attainment. There is no... [end of fragment].
This is the aspiration of the Mahāyāna. This precisely illuminates the meaning of the "one liberation" taught by the Buddha in the *Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*.

Our intention was that we too had attained this Dharma and reached *nirvāṇa*. Now, the single phrase "only now do I know it" is precisely a rebuke for our dull faculties and shallow wisdom, for not having awakened early to this wondrous Dharma.
One must understand that Cundabhadrā and the others were already [enlightened] in the past.
Those who have long served within the imperial palace have seen everything without exception as the World-Honored One handled them from beginning to end.
It was like when he first poked his head out and said, "In the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am honored. At that moment, one might think, "I shall realize enlightenment here.
Yet throughout forty years, as things were revealed at every turn, I simply failed to realize enlightenment at every turn—until this very assembly where he finally let down his eyebrows.

The intermittent light emerged as he emerged from samādhi to extol his virtues, employing both dharma-explanations and parables; yet, for the most part, these were like playing the Ninefold Shao music for the deaf.
Only when he spoke of the causal conditions and the illusory city did they finally attain clarity. One may say they were the height of dullness and stupidity.
Thus reproaching himself, he was in the same mold as Śāriputra’s self-reproach and the four disciples’ discourse on the parable of the impoverished son. △
Second, the explanation by way of similes. This also has two parts. First, a brief citation of the simile:
"Just as one who lacks wisdom... [omitted] ...and thus considers their own meager wisdom to be sufficient."
In the Parable of the Burning House, the Tathāgata said: "Those who possess wisdom attain understanding through parables.

Since this has already been explained by way of a parable and further by way of causes and conditions, how can it be said that they lack wisdom? Looking now at the Chapter on Expedient Means, one does not yet know where the meaning of this teaching leads.
It was previously said that they did not know; now they do know. Because their realization came late, [it is said they were ignorant].
Regarding the phrase "like one who lacks wisdom," the following section provides an inquiry and clarification. Why is it said to be like one who lacks wisdom?

To say nothing of the immeasurable wisdom possessed by the Tathāgata, which was originally intended for me to attain, I have failed to seek it diligently; instead, I am content with a mere small measure of wisdom.
Is this not indeed a great folly? By observing the two characters "should-attain" (應得), one can clearly understand what has been newly realized today.
One penetrates the wondrous clarity of original enlightenment and opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; thus, all darkness is utterly extinguished.
△ Second, the actual presentation of the analogy, divided into two parts. First, the opening of the parable, which further has two parts. First, being intoxicated and unaware.
World-Honored One, it is as if there were a person who went to the house of a close friend; [the friend] tied a pearl inside the person's garment and departed with them.
This is the Parable of the Tied Pearl, concerning the Prince on the Neck (*Kandhaka*) forming a karmic connection. Tiantai says: "The person" refers to those of the Two Vehicles;
"the close friend" refers to the Sixteenth Prince; "the house" refers to the teachings of the Mahāyāna; and the phrase "drunk with wine" [refers to their initial state].

This means that at that time, their great capacity for awakening was briefly aroused and ignorance was temporarily suppressed, enabling them to hear the sutra and gain a slight understanding within their minds, as if arriving at the home of a close friend.
However, because their ignorance was still heavy, they once again lost their way, like one who has fallen asleep after drinking wine.

There are two meanings of "intoxication": first, heavy intoxication, wherein one is entirely unaware; second, light intoxication, wherein one perceives slightly but soon forgets, which is also termed "non-awareness.
Although there are these two meanings, they ultimately result in the "tying of the jewel," like the metaphor of the poison-drum. Regarding the phrase "when it is time to act" (*dang xing*):

this clarifies that when the Prince’s spiritual capacities manifest elsewhere, he adapts to conditions and responds accordingly; thus it is called "time to act. This refers to the propagation of the Dharma and transformation.
He knew it was not his private business; therefore, it is called "official business. The priceless jewel is the true wisdom of the suchness of the one vehicle’s true reality (*tathatā*).
"Tying it inside the garment" means that shame, remorse, and patience can conceal ugliness and anger, as well as ward off external evils—this constitutes the outer garment.
The mind of faith and joy internally wraps around the roots of goodness—this constitutes the inner garment. At that time...
Hearing the Dharma and having a slight inclination toward faith and joy is the seed of the wisdom of the immediate cause (*vyañjana-hetu*).
Such a person lies drunk and unconscious of it; even if they obtain a small measure of realization, they consider it sufficient.

Tiantai says: "Drunk and lying down, one does not wake" means that during the interval between [the previous state and awakening], one is indolent and regresses, failing to receive the Great Dharma because the mind of ignorance is heavy.
"Seeking again, yet not remembering" means that after rising, one wanders; this indicates that during the interval, one is met with the minor teachings of the transformation of the Three Vehicles.
Because the roots of goodness desire to sprout and one grows weary of suffering while seeking joy, it is said: "Having risen, one wanders."

This explains the obscuration of ignorance: because one does not know how to turn back toward the source to seek the clothing and food of the Mahāyāna, it is said that one seeks the clothing and food of the Hīnayāna in another land.
If one compares the Buddha and Māra, the realm of birth-and-death (saṃsāra) under the sway of Māra is "another land," while both the Great and Small Vehicles of the Buddha-Dharma are one's "own land.
Even when comparing the Great and Small Vehicles themselves, the Hīnayāna has not yet escaped birth-and-death; thus, it remains "other."
The Mahāyāna is the land from which one is eternally liberated from birth and death; it is one's own original country, the ultimate return to the source.

This refers precisely to turning one's back on the Mahāyāna country and going instead to the soil of the Hīnayāna—failing to know how to draw sustenance from the pearl, yet seeking to support oneself through hired labor.
"Obtaining the price of a single day" means being content with what little one has gained. Regarding "food, clothing, and so forth," the *Zhijin* (Record of Sounds) says:
This is a metaphor for the five hundred people who, having become deluded regarding their original nature, fell into the five realms of existence.

Unable to avoid seeking the food and clothing of the blessings of humans and devas, they venerate water and worship fire, observe the precepts of oxen and dogs, and laboriously strive to seek them out—a process that is exceedingly difficult and arduous. △ Two.
A close friend awakened him.
Later, that friend encountered him (and asked), "What has become of your food and clothing?
and so forth, until [he explained] how he had sown the seeds from the great penetration of the jewel down to the present forty years later. Therefore, it is said, "later encountered."

[Zhaozhou] saw him. Zhizhi said: "This follows the parable of the impoverished son. It corresponds to the elder’s third turning, when [the son], with his body covered in dust and dirt, happens upon the place where refuse is being cleared;
[the elder] employs skillful means to see his son. That [text] says, 'Ho! You man!

This describes the time of Prajñā, when both the ultimate and the conventional are simultaneously transcended. Therefore it says, 'You have always been doing this,' which describes not yet having attained the ultimate and the conventional."
It is all one and the same. Therefore it is said: "What is the use of clothing and food? and so forth, up to "it is thus.

"Alas!"—this is the sound of a shout to awaken [the mind]. "Dharma-vin" (丈夫) is a beautiful epithet for a man. Since you are already addressed as a "Dharma-vin," it is known that your fundamental vision possesses a majestic and lofty spirit;
it is simply that you have not yet unfolded it. If you were to attain the perfection of merit and wisdom, you would be revered by devas and humans, and turn back [samsara].
"O Great Wheel! How could he not be a truly great man? Why speak of food and clothing? These are the words of a most strange friend.
Even if there were truly no jewel and one had to endure such hardships, they might still be bearable. But now, the divine jewel is inherently present;
it can naturally bring about great abundance. If it were brought forth, it could even universally relieve the myriad beings."
[The Buddha said: "How is it that you strive so diligently for nothing but food and clothing? Therefore, he gave him the jewel below to show him:
'In the past, I wished to bring you peace and happiness... [omitted] ...to seek a livelihood for yourself in such a manner is truly foolish.'"
This explains the matter of tying a priceless jewel within one’s robe; that is to say, when I was among the sixteen princes, I have previously spoken of it for you as well.

The "Record of Knowledge" states: "In such-and-such a month and year" refers to the time when the Buddha Jñāna entered meditative absorption for eighty-four thousand *kalpas*, and the sixteen princes served as lecturers. The passage above says: "At ease with the five desires..."

"Arbitrarily. This metaphor refers to the enjoyment of the fruition upon attaining Buddhahood, which is the adornment of the true recompense (*sambhoga-kāya*), where wisdom and principle are perfected.
This statement uses the "priceless jewel" and other such items as a metaphor for the Buddha’s cultivation of the great seeds during his causal stage.
"That which now exists" means that the Dharma-nature, previously pointed out, has been inherently present from the beginning and has never been lost; yet you do not know this.
Obstructed by ignorance, although they obtain a small fruit, they forget its great cause; thus, while undergoing diligent toil, sorrow, and affliction, their folly may be said to be extreme.
The preceding section generally belongs to the exposition of the teaching; from here on, it provides instruction for awakening and entry.
"You may now trade this jewel for whatever you require; thus you shall always have your wishes fulfilled and never lack anything.

This exhortation to trade is an analogy for receiving the prediction of attaining Buddhahood. The *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states: "Although the price of the jewel is immeasurable, it must be traded before it can be of practical use.
Likewise, although the internal realization of the *liàoyīn* (the cause of completion) is ultimate, it must rely upon past seeds [of cultivation]."

It is easy to manifest in practice because one’s former understanding of a single thing as the understanding of all things is now exchanged for the present practice of a single action as the practice of all actions.
Just as the substance of a jewel is inexhaustible and its exchange is infinite, one must listen further and cultivate further before the functional power of this treasure can be fully revealed.
It is like obtaining a *maṇi* jewel in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which must undergo ten kinds of polishing before it can rain down treasures.

When one's practice and understanding are in accord, one is then worthy of the Buddha’s prediction. From this point onward, one possesses the robe of the patience of cessation (*śānti-kṣānti*) and the food of *Śūraṅgama*.
With immeasurable jewels for self-cultivation and transforming others, the state of non-effort (*anābhoga*) is inexhaustible for both oneself and others.
The "Knowledgeable One" says: to realize the fruit through the cause is called "exchange" (*mào*); to achieve the great from the small is called "transformation" (*yì*). △ Second, the combination.
The analogy is divided into two parts. First, the union with the state of being intoxicated and unaware:
the Buddha was likewise when he was a bodhisattva; [up to] his vow for omniscience remains intact and has not been lost.
The preceding section establishes the thesis through analogy; the subsequent section clarifies the essential point through the Dharma. Since the Dharma and the analogy are identical, it is said:
"The Buddha is also like this. The Direct Pointing states: "At the time he was a Bodhisattva, when [the Buddha] pointed to himself as one of the sixteen śrāmaṇeras, that was the mind of omniscience."

The *Lotus Sūtra* comprehensively subsumes the myriad practices of both the provisional and the real; however, because one merely received them in a vague and superficial manner, they were soon forgotten.
The passage following "having attained the stage of an Arhat" generally describes how past delusions regarding the partial and small [vehicles] remain undispersed;

it correctly clarifies that the seeds of the Path from former conditions still persist. In Tiantai’s topical outline, this corresponds to the four phrases beginning with "The Buddha was likewise," which correspond to the analogy of the tied jewel.
Then, following the two subsequent lines: "Together intoxicated, we were unaware. Having attained [this state], one should rise and wander forth.
△ Second, the convergence of friends' awakening:
"Now the World-Honored One has awakened us... (up to) ...yet you claim to have truly attained parinirvāṇa."
This correctly clarifies the present awakening. The phrase "awakening us" refers to the exposition of the three stages of instruction (*triparivarta*).

It also summarizes the passage from the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paryāya*) which states: "Although I speak of *nirvāṇa*, this is not yet the true extinction," and so forth. The remainder is as explained previously, combining it with the passages on the reprimand and the display of the jewel.
“World-Honored One, it is only now that I truly know myself to be a bodhisattva” (up to) “I am filled with great joy at having attained what I never had before.

This directly clarifies the expression of gratitude for receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). It points directly to the fact that one delivers sentient beings who are of the same nature as oneself, severs afflictions that are of the same nature as oneself, studies dharma-gates that are of the same nature as oneself, and accomplishes the Tathāgata who is of the same nature as oneself; therefore, it says, “it is only now that I know. [This refers to] mind, Buddha, and sentient beings.
Third, non-differentiation. The triad of faculty, object, and consciousness—both in essence and function—is *tathatā* (suchness); therefore, one receives the prediction of *tri-bodhi*.
The following three phrases conclude the initial expression of exultant joy at the beginning of the chapter. II. Verse Recitation. This is divided into two parts.
Within a single verse, their minds attained understanding.
At that time, Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the others, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Having heard the voice of the unsurpassed, peaceful prediction [of our enlightenment]... (up to)... we individually repent of all our transgressions."
The first four lines of the verse express the joy and gratitude for receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). The final two lines express the confession of faults;
by saying "I repent of all my transgressions," one reveals the depth of today’s realization and the intensity of one's sense of shame and remorse. II.
The verse on the personal statement of realization, divided into two parts: A. The verse on the Dharma-exposition.
Regarding the Buddha-treasure, they had attained but a small portion of nirvāṇa;
in their verses, they claimed for themselves that they had already attained extinction. Now, however, they realize this:

when they first heard that the wisdom of the Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable, it seemed as though it were separated from them by thousands of miles; they did not know at all what kind of realm it was. Now, finally...

The contemplation of the reality of all phenomena used by Bodhisattvas to transform others is called 'skillful deliverance' (*qiǎo dù*). △ Fifth, praising [the teaching] in terms of its fruit.
Furthermore, there are five [points]. First, clarifying proximity:
"There are sentient beings who seek the Buddha-way" (up to) "they shall attain proximity to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
This passage praises the Dharma by way of its fruit. One should know that "it must be near" refers to what Tiantai calls the "near station" within the *Anraku-gyō* (Practices of Peaceful Conduct).
This fruit of Bodhi has as its essence the sphere of knowledge and vision of the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom;
it is of two kinds: first, the Bodhi of the initial mind, which is the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*); second, the Bodhi of the final mind, which is...
"Wondrous Enlightenment. What is now called "near" refers precisely to being close to the Bodhi of the First Abode (Prathamābhūmi). △ Second, the opening of the analogy:
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, it is like a person who, parched with thirst, requires water... [up to] "...his mind is resolved that the water must be near."
This further clarifies the Dharma through a parable. This parable is to be understood on two levels. First, seeking water on high ground indicates that it is still far off;
this pertains to the provisional (upāya). Second, seeking water in moist soil pertains to the real (tattva).

Some point out that those, whether lay or ordained, who practice the bodhisattva path and suffer from thirst and exhaustion require water; this is a general indication of the urgency with which they seek the Way, pointing directly [to their condition].
It is said: "Thirst" is a metaphor for the oppression of the burning house of the triple world; "exhaustion" is a metaphor for not yet attaining the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
"water" is a metaphor for the principle of the true suchness (tathatā) of the threefold equality; "needing water" is a metaphor for diligently seeking the Buddha-way.

The "high plateau" is a metaphor for the provisional teachings of the Āgamas and Vaipulya sūtras. To analyze form and clarify emptiness is called "digging"; to fully awaken to the twelve links of dependent origination is called [the completion of the well].
He pierced through [the veil] and attained the principle of partial emptiness, which was like dry soil. For two years, he sat and maintained this partial emptiness as the ultimate goal;
yet only the Buddha knew that it was not true *nirvāṇa*. Thus it is said: "He knew the water was still far off.
Without ceasing his efforts, he used the *prajñā* of twenty-two years to sift and refine [his realization], yet he remained outside the gate, lodging for the night in the grass.
The character "ān" (菴) is used as a name for a child; this is a metaphor for seeing moist soil and thus obtaining a name for the child.

One thereby comes to know the family estate of the elder. This is a metaphor for gradually reaching the mud. Once the family estate is known, it will certainly be entrusted [to one]; this is a metaphor for knowing that water must be near.
The two characters "definitive" (niyata) refer to opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, severing doubt, and engendering faith. This is an illustration of the Dharma by means of a metaphor.

This explains "proximity.

they all pertain to the four characters of this sutra, and their meaning is profound. Thus, there is no gateway previously described as difficult to understand or difficult to enter that one will not penetrate.
The following further clarifies its profound and immeasurable nature. That is to say, this treasury of the sutra first proceeds from all phenomena back to mere emptiness;

Therefore, it is called "profound. Furthermore, from the limit of reality, it turns back to contemplate all phenomena; they cannot be grasped from the front, nor can they be avoided from behind, being like Mount Sumeru.

therefore, it is called "profound. From the Ten Abodes up to Equal Enlightenment, it is likened to traveling five hundred *yojanas* before reaching the place of treasure;

therefore, it is called "distant. Even having reached Equal Enlightenment, one is still separated by a single layer. How could this be easily reached by ordinary people? Therefore, it is called "non-existent."
"Human beings can reach it. This refers to the final three phrases, meaning that having now received the Buddha’s transformation and attained fulfillment, they have become bodhisattvas;

"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* (up to the point where it says), 'you should know that they are those of overweening pride,' these must be the eight thousand newly resolved bodhisattvas and the five thousand who rose from their seats and departed. "Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there are good sons (or daughters of good family) [who wish to preach this sutra], they should then extensively expound this sutra for the fourfold assembly.

"The Tathāgata’s chamber" refers to [the great compassion] among all sentient beings... "The Tathāgata’s seat" refers to the emptiness of all phenomena.
This explanation clarifies three kinds of protective sheltering. That is to say, the Dharma-preacher should first give rise to the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings;

Compassion (*karuṇā*) can uproot suffering; because great loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*) can establish sentient beings in peace, it is metaphorically called the "Tathāgata’s dwelling.

This means that by expounding the Dharma through the two wisdoms of the provisional and the ultimate, one accords with the essence of the absolute and the conventional to adorn sentient beings. Even if there should be those who cling...

Therefore, the two gates of compassion and wisdom are likened to the Tathāgata’s robe. Furthermore, this points to the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus), as well as the phenomena of the ultimate and conventional truths.

The very essence of reality is entirely empty; this constitutes the Tathāgata’s seat. Because all phenomena are without self and without what belongs to a self, one perceives the twelve classes of sentient beings within the triple world as being like reflections in a mirror or flowers in the sky. Thus, one first ceases to hold the view of them as real sentient beings and settles the mind.
One then preaches the Dharma for these illusion-like sentient beings; therefore, the emptiness and quiescence of all phenomena constitute the Tathāgata’s seat.

The preceding statement asks how one should preach and further explains that it must be preached in such a manner; this is sufficient to demonstrate that if it were otherwise, it would not conform to the proper method of preaching the Dharma.
The fact that the term "Tathāgata" is mentioned three times indicates that these three types of ritual protocols all follow the established traditions of the Tathāgata.
Tiantai asked: For what reason are these three dharmas designated as the "Dharma Master"? He answered: It is based on the phenomenal level (*vastu*).
One must ascend the hall, adjust one's robes, and take one’s seat before one may proclaim [the Dharma]. Furthermore, compassion gives rise to all that is good;

"Abiding therein" means that one subsequently preaches this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* with a mind free from indolence.
"Therein" refers to the three dharmas. By not being indolent—that is, by employing diligence—one adorns these three dharmas and is thus able to preach them extensively.
Tiantai says: "The five kinds of Dharma-preachers use these three dharmas as their own standard of conduct; therefore, it is said 'abiding.'"
Within this context, because one employs these means to transform others, it says, "with a mind free from indolence," and so forth; this is the proper exhortation to practice.
△ Second, clarifying the benefits, which is divided into five parts. First, dispatching emanated persons.
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, in other lands I shall dispatch transformed beings to assemble for them a congregation to hear the Dharma.
This clarifies that the Tathāgata bestows his empowerment to dispatch a multitude to gather for the teaching. Tiantai says: "If one's initial resolve is not yet pure..."
For now, one may only dispatch emanated beings; it is not yet appropriate to dispatch emanations of the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of supernatural beings.
If one were to see devas and nāgas, they might rely on this to become arrogant, which would obstruct and damage their path. Therefore, they must not be allowed to see them.

If the mind is free from attachment and reliance, then one is already capable of seeing the Buddha—how much more so for devas and nāgas, up to those who have attained *dhāraṇī* and realized their own benefit? △ Second.
He dispatched a multitude of emanations, and also dispatched emanated bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs (up to: who heard the Dharma, believed and accepted it, followed it, and did not oppose it.

The previous [passage] spoke of dispatching emanated persons, but it was not clarified what kind of persons these were; it merely stated that they were for the sake of assembling a crowd to listen to the Dharma.
He appears to be a guide for people. This refers to the assembly of disciples.
Since they are those sent by the Tathāgata to transform others, they have received the Buddha’s command and come for the sake of the Dharma; upon hearing it, they will surely believe and accept it.
At all times and in all speech—whether provisional or real, great or small—they will comply with it without exception. △ Third, the dispatching of the eight classes of beings.

If a Dharma teacher is in a secluded place—ranging from such a location up to one where asuras and other beings listen to their preaching—a "secluded place" refers to a desolate spot where no people are present.
When the environment is tranquil and the mind is at ease, it is said that ghosts and spirits come to dwell there.
How much more so when this occurs by the mandate of the Buddha; this is a manifestation of the mutual resonance between the Way and its response. *Zhizhi* says:
Previously, he sent forth a manifested assembly to listen to the Dharma; now, he truly dispatches a celestial assembly to protect the Dharma.
In both cases, he uses his supernatural powers to provide protection. △ Fourth, seeing the Buddha’s body.
"Although I am in another land, I shall from time to time cause the Dharma-preacher to behold my body.
What was previously stated—that he dispatches celestial hosts to listen to the Dharma—whether they remain hidden or manifest, seems not yet definitive;
here it says "he beholds," which means looking face-to-face. The *Zhizhi* (Direct Pointing) says: "This is the Dharma Master’s mind resonating with the Buddha’s mind. It is an inspiration.

The Way should be practiced through mutual engagement; therefore, the Tathāgata manifests his physical presence to protect [beings], allowing them to see him from time to time, so that the sincerity of his mind in preaching the Dharma may be clearly perceived. △ Fifth, Bestowing Dhāraṇīs.
If one forgets the phrasing or the punctuation of this sutra, I shall explain it again for them so that they may attain completeness.

What was previously called "seeing [the Buddha] from time to time" and what is here called "I shall explain it again for them" both refer to the Dharma-preacher being in resonance with the Dharmakāya.
If one were to speak only of seeing the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*, or hearing the preaching of the Dharma by the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*, then [the connection] would be remote. △
The two verses are divided into two parts. First, the general exhortation:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Those who wish to abandon all indolence should listen to this sutra; it is difficult to hear, and those who can believe and understand it are also rare."
This is a general verse concerning the section on those who practice the bodhisattva path with excellence. "The indolent" refers to those of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas).

It is difficult for them to hear and difficult for them to believe, as this follows from the preceding discussion on being deep, firm, profound, and remote. When people have not yet attained the principle, indolence naturally arises.
All who wish to abandon indolence should, in accord with the underlying principle, listen to this sutra.
Through the perfect integration of principle and wisdom afforded by this sutra, even hearing it for a brief moment brings one closer to Bodhi; how much more so by hearing it over a long period?
Yet this sutra is difficult to hear and difficult to believe; those who can believe and accept it may be said to be like the udumbara flower. △ Second, the verse summary of the preceding section.
Two: One verse praises the sutra.
It is like a person who, thirsty and needing water, digs at a high plateau (until) they know for certain that water is near.
This verse uses the metaphor of finding water at varying distances, as explained previously.
"Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that such people as these... are close to the Buddha’s wisdom.

This section combines the parable with the verse. To say that this sutra is a "profound sutra" means that the various sutras spoken during the forty years prior were shallow and explicit, not yet discussing the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*);
it is only now, with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, that the gate of skillful means (*upāya-mukha*) is opened.
It reveals the true mark, stating that all śrāvakas are themselves bodhisattvas; this is therefore deeper than what preceded it and is the king among all sūtras.
If one can contemplate this with careful discernment, one will not be far from the Buddha-wisdom.

"If a person speaks this sutra, they should enter the Tathāgata’s chamber" [up to] "abiding here, one preaches the Dharma.
This verse marks and explains a section, which has already been clarified previously. "Fearlessness" refers to the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). [The details are] extensive.
To explain through differentiation is to practice both the provisional and the ultimate simultaneously.
When preaching this sutra, if there are those who revile one with evil speech... [down to] ...preaching the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

"It is exhausted.
