first, it means that if the Dharma Master is reading the sutras in a solitary location and forgets any passages or verses, I shall manifest my body to explain them for him. Second, if he is in a secluded... [text ends].

"This person delights in preaching the Dharma, making distinctions without hindrance" (up to) "attaining the vision of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
These eight phrases stand independently. They extensively clarify that the Dharma Master possesses unhindered eloquence and his mind is in accord with the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Because all Buddhas protect and cherish them as their own children, the sublime Dharma they expound causes listeners to perceive the Truth and attain the stage of joy;
furthermore, they entrust them to human and celestial beings to draw near to Mahāyāna teachers and study, so that they may swiftly obtain the wondrous fruits of the Mahāyāna.

The *Yinzhi* (Record of Sounds) states: "The final four lines serve as the thematic basis for the last two chapters. From 'If one draws near' onwards is the exhortation.

The "Introductory Section" (Kāraṇamukha). Following the previous section, this establishes the foundation for the attainment of the fruits of spiritual merit by those who become disciples of this sutra;

it serves as the introduction to the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa" that follows. This single chapter of the sutra exclusively elucidates the phrase: "the teaching of the Dharma for bodhisattvas."
The first half of this chapter teaches the Dharma for bodhisattvas acting as disciples; the second half teaches the Dharma for bodhisattvas acting as teachers.
The subsequent chapter, "Seeing the Jeweled Stūpa," clarifies solely the single phrase "protected by the Buddha's mindfulness.
It is seen that the Buddhas who provide such protection exist throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions.
The sectioning of the eleventh chapter, "The Appearance of the Jeweled Stūpa," states: This chapter is judged to be that which reveals the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*).

It is so designated because it displays the true realm of the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding *dharmakāya* and *tathatā*, desiring to cause sentient beings to know this and see this; this is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Indeed, this true realm of the Dharmakāya— wherein the sutra’s initial ray of light shines eastward, perfectly manifesting the phenomena of the Dharma-realm from the beginning to the end of both sentient beings and Buddhas—
is a universal demonstration of the wondrous nature of the mind and objects of all living beings.
Because the audience had not yet awakened to their own minds and failed to realize what was before their eyes, they have now received the Tathāgata’s various instructions and have attained faith.

The Buddha said: "Each of you has known for yourselves that you shall become Buddhas and has received a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). Although you believe in your own minds, you have not yet believed in the true realm of the *dharmatā*.

Therefore, as the World-Honored One approaches this point to reveal the permanence of the *dharmakāya*, he beholds a stupa of the seven treasures miraculously emerging from the earth, wherein the entire body of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna is present, in order to eliminate the view of arising and ceasing."
This Sahā world is transformed into a pure land three times in order to eliminate the attachment to purity and impurity.
Furthermore, the Buddhas of the ten directions fill its midst, clearly manifesting that every atom and every land within the *dharmadhātu* is, upon contact with the eye, nothing but the true realm.

This is the knowledge and vision of the True Buddha. The *Dàkuǎn* states: "From this chapter onward, through the three gates of Expedient Means (*upāya*), Parable (*dṛṣṭānta*), and Causal Conditions (*nidāna*), it causes..."
Those of the three faculties each attain realization and receive the prediction of enlightenment, becoming Dharma Princes who succeed to and uphold the lineage of the Sages.
By completing the two characters "awakening" (kai-wo), one also completes the section on the gate of wisdom being difficult to understand and difficult to enter.
Once awakened, in order that they may resolve to propagate the sutra and perform the deeds of a Dharma Master, the "Dharma Master" chapter first extensively praises the Dharma.
Regarding the Master’s merit: fearing that [the assembly] might not be willing to accept and uphold [the teaching], he relied upon Prabhūtaratna to personally present the model of the stupa.
Each of the Buddhas of the ten directions brought a single scroll of the Great Sutra as testimony, presenting it face-to-face so that people might see it directly once.

Only then would they be willing to make the vow to accept and uphold it; subsequently, they were able to enter. Thus, with the two characters "completed" (了) and "shown entry" (示入), this matter is also concluded.

The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable; thus, the first half of this chapter demonstrates the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, while the second half causes [the disciples] to make vows and uphold [this teaching].
This is what is meant by "a single drop of ink forming two dragons. The significance of this chapter is not slight; having already seen the stupa and further heard its sound, one should...
Those who hear and see this will surely not fail to conceive thoughts of its extraordinary nature. Possessing such thoughts, they will inevitably seek to open the stupa.

From this, [the Buddha] initiates the gathering of his emanations, the transformation of the pure land, the proclamation of the lifespan, and the manifestation of spiritual powers—many such wonders as these.
All of these are for the sake of those with new records [of faith], to broaden their perspective and exhaustively reveal the Buddha’s knowledge.
It is seen. Thus, the stupa represents the Dharma-body, which is the principle that is seen; the character "see" (見) refers to the person who is able to see.
Since this is a direct vision at this stage, when the earth subsequently transforms and the Buddhas assemble, there will be no realm whatsoever that is not directly known.
Therefore, this knowledge and vision does not depend solely upon the future attainment of Buddhahood and the subsequent perfection of merit and wisdom.
Thus, one immediately attains a small portion of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Otherwise, how could one fulfill the Tathāgata’s great purpose for appearing in the world?
△ Second, revealing the wondrous realm of the single truth. The Tathāgata issues this call:
Seeking its circulation is divided into two parts. First, the prose section, which is divided into three. First, the emergence of Prabhūtaratna, which is further divided into six.
First, the appearance of the stupa.
At that time, before the Buddha, there was a stupa made of the seven treasures, adorned with various precious objects.

This clarifies the characteristics of the stupa. "At that time" refers to when the people of the three cycles give rise to the wisdom of initial awakening (*shiqiao*) and perceive the principle of original awakening (*benjue*).
Regarding the "seven treasures," the Direct Pointing says: they symbolize the wondrous wisdom of the stages of faith, abiding, practice, transference, and the grounds (*bhūmi*). Treasure.
The *stūpa* represents the realm of ultimate reality (*dharmatā*) and is the locus upon which the *dharmakāya* relies.
Because it realizes and dwells in the perfect principle of the five stages—such as the stage of "abiding"—through the wisdom of the provisional and the real, it is five hundred *yojanas* high.

Because wisdom penetrates the three aggregates (*skandha*) and the seven elements (*mahābhūta*), all of which are the *tathāgatagarbha*, it is two hundred and fifty *yojanas* wide. In terms of the measurement of *yojanas*, its height is twice [its width].

The ten thousand *li* represent the simultaneous transformation of the environment and its inhabitants (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), transcending both the ultimate and conventional truths (*paramārtha-saṃvṛti-satya*). The breadth of ten thousand *li* represents the single true mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*).

Because the three cycles [of teaching] have shattered the heavy defilements of the two attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) and the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-bhūmi*), the stupa is seen to surge forth from the earth.
Because non-reliant wisdom (*anāśrita-jñāna*) accords with the non-reliant principle (*anāśrita-tattva*), the stupa abides in mid-air. Thus, in various ways...
The multitude [of features] refers to concentration and wisdom. That which adorns them is all that is contained within the single principle.
There are five thousand railings and ten million grottoes and chambers, reaching as high as the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings.
Tiantai said: "The railings represent the Dharma of *dhāraṇī*. The thousands of myriad chambers signify immeasurable compassion, and are also immeasurable empty rooms.
The banners and pennants are the superior marks of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). As for the hanging jeweled necklaces..."
The merits of the forty stages adorn the Dharma-body above and clothe sentient beings below. The ten billion jeweled chimes represent the eightfold voice and the four types of eloquence.
The fragrance emanating from the four sides represents the wind of the Path of the Four Truths blowing the scent of the four virtues.
The banners and canopies composed of the seven treasures symbolize that the myriad differentiated practices all flow from the principle and wisdom of the seven stages.
It rises four *yojana*s high. This signifies that the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*) transcends the four currents of existence (*catasra oghāḥ*).

The universal assembly of all Buddhas signifies that causal practices encompass the ocean of the fruit. In this state of non-action, cause and effect mutually trust one another.
Indeed, essence and function are identical as one: the three transformations of the land create a land of quiescence, wherein the two Tathāgatas are unified as one.
True Suchness: the three bodies as one essence, the four lands as one mind. The great dream of the ten dharma realms is suddenly and completely unveiled;
the boundless fruit of Buddhahood is accomplished in a single instant. The grand undertaking of the Trace Gate is now nearing its completion.
Summoning the assembly to circulate [this teaching] and succeed to the Buddha’s wisdom-life.

The sectioning of the twelfth chapter, "Devadatta," states:

This chapter, together with the following ten chapters, collectively serves to awaken one to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; furthermore, the preceding [sections] have already determined the opening.

The Buddha’s knowledge and vision consists of nine chapters in the sutra text. To "show" the Buddha’s knowledge and vision occupies only one chapter, whereas to "awaken to" the Buddha’s knowledge and vision comprises all eleven chapters.

Why is it that their breadth and brevity differ? One must understand that "opening" the Buddha’s knowledge and vision refers only to the three cycles of opening and revealing, which conclude after the three rounds of bestowing predictions across the nine chapters. However, as for "showing" the Buddha’s knowledge and vision...

This directly reveals the wondrous nature of the mind and its objects before one’s eyes, causing delusive emotions to dissolve in the present moment. Once the Dharma-body is manifested, the Pure Land is perfectly present.
If you understand this, you will immediately know where to return; what need is there for further words? As for those who awaken to the Buddha’s vision and knowledge:

Although those of the Śrāvaka vehicle have realized their own minds, they still possess the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance accumulated over kalpas that have not yet been exhausted, and their narrow and inferior views have not yet been forgotten;
therefore, they must undergo manifold methods of cultivation and treatment before the Dharmakāya can become pure.
Furthermore, fearing that when engaging with the world to benefit sentient beings, they might lack skillful means (*upāya*), various methods for protection are preemptively indicated so as to...
That they do not fall into ordinary sentiments and do not give rise to alarm or fear is precisely the vast compassion of the Tathāgata;

it is what is called the metaphor of providing medical prescriptions in advance. However, as for the initial stage of awakening, those who have already mastered many categories and names [should proceed accordingly].

This reveals that there are difficulties and ease in realization. Because the śrāvakas have long harbored fear regarding the long duration of the Buddha-way, they have not given rise to a sense of joyful aspiration.
Now that they have received their predictions, they must nonetheless pass through many more kalpas before they can attain the fruit of realization.
Fearing that they might again give rise to the habitual tendencies of the past and lack the resolve to seek diligently, the World-Honored One himself cited his own past lives:

how he sought the sublime Dharma with such vigor that he did not spare even his own body or life, until today he finally attained the ultimate realization—thus demonstrating the difficulty of this awakening.
Furthermore, fearing that those of inferior capacity might shrink from the difficulty and fail to advance, he further cited the story of Mañjuśrī entering the Dragon Palace.
When the eight-year-old dragon girl who was to be converted offered her pearl, she immediately attained perfect enlightenment.

How much more so for one who, in the midst of the ocean—the realm of drowning in birth and death—was a dragon, a being characterized by great anger and extreme venom, and a woman, a vessel of feminine softness and turbid defilement;
she may be called the most difficult to convert, yet she instantly transformed from an ordinary person into a sage and realized Bodhi. Why is this?
Is it not easy? It is truly because one relies upon the Great Wisdom as one's support.

The intention is that those who are suited to this teaching should, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, rely upon the most excellent spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), so that they may preserve the ultimate state of wondrous awakening and never fall into the stages of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Therefore, this is listed as the foremost of awakenings. Tiantai said: "Devadatta" means...
Devadatta is so called because he was obtained by requesting him from the gods. He was the son of Droṇodana and the biological elder brother of Ānanda.
In the *Mahāyāna-śāstra-praśna*, it is asked: "Since that Devadatta was an enemy of the Buddha in lifetime after lifetime, why is he called a great bodhisattva? The answer is as follows:
If they were enemies, how could they meet one another life after life? It is like two people traveling in opposite directions, east and west;
as they take each step, they grow further apart. How could they remain companions? The *Mahāmegha Sūtra* states: "Devadatta is inconceivable;
the karmic practices he cultivated were identical to those of the Tathāgata. Yet, he personally committed the three heinous crimes and incited the king to commit murder."
The father harms the mother—such matters as these are all the skillful means (*upāya*) established by the Great Being to teach and transform others.
By acting through what are not the [conventional] paths, he penetrates the Buddha-way; it is merely to instill fear in evil people so that they may refrain from committing evil. Zhizhi says:

"In the preceding chapter, the manifestation of the stupa, the appearance of the body, and the three transformations of the Pure Land were shown to those of the three capacities to demonstrate the realization of the perfect practice; yet in reality, it is like..."
The realm of future fruits is fully revealed herein. Now, where there is a fruit, one must trace it back to its cause;

therefore, within this self-narrative of seeking the Dharma and forgetting the self amidst the causes, it perfectly accords with the original vow of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna to come for the sake of the Dharma.
This is why this chapter follows the "Appearance of the Stupa" and immediately concerns the transmission of the Sūtra.

This is the general heading. What follows all expresses the reality of tirelessness, extending even to the case of Constantly Non-Disparaging;
these are all matters concerning tirelessness. Generally speaking, the two characters "lassitude" and "weariness" are the root of all sufferings. Once lassitude arises, [all else follows].
Not only would the Buddha be unable to achieve [enlightenment], but the Dharma could not be sought, and one would likewise be unable to escape the worldly web.
△ Second, the actual explanation of seeking the Dharma:
Throughout many kalpas, he constantly acted as a king (up to) sparing neither his own flesh, hands, nor feet, nor even his life.
This clarifies that sacrificing one’s body in the past to seek the Dharma is the very embodiment of tireless diligence. Zhizhi says:
He constantly made vows to seek the Way as a king; it was not merely for the sake of the rank of a prince, but to fulfill the six pāramitās.
This is the aspiration of the Mahāyāna. Diligently practicing giving and so forth constitutes external giving; giving one's head, eyes, and so forth constitutes internal giving.
By citing these acts that can be performed, it serves as an exhortation for those who receive and uphold [the teachings] not to succumb to indolence or weariness.
At that time, the lifespan of the people of the world was immeasurable; [I] shall serve as their attendant for the rest of my life.

When human lifespan is immeasurable, it is truly an *utkalpa* (increasing eon). The glory of the human world is exceedingly long and enduring, and the pleasures of a king are likewise sufficient for enjoyment.
That one should nonetheless renounce their position and abdicate power without looking back is entirely for the sake of the Dharma, and not otherwise.
The worldly glory is comparable to this. That he issues a proclamation and must strike the drum is to sound forth his mind seeking the Dharma.

That his search for the Dharma extends to the four quarters is that he seeks it everywhere without ceasing. When he asks, "Who can preach the Mahāyāna for me?", he demonstrates that what he seeks is not the provisional vehicle or its minor fruits.
The phrase "supplying him for the rest of my life, truly there shall be no weariness" is precisely appropriate.
Section: Don (pinyin: yuán). △ Third, seeking out a Dharma Master.
At that time, there was a *ṛṣi* who came and addressed the King, saying: [up to] "If you do not oppose me, I shall proclaim the teaching for you."
Since the sincerity of one's invocation is genuine, the response will inevitably be verified; that the immortal came was, in principle, precisely as it should have been.

However, that the immortal said, "I possess the Mahāyāna," was likewise a manifestation in accordance with the capacities of those present; he was not the kind of immortal commonly referred to in ordinary parlance.
The name of this sutra is *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. The immortal must surely have received its name from a teacher of the past; thus one knows that this sutra has flowed down from a beginningless time.
The king vowed to provide lifelong offerings once he had found a teacher, and the immortal vowed not to refuse him, promising instead to expound it for his sake.
As these two vows were mutually firm, the *Saddharma* manifested of itself. One must know that it does not deviate from this.
With a single word, the Rishi did not merely enter into a solemn covenant with the King;
rather, throughout hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes, as emanations of the Tathāgata, he endured grievances and suffering within various forms of existence, never failing his vow.
This was the fulfillment of the Rishi’s wish. △ Four: Receiving the Dharma and Practicing it.
Upon hearing the words of the seer, the king rejoiced and leaped for joy; he served him with such diligent devotion that nothing was lacking.
He renounced his precious throne as if discarding a drop of mucus, treating his own nobility like that of a servant.

By humbling himself in this way, he made it known to all under heaven that there exists one who is most noble. This sufficiently demonstrates the World-Honored One’s bitter toil for the sake of the Dharma and for the sake of humanity. Furthermore—
It has come to this day. "Providing what is required" means providing what is desired. That which the rishi desires does not lie in fruits or melons, but in refinement.
Because the World-Honored One takes the Dharma as his person, he ascends mountains and treads through mountain streams;
there is no morning in which these are not prepared, and no evening in which couches and seats are not provided. Thus, day and night, there is no lack.
The interval [of time] may be called one of extreme toil and hardship. Furthermore, it must pass through a thousand years; this may be called the ultimate in endurance. Alas!
How firm is such a heart free from weariness and indolence! △ Second, the verse summary, divided into five parts. First, the verse on the duration of seeking the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"I recall past kalpas, for the sake of seeking the Great Dharma.
This verse clarifies that he sought the Great Dharma over a vast duration of time, thereby marking the firmness and stability of his diligent perseverance. As for "I recall":
That is to say, the Tathāgata, by means of his knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), perceives the distant past as clearly as he sees today.

This is to declare that his own account is not false, so as to cause those who have newly awakened their mindfulness to remember that when they attain Buddhahood in the future, they shall seek the Dharma within the causal stage just as he does today.
△ Second, the verse correctly clarifies the seeking of the Dharma.
Although he served as a king of the world, he did not crave the pleasures of the five desires (up to: his body would become that of a slave).
Worldly people take the false for the true, and thus regard the five desires as ultimate bliss. The man of realization knows all things to be illusory and does not crave worldly pleasures;
seeking the Dharma Master, he does not begrudge the sacrifice of his own life. This may be called "valuing what is truly worthy of value."
The former was called "beating the drum"; this is called "striking the bell. It is simply to make the earnest mind seeking the Dharma heard throughout the four quarters.
△ Third, a verse on obtaining a teacher who expounds the Dharma.
At that time, the Rishi Asita came and addressed the Great King, saying: "I shall explain it for you. Asita means "Incomparable" (Anupama).
However, because his fruit was named Devadatta (Heavenly King), he was called Devadatta by men; thus, he was named "Incomparable" (Asita) based on these three factors.

The meanings of the names in these three instances all accord with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; therefore, he was the teacher of the *Lotus Sūtra*. This is intended to clarify that [the Buddha] exists.
"Such causes produce such effects. This is intended to make those who have newly taken up the records understand that cause and effect are clearly manifest.
The prose states, "not contradicting me," while the verse says, "able to practice. One must first perceive that there is no contradiction before one can practice;
only when one is able to practice does one not contradict [the teaching]. △ Fourth, the verse on receiving the Dharma and putting it into practice.
At that time, when the King heard the words of the seer, great joy arose in his heart... (up to) "he diligently sought the Great Dharma.

He then followed the three characters. To see and obtain [the truth] without any lingering attachment and without any delay is precisely what is meant by the phrase "sacrificing the kingdom and entrusting oneself.
The sentiment contained in the two characters refers to being single-mindedly earnest. When people of the world undertake a task, they act with such dedication.
One then feels weary; it is simply that one’s emotions do not dwell upon this. If the emotions dwell upon the wondrous Dharma, how could body and mind possibly experience weariness?
Yet, this endurance of suffering and toil is by no means for the sake of body and mind alone.
It is also because all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, and one must simply diligently seek a true teacher and begin with oneself. Its intent is solely to...
New students must not be attached to minor fruits; they ought to be courageous and vigorous in seeking advancement to perfect themselves and thereby perfect others.
That which bears fruit on trees is called *guǒ* (fruit); that which bears fruit on vines or grasses is called *luò* (gourd). It is also said: *guǒ* refers to peaches, plums, and the like;
*luò* (pronounced *luǒ*) refers to melons, gourds, and the like. △ Fifth, the concluding verse summarizes the proof and exhorts faith.
"Nor is it for my own sake or for the pleasure of the five desires"—this [passage] up to here summarizes the preceding text.
It instructs the assembly that they should believe and study. The previous statement, "seeking the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings," demonstrates the breadth of his public-mindedness;
this present statement, "not for one's own bodily desires or pleasures," demonstrates the severance of his private attachments.
However, if one were to seek with such diligence and yet the Dharma could still not be attained, or the Buddha could still not be realized, then why would I need to repeat myself so profusely?
If one seeks it once, one attains it; if one attains it once, one realizes it. This is why I do not spare my words to speak for you.
It is simply that I wish those who have newly taken up this record to remain free from indolence and weariness, so that they may surely attain it.
The reality of attaining Buddhahood. △ Second, the conclusion and correlation of past and present, divided into two parts. First, the formal correlation:
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus... (up to)... "The seer of that time was none other than Devadatta."
This clarifies that the Dharma is not different across antiquity and the present, and that there are no two teachings. Zhizhi said: "My body is the King’s body;
though their forms differ, their minds are one and the same. "The Immortal is identical to Datta; though their names differ, the Dharma is one and the same.
I have attained Buddhahood through the Dharma, which is thus inconceivable; the Dharma is transmitted through the Teacher.
"I am indeed the teacher of the inconceivable. [△@△] The following clarifies the inconceivable teacher.
The meaning is that he who refined and perfected me is the present-day Daḍa; he who grinds and polishes you is the present-day Śākyamuni.
Since it is so now, it was likewise so in the past. How could one not believe this? △ Second, clarifying the karmic reward, divided into two parts.

First, it clarifies that the disciples’ fulfillment of their karmic retribution was due to Devadatta as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); [it continues] up to "all were due to Devadatta as a spiritual friend."

Although this passage clarifies that [the Buddha] received his reward as a result of his own causes, it actually attributes the merit to his teacher. The intention is to instruct the assembly not to fail the teacher’s instruction today.

While other sutras mostly describe the seeking of one's head, eyes, and so forth, these are for the sake of the Buddha fulfilling the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), along with the preceding five perfections;
only this sutra speaks in terms of transmitting the Dharma, thereby simultaneously fulfilling the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).

This is the Dharma. Thus, the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "If it were not for the spiritual friend Devadatta, one would never have known that the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable merits. Therefore, this also says, "causing me to be fully endowed," and so forth.
Regarding the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), Tiantai says: first, attraction through giving; if one desires wealth, one attracts them by means of wealth.
1. *Dāna-saṃgraha* (Gathering through giving): If there are those who desire the Dharma, one gathers them through the Dharma. 2. *Priyavāda-saṃgraha* (Gathering through kind speech):
By means of words that are virtuous and gentle, one accords with sentient beings, comforting and instructing them. 3. *Arthacaryā-saṃgraha* (Gathering through beneficial conduct):

The Bodhisattva initiates actions of body, speech, and mind as appropriate, enabling each sentient being to receive benefit. 4. *Samānārthatā-saṃgraha* (Gathering through common purpose): The Bodhisattva, by means of the Dharma...

The Eye clearly perceives the faculties and conditions of sentient beings; it immediately divides its forms and disperses its reflections, harmonizing its light with the dust of the world to engage in their common affairs.
Fourth, regarding "inclusive guidance": it accords with what sentient beings cherish in their hearts to lead them through sympathetic connection, gradually causing them to enter the Mahāyāna.
As it is said: "First one uses the hook of desire to draw them in, and later causes them to enter the Buddha-wisdom. All other matters are as explained in the relevant sections.

Commentary on the "Chapter on Expedients": This refers to the attainment of perfect enlightenment and the deliverance of sentient beings; these merits of the two benefits are entirely reached through the teacher’s refinement.
Furthermore, it is seen as proof that one does not contravene the teacher’s instructions. II. Clarifying that the Wondrous Fruit of the Dharma Master Shall Be Attained.
This is divided into three parts. First, the realization of the fruit.
The Buddha addressed the fourfold assembly: "Devadatta... [the world] shall be named Heavenly Path.
In this passage, the Tathāgata originally cited a remote cause as a teaching for the sake of the Dharma, intending to lead new practitioners toward firmness and diligence;
thus, the words of the prediction arrived unexpectedly. Examining the preceding and succeeding sections of the sutra, it is evident that Devadatta was not included in that assembly.
Another sutra states: Because he had harmed the Buddha, he was reborn in the Avīci Hell. The Buddha sent Ānanda to inquire whether he experienced suffering or bliss.
Huida replied, "I am here as if in the bliss of the third dhyāna heaven. Ānanda asked, "When will you emerge? Huida replied, "I shall wait for Śākyamuni to enter hell;
once he has, I shall immediately leave. Ānanda said, "How could the World-Honored One ever [enter hell]?"
Regarding the "portion of entering hell," Dà (Dharmatāla) said: "How could I possibly have a portion for exiting hell?

From this, one knows that the place where the Tathāgata bestowed his prediction was precisely the point where Dharmatāla was certain not to receive [a different fate]; how extraordinary! One must fix one's gaze well upon this point.
As for the fruit being called "King of Heaven," Dàkuǎn says: "Possessing great majestic power, he accomplishes the Tathāgata."
Great causes yield great fruits. As for this world named Deva-patha, the path of the gods has no partiality; it is always with those who do good.

One must understand that Deva’s present hatred was, in fact, the sublime Dharma of the past, and Śākyamuni’s present adversary was his spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) of the past. How can one regard these two as different?
△ Second, the conversion and deliverance.

At that time, the Buddha T'ien-wang (Devarāja) dwelt in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas, [until] they attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and reached the stage of non-retrogression.

Although the adornments of his primary and secondary bodies (*sambhoga- and nirmāṇa-kāya*) are not explicitly recorded, one may generally know them by observing those who benefited from his preaching of the Dharma.

The Buddha preached the Dharma for twenty intermediate kalpas, extensively expounding the Three Vehicles until those who attained the fruits were numerous and inexhaustible. △ Third, after his parinirvāṇa.

therefore, it is called non-arising. "Non-emergence" means that the realm governed by the Tathāgata is, in its entirety, identical [to this]; therefore, there is no [emergence].
One may emerge. As for "not arising," it is because one has entered into principle (*li*). Both skillful means and the teaching of principle are entirely quiescent.
However, this principle of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) cannot be named by names; therefore, its nature is empty. It cannot be characterized by characteristics;

therefore, its appearance is empty. Thus it is said to be "nameless and signless. This reiterates the previous statement regarding "non-existence" and so forth. Below, it further says "no... [and so on].
"Omnipresent" (sarvatraga) means that the essence of the wisdom of the Middle Way contemplation possesses no existence in either of the two extremes.

"Immeasurable" (apramāṇa) means that it does not possess the quantitative limits of the aggregates, elements, or sense bases. "Boundless" (ananta) means that it is not like partial or limited phenomena.
"Unobstructed" (apratigha) means that it universally enters into all phenomena. "Unimpeded" (anāvaraṇa) means that there is nothing capable of obstructing it.
Therefore, although there are many phrases herein, in reality they simply mean that the characteristics of the objects of contemplation are fused and all phenomena are empty. △ Third, the conclusion:
"But by means of causes and conditions... up to "...this is called the second station of intimacy for a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
This summarizes the preceding phrases: they are nothing other than causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Tiantai says:

"The preceding [passage] directly clarifies the contemplative wisdom of the Middle Way, which is neither understanding nor delusion, and transcends the characteristics of the two extremes. Now, it clarifies the simultaneous illumination of the two extremes:

from the causes and conditions of delusion, birth and death arise; from the causes and conditions of understanding, nirvana arises. Thus, by means of the single phrase 'causes and conditions,' the meaning is opened up."

Regarding the two objects: furthermore, because there is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there is *nirvāṇa*; because there is the arising of inversion, one is born into birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

This clearly manifests the meaning of the twofold illumination. The *Yinzhi* (Sound-Knower) says: "The previous statement that 'all dharmas are empty' meant that the objects and wisdom of all dharmas—the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)—are all empty.
Now, to speak again of 'existence,' it is merely existence by way of dependent origination, not [existence] from the beginning."
It exists. Since it is in no way non-existent, for one to now say it is non-existent arises from delusion; thus one speaks of its non-existence, yet it is not originally non-existent.
That which is neither existent nor non-existent is the mark of the true Dharmakāya. This is what the upholder of the sutra [should understand].
One should always delight in such contemplation and draw near to it. △ Second, the verse summary, divided into three parts. First, the verse that sets forth the chapter:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

If there is a bodhisattva who, in the future evil age, wishes to preach this sutra with a mind free from fear, he should abide in four dharmas as stated above when wishing to preach this sutra. He is "without fear" because he abides in the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*).
Although his mind may not be startled or terrified, he must further enter the sphere of practice (*caryā-vastu*) and the sphere of proximity (*sevā-vastu*); only then will it be possible.
△ Second, the verse on the practice of cultivation:
"He should enter the sphere of practice and the sphere of proximity... [up to] ...and the *caṇḍālas*, non-Buddhists, and brahmins."
"Entering" means to realize and enter [the state]. "Abiding" refers to being externally distant from the clamor and bustle of the world, while internally remaining close to the principle (*li*).
It does not mean that one must remain entirely aloof from all things. This verse [describes] first, avoiding kings; second, avoiding violent amusements; third, staying far from butchers;
and fourth, staying far from those of false wisdom. The meaning is as explained previously.
One should not associate with those of overweening pride (up to: nor should one associate with any female lay devotees).
Regarding the scholars of the Tripiṭaka: when the Buddha was in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, he preached the Sūtra Piṭaka for the sake of Ājñātakauṇḍinya and others.
In Rājagṛha, he taught the Vinaya Piṭaka for Sunakṣatra. At the side of the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī, he taught the Abhidharma Piṭaka—the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna—for the son of the Vṛji clan.
Those called "Arhats" by name are so designated only nominally; they have not truly realized the fruit. Those who seek extinction in the present life do not belong to the Mahāyāna.
Because they are [like] vessels [of impurity], those who propagate the Lotus Sūtra must not associate closely with them.
Even if such persons approach with good intentions, one must not draw near to them or treat them with intimacy.
"Those with good intentions" refers to those of the Lesser Vehicle who wish to hear the Buddha-way. "Fearless" means not harboring expectations.
For example, the Venerable Zuoxi never spoke a single word of Dharma for the sake of profit, nor did he ever accept so much as a hair’s breadth of wealth on account of the Dharma.
Only by maintaining such a mind can one be said to be without expectation. As for those who are not male...
This includes eunuchs and those whose physical and mental natures are impure;
one must not associate with them. One should likewise not associate with butchers, executioners, and all such persons. Do not associate with any of these people.
To carve meat into pieces is called *tu*; to mince meat finely is called *kuài*. Furthermore, one who kills people is also called a *kuáikuài*.
To buy low and sell high is called *fàn*; to advertise one’s own affairs is called *xuàn*. To live by killing is for one’s entire being to be an occupation;
to advertise oneself through lust is for one’s entire being to be stained. To associate with such persons is not merely useless—it is harmful.
[The character for] *huài* (pronounced *sēng*).
[From] "various games such as dangerous sumō" up to "by these two places one can preach with peace and joy.
As for the "two places," they refer to the two locations where he travels. The Dharma Master is able to travel in this manner; he is able to act in this way.
When one draws near [to this], the multitude of difficulties will not trouble them; thus, they shall dwell in peace and happiness. △ Third, the verse on the accomplishment of practice:
"Furthermore, one does not practice the superior, middling, or inferior dharmas... this is called the bodhisattva’s sphere of practice."
Tiantai says: This verse refers back to the principles and practices of the superior, middling, and inferior [vehicles], which are the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
Now, speaking from the perspective of "abolishing the provisional," it is said that they are "not practiced. Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are mundane dharmas and are therefore unreal;

unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are supramundane dharmas and are therefore real. Yet both the mundane and the supramundane are merely provisional designations. Since one contemplates all dharmas as being thus...
The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is simply the single, ultimate emptiness. How, then, could there be birth-and-death to be severed or nirvāṇa to be realized?
As it is said: "Nirvāṇa and birth-and-death are equal to flowers in the sky. Therefore, both real and unreal phenomena do not function.

Since the internal is not differentiated as the true mark, how could the external be differentiated as male or female? Since the internal and external are thus one and the same, the nature of defilement and purity—
Emptiness. To act all day long without acting at all—therefore it is said that one does not grasp any dharmas.
That which is "neither knowing nor seeing" is not a lack of knowledge or vision; rather, it is the equality of the single principle, wherein there is nothing that is not known or seen.
One who acts thus may be considered a bodhisattva practicing prajñā.
"All dharmas are empty and non-existent" (up to) "this is called the place frequented by the wise.
This separate verse concerns the practice of approaching [the truth]. The *Yizhin* (*Yizhi yin*) states:

"From 'All' downwards, the verse praises the contemplation of all dharmas as being empty according to their true nature, and as having a nature of non-existence like space. The single phrase 'there is no permanence' is an interpolation."
Practice is without pattern; it is likewise without arising or ceasing. The verse [above] spoke of non-arising, while the prose [here] speaks of non-existence;

thus, they manifest alternately before and after one another. [△@△] There is no permanent abiding, which means not dwelling in existence or non-existence. Arising and ceasing mean not dwelling in emptiness.
Having attained this non-dwelling in both emptiness and existence, this is precisely the sphere of practice for the wise.

To engage in inverted conceptualization regarding the existence or non-existence of all phenomena [up to] abiding immovably like Mount Sumeru—this is a verse reiterating the practice of conduct within the stage of cultivation.
The *Yinzhi* (Sound-Knowledge) commentary states: "The verse says that those who are free from inversion certainly do not engage in conceptualization;
however, for those who possess inversion, they then conceptualize the existence or non-existence, right or wrong, and reality or unreality of all phenomena, as well as their arising."
It is extinguished. Being "below" refers to those who uphold this sutra; having realized that these are inverted discriminations, their minds will become unsettled.
They should therefore practice self-restraint in a secluded place to make the mind tranquil and as immovable as Mount Sumeru.
Only then can one achieve the Practice of Peaceful Abiding (*anurakṣaṇā-pratipatti*).

To contemplate that all phenomena (*dharma*) are non-existent, up to [the realization that they] eternally abide in a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*), is called the "proximate dwelling" (*upaniṣad*).
As the preceding verse stated: "Settle the mind like a mountain; wisdom is clarity. This contemplation of all phenomena as equal is the clear object, like space.
"Emptiness" means that all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent. "Lacking solidity" means that all phenomena are like illusions.

"Neither arising nor emerging," and so forth, summarizes the single characteristic of eternal abiding. It is said that only when a Bodhisattva can contemplate in this manner do they attain the peace and joy of intimacy.
If there is a bhikṣu who, after my parinirvāṇa, experiences no timidity when preaching this sūtra, this indicates that his practice has been perfected.
When his practice is perfected, his external demeanor will not falter; when the principle is perfected, his inner mind will be free from obstruction.
Therefore, when preaching the sūtra, he is without timidity.
"At times, the Bodhisattva enters a quiet chamber... his mind is peaceful and secure, free from any timidity.

This explains the cause of peace and bliss. Tiantai says: "Because he enters a quiet chamber to cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he ceases transgressions and evils and attains the realization of *pudgala-nairātmya* (the selflessness of persons);
thus, externally, he is not harmed. Because he cultivates wisdom through right mindfulness, [internally, he is not harmed]."

Being free from all attachments, one attains the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and is inwardly free from inversion; this is what it means for the mind not to be timid or weak, and it is precisely what is called "peaceful and blissful practice" (*sukha-vihāra*). Question: Previously, you taught that one should not associate with kings and others, yet here you again teach that one should preach and transform them. What is the intention behind these two teachings? Answer: Regarding the previous instruction not to associate with them: [it was intended for those who have not yet attained realization]. As for the present teaching: [it is for those who have already realized the truth].
