Because the practitioner’s own self-benefit has not yet been fully realized, they fear being moved by worldly power and profit.

Furthermore, since the other party lacks sincere seeking while the practitioner desires to draw near, it would inevitably lead to being detested by others. Now that one has arisen from meditative concentration, the mind is set upon benefiting and saving others;
moreover, as their mind is peaceful and stable, they do not perceive any worldly power or profit worthy of honor. Thus it is said.
The Dharma: This is the fundamental essence of the Bodhisattva’s propagation of the sutra. △ Second, the conclusion on the fulfillment of practice:
Mañjuśrī, this is called the Bodhisattva abiding in the first dharma and being able to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in future ages.
This is the invocation of Mañjuśrī, concluding his inquiry. Regarding the "first dharma," it refers to the peace and happiness of one's own body.

Although the heading mentions the body alone, the text encompasses both speech and mind; in reality, the three karmas are presented together. You asked later how one can preach this sutra in the evil age;
if a bodhisattva abides in this first dharma, they will be able to preach this sutra in future generations. △ Second.
The peaceful conduct of speech. This is divided into two parts. First, the prose section. This is further divided into two. First, the heading of the chapter:
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata... [until] one should abide in peaceful conduct.
This is the purity of speech. To propagate the sutra in the Dharma-ending age, if one’s words are not correct, the resulting calamity will also be severe.
△ Second, the explanation of practice, divided into two parts. First, the practice of cessation.
Whether when speaking aloud or when reading the scriptures, one should not take pleasure in speaking of the faults of persons or of the scriptures.
"Speaking" refers to discourse before an assembly; "reading" refers to the words of one's own private recitation. Whether speaking or reading:

In no case can one say that either the person or the scripture has committed a fault. Prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the provisional teachings of the seven stages of skillful means were spoken by the Buddha according to the capacities of beings as teachings of incomplete meaning (*neyārtha*). If a person hears and accepts them, there may be the fault of delighting in the partial and inferior;
yet, since the Dharma fundamentally accords with capacity, what fault could there be? If one were to say that the Dharma itself possesses a fault, then people would harbor affliction and confusion.
This is not for the sake of oral pleasure.
Nor should one treat other Dharma masters with contempt (up to: nor should one give rise to a mind of resentment or aversion toward those who propagate this teaching).
One who transmits the scriptures must not rely on the Perfect Teaching to disparage Dharma masters of the Small Vehicle. — Tiantai.
It is said: "Not speaking of the long and the short" means that ordinary people in the world all loathe hearing of their own faults;

therefore, one does not speak of their shortcomings. Those who love praise will surely be prone to slander; therefore, one does not extol their virtues. This refers to not speaking of any person at all. Next, it specifically mentions the *śrāvakas*:
since the faculties and natures of *śrāvakas* are not fixed, praising them would cause them to regress from the Great [Vehicle] and take up the Small; whereas slandering them...
Thus, both the great and the small are lost; therefore, both censure and praise are inappropriate. Regarding "not giving rise to resentment or aversion":
if one claims that the person from whom one received [the teaching] or the Dharma one has inherited obstructs one's own path, this is a mind of resentment.
If one claims that such a person or their Dharma is base and inferior, this is a mind of aversion. Once the mental faculty is stirred, speech immediately issues forth. To block [this]:
This is the source of what has been taught; therefore, one should not give rise to resentment or aversion. △ Second, regarding contemplative practice:
because one skillfully cultivates such a mind of peace and bliss... (up to) ...one explains it for them so that they may attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Since the practitioner has already contemplated the emptiness of all phenomena, their mind dwells in the principle of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) without any grasping or attachment;

this is precisely the well-cultivated mind of peace and bliss. Because they do not cling to the great while disparaging the small, the teachings they expound do not conflict with the listener's disposition.
When there are difficult questions, they respond by means of the Mahāyāna, thereby gradually leading others into the Buddha’s wisdom; hence it is said, "to cause [them to enter]."
One attains the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). △ Second, the verse summary. This is divided into three parts. First, the verse that sets forth the chapter.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
The Bodhisattva always delights in preaching the Dharma for peace and security (up to: taking his place upon the Dharma-seat, he preaches according to the questions asked.
The meaning of the verse here does not overlap with the prose; rather, it refers to the Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom, which preaches as the occasion arises.
The former [section] spoke of purity of speech; this further teaches the purification of both body and mind. The Bodhisattva desires to attain peace...
The teaching on the hidden dharma must require both internal and external purity. Regarding "purifying the ground": externally, this means being free from the ten afflictions;
internally, it means wisdom is suchness (*tathatā*). This is entering the Tathāgata’s chamber. "Providing a seat" means contemplating that all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty.

"Anointing the body with oil" means attaining physical peace and happiness. "Washing away dust and grime" means removing afflictions and distress. "Wearing new, clean clothes" means being fully endowed with...
Regarding the power of patience: one dons the robe of the Tathāgata, takes one’s place upon the Dharma-seat, and ascends the seat of the Tathāgata.
Only when these three conditions are fully met can one preach the Dharma; hence it is said, "he preaches according to the questions asked. △ Second, the verse on the method of practice.

If there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs [up to] who explain the subtle and wondrous meaning with a serene countenance, it is because they have not yet attained realization of the characteristics of dharmas (dharmalakṣaṇa);
therefore, they must rely on the practice of seclusion so that both parties may remain free from fault.

Now, since they have already attained realization of the characteristics of dharmas, they explain the subtle and wondrous meaning with a serene countenance. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the mundane is entirely the ultimate truth (*tathatā*).
It causes people to delight in hearing it; therefore, it is called "subtle and wonderful. "With a serene countenance" means preaching the Dharma with joy.
If there are difficult questions, one answers them according to their meaning (until) they gradually increase in merit and enter the Buddha-way.
There are two types of difficult questions. The first is when a wise person poses a question, engaging in repeated debate and mutual stimulation to bring forth what has not yet been revealed.
The second is when a fool harbors doubts that have not yet been resolved; in such cases, the Dharma Master may cite causes and conditions [to provide clarification].

Alternatively, he establishes parables to open and develop their mental ground; by discerning names and characteristics, he causes them all to resolve their minds, leading them from provisional means toward the ultimate reality and into the Buddha-way.
One eliminates the mind of indolence and the thought of laxity, and preaches the Dharma with a heart of compassion free from all sorrow and affliction.
Preaching the Dharma with a compassionate heart means being without resentment or aversion; thus, one is free from all sorrow and affliction.
Preaching the Dharma means being solely diligent and energetic; thus, one eliminates all forms of sloth and indolence.
"Day and night they constantly preach the unsurpassed Way of the Buddha (up to) this is the great benefit, peace, and bliss of making offerings.

This verse refers to the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*). While the prose commentary merely states that he answers by means of the Mahāyāna Dharma, the present text specifies that he "preaches the unsurpassed Way."
The former statement says, "May one attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*)," while this statement says, "May one fulfill the Buddha-way. A commentary on these words states:
"This is because he preaches the Dharma with a heart of compassion; thus, he obtains great benefit. There are five aspects of his bringing peace and happiness:
first, preaching continuously day and night; second, preaching with immeasurable causes and analogies; third, preaching so as to cause all to rejoice; and fourth, not hoping for the four requisites."
It is said: "The fifth is to preach the path to Buddhahood with a mind of loving-kindness. A single phrase of preaching the Dharma with a compassionate heart is the most important.
Therefore it is said: "This is of great benefit," and so forth. △ Third, the verse on the fulfillment of practice.

"After my parinirvāṇa, if there are bhikṣus (up to: who likewise do not expel [others], because they abide in patience, those who preach the Dharma in the final age will be able to speak as described above; they will not only avoid harm and peril, but shall also attain inexhaustible merit.
The *Yinzhi* says: "There are five ways in which there is no harm: first, no sorrow or grief; second, no..."
1. No verbal abuse; 2. No fear; 3. No dread; 4. No swords or staves; 5. No expulsion.
All these arise because one preaches the Dharma without envy or anger, so that no afflictions are produced.
The wise person thus skillfully cultivates the mind (up to the point where it) cannot be fully exhausted even by means of calculation or analogy;
this clarifies that they are endowed with all merits. That is to say, even if one were to speak for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, one could not exhaust [the description].
Its efficacy lies in the single phrase "skillfully cultivating the mind. If one does not skillfully cultivate the mind, one cannot even avoid suffering, let alone...

Virtuous One. Question: The text designates "peace of mouth" (*mukha-sukha*), yet what is described therein pertains entirely to the mind (*manas*). For example, it says: "Eliminate sloth and indolence;
preach the Dharma with a compassionate mind; simply maintain single-minded mindfulness; let the mind be free from envy and anger," up to "skillfully cultivating the mind.
How could this ever be called "peace of mouth"? Answer: Although the text mentions three [aspects], the meaning is non-dual. Body...
The mind does not act [inappropriately]; the mouth does not move [inappropriately] because of the mind. The mind is the foundation of body and speech;

therefore, this is a constant teaching. △ Third, the Practice of Mental Tranquility. This is divided into two parts. First, the prose section. This is divided into three parts. First, the presentation of the heading.
Furthermore, regarding the passage from "Moreover, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva...

up to "...those who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra," the phrase "when the Dharma is about to perish" refers specifically to the period of the final five hundred years when strife is firmly entrenched.
If a bodhisattva dharma-preacher wishes to read and recite this sutra, they must first rectify their own intention.

When the mind is correct, the Dharma is such that all phenomena are as they truly are. △ Second, the explanation of practice, which is further divided into two parts. First, the practice of cessation (*śamatha*):
One should harbor no thoughts of jealousy, flattery, or deception, nor should one disparage or revile those who study the Buddha-way by seeking out their faults.
This explanation clarifies the characteristics of practice (*pratipatti*), whereby one attains peace and happiness of mind. Tiantai said: "Those of the Two Vehicles wish to transcend birth and death;
therefore, they first eliminate craving and desire. Bodhisattvas wish to transform sentient beings; therefore, they first eliminate anger and [wrong] views."
Envy is a defilement of anger; flattery is a defilement of views. Envy and jealousy contradict the mind of compassion and are not the method for transforming others.
Flattery and deception deviate from the path of wisdom and are not the method for one's own practice.
If wisdom is obstructed, how can one seek the fruit of Buddhahood above? If compassion is hindered, how can one transform sentient beings below? Therefore—
If a bodhisattva wishes to rectify their own mind, they must most urgently abandon [such conduct]. Furthermore, regarding "one should not disparage or revile others":

this precept means one should not rely on the perfection (pāramitā) of one’s own practice to criticize or seek out the shortcomings of those who follow the provisional teachings (upāya). If one should treat others with contempt or revile them, one will cause their roots of goodness to regress.
"If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī... [you] are a person of negligence because you are lax in the Path.
This clarifies that the seven groups of people, including both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, should be viewed with equal eyes.

Even if each has their own attachments, they should be disciplined according to the circumstances and transformed according to their capacities; do not cause them distress, lest they look [for faults].
One sees the Dharma-gate of the equality of the Mahāyāna, which encompasses everything; thus, it causes one to forever sever doubt and regret, settling the mind upon the Path.
Immediately after speaking these words to that person, he uttered the words of his distress: "The Dharma Master should not reprimand the Hīnayāna with the perfect principle.
Moreover, those who rely on expedient means look toward the Great [Vehicle], yet they fundamentally fear the circuitous route; therefore, it is said they have departed from the Path."
It is extremely distant. Since those of the Lesser Vehicle lack aspiration, they will ultimately never attain the Buddha-way;
since they are weary of birth and death, they will ultimately never transform sentient beings. Therefore, it is said that they are negligent and indolent.
Furthermore, one should not engage in frivolous speculation (*prapañca*) regarding the various dharmas or contend over them.
Frivolous speculation consists of speaking indeterminately about all dharmas—namely, mundane and supramundane, defiled and pure phenomena.
When a Bodhisattva propagates the sutras in the final age, they must declare that the defiled dharmas of birth and death are definitively impure, and that Nirvana is holy.
The Dharma is definitively not mundane; pray do not confuse it. Furthermore, it is inappropriate to take what is great and reduce it to the small, thereby giving rise to contention.
To teach the Dharma in this manner brings peace and joy to the mind. △ Second, Contemplative Practice.
One should give rise to thoughts of great compassion toward all sentient beings.
This directly counters the aforementioned lack of envy and the absence of a mind free from flattery and deception.

That is to say, the Dharma-preacher should, regarding the twelve classes of beings within the triple world, intend to uproot their various sufferings and afflictions through great compassion; this is his fundamental purpose. Yet, [if he harbors] envy...
One should not harbor a jealous mind.
One should conceive of all Tathāgatas as one’s compassionate father.

This contrasts with the previous injunctions against disparaging them and so forth. The term "all Tathāgatas" encompasses those of the three periods of time; that is to say, for anyone who studies the Buddha-way...
These individuals are precisely the assembly that shall attain Buddhahood in the future.

Since those who propagate the sutras already regard the Tathāgata as their father, how could they, in turn, give rise to contempt or abuse toward those who come, seeking out their faults and shortcomings?
One should conceive of all bodhisattvas as great teachers (upādhyāya), and should always, with a profound mind, pay them homage and prostrate.
This contrasts with the previous instruction not to cause distress to those seeking the three vehicles;

rather, one should, with a profound mind, revere all bodhisattvas of this land and the ten directions as if they were great teachers. How could one [behave otherwise] toward those of the three vehicles?
On the contrary, why do you instead give rise to vexation and confusion by speaking of their faults?
He teaches the Dharma with equanimity toward all sentient beings (up to) and does not speak excessively.
This contrasts with the aforementioned [faults] such as frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*); that is to say, through equanimity there is no contention, and by following the Dharma, one does not...
Regarding "idle proliferation" (*prapañca*): that it is neither much nor little depends upon the sharpness or dullness of the practitioner's faculties. △ Third, the accomplishment of practice:
"Mañjuśrī, this bodhisattva mahāsattva... [up to] ...reveres, honors, and praises [him]."
This concludes the proof of the third "Peaceful and Joyful Practice.
Because I am able to preach the Dharma with equanimity, not only do people not disturb me, but there are those who naturally respond to my spirit and seek to be my good companions in study;
they successively uphold it and successively revere it, until its circulation becomes inexhaustible. △ Second, the verse summary, divided into two parts. First:
The Verse on the Practice of the Dharma:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one wishes to expound this sutra, one should abandon envy, anger, and pride... [until] saying, 'You shall not attain Buddhahood.'"

This verse concerns the practice of *śamatha*. It means to cease all unwholesome dharmas and refrain from practicing them, while constantly cultivating the single phrase of integrity and straightforwardness;
this is what should be practiced.
These sons of the Buddha, when teaching the Dharma, are always gentle and capable of forbearance (up to) teaching the Dharma without obstruction.
This verse concerns contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*). It states that when a Bodhisattva practices the Path out of compassion for sentient beings, he does so not for his own sake;
such a Great Teacher I shall revere. The remainder may be understood by comparison with the prose commentary. △ Second, the verse on the fulfillment of practice.
Regarding the third dharma: a wise person such as this should guard their single-mindedness and practice with peace and joy, being honored by immeasurable multitudes.
The verse says: "The wise person should maintain a single mind; once the mind has returned to oneness, there is no practice that cannot be accomplished."
Zhizhi says: This chapter takes correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) as its essence. When correct wisdom manifests before one, intentional karma becomes pure;
thus, one is able to be compassionate toward all, to revere all, to distance oneself from all evils, and to give rise to all virtues.
Above, this accords with the Buddha-mind; below, it accords with the minds of ordinary beings. Naturally, one will be revered and honored by humans and devas. △ Four Vows.

May there be peace and happiness. This is divided into two parts. First, the prose section, which is further divided into two. First, the explanation of the ritual practice, which is further divided into three.
First, the heading: Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva... (up to) "those who uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*."
This indicates the fourth vow for peaceful conduct (*sukhavihāra*). When one’s body, speech, and mind are conjoined with compassion, they are equalized within a single principle.
Preaching the Dharma through the wisdom of this single principle, there is no dharma that is not perfected and no being that is not delivered.
How can the peace and happiness thereof be fully described! △ Second, the practice of the Dharma:
[The text proceeds] from among householders and renunciants... to generating great compassion for those who are not bodhisattvas.
This clarifies that one should universally save all sentient beings through compassion. *Zhizhi* says: "In the preceding three chapters, the seven classes of followers were extensively cited.

Here, 'laypeople' refers to those such as upāsakas who have already resolved their minds [to attain enlightenment]; 'those who have left home' refers to those such as bhikṣus who have already resolved their minds.
Although they have all resolved their minds, they possess only faith and understanding; they have not yet realized [the truth]."
Because they possess the noble wisdom of self-realization, one should arouse great compassion for them and grant them the equal joy of the Dharma.

As for those who are not Bodhisattvas—namely, the ten types of persons previously cautioned against as those whom one should not associate with—it is because they do not yet know the Tathāgata’s impartial great wisdom;
although they possess the Buddha-nature, their afflictions within the three realms are profound and heavy.
One should give rise to great compassion toward them, deliver them from suffering, and cause them to likewise realize bodhi.
One should form this thought: "Such persons (up to) do not perceive, do not inquire, do not believe, and do not understand."

This teaching for the Bodhisattva Dharma Master involves forming a mental resolve and making a vow regarding the realm of those to be saved; this serves as the basis for the salvation of sentient beings.
*Zhizhi* states: "Ordinary and Hinayana practitioners, both within and without the triple world, have lost the Tathāgata’s impartial great wisdom.
This is a mental resolve based upon the correct causal Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*). It is the Tathāgata’s skillful means, expounding the Dharma according to what is appropriate.
"Not hearing, not knowing, and not awakening" refers to forming a mental focus based on the Buddha-nature as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
"Not inquiring, not believing, and not understanding" refers to forming a mental focus based on the Buddha-nature as the liberating cause (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*).

Having formed these three reflections, out of compassion for those in both the monastic and lay communities, one should, before the Buddhas of the ten directions, give rise to great loving-kindness and compassion and make a vow to deliver them.
They dwell together within this Dharma;
although that person does not inquire about, believe in, or understand this sutra, [the Buddha] leads them and causes them to abide within this Dharma.

This is the formal formulation of the vow. Zhizhi says: Because ordinary people and those of the Lesser Vehicle do not inquire into the meaning and principles of this sutra, and even if they were to ask, they would not believe it;
and because they do not believe, they do not understand. Therefore, one should make this aspiration:
"When I attain Bodhi, wherever I may be, I shall, by the power of my supernatural penetrations and wisdom, lead [beings] [to this teaching]."
...causing them to abide within the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This is brought about by the two minds of great kindness and great compassion mentioned above.
As for "what stage," this refers to the period after attaining the Way, whether in this world or another; it is thus a designation that is not yet fixed.
"Supernatural powers and wisdom" refers to the virtues of *prajñā* (wisdom) and liberation (*vimukti*). To abide within these dharmas is the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This...
The four practices are precisely equal to the Four Great Vows; how excellent that the power of aspiration must not be lacking!
Those with resolve should understand this deeply. △ Third, the conclusion, divided into two parts: first, the summary of being free from fault.
Mañjuśrī, when this bodhisattva-mahāsattva... [up to] "preaches this Dharma, there is no fault.
This is the vow of the "Practice for Peace and Bliss" (Anrakugyō). Tiantai says:

"The summary here regarding 'no fault' is because, by establishing the great vow, one immediately enters the Tathāgata’s chamber; thus, there is no fault of anger. One knows that the fourfold assembly has faults..."

To sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat is to be free from the fault of indolence; by restraining the mind through one's vow, one puts on the Tathāgata’s robe and is thus free from the fault of flattery and crookedness.
Being free from these various faults constitutes the perfection of practice. II. Specifically concluding with compassion.
He constantly acts as a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī (up to: he is able to cause all who hear him to attain joy).

Because he has perfected the practice of loving-kindness, he gathers the offerings of the fourfold assembly and of devas and humans. Because his vows have been fulfilled, he causes them to listen to the Dharma.
Through the Buddha’s supernatural power and the protection of the devas, the Tathāgata’s seat was established. Because they do not cling to dharmas, all who hear this are filled with joy.
Why is this? It is because this sutra is protected by the supernatural power of all Buddhas.
This explains that the practice of the vow has been fulfilled; even the Buddhas of the three periods of time all protect it, let alone the devas.

The "Commentary on the Meaning" (*Yinzhi*) states: "The *Zhao* Dharma Master’s chapter [on this] says: 'This sutra is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas; it must not be recklessly bestowed upon others.
This refers to the intent of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who guard it. Furthermore, one should know that one must abide in patience regarding the sphere of practice.
To humble oneself before the ground and so forth is to don the Tathāgata’s robe. To dwell near and contemplate the emptiness of all dharmas and so forth is to sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat.
This section on the mind of compassion is to enter the Tathāgata’s chamber. When these three dharmas are accomplished, this is the true practice of peaceful dwelling.

△ Second, the formal praise of the sutra, divided into two parts. First, the Dharma-exposition, which is further divided into two. First, revealing that [the Buddha] did not [preach it] in the past...
"It is so. Mañjuśrī, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—even down to its very name—is impossible to hear.
This passage correctly clarifies that it is protected by all Buddhas; it serves as the basis for the chapter on establishing metaphors that follows, namely, this "Wondrous" [Dharma].
The Dharma is inherently revered; therefore, those who uphold this sutra are likewise revered because of it.
Even in the immeasurable lands of the ten directions, one might not even be able to hear its name.
Since this sutra is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas, which they constantly guard, how could it be bestowed upon others recklessly? II. Explaining that it has only now begun.
How much more so for those who have obtained the opportunity to see, receive, uphold, read, and recite it?
Since its name has not been heard in immeasurable lands, all those who today obtain the opportunity to see, hear, receive, and uphold it— [are indeed rare].
This is due to the Tathāgata’s four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa-citta*).

If a Bodhisattva Dharma-preacher does not possess the various forms of patience (*kṣānti*) and does not give rise to vows (*praṇidhāna*), how could he be able to protect and maintain the Tathāgata’s teachings, or preserve and bring his transformation to fruition?
II. Explanation by Analogy. This is divided into two parts. First, the analogy of not giving the jewel. This is further divided into two. First, the opening of the analogy.
Mañjuśrī, it is like a powerful king (up to) raising various armies and setting out for a punitive expedition.

This is a metaphor for having recently come from immeasurable lands—having been protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas as described in the preceding chapter—to hear [this teaching] and arrive here.
This single analogy is presented to conclude the general framework for the fourteen chapters on "opening the provisional to reveal the real.
The *Sūtra of the Arising of the World* states: "During the kalpa of increase, four wheel-turning kings appear in succession.
First, when the human lifespan in the four continents under Mount Sumeru is fifty thousand years, an iron-wheel-turning king appears in the world, ruling over one continent. He exerts [his power]...
When the *ge* (spears) first became established and the human lifespan was sixty thousand years, a copper-wheel-turning monarch (*tāmra-cakravartin*) appeared in the world.

He ruled over two continents; they submitted upon the shaking of his majesty. When the human lifespan was seventy thousand years, a silver-wheel-turning monarch (*rūpya-cakravartin*) appeared in the world.

He ruled over three continents; they were brought to submission by the dispatch of envoys. When the human lifespan was eighty thousand years, a gold-wheel-turning monarch (*suvarṇa-cakravartin*) appeared in the world. He ruled over four [continents].

Throughout the world, all were transformed by the mere sight of his presence; they were all turned toward and responded to the True Dharma through its timely application. Hence, he is called a *cakravartin* (Wheel-Turning King). Direct Pointing says:
"In terms of phenomena, the Wheel-Turning King is a metaphor for the Buddha. 'Powerful strength' is a metaphor for the Buddha’s heroic vigor.

'Majestic authority' is a metaphor for the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real in the *Avataṃsaka*. 'Various kingdoms' refers to the twenty-five realms of existence as well as the provisional lands beyond the [ten] directions. 'Subduing' refers to..."

Using wisdom to destroy delusions is like a minor king who is disobedient; this is a metaphor for the false attachments and biased perversions of ordinary beings and those of limited capacity, which are difficult to transform.

The king’s military campaign to subjugate him is a metaphor for employing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as aids to the path, along with the fifty-five distinct stages of differentiated contemplative practice, to strike down the demonic armies of birth and death and thereby purify the single, true Dharma-realm. In terms of principle, the king is a metaphor for the fundamental [nature].
The principle of awakening: the metaphor of majesty represents fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); the various kingdoms represent the aggregates, bases, elements, the three greats, and so forth;
the minor kings represent the various mind-kings and mental factors; and the military campaign represents reliance on provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).

From the three gradual stages up to the fifty-five positions, culminating in the two awakenings of Equality and Wondrous Enlightenment, it penetrates from beginning to end—a single thought-moment of perfection.
Illumination. When the ten directions are severed at their source, the body-faculties and the vessel-world shall, in a single thought-moment, be transformed into supreme awakening.
[The King] saw among his troops those who had performed meritorious service in battle—[ranging from] elephants, horses, and chariots to slaves and commoners.

The multitude of soldiers is a metaphor for skillful means and wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*). Their merit is a metaphor for the destruction of the two attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*).

Their joy is a metaphor for sentient beings realizing the principle of the threefold equality at the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*). Bestowing rewards according to their merit is a metaphor for initiating practice based on that principle; it signifies that the fruit realized from causes is unfailing.
There are seven kinds of rewards, which are metaphors for the seven treasures of the noble ones (*ārya-dhana*). The first, fields and houses, is a metaphor for the Mahāyāna.

1. *Śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* correspond to the two villages and cities, which metaphorically represent the fifty-five stages of the principle of suchness (*tathatā*). 2. The set of robes corresponds to the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*). 3.

The precious jewels correspond to the principles and practices of differentiation. 4. The vehicles correspond to the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate truth (*upāya-jñāna* and *paramārtha-jñāna*).

The six classes of people represent the practice of differentiated wisdom (*pratisaṃvid-jñāna*). The above collectively clarifies that during the forty-year period, the provisional wisdom was equal to the sheep, deer, and ox carts;
however, the bright pearl from within the topknot was not given to them. (Up to this point: the King and his retinue would surely have been greatly astonished and marveled.
Tiantai says: This metaphor illustrates that the *Lotus Sūtra* is not preached at the wrong time, nor is it expounded for those who lack the capacity.

The "topknot" (*śikhā*) symbolizes the provisional; the "jewel" symbolizes the real. The real is concealed by the provisional, just as the jewel is hidden within the topknot. The "summit of the head" symbolizes the ultimate fruit.

To transcend the death and rebirth of the mundane realm (*bhavāgra*) is a minor achievement; to transcend the death and rebirth of the transformative realm (*nirmāṇa*) is the great achievement. Without having attained this great achievement, [the Buddha] bestows...
The topknot jewel. All the ministers were filled with doubt and wonder. This is a metaphor for when the great capacity of sentient beings has not yet been stirred;
when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is preached for them, those of the Two Vehicles feel doubt, while Bodhisattvas must surely feel wonder. △ Second, the combined parable.
Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata is also like this... [up to] ...the holy sages and generals fight alongside him.
This is an analogy consistent with the Dharma, clarifying that the merit of the sutra is exceptionally superior. Zhizhi says: "The Buddha corresponds to the Wheel-Turning King;
meditation and wisdom correspond to his majestic power. Attaining the Dharma-nature land and reigning over the triple world corresponds to subduing all kingdoms and demons."
Those who do not submit are the petty kings who are disobedient; those from the Three Vehicles upward are the worthy (xian); those above the three stages of worthiness are the sages (sheng).
Taken together, the four teachings and the fifty-five stages encompass all the worthy and sages of the Tathāgata.
To engage in battle with them is to use the contemplative wisdom of these fifty-five stages to confront and defeat both my [the practitioner's] afflictions and their dharmas.
This refers to the grasping and the fifty kinds of *skandha-māras*.
Those who possess merit also have their minds rejoice (up to) guiding their minds so that they all rejoice.

Tiantai says: "Roots and powers" refers to the five roots (*pañcendriya*) and the five powers (*pañcabala*). By cultivating these roots and powers, one does not fall into [the realms of] leakage (*āsrava*).
The cycle of birth and death within the six realms is thus called "outflow-free" (anāsrava). Nirvana is the true emptiness of the Lesser Vehicle;

it can prevent the errors of views and afflictions and repel the enemy of birth and death, and is therefore termed a "city. "Direct Pointing" states: "Those with merit" refers to the realization of the fruits through the four teachings;
"the four assemblies" refers to those at the stage of the causal ground; and "various sutras" refers to the forty years of the Lesser Vehicle.

The various teachings cause one to experience results according to their causes, each conforming to its respective intent; thus, the multitude’s hearts are gladdened. This corresponds to the section on the Holy King’s bestowal of rewards:
meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) corresponds to fields and houses; liberation (*vimukti*) and the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*) correspond to villages;

the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) correspond to clothing, utensils, and precious jewels; and the city of Nirvāṇa corresponds to the capital city. By guiding them in this way, he brings joy and binds their hearts [to the Dharma].
Although he rejoiced, [the Buddha] did not preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for him.
This corresponds to the single phrase "the holy king does not give the crest-jewel," as it was intended to wait for the proper time. △ Second, the directions.
The analogy of the jewel is divided into two parts. First, the introduction of the analogy:
"Mañjuśrī, like a wheel-turning monarch... [he] does not give it to others recklessly, yet now he gives it."

The metaphor of untying the topknot illustrates the opening of the provisional (upāya); the metaphor of bestowing the jewel illustrates the manifestation of the real (bhūta). Because [the Buddha] kept it secret and did not speak of it for forty years, it is said:
"He does not give it to others recklessly. △ Second, the synthesis of the metaphors.
The Tathāgata is also like this... (up to) "at that time, the Tathāgata was also greatly rejoiced.
This illustrates the correspondence between the Dharma and the metaphor. Zhizhi says: "The Tathāgata is a king over the three realms, not merely over the four continents.

The Buddha is the King of Dharma, not merely a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*). By means of the Dharma he teaches and transforms, causing beings to leave suffering behind and attain [liberation]."

Joy is not merely the attainment of power through forceful suppression. As the *Miaole* (Cloud of Wondrous Joy) says: "Regarding the vision of the worthy and noble ones," the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:

"By knowing suffering, one destroys the demon of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*); by abandoning accumulation, one leaves behind the demon of afflictions (*kleśamāra*); by realizing cessation, one leaves behind the demon of death (*mṛtyumāra*); and by cultivating the path, one destroys the demon of Māra.
The reason why the demon of Māra is not mentioned here is that in the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), one primarily abandons these three demons. This has already been established.
The meaning of "destroying the heavenly Māras" is that one who attains the Path will inevitably subdue the Māras. One who achieves great merit is as follows:

when the Tathāgata sees that the followers of the Lesser Vehicle eliminate suffering and its origin within the realm of the world, it is called "waging war against the aggregates" (*skandha-yuddha*). Upon reaching the Prajñā [wisdom], they shatter ignorance and emerge from the *parināmika* (transformative) existence;
this is called "great merit. Therefore, the three poisons and so forth are for now explained within the context of the Lesser Vehicle. The three poisons are, namely, greed... [and so on].

Hatred and delusion: when they exist within the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), they are called the "perverse three poisons"; when they exist within the afflictions of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*), they are called the "correct three poisons.

They do not transcend these two types of affliction—views and mental cultivation. The Tathāgata, having seen that all worthies and sages have already severed both views and mental cultivation, has emerged beyond the triple world.
They are not ensnared by the net of Māra; having shattered ignorance, they emerge from the realm of transformation. Therefore, it is called "Great Joy.
This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* can cause sentient beings [to attain this state], such that what was previously unsaid is now spoken.

All who hear this sutra shall universally attain Buddhahood; therefore, it is said that they reach "all-encompassing wisdom" (*sarvajñā*). Regarding the phrase "many enemies and difficult to believe":

"many enemies" refers to the fact that this sutra is not easily preached, as exemplified by the five thousand who withdrew from their seats. "Difficult to believe" refers to those of middling or inferior capacities.
Thus, it was previously stated that even while the Tathāgata is present, there are still many who harbor resentment and jealousy. This has not been explained before.
This is because their faculties were not yet mature; that it is taught now is because the proper time has been fulfilled.
Mañjuśrī, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—like a long-guarded bright jewel—is finally bestowed upon them now.
This concludes the teaching by means of both analogy and dharma. This alone is the single reality; there is nothing else, hence it is called "foremost.
Only Buddha after Buddha can know it, hence it is called "profoundly deep. Once the life of wisdom has been sustained, the Buddha then manifested his parinirvāṇa.

Therefore, it is said that "it was bestowed at the very end. The final three lines cite a metaphor to provide a dual conclusion, demonstrating that the revelation of the reality is rare and marvelous.
[The Buddha says: "Mañjuśrī, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*... (up to) ...I shall now expound it for you all."
This concludes the preceding section on the exhaustion of the fetters through the Dharma.

It means that this sutra is that which all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and three periods of time collectively cherish and delight in, guarding it throughout the long night; it is the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*). It is not spoken of recklessly;
it is the esoteric treasury (*guhya-kośa*). Precisely because of this secret Dharma, it is the most supreme and most vital, incomparable to other dharmas or other sutras. Just as...
The crest-jewel of the Wheel-Turning King is the most honored, the most secret, and the most cherished;

it cannot be compared to other fields, houses, or treasures. Since today I have expounded this most honored and most secret Dharma for you all, and you have obtained it, how could you ever regard it as being like other teachings or ordinary sutras? Furthermore, within this...
The intent of the sutra is that although it places primary emphasis on the Dharma, in reality, those who receive and uphold the teachings will naturally develop reverence for it;
by purifying their body, speech, and mind, they shall make firm their vows, thereby perfecting the peaceful and blissful practices for propagating the sutra in the final age.

△ Second, the verses in praise. This is divided into two parts. First, the verses on the methods of practice. This is further divided into two. First, the verses that skip ahead to the methods of practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
By constantly practicing patience and showing compassion for all, one is able to expound the sūtras praised by the Buddha.

In the preceding prose, the accomplishment of practice was explained in general; now, it is specifically revealed in these verses. "Constantly practicing patience" refers to the accomplishment of practice by donning the robe of patience.

△ 2. Purification of the Three Obstacles. Divided into three parts: 1. Transformation of the obstacle of retribution to obtain the present...

sentient beings delight in seeing [him], longing for him as if he were a holy sage, and celestial youths serve him as attendants.
This clarifies the transformation of the obstacle of greed. One who has much greed is treated with contempt by others; furthermore, it obstructs rebirth in the Brahma world.
Now, since one is seen with pleasure as a human being, one is not treated with contempt. Since celestial youths serve one, one attains rebirth in the Brahma world.
This is why subsequent retribution is transformed.
Weapons and staves do not strike him, and poisons cannot harm him; he wanders without fear like a lion king.
This clarifies the transformation of the obstacle of anger (*dveṣa*). By abandoning anger, one eliminates the internal knives and arrows; when encountering harm, the external knives [do not strike].
They are not harmed; therefore, it is said that "swords and staves do not strike them. Anger is the poisonous drug that destroys loving-kindness and compassion.
When loving-kindness and compassion flourish, poison cannot cause harm. Anger is the internal organ of harsh speech;
when there is no anger within, the mouths of those who would revile one naturally close. Because they are free from all things that provoke fear, they wander about without fear, like lions.
He is a king.
The light of his wisdom shines like the sun.
This clarifies the transformation of the obstacle of delusion (*moha*). Delusion is able to obstruct wisdom; now that the obstacle of delusion has been removed, it causes—
Wisdom is clear and penetrating, like the light of the sun. Regarding the phrase "those who previously turned [the wheel] extinguish the three obstacles and the three poisons":
it is because within this Secret Treasury, the encompassing of all dharmas is inexhaustible. Furthermore, wherever this sutra resides, all Buddhas rejoice;
therefore, those who uphold it shall have no sorrow. This sutra can deliver all beings from birth and death; therefore, those who uphold it shall have no illness. This sutra...
Like the udumbara flower, it is unstained by even a single speck of dust; therefore, those who uphold it will have a fresh and white complexion. This sutra possesses immeasurable sublime virtues;
therefore, those who uphold it will never be exhausted. This sutra is protected by all Buddhas; it causes those who uphold it not to be born into lowly or base circumstances.
This sutra is adorned with ten thousand forms of goodness; it causes those who uphold it not to be born with an ugly appearance. Since the three obstacles [have been removed]...
It transforms. The three poisons are secretly eliminated. Thus, it is like yearning for the worthy and holy, like a lion king, and like the shining sun.
By means of these three "like" characters, this Dharma is revealed with nothing left unexhausted. △ Second, a general explanation of the transformation of all hindrances.
If, within a dream, one sees only auspicious matters (up to) being surrounded by a multitude of bhikṣus while preaching the Dharma—
