“World-Honored One, such a matter as this is difficult for the world to believe... that you have brought us into birth—this matter is difficult to believe. This is because the cause and the phenomenon are contrary;
therefore, an inverse analogy is raised for investigation in order to reveal the fundamental reality.

*Zhizhi* says: “For example, there is a person” is a metaphor for the Buddha. “With beautiful complexion and black hair” is a metaphor for the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Trace Gate. “At the age of twenty.”
5. This is illustrated by the analogy of a prince who leaves home and attains the Way; yet it has been barely forty-odd years since he did so—what is called "a short period of time.

This uses a recent event to cast doubt upon the distant past, as when a hundred-year-old man is pointed out as one's son. This serves as a metaphor for the Bodhisattvas emerging from the earth, all of whom have long cultivated their virtuous deeds;
they are certainly not Buddhas newly manifested through conversion today. Thus, the hundred-year-old man is used to represent those who are young.
The father serves as a metaphor for all Bodhisattvas who approach the void to pay homage and offer praise; thus, one distances oneself from the fundamental [truth] while suspecting the proximate.
Moreover, since the relationship between father and son is inherently appropriate, why should their ages alone be so contrary? Therefore, it is said that this matter is difficult to believe.
However, herein there is a fixation on the迹门 (Ji-men, the Gate of Traces) and taking the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) as primary, thereby doubting the fundamental gate (benmen).
Using what is not a companion: at the outset, one uses the traces to cast doubt upon the fundamental; it is not expected that by means of the fundamental, the traces will be shattered.
These are all questions of skillful means (*upāya*). Only this mutual reversal between the principal and the companion constitutes the primary intent;
as for the rest, there is no need for erroneous correlation. △ Second, the combined analogy.
The Buddha is also like this; from the time he attained the Way until now, he has led [beings] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

This passage cites the Dharma to correspond with the metaphor, thereby manifesting the ultimate goal of the fundamental source. Direct Pointing (Zhizhi) says: "The three phrases beginning with 'The Buddha is also... refers to this.
The beauty of their complexions reached its peak by the age of twenty-five. Among this great assembly, those who were a hundred years old were like children.
Within this, the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*) are not excluded: practicing diligently and with vigor is the perfection of effort (*vīryapāramitā*);

skillfully entering, emerging from, and abiding in [meditative states] is the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*); immeasurable samādhis are the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); and attaining the Great... [text fragment ends].
Supernatural powers are the perfection of aspiration; long cultivation of the holy life is the perfection of ethical discipline; cultivation of all wholesome dharmas is the perfection of generosity;
skill in question and answer is the perfection of skillful means; being a jewel among men is the perfection of power; being exceedingly rare is the perfection of patience.
Since patience is placed last, it corresponds to abiding in the stage of gentle patience. Today, the World-Honored One has descended, corresponding to the age of one hundred years.
People refer to the youth as the father. Tiantai says: "The nine successive concentrations (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti) are skillful entry;

the lion’s bound-fury samādhi (siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi) is skillful exit; the leap-over samādhi (vyutkrāntaka-samādhi) is skillful abiding. This is the meaning of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings (zàng-tōng).
From the first stage (bhūmi) to the tenth stage is called skillful entry. Entering the gate of profound mystery from the tenth stage, one again practices the affairs of an ordinary person.
"Skillfully emerging" refers to the wondrous enlightenment being all-pervasive; this is called "skillfully abiding. This is the intent of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*).
"Skillfully entering" refers to the *dharmatā-samādhi*; "skillfully emerging" refers to the *śūraṅgama-samādhi*; and "skillfully abiding" refers to the *rāja-samādhi*.
This is the intent of the Perfect Teaching (*ekayāna*). △ Third, the request for an answer.
It has not been long since the World-Honored One attained Buddhahood (until: ...), yet he has fully mastered everything known by a Buddha.

The two phrases beginning with "The World-Honored One" are words that are truly difficult to believe. The three phrases beginning with "We" indicate that we understand in our minds that the Tathāgata’s speech is based on a standard;
that is to say, we know for certain that the Tathāgata intends to manifest his distant origins, and this is spoken according to what is appropriate.
It is said that the assembly of beings who have emerged from the earth does not speak falsely; knowing all things without fail, they do not speak erroneously.
This is known exclusively by me, Maitreya, and my peers. As for those of later learning and beginners, it must be proclaimed and clarified by the Tathāgata before they can understand.
Nevertheless, even those bodhisattvas who have newly resolved [to attain enlightenment], upon hearing this matter, will not give rise to doubt.
Tiantai says: "Those currently making this request are specifically for the sake of those with newly resolved minds in the future and the present.

Because their practice is shallow and their faith is slight, they are prone to giving rise to slander; through slander, they fall into suffering. Those who are non-retrogressive, although able to believe, [do not fall into such error]."

[They] slander [the teaching]. This cannot increase the Path. However, if it is analyzed and explained, those who slander will come to have faith, and those who already have faith will further increase their progress on the Path.
[△@△] Although we ourselves believe this, for the sake of those who have newly resolved to attain enlightenment, hearing these words may give rise to doubt.
Since Maitreya himself has clearly and explicitly stated this, one knows that Maitreya’s own doubts were originally identical to those of Zhiji and Mañjuśrī.

There is no difference. Throughout these repeated arguments and refutations, there is nothing that does not aim to resolve the doubts of later students and strengthen their faith, so that they may achieve unexcelled bodhi.
A connoisseur asks: "In the analogy, the young father points to Laozi, and Laozi points to the young father."
Question: Within the Dharma, it is appropriate for the young to point out the old, but why is it inappropriate for the old to point out the young?
Answer: This should have been included in the text; perhaps the translator overlooked it. However, the meaning directly emphasizes that the father is young and the son is old on one side;

therefore, it is not appropriate for the old to point out the young. Question: Where in the sutra text is it seen that the old recognizes the young as his father? Answer: In the first section, "The Initial Eruption."

When emerging [from meditation], after completing the prostrations and praises to the Buddhas of the three periods and the ten directions, he then alone pays his respects to Śākyamuni; this is the point where the old man recognizes the young.
△ Second, the verse summary, divided into two parts. First, the summary of the Dharma-exposition.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"In the past, the Buddha left the Śākya clan to renounce the world; it has not been long since he sat beneath the Bodhi tree near Gayā."
This verse refers to those who cling to recent events; that is to say, they have seen him leave home and attain enlightenment, which is commonly known by people, yet in reality it has not been long.
How can these sons of the Buddha, whose number is immeasurable, be believed? [The text continues from "their number is immeasurable" up to] "...how can they be believed?"
This verse raises doubts regarding the distant origin [of the text]. It suggests that the multitude was beyond reckoning and had long practiced;

their supernormal powers and samādhis surpassed all others, as they were all products of prior study. By the single phrase "a lotus flower in the water," the upper part metaphorically illustrates being unstained by worldly dharmas, while the lower part metaphorically illustrates emerging from the earth. Those who are thus are all gradually and reverently devoted to the Tathāgata.
At first glance, it appeared as if created by the Tathāgata himself; yet when one examines the facts, they are vastly remote, while observing its expression, it is again strikingly lifelike.
This is truly something difficult to believe.
"The Buddha attained the Way so recently, yet that which he has accomplished is so vast; we pray that you will dispel our doubts and explain this according to reality.
This verse concludes the request for an answer. That is to say, if the World-Honored One had attained enlightenment long ago, there would be no cause for doubt;
nor would there be cause for doubt if the assembly to be converted were small and few. Yet now, in such a short and recent time, he has transformed this inconceivable multitude.
It is not only those whose afflictions have been deep and wisdom shallow from the outset who harbor doubts;

even those currently receiving transformation through the teaching cannot avoid doubt. If such matters were not proclaimed and revealed by the Tathāgata, they would instead increase their karmic burdens. II. Verses on the Parable.
For example, a person in the prime of youth, twenty-five years of age, [doing something] that the whole world does not believe—this is the meaning of the analogy, explained exactly as before.
However, while the long prose version speaks of the father’s handsome complexion and black hair, the verse speaks of the son’s white hair and wrinkled face;
thus, they appear alternately in the preceding and following sections. (The character *zhòu* is pronounced *zòu*.)
The World-Honored One has likewise attained the Way for but a very short time, yet he dwells in the space below.

Since Maitreya claimed not to recognize a single person, how could he know that their resolve was firm and fearless, that they had practiced the Path through distant kalpas until their minds were determined in patience, and that they were praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions? As for what he called "not recognizing" them—

This is precisely the ultimate limit of consciousness. However, for those who have newly resolved their minds and those in the future who do not yet truly understand consciousness, [the purpose] is to enable them to realize the realm of Maitreya’s non-consciousness.
"We have heard this matter from the Buddha and are without doubt" (up to) "we abide in the stage of non-retrogression.
The Tathāgata’s intent in bestowing his teachings is firm and urgent, and the Bodhisattva’s sincerity in assisting in the transformation of beings is likewise earnest.
That Maitreya’s request is pressing at every step does not mean that the Buddha does not bestow subtle compassion; it is simply that [Maitreya] desires to practice.

If a person’s faculty of faith is firm and solid, they wash away the defilements of the mind and gradually enter an auspicious state; yet, should they become slightly attached to their state of doubt, they will fall into the evil realms.
One whose profound compassion and sincere resolve for compassionate salvation are as earnest as these is truly equal to a Buddha.
This concludes the brief elucidation regarding the movement of attachments and the arising of doubt.

The sixteenth chapter, "The Lifespan of the Tathāgata," states:

Regarding the intent of this chapter’s inclusion, it arises from Maitreya raising doubts, to which the World-Honored One responds by teaching his lifespan in order to reveal the subtlety of his fundamental and manifested traces (*honjaku*).
Exhausting my private efforts, I shall refute the views of the two vehicles regarding birth and extinction, thereby reaching the ultimate principle of the *dharmakāya*. Following...

Because of universal response, the concealment and manifestation [of the Buddha] are unimpeded; only then does one come to know that the Tathāgata’s wisdom is profoundly deep and immeasurable, and that the gateway to this wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter.
The intent is that for those who practice and study, if they do not penetrate the *dharmakāya*, it is ultimately not a true realization and cannot be called the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
In the "Jeweled Stūpa" chapter, although [the Buddha] distantly relies upon the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna... [text fragment].
The Dharma-body was revealed; yet the great assembly believed only in Prabhūtaratna and did not recognize that Śākyamuni and he were one and the same body, possessing the power of a single wisdom.
Because the śrāvakas perceived and knew only the one who preached the Dharma at the Deer Park as the true Buddha, they remained unaware that there was still a further reality beyond.
Furthermore, hearing that [the Buddha] was about to enter parinirvāṇa, they were moved to arise once more.
With a mind set on extinction, although they hear the bestowal of prophecy, they merely understand it as the Buddha’s words and have not yet awakened to the Buddha’s mind;
thus, they will ultimately find it difficult to attain the fruit of Bodhi from afar. Since their awakening is not yet true, how could their cultivation be real?

Then the Tathāgata’s original intent for appearing in the world would never be fully realized. Although he previously provided various indications, these were still dependent upon others; now, at this point, the Tathāgata...
Exhausting his supernatural powers, he reveals his true intent; thus, he demonstrates that the lifespan of the Dharmakāya is immeasurable.

Furthermore, by means of the analogy of the physician, he clarifies that although it ceases, it does not cease, and directly causes those of the Two Vehicles to realize that birth is non-birth, thereby personally attesting to the Dharmakāya.
While the true cause has already been planted, this chapter fully elucidates the principle; from the following chapter onward, there is merely further differentiation.

It is merely a matter of merit. Daokuang says: "This sutra begins with the teaching of the *Sūtra of Immeasurability*, entering the immeasurable samādhi, and emitting immeasurable light, thereby manifesting the immeasurability of the Tathāgata’s phenomena in every respect.
In the two chapters on Expedient Means and Parables, it manifests the immeasurable skillful means of the Tathāgata.
In the Chapter on the Medicinal Herbs, one sees the immeasurability of the rain of Dharma. In the Chapter on the City of Transformation..."
The immeasurable number of kalpas is revealed; the immeasurable knowledge and vision [of the Tathāgata] is revealed; the immeasurable śrāvaka disciples he transforms are revealed;
in the "Treasure Stūpa" chapter, the immeasurable emanated bodies are seen; and in the "Earth-Sprouting" chapter, the immeasurable bodhisattvas he transforms are seen.

Nevertheless, these are all merely peripheral matters concerning the Tathāgata’s responsive manifestations (*nirmāṇa*). They have not yet fully revealed the equality and immeasurability of the dharmakāya’s life of wisdom (*prajñājīvita*).
Therefore, this chapter specifically discusses the immeasurable lifespan of the Tathāgata, manifesting that he attained enlightenment long ago, prior to even the kalpas as numerous as motes of dust;
hence it is titled "The Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata. "Tathāgata" is a general designation for all those throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
"Lifespan" (*āyus-pramāṇa*) is a principle shared equally by the holy and the ordinary. While sentient beings cling to appearances and are deluded, [the text continues].
Distinguishing between the long and the short, the Tathāgata penetrates the source and the bottom to realize non-arising (*anutpāda*).
From his descent of spirit and manifestation of birth to his proclamation of extinction (*nirvāṇa*), all were manifestations shown in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.

Now, wishing to open the final profound gate for those who have newly entered the records and who are timid regarding the views of arising and ceasing, he most fully reveals the immeasurable life of the True Heaven. For this reason, it is named [the *Amida Sutra*].

Chapter. △ Second, the detailed exposition on severing delusions and generating faith. This section is divided into two parts. First, the admonition to believe and the earnest request. This is further divided into three parts.
First, the Tathāgata’s admonition to believe.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas (up to): "You all should believe and understand the Tathāgata’s words of truth.
"Truth" refers to that which is real and without falsehood. For forty years, the Tathāgata has employed skillful means.
I have explained everything else in full detail, yet this fundamental source alone has not been revealed. This is not because I am being deliberately solemn or hesitant.
As soon as one opens their mouth, if it is not that their faith is insufficient, it is that their understanding is not yet penetrating.

If one lacks both faith and understanding, will they not bring this great matter to an end within the realm of delusion? Now, seeing that the roots of faith among the assembled congregation are already pure, [I shall speak].

The time has now arrived; how can you simply remain hidden and patient? Yet, even before speaking, I have called for awakening three times and issued three warnings, all intended to cause the assembly to give rise to faith and understanding.
Once you have attained sufficient faith, you will naturally penetrate through to full comprehension.
To understand thoroughly is to attain through faith; this single word "faith" is truly the root source of realization and awakening.
II. The Assembly’s Repeated Request:
At that time, the great assembly of Bodhisattvas, with Maitreya at their head... (until) "...we shall faithfully accept the Buddha’s words."
When the Tathāgata himself speaks, it is called the "Ultimate Truth. When Maitreya and others hear it, they recognize it immediately as the Buddha’s word;
there is no word of the Buddha that is not the Ultimate Truth. When the Tathāgata called out three times, Maitreya and the others made their request three times;
when the Tathāgata gave his charge three times, Maitreya and the others accepted it three times. They already knew it within their own hearts.
Duan’s subtle and profound faith has indeed reached its fulfillment; yet, because the World-Honored One had never explicitly spoken it out, there was no basis for his understanding and awakening.
Therefore, after three requests, he again made a solemn entreaty; his resolve to seek understanding was truly earnest and ultimate.
△ The World-Honored One’s second admonition.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the bodhisattvas had made their request three times without ceasing, addressed them, saying: "Listen attentively.
Since they had requested three times without stopping, he further accepted their plea four times; for this cannot be done by those who lack profound faith.

The World-Honored One already knew that Maitreya and the others were capable of receiving and upholding [the teaching], yet he necessarily called out to you again and once more exhorted you to listen attentively.
This is because this matter is profoundly deep and subtle; I only fear that you might incidentally give rise to doubts or obstructions.

II. The direct answer to the question, divided into two parts. A. The prose explanation, further divided into two. 1. The teaching by way of Dharma, further divided into two. a. Benefiting sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, further divided into two.
i. Clarifying the benefit of sentient beings in the past, further divided into two. 1. Manifesting according to the immediate inclinations of those ready to be awakened.
Regarding "the power of the Tathāgata’s secret supernatural penetrations" up to "attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*":
as for the "Tathāgata’s secret [powers] and so forth," this refers to what was previously promised and cautioned in the preceding chapter, stating:
"I now wish to reveal and proclaim the wisdom of all Buddhas, up to the three kinds of powers—the sovereign supernatural penetrations of all Buddhas. From this point downward:

This is precisely what is being manifested. The previous statement referred to the sovereign supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of all Buddhas; this present statement refers to the secret supernatural powers of the Tathāgata.

This correctly permits the mutual illumination of their characteristics. "Tathāgata" is the general designation for the ten directions and the three periods of time as cited in the title of this chapter.
"Secret," etc., refers to the two characters "Life Span" (*āyus-pramāṇa*) in the title. This single phrase summarizes all the aforementioned Buddhas.
The phrases such as "wisdom" and so forth are secret; they are realized only by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time.
They are esoteric; they are protected only by all Buddhas. "Divine" means that the nine realms cannot fathom them. "Penetrating" means that the three periods of time cannot alter them.
What are called the "Tathāgata’s lifespan" and the "wisdom of all Buddhas" are, in intent, but a single phrase; this is the essential core of the Root Chapter.
The meaning is fully contained herein. Regarding the phrase "all the worlds," etc., this collectively refers to the nine realms that cling to recent traces and fail to know the distant origin;
thus it is said that all consider Śākyamuni to be a newly accomplished Buddha. This also restates the previous words of Maitreya’s doubt.
△ Second, refuting the near to reveal the far, divided into two parts. First, specifically revealing the long duration, which is further divided into two.
This is the first teaching.
However, son of good family, it has actually been hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas since I truly attained Buddhahood.

From this point downward, the text directly refutes attachments and dispels delusions in order to reveal the primordially remote origin. Above, [the Buddha] cautioned [them] to listen attentively and believe.

This refers to that very point. Since the Tathāgata has already stated that his attainment of Buddhahood was long ago, the misconception that he attained enlightenment recently at Gayā—namely, the attachment that the father is young while the son is old—can now be refuted.
△ Second, the explanation by way of analogy, which is further divided into three parts. First, citing an analogy to pose a question.
"For example, [if there were] five hundred thousand million billion [worlds] (up to the point where one could contemplate, calculate, and know their number)—Tiantai says:
Other sutras clarify large numbers by using metaphors such as 'unspeakable' dust motes and sands; however, this present sutra uses them as a metaphor for long life.
Even the realms directly beneath a single dust mote that has been marked are already unspeakable, let alone those beneath it."

How could the realm of dust be described? Since even the realm of "lower dust" and "not lower dust" cannot be described, how much less could the dust within the worlds of "lower dust" and "not lower dust" be described? Furthermore, it is said that there are even more than this;
how then could that be described? A *nayuta*—this is translated as ten billion (*koṭi*). An *asaṃkhyeya*—this...
It is called "innumerable. [△@△] The previous statement regarding the duration of the kalpa until Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū’s parinirvāṇa did not exceed taking a single trichiliocosm as dust particles;
nor did it go beyond saying that a single point is placed beneath a thousand lands.
Now, it is said that one takes five hundred thousand million billion nayutas of asaṃkhyeya worlds and reduces them to dust;
then, having passed beyond even more such vast lands, one places a single speck. Thus, its transcendence of numerical measure is immense.

The Tathāgata says that [this teaching] was given at the place of the Buddha Jñānavatī, where he preached the Dharma for the prince; this was already spoken as a discourse revealing the original source.
However, at that time, he explained the causes and conditions for those of inferior capacity, first revealing a single aspect to serve as a definitive conclusion for this section.
Now, reaching this point, he reveals the original source in its entirety, so that a beginner may grasp it upon hearing it once, without the need for prolixity. This is even more so.

In the previous "Admonition and Permission" section, it was stated that the sovereign power of the Buddhas' supernatural penetrations (*ṛddhi*), the power of the lion’s majestic springing (*siṃhavijṛmbhita*), and the power of great might and ferocity do not transcend this chapter. Second, the answer is given by way of [the disciples'] ignorance.
Maitreya Bodhisattva and the others addressed the Buddha together, saying: [up to] "Such worlds as these are immeasurable and boundless.

Among these, three types of people are mentioned who do not know [them]: those who have reached the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), also called *abhibhūti* (in Chinese, *bùtuǎnzhuǎn*, "non-retrogressing").
Maitreya answered that this is known neither by calculation nor can it be reached by the power of the mind; thus, he has already cut through [the doubt].
This utterly severs the life-faculties of the three classes of beings. How excellent is the sincerity of your assistance in this transformation; your kindness is no small matter.
Next, he raises the point regarding the ignorance of these three classes: namely, that although the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas possess untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna), [they lack...]

To contemplate by means of this is already remote. If one were to limit it to the boundaries of the world-systems, or calculate it by means of the number of worlds as fine as motes of dust, even a non-retrogressive Bodhisattva, though they have reached the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyak-saṃbodhi), does not forget these quantities, yet they do not fully comprehend them.
That they do not fully comprehend them is because a portion of the characteristics of arising has not yet been extinguished; how then could they know the Tathāgata?
This is a secret supernatural power; therefore, it is simply stated that "this world is immeasurable and boundless.
△ Third, the combined manifestation of its long duration:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of great bodhisattvas... [up to] "hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeya kalpas."

This correctly reveals the fundamental point. The Direct Instruction says: "Taking the aforementioned lands already covered by dust, as well as the five hundred trillion nayuta asaṃkhyeya lands in between that have not yet been covered by dust—all these lands of the eastern direction, both those covered and those not covered—grind them all completely into dust.
Let each particle of dust represent one kalpa, following the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment."
"Come. Furthermore, it passes through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of such eons. The Essential Explanation (*Yaojie*) states: "The lifespan of all Buddhas is entirely immeasurable;
the lifespan of sentient beings is likewise so. It is only because they are deluded regarding their own wisdom that they falsely pursue birth and death.
For example, if one falls into a single hell and remains there for countless eons, is this not an immeasurable lifespan? If indeed it were not..."

If one remains deluded and falls [into error], how does this differ from [the state of] a Buddha? [△@△] Those who clearly proclaim these words do so because the capacity [of the audience] has matured and faith has been established;

it is not that they previously withheld them through skillful means to accommodate the capacities of others by remaining silent. When it is said that he has been a Buddha since the past, this refers solely to the past.
There have already been inconceivable kalpas; yet if one continues to investigate and trace them back, each preceding stage is itself without beginning.
Once it is known that each preceding stage is without beginning, one recognizes that each succeeding stage is likewise without end.

Considering the total lifespan across the three periods of time, how could it ever be exhausted? Question: If it is thus vast and boundless without end, who can know that this lifespan is so long and far-reaching?

Answer: It is said that the Tathāgata is not seen; this is because he now wishes to manifest and proclaim the wisdom of all Buddhas. Since it is called "Buddha-wisdom," it is known and seen only by a Buddha.
Therefore, neither any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor even non-retrogressive bodhisattvas, can know or see it;
only those who have attained solitary awakening (pratyekajina) can know and see it. Because it is thus inconceivable and immeasurable, it is so called.

This is the power of sovereign spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*). △ Second, the appropriateness for benefiting sentient beings. This is divided into three parts. First, the place where they benefit sentient beings:
"From that time until now, I have constantly remained here (until) leading and benefiting sentient beings in incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) lands."
This clarifies that the appearance of the Buddhas in the world is due to the power of secret spiritual transformations (*ṛddhi*). The *Yinzhi* (Sound-Knower) commentary states:
"Although they manifest birth, they are in reality not born. Since the kalpa of dust-motes, they have either been in this Sahā world or have manifested in other lands."
Nevertheless, while the oceans of lands inherently possess distinctions of "this" and "that," the Dharma-body pervades them all to guide and benefit sentient beings;

this is why it constitutes the secret, primordial foundation. [△@△] I, the fool, maintain that the previous citation of the lifespan revealed that the Dharma-nature body is infinite throughout the three periods of time, while this citation of the lands reveals that the Dharma-nature land is boundless throughout the ten directions. Thus...
With such a body, dwelling in such a land, preaching such a Dharma, and transforming such a multitude—within this interval, what Dharma was not preached?

What being was not delivered? It is as if one sees only the imperial wind forming a single expanse, unaware of where any boundaries lie; from beginning to end, it is solely thus. △ Second: Wiping Away.
The traces [of his activity] are suspect. These good sons, in the interval between [then and now], up until this very day, have all distinguished [the teachings] through skillful means.
As the commentary says: "From kalpas as numerous as motes of dust until today, in the interim, he may have spoken of receiving the prediction from Dīpaṃkara."
The initial arousal of the bodhicitta is regarded as the beginning, while entry into nirvana is said to be the ultimate end.

That the retributive and transformational bodies are not devoid of arising and ceasing is entirely a distinction made by the provisional wisdom of skillful means; this is why they are considered the proximate traces of supernatural power.

[△@△] The previous statement spoke of "coming from this," while the present statement refers to "this intermediate stage. These two instances of the character "this" (是) are precisely the secret divinity.
This is a profound point. Those who observe it must not treat it with negligence. These two characters, "intermediate" (zhōngjiān), are by no means superficial or mundane.
Since he has cited "inconceivable kalpas as numerous as motes of dust," the manifestation of birth and extinction within that interval is likewise inconceivable.
When Dīpaṃkara Buddha mentions the "last" [kalpa], the word "etc. (děng) refers to all the inconceivable kalpas prior to Dīpaṃkara in which [the Bodhisattva] performed his practices.
These all refer to the skillful means of manifesting birth. Since it is said that he manifests birth, he must likewise manifest extinction;
therefore, it is further stated that he enters nirvana, meaning he manifests extinction during the interval of inconceivable eons.
This is also a skillful means (*upāya*). Thus we know that the World-Honored One, throughout immeasurable kalpas of the past, has distinguished such wondrous Dharma through skillful means;
and throughout immeasurable kalpas of the future, he shall likewise distinguish it through skillful means.
We know that while empty space may come to an end, skillful means are inexhaustible. △ Third, clarifying the benefit of sentient beings.
"O sons of good family, if there are sentient beings [up to] who likewise manifest by saying they shall enter *nirvāṇa*.
The preceding statements showed birth and death; however, it was not yet clarified for what reason these were shown.
Here, for the first time, the reasons for showing birth and death are clarified. 'If there are sentient beings' refers to those within the nine realms who come to my presence."

This is the moment when principle and wisdom meet in profound stillness and the karmic capacity is activated in resonance. The Buddha-eye is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom that shines universally without omission;
this is the subject of contemplation (*nirūpaka*). Faith and the others are the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), which constitute the capacities for sharp or dull realization;

these are the objects of contemplation (*nirūpya*). Among the five faculties, wisdom is the "revealing cause" (*vyañjanahetu*), while faith, diligence, mindfulness, and concentration serve as the four conditions (*pratyaya*).
As for the causes, there are differences of sharpness and dullness, as well as greatness and smallness.

According to those who are to be saved, because their capacities and inspirations differ, the manifestations of the response vary. The phrase "in every place" refers to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeya lands.

The names and so forth mentioned therein do not go beyond having the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body) as their essence; however, the names follow [the specific circumstances].

Regarding "expedient transformation," there is the name "inconceivable. As for the distinction between great and small [lifespans], the "great" refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), while the "small" refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body).
This is also a manifestation according to the capacities of beings (*yathā-vainayika*), showing the differences in the length of their lifespans.

This completes the two characters "middle" and "end" mentioned above; it is also the manifestation of non-arising as arising. This completes the phrase: "I spoke of [having served] Dīpaṃkara Buddha and others. It is also...

Furthermore, the manifestation of speech and so forth refers to those who are to be transformed through the means of *parinirvāṇa*. Thus, for them, there is no extinction, yet extinction is manifested;

this is precisely what completes the previous statement regarding their entry into *nirvāṇa*. Such is the general clarification of the Buddha-activities of the Trace Gate (*jìmén*), which are like the moon in water or flowers in the sky.
Dàkuǎn says: "To investigate the reality, there is not a single thing that is not the Tathāgata."
There is not a single name that is not the Tathāgata’s title; there is not a single kṣaṇa that is not a time of the Tathāgata’s manifestation;
there is not a single place as small as a mustard seed that is not the site of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa. It is so in every atom, so in every world-system, and so in every thought-moment.
Each and every thing is thus. How could it be limited by a single body, a single name, a single time, or a single place?
This reveals that, through secret spiritual powers, he manifests this very appearance within the past.
Furthermore, by means of various skillful expedients (*upāya*), he preaches the subtle and wondrous Dharma, enabling sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy.

The previous statement showed that birth and extinction are not the same; this passage clarifies that the Small and Great Vehicles are no different. "Various skillful expedients" refers to the provisional (*prajñapti*);

"preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma" refers to the real (*tattva*). By using the provisional to explain the real, all return to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); one sees that phenomena are non-dual.

Furthermore, the Dharma taught accords with the specific nature of each being, thereby causing them to rejoice. This correctly completes the four characters "skillful means" (*upāya*) and "differentiation" (*vibhāga*).
From this, one knows that within the first four characters, both the provisional and the ultimate teachings are fully encompassed;
it is not the "differentiation" as commonly understood. △ Second, clarifying the benefit of beings in the present, divided into two parts. First, clarifying the response of the faculties.

"O sons of good family, when the Tathāgata perceives that sentient beings delight in inferior teachings, possess meager merit, and are heavily defiled—this section completes the preceding [passage], from which it follows:
'Since that time, I have constantly remained in this Sahā world, preaching the Dharma and transforming beings.

'Perceiving sentient beings' refers to the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) discerning their capacities; it specifically indicates a class of beings with dull faculties and heavy defilements."

I shall speak concerning those who are heavy [in their defilements]. Those who delight in the Lesser Dharma possess thin merit and heavy impurities; consequently, they lack the aspiration for the Mahāyāna.

For this reason, they cling only to the immediate traces and fail to comprehend the secrets of the distant origin. "Thin merit" means that the functional efficacy of the two virtues—the conditioned and the ultimate—is weak and inferior.

"Heavy impurities" means that the afflictions of view and thought have not yet been eliminated. Thus, because the virtuous causes are minute while the stains of delusion are heavy, [they do not attain realization].

Knowing the fundamental source of the far-reaching, one can only manifest birth and extinction for the sake of others. △ Second, clarifying the manifested transformation. This is divided into two parts.
First, manifesting birth where there is no birth. This is further divided into two. First, manifesting birth.
For these people, I say that I left home at a young age and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This clarifies that on this day I conceal my excellence and manifest inferiority by displaying the eight phases of attaining enlightenment;
it is intended to provide a skillful means to draw near those of inferior capacity.
"However, since I truly attained Buddhahood... (up to) "...causing them to enter the Buddha-way, I speak thus.
This is a summary that concludes all the secret supernatural powers within the "original" and "traced" [teachings], speaking in this manner.

The first two phrases conclude and demonstrate the manifestation of the original; the latter three phrases conclude and demonstrate the clarification of the trace. △ Second, the benefits. Divided into two parts. First:
"Clarifying form and sound.
Good sons, all the sūtras expounded by the Tathāgata (down to) all that he has spoken are real and not false.

This clarifies how his manifested forms and sounds benefit sentient beings in the present life. "Expounding" refers to the teaching of sound; "demonstrating" refers to the regulations of form. It is a direct pointing.

It is said: This extensively clarifies the fundamental reality (*dharmatā*). Three matters are cited to encompass all matters; each matter is briefly explained in terms of essence and function, as well as self and other.
The explanation of "one's own body" is directed toward the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages, extensively clarifying the beginning and end of the Dharma-nature body.
The explanation of "the bodies of others" is directed toward those of the Two Vehicles and the sentient beings of the Six Realms. Extensively...

This explains the beginning and end of the two bodies of transformation and response. Furthermore, the three bodies are collectively termed the "self-body," while the nine realms are all termed the "other-body.
Regarding the term "explaining": it is for the purpose of elucidating the causes of all these bodies and what they respond to.
"Manifesting one's own body" refers to manifesting the Dharma-nature body in response to those on the stages (bhūmi). "Manifesting the other-body" refers to responding to the nine realms.

This indicates the manifestation of the various transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). Furthermore, the three bodies collectively manifest one's own body; all other manifestations that adapt according to the capacities of beings are the manifestation of other bodies.
Regarding those that demonstrate one's own affairs: as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the teachings on the lifespan are all one's own affairs.
Those in the *Āgama*, *Vaipulya*, and *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras are all termed the affairs of others. As for the statement that "the final conclusion is entirely real and not false," it means:
Self and other are of one suchness; essence and function are of one accord. Whether provisional or ultimate, all are dharmas for transforming others, and none are in vain.
The above clarifies the Tathāgata’s unobstructed dharma-realm of affairs. △ Second, the explanation of "not being in vain," which is further divided into two parts.
First, not being in vain through the illumination of principle.
Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata knows and perceives things as they truly are—[up to] there being neither one who remains in the world nor one who has entered parinirvāṇa.
The following section provides a general explanation that the benefit of sentient beings is not in vain. Here, we first explain that the benefit of the physical form is not in vain. Tiantai says:

"The response-body (nirmāṇakāya) does not depart from the dharma-body (dharmakāya). The dharma-body is formless and likewise has no arising or ceasing. Yet, sentient beings experience arising and ceasing."
The capacity [of the sentient being] is moved by the Dharmakāya; thus, the Tathāgata’s power of vow arises and ceases in concert with it.
Therefore, by means of the three realms, it is shown that what is revealed is not in vain. Zhizhi says: "This uses fundamental wisdom to explain that the three realms are like an illusion."
The three matters indicated by the light are all Buddha-activities within a dream;
they are summarized and returned to the single principle of true purity, the unobstructed *dharmadhātu*. [△@△] The phrase "the characteristics of the triple world" serves as the general heading.
Thus, regarding all these characteristics, the Tathāgata perceives them with the Buddha-eye exactly as they are, without error. The multitudes of the triple world...

Birth consists of two kinds of birth and death: the birth and death of segmented continuity (*paricchinna*) and the birth and death of transformation (*pariṇāma*). These are absent when seen and known by the Tathāgata.
The Two Vehicles possess the mind of withdrawal and the notion of attaining extinction while remaining in the world; these are absent when seen and known by the Tathāgata.

Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "When the Tathāgata abides in samādhi, he perceives that the seeing, the objects of seeing, and all perceived appearances are like flowers in the sky—fundamentally non-existent."
Neither real nor unreal, neither suchness nor different—(up to: the Tathāgata clearly perceives this without error.
By means of the wisdom of the Middle Way, he brings [all things] back to the three realms as being neither real nor unreal. Pointing directly, it says:

"The three matters shown above are all true, eternal, profound, and quiescent. This concludes by returning to the truth that the ultimate and the conventional are one and the same, which constitutes the principle.

The Dharma-realm of non-obstruction regarding phenomena. [△@△] Since the Tathāgata knows that the birth-and-death of the sages and ordinary beings within the triple world, as well as nirvāṇa, are all entirely like illusions and thus do not truly exist, it would seem unnecessary for him to manifest birth and manifestation of extinction, or to speak of himself and others—these three aforementioned matters.
For what purpose, then, were they established? One must understand that although the characteristics of the triple world are not real, [they nevertheless appear].
Furthermore, it is not empty. Sentient beings of the six realms do not realize that it is not different, yet they view it as different.
The *śrāvakas* of the two vehicles do not recognize that it is not suchness (*tathatā*), yet they perceive it as suchness.

Since their views regarding emptiness and reality, or sameness and difference, have not been forgotten, they cannot help but engage in provisional designations (*prajñapti*). When viewed through the power of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, [it is] empty...
The characteristic of reality cannot be apprehended; the characteristics of identity and difference likewise cannot be apprehended.

Fundamentally, these are not unlike the illusory and false perceptions of the people within the three realms. Thus, all that exists—birth and death, nirvana, the void and the real, identity and difference—is of this nature.
Therefore, the Tathāgata perceives all things with perfect clarity and without error. Thus, he manifests birth within the unborn and manifests extinction within the non-extinguished;

even when speaking of himself or others, it is all true and not false. The two characters "clear perception" (mingjian) refer to the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), which encompasses the five eyes.
△ Second, [the teaching] is not in vain as it accords with the capacities of beings.
Because sentient beings possess various natures (up to) various conceptualizations and discriminations.
The preceding section clarified the lands upon which the twenty-five states of existence depend; this section clarifies the sentient beings who depend upon them. *Zhizhi* says:
"The categories of the twenty-five states of existence vary in their goodness and evil, and their faculties and natures are not uniform; therefore, they have 'various natures' based on these."
Because the nature of the arising of karma is not uniform, there are various desires. Because one is led by karma in manifold ways, there are various formations (*saṃskāra*).
Formations in turn give rise to karma, and karma in turn gives rise to formations; thus, there are various recollections, conceptions, and discriminations.
The above cites the first two of the three modes of continuity.
It is intended to cause various roots of goodness to arise (up to: so that the Buddha-activities performed have never been abandoned for even a moment).
This directly addresses the capacities of sentient beings by bestowing the benefit of one's own and others' voices.

Because it is intended to cause those of gradual and sudden capacities to give rise to various roots of goodness, it manifests various deeds involving both one's own and others' bodies. *Zhizhi* says: "This clarifies the four wisdoms and three [bodies] of the Buddha."
The body extracts the suffering of sentient beings from the burning house, ensuring that karmic fruits do not continue in succession. "Causing" refers to the teaching of one great eon.
"Giving birth to all below" points to the general description of the nine realms. "By means of various [methods]" refers, in the near term, to the past forty years;
in the distant sense, it corresponds to the preceding text, "from this time onward. The wisdom that benefits living beings is like the revolving sun.
It is empty; therefore, it is said that it has never for a moment been abandoned. The above clarifies the Tathāgata’s dharma-realm of unimpededness in all things.
[△@△] Desiring to cause various roots of goodness to arise, the beings of the nine realms each obtain their benefit.
Furthermore, by means of numerous causes, conditions, parables, and expressions, these skillful means are extremely manifold. These various teachings spoken constitute the Dharma-gates as well.

How much more so, then, after eons as numerous as the dust motes of a kalpa? If one considers such extensive teaching and transformation, it is no wonder that the multitude who emerge through accomplishment is so vast;
