it is indeed a teaching of skillful means. Sentient beings do not recognize the Tathāgata’s skillful means, and as he emerges from one place and passes away in another, they say, "He has entered parinirvāṇa.
△ Third, a verse on his non-extinction in response to future opportunities.
"I see all sentient beings submerged in suffering and affliction... (until) I then emerge to preach the Dharma for them.

Tiantai says: "This verse refers to the future. While the prose [commentary] merely mentions the four characters 'eternally abiding and not perishing,' this verse now elaborates upon that text in detail.
Furthermore, the reason I manifest extinction is because sentient beings are submerged in suffering and affliction."
Because they see that the Buddha is always present, they fail to give rise to reverence and instead become arrogant and self-indulgent; therefore, he does not manifest his body.

He waits until they have developed a thirst for, and a longing for, him, and through that, he manifests birth once more to preach the Dharma to them. This means that while his manifestation of the body is not extinguished, [he remains hidden from those who lack devotion].
The subsequent statement clarifies that while manifesting the lands, he does not pass into extinction.
Such is his supernormal power (*abhijñā*) that, throughout incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), he scatters [offerings] to the Buddha and the great assembly.
This verse follows upon the previous description of his appearing and disappearing, or being here and there; all of this is due to the power of the Buddha’s supernormal abilities.
It is so. In reality, the Dharma-body dwells through incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, yet it neither leaves this Vulture Peak nor any other place.
This further demonstrates that the Dharma-body pervades all locations, being neither present nor absent.
Some say that when the three calamities destroy the world, the entire universe perishes; one wonders then where the Buddha remains. However, when the kalpa is destroyed...

This is the perception of sentient beings. My own land, however, is fundamentally peaceful and secure; this further reveals that the Dharma-nature land is truly eternal and imperishable, and is neither existent nor non-existent.
The passage beginning with "Heavenly beings and humans" clarifies that the primary retribution (the physical body) is likewise imperishable.

Below the phrase "gardens and groves," it clarifies that the *niśrita-vipāka* (dependent retribution) does not perish; these all emerge from the realm of the actual adornment of the *vipākaphala* (fruition of retribution).

Within this realm, there are also immeasurable sentient beings who sport and enjoy themselves with happiness, unlike those in the *sahā-loka* (the world of endurance) whose karmic retributions are profound and heavy.

The striking of the celestial drum signifies that the Buddha speaks of his own accord without being questioned. The raining of flowers upon the Buddha and so forth signifies the Buddha’s [manifestation of his power].
This explains the stages of the noble ones (*ārya*). The constant performance of various music symbolizes the inexhaustibility of the Dharma-joy.

Such a realm is entirely the manifestation of the Buddhas' wisdom and spiritual powers (*abhijñā*), unfolding the wondrous realm of the *dharmatā* of the Original Gate (*mūla-dvāra*), which has existed eternally since antiquity;
it is also the sublation of the provisional traces of the three transformations of the Sahā world.
"My pure land is not destroyed, yet the multitudes see it as being consumed by fire" (up to) "they do not hear the names of the Triple Gem.
The single phrase "the pure land is not destroyed" clarifies that the principle does not change.

That which appears to change is brought about solely by the causal conditions of the evil karma of sentient beings. The Triple Gem abides eternally in the world, yet sentient beings themselves [fail to perceive it].
If one is able to hear [this], how can it be anyone else’s fault? This verse expands upon the prose passage concerning those of meager virtue who have not planted roots of goodness;
for all those who cultivate merit and are gentle and upright, it is said that a Buddha is difficult to encounter.
This verse refers to a certain class of people who do not lose their original minds and attain awakening upon hearing the Dharma.

Because they have long cultivated merit and are gentle, upright, and honest, they achieve the four practices of peaceful dwelling. They are not like those sentient beings burdened by transgressions who have never heard of the Triple Gem;
therefore, they are able to behold my true and manifested bodies and hear my teachings on the fundamental and the trace. For this reason...

Because the assembly is equal [to that of the previous kalpas], it is said that his lifespan is immeasurable. If these are sentient beings who have not seen the Buddha for a long time due to their evil karma, he merely says that a Buddha is difficult to encounter.
The two characters "or at times" (*huò shí*) are indeterminate terms; sometimes he speaks of the lifespan, and sometimes he speaks of the difficulty of encountering a Buddha.
All of this is a skillful means (*upāya*) adapted to the capacities of the audience. This verse concludes the extended [explanation].

"Practicing in this way, since I attained Buddhahood it has been exceedingly long ago," and so forth; from "after a long time they see the Buddha" downwards, the verse concludes with "some see the Buddha, while others do not," and so on.
Such is the power of my wisdom; the light of its insight illuminates the immeasurable, and this lifespan of countless kalpas was obtained through long-cultivated practice.
A commentary states: "The previous [verse] spoke of the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*), while the present one speaks of the power of wisdom (*jñāna*).

Supernatural faculties manifest the affairs of one's own and others' bodies, whereas wisdom explains the affairs of one's own and others' bodies. Thus, by means of these verses, it is shown that the measure of the Dharmakāya’s lifespan is not shallow. Its lifespan—
The command was issued. The verse states that the lifespan of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is not extinguished. This corresponds to the prose passage which says:
"The lifespan I have accomplished while originally practicing the bodhisattva path is still not yet exhausted. Therefore, it is said: "That which is obtained through long-cultivated practice.
These four lines complete the general promise to speak; herein, the Tathāgata now wishes to manifest and proclaim the wisdom of all Buddhas.
Regarding the section on wisdom: I have previously granted you the wisdom to manifest and proclaim it as described above;

yet the fundamental and manifested aspects of my power of wisdom are merely such as this. With the light of wisdom illuminating the immeasurable, I bind together the power of sovereign spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*);
with an immeasurable lifespan, I bind together the power of the lion’s majestic stride (*siṃhavikrīḍita*). These are obtained through long-term cultivation.

The summary verse concludes with the phrase "the power of great majesty and fierce strength. The reason all three [verses] mention "power" is that by means of this, one can destroy delusions and eliminate doubts, set aside the provisional traces to reveal the fundamental reality, and enable those who hear it to realize the stage and obtain benefit. Only these four lines conclude the entire chapter.
II. The verse states: "All is real and not false."
"You who possess wisdom, do not harbor doubts regarding this; you should sever them so that they are forever exhausted. The Buddha’s words are truly not false.

This instruction is intended to inspire the utmost genuine faith, meaning: "You, Maitreya and others, having heard the above account of the longevity of his life and the universal pervasiveness of his teaching of the Dharma, ought not to doubt that those who attain the Way will do so swiftly and achieve great accomplishment."
Furthermore, should there be any lingering doubt, it shall be made to cease forever. You must know that what I, the Tathāgata, have spoken is neither deceptive nor false.
△ Second, the verse on the parable, divided into two parts. First, the verse on the opening of the parable.
It is like a physician who, through skillful means, speaks of a death that is actually a cure for the sake of treating a mad son; no one can say he is speaking falsely.
This is the meaning of the single verse’s parable, which is summarized here because it was already explained in detail in the prose. △ Second, the verse that correlates with the parable.
"I am also the Father of the World, the savior of all who suffer" (up to) "those fallen into the evil realms.
This single verse-line is appropriate for the Dharma. The two lines "I am the Father of the World" [express] that although there is no birth, birth is manifested.

The two lines concerning ordinary beings [express] that although there is no cessation, cessation is displayed. The four lines beginning with "Because of the view of permanence" explain and clarify the manifestation of cessation.
I constantly know whether sentient beings practice the Path or do not practice it, and I preach various dharmas according to what is appropriate for their deliverance.
"Constantly knowing" means that with the Buddha-eye, one discerns their capacities without anything being unclear.

"According to what is appropriate" means manifesting bodies that accord with each type of being and preaching dharmas that accord with each type of being; all of these are expedient means employed because there is no other choice.
Each time he forms this thought— “By what means can I cause sentient beings to enter supreme wisdom and swiftly achieve the Buddha-body?”—
this precisely articulates his fundamental intent for delivering living beings. It is evident that he speaks of the provisional and the real, clarifies the original and the manifested,
and that his essential purpose is not otherwise than to cause all sentient beings to enter supreme wisdom and realize their inherent Tathāgata-nature as Amitāyus.
[This concludes the section. Having finished the opening of the near and the manifestation of the far, the topical outline of the seventeenth chapter, "Distinguishing Merit," states:

Regarding the intent of this chapter's arrival, it is because, through hearing the teaching on the extreme longevity [of the Buddha], one has already realized that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding.
Furthermore, upon seeing the three transformed pure lands, one realizes that the realm of the triple world is nothing but mind.
Taking this true faith as the cause, one may accord with the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding true fruit. Only by relying on this to uphold the sutra can one attain wondrous benefit.

Moreover, since the Dharma-body is eternally abiding, the pure land of the world is not separate from one's own place; therefore, I urge those capable of forming such a contemplation to do so. This is...
This constitutes the characteristic of profound faith and understanding. Therefore, the merits are distinguished as being inconceivable.

Upon reaching this state, the sentiments of arising and ceasing are forgotten and the views of purity and defilement are extinguished; when wondrous realization has reached its ultimate limit, one is then truly upholding the sutra. Thus, this chapter [is presented].
Tiantai judges that the five kinds of Dharma masters belong to the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxingwei*).
Thus, one knows that the intent of upholding the sutra lies in wondrous awakening, not in the literal words. Therefore, it is able to transcend all conditioned merits. Tiantai says:
"The Buddha’s teaching on the Lifespan [Sutra], the disciples who emerged from the earth in the past, and the disciples currently at Vulture Peak all obtain various benefits."

Regarding the statement on "merit," as there are differences in its depth and shallowness, it is here distinguished. This passage constitutes the second section on the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) within the Root Chapter.

While, according to the merit of merely hearing the sutra, this would belong only to the remaining [categories], now, based on the words "you shall attain bodhi," it is likewise treated as a bestowal of prediction.
According to the *Dharmaparyāya-śāstra*, this passage is divided into two types: the power of the Dharma and the power of practice.
Regarding the power of the Dharma (*dharmabala*): it is called "power" because it is accomplished through the Dharma. There are five kinds:

first, realization (*sākṣātkriyā*), which refers to those who have attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), numbering six hundred and eighty million billion, up to those who shall attain *bodhi* in a single lifetime.

Second, faith (*śraddhā*), which refers to those who have resolved their minds on enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), numbering as many as the atoms in eight worlds. Third, making offerings (*pūjā*). This refers to...
When a bodhisattva attains great benefit from the Dharma, it is as described when celestial flowers and so forth rain down from the void;

this corresponds to the present chapter. Fourth is hearing the Dharma, as in the Chapter on Rejoicing. Fifth is reading, reciting, upholding, and explaining: "reading and reciting" is as in the Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master;
"upholding" refers back to the three chapters on the *Anrakugyō* (Peaceful Practices) which encourage its retention; and "explaining" [is as follows].
As for these, the two chapters on "Supernatural Power" and "Entrustment" both pertain to the power of the Dharma. As for the power of practice: asceticism is like the "Medicine King" chapter;
teaching and transforming others is like the "Wonderful Sound" chapter; and protecting against difficulties is like the two chapters on Avalokiteśvara and the Dhāraṇī.

The manifestation of merit is as described in the "Chapter on the Adorned King" (Zhuangwang pin). The protection of the Dharma is as described in the "Chapter on Samantabhadra" (Puxian pin). A commentator says:
"This, too, is the empowerment and protection bestowed by the sovereign supernatural powers of all Buddhas. Otherwise, how could one discuss the span of a Buddha's life in such a brief period?"
Since these merits pervade the entire great assembly, how could they not be swiftly accomplished? This correctly illustrates the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter:
the immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits of the Tathāgata. II. General Bestowal of the Prediction of the Dharma-body.
Divided into three parts: 1. The Sūtra-author’s General Introduction.
At that time, the great assembly heard the Buddha’s discourse on the span of his life (up to the point where) incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings attained great benefit.
This is a general indication of the attainment of benefit. As for the term "great assembly," it collectively refers to the nine realms; these are the capacities [of beings] who receive the benefit.
Hearing of the Buddha’s long and far-reaching lifespan is a dharma that brings benefit; it yields great advantage, as explained in detail below.
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s differentiation.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva... [until] "attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Buddha summoned those who were ready to receive the teaching (*yathābhavya*) and specifically analyzed it for them, as described above regarding the merits realized through hearing this sutra.

At the end of the sixth fascicle, there is a general summary of the teachings expounded in the superior grade. Regarding "the patience of the non-arising," Tiantai says: "Entering the Perfect [Teaching]."

This teaches the ten stages of abiding (*daśabhūmi*). Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "In the first stage, the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-bhūmi*), one resolve gives rise to all resolves;
one attains the Tathāgata’s single body that is an infinite body, the pure and wondrous Dharma-body, which serenely responds to all things.

This is precisely this meaning. Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Commentary* states: "A" signifies the principle of entering non-arising (*anutpāda*). The principle of non-arising universally encompasses [all phenomena].
Regarding the ten thousand dharmas: when a bodhisattva attains this non-arising and penetrates the emptiness of all phenomena, they sever all hindrances.
Furthermore, there are a thousandfold more bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who attain the dhāraṇī-door of hearing and retaining.
The *Śrutadhara-dhāraṇī* (Dhāraṇī of Hearing and Retaining). One enters the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśabhūmi*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains three types of dhāraṇīs: first, the *Śrutadhara-dhāraṇī*. One who attains this does not forget or lose any speech or phenomena heard by the ear;
thus it is called "hearing and retaining. Second, the *Vijñapti-jñāna-dhāraṇī* (Dhāraṇī of Discerning Knowledge). Third, the *Ghoṣapraveśa-dhāraṇī* (Dhāraṇī of Entering Sounds).

Regarding the *dhāraṇī*: consult the *Fanyi mingyi* (Explanations of Translation Terms) for a detailed account. "A thousandfold" means it is a thousand times more than the aforementioned number of sands.
"Hearing and Retaining" (*śrutadhara*) pertains to the faculty of the ear. The two types mentioned above both pertain to self-awakening (*svasaṃvedana*).
As one proceeds from these stages, the positions become increasingly superior and the numbers become increasingly vast; therefore, both of these are calculated by means of the metaphor of sands.
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in another world-system who attained the unhindered eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*).
This refers to attaining such joyful speech and entering the stage of the Ten Deeds (*daśabhūmi-pratipatti*). As the "Chapter on Dedication" (*pariṇāmanā-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states:
"The Bodhisattva attains the inexhaustible treasury of definitive eloquence and expounds all the equal dharmas of the Buddhas. This is what that passage means.
One world-system is a small chiliocosm. Compared to this, a thousand times the number of sands [in the Ganges] is immeasurable.
This pertains to the benefit of the faculty of the tongue.
Furthermore, there are [beings] as numerous as the atoms in another world-system who attain hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of immeasurable *varta-dhāraṇī*.
Regarding this *varta-dhāraṇī*, it enters the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states: "To revolve (*varta*) means to turn.

It refers to revolving and discerning, whereby one destroys the delusions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and manifests the Buddha-dharma as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. This "one world" refers to the Middle [World].

Regarding the "thousand worlds": because one realizes the principle of the threefold equality on the first stage (*bhūmi*), it is the merit of the mental faculty (*manas*) among the six sense faculties.
Since the mind is able to silently encompass the ten directions and the three periods of time, it is said that one "attains the *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī*."
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in three thousand great thousandfold world systems who are able to turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma.

(The meaning of "irreversible" is as seen previously. These enter the second stage (*bhūmi*). According to the eight births mentioned below, these [bodhisattvas] should attain the fruit of *bodhi* after ten births.
The above constitutes the enumeration; from the ordinary person to the sage, the numbers increase from few to many, clarifying this progression.
Next, proceeding downward from the intermediate chiliocosm to the small chiliocosm, the numbers decrease from many to few, clarifying the sequence of reduction.
It can be seen that those who attain the great fruits are even fewer still.
Furthermore, there were bodhisattvas numbering as many as the atoms in two thousand lands of the central world-system, who were able to turn the pure wheel of Dharma.

This marks their entry into the third stage (*bhūmi*). Regarding the calculation based on two intermediate world-systems (*dvisāhasramadhyama-lokadhātu*): one thousand Sumerus constitute a small world-system (*sāhasracūḍika-lokadhātu*);

one thousand times that small world-system constitutes an intermediate world-system; and one thousand times that intermediate world-system constitutes a great world-system (*trisāhasramahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*). The present figure refers to twice the number of an intermediate world-system.

This is a reduction [of the number]. Regarding the "Pure Wheel of Dharma": since the first two stages have already been free from defilement, the third stage is now able to emit the wondrous light of True Suchness (Tathatā); thus, the Dharma that is turned is entirely pure and unstained.
Furthermore, there are those who, from [the stage of] a small chiliocosm up to eight births, shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
○ Eight births to enter the fourth stage; seven births to enter the fifth stage; six births to enter the sixth stage; five births to enter the seventh stage.
[△@△] These are based on the stages and their respective numbers. As for why the text does not provide a sequential correspondence, it may be because they attained them at that specific time.
Regarding "merit" (*guṇa*): it is not that its numerical positions are inherently fixed. Furthermore, the Buddha’s speech is skillful;
by mentioning one corner, the other three corners are implied. Alternatively, it may be that the translators abbreviated the text, perceiving its underlying interconnections.
Furthermore, there are four sets of four *cāturdvīpaka* worlds (up to) where four beings shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Herein, there are these four groups, as numerous as the atoms within four *cāturdvīpaka* worlds, who have entered the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, there are those who will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* after three more births within three sets of four-continent worlds (*cāturmahādvīpaka*).

These consist of a multitude of beings as numerous as the atoms in three sets of four-continent worlds who have entered the ninth stage (*navamī bhūmi*); from this point, they require only three births to reach the state of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*).
Furthermore, there are those who, having passed through two sets of four continents (up to) two more births, shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Those who have ascended to the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) possess a number of beings equal to the dust motes of two sets of four continents; compared to the state of wondrous enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), they have only two births remaining.

Furthermore, there is one [bodhisattva] who, within one more birth, shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. In one life, they enter the diamond-like mind (*vajra-citta*) of equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
From the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) up to equal enlightenment, they sever one grade of ignorance (*avidyā*) at each stage, totaling forty-one grades.
Having further severed one final grade of subtle ignorance, they enter the Subtle [Wisdom].
This is the stage of awakening. However, the attainment of the Way in this Fundamental Gate (the *Lotus Sūtra*) exceeds that of all other sūtras by several multiples.

It is not only because the number [of those attaining it] is great; it is also because the period of cultivation and refinement has been long. Having manifested traces based upon the fundamental reality, [the Buddha] has guided and led beings everywhere.

Having encountered [these teachings] repeatedly during the intervening periods, they have been matured time and again, and are now tamed in this present life, converging toward the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. After the *Lotus Sūtra*, there are those who attain the Way, like one gathering ears of grain (*kuñcana*).
"Collecting ears" (*śikṣi*): "Gathering" (*tṛṇa-śikṣi*) refers to the manner in which farmers gather up the remaining ears of grain in the fields.
Furthermore, there were sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in eight worlds who [attained] the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
In this context, the number is stated as being even greater than the aforementioned count—namely, the number of dust motes in eight worlds.

"Sentient beings" here refers specifically to those at the stage of the purification of the six sense faculties; upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching on his lifespan, they immediately resolve for perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Thus, the true cause has already been planted, and they become persons destined for future Buddhahood. This may be called a succession of the flames of wisdom that is inexhaustible.
...Thus it was. △ Third, the assembly’s offering:
When the Buddha had spoken these words regarding the various Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas (up to) singing immeasurable verses in praise of the Buddhas.
At that time, the assembly, having heard the profound and far-reaching Dharma, attained great benefit. Desiring to repay the Buddha’s kindness, they prepared offerings;

this was also a symbolic act to express their understanding. While the previous Gate of the Trace had opened the provisional to reveal the real, and the bodhisattvas therein had all attained realization and entry, no offerings were presented because the Great Matter had not yet been completed. Now, with the opening and revelation of the Fundamental Gate, the Great Matter [is fulfilled].
Once this had been made manifest, Maitreya offered a comprehensive summary to express his understanding; thus, he represented it through the act of making offerings.

[△@△] This section was also arranged by the compiler of the sutra. Following the phrase "at the time of attaining the great benefit of the Dharma," there should have been the phrase "those various bodhisattvas."
This may be an abbreviation of the text. Once the Buddha had already distinguished all the merits, the bodhisattvas immediately presented their offerings;
this indicates that [Bodhisattva] Xijian (Joyful Vision) attained the Dharma and was filled with joy.

Furthermore, within the verses it is clarified that Śakra and Brahmā came from as many buddha-lands as there are sands in the Ganges, scattering offerings upon the three Buddhas and the various bodhisattvas; this signifies the completion of the matters of the Root Chapter.

Because the cause has penetrated to the fruit, the perfect understanding has already been realized; this is the auspicious omen that the aforementioned beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, the raining down of sandalwood and other fragrances symbolizes that their essence is endowed with the fragrance of the ten inexhaustible treasuries of precepts;
this is the auspicious omen that a thousandfold more bodhisattvas have attained the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining. The celestial drum resounded spontaneously and wondrously.
The sound was deep and far-reaching, signifying the possession of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*);

this was an auspicious omen that bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms within a world-system, had attained the unimpeded eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*). Furthermore, a thousand kinds of celestial garments rained down, signifying the possession of the virtue of patience;
this was an auspicious omen that bodhisattvas had attained the *āvartanī-dhāraṇī*. Necklaces hung down, signifying that the Dharma-body is endowed with myriads of virtues.
This is the auspicious omen of the Bodhisattva turning the pure wheel of Dharma that never regresses. As for its pervading the nine directions:
by including the lower direction within the primary assembly, it symbolizes the universal benefit of the nine realms.

The incense from the precious burner pervades and reaches the entire great assembly, symbolizing the universal fragrance of the wisdom and virtue of the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages. The banners and canopies extend successively up to the Brahma Heaven.
The manifestation of the ten stages signifies that their merit universally covers all; this is an auspicious omen of attaining Bodhi within ten births.
The wondrous voice praising the Buddha signifies dwelling together with the Buddha; this is an auspicious omen of Equal Enlightenment being adjacent to the ultimate fruit.
Such occurrences are all due to the fact that all the merits possessed by the Tathāgata have been fully manifested here, and thus appear simultaneously.
△ Third, the understanding and realization of the assembly present at that time. This is divided into three parts. First, a verse on the understanding and realization of the assembled multitude.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat (until) joined his palms toward the Buddha and spoke these verses.
The Buddha spoke of this rare Dharma, never heard before... [until] "joy pervades his entire body.
The Tathāgata expounded it first, and Maitreya subsequently versified it in detail; thus teacher and disciple were in perfect accord, truly sharing the same essence despite different forms.
Now that Maitreya has received his station, he will immediately attain Buddhahood in the future; thus we know that Maitreya—

The "Verse of Encouragement" (*le-sòng*) refers to the Buddha’s own verse. The first two lines praise the great event of the Revealing the Original [Enlightenment] (*běnmén dàshì*), which is a rare and marvelous teaching.

The phrase "World-Honored One" and the following two lines praise the three kinds of power of the sovereign supernatural powers (*zìzài shéntōng*) of all Buddhas. The section beginning with "Innumerable... [and so forth].
This general verse praises the great number of benefits obtained by the sons of the Buddha, and their immeasurable joy. △ Second, the verse on the Tathāgata’s discernment:
"Whether abiding in the stage of non-retrogression or attaining dhāraṇīs" (up to) "...like space, it is boundless."
The merits distinguished by the preceding eight lines of verse are as previously explained. The final four lines conclude that the benefits are inexhaustible.
Since Maitreya’s realization was profound, he knew that these benefits were inconceivable;
therefore, he reiterated them so that those who were lingering in their tracks or harboring doubts would understand clearly and without obstruction, further recognizing Maitreya’s manifested trace.
This is a crucial point. △ Third, the verse on the assembly’s offerings:
"Raining down *māndārava* and *mahāmāndārava* [flowers]... to assist the unsurpassed mind."
This verse concerns the offerings made by the assembly; all are auspicious omens.

Furthermore, the verse clarifies that there were countless Śakras, Brahmās, and other devas, each holding exquisite flowers, who came from outside countless Buddha-lands, having arrived to celebrate the Dharma.
The incense and flowers scattered were like auspicious snow, falling in profusion and fluttering gracefully like flocks of birds;
these were all inconceivable omens. The remainder may be understood according to the text. The final four lines conclude the preceding omens.

That is to say, as for these many inconceivable auspicious omens mentioned above, they occurred because the Buddha’s fame reached throughout the ten directions, causing the various devas to come from afar;
this is why there was an immeasurable rain of flowers. Furthermore, one sees the multitude who were benefited thereby.
All are inconceivable. Thus, various activities such as burning incense, scattering flowers, holding canopies, and offering praise are all inconceivable;
none fail to assist in the manifestation of the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), so that all who see or hear may derive benefit.

What follows is a comparative calculation of this merit. △ Second, a general explanation of the merit.

If there are good sons or good daughters [up to] that which cannot be known even by calculation or analogy—this is a comparison based on depth and shallowness, showing that phenomena do not surpass principle. As stated above, it is "faithful understanding in a single thought-moment."
For if one can have faith, then the source is remote yet certainly has a basis for reliance; if one can achieve understanding, then the source is remote yet clearly and penetratingly realized.
Within a single thought-moment, one has already attained the principle of the Dharmakāya. As for those who practice the five pāramitās, their practice is not lacking in breadth;

Although this may take a long time, it does not equal even a single moment of faith and understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*). The former still belongs to the realm of striving for external signs and achievements, whereas this is the sudden, expansive realization of the source of principle.

The middle four lines clarify that by virtue of these causes and conditions, one attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), and thus remains securely established for many kalpas with an undisturbed mind. The final four...

It is said that after my parinirvāṇa, those who uphold [this teaching] in such a manner—benefiting both themselves and others—should establish monasteries for them, providing for the community of monks no differently than they would for me. This is intended to strengthen their resolve to uphold it.

The bathing pools represent the eight liberations; Great Nirvana is the cave of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); gentleness and patience serve as clothing;

The Dharma-realm. The same applies to the other five perfections (*pāramitās*). Although their phenomenal aspects are slight, the movement of the mind is exceedingly vast.

It is superior. Therefore, it is further likened to space, which is boundless and immeasurable, swiftly reaching all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*). One should understand this comparison.

therefore, its merit is as boundless as space. Not only is the merit boundless, but it can also enable the practitioner to swiftly reach all-knowledge.
Its supreme excellence can be fully understood. This fourth section on the evaluation of merits makes its superiority evident.
△ Fifth: The Correct Practice of the Six Perfections.
"If a person reads, recites, accepts, and upholds this sutra... [until] their faculties become sharp, their wisdom profound, and they are skilled in answering difficult questions.

The *Miaoxuan* states: "When one reaches the fifth stage (*wupin*) and the perfect contemplation (*yuan guan*) has somewhat matured, principle and phenomena are about to merge; engaging with phenomena does not obstruct principle."
In principle, there is no separation from phenomena; therefore, one fully practices the six pāramitās. When practicing giving (*dāna*), one is free from attachment to the two extremes.
Regarding the ten dharma realms and their environments and inhabitants, one gives all things away in a single act of relinquishment—giving wealth, body, life, and fearlessness.

When observing precepts (*śīla*), one regards praise and blame with equal indifference, making no distinction between them; regarding the five categories of gravity and lightness, one commits no transgression whatsoever.
When practicing patience, one gives rise to the patience regarding the quiescence of phenomena and so forth, bearing and enduring with fortitude.

When practicing diligence, both body and mind are pure, uninterrupted and without regression. When practicing dhyāna, one enters into the various meditative absorptions, such that stillness and distraction do not hinder one another.
When practicing wisdom, one thoroughly investigates and penetrates both the provisional and the ultimate truths;

even mundane knowledge regarding livelihood and industry does not contradict the true mark (*dharmatā*). One fully explains the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and within right contemplation, it is like adding fuel to a fire.
Therefore, it is said that one correctly practices the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). Among these six perfections, giving (*dāna*) is not specifically mentioned here.

As for "giving," explaining it for others already encompasses the meaning of the "Dharma-giving. Among the five stages, the first three stages constitute the position of *śrutamayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from hearing), during which one practices the six perfections concurrently.

The [next] stage constitutes the position of *cintāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from reflection), during which one practices the six perfections formally. The [final] stage constitutes the position of *bhāvanāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from cultivation);

One stage is divided into two minds; these five stages constitute the ten levels of faithful mind (*śraddhā-citta*). This is the stage of the iron wheel where the six sense faculties are purified. *Myōryaku* asks:
Why are there only four levels of faith established during the present [Buddha’s lifetime], while five stages are established after his extinction? He answers:
Since their meaning is identical, there is no distinction between the four and the five; it is merely that after my parinirvāṇa, the practice of reciting and chanting is added as the first category.

According to the *Fanyi mingyi ji* (Collection of Translated Names and Meanings), *candana* translates in meaning as "medicine. The *Ci'en zhuan* (Biography of Xuanzang) states that it is a type of tree.

the full name is *sumanā*, also called *sūmara*; this is translated as "well-restraining the mind. Its flower is yellowish-white and extremely [beautiful].

Before long, one attains entry into the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), the Copper Wheel, and is able to manifest the eight aspects of a Buddha. The fifth grade and the fourth grade are identical;

this is the stage of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-prajñā*). If one discusses entry into the stages generally, it constitutes the stage of the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*).

However, there is a distinction between those in the presence of a living Buddha and those after his parinirvāṇa. This "ground" (*bhūmi*) is precisely the true realm of the ultimate reality (*tathatā*). It is...

This is the field of enjoyment for all Tathāgatas. Now that the Son of the Buddha has attained the perfect fusion of principle and phenomena, benefiting both self and others, and having extensively practiced the six pāramitās to accord with True Suchness (tathatā), he partakes in the same enjoyment as the Buddhas; thus, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—
All are contained therein. The classification of the five grades and the evaluation of the four grades of merit have now been completed.

Regarding the intent behind the arrival of this chapter, "The Merit of Rejoicing" (Chapter 18), it is stated that since the previously analyzed merits of upholding the sutra are already exceptionally sublime, [this chapter follows].

However, because the benefit of that [previous practice] was not yet exhausted, one now surpasses eighty years of extensively giving the necessities of life consisting of the seven treasures to the sentient beings of the six realms across four million billion *asaṃkhyeya* worlds—

thereby causing each of them to attain the merit of the four fruits of the path— merely by the merit of a single thought of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) at the end. It is not equal to this final person’s single thought of sympathetic joy.

Regarding "rejoicing" (*muditā*): this is intended specifically to manifest the superior benefits of this teaching, thereby strengthening the aspiration and resolve of those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Tiantai says: "Rejoicing" means to accord with both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*), such that they are non-dual and without distinction. "Rejoicing" is to celebrate both oneself and others.

Upon hearing the profound and abstruse Dharma, one rejoices because there is the merit of reality (*tattva*) in accordance with principle, and the merit of skillful means (*upāya*) in accordance with phenomena. This is celebration.
One possesses wisdom oneself; one rejoices in the compassion of others. By synthesizing and expounding upon both provisional and ultimate wisdom and severance, it is said:

"The Merit of Rejoicing" (Sui-hsi Kung-te) directly points out that the preceding chapter concerns the merit obtained from personally hearing the Buddha’s teaching on the span of his lifespan, whereas this [chapter] concerns briefly hearing this Dharma within the assembly for its dissemination after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, and awakening in a single thought-moment.
The mind gives rise to joy, and one immediately attains extraordinary merit; therefore, it is called "merit of sympathetic joy" (*anumodana-puṇya*). In terms of its meaning, there are four aspects:
first, following after others and giving rise to reverence through joy; second, following after the Dharma and giving rise to faith through joy;
third, following after principle and giving rise to understanding through joy; and fourth, following after phenomena and giving rise to practice through joy. All within a single thought-moment.

It encompasses both persons and dharmas, and its principle and phenomena are perfectly interfused; thus, its merit is immeasurable, as explained extensively in the commentary on the *Pranidhāna-paṭala*.

[△@△] In the preceding chapter, among the five stages, only the text of the first, the "Chapter on Rejoicing," merely indicates the characteristics of persons without yet providing a comparative calculation.
Therefore, Maitreya, seizing the opportunity to inquire of the Buddha, extensively calculates the first chapter, through which one finally comes to know the latter four chapters.
The merit is seen to be truly inconceivable. △ Second, the evaluation of the qualities of the two types of persons; first, the merit of the initial stage.
This is divided into two parts. First, the question:
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva... [up to] "obtains how much merit? and then spoke in verse.
After the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One, if there are those who hear this sutra and are able to rejoice in it, how much merit will they obtain?
Although the preceding chapters have already provided a comparative measurement, the Tathāgata did not fully elaborate upon this in the first chapter.
His intention was to wait for Maitreya’s inquiry before speaking. What Maitreya now asks concerns specifically those of the first category;
however, all sentient beings who rejoice [in the merit] are persons destined to attain Buddhahood in the future and are to receive their prediction of enlightenment from Maitreya.
Therefore, he asks this particular question. Furthermore, it serves to stimulate the profound resolve of those in the present who uphold this sutra.

△ Second, the response. This is divided into two parts. First, the prose section. This is further divided into two. First, the response for those who rejoice within their own minds. This is further divided into four.
First, mutual instruction through successive transmission.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva... [up to] "...having heard this sutra and rejoiced.
This passage identifies those capable of hearing it: first, it specifically designates the fourfold assembly; next, it generally refers to all people, both old and young.
Regarding "other wise ones," Zhizhi directly points out that this refers specifically to a certain class of those with sharp faculties who,
after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, personally hear this sutra at the feet of a Dharma master and attain sudden spiritual realization.
Having attained something in one's mind, it is said that after rejoicing,
one departs from the Dharma assembly and goes to other places, where one expounds [the teaching] according to one's ability for virtuous friends and spiritual teachers.

This clarifies the one who is able to rejoice: having attained some understanding of this sutra themselves, they go elsewhere and expound the sutra they have heard for others according to their capacity. "Elsewhere" refers to wherever they may go.
This refers to monastic quarters, cities, towns, and the like. "As one has heard" means not adding to what was said by others nor diminishing what one has heard oneself.
"Expounding according to one's ability" means explaining in accordance with what one has heard, to the extent of one's own capacity.

A city (*nagara*) is a place where the populace gathers; it was first built during the time of the Yellow Emperor (*Huangdi*) for the purpose of housing the people. A town (*grāma*), on the other hand, is...

Regarding cities and towns: four counties constitute a *du* (capital), and four *jing* (wells) constitute a *yi* (town). A *mo* is a road between fields; those running north-south are called *qian*, while those running east-west are called *mo*.
Villages, settlements, fields, and hamlets—these are all places where the Dharma may be expounded according to one's capacity for the sake of the fourfold assembly.
These are the first stratum of those who transmit the teaching.
When these people have heard [the teaching], they rejoice; (up to: they also rejoice and teach it to others.

"These people" refers to the aforementioned parents and kinsmen. "Having heard" means that upon hearing even a small portion of the Dharma as it was expounded according to their capacity, they are likewise able to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) and teach it to others. This is the second stage of transmission.
"To teach others" refers to other people; this is the third stage of successive transmission.
In this manner, it is passed on in succession until the fiftieth person.

"In this way" (如是指前) means that as each preceding person successively gives rise to the next, they take the one before them and expound the teaching according to their capacity, passing it on in turn.
The oral tradition has been passed down thus: we have already reached the fiftieth person.

Now, let us merely take the merit obtained by the single thought of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) of this very last fiftieth person and compare it [to other merits]. △ Second, establishing the standard for measurement.
Ajita, regarding these fifty [kalpas] (up to) those who are thus numbered among sentient beings:
first, the maximum number of worlds is cited; next, ten classes of sentient beings are cited. Since each world possesses all ten classes, the number of sentient beings is immeasurable.
The "sentient beings of the six destinies" is a general enumeration. [The term] *pū* is in the Sanskrit language.
*Pudgala*. This is translated as "one who repeatedly takes rebirth," meaning that one undergoes birth again and again within the various realms of existence (*gati*).

Furthermore, because they arise from the combination of manifold phenomena (*dharma*), they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*). These manifold phenomena refer to the five aggregates (*skandha*) and the six sense faculties (*indriya*), which together constitute the two categories of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).
Birth from eggs refers to fish, birds, tortoises, snakes, and the like. Birth from a womb refers to humans, domestic animals, *nāgas*, and *ṛṣis*.
Moisture-born refers to wriggling and crawling creatures. Transformation-born refers to those that molt and fly. With form refers to spirits of auspicious and inauspicious portents.
Formless refers to those that are empty, dispersed, or dissolved. With thought refers to gods, ghosts, and spiritual intelligences.
Without thought refers to spirits whose essence has been transformed into earth, wood, metal, or stone. Those who are neither with nor without thought...
It is like the *pulu* insect, which originally has no notion of being a bee; yet, because it is carried by a *gonglo* (wasp), it becomes a bee. This is not a case of lacking a notion.

It is also like the *tuxiao* (owl) and its kind, where once the offspring are formed, the mother is devoured by them. Since they are born from one another in this way, this is likewise not a case of lacking a notion.
The category of "those without feet" and so forth encompasses all such beings without exception. These and others are included in the above. This is...
In summary, the sentient beings who are to be transformed are as vast as this. Next, the person capable of bestowing [the gift] is introduced:

This indicates the objects to be bestowed. For all these ten classes of sentient beings, let each individual be given the seven treasures filling one Jambudvīpa;

After the thought "and he makes this reflection" [is expressed], the gift of Dharma (dharmadāna) begins.
As for the reason for this:
he immediately assembled these sentient beings and proclaimed the transformation of the Dharma (up to) all attaining mastery and being endowed with the eight liberations.
"Immediately assembled" means that he collectively summoned the ten classes of sentient beings from four million *koṭis* of nations. He proclaimed...
As for "extensively" (布): it refers to using the Dharma-wheel of the Four Noble Truths to reveal, instruct, and transform [beings], so that they all attain awakening and entry.
Thus, at one time, they all fully realized the four fruits, severed birth and death within the realm, and realized nirvana beyond the realm.
*Srotāpanna* is the first fruit; this is translated as "Stream-enterer. *Sakṛdāgāmin* is the second fruit; this is translated as "Once-returner. *Anāgāmin*...
These are the three fruits. This [fruit] is called "Non-returner" (Anāgāmin). The Arhat is the fourth fruit; its meaning is revealed in the Preface Chapter.
"Exhausting all outflows" (āsrava) means being free from suffering. "Attaining mastery" means attaining bliss. △ Third, the question-and-answer section clarifies the merit.
"What do you think? As for this great donor... let alone causing others to attain the fruit of Arhatship.

The recipient of the teaching, upon hearing this established comparison, realized within his mind that even if one were to give immeasurable wealth to all the immeasurable sentient beings in immeasurable worlds, the scope of such material giving would already be beyond measure. Material wealth—
The merit of material giving is already immeasurable; how then could the merit of the gift of Dharma be measured? △ Fourth, the formal comparison:
The Buddha told Maitreya, "I shall now speak to you clearly... [up to] ...that which cannot be known through calculation or analogy."
This is compared by way of the Dharma; it is truly beyond measure. Furthermore, as with the aforementioned donor, while material giving cannot be compared, that is certainly so.
As for the infinite number of people who realize the fruit of Arhatship, attain profound meditative concentration, and possess liberation—[this too is beyond measure].
This does not even equal the merit of a beginner who hears a single verse, much less one who merely rejoices in it.
To say that such calculations and analogies do not equal even a fraction [of the latter] is an exaggeration; this is not so.

One must understand that while the realization of the four fruits by immeasurable people belongs entirely to the provisional teaching and is of incomplete meaning, planting the seed of a single thought of rejoicing in a single verse of this sutra now—
The cause of the Mahāyāna leads inevitably to the attainment of Buddhahood; this union of the provisional and the real is truly beyond compare.
It is like a poor man who, by holding a single character of the Son of Heaven, immediately surpasses all his ministers in status.
That which he values does not reside in the person, but in that single character. The comparative evaluation in this sutra is likewise so.
Ānanda, these fifty persons, up to the fiftieth, cannot be compared even to an asaṃkhyeya [number].
The former were compared by means of the external to the internal; this is compared by means of the internal to the internal.

That is to say, the words of the very last person, transmitted through successive tradition, are the fewest, yet the merit they obtain is still immeasurable; how much more so for those at the beginning of the Dharma assembly!
Within this, how could the merit of one who hears but a single phrase and is able to rejoice therein be easily measured?
△ Second, clarifying those who come from outside to hear the Dharma, divided into four parts. First, going there oneself.
Furthermore, Ajita, if a person—for the sake of this sutra—[receives] precious carriages, palanquins, or celestial palaces;
"if a person" refers to the fourfold assembly and those with wisdom. For the sake of this sutra, one sees their faith as they go to the monasteries;
one sees their sincerity; and whether sitting or standing, one sees their profound respect, which is not merely ordinary.

This is comparable to those who, while playing and acting with haste, do not practice cultivation, yet listen for even a brief moment. Although not much time has passed, the seeds of the Way have already been sown;
this is the attainment of the true cause. "Transforming the body" refers to passing through the veil of death and changing one's birth.

Obtaining a superior and exquisite vehicle is the retribution for the merit of traveling toward [the goal]; obtaining a precious palanquin is the retribution for the merit of standing and listening. One mounts it...
The celestial palaces are the retribution for the merit of entering the monastic quarters. These three [attainments] all arise from a single thought of sincere faith;
taking the hearing of this wondrous Dharma as the cause, and the concurrent cultivation of the ten wholesome actions as the condition. △ Second, the sharing of seats.
Furthermore, if there is someone who sits in a place where the Dharma is being preached—up to and including the seat of a Wheel-Turning Sage King—the previous section concerned oneself;
this one additionally encourages others. To be able to share one’s seat possesses the virtue of aiding others;
therefore, upon changing bodies, one attains the position of a king’s throne, thereby universally benefiting ministers and subjects. △ Third, encouraging others.

Ajita, if there is another person [who, from the point of being born until death] is neither dark-skinned nor possesses anything loathsome, yet speaks to others and exhorts them to listen, then their intention to benefit others is earnest. Therefore, the benefit is doubly vast and the retribution is doubly superior.
As for the *dhāraṇī*, once a Bodhisattva has attained it within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), they dwell together with those who have reached the ten stages;

their karmic retribution is not slight. One should know that such a person likewise possesses the merit of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Regarding the sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*) and so forth, these pertain to the mind (*manas*).

Not being mute or dumb pertains to the tongue. Later in the text, "the nose is long and straight" refers to the nose faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*). "Seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma" pertains to the eye and ear faculties. All others pertain to the body faculty (*kāyendriya*).
Here, the retribution for the mouth alone is clarified: having indistinct sounds is called muteness (*mūka*); being entirely deprived of sound is called dumbness (*mūka*).
Now, because of praising his name and exhorting him to listen, the retribution is that he shall not be mute or dumb for thousands of millions of births.
One is able to hear and receive [the teaching] oneself; one then places the wondrous lotus flower in one’s mouth, and thus the mouth has no foul odor.

This refers to the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*) when discussing merit. As for the tongue always hanging down, this speaks in terms of physical appearance (*rūpa*). Tarnish, blackness, coarseness, yellowness, and gaps are all dental ailments.
When they are corrected, they turn outward; when they are crooked, they turn inward. Now, by virtue of reciting this sutra and exhorting others to listen, throughout hundreds of thousands...
When born, one’s teeth are free from such ailments; these are the internal characteristics of the mouth. Features such as the lips not hanging down are external characteristics of the mouth.

If they hang down, they are long; if they are drawn back or shriveled, they are short. If coarse and rough in form, they are unfit to behold. If afflicted with sores or warts, their odor is unfit to smell.
If deficient or broken, they are exposed. If crooked or slanted, they are distorted. If thick and large, they manifest stupidity. If dark brown or black...
To speak of their obstructions: now that it is stated in the sutra that one should be encouraged to listen, none of these ailments exist.
Both mouth and tongue are thus pure; hence it is said, "there are no things loathsome. (Zhěn [pronounced zhěn], Kuò [kuài in the level tone], Qiān [pronounced qiān]).
The nose is neither flat nor crooked (up to: seeing the Buddha, hearing the Dharma, and faithfully accepting his instructions. Exhorting others fundamentally pertains to the body and speech;

previously, the retribution of speech was explained in detail, while here both the faculty of the body and the faculties of the eye, ear, and mind are included within "seeing the Buddha, hearing the Dharma, and faithfully accepting his instructions. Thus it is known that this refers to the exhortation to practice.
Upon hearing this with the mind, within a mere moment, one experiences the purification of the six sense faculties for hundreds of thousands of lifetimes.
How wonderful! This sublime Dharma is truly inconceivable. [Characters: 匾 (pinyin: biǎn), 匚@虒 (pinyin: tī), 音 (pinyin: yīn).

"The merit obtained by the person at the end shall now be analyzed" (up to) "the three knowledges and eight liberations."
The long passage merely states that he "proclaimed the transformation of the Dharma" and "instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened" [the assembly].
This clarifies that the world is entirely impermanent, like foam on water or like bubbles and mirages. It further exhorts one not to crave worldly pleasures but to savor the joy of the Dharma;
this is an exposition of the skillful means of the Four Noble Truths, intended to lead them to realize *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. As it is said: "This body is impermanent, unsubstantial, and fleeting."
It is of a nature subject to decay. This body is like a mass of foam that cannot be grasped; this body is like a bubble that cannot endure for long;
this body is like a mirage, born from craving, and so forth. △ Third, the verse on correct logical analysis.

This may be understood. △ Second, the verse on listening to the Dharma externally. This section has four parts. First, the verse exhorting one to listen to the sutra:

The Mahāyāna: because one enters the chamber of the Tathāgata, such is the resulting retribution. △ Third, the verse on sharing a seat to listen:

It is established within the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*) and takes the weaving of delusion as its boundary; therefore, there are the four directions.

Why does this act as a cause for suffering? The answer is: because they lack wholesome causes, even those who do not slander [the Dharma] may fall.

One falls into the evil realms due to slander, yet it is necessarily through such gain that one is saved—just as a person who has fallen to the ground must rise from that very ground. Therefore, by means of "correct slander," one is brought back from the "false fall."
"Mahāsthāmaprāpta, what do you think? ... [up to] 'one who does not regress from supreme enlightenment'—this is the point where the ancient and the modern are brought together;

it is even better to look at this. You must know that whether one previously believed or slandered, whether one endured patience or humiliation, whether there was suffering or joy, the heterodox or the orthodox, the contemptuous or the respectful—all these are, in essence, just this single person of today."
The countenance of Gautama; thus, I now speak these words with faith. Could this be anyone else? Tiantai says: *Bhadrapāla* means "Good Protector" (*Śanshǒu*).
This means that if sentient beings hear his name, they will ultimately attain *samyak-saṃbodhi*; hence he is called "Good Protector.
He is also called "Worthy Head" (*Xiánshǒu*), for his rank is that of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi-samāsanna*), making him the foremost among the worthy. The Supplement (*Bǔzhù*) states:
There are those who have composed sectional summaries (*piṇḍoddāna*) consisting of five hundred [verses] regarding the bhikṣuṇīs, which cause considerable confusion.
Their intention is that for the two monastic communities, one should mention only the *bhikṣus*, and for the laity, only the *upāsakas*.

Furthermore, they argue that since the *Sahasrabuddha-nidāna-sūtra* mentions only "contemplating the Buddhas" (*si fǒngděng*), it likely omits the word "nun" (*ni*). However, according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it says "Siṃha... [and so on].
The five hundred bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, including the upāsikās, constitute the fourfold assembly.
Since Siṃhacandra was himself a bhikṣu, he should not be referred to as a *bhikṣuṇī*; thus, it is said that there would be an inconsistency. Now, examining the *Nidāna-sūtra*, it says:
"Five hundred upāsakas contemplated the Buddha and attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); [the mother of] Uttara was virtuous..."
The five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, including the virtuous bhikṣuṇīs, were no longer subject to outflows and attained arhatship.
Furthermore, the *Nidāna-sūtra* was also translated by Kumārajīva; how then could one dare to definitively claim that the word "bhikṣuṇī" is missing?

Moreover, as for the name "Nisi," I have not seen it appear in other sūtras, and thus I do not dare state it with certainty. Should I later encounter the term "Nisi," [I shall provide further clarification].
Only then will the name be appropriate. △ Third, the conclusion: the summary of benefits and the exhortation to uphold.
"Mahāsthāmaprāpta, you should know that this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*... [up to] ...one who upholds, reads, recites, explains, and transcribes this sutra."
This section of the sutra is exceptionally profound; it is precisely this passage that constitutes the core of the entire chapter’s efficacy.
It is nothing other than an instruction for people to believe and uphold [the teaching]. Tiantai said: "The sutra truly possesses power and will ultimately bring about great fruition.
One must diligently practice the five kinds of conduct. These five kinds of conduct refer to the practices of the five types of Dharma-preachers. △ Second, the verses.
The Verse Summary. It is divided into two parts. First, the verse on the causes and effects of faith and slander, which is further divided into two. First, the verse on the fundamental matter.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"In the past there was a Buddha named King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja)" (up to) "...jointly honored by devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits.
This verse encompasses all twenty-two thousand koṭis of Buddhas. The *Yinzhi* (Sound-Knowledge) commentary states: "Immeasurable spiritual wisdom" refers to the *dharmakāya*.

"Majesty" (*wei*) refers to the guidance of all beings; this is *prajñā*. "Sound" (*yin*) refers to the section on devas and humans below; this is *vimukti*. "King" (*wang*) refers to... [the rest of the passage follows].
The name is used to illustrate its actual meaning. △ Second, the verses on the original events (*nidāna*). This also has four parts. First, the verse that doubly indicates the two persons:
"At the time after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the Dharma was about to perish... (until) at that time the fourfold assembly clung to the teachings."
This verse refers to the period immediately following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when these two types of people appeared. "Not slighting" refers to the masters who uphold this sutra;

the "fourfold assembly" refers to those who were arrogant toward the Dharma. This is a paired presentation of faith and slander. As for "those attached to dharmas," they are the class of people who cling to a self and fixate on signs.
The *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* states: "If a wheel of swords were to slaughter the people of Jambudvīpa, that loss would still be small."
Those who preach the Mahāyāna with a mind that grasps at attainment commit a sin greater than that. △ Second, the verse clarifies their gains and losses:
When the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging went to their places, they [the disparagers] were able to endure his treatment.
The Bodhisattva went to their place to receive their teachings; thus, the True permeates the delusory.
Possessing the reality of "Not Disdainful," he endured their insults and abuse; this is truly the ability to dissolve the delusory. He thereby attained the name "Not Disdainful.
△ Third, a verse on the retribution for faith and slander.
When his transgressions were exhausted and he approached the end of his life (until: gradually perfecting merit and swiftly attaining the Buddha-way). A supplementary note states:
Because the fourfold assembly treated him with contempt, he was given the name "Never-Disparaging. Furthermore, he was able to endure all instances of being struck or pelted with tiles and stones.
Consequently, all his karmic offenses were thereby brought to an end; thus, at the time of his death, he fully heard the wondrous Dharma.
He immediately attained the purity of the six sense organs. △ Fourth, the verse concludes by correlating the past with the present:
"At that time, 'Not-Disparaging' was none other than myself... [omitted] ...life after life, he upheld such a sutra as this."
This verse clarifies that the persons and dharmas of the past and present are non-dual. The *Yinzhi* (Record of Sound Knowledge) states:
"From 'At that time' onwards, the verse praises the teachers of the past causes and present fruits, showing that the merit of transmitting the Dharma is not in vain. From 'At that time [the four...
onwards, the verse praises the assembly of past causes and present fruits, showing that listening to the Dharma before the present Buddha is not without cause. From 'In my previous life' onwards..."
Seeing that the Buddha’s past act of exhorting others to listen to the sutra served as the cause, his present act of revealing it so they may abide in nirvana constitutes the fruit.
The section beginning with "From lifetime to lifetime" clarifies his long-term perseverance without weariness; this corresponds to the preceding passage:
"If, in past lives, I had not accepted, upheld, read, or recited this sutra," and so forth. II. The Verse Summary Exhorting Upholding.
For billions upon billions of kalpas, even unto the inconceivable, they shall encounter Buddhas in every lifetime and swiftly attain the path of Buddhahood.
This is the general instruction: having obtained the sight and hearing of this wondrous Dharma, one must not regard this seeing and hearing as something easy to achieve.
Since time immemorial, I have exhorted others in every lifetime to uphold this sutra; I have done so for billions upon billions of kalpas until now.
It is only after inconceivable eons that one may hear this Dharma once; thus, hearing this Dharma is not easy.
Furthermore, after as many such eons, only one Buddha appears in the world to expound this Dharma once; thus, the preaching of this Dharma is also not easy.
For this reason, I earnestly exhort you Bodhisattvas: after my parinirvāṇa, you should uphold it with a single mind.
"Speak thus! Do not give rise to doubt; you shall surely and swiftly realize the unsurpassed, ultimate fruit.

For your sake, I guarantee this matter—it shall never prove false. When the World-Honored One exhorted the people, it may be said that he was as resolute as "cutting through nails and iron," far beyond mere "shedding tears of blood.
We truly must not disparage or neglect ourselves. Thus ends the first three and a half chapters, which clarify [the preceding points].
The Merit of Propagating the Sūtra is hereby completed.
*The Lotus Sūtra: A Manual for Transmission*, Scroll Eight.
