Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhixiang of Mount Hengyun in Chu.
The sectioning of the twenty-first chapter, "The Supernatural Powers of the Tathāgata," states:
This chapter follows the extensive explanation of the merit of upholding the sūtra and further demonstrates the practice of upholding it oneself.
Thus, the immediate recipient of the teaching has attained perfect enlightenment to the ultimate degree, thereby fulfilling the Tathāgata’s original intent for appearing in the world.
Furthermore, having obtained the assembly of those who emerged from the earth to uphold the sutra, the Tathāgata rejoices and employs his supreme spiritual power to certify this realization.
Moreover, he desires to lead the recipient to penetrate the equal Dharma-realm, directly causing them to behold the Buddha-field before their very eyes.
The Pure Land is perceived in the present moment; since the benefit of the Dharma is now complete, the family enterprise of the Dharma King may be entrusted.
Nevertheless, the fact that the discourse begins with the assembly emerging from the earth precisely demonstrates that the virtues of one's own mind-nature are fully perfected.
This constitutes the entire body of the Lotus Sūtra. Therefore, the Tathāgata immediately manifests his supernatural powers:

light rays are emitted from every pore of his body, his tongue reaches up to the Brahma-heaven, and the earth trembles everywhere. This is what is meant by "revealing himself throughout his entire being" and "turning everything over from its very depths.
All Buddhas likewise emit light rays to manifest that the Way of Buddha-to-Buddha is identical; all the Buddhas of the ten directions are one and the same.
While sitting amidst the light, a voice issued from the air, praising from afar Śākyamuni for preaching the Lotus Sūtra;

this manifested the mutual resonance of the minds of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions. The worlds of the ten directions were pervaded without obstruction, as if they were a single Buddha-land.
Thus, he brilliantly illuminates the true realm of the Dharmakāya to eliminate the limited minds of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
When the World-Honored One has reached the ultimate limit of his supernatural powers (*ṛddhibala*) in extolling the merits of this sutra,
that which remains unexhausted consists of all the dharmas of the Tathāgata, all his sovereign supernatural powers, all the secret treasuries, and all that is profoundly deep.
All such matters are proclaimed and clearly expounded within this sutra. Having long kept silent regarding this essential point, it is now being spoken.
Because it was difficult to believe and difficult to understand, it has now been believed and understood—namely, the realization of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The merit of upholding this is likewise beyond the reach of thought. Having been revealed to this extent, the manifestation of the principle is complete; therefore—
Exhausting the Buddha’s supernatural power, he seals it with a seal of authentication; thus, this chapter is judged to be the ultimate revelation of the principle.
Since the revelation of the principle is now complete, the entrustment follows next. The old commentaries judge that from this point downward, all belong to the section on the Propagation.
Zhizhi says: "From the 'Emergence from the Earth' chapter up to these seven chapters, all constitute the activities of the Revealing of the Original Gate."
The "Chapter on the Emergence" reveals the great function of the original gate; the "Chapter on the Lifespan" reveals the great essence of the original [Buddha-body].

The three chapters on the "Distinction of Rejoicing" and the "Dharma Master" reveal the great power of the original; the "Chapter on the Unconquerable One" reveals the great practice of the original. Now, the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" reveals the great fruit of the original.
Regarding what is called the "great fruit," it corresponds to what is said in the "Parable Chapter": "The Tathāgata has accomplished immeasurable..."

The powers of knowledge and vision, the fearlessnesses, the great power of spiritual transformation, as well as the power of wisdom, and the perfection of skillful means and wisdom—all these are subsumed within the great fruit. This concludes the fourteen chapters of the Section on Traces.
These [teachings] generally belong to the Tathāgata’s wisdom. From the "Original Gate" (Honmon) up to these seven chapters, they also belong to the Tathāgata’s spiritual power (*ṛddhi*).

However, while in the preceding six chapters spiritual power and wisdom proceed in tandem, this chapter alone represents the ultimate purport of the entire "Original Gate," and because it seeks to sweep away all traces of the activity of wisdom and power, it uniquely manifests ten kinds of spiritual power.
In a single moment, he directly causes the worlds of the ten directions to become one single land, and all sentient beings of the nine realms to ascend simultaneously to the stage of Buddhahood;
this is the fulfillment of the Elder’s intention through the power of his physical strength. Tiantai says: The meaning of "Tathāgata" is as explained previously.
Regarding "supernatural power" (*ṛddhi*): "Supernatural" (*shen*) means unfathomable, and "power" (*li*) refers to efficacious function. Being unfathomable is like heaven (*tian*).

The substance of this [teaching] is profound; its application and function involve a great power of transformation. Because it intends to entrust the profound Dharma, ten kinds of divine manifestations are displayed;

therefore, it is titled the "Chapter on Divine Power. From here until the end of eight chapters, there is a general clarification of the entrustment and circulation [of the teaching], divided into three sections.
First, these two chapters, "This" and "Entrustment," clarify the entrustment and circulation, which are further divided into two parts.

First, clarifying how the Bodhisattvas received their mandate to propagate the sutra. This section has two parts. First, the prose exposition (*gadya*), which is divided into three. First, the Bodhisattvas receiving their mandate, which further has two parts.
First, the narrator’s description of the ritual protocol.
At that time, the multitude emerging from the earth— equal in number to the atoms of a thousand worlds (up to) gazing upon the Honored One’s countenance with single-minded palms joined—
took their original purpose for coming, which was to propagate the Great Dharma, as secondary;

because at that moment the Buddha had not yet finished instructing the assembly by resolving their doubts and revealing the great matter of the Original Gate, they did not have the leisure to state their reasons for having come.
And thus they make their vows. However, regarding the two gates of the Trace and the Origin, there are two levels for each in terms of the capacity of those who propagate [the teaching].

For instance, when the Tathāgata of the Trace Gate calls for volunteers to propagate [the teaching], although the newly recorded ones have all made vows, whether in this world or other worlds, this truly does not yet accord with the Buddha’s original intent.
It is only upon surveying the eighty quadrillion bodhisattvas that the *Dhāraṇī* Chapter and [the subsequent chapters] first appear.
One shall practice in peace and happiness, thereby ensuring the Dharma is propagated in accordance with the True Dharma. Now, this "Sudden Appearance" (Honmon) section also possesses two layers.
The preceding three chapters on the Entrustment and the Joyful Acceptance of the Dharma Masters do not yet fully exhaust the Tathāgata’s original intent.

Only now, with the emergence of the great assembly from the earth and their respective declarations of their original vows, can the Tathāgata’s long-held concerns be fully realized; thus, his heart may be set at ease. It is necessary...

Know that among those who propagate these two gates, those in the former stage can only benefit themselves, whereas those in the latter stage attain the great function of True Suchness (tathatā) and shoulder the entire burden.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has dispelled his concerns and manifested divine joy and fortune;
this is for the purpose of entrustment. 2. Taking an Oath to Propagate the Sūtra.
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One... [up to] "...explaining it, copying it, and making offerings to it.

The commentary notes that if one examines the meaning of these words, there are two differences from what preceded regarding the breadth or narrowness of the location and the slowness or urgency of the mind.
As for those who made various vows in the "Chapter on the Retention," why is it that although figures such as Bhaiṣajyarāja each made their own vows?
They travel back and forth between this world and other worlds throughout the ten directions to uphold this sutra;
yet, because they merely obey the Buddha’s command and have not attained the Buddha’s mind, the Buddha does not entrust them with his final, peaceful repose.

It is only these multitudes, as numerous as the dust motes in a thousand worlds, who have made their vows; when one speaks of their location, it is said: "In the world after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, wherever the World-Honored One’s emanations reside..."
The places where the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa are the places where this sutra is upheld;
they are immeasurably vast, extending not merely to the worlds of the ten directions where one Buddha travels back and forth after his passing, for the Buddha’s emanations are infinite.
Because the worlds are also infinite, he raised his mind and said: "We ourselves also desire to attain this truly pure Great Dharma.
This is the mind that upholds the sutra—tireless and expansive. It was not like the words of the eighty trillion nayutas of bodhisattvas, who had said:
"We respectfully believe in the Buddha and will endure all these evils; we only pray..."

The World-Honored One, while in another land, beheld them from afar and protected them out of fear that they might seek protection through evil means; ultimately, their affairs relied upon the Buddha.
Now, this great assembly desires to attain the truly pure Dharma for themselves; thus, they do not rely on the Buddha above nor do they fear evil below.
Therefore, having received the Buddha’s command and satisfied his heart, he immediately manifested his supernatural power to entrust [the teaching] to them. △
Second, the manifestation of the two Buddhas’ supernormal powers. This is divided into two parts. First, the assembly present before them:
At that time, the World-Honored One, before the entire assembly including Mañjuśrī and others, as well as humans and non-humans...
All that follows is arranged as a narrative by the compiler. The Buddha employs ten kinds of spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*) to entrust [the teaching].
Those who understand the meaning say that Mañjuśrī and others represent the "long-term residents," while Xingxiang (Manifest Practice) and others represent the "newly arrived residents.
Furthermore, in the past, under the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa, Mañjuśrī was the Dharma Master Varaprabha, who instructed the eight princes; the eighth of these was named Jyotiṣprabha (Flaming Light).
Regarding the lamp: it was at the time of Dīpaṃkara that Śākyamuni first gave rise to the Great Mind; therefore, Mañjuśrī is called the elder who has long resided in this Sahā world.
Now, before this assembly, he manifests great supernatural power, desiring to entrust this sutra to his native land.
II. The Actual Manifestation of Supernatural Power, divided into ten sections: 1. Extending the Tongue to Symbolize...
Truly. He manifests great supernormal power by extending his broad and long tongue upward as far as the Brahma-world.
By means of this broad and long tongue, the Tathāgata manifests a great supernormal power that transcends the world and universally covers all things.
Tiantai says: The phrase "manifesting great supernatural powers" serves as the general heading, while the ten subsequent items are the specific details. Regarding the manifestation of the tongue:

this reveals that all that is expounded in the present sutra—the opening of the three to reveal the one, the provisional and the real, the original and the trace, the bestowal of predictions upon the śrāvakas, causes and conditions, and parables—is entirely truthful and not false. Were it otherwise, how could he manifest such a broad and long tongue?
Is this not a mark? His speech throughout the three periods of time is never false. His tongue can reach his nose;

while the tongues of those who have mastered the Tripitaka reach the hairline, the Buddha’s tongue now reaches the Brahma Heaven, surpassing both ordinary beings and sages, extending to the summit of the Pure Heavens. Since these marks are so extraordinary, [how could he be an ordinary person?]
This teaching is all the more trustworthy. △ Second, the manifestation of the sublime through the emission of light:
From every pore, he emits immeasurable [light] (up to) extending his broad and long tongue and emitting immeasurable rays of light.
This is the Tathāgata’s great supernatural power, which manifests through the light of his pores and pervades the ten directions without obstruction.
Throughout the sutra, light is emitted on three occasions. On the first, light is emitted from the white tuft between his eyebrows;

that it illuminates only eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction is specifically to manifest this realm within the scope of the near and accessible, for the sake of all who have not yet understood.

This is to cause them to know and recognize it. Next, at the site where the three transformations of the land occur, he likewise emits this light, illuminating five hundred *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sand worlds in the eastern direction.
In this manner, he successively illuminates all eight directions, making the lands in these directions even more excellent than those previously mentioned.
This expands the preceding realms, causing their knowledge and recognition to increase and broaden deeply.
It reaches the ears. Previously there was but a single hair; now there are all hairs. Previously there was but a single color;

now there are countless colors. Previously it illuminated but a small area; now it illuminates the ten directions. This is what is meant by using countless skillful means to gradually lead one into the Buddha’s wisdom.
At first it was said to be profoundly deep, immeasurable, difficult to understand, and difficult to enter; reaching this point, one has penetrated to the very summit and through to the other side.
"Bottomless. There are no remaining aggregates (*skandha*). Tiantai says: "Every pore of his body emits light, pervading the ten directions so that there is nowhere it does not illuminate.
This signifies that the principle of the two gates is one, and that the realm of wisdom is ultimate.

Previously, in the Trace Gate, the white tuft emitted radiance beginning from the east, signifying that through the seven stages of expedient means, one first perceives the single principle. Now, in this Root Gate, since...

It is finished. They emit all-encompassing light that illuminates all lands, enabling those at the initial stage of the causal path to ultimately reach the ultimate Buddha-wisdom of Equal Enlightenment.
The emanated bodies of these Buddhas are likewise so; since these characteristics are identical, their benefit to beings within their respective lands is also the same.
△ Third, simultaneity of extension and contraction.
From the time Śākyamuni Buddha [manifested] beneath the jewel tree until he subsequently withdrew his tongue-mark, this Tathāgata took what was brief and made it long;
through the illusory transformation of the three periods of time, he manifested the great power of simultaneity between extension and contraction.
At one time he extended his tongue for a hundred thousand years; were it not for great supernormal power (*mahā-ṛddhi*), how could he have withdrawn it?

Having withdrawn it, he spoke in response to the previous statement about extending the tongue, pointing directly: "The Buddhas realize the equality of the three periods of time (*tryadhva-samatā*), such that the ultimate and the conventional are of one suchness (*tathatā*);
thus they are able to extend a single instant (*kṣaṇa*) into an eon (*kalpa*), and contract an eon into a single instant. This is because of their mental capacity (*citta-mātra*)."
If they do not exist, then the measure of the *dharmadhātu* ceases; yet the *dharmadhātu* is immeasurable, and its extension or contraction is like an illusion.

This is the Buddha’s ordinary enjoyment of *samādhi*; it is called "spiritual power" (*ṛddhibala*) only because it is directed toward those with new capacities. △ Fourth, coughing and snapping the fingers.
At that moment, they coughed and snapped their fingers together; these two sounds reached throughout the ten directions.

This demonstrates that the Tathāgata possesses the great supernormal power of manifesting universally throughout the ten directions without obstruction through the sounds of his coughing and snapping of fingers.
After withdrawing the mark of his tongue, he was about to produce a sound; hence it is called "coughing" (*kṣiṅ-kai*).
Why speak of "spiritual power" (*ṛddhi-bala*) regarding this coughing and snapping of fingers? Spiritual power is perceived within these four characters: "all together at one time.
This is because the emanated Buddhas within the three transformations of the land are infinite in number. Such a multitude of Buddhas all coughed and snapped their fingers simultaneously.
Śākyamuni was not first, and his emanations were not later; these two kinds of voices simultaneously pervaded the ten directions.
Is this not a great supernatural power? You must know that I, the Tathāgata, through my total embodiment and great function, directly manifest the natural splendor of the original ground.

To cause all people to penetrate the profound barrier and the golden lock, and to possess the eye of the crown of the head—such that even coughing, spitting, or swinging one’s arms are all instances of the supreme mechanism—this is precisely the intent behind the Buddha’s holding up the flower at the assembly for the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The four supernormal powers mentioned previously were manifested from the Buddha’s own body, and the same was true for his various emanation Buddhas. As for the six supernormal powers below, they...
This is manifested through the power of the Buddha’s voice and light, and by being permeated by the power of the Buddha’s voice and light, appearing in successive stages.
*Qǐng* (pronounced with the upper tone) and *kài* (pronounced *kǎi*). △ At the fifth stage, there are six kinds of earth-movements.
The grounds of all Buddha-worlds trembled in six ways;
this was the manifestation of the signs of the grounds throughout the ten directions through the power of this Buddha’s voice, light, and majestic spiritual authority (*prabhāva*).
The spiritual power does not reside in the trembling itself, but is seen in the eight characters "all Buddha-worlds' grounds tremble in six ways. Thus it is with the Tathāgata.
The exposition of the two gates of the original and the trace regarding the great matter of transcending the world is now complete; therefore, he protrudes his tongue to manifest the ultimate truth.
When the assembly beholds this sign, they believe that the Tathāgata’s words are free from falsehood.

The Buddha further wishes to fully reveal within his white curl (*ūrṇā*) the signs of the ten realms of existence, so that people may understand that it is not only a single hair that is thus. Then, the hairs—
There is not a single pore that is not thus. When it is so for form, then form pervades the ten directions.
Since form is thus, sound is likewise so; this is why the sounds of clearing one's throat or snapping the fingers all pervade the ten directions.
Furthermore, while form and sound pertain only to the eyes and ears, the nose, tongue, body, and mind have not yet been manifested.
Therefore, he now displays great supernormal power once more, such that all Buddha-worlds respond here to what is felt there, resulting in the six kinds of earth tremors.
These six kinds of tremors precisely manifest the full revelation of the great function of the six sense faculties, so that the assembly may, through this—

Knowing that one's own faculties, sense objects, and sense fields pervade the entire Dharma-realm, one will no longer doubt why the wisdom of all Buddhas is so profoundly deep, immeasurable, difficult to understand, and difficult to enter. △ Sixth, Universally Beholding the Great Assembly.
Among them, the sentient beings, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and so forth, all rejoiced greatly at having attained what they had never experienced before.
This was due to the inconceivable power of this Buddha’s voice and light, which opened the way for the sentient beings of the ten directions to behold these supreme signs.
"Sentient beings" refers to all sentient beings within the worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions that were previously shaken.
By what means do these sentient beings come to see the immeasurable Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and the fourfold assembly of the Sahā world?
It is by the spiritual power of the Buddha. For it is only through the manifestation of the Buddha’s spiritual power that this is possible. Thus it is said.
Suddenly causing all sentient beings to simultaneously and equally attain perfect enlightenment, opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Once this knowledge and vision are opened, there is nothing that is not seen. Although the worlds are thus vast and distant, and the various sages are thus numerous, they all appear with distinct clarity;
seeing them perfectly without shifting, how could one not feel great joy? One attains...
"How marvelous! △ Seventh, a voice issues from the sky.
Immediately, the various devas in the void [proclaim]: '...you should also pay homage and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha.'"
This inconceivable power of the Buddha’s voice and light causes the devas of the ten directions to see the signs of his supreme exhortation to offer worship.
By what means could these devas have heard that in the Sahā world there is Śākyamuni, who is preaching this Great Dharma for the sake of the bodhisattvas?
It is also due to the Buddha’s spiritual power. Only the Buddha can manifest and reveal it through his spiritual power.
Therefore, within the perfect interfusion of the ultimate and the conventional, these sounds are produced and these words are spoken:
to make known this Triple Gem to these sentient beings and to instruct them to rejoice with a profound mind. One thus knows that such a profound realm cannot be realized without such a profound mind;
for this reason, this prostration and offering are unavoidable. △ Eight: Hearing the Sound... up to [the end].
Veneration.
When those sentient beings heard the voice from the midst of space (up to) they all together scattered [flowers] from afar toward the Sahā world.
These sentient beings of the ten directions, having been graced by the Buddha’s radiance and having heard the voice from space, thereby came to know that the Buddha had appeared in the world.

This is the manner of making offerings. When those sentient beings heard the voice from mid-air, why did they immediately join their palms, call out the name [of the Buddha], and present various kinds of precious objects from afar, scattering them throughout the Sahā world? This was also due to the Buddha’s spiritual power.

It is solely because the Buddha manifests through his supernatural power that all beings—whether oneself or others—throughout the entirety of the ten directions of the Dharma-realm, universally attain the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).
Since there is no distinction between self and other, each person makes various offerings within their own dwelling place.
If one discusses the two types of awakening—the original (*mūla*) and the initial (*ādi*)—then all people, regarding the sixth supernatural power...
Within [the stupa], he has already seen Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna dwelling together in one tower.
As for the emanated Buddhas and all the Bodhisattvas, he has clearly perceived them all. Why, then, would it be necessary for the devas and humans to announce this again?

It should be known that by hearing this sound, he gains yet another layer of intimacy. This is why it is said that [the teaching] is directed toward the Sahā world; it is intimate regarding its location and accords with reality.
The name "Coming" (Lai) accords closely with the underlying principle. Since there is that toward which one is directed and that which is revered, one knows that there is nothing not illuminated;
this may be called truly attaining the Buddha’s knowledge. △ Ninth: The Offering Objects Form a Canopy.
The various objects scattered [as offerings] came from the ten directions and completely covered the Buddhas throughout this realm.

Furthermore, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, the sentient beings of this Sahā world were likewise able to see the manifestations of the various offerings being presented in each of the ten directions.
Those flowers, incense, necklaces, and so forth, arrived like a gathering of clouds; by what means did they come?
It transformed into a jeweled canopy covering all the Buddhas. This could not have been accomplished without the Buddha’s supernatural power.

One must know that these objects came from the ten directions; this was the gathering of great functions into one place, transforming them into a jeweled canopy. This was the dispersal and subsequent re-aggregation [of light].
It was precisely as the Tathāgata, having finished preaching the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, again entered the *Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings*.
The Buddhas of this realm are the entire body itself. "Pervasive coverage" means there is no Buddha who is not included.

To pervasively cover all these Buddhas of this realm is precisely what is meant by "gathering the great function back into the entire body," wherein all that was to be done has been accomplished and knowledge and vision have become perfect—what is called the wondrous cloud of compassionate shade covering the ocean of *nirvāṇa*. △ Tenth: Pervading a single Buddha-land.
At that time, the worlds of the ten directions were unimpededly accessible as if they were a single buddha-field.
This summary is due to the Buddha’s spiritual power; the worlds of the ten directions and the Sahā world were all completely interfused, appearing as a single buddha-field.
"World" (*loka*) is the general term for both the environment and the beings—the two types of retribution. For now, [we shall consider] the environment...
The realms have no inherent boundaries or territories; these are all merely conventional designations. As for the primary retribution of sentient beings, they are fundamentally of one principle.

Yet, due to the deluded arising of knowledge and views, various sensory objects are allowed to create separation and obstruction. What is called "the blazing creation of difference within that which is neither identical nor different" is entirely delusion.
Once this false construction is established, knowledge and views are falsely divided. This is why it is said to reside in the eye.
It is divided into seeing; when it is in the ear-cavity, it is called hearing. Thus, it is said that the original single pure brightness is divided into six harmonious combinations.
For immeasurable kalpas, the World-Honored One has realized this unimpeded, wondrous principle.

Observing that all people remain in the great night of ignorance, difficult to dawn upon, he has appeared in the world specifically for this great cause and condition to reveal and instruct them. Now that...

The teaching has been fully revealed, and the knowledge and vision of all people have likewise reached their ultimate limit. This overturns the previously deluded realm and transforms it into the field of great enlightenment.
Therefore, throughout the worlds of the ten directions—places that were formerly inaccessible, unpenetrated, most obstructed, and most hindered—they are now suddenly and completely permeated.
Thus it is said: "To penetrate without obstruction is as if it were a single Buddha-land. As...

The discourse begins with the manifestation of auspicious signs through the emission of light; it proceeds through the emergence from meditative concentration, the praise of virtues, the provisional opening of the gates, and the revelation of the ultimate reality.

It discards the traces to manifest the fundamental source across twenty chapters of scripture. Herein lies the profound discussion of the *Saddharma*; herein the sublime spiritual powers are wondrously manifested;

herein the fundamental and the trace are harmoniously integrated; herein the living beings and the Buddhas realize the same truth; and herein false and deluded cognition and vision are transformed into the state of all Buddhas.

Regarding knowledge and vision: at this point, there is not a single place as small as the point of a needle where it is not the Buddha’s knowledge, nor a single speck of dust where it is not the Buddha’s vision.

Only now is fulfilled the original mind and original vow of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world for the sake of the one great cause and condition—to reveal, instruct, awaken, and lead others into [enlightenment].
According to the intent of the sutra, the main body of the Honmon (the Essential Gate) should conclude here. The Buddha then manifests...
The section on supernatural powers is concluded. △ Third, the summary and exhortation to uphold [the teaching], divided into four parts. First, the praise and entrustment:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Superior Progression Bodhisattva and others... (up to) "the merit of expounding this sutra cannot yet be fully exhausted."

Since the original intent of appearing in the world has already been fully revealed, and the assembly has likewise each attained perfect realization, he merely summons his disciples from the lower realms to entrust them with the teaching. Furthermore, at the time he manifested his supernatural powers:
Regarding the presence before the assembly of Mañjuśrī: since Mañjuśrī had already received the command to propagate [the teaching] during the time of Candrasūryapradīpa Buddha,
and Bhaiṣajyarāja had likewise received the command to propagate it before the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa,
he manifested such supernatural power (ṛddhi) before these bodhisattvas because they were all elders who had previously witnessed [him].
The Buddha likewise manifests himself in this way; now, beholding these signs once more, the intent to propagate [the Dharma] is renewed.

As for those such as Shangxing and others, who have never seen such things before, having now witnessed such supernatural power even once, their resolve to receive the mandate and propagate it becomes even more urgent.
They will surely pray to fulfill Bodhi before they cease, and shall also cause the newly recorded Śrāvakas to find peace of mind in the myriad [teachings].
[He] acts. There are no other thoughts. Therefore, he declares: "The spiritual power of all Buddhas—this is but a small portion;
there remains that which is inconceivable. This concludes the proof of the great enterprise of the true teaching of the Original Gate.
From the words "If I, by this spiritual power," onwards, he begins the entrustment and circulation, saying: "If I, by this spiritual power, manifest [it] in the..."
Even if one were to spend immeasurable eons, proclaiming the merits of this sutra for the sake of entrustment in every single eon, one could still not exhaust them.

Thus, we know that the preceding section concludes what has gone before, while the subsequent section introduces what follows; it is only here, between the two pillars of the "Correct Teaching" (dharmakāya) and the "Circulation" (pravartana), that the formal conclusion begins.
If one were to explain this as a single continuous flow, then this supernatural power would pertain solely to the circulation.

As for this manifestation, the observer must exercise discernment. Generally, whenever the Buddhas and Tathāgatas manifest supernatural transformations, there is always a great underlying cause and condition.
Thus, at the very beginning, wishing to open up the provisional and reveal the real by bestowing predictions upon those of the three capacities, they briefly emitted a single ray of light.
Now that the Trace Gate is nearing its conclusion, and as they further wish to open up and reveal the Great Matter of the Origin Gate, they once again...
This light was extensively emitted. Now that the primary teaching (the *zhengzong*) has been completed, these ten kinds of spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*) are manifested;
thus, the intention to promote and circulate [the teaching] is hereby aroused. △ Second, the summary and entrustment.
To state it briefly: all that the Tathāgata has [taught] up to this point has been proclaimed and revealed within this sutra.
This summarizes and consolidates what was previously explained regarding the provisional and the real, and the primary and secondary aspects of the teaching;

all these points are now presented together as a summary of the essential purport of the entire sutra, entrusted to the Bodhisattvas who have emerged from the earth so that they may grasp its vital core.
Thus, it was circulated everywhere. Therefore, it is said: "To state the essentials: the Tathāgata here refers collectively to all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
"Dharma" refers to the Dharma realized by each of these Buddhas-Tathāgatas at their respective sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
As for the phrase "all that exists," this refers to what was previously praised at the very beginning of the main teaching (*śarīra-dharma*) upon emerging from meditative absorption.
The virtues— the ten realms and ten suchnesses, the provisional and the real of the Great and Small Vehicles, the revelation through the three turnings of the wheel,

the bestowing of predictions upon the śrāvakas, up to the praise of the Dharma-preacher, the exposition of the practices of peaceful dwelling, the causes and conditions of the earth-emerging bodhisattvas,
the long duration of the Buddha’s lifespan, and so forth— all these are every single dharma possessed by the Tathāgata. These belong to the Buddha’s wisdom and his sovereign spiritual powers.
He immediately emitted light and shook the earth as before; lengthening and shortening time occurred simultaneously, such that eighty minor kalpas were perceived as being like half a day.
He received the great assembly into the void and transformed the Sahā world in an instant, manifesting the ten kinds of divine powers described above.
All of these are the sovereign spiritual powers of the Tathāgata; they belong to the Buddha’s supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*).
Regarding the "Secret Essential Treasury" (*guhyaka-kośa*): it is guarded by all Buddhas. "Secret" (*guhya*) means esoteric; "essential" (*yao*) means vital and urgent.

Are not the ten dharma-realm manifestations that appeared within the light previously mentioned secret and essential? Is not the wondrous stupa of Prabhūtaratna that surged forth from the earth secret and essential?
Essential. Are not each of the bodhisattvas appearing below, as well as the immeasurable multitudes emerging from the Dragon Palace, all essentials that were previously unmanifest?
Now, within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, each is revealed so that those who see or hear them may ultimately reach Bodhi.
These are all the Tathāgata’s secret and essential treasury; therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] has long remained silent.
This is the essential point. These matters belonging to the Tathāgata’s samādhi, which are exceedingly profound, are as follows:
namely, the account of Mañjuśrī and the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa; the account of the World-Honored One regarding Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū; and the account of Devadatta.

The matter of the dragon girl attaining Buddhahood; the matter of the transformation of the assembly emerging from the earth; the matter of the conduct of Sadāparibhūta; the matter of the provisional being set aside to reveal the real;
and the matter of the traces being abandoned to reveal the fundamental—these are all difficult to fathom and difficult to know; they are the profoundly deep matters of the Tathāgata.
These belong to the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision. Therefore, the "Parable Chapter" states:
"He has already fully perfected immeasurable samādhis, wisdoms, supernormal powers, knowledges, and pāramitās; now he wishes to entrust these four dharmas to the bodhisattvas.
This is stated by summarizing the essentials; therefore, it says they are all proclaimed and clearly expounded within this sutra. Furthermore, one must...
To know these four dharmas is precisely what is established by the fivefold profound meaning (*pañca-gambhīrārtha*). "All dharmas" refers to the name of the wondrous Dharma (*saddharma*).
Once sovereign spiritual powers (*vibhutva-ṛddhi*) have been clearly perceived, doubt is severed and faith arises; this is the function.

The secret treasury of essentials is that which integrates all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) and returns them to the essence of the single true mark (*ekalakṣaṇatathatā*). The profoundly deep matter concerns cause and effect.

This must be thoroughly penetrated; it is the doctrine esteemed by the One Vehicle. These four phrases alone encompass the entire purport of this sutra. Thus one may perceive the intent of the scripture:
having perfected the orthodox teaching and summarized its essential meaning, they are entrusted to the various bodhisattvas, at which point the transmission truly begins.
△ Third, the exhortation and entrustment.
Therefore, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, you all should erect stupas within these [places] and make offerings to them.
Furthermore, you must summon those such as Śikhin to protect and circulate [this teaching].

However, for it to be circulated, it ultimately requires that one single-mindedly receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, transcribe, and practice according to the teaching. Only by possessing these six matters is one capable [of this task].

Regarding the responsibility: in whatever land this scripture exists, and wherever there are those who practice this scripture, one by one they must be commanded to ascend [to the heights] and so forth; all should erect stupas and make offerings.
This is what is meant by "ascending. The four extraordinary powers belong entirely to this scripture and reside within these persons, thereby continuing the life of wisdom.
Therefore, you should pay respectful homage. △ Fourth, the explanation that establishes the entrustment.
Why is this so? You should know that this place is where all Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa.

This correctly explains its meaning. Regarding the previous statement that "wherever this sūtra volume is located, a stūpa should be erected," it is because the essential teaching within the sūtra requires four matters. As for "this place," Tiantai says it refers to the location where the sūtra is;

he explains the aforementioned "profound matter" as the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), the aforementioned "secret treasury" as the attainment of bodhi, and [the aforementioned] as the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
All dharmas above [this] enter nirvāṇa, thereby explaining the aforementioned supernormal powers. These four essentials encompass the entirety of the sūtra’s text;
therefore, stupas should be erected for each of them. As for what is meant by "essentials": attaining bodhi is the *dharmakāya*;
turning the wheel of the Dharma is *prajñā*; entering nirvāṇa is *vimukti*. These three dharmas constitute the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*), within which the Buddha dwells.
This is the meaning of "stūpa. △ Second, the verse summary, divided into two parts. First, the verses on the ten kinds of supernormal powers.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Buddhas, saviors of the world, abide in great supernormal powers" (up to) "manifesting immeasurable spiritual powers.
The first four lines constitute a general summary. When the Buddhas appear in the world, they abide in great supernormal powers;

there is nothing they do that is not for the sake of saving those who have not yet heard the Buddha-way. The reason they manifest such spiritual powers does not stop at this [duality] of existence and non-existence.

This is the measure. It is nothing more than bringing joy to sentient beings and causing them to advance deeply into the path. Regarding the four lines beginning with "The tongue-mark" (*jihvā-lakṣaṇa*), the verse praises the pervasiveness of the Dharma-body throughout the ten directions.
Now, both the new and old inhabitants of this Sahā world, as well as the sentient beings from the nine realms gathered from other regions, shall all hear this great enterprise of the True Doctrine.
Each will give rise to the mind of the two benefits (self-benefit and benefit for others), and their seeking shall be fulfilled.
The Way. Why was it so earnest? Therefore, he extended his tongue and emitted light, manifesting this rare phenomenon to provide a seal of verification for what was received in the preceding text.

His clearing of his throat and other such acts caused the sound of the verses to pervade the ten directions, universally proclaiming this to both this world and others, so that they might know that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Dharma would be transmitted to those who could receive it, fulfilling the original intent of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world. It is not [otherwise].
This is for consolation. The reason he manifests immeasurable supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) is to initiate the subsequent entrustment and circulation [of the teaching].
Among the ten kinds of supernatural powers mentioned previously, only these four are singled out; the remainder are all subsumed within the two characters "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*).
△ Second, the verse summary of the essential entrustment, divided into three parts: First, a general verse summarizing the four dharmas.
Because he entrusts this sutra, he praises those who receive and uphold it, up to the point that its limit cannot be found.
This summarizes four points; however, it simply states "because he entrusts this sutra" and extends to "the limit cannot be found."
It encompasses four meanings. Since these meanings are boundless, the merit of the person who upholds them is likewise boundless.
△ Second, the separate verses on the four dharmas, divided into four parts. First, the verse on all dharmas.
"One who can uphold this sutra has already seen me... [and] teaches and transforms all bodhisattvas.
This verse encompasses all the dharmas possessed by the Tathāgata. Tiantai says: "To uphold the Dharma is to uphold the Buddha-body."
This is because all phenomena do not transcend the transformer and the realized one, as well as that which is transformed and that which is realized.
△ Second, the verse on sovereign spiritual power:
"Those who can uphold this sutra shall cause me and my emanated bodies (down to... to also attain joy."

The signs of the movement of supernormal power arise from within joy. If there are those who can uphold this sutra, it is not only that the Buddhas of the present manifest their supernormal powers to praise them;
all Tathāgatas of the three periods and ten directions likewise manifest their supernormal powers to praise them in this same way.
△ Third, verses on the secret and essential treasury.
The secret and essential Dharma attained by all Buddhas while seated at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) shall also be attained before long by those who can uphold this sutra.
The secret, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma attained by all Buddhas at the site of enlightenment is known only by a Buddha and a Buddha;
if one can now recite and uphold this sutra, then one will not be far from the site of enlightenment.
Before long, you too shall attain this wondrous Dharma. △ Fourth, the verse on the profoundly deep matter:
"Those who can uphold this sutra [regarding] the meaning of all dharmas... shall ultimately abide in the One Vehicle."

The previous statement that "one shall before long attain this Dharma" refers to self-benefit. This present statement regarding the "inexhaustible method of joyful exposition" refers to benefiting others.

That is to say, if one can uphold and recite this sutra, one will attain joyful exposition regarding the Dharma, its meaning, and its terminology, thereby perfecting the four types of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*).
In preaching the Dharma without obstruction, it will be like wind entering space, entirely free from hindrance.
Having attained such eloquence, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, they will be able— just as the Buddha—
to teach this wondrous Dharma of the true mark to sentient beings by means of various causes, conditions, parables, and expressions,
following the sequence of all the sūtras and teachings spoken by the Buddha. They shall awaken themselves and awaken others, shattering the darkness of ignorance, just like [the sun].

The light of the sun and moon shines everywhere without exception; thus, they are able to teach and transform immeasurable bodhisattvas, leading them to the ultimate, wondrous fruit of the One Vehicle.
Is this not indeed the profound matter of the Tathāgata? △ Third, the concluding verse of summary and exhortation.
Therefore, those with wisdom who hear these merits and benefits will be certain and free from doubt.
This verse summarizes the four dharmas; it states that if one can uphold these four dharmas and faithfully accept this sutra, one will ultimately attain Buddhahood without fail.
Following the manifestation of supernatural powers, the Tathāgata correctly expounded the propagation [of the teaching], and thus he addressed [the assembly]:
The essential meaning of the entire sutra concerning the Bodhisattvas such as Śūraṅgama does not exceed these four dharmas, which are elucidated repeatedly;
since they were originally intended for entrustment, the conclusion states: "Such a person will certainly have no doubt regarding the Buddha-way."
Thus, this long passage, including both prose and verse, precedes the section on the entrustment and dissemination;
it serves both to conclude what has preceded and to introduce what follows, for after this concludes, the "Chapter on Entrustment" (Zhūlèi pǐn) is established.
The twenty-second chapter, "Entrusting," states in its sectioning:

Because the preceding exposition has already perfected the revelation of principle, the capacity of the audience has already thoroughly awakened to the mind, their faith and understanding have become authentic, and the primary cause for attaining Buddhahood is fully established; this is thus the fundamental purpose of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world.
The period of gestation is now complete. It is just as when a patriarch and his son have forgotten their worldly attachments; he then entrusts the family estate to him.
Thus, the teaching on the "entrustment" (parindanā) is spoken to bring the disciples' faith and understanding to its conclusion. From the section on Devadatta up to this point—

The eleven chapters of the sutra collectively serve to awaken one to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Together with the preceding twenty-two chapters, they generally constitute *śraddhā-vimukti* (faith and understanding).

Taken as a whole, they belong to the category of revealing the principle (*li*) as the cause. The final six chapters reveal practice (*xing*), clarifying that realization and entry (*zhengru*) constitute the fruit.

The *Yaojie* (Essential Explanation) states: "To entrust by means of words is called *zhuchi*; to bind by means of the Dharma is called *leiyi*. This is intended to ensure the transmission and continuity of the wondrous [Dharma]."
The Dharma reaches fulfillment without end; therefore, it is called "entrustment" (*parindanā*), serving as its transmission for universal circulation.

Now, although the assembly has not yet concluded, the reason the entrustment is spoken of so abruptly is that this sutra establishes its essence through wisdom and perfects its virtues through practice.
Having previously opened up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to clarify the Great Matter, the method for establishing the essence is now complete; thus, the entrustment is proclaimed.
The essential point of the Buddhas handing down the transmission from hand to hand is exhausted here.

For those who would later perfect their virtue through practice, there is nothing other than to embody these preceding teachings and extend them into action; there is no separate method. Since there is no separate method, this entrustment is most appropriate.
△ Second, explaining the Tathāgata’s entrustment by stroking the crown of the head, divided into two parts. First, specifically explaining the entrustment.
Furthermore, there are three [points]. First, the entrustment by the Tathāgata.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha—[omitting the intervening text]—caused all sentient beings to hear and know it universally.

The supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) described in the preceding chapter was for the purpose of gladdening sentient beings and enabling them to achieve the joy of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*); therefore, he manifested himself seated upon his throne.

This reveals the sovereign nature of the fruit-body. Now, for the sake of entrustment and circulation, although this constitutes the accomplishment of a Bodhisattva’s own practice, it is nonetheless the Buddha’s own business to ensure the continuity of the life of wisdom; therefore, he rises from his seat and again manifests his supernatural power.

Zhizhi says: "Raising the hand symbolizes the provisional (expedient means), while stroking the crown of the head symbolizes the real. Relying upon the provisional power of all Buddhas, [the real is] revealed."

The reality of intrinsic nature thus accords with the intent of universal circulation. Raising one hand to universally stroke the crowns of the heads of immeasurable bodhisattvas is a great supernatural power;

this is the Tathāgata’s empowerment through the activity of body (*kāyakarman*). The above constitutes the narrative framework provided by the scribe of the sutra, serving as the basis for the conclusion and verification in the "Dharma-preacher" chapter (*dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*) regarding the case of the Tathāgata stroking their heads with his hand.
The second says: "For immeasurable kalpas, I have practiced this dharma that is difficult to obtain;
I now entrust it to you. This is empowerment through the karma of speech. The third says: "You should with one mind propagate this dharma and cause it to increase extensively.
This is empowerment through the karma of mind. This concluding testimony of the "Dharma Master" chapter constitutes the Tathāgata’s [empowerment].
This is the case regarding the entrustment of the Tathāgata’s work; it is precisely these three points that are empowered.

One sees therein the full unfolding of the Tathāgata’s great compassion, manifesting as both lack of parsimony and fearlessness. [△@△] Upon careful reflection on the words of this entrustment, he says:
"For immeasurable eons, I have cultivated this dharma so difficult to obtain. Within this, there are hardships and sufferings that I cannot bear to describe in detail."
Was it only at the abode of the Rishi Asita that he endured suffering for a thousand years, or was it when, as Sadāparibhūta, he practiced the Way for hundreds of millions of kalpas?
One must know that throughout kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, he sacrificed his body and life;

furthermore, how could there have been even a space the size of a mustard seed in this Sahā world where he did not do so? All of this was solely because of the difficulty of attaining this Dharma. Now, by means of this difficulty—

"This Dharma that has been attained is entrusted to you. You should simply reflect upon your own diligent efforts and the difficulty of its attainment; you should likewise consider my own diligent efforts and the difficulty of its attainment.
Will you not then exert your full strength to propagate it? This constitutes the most earnest and poignant of the Buddha’s exhortations to Upariṣṭa and the others.
Furthermore, observe that at the beginning it says, "Extensively cause it to increase," and at the end it says, "Cause all..."
Sentient beings everywhere hear and know this. Furthermore, this demonstrates the utmost urgency with which our Buddha does not abandon even a single sentient being.
Readers should feel profound shame and remorse.
"Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata possesses great compassion" (extending to) "do not give rise to stinginess.
This is precisely the meaning of the entrustment (*parindanā*). From "Why is this so?
down to "great donor," the Buddha cites his own grand character as the primary principle, teaching that one should practice by emulating his conduct. Zhizhi says: "Great Compassion."

Compassion is the Tathāgata’s chamber; one should give rise to two kinds of mind as described in the "Chapter on Peaceful Abiding" (Anraku-hon). Freedom from stinginess and parsimony is the Tathāgata’s robe;
one should act according to the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (Hōben-hon), for if one were to convert others by means of the Lesser Vehicle, one would fall into stinginess and greed.
Fearlessness is the Tathāgata’s seat; one should preach this sutra with a fearless mind, as stated previously. Tiantai says: "The Buddha’s wisdom..."
This is the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). It is the Tathāgata’s wisdom. It is the wisdom of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*).
It is spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*). It is the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Within the Tathāgata’s chamber, he is able to bestow these three kinds of wisdom upon sentient beings;
even within his seat, he likewise knows this. Thus, within the robe, the seat, and the chamber, each possesses the three wisdoms. By means of these three matters, [he] propagates...
"By means of the sūtra, one benefits others, causing them each to attain the function of the three wisdoms of the stage of fruition. The passage beginning with "You all...
is the entrustment [of the teaching], exhorting you to emulate the aforementioned practices and so forth to bring universal benefit. First, it says "you should learn," and again, "do not be stingy.
Such an entrustment may indeed be called most earnest.
"If in future ages there should be good sons (or even down to) ... they will have already repaid the kindness of all Buddhas.
This is a formal entrustment for circulation in future ages. Tiantai says: "If their roots are deep and their wisdom sharp..."
I shall speak directly of the Buddha’s wisdom. If you are not yet capable of receiving it, I shall instruct, benefit, and gladden you through other profound teachings.

The Buddha’s wisdom is profound, whereas other teachings are not; skillful means are "other," but not profound; the sequential teaching of the Separate Vehicle (Bie-jiao) is both "other" and profound.
If you can employ these other profound teachings to assist in proclaiming the Buddha’s wisdom, that is skillful repayment for the Buddha’s kindness.
This is called the "Instruction and Entrustment. It corresponds to the case of the entrustment found within the "Chapter on the Completion of the Jeweled Stūpa.
2. The Bodhisattvas Receive [the Teaching].
At that time, the various Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas... (up to)... "So be it, World-Honored One; may you have no further concern."

Tiantai says: Since the Buddha has entrusted [the Dharma] through his three karmas, the Bodhisattvas also receive it through their three karmas. Uttering voices together is receiving it with the mouth;
bowing the body and so forth is receiving it with the body; and rejoicing is receiving it with the mind. "As the World-Honored One has commanded" refers to this.
"Receiving [the teaching] from the Tathāgata, the Great Donor," refers to entering the room.

"One who fully practices and receives the instruction without any stinginess or parsimony," refers to putting on the robes. "Vowing not to have any anxieties," refers to receiving the instruction that there is nothing to fear and thus sitting upon the seat.
These two gates—the fundamental and the phenomenal—of this sutra repeatedly teach people to make vows and attain universal penetration.
The sutra states: "The intent is that the Great Dharma is difficult to practice and people are likewise difficult to lead to faith.
Who can awaken to this wondrous Dharma, penetrating from antiquity to the present? Who can use this wondrous Dharma to benefit others and oneself?

For forty years, with a heart of blood and bitter words, I have labored until, at the assembly of the Lotus Sutra, those who first turned their minds toward this Dharma gate were found. Once they were able to believe and accept it," [the Buddha spoke thus].
