This sutra can greatly benefit all sentient beings—[up to: like a merchant who has reached the ocean, or like a torch that dispels darkness.
Daokuan said: "This sutra is an inexhaustible treasury; therefore, it can benefit all sentient beings.
This sutra is like a cool pond, enabling those who are parched and exhausted to all obtain the supreme flavors of ambrosia and clarified butter, so that their entire bodies are purified."
Because it is cooling, this sutra is like fire; it can cause the cold ashes and withered wood to burst forth into the flames of wisdom.
Because it provides adornment where there is no merit, this sutra is like clothing; it enables those who lack adornments to don the raiment of the Tathāgata.

Because it provides refuge where there is no protector, this sutra is like a master; it enables those without reliance to recognize the true Lord. Because it nurtures those who are weak and lost... [it is like a mother].
It is like a compassionate mother for those who, in a foreign land, do not know how to return home. This sutra is like a boat, for it can carry sentient beings to the other shore.
This sutra is like a physician, for it can heal the physical and mental illnesses of sentient beings. This sutra is like a lamp.

Because it can shatter the darkness of the long night of birth and death, this sutra is like a treasure. Because it can cause the destitute son to obtain whatever he requires as he wishes, this sutra is like a king.
Because one may rely upon the King of Great Vows amidst the sufferings of birth and death, this sutra is like the ocean.
Because one obtains the treasure of great wisdom within the sea of afflictions, this sutra is like a torch. Once the flame of wisdom is ignited, there is no...

This is because it clarifies that [suffering] is suddenly exhausted. [△@△] Indeed, this sutra’s great compassion is inexhaustible, and it likewise resides within the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*).

Once knowledge and vision are opened, what joy would not be complete? Not only do ordinary beings attain the bliss of liberation, but it also enables all sages to attain the unsurpassed, wondrous bliss of the Buddha-fruit. △ Third, the summary conclusion on the transcendence of suffering.
This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is also like this... [up to] ...it can untie all the bonds of birth and death.
This summarizes the two sublime functions of uprooting suffering and bestowing happiness. Daokuang says: "All sufferings" refers to the five signs of decay and the eight types of suffering.
"All illnesses" refers to the two illnesses of body and mind. "The bonds of birth and death" refers to the *pariccheda-vibhāga* (segmented) existence.
It is transformation. Although the above has employed various metaphors to clarify this Dharma, ultimately no analogy can reach it.
Thus, the Great Sūtra states: "O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata uses all manner of metaphors to explain various matters, yet there is no metaphor that can illustrate this Dharma.
Why is this? Because the paths of mind and intellect are cut off; it is inconceivable."
Therefore, although this concludes the extraction from suffering, when suffering is exhausted, bliss arises spontaneously; thus, the meaning of "bestowing bliss" is contained therein.
△ Third, the profound merit of upholding the sutra, divided into two parts. First, the merit obtained by hearing the entire sutra.
If a person hears this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the merit they obtain will likewise be immeasurable.
Although this passage mentions hearing the sūtra and transcribing it, it actually encompasses all six types of Dharma-preachers and ten kinds of offerings;
thus, it encourages the practice and upholding of this sūtra, for which the merit is immeasurable. This is expressed by saying that it is measured by the Buddha’s wisdom.
As for those who do not grasp its limits: it is not that there is nothing else; rather, the merit of this sutra is so manifest and immeasurable that it cannot be fathomed.
This does not mean that the Buddha’s wisdom fails to perceive it. *Campaka* means "golden flower" or "yellow flower.
*Sumana* means "flower that well-restrains the mind. *Pāṭala* means "reborn flower. *Vārṣika* means "rain flower," as it blooms only during the rainy season.
Therefore, it is further stated that "summer-blooming flowers" refers to *nāga* flowers, which means "variegated flowers," and *mallikā* flowers, which means "jasmine flowers.
It is also called "garlands" because these flowers can be made into garlands. Furthermore, oil is perfumed with flowers to extract their fragrance.
△ Second, citing the merit obtained from hearing this chapter, divided into two parts: 1. Estimating the magnitude [of the merit].
"O Rājakuśalagandha, if there is anyone who hears [this]... up to... being born upon a jeweled throne within a lotus flower.
This passage above clearly explains the merit of receiving, upholding, transcribing, and making offerings to the entire sutra;

it further uniquely reveals that the merit of hearing and upholding even a single chapter is likewise immeasurable. This is because this single chapter encompasses the entirety of the sutra, not merely one part.

The title of this chapter, "The Entire Scripture," refers specifically to the two characters *Bhaiṣajyarāja* (Medicine King); these two characters likewise encompass the entire scripture. The *Dàkuǎn* states:
"If there be anyone who hears [the following]" refers generally to all people; subsequently, it is specifically applied to women to illustrate the point.
Since the wisdom of women is inferior, those who are able to believe and uphold [this teaching] will immediately transform from female to male. Why is this? Furthermore, as for those who abandon...
To sacrifice one’s own arm is something that cannot be done by one who is not a great man (mahāpuruṣa) who has realized the emptiness of both self and dharmas.
Regarding the "final five hundred years," the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* states: during the first five hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, liberation will be firm;

during the second five hundred years, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) will be firm; during the third five hundred years, learning (*bahuśruta*) will be firm; and during the fourth five hundred years, merit (*puṇya*) will be firm.
The five types of strife will become firm; this refers to the final five hundred years. At this time alone, roots of goodness are rare.
If a woman is able to uphold [this teaching], she is indeed a great man and shall obtain exceptionally superior merit.
As for those who, at the end of life, are born in Sukhāvatī, it is because they have been able to renounce their most profound attachments to Saṃsāra.
They are no longer afflicted by desire (and so forth, until: all other adversaries are utterly destroyed.

Because they are born in a Buddha-land, they are far removed from the causes of birth within the triple world (*tridhātu*). They attain the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of a Bodhisattva; this indicates that these supernormal powers are not those of a minor fruit.

"Patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) refers to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*). As for "the purity of the faculty of the eye," it is because of the Buddha’s knowledge.
This is because they are seen to be opened and made clear. To say that one sees all Buddhas and hears all their voices is due to the power of upholding and expounding this sutra.
Thus, the fact that the power of the Dharma is so inconceivable is none other than because its essence exceeds that of a diamond (*vajra*);
neither water nor fire can alter its virtue. It is only able to destroy all demons, slay all thieves, and demolish all [obstacles].
The army has eliminated all enmity; therefore, it brings about the joint praise of the thousand Buddhas, which cannot be exhausted.
Good son, among the hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, there is no one whose wisdom and meditative concentration can equal yours.
One who upholds this sutra enters the chamber of the Tathāgata and sits upon the Tathāgata’s throne as a true son of the Buddha;
therefore, the Buddhas of the ten directions collectively protect them. The wisdom of such a person transcends the three realms, and thus worldly wisdom cannot compare to it.

When the provisional and the real are simultaneously integrated, even the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot equal them. Having attained the Supreme Vehicle, they cause even the Bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings to... [be surpassed].
They are able to be equal [to the Tathāgata]. One who is thus is protected by the Buddha through the power of upholding this sūtra; therefore, they are equal to the Tathāgata alone.
O Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, the merit obtained by this bodhisattva is as described above.
This Bodhisattva refers specifically to Bhaiṣajyarāja. One who has accomplished such merit is established as proof of the intention that the merit of upholding this chapter is inexhaustible.
This is because Bhaiṣajyarāja did not spare his own body or life for the sole purpose of circulating this sutra.
If a person can rejoice in and praise its excellence, then the wondrous lotus will blossom; thus, fragrance issues from their mouth.

It has emerged! If a person can hear this chapter and rejoice in it with sympathetic joy, their entire being will experience a sense of celebration and liberation, like the rare encounter with ox-head sandalwood.
If a person can give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy, they shall obtain all those dharmas that are difficult to attain.

Thus, from the pores of his body, such fragrance was produced. Although this body is impure, its ability to produce fragrance now is a testament to the Bodhisattva’s light regard for the body and profound esteem for the Dharma, as well as his overcoming of attachment. Furthermore, it is not merely that fragrance is produced;
he also attains all the various merits of a Bodhisattva mentioned above. (Supplementary Note: *Sūtra of King Aśoka*)
It is said that when King Aśoka invited the Saṃgha for a meal offering, there was a bhikṣu named Utpala whose mouth emitted the fragrance of an utpala flower.
The king suspected that the young bhikṣu was holding incense in his mouth and immediately ordered him to rinse his mouth with water.
After he had rinsed it, the fragrance became even more intense. The king asked, "How long have you been holding this fragrance? He replied, "I am not holding any fragrance. It is from my past..."
In the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, I served as a high-seat Dharma teacher and praised the Buddha-dharma.
Consequently, for forty-nine billion years, I was born among humans and devas, and this fragrance constantly issued from my mouth.
Having heard this, the King increased his reverence even further. Now, when he says "I rejoice" and praises what is good, the fragrance issues from his mouth; thus it is manifested.
This is the retribution. △ Second, the entrustment.
Therefore, from "O Śuddharaśmiprabha" (until) "the kumbhāṇḍas and others will find an opportunity.
The Tathāgata alone entrusts this chapter to those who are the appropriate recipients. In the age of the Dharma’s decay, only ascetic practice can fully preserve it.
By means of right livelihood, one attains faith and joy. In the final five hundred years, the times will be extremely evil; in Jambudvīpa, the people will suffer extreme misery.
It is solely because of this moving Buddha’s profound compassion that he specifically entrusts [this teaching].

Even among the evil Māras and their followers, there are those who do not wish for even a single phrase to be in accord with the Dharma. Many evil Māras, demons, and spirits do not desire what is correct, fearing that [the truth] might prevail.
Those who practice asceticism while propagating the True Dharma may be possessed by malevolent spirits; such harm is no small matter.
Therefore, I specifically entrust this to you.
“Sukhāvatīvyūha-rāja, you should, by means of your supernormal powers, [protect them] until their illnesses are extinguished and they attain neither aging nor death.
Previously, he entrusted me with a single chapter; now, he entrusts me with the entire sutra.

When it says “to protect by means of supernormal power,” it means that those practitioners shall achieve success without being aware of or knowing how it is accomplished. However, in the evil age, there are demons, ghosts, and the like who are not...
Furthermore, through the empowerment of the Bodhisattva’s supernatural powers, it is difficult for practitioners to encounter any obstacles.

This sutra alone is called the excellent medicine for the illnesses of the people of Jambudvīpa because the illness of the people of Jambudvīpa lies in their lack of faith, whereas this sutra can sever all doubts and give rise to all forms of faith. Their illness also lies in their lack of wisdom, and this sutra...
It enables one to awaken to and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. When the ailment lies in stubbornness and rigidity, this sutra teaches people to don the robe of patience.
When the ailment lies in indulging in various sensory desires, this sutra can uproot sentient beings from their attachments everywhere.
For anyone with such ailments, upon hearing this sutra even once, there is none that is not eliminated. Once the ailments are removed, the Dharma...
Their physical stature increases; therefore, they are said to be neither aging nor dying.
Suvikrāntavikramin, if you see anyone who receives and maintains this sutra (up to) filling a vessel with powdered incense and scattering it over them.
The previous teaching was intended to inspire respect for this sutra; the present teaching is to instruct one to make offerings to those who uphold the sutra.
To honor the person is truly to honor the Dharma. Flowers symbolize causes, while incense symbolizes virtues.
By scattering flowers laden with fragrance as an offering, one celebrates the fact that the causes and virtues of the sutra-upholder are fragrant.
Having scattered [the offerings], one should form this thought: "I shall deliver all sentient beings from the ocean of old age, sickness, and death.

One should instruct those present according to their capacities to make offerings; they must surely be pure both internally and externally. Externally, they offer incense and flowers; internally, they maintain sublime understanding.
May you not consider yourself a sage while regarding others as ordinary. You should know that for the upholder of this sutra, before long—
In this interval, one may enter the stream of the sages and realize Bodhi. To speak of taking grass and so forth is not only a matter of reaching the ultimate principle;
it is also the actualization of Equal and Perfect Enlightenment based upon concrete events.

For example, when the World-Honored One sat beneath the Bodhi tree upon a seat of auspicious grass (*śālistamba*) and attained the Way of the Buddha, his defeat of the demonic armies was an event that occurred prior to his final realization. [He then] turned the wheel of Dharma...

The turning of the Dharma wheel is an event that occurs after attaining the Way. Blowing the conch and beating the drum are means to summon the sentient beings of the nine realms and benefit them by preaching the Dharma.
Therefore, those who seek the Buddha-way (up to this point) should give rise to such a mind of reverence.
This is a summary exhortation to uphold [the teaching]. Previously, the entrustment was directed to a single individual; thus, it was for the purpose of respectful circulation.
Now, it is universally entrusted to all who seek the Buddha-way: if one sees anyone who receives and upholds this sutra, one should generate a mind of reverence as described above.
The formal answer is now concluded. △ Third, the benefits.
When this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja" was being preached—up to the point of the *dhāraṇī* of the speech of all sentient beings—the essential commentary states:

Upon joyfully seeing and hearing this sutra, one immediately attains the samādhi of manifesting the body; and after performing the self-immolation by burning the body, one immediately attains the *dhāraṇī* of speech.
This is because, having realized the Dharma-body and departed from all marks and views, one penetrates and accords with the wondrous perfection.
Thus, when he reached the point of burning his arm, he enabled the śrāvakas to attain the Samādhi of Manifesting the Physical Body. Now, to speak of this past event:
it was by awakening to the matter of burning his body and burning his arm that the Bodhisattva attained the dhāraṇī of understanding all languages.
This was because he was able to detach from all views and attachments, penetratingly realizing the wondrous perfection. This is what is meant by "through ascetic practice..."

This constitutes the attainment of perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*). Yet all have attained *samādhi*, and furthermore, those who have attained *dhāraṇī* attain the *samādhi* of manifesting their own bodies;
they divide their forms according to the species [of beings] and maintain mastery over speech, preaching the Dharma according to the species.

These two states are essentially mutually requisite, and both are realized through the wondrous Dharma; therefore, when the "Chapter on Wondrous Sound" was preached, the assembly of Bodhisattvas also attained this *samādhi*.
And the dhāraṇīs. △ Fourth, the conclusion and praise by Prabhūtaratna:
The Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, from within the jeweled stupa... benefits immeasurable all sentient beings.
The people of the末法 (mofa) age regard conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as supreme. The Tathāgata wishes for this sublime Dharma to circulate throughout the five turbidities;
it is only through ascetic practice that their minds can be easily aroused, and only through ascetic practice that their resolve can be firmly established.

Śrīkṣetra also knows that only this can be practiced in Jambudvīpa and can eliminate the habitual tendencies toward conditioned phenomena; therefore, he specifically entreated the Tathāgata to speak [of it].
This is the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-pūrvayoga*. It is intended to ensure the firm establishment and circulation of this newly recorded [text].

The Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna originally came to bear witness to the sutra; now, seeing the Elder King (Śubhavyūha) make such a request and the World-Honored One provide such a response, he further praises the excellence of the sutra and entrusts it for its circulation. Thus, eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas attained [realization].
That the Medicine King has attained this is entirely the achievement of his past sovereign merits; therefore, his goodness is extolled and his virtue is made manifest.
Were it not for long-term cultivation and actual realization, how could he have posed such questions and brought about such benefits?
The twenty-fourth chapter, "The Chapter on Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara," states:
This chapter specifically reveals the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra, which is the actual realization of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), the True Suchness (*tathatā*) of the level ground.

Having already attained this, he further realized the ninth stage (*bhūmi*), manifesting the great function of *tathatā* (suchness). With mastery over both form and mind, he attained the *māyopama-samādhi* (illusion-like samādhi) and occupied the rank of Dharma Master.
Upon reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samāpatti-bodhi*), he manifested emanations to preach the Dharma; for this reason, he was specifically named "Wondrous Sound" (*Ghoṣa*).

As for the Tathāgata’s emission of the two lights from the fleshly protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) and the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*) at this point: the protuberance is the mark of the crown of the head.
The "manifestation" represents the fruit, while the "hair" represents the cause; because the present cause and fruit are in accord with realization, they are symbolized by these two lights.

Since the *ālayavijñāna* is utterly purified, the land is named Pure Light (*Vimalaprabhā*). Because pure wisdom accords with the fruit, the Buddha is titled Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom (*Vimalapuṣpasūryarājajñāna*).
Furthermore, the bodhisattvas of this stage are wondrously in accord with the Buddha-mind; through making offerings to the Buddha, they attain [merit] as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
Samādhi. By means of the fruit, one returns to the cause; thus Śākyamuni’s light illuminates his body, manifesting function from essence.
Therefore, he vows to go to the Sahā world to perform all Buddha-works through the wondrous power of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
Thus, without rising from his seat, by the power of samādhi, he magically creates various precious lotus flowers, intending to manifest the re-establishment of the true cause. From this stage...
The Bodhisattva’s pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; he is able to transform afflictions into sublime practices.
Therefore, he arrives surrounded by eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas. Because the cause accords with the fruit, he pays his respects to the World-Honored One.
Because he wondrously accords with the Dharma-body, he meets with Prabhūtaratna. Furthermore, this sutra establishes its substance through wisdom; it was initially initiated by Mañjuśrī.

Therefore, awakening is the fruit while the mind is the cause. Now that he has realized True Suchness (Tathatā) and yet beholds Mañjuśrī, it is only then that the beginning and the end accord, and cause and effect correspond in mystery. Thus, his ability to manifest a body and preach the Dharma is indeed fitting.
Furthermore, one must understand that the manifested body is the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) which realizes the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*).
This is distinct from the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Avalokiteśvara mentioned later. Because this [body] enters and emerges from *samādhi*, it manifests the appearance of coming and going.
As for the universal gate manifestations (*samantamukha-nirdeśa*) of Avalokiteśvara, however, they are all-pervasive. Those who observe should understand this point. *Yaojie* (Essential Explanation).

Regarding the one named "Wonderful Voice" (Ghoṣadatta): he has deeply realized the wondrous Dharma and is able to expound it with a wonderful voice according to the needs of beings, thereby circulating this Way.

Although his name is "Wonderful Voice," his reality manifests wonderful conduct. Observing how he planted the causes in the past at the abode of the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Sound King (Meghasvararāja), he offered music and presented an alms-bowl, aspiring to have a wonderful voice for preaching the Dharma and to follow in wonderful conduct.
It is so. Therefore, the Buddha Śākyamuni was born in the land of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna; he is indeed able to possess such supernatural power.

Now, in order to cause practitioners to embody his wondrous conduct and preach the Dharma according to their needs, thereby propagating this Way, the "Chapter on the Wondrous Sound" is taught for the circulation of wondrous practice.
Indeed, by embodying the wondrous sound, one does not become obstructed by verbal expressions; by being able to respond accordingly, one is not limited [by form].
The traces of the mind are neither stagnant nor restricted; this is why they constitute wondrous practice (*miao-xing*).

Following this, there are further the practices of perfection (*yuan-xing*) and constancy (*chang-xing*), which succeed the aforementioned ascetic practice (*ku-xing*). One who wishes to achieve virtue through practice must first refine the mind and exert bitter resolve;
only then can one attain the wondrous. Only after attaining the wondrous can one achieve perfection; only after achieving perfection can one truly enter into accord (*zhen-qi*). △ Two: Clarification.

The Wondrous Sound comes and goes, exhorting the disciples to receive and study [the teaching] so that it may be widely circulated. This is divided into six parts. First, the Emission of Light to Summon from the East:
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha emitted the light of the mark of a great man (up to) the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*), whose radiance shone everywhere throughout that land.
"At that time" refers to the period after the Tathāgata had spoken the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-pūrvayoga* and was about to summon Gadgadasvara to this place.
From this point until the passage where Mañjuśrī asks the Buddha what karmic conditions have caused these preliminary auspicious signs to appear, all is the text compiled by the sūtra-reciters.
Regarding the Buddha’s special emission of light from the *uṣṇīṣa*, it was by means of that pure light...
In the land of Śobhavatī, the Buddha’s body was six million eight hundred thousand yojanas in height, and the bodies of the bodhisattvas were forty-two thousand yojanas.
Although their physical dimensions were thus immense, they did not at all transcend the light of the Tathāgata’s marks of a great man.
Furthermore, because the Buddha wished to demonstrate to people the great fruit realized by the bodhisattvas, he emitted light from between his eyebrows.
This is intended to demonstrate to others the great causes cultivated by Bodhisattvas. Previously, the first light illuminated eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction;
this was intended to cause the śrāvakas who abide in silence to shatter the aggregates (skandhas) and the elements (dhātus).
Now, these second lights illuminate hundreds of eight million billion nayutas of Buddha-lands in the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.

This Bodhisattva who wishes to uphold this sutra must first exhaustively destroy ignorance as vast as the sands of the Ganges before they can reach the World Adorned with Pure Light and realize the Single True Dharma-realm. The Buddha there is named Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom;
it is by purifying attachment to dharmas that one attains conduct free from defilement and wisdom free from clinging, thereby becoming a Buddha of the Dharma-body and Wisdom.
The light of Śākyamuni illuminates that land. One aspect signifies that the ultimate fruit is equally realized;
the other reveals that the World-Honored One’s radiance is vast and inconceivable. Tiantai says: "The marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa) constitute an ocean of great marks.
The merit of all the body hairs does not equal the merit of a single secondary mark (anuvyañjana); the merit of all the secondary marks does not equal [the merit of] one..."
Regarding the merit of the marks: the various marks, progressing from the lower upward, each surpasses the preceding one; yet they do not equal the merit of the *ūrṇā* (white tuft of hair).

The *ūrṇā* does not equal the merit of the *uṣṇīṣa* (fleshly protuberance on the crown). Now, emitting the supreme light from the top of his head, he summons his original disciples to clarify the most ultimate and wondrous Dharma.
This mark of the *uṣṇīṣa* is obtained through filial obedience toward teachers and elders; [likewise is] the *ūrṇā*.
It is attained through the purity of a single path. Now, he emits this light for the purpose of causing this Dharma to be propagated.

Question: The Buddha has disciples who fill the ten directions; why does he merely emit light to summon Wondrous Sound from the east and speak of Avalokiteśvara of the west, rather than addressing all eight directions?
Answer: This has a symbolic significance. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The sun..."
With what intention does the moon traverse Jambudvīpa? It is its desire to dispel the manifold darkness with its radiance. The east is where its light begins; the west is where it ends.
That which has a beginning and an end—can that be anything other than a sage? Those who have not yet resolved to attain awakening are caused to resolve upon it;
those who have not yet reached the ultimate goal are caused to reach it. As it is for one bodhisattva, so it is for all the assembly.
However, as it is in one direction, so it is in all directions. The Sage did not trouble himself with prolixity; by citing one, he encompassed all.

Therefore, he merely mentions the east and west. II. Receiving the Command to Come West. This section is divided into two parts. First, the circumstances for his departure, which further has five sub-sections.
First, the narrator describes [the Buddha’s] merit and wisdom.
"At that time, in the land of Universal Pure Light Adornment... (up to) they all fully accomplished profound wisdom.
From "At that time" downwards, it describes the countless Buddha-lands of Universal Pure Light Adornment; hence, it says "all.
From "There is one" downwards, it means that in each of those lands there is a single Body of Wondrous Sound to serve as the appropriate vessel for the teaching. This concludes the preceding section.
This merely describes the land where Gadgadasvara dwells and the teacher he serves; here, it specifically describes Gadgadasvara himself.
Since he has long planted roots of virtue and made extensive offerings to the Buddhas, it is evident that his merit is complete.
As his merit is complete, his wisdom is accordingly vast; thus it is said that he has "accomplished profound wisdom."
He attains the Samādhi of the Wondrous Banner Mark (up to) as many great samādhis as there are sands in the Ganges.

*Miaole* says: "Samādhi belongs to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). In contrast to wisdom (*prajñā*), it is termed 'merit' (*puṇya*). It is already distinct from the [other] three teachings; how could it be the same as what exists in the world?"
Furthermore, these sixteen [phrases] are all alternative names for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*. The word "attainment" (*pratilambha*) applies universally across the sixteen phrases;
it signifies actual realization. The *Yinzhi* (Sound-Knower) says: "This is also brought about by the fulfillment of both merit and wisdom.
Below, the scriptural text itself contains sixteen sections that explain and allow one to see the reality of this samādhi. Otherwise, this section would be in vain.

The literal meaning of the characters [in the title] has no bearing on the significance [of the content]. These sixteen are the primary ones; since there are many other samādhis besides them, the word "etc.
(等) is used. The *Yāojie* (Essential Explanation) states: "Samādhi" is here translated as "right concentration" (正定), and it is also called "right reception" (正受).

This refers to the dharma experienced within right concentration. As for "the mark of the wondrous banner" (妙幢相), it signifies the subduing of the heterodox to manifest the orthodox, yet without abiding therein.

This is the mark (*lakṣaṇa*). The supplementary note states: "The essence of the three thousand [realms] is quiescent; vertically transcending all, it is a mark while being markless—this is named the 'Exquisite Banner Mark' (*Sudharmadhvaja-lakṣaṇa*).
The *Dharmapada-samādhi* (Lotus Samādhi) refers to deeply entering the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and realizing all true marks (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

The *Vimalaguṇa-samādhi* (Pure Virtue Samādhi) means that all virtues are truly pure, such that nothing can defile them. The *Rājanirghoṣa-samādhi* (King’s Play Samādhi) signifies the sovereignty of fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*).

There is no stagnation or attachment. "Sukhāvatīrāja" (宿王) is an alternative name for the Moon; through skillful means and wisdom, it illuminates the capacities of beings and adapts with exquisite artistry.
Thus, when there is no object of focus, illumination is eternally quiescent. It does not focus on the compassion of the partial or small vehicles that takes arising phenomena as its object;
rather, it focuses without focusing, for it focuses upon the great compassion of equality. As for the Seal of Wisdom, it integrates all phenomena—the single mind and the threefold wisdom.
It is so called because it seals all dharmas. "Understanding all languages" means realizing that all are true teachings.
"Gathering all merits" means the perfection of the myriad virtues; as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to gather the merits of all samādhis.
"Pure Samādhi" means that not even a speck of dust can stand; the six sense faculties are free from defilement.
Because they exercise mastery in mutual application, those who sport with supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) possess sovereign power over transformations and manifestations.

They exercise sovereign power in transforming sentient beings, roaming through all worlds as if in child’s play. Because it can destroy the darkness of ignorance, the torch of wisdom (*prajñā-ulkā*) is like a lamp that dispels the dark;

thus, the Great Equal Wisdom is like a torch that removes darkness. Because it universally encompasses sublime conduct and is inherently endowed with myriad virtues, the King of Adornments (*vyūha-rāja*)... [is so called]. Regarding conditions (*pratyaya*)...
"Perfected Adornment" refers to the mastery of unimpeded integration. "Pure Radiance" refers to the attainment of the illumination of wondrous wisdom;

as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the defilements of any other samādhis. Furthermore, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "Among all phenomena, one perceives no defilement.
"Pure Treasury" refers to the attainment of the treasury of the Dharma-eye, wherein a single thought-moment of pure mind is fully perfected.
The merit of the provisional and the ultimate encompasses all things; thus it is "unshared," meaning that the two vehicles cannot attain it.

"The revolving sun" refers to the universal illumination of the great trichiliocosm; because true wisdom relies upon emptiness yet does not dwell in emptiness, one attains such samādhis as are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—meaning they interpenetrate and harmoniously encompass one another in infinite layers—all of which are possessed by the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound.

It is because they possess these qualities that they are able to accomplish sublime practice and circulate the sublime Dharma. △ Second, the passage concerning being illuminated by the Original Teacher:
"The light of Śākyamuni Buddha shone upon their bodies" (extending to) Bodhisattva King of Adornment and Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja.
The arrival of Gadgadasvara was sent by the Buddha himself; were it not for the Tathāgata’s light reaching him, he could not have proceeded to this Sahā world.
Thus we know that Gadgadasvara’s coming and going occurred entirely within that light.

Although it is said that he passed through worlds as numerous as the sands of eight hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges Rivers, in reality he did not depart from this single ray of light. Therefore, Gadgadasvara is...

This is the primordial existence within a single ray of light. From this context, the phrase "Śākyamuni’s light shines upon his body" is extracted specifically to make people know that there is a source; yet many people overlook it—who can be blamed for this?

Once the wondrous sound has been produced and he addresses the Lord, it signifies that wondrous practice is about to arise, which is the functioning arising from the essence. Since it says "having gone,"...
"Approaching" means drawing near. "Immovable yet moving" refers to making offerings to Śākyamuni; this is the practice returning to its essential nature.
The arrival of Gadgadasvara signifies that perfect practice has been accomplished. Furthermore, the mention of seeing Mañjuśrī indicates the fulfillment of wisdom-practice.

Bhaiṣajyarāja represents the capacity of practice to universally heal, while Śūradatta symbolizes the flourishing of myriad practices. Rājanirghoṣa... [text ends]... represents the King of Constellations.
The Flower is the essence and function of Suchness (tathatā). The King of Adornment is the true cultivation of wondrous conduct.
By means of supreme practice, he universally delivers sentient beings; his medicine is unsurpassed. This is the fundamental aspiration of the Lord of Wondrous Sound and Speech.
△ Third, the Teacher’s admonition not to harbor disparaging thoughts.

At that time, from the passage concerning the Buddha Śubhavyūha-rāja-saṃkusumitābhijña up to the point where it says, "If one conceives thoughts of inferiority regarding the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or their lands," this is the instruction and command of our Original Teacher;
it is intended to encourage diligent and focused practice. Tiantai said: "However, Miaoyin (Gandhahastin) is a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body;

therefore, he accomplished his purpose without formal solemnity. Upon arriving here and seeing the impurity [of the land], how could he have conceived thoughts of inferiority? Or perhaps [the text] fears that he might have done so."

The realized ones, therefore, rely upon that [the external] to regulate this [the internal]. Now, the Buddha-body corresponds to the principle; one must not see its humble form and thereby forget its majesty.
This is the admonition regarding the Tathāgata’s seat. Furthermore, both teacher and disciple are fully endowed with wisdom and the severance of afflictions;
since the teacher has manifested skillful means (*upāya*), the student should conceal the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). This is the admonition regarding the Tathāgata’s robe.
Furthermore, the circumstantial retribution (niśraya-vipāka) is that which is evoked by the primary retribution (mūla-vipāka).

As the Tathāgata’s compassion extends throughout the trichiliocosm, it is appropriate to attend both to the high and the low; one must not observe the circumstantial while neglecting the primary. This is an admonition regarding the "Tathāgata’s Chamber.

[△@△] Since the signs of movement have arisen and activities have become boundless, the Master’s instruction is especially weighty at the time of departure. Moreover, the Tathāgata has emitted rays of light.
This was originally intended to encourage the true cultivation of disciples; thus, the wondrous sound was suspended and proclaimed for the sake of circulation.
In the circulation of the wondrous Dharma, one must not discriminate between people based on their nobility or meanness, nor speak of distinctions of high or low regarding their dwellings.

If the sentiments of purity and impurity are not forgotten, the mind of "self" and "other" will immediately arise. If one's own practice is not perfected, how can one widely benefit others? Therefore, the Wise One...
The Buddha cautioned them, saying, "Do not hold it lightly. From "Good sons" downward, he separately explains that one must not disparage the *parivṛtti-āśraya* (the dependent retribution).

From "The Buddha’s body" downward, he separately explains that one must not disparage the *mūla-āśraya* (the primary retribution). From "But your own body" downward, he uses that [example] to manifest this [point]. Therefore, the Tathāgata manifests the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
When the Wisdom-Buddha speaks of the marks of a Great Man, his general intent is to cause both the great and the small to be forgotten; only then can the teaching be propagated.
[End of section]. △ Fourth, receiving the mandate and relying on the power of the teacher:
Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound addressed his Buddha, saying... [up to] "...the adornment of the Tathāgata’s merit and wisdom."
The Original Teacher taught this by way of the admonition not to underestimate either the physical environment or its inhabitants.
Yet, when Gadgadasvara said, "That I have now come to the Sahā world to approach Śākyamuni and see Mañjuśrī and the others is not by my own power, but by the power of the Tathāgata;

every step of my journey today has been undertaken solely by relying on the Tathāgata’s playful manifestation of supernatural powers," he demonstrated that once one has attained the Buddha’s playful mastery, how could it be otherwise?
When the unevenness of high and low enters my eyes, even my own body of forty-two thousand yojanas is likewise adorned by the merit and wisdom of the Tathāgata.

Having attained the adornment of the Buddha’s wisdom, how could the inferior and small forms of those Buddhas and Bodhisattvas further obscure my mind? One must know that this is the second [mark] of the Tathāgata.
The name [of this Bodhisattva] is the very mastery by which Wondrous Sound is able to enter the Sahā world.
Thus, although he manifests in various forms and preaches various dharmas, all of these do not depart from the reality of suchness. △ Fifth, the actual manifestation of his arrival.
It is divided into six parts. First, the dispatching of Padmaśrī.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, without rising from his seat... [using] *cāmpeya* flowers and *vaiḍūrya* jewels as its pedestal.
The *Zhiyin* (Sound-Knower) commentary states: This section describes the arrival of Gadgadasvara. It explains the first [samādhi], the "Exquisite Banner" (*Sudhvaja-lakṣaṇa-samādhi*).

Because "exquisite" (*miao*) refers to the Exquisite Mind (*miaoxin*), and because a "banner" (*dhvaja*) possesses the function of suppressing the heterodox and assisting the orthodox, it uses the lotus flower to symbolize its characteristic.
From the words "Thereupon" (*yúshì*) below, the formal manner of entering samādhi is indicated, clarifying the relationship between Gadgadasvara and Śākyamuni.
The Dharma-body is seen through its characteristics: namely, that while remaining unmoving, it ascends and pervades all dust-motes and lands simultaneously.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "A bodhisattva, while in a single Buddha-land, hears the Dharma and receives and upholds it;

without his body moving, by the power of samādhi, he manifests his presence in every location within unspeakably many assemblies of Buddhas, yet he does not arise from meditative concentration, and in each instance he produces [transformations]..."
One may speak of the body of samādhi. In this sequence, all lands are inexhaustible; such is the case.
By means of the power of the samādhi below—namely, the power of the Samādhi of the Wondrous Banner Mark—it can render the distant near.
Therefore, although [the Buddha] was outside worlds as numerous as the sands of eight million billion nayutas of Ganges Rivers, he was not far from the Dharma-seat on Vulture Peak.

It is able to manifest precious lotus flowers. Regarding the statement that there are eighty-four thousand [petals], one meaning is that this expands the capacity of the mind to accord with the numerical categories of the Dharma-gates;
another is that it shows how numerous the followers of the Dharma of Wondrous Sound (Ghoṣadatta) are.
Below the section on Jambudvīpa, the characteristics of these flowers are described. On the banks of the Jambu River in the Western Regions, there is this *candana* tree which drips...
When water enters the earth, the soil turns the color of gold; other golds, being of inferior kind, lose their luster and appear like ink.
This is the most excellent. As for "vajra" (diamond), it is formed from gold and possesses the dual meanings of hardness and sharpness; being hard, no object can destroy it.
If it is beneficial, it can destroy all things. *Cintāmaṇi* (甄叔迦) is translated here as "parrot-beak.

The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that there is a *cintāmaṇi* tree whose flowers are red and as large as a hand; this jewel resembles them. The "platform" refers to the central platform within the lotus flower.
However, when Miaoyin (Wonderful Sound) was about to arrive, this sign first appeared; it corresponds precisely to this sutra.
Therefore, in the following section, Mañjuśrī asks for what reason this auspicious omen has appeared. The Buddha answers that it is because they are listening to the Lotus Sūtra;
its meaning is thus clear. △ Second, Mañjuśrī asks about the omen.

At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, [proceeded] until he reached a dais made of *cintāmaṇi* and *vaiḍūrya* and *jāmbūnada* gold and *candana* wood, with a pedestal of *kiṃśuka* and *tāla* wood, and a base of *gośīrṣa* sandalwood and *uragasāra* sandalwood, adorned with *vaidūrya* and *sphaṭika* gems, and a platform of *cintāmaṇi* and *vaiḍūrya*.

Seeing these signs, Mañjuśrī posed a question in order to inquire about the purpose of Gadgadasvara’s arrival, thereby eliciting what Gadgadasvara had been harboring within him. △ Third, the Tathāgata’s response.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha (up to) also desired to make offerings and listen to the Lotus Sūtra.

The Commentary on the Sounds of Wisdom states: "Although this section consists of a question and answer following the previous section, in reality it concerns the Samādhi of the Auspicious Banner Mark."
This demonstrates the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*. [△@△] However, Mañjuśrī acts as the questioner for the sake of all people in order to manifest this samādhi;
this clarifies that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* cannot be brought to ultimate completion unless one possesses fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). △ Fourth, Mañjuśrī requests to see [the Buddha].
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: [up to] "May that Bodhisattva come so that I may behold him.
This section constitutes the questions and answers resulting from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, demonstrating the third, the *Vimalaguṇa-samādhi*.

Now, "purity" (*vimala*) refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which is inherently undefiled; "virtue" (*guṇa*) refers to the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), as well as their physical forms and majestic deportment.
These are all the merits inherently possessed within the Dharmakāya. When Mañjuśrī asks, "What roots of goodness have been planted?
he intends to reveal for the sake of others that the purity of the Dharmakāya is itself the root of all virtues. When he asks, "What merits have been cultivated?
he likewise means that the practices arising from this pure Dharmakāya constitute the accomplishment of merit. And thus, one is able to...
One who possesses such supernormal powers (abhijñā) is endowed with the roots of goodness and merits described above;
only then can they transform the distant into the near and the non-existent into the existent, manifesting various lotus flowers and thereby accomplishing these supernormal powers.

Mañjuśrī further asked for the name of the samādhi, to which [the Buddha] replied that he wished to follow the name "Pure Virtue" (viśuddhaguṇa) in order to enter the reality of Pure Virtue and practice accordingly.
May we thus achieve resonance of like sounds, so that we may perceive the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) manifested by the wondrous voice.

Since physical characteristics and the like belong to the retribution-body (*vipākakāya*) and the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), [the text] says "I only pray," meaning that it is the very body of the Bodhisattva;

were it not for the empowerment of the Buddha’s power, one would likewise be unable to see it. As the ancients said: "Within the shadows of the colored clouds, the immortal appears, holding red gauze in his hand."
The fan covers his face. You must urgently look at the seer; do not look at the fan in the seer’s hand.
Now, when Mañjuśrī seeks to see Gadgadasvara, he inquires after both his physical appearance and its dimensions.
This indicates that he does not merely wish to see the seer, but desires to see the fan as well. [△@△] Mañjuśrī does not mean that he himself has not seen it, yet he insists on seeking it out.

[The Buddha] saw this. His intention was to alert those who have not yet realized this principle so that they might advance toward it. He asked what roots of goodness were planted, what meritorious deeds were cultivated, and what samādhis were practiced;
he intended to gauge the extent of their inclinations and how they were able to possess such great supernormal powers.
[He thought: "To what extent do we revere and look up to them? To what extent do we wish to diligently practice their path? To what extent do we feel inspired?"
How could this be Mañjuśrī clarifying his own quest? △ Fifth, attributing the merit to Prabhūtaratna:
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha... (until) "he shall manifest his form for you all."
○ When Mañjuśrī requested the Buddha to manifest a sign, the Buddha did not personally command him, but instead deferred to the venerable Prabhūtaratna Buddha;
this was to demonstrate the fourth samādhi, the "Play of the Constellation King. △ Sixth, the Ancient Buddhas Exhorting Action.
At that time, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna addressed those bodhisattvas... [down to] Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, saying, "I wish to see your body.

O Pure Light Adornment, although you are separated from this Sahā world by a distance of one hundred and eight million *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sands of lands, since you have already entered meditative concentration there, how easy it is for me to summon you here with a single voice!
How near! What is this if not the *Vyūharāja-samādhi*? There is further explanation for this: the World-Honored One did not summon the practitioner himself;
previously, he summoned him with light, and as the lotus appeared simultaneously, it was clear that Subhūti had already arrived.
Now, Mañjuśrī wishes to cause him to see the physical body (*rūpakāya*) once more. If it were not for the summons by the Ancient Buddha, from where would the physical body come?
It can be seen. Therefore it is said: "Mañjuśrī wishes to see your body.

Yet, when Mañjuśrī wishes to see Gadgadasvara, this is wisdom (*jñāna*) without practice (*caryā*), which is not manifest. When Gadgadasvara wishes to see Mañjuśrī, this is practice without wisdom, which does not proceed.
△ Second, the actual arrival. This is divided into six parts. First, the principal figure and his retinue arrive together:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara vanished from that land (until) hundreds of thousands of celestial musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.
This demonstrates the fifth, the objectless samādhi (*anālambana-samādhi*). Regarding "objectless": it is so called because it does not take any objects as its focal point.
If there were an object, how could one disappear from that and emerge here?

Furthermore, how could it cause all the bodhisattvas to come forth together, and how could it cause the flowers to rain down of their own accord, the ground to move of its own accord, and the various musical instruments to play spontaneously?
Ah! Only now do I realize that the power of unconditioned compassion covers all living beings, like the reflection of the moon appearing upon the waters of a thousand ravines.
△ Second, the description of ascending the platform:
This Bodhisattva’s eyes were like the broad petals of a great blue lotus flower... (omitted)... bowing his head to the Buddha’s feet and offering him a necklace.

This demonstrates the sixth, the Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom (Jñāna-mudrā). "Wisdom" refers to the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (Kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna) of the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, which corresponds to the Buddha’s Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (Pratyavekṣaṇa-jñāna). "Seal" means that the two wisdoms of the Buddha and the Bodhisattva mutually seal one another without alteration.
Furthermore, regarding the "Seal of Wisdom": when Gadgadasvara was about to come to this Sahā world, he manifested a lotus flower and offered a jeweled necklace.
He manifests various bodies and preaches various dharmas, having already caused eighty-four thousand who came to this assembly to all attain the Samādhi of Manifesting All Form-Bodies.
It is these immeasurable Bodhisattvas of this realm who have likewise attained this samādhi and dhāraṇī.
This is what is meant by: "The vast array and the myriad phenomena are all sealed by the One Dharma."
Regarding the passage "The Bodhisattva descends": this should correctly refer to Mañjuśrī’s desire to see the size and appearance of [the Buddha’s] physical form.

There are eight types [of comparisons]: first, eyes like the blue lotus (*utpala*). In India there is the blue lotus; its petals are long and broad, and the distinction between the blue and white is as clear as the shape of an eye.
Second, a face surpassing the full moon. The phrasing here seems inverted; it should rather be said that his countenance is upright and handsome.
Even if one were to combine hundreds of thousands of millions of moons and exceed this number, it would still be correct.

To take hundreds of thousands of millions of moons and condense them into a single month—this may be called vast—and yet to say that [Gandharva’s body] exceeds even this, shows that when the Wondrous Sound (Gandharva) came here, his body forty-two thousand *yojanas* in height remained unhidden; thus we further know the physical form described by Mañjuśrī’s question.
"Great or small—how could you not know this? he asked. "The three bodies are all golden in color. Yet, such a golden body is possessed only by a Buddha;
that the Bodhisattva now possesses it is precisely why he has attained the Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom (Jñānamudrā). His four bodies are fully adorned.
This adornment is not an external adornment of physical form, such as necklaces and the like; rather, it is the result of what was cultivated in the past."
The reply: It is adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of merits, just like the adornments of a Buddha. Its fivefold majestic power is blazingly intense;
that is to say, this Bodhisattva’s compassionate majesty encompasses and gathers all. That the lands of the countries he passes through all tremble is his "majesty" (wei).
That the heavens rain down jeweled flowers and various musical instruments sound of their own accord is his "virtue" (de). Having cited these, the rest may be inferred.
By analogy: sixth, the radiance of the six lights shines forth; this is not the emission of light, but rather the constant light inherent within the body of purple-gold.
Seventh, the various marks are fully complete; since it says "various marks" and also "fully complete," there must be the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics;
otherwise, what would it mean to be "fully complete"? Eighth, the physical body is firm and solid.
Generally, all physical bodies are subject to decay; yet this Bodhisattva’s body is like that of Nārāyaṇa.
Master Zao said: "Nārāyaṇa is the name of a powerful deity. He is upright and exceptionally beautiful, possessing peerless valor and strength, and his body is extremely firm.
The three phrases beginning with "He entered the seven-jeweled tower" and ending with "descended to observe and came here" refer to this tower.
This is not the same as the eighty-four thousand lotus pedestals manifested previously; moreover, what was called "cāmpeya" earlier refers to the seven treasures.
Alternatively, it may be that Miaoyin (Ghoṣadatta) vanished from that land and, together with the various bodhisattvas, mounted a seven-treasure pedestal.
Therefore, it is said that he "arrived at this Sahā world. That he was previously described as "entering the pedestal" and later as "descending from the pedestal" is sufficient evidence [of this].

Mañjuśrī’s inquiry regarding deportment and movement becomes even clearer. By using the term "price" (mūlya), it clarifies that with a most precious jewel one makes an offering to the Most Honored Buddha;

this signifies adorning the Dharmakāya with the Dharma-jewel. This precisely corresponds to the World-Honored One’s reply to Mañjuśrī, stating that one should make offerings to, attend upon, and prostrate before me. All of these matters are...
It does not emerge apart from the single dharma sealed by wondrous wisdom; therefore, it is called the Samādhi of the Wisdom-Seal Manifestation.

△ Third, inquiring after his health and transmitting the imperial decree, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... [omitted] ...are you at ease, with little affliction, and able to endure as you dwell long in this world?"
This demonstrates the seventh samādhi, "Understanding All Languages. He transmits the words of that land to inquire of the Buddha of this land;
yet these words of greeting are all the languages of sentient beings, which only Subhūti’s Wondrous Voice can understand.

Therefore, "few illnesses" refers to an inquiry concerning the body; "few afflictions" refers to an inquiry concerning the mind. "In your daily life" and below inquire whether the body is free from illness.
"Worldly affairs" and below inquire whether the mind is free from affliction. The above inquiries concern the teacher who is capable of instructing.

"Are you not burdened by many [tasks]" and below inquire whether the capacities of those to be converted are complete or not, and whether the various latent defilements (*anuśaya*) have been eliminated. "Are you not lacking in filial piety" and below inquire...
"Sentient beings' mundane affairs" refers to matters below [the level of] reverence. "Questioning sentient beings' supramundane affairs" refers to the ability to subdue those below.
"Questioning whether there are obstacles of Māra regarding the practice of the True and the Mundane for sentient beings" all concern Buddhas of the present life.
"Those long extinguished in Nirvāṇa" concerns the coming and going of past Buddhas. Furthermore, "inquiring after their welfare" also concerns past Buddhas.

Regarding the matter of body and mind, Tiantai states: "In this sutra, there are three instances where inquiries are made concerning illness and affliction. Former masters have explained these through three meanings:

first, to accord with the manifestation of transformation within the realm of common residence (*sahā-loka*), wherein the manifested birth-body (*janma-kāya*) shows itself to be identical to human phenomena;

second, regarding ritual propriety, as it is naturally so; and third, regarding the three bodies (*trikāya*), as it encompasses both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. This is as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra*.
It is said that the *Avataṃsaka* is the characteristic of arising of the Mahāyāna, while the *Nirvāṇa* is the characteristic of cessation of the Mahāyāna.

In the section on the "Peaceful Practices" (*Anurakṣita-caryā*), with the exception of the instances of "not filial" and "not respectful," all other occurrences of the character "不" (bù) are pronounced as "否" (fǒu).

From "no excessive greed and desire" up to the phrase "no stinginess and pride," the character "無" (wú) at the beginning of the sentence extends throughout the following text; that is to say, from no greed and desire, up to no stinginess.
"Is there no pride? Is there no lack of filial piety up to no wrong views?"—these three phrases, the word "no" (無), should also be read as applying throughout them;

that is, "is there no lack of filial piety," and so on, up to "is there no wrong view? The phrase "a single thought of a wholesome mind" subsumes the phrase "the five sensory faculties not being unified.
That which subsumes is the mental faculty (*manas*); that which is subsumed refers to the five sense organs, such as the eye and so forth. This means to gather and bring them to stillness.
"Quietude" means non-negligence (*apramāda*). "Peaceful and joyful practice" (*anurakṣa-pratipatti*): the character *xing* (practice) is pronounced in the level tone (*ping sheng*).

From the passage "Sentient beings are easy to deliver" onwards, all constitutes the Dharma taught by Gadgadasvara to the assembly on behalf of his inquiries. [Regarding the afflictions: greed, anger, ignorance, and pride.

The four dull afflictions (*mṛdu-kleśa*): envy (*īrṣyā*) and stinginess (*mātsarya*). The two secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*): false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). The one sharp affliction (*tīkṣṇa-kleśa*):
[the remaining] wrong views. The various *māras*: namely, the *kleśa-māra* and the *skandha-māra*. These are all that the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayānika*) cannot swiftly sever.
With these various obstacles, it is not easy to deliver sentient beings. Furthermore, the ten terms from "greed" (*lobha*) to "stinginess and pride" (*mātsarya-māna*) are...
In summary: lack of filial piety is anger (*dveṣa*), which is also an unwholesome mind; lack of respect is delusion (*moha*), which is driven by wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
The domination of the five senses is an abundance of greed and desire (*rāga*); failure to subdue the various Māras is the flourishing of stinginess and envy (*mātsarya-īrṣyā*).
These are all things to which the people of this Sahā world are habituated; therefore, Gadgadasvara borrowed [the power] from the Tathāgata.
The nostrils serve to expel breath for others. Furthermore, inquiring after the health of Prabhūtaratna as he listens to the Dharma serves as a reminder to people to listen attentively.

His enduring presence for a long time serves to dispel the weariness of others; by relying on this, he inspires them so that all sentient beings may each hear the wondrous sound and each understand the wondrous speech.

The twenty-fifth chapter, the "Universal Gate" (Pumenpin) of the Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, states in its commentary:
The intent of this chapter is that through the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra, the causal stage of initial awakening is perfected, thereby wondrously harmonizing with the ocean of the fruition.
Flowing against the current, they manifest clouds of bodies of the ten dharma realms, responding without thought.

These are what are called the bodies of the noble lineage, appearing simultaneously; this is precisely the manifestation of the "spontaneously born body of the same class that arises without volition."
Because the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) manifests through the eternal extinction of fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), it is called the "Universal Gateway Manifestation.

This is truly because the Great Being, by virtue of the power of the diamond-like samādhi (*vajra-samādhi*) and the permeation of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*) which are like an illusion at the initial stage, attains the manifestation of the cessation of birth-and-death and the quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*).

Thus, he transcends both the mundane and supramundane realms; above, he accords with the power of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and below, he harmonizes with the yearning for compassion (*karuṇā*). By means of this single [wisdom], he is able to...

His body universally responds to all, attaining three kinds of wondrous functions. Thus, there are the thirty-two manifestations, the fourteen fearlessnesses, and the nineteen modes of preaching the Dharma;
regarding the seven calamities and the two requests, there is nothing to which he does not respond.

This demonstrates the perfection of wondrous conduct and the accomplishment of the merits of the Lotus Samādhi. Wondrousness reaches its ultimate here; therefore, by means of the three kinds of intention—
This is the realization of virtue through the practice of the birth-body; the sacred intent is clear and can be seen through profound contemplation.

Nevertheless, although the wondrous practice is perfected, there remains the fear that the practitioner’s residual habits and the shadows of objective conditions may not be fully exhausted; thus, the three kinds of empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna) are further explained.
Only then can one achieve the wondrous fruit. Therefore, the text concludes with these three grades. Tiantai cites the *Bie xing xuán* (Profound Meaning of the Separate Practice), which states:
"Guanshiyin is the authentic name in the Western Land; it is called Āryāvalokiteśvara, which translates here as 'Observer of the World’s Sounds.
Subject and object are perfectly integrated, and both existence and non-existence are fully elucidated. It illuminates and exhausts the true nature, examining both the root and the branches."
Therefore, it is called "Contemplation" (Guān). "World-Sound" (Shìyīn) refers to the objects of contemplation. Myriad phenomena flow and change, separated and distinct;

though their sounds are diverse and their cries differ, all alike receive liberation from suffering. Through the Bodhisattva’s vast compassion, they are universally rescued at once, and all are led to deliverance. Hence, he is named Guānshìyīn.
This is an instance where both the object and the wisdom are raised together, and the subject and the object are designated as a pair. [The Universal Gate] (Pǔmén).
"Universal" (*pu*) has the meaning of pervasiveness. "Gate" (*men*) refers to that which enables passage. By employing the single reality-mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*), one opens the ten universal gates;
because there is no obstruction whatsoever, it is called the Universal Gate. This is the general explanation. The specific explanation consists of two types: the common and the particular.

The common explanation comprises ten pairs, while the particular explanation comprises five single items. Regarding the ten pairs: first, "person" and "dharma" serve as the names. In this chapter, there are two turns [of explanation].

Regarding the names derived from the questions and answers: "Person" refers to Avalokiteśvara, named according to the preceding dialogue; "Dharma" refers to the Universal Gate (Samantamukha), established according to the subsequent dialogue. Both are named after their compassion.

As for "Avalokiteśvara," it signifies great compassion that uproots suffering, based on the preceding dialogue, wherein hundreds of thousands of afflictions are all liberated. As for the "Universal Gate," it is [great compassion]... (Note:

"Both fulfilled. Regarding "Universal Gate" (Pumen): this reveals the performance of benefiting others; it refers to beholding the thirty-two bodies with the eyes and hearing the teachings of the nineteen honored ones with the ears.
Seventh, it is named according to the provisional and the real: "Avalokiteśvara" (Guanshiyin) refers to illuminating the realm of real wisdom according to one's own intent;

This is precisely the five-character exegesis of the Universal Gate (Pumen) of Avalokiteśvara. First, regarding "contemplation" (*guan*), there are also many types:

analytical contemplation (*xi guan*), essential contemplation (*ti guan*), sequential contemplation (*ci di guan*), and perfect contemplation (*yuan guan*). Analytical contemplation means extinguishing form to enter emptiness (*kō*).
Essential contemplation means that form itself is emptiness. Sequential contemplation proceeds from analytical contemplation up to perfect contemplation. Perfect contemplation...
This refers to analytical observation (*vibhajana-vipaśyanā*) up to sequential observation (*anupūrva-vipaśyanā*), all of which are the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Faculties: The faculties of the Tathāgata, and the faculties of humans and devas, consist in not committing any evil and practicing all that is good.

The faculties of Bodhisattvas consist in putting others before oneself and being compassionate, benevolent, and yielding. The faculty of the Buddha consists in entering into all phenomena through the contemplation of equality. One.
All are people who have transcended the world; there is but one path for escaping birth and death. Now, setting aside the previous three, we take only the capacity of the Buddha’s voice as our basis.

if one does not attain universality, it is a biased dharma. If a dharma is biased, how can it respond with perfect completeness? This is a brief summary.

The ten aspects of the universal illumination of the Dharma are: first, the universality of compassion; second, the universality of the great vows; third, the universality of cultivation; fourth, the universality of severing delusions; fifth, the universality of entering the Dharma-gates;
sixth, the universality of supernormal powers; seventh, the universality of skillful means; eighth, the universality of preaching the Dharma; ninth, the universality of maturing sentient beings;
and tenth, the universality of making offerings to all Buddhas. Having grasped this meaning, one should apply it analogously to all phenomena.
There is nothing that is not universal. This explains ten meanings, as detailed in the *Kezhu* (Sectional Commentary); they are not cited here at length. Fifth, regarding the "gates":

from the conventional entering emptiness, emptiness is pervasive while the conventional is obstructed; from emptiness entering the conventional, the conventional is pervasive while emptiness is obstructed.
If one is biased in their penetration, it is not universal; if one is obstructed, it is not a gate. The Middle Way is neither empty nor provisional;

it correctly penetrates the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) and simultaneously illuminates the two truths. Therefore, it is called the "Universal Gate" (*samantamukha*). 4. The Number of Persons. The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati: "Good son, if there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings.
This is the direct answer regarding causes and conditions. Tiantai says: "The capacities of the ten dharma realms are in fact immeasurable; yet it is said..."
"Hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis" does not mean that these numbers are common to all ten realms.

Rather, it refers to as many people as there are for a single karma—for instance, when those in a single hell collectively undergo one suffering, one may infer from that suffering that they share the same karma.
By analogy, this is the case for all other destinies as well. Thus, we know that these numbers are intended to indicate the shared nature of karma. This...
The multitude of capacities among those addressed is vast, thereby manifesting that the contemplation is profound and the response is great. [△@△] To cite several instances:
the phrase "if there be" is an indefinite expression; it may refer to one person, ten people, a hundred, a thousand, or even up to immeasurable people—this is the intended meaning.

This clarifies that they are currently beset by calamities and distress. Among them, there are those who possess many sufferings alone, those where many people undergo one suffering, those where one person undergoes many sufferings, and those where one person undergoes few sufferings. "If one hears of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and single-mindedly invokes his name..."

This refers to the intermingling of good and evil, which together constitute the "trigger" (the karmic condition). Through evil one encounters suffering; through good, one hears the name [of the Bodhisattva]. The *Dakuan* states:
"The two characters 'one' and 'mind' are the root for escaping calamity. This precisely means that when the mind is gathered into a single point, it is the very moment Avalokiteśvara appears.
For the Bodhisattva and sentient beings share the same essence, pervading all beings.
Within the minds of those who are born, the name of the Bodhisattva pervades the ears of all sentient beings;
yet, because they refuse to focus their minds with single-minded devotion, they follow after sounds and wander on, remaining separated from the Bodhisattva by a distance of a thousand li.

If one can invoke the name with single-mindedness, then Avalokiteśvara will not be far from that very place. If hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of suffering sentient beings were to do so together—
At that time, by single-mindedly invoking the name, they shall simultaneously be freed from all suffering and affliction. △ Fourth, Liberation:
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva immediately beholds their voices, and they all attain liberation.

Tiantai says: "The fact that hearing [the name] above immediately results in its being invoked shows that the capacity (ji) is swift; the fact that invoking it now immediately results in verification shows that the response (ying) is swift.

This also reveals the response that is perfectly pervasive. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"Immediately" means that at the moment one invokes my name with single-mindedness, without interruption or cessation, the four marks [of birth, abiding, change, and extinction] are simultaneously empty. It is not...

Would this not result in universal liberation? △ Second, the specific answer regarding liberation from suffering. This is divided into three parts.

The fire of karmic retribution ranges from the hells up to the first dhyāna; in all these realms, there is a blazing conflagration that none can escape.

That which can destroy the roots of goodness and cause one to fall back from higher states to lower ones is all termed "fire. The fire of afflictions pervades the three vehicles; the śrāvakas fear the [threefold suffering].

fire cannot burn them.
That it cannot burn is because when one calls upon the Name with a single mind, the fire of one's own mind is extinguished—how much more so for all other fires!
All objects arise from the mind; if the mind does not arise, delusive conditions naturally cease.
Yet, at the very moment of a raging, fierce fire, how many are there who can forget themselves within the realm of non-action, remaining neither startled nor terrified?
That one meets fire without being burned is due to the spiritual power of the Bodhisattva and the power of one’s own mental resolve. △

When the object reaches [the senses], the spirit is cast into it—this is the natural force of things. It is like seeing and loving: [if one sees the Buddha with love, one is not burned].

A red light appeared, and he was ultimately able to reach the shore; all of this was due to the appropriate application of spiritual power (*ṛddhi*). Regarding the explanation of the three contemplations:
as for the waters of karmic retribution, from the hells up to the second dhyāna, there is no one who can escape them. The waters of evil karma pervade the three realms;
various evils destroy wholesome karma, and all such things are termed the waves of evil karma. The waters of affliction (*kleśa*) likewise pervade the three vehicles. As for...
This refers to the great river of afflictions, which can sweep away even fragrant elephants; those blinded by ignorance cannot escape from it.

When Śrāvakas attain the second or third fruit, this is called a "shallow place"; for those beyond training (aśaikṣa), it is the "far shore. For Pratyekabuddhas, the attenuation of habitual tendencies constitutes the "shallow place."

In the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), the exhaustion of both active and latent afflictions constitutes the "other shore. In the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*), the severing of the four abiding delusions (*catur-vāsana*) is the "shallow stage," while the severing of ignorance (*avidyā*) is the "other shore.

In the Perfect Teaching (*pūrṇa-yāna*), the purification of the six sense faculties during the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) is the "shallow stage," while entering the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*) is the "other shore.
The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states: "Third, by observing hearing and causing it to turn inward, one enables the multitude who hold the Name..."
When born [in such a place], water cannot harm them. Yet water fundamentally belongs to the ears; it arises from what is heard. When there is craving, water is produced;
when there is anger, tears flow. By means of the Bodhisattva’s revolving away from the sound of hearing, those who invoke his name are freed from the peril of water.
△ Third, the peril of rākṣasīs.
"If there are hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, or billions of sentient beings" (up to) "for this reason he is named Avalokiteśvara.

Tiantai’s explanation of the objection also has three parts. First, the literal commentary: when entering the sea to seek treasures, one does not travel alone, though the number of companions is not fixed;
here, a general total is cited, simply stated as "hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, or billions. The phrase "for the sake of seeking" [refers to] what follows. It emerges.
Regarding the name by which he seeks [his goal], the character "equal" (等) encompasses all various treasures. As for "must enter the great ocean":

because the ocean is the gathering place of all treasures, the *Xiányújīng* (Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish) states: "Agriculture yields a hundredfold; commerce yields a thousandfold; official service yields ten thousandfold;
but entering the sea and returning safely yields immeasurable multiples. Therefore, one must certainly enter the sea. [△@△] Even if...
This refers to those who happen to encounter it by chance; it is not necessarily the case for all who enter the sea. This section should emphasize the two characters "black wind" (*kṛṣṇavāta*).
Following the previous accounts of water and fire, this corresponds to the peril of wind. Otherwise, it would be redundant with the previously mentioned peril of ghosts.
When encountering wind upon the great ocean, it is already most terrifying; how much more so when that wind is black, causing all who head toward it to lose their way.
One will undoubtedly end up falling into the realm of ghosts. Rākṣasas are ghosts that devour humans; they are even more terrifying than that.

Next, the text clarifies the capacity [of the name]: it means that precisely at a time of great terror, if among a multitude of people even a single person invokes the name, then everyone shall be spared from this harm. Is this not due to the majestic power of the Bodhisattva?

How sublime! It is that one person alone who invokes the name; it is one person whose spiritual resonance is manifest. While the collective response has not yet been revealed, how could the response indiscriminately extend [to all]?
Nevertheless, though the multitude may be silent, their hearts seeking salvation must be urgent. When the heart is urgent, the spirit manifests.
This principle is likewise appropriate. This too is encompassed by the inconceivable great compassion of the Bodhisattva. Second, the citation of evidence:
There were over a hundred people from foreign lands who sailed from Siṃhala Island toward Funan. They encountered a violent wind and fell into the realm of ghosts.
All were struck with great terror and invoked the holy name. Among them was a śramaṇa of the Hīnayāna who did not believe in visualization.
The sound was heard, and the ghost subsequently took the śramaṇa’s food. Because of this, the scholar Xuéchēng also managed to escape the calamity.

Regarding the interpretation of the "three contemplations," it clarifies not only the winds within the world-system, but also that black karma (*kṛṣṇa-karman*) is likewise called "wind. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states:

"The fierce winds of resentment blow upon the fire of the sinful mind, constantly causing it to blaze; they blow the merchants of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and cause them to fall into the evil destinies."
The wind of karmic retribution reaches up to the third dhyāna; the wind of evil karma pervades the three realms; the wind of afflictions pervades the three vehicles.
This is explained in detail as clarified in the annotated commentary (*kezhù*). Nevertheless, by reciting the name even once, one attains liberation from suffering in all cases;

this demonstrates the reality of seeking out voices to rescue those in distress. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Sixth, the refined clarity of hearing-penetration pervades the entire Dharma-realm; thus, all that is obscure..."
