Darkness. Its nature cannot be complete. Since there is no black wind, one will not fall into the various realms of ghosts.
From this point downward, [the text] parallels the preceding sections on water and fire to provide a concluding answer to the question asked by the immediate audience: "By what causes and conditions?
This refers to "by these causes and conditions. *Fǎng* (pronounced *fàng*). △ Fourth, the King’s Objection.
Furthermore, if there is a person who is on the verge of being harmed—[continuing until]—they immediately have their body severed piece by piece and yet attain liberation.

○ The explanation of Wangli (Wang Li) also has three parts. First, the commentary on the text: encountering disaster is suffering; invoking the name is goodness, which constitutes the "stimulus" (*jī*).
Attaining liberation is receiving the "response" (*yìng*). Second, citing evidence: the *Yingyan zhuan* (Biographies of Verified Responses) states that formerly, during the Dàyuán [era]...
In P'eng-ch'eng, there was a man who was falsely accused of being a bandit. This man had habitually enshrined a golden image within his topknot.
When he was led beneath the blade for execution, he heard only the sound of metal; though struck three times, his neck remained uninjured.

Upon inquiry, it was discovered that the golden image within his topknot bore three marks on its neck. Other instances need not be cited at length. Thus, those who explain [the matter] through the Three Contemplations find their evidence confirmed.

The retribution for blades and clubs extends from the hells up to the heavens of the desire realm. The blades and clubs of evil karma pervade the three realms, while the blades and clubs of afflictions pervade the three vehicles.
This means that whatever wholesome causes one cultivates are treated as the blades and arrows of the three poisons;

evil karma destroys the wholesome mind, cutting through the skin of precepts, the flesh of meditative concentration, the bone of wisdom, and the subtle marrow of the heart. If one can [practice] with a sincere mind...

Reciting the Name: In this way, there is no sword or staff from which one will not be liberated. [△@△] It is said that when one is about to be harmed, and at the very moment of execution, one is able to bring the subject and object into confrontation;
by reciting the Name once, the blade breaks into pieces, and both the capacity to act and the object of action are extinguished and forgotten.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Fifth, the hearing-faculty is perfumed and perfected as hearing; the six faculties are dissolved and restored, becoming identical to the hearing of sound. This enables...
Their weapons and spears are like slicing through water or blowing across light; their nature is without agitation, brought about by spiritual power.
△ Fifth, the peril of evil spirits.
If even the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system [cannot do so], how much less could they look upon one with an evil eye, let alone inflict harm?
○ There are also three parts to the explanation of the calamity of ghosts: first, the literal commentary. From "If the three-thousandfold" downward marks the location;

from "wishing to come" downward clarifies that encountering such a calamity is suffering; from "hearing his name" downward shows that calling the name is virtuous—this is the "stimulus. Ghosts cannot cause harm.
This is a response to that [previous] request. The previous statement that "those who drift and fall enter the realm of ghosts" refers to ghosts coming to harass people;
this statement that "ghosts fill the great trichiliocosm" refers to ghosts arriving among humans. What was said—that the entire universe is filled with ghosts—is indeed a reality.
One does not perceive the Middle Way within the teachings. In this Sahā world, there are ghosts through whom even a needle cannot be inserted;
yet, if a person can recite [the Buddha’s] name, the ghost’s mind is immediately extinguished—is this not like snow falling upon a red-hot furnace? Second, the citation of evidence:

this matter has already been manifested in the aforementioned section on the difficulty of the rākṣasas, so it need not be recounted here at length. Third, the explanation through contemplation: if it concerns karmic retribution...
Regarding ghosts: from the hells up to the celestial palaces, this danger exists everywhere. For instance, within the hells there are powerful ghosts who torment the sinners;
among the hungry ghosts (preta), there are malevolent ghosts who harm the lesser ghosts; among animals, there are malevolent ghosts that devour them;
and as for the heavens, the *Āgama* Sūtras state that there are powerful ghosts who sit upon the throne of Śakra. Śakra...

The *Śāstra on the Great Wrathful One* states: "The light of ghosts is likewise blazing," and so forth. Ghosts of evil karma pervade the three realms; for instance, greed, anger, and delusion all carry the meaning of being "ghosts.
Ghosts of affliction (*kleśa*) pervade the three vehicles; as it is said that the mind of views is a male ghost and the mind of craving is a female ghost.
Among these, the proclivities of views (*dṛṣṭi-anuśaya*) throughout the three realms number eighty-eight, while craving—which is synonymous with volition (*cetanā*)—numbers eighty-one.
It is not false that this great trichiliocosm is filled with ghosts; even those of the Two Vehicles encounter such demonic afflictions.
For Bodhisattvas, there are the ghosts of ignorance and the rākṣasas of folly. If one can recite the name of the Bodhisattva with a sincere heart, none shall fail to attain liberation.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Fourth, by severing delusive thoughts and harboring no intent to harm, one causes all sentient beings..."

The ghosts who have been born there cannot harm them. When those who hold the name receive their benefits, not only do [the ghosts] dare not inflict harm, they would not even dare to cast a malevolent glance at them. △ Sixth, the difficulty of shackles and fetters.
Furthermore, suppose there is a person, whether guilty or innocent, (up to) all are completely severed and destroyed, and they immediately attain liberation.

The explanation of the difficulty regarding shackles and fetters also has three parts. First, the word-by-word commentary: "Furthermore, etc. first indicates those who are guilty and those who are innocent.
"Manacles and shackles" below signify that encountering calamity is suffering. "Reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara" below signifies that calling upon the name is goodness;
this constitutes the stimulus (*ki*). "All are completely severed and destroyed," etc., signifies the response (*ō*). Regarding "those with offenses or without offenses":

some actually have offenses, some are ultimately without offense, and others have not yet been determined through investigation—all of these are imprisoned and detained. [△@△] As for those without offense, they should...

Nevertheless, even those with offenses are exempted. Why? This clarifies that the Sage’s mind is impartial; it fundamentally takes the rescue of those in captivity as its duty, regardless of whether they have committed an offense or not.

What is on the hands is called *xiǔ* (handcuffs); what is on the feet is called *xiè* (fetters); what is on the neck is called *jiā* (a neck-shackle); and what binds the body is called *suǒ* (chains).
These are the names for the three types of wooden restraints and one type of iron restraint. To "bind" (*jì*) means to bind and obstruct; to "inspect" (*jiǎn*)...

This refers to being bound and sealed. Being bound does not necessarily entail being sealed, but being sealed certainly entails being bound. To be both bound and sealed causes one’s grief and fear to be even more profound.
If one can invoke the name [of the Buddha], the heavy gates will open of their own accord, and the iron and wood will easily crumble.

Second, the citation of evidence: The *Yingyan Zhuan* (Biographies of Verified Responses) states: Gaihu was a native of Shanyang. He was imprisoned and sentenced to death. For three days and three nights, his mind remained without interruption [in its devotion].
He stopped. Immediately, he saw Avalokiteśvara emitting light that shone upon him; his shackles fell off and the door opened.

He followed the light and traveled twenty *li* until the light ceased. Commentary on the Three Contemplations: First, regarding the shackles and fetters of karmic retribution—this applies to the three miserable realms (*durgati*) and humans, as need not be stated explicitly.
The *asuras* also possess the five bonds. Only those in the northern continent (*Uttarakuru*) and the heavens are naturally free of these.

Difficult. Second, the shackles and fetters of evil karma: if a person cultivates wholesome dharmas, yet their mind is shrouded by evil karma such that the wholesome dharmas are ruined, they are then bound by evil karma;
within the three realms, there is no means of liberation. Third, the shackles and fetters of afflictions (*kleśa*):
those of the three vehicles who have not yet reached the ultimate are all bound by afflictions and cannot attain [liberation] for themselves.
If one can recite the name of the Bodhisattva with a sincere heart, all shackles and fetters will be liberated. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"Seventh, when the nature of sound is perfectly extinguished, one is free from all defiled delusions. Once these deluded objects are removed, what remains to bind one?
This is why those who hold the name attain liberation. 7. The Peril of Enemies and Bandits.
If the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were filled with hostile bandits (up to the point where), by merely reciting their names, one immediately attains liberation.

The explanation of this "difficulty of hostile bandits" also has three parts. First, the literal commentary: "The three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system" indicates the locus of the difficulty.

The phrase "filled with hostile bandits" indicates the difficulty of the journey. "Filled with" reveals that the country is vast and the bandits are numerous; it shows that the power of the Sage can provide salvation.
Hostiles inevitably take one's life, whereas bandits merely seize one's wealth. Now, since they are both bandits and hostiles, it is certain that both one's wealth and life will be taken.
This is truly terrifying. [△@△] The treasure is precious, yet the road is perilous; the bandits are at hand and moreover hostile—this is a source of harm.
How could this be a trivial or superficial matter? Within this context, one person earnestly exhorted others to recite the name, saying:

"The Bodhisattva is able to bestow fearlessness upon others; if one recites his name, one will surely be liberated from suffering. How is this different from hearing a great thunderclap during a long drought?

When the entire caravan recites together, how is it different from a solitary traveler meeting their parents? These are all instances of knowing the agreement [of the Dharma], whereas the other two are knowings of the individual.
If they were to vanish [without speaking], how could they not have brought about liberation? As for the caravan leaders and others, they were those who had encountered disaster.

"Caravan leader" (*śreṣṭhin*) refers to one who can distinguish between the noble and the base, is skilled in understanding wealth and profit, and through deliberation acts with propriety; such a person is fit to be the head of a merchant caravan. The passage following "one person below" clarifies the sequence of the mechanism:
first, providing comfort; second, exhorting them to call out the name [of the Buddha]; third, praising the holy virtue; and fourth, all raising their voices together.

That which provides consolation serves to quell one's terror. That which encourages the recitation of the name establishes the supreme strategy. That which extols the virtues serves to encourage and steady one’s resolve.

Second, the citation of evidence: According to the *Yingyan Zhuan* (Biographies of Verified Responses), when Seng Huida was digging for licorice on the Loess Plateau in the second year of the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty, he encountered hungry Qiang tribesmen who were in the midst of capturing people for food; he immediately captured them.
Huida was confined within a pen, where the fatter animals were selected first for slaughter. Terrified, Huida focused his mind solely on reciting the name [of the Buddha] and chanting this sutra.
When the others had all been eaten, only Huida and a small child remained; it was intended that they would be taken for food the following morning.

Fotudao continued his recitations throughout the night, yet it seemed as though he felt no divine response. As dawn approached, the Qiang came to seize him; suddenly, a fierce tiger burst forth from the grass, roaring incessantly.
The Qiang fled in all directions, and the tiger gnawed a hole through the fence before departing.
Fotudao and the children were all spared from harm. Regarding the three contemplations on resentment, the first concerns the enemy of karmic retribution (*vipāka-vaira*). From the ground...
From the hells up to the sixth heaven, there is everywhere strife. There are two kinds of enemies of evil karma: first, the enemy of much evil when one practices virtue;
second, the enemy of the afflictions (*kleśa*), which for those of the Three Vehicles is a mind hostile to the supramundane.

Prajñāpāramitā is the caravan leader; the five perfections and various practices are the merchants; the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and the ultimate reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) are the precious treasures;
and the six obscurations are the hostile bandits. If one can single-mindedly invoke the name [of the Buddha], all hostile bandits shall be liberated.

The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states that the eighth [attainment] is "the cessation of sound and the perfection of hearing, universally generating the power of compassion. This is because when sound and hearing stand as two, self and other become adversaries;
when sound ceases and hearing is perfected, there is no dependence on internal or external. Thus, one is able to extend universal compassion and repel adversaries.
△ Second, the summary of the supernormal powers.
"The majestic power of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, Akṣayamati, is thus sublime.
Tiantai says: "Since the power of Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom is so great, his protective guardianship is likewise vast. It does not merely respond to the seven calamities;
one should know that he is able to rescue and protect throughout the entire Dharma-realm. Therefore, it is called 'sublime' (*weīweī*). 'Sublime' serves as a further clarification."

The phrase "highly accumulated" (*gāolèi*) refers to this. The power of Avalokiteśvara transcends the two types of death—homogeneous and segmented—and vertically responds between the two lands of the provisional (*fāngbiàn*) and the true-recompense (*shíbào*).
Therefore, it is called "repeatedly manifesting. Having been repeatedly bathed by divine response, it is called "highly accumulated.
The response to objects through the faculty of speech is now concluded. II. Response to objects through the faculty of mind. This is divided into two parts. First, detachment... [text truncated].
The three poisons.
If there are sentient beings who have an abundance of lust (up to) they will then be able to leave delusion behind.
Tiantai says: These three are collectively called "poisons" because they are able to inflict harm upon the practitioner. However, there are also instances where they appear individually.
This is merely a repetition. While "greed, anger, and delusion" would suffice as single terms, they are listed here in pairs;

therefore, it says "sexual desire and so forth. To love oneself is "desire" (yù); to love another is "lust" (yín). To be angry with oneself is "resentment" (èi); to be angry with another is "anger" (chēn).

To be deluded regarding oneself is "folly" (yú); to be deluded regarding another is "delusion" (chī). Here, it clarifies that although the three poisons are predominant, the power of a Bodhisattva can still...
If one can attain detachment from this, how much more so for those who are young? The Essential Explanation states:

"Detachment from desire arises through the power of the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of hearing, which removes the dust and prevents one from being carried away by forms. It is because sentient beings conjoin with sensory objects through the habit-energy of desire that they are carried away by forms."

Once one is blessed by this wondrous power, sensual desire dries up and withers; the faculties and their objects no longer meet, so that even if seductive forms appear, they cannot plunder or disturb the mind.
As for those who have abandoned anger: because the faculties and their objects are perfectly interfused, there is no force of subject-object opposition.

For anger arises from the violation of one's feelings and is produced in response to external objects; when there is perfect interfusion, there is neither violation nor opposition, and thus anger ceases.

One may become free from it. To be free from delusion means to possess the power of revolving back toward luminosity through the elimination of defilements, such that one is clear, penetrating, and unobstructed.

For delusion is obscured by false objects and shrouded by ignorance; when defilements are eliminated, there is no longer obscuration, and when one is clear and penetrating, there is no longer concealment.
Thus, one is able to revolve back toward true luminosity and forever depart from the darkness of delusion. △ Second, manifesting majestic spiritual power.
From "The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Inexhaustible Intent" (up to) "...therefore sentient beings should always keep him in mind.
The phrase "it is thus" refers to the aforementioned three poisons. The word "etcetera" includes pride, doubt, and all [wrong] views.

However, although all ten fetters and proclivities are profound delusions within the triple world, the three poisons are particularly grave; therefore, they are singled out for mention. This is intended to...
To be free from the three poisons and yet be called one of great majestic power and vast benefit:
this is because while the previous seven calamities were merely external conditions, the three poisons are the stubborn knots of beginningless ignorance within all sentient beings.

With roots so deep and firm, how could they be severed easily unless by means of great majestic power and great fierce strength? If the three poisons are not eliminated, one will [continue to transmigrate].
What could emerge from death? Now that all delusions have been dissolved and forgotten, the single truth should naturally be revealed;
thus, it will not be difficult to awaken to and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Therefore, it is said that there is much benefit.

While among the previous seven difficulties it was simply said to "single-mindedly recite the name" or "recite his title," the present text necessarily says one must "constantly keep him in mind. This is because...
The three poisons are subtle and profound; their prevention must be meticulous. If sentient beings can constantly maintain mindfulness and reverence, from where could the poisons arise?
Should they momentarily forget their mindfulness, then delusive objects will compete to gather and the three poisons will erupt.
Therefore, practitioners must always keep the sacred realm of the Bodhisattva in mind. △ Regarding the Three Bodies’ Responsive Mechanism to Objects, divided into two parts. First:
The explicit explanation of the sincere seeking [of a son] has two parts. First, the seeking of a male child:
"If there is a woman who wishes to seek a male child" (up to) "...she shall give birth to a son endowed with merit and wisdom."
The *Zhīyīn* (Commentary on the Sounds of Knowledge) says: Generally, a woman’s status is exalted by the nobility of her husband;
however, physical beauty is difficult to maintain, and a husband’s affection is seldom constant. Only the birth of a son can provide lasting reliance. Therefore, women inevitably desire sons.
If a son born lacks fortune, the family cannot flourish; if he lacks virtue, his reputation cannot prosper; if he lacks wisdom, his person cannot be distinguished.
Noble one, without the path of wisdom one cannot practice; therefore, one seeks a bodhisattva, which is equivalent to desiring to give birth to a son endowed with merit and wisdom.
Yet, such a seeking will surely be fulfilled because the bodhisattva merges their form and returns to hear the Way at the Immovable Place of Enlightenment.
This continues up to each respective Buddha; it is by the power of being a Dharma Prince.

Since the Bodhisattva has already fulfilled the way of a son toward all Buddhas, he causes whatever is sought to be obtained immediately. [△@△] Among worldly people, there are still many who give birth to sons and daughters without seeking them;
yet here, when it says "one who wishes to seek," it refers to one who has a specific aspiration or desire. To prostrate and make offerings is sincerity.
If one seeks [a son], he shall be born endowed with merit and other such qualities; this clarifies the mutual resonance between the Way and its response. △ Second, seeking a daughter:
if one desires to seek a daughter, she shall be born upright and possessed of auspicious marks, having planted the roots of virtue in past lives, so that all people love and respect her.
The Connoisseur of Sound said: "A woman who is not upright—though her appearance may be beautiful, her inner governance will not be established.

One who lacks proper features—though her mind may be upright, what is seen outwardly will not be honored. If one has not planted the roots of virtue in past lives, they will not know how to revere the Triple Gem, nor will they inspire love and respect in others.
Yet, when a Bodhisattva seeks such a person with sincerity, she will surely be born as such."

As for this woman: because her six sense faculties are perfectly interfused and her illumination is non-dual, she has even received and followed the secret Dharma-gates of the Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, receiving them without error. As the *Book of Changes* says: "How ultimate is the primal source of Kun!"

Thus, she follows and sustains Heaven. Now, because the Bodhisattva’s body of perfect penetration is both luminously illuminating and capable of receiving and sustaining, she possesses the Way of Kun (Earth).
As Kun is thick and bears all things, she has caused a woman to appear—one who is receptive, vast, brilliant, upright, and endowed with auspicious marks.
Yet, the three poisons are the very nature constantly possessed by sentient beings.
If there are many, the harm is profound; yet the two-fold seeking is the constant, natural inclination of sentient beings.

If there are few, the lineage will be severed; thus some loathe their abundance while others fear their extinction. To honor the Sage with even a single thought is called making offerings to the Sage’s image;
that all these responses occur is the inconceivable, wondrous function [of the Buddha]. △ Second, concluding that the merit is not in vain.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, Immeasurable Intent, possesses such power (up to: that blessings are never in vain.
This concludes the discussion on how physical actions correspond to the needs of sentient beings without fail.

Fearing that skeptics might say, "There are those who perform prostrations yet do not receive the fulfillment of their vows," he therefore says: "If one can pay respectful homage and prostrate, the merit obtained will certainly not be in vain."

"Discarded" (*qi*) means "wasted" (*tángyuán*); it refers to being thrown away in vain. The reason one does not receive a response is that the resonance [of the invocation] has not yet reached its fulfillment;
it is not that the response is insufficient. The separate answer regarding liberation from suffering is concluded. △ Third, the answer exhorting the holding of the name, divided into three parts.
First, the exhortation to hold the name.
Therefore, all sentient beings should receive and uphold the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Tiantai says: "The above has explained the causes and conditions for which Avalokiteśvara received his name; its power is vast and great.

Since his physical form and substance have not been discussed, but only his name and virtues have been described, those who wish to take refuge in and revere him should properly uphold his name; hence, the upholding of the name is mentioned."

This is for the purpose of exhortation. [△@△] "For this reason" refers to the aforementioned rescue from the seven calamities, the departure from the three poisons, and the fulfillment of the two kinds of seeking;
it is because of these various majestic spiritual powers. "All should" is a broad exhortation to uphold the Name.

This means that since Bodhisattvas possess such great majestic spiritual power, it is not only those who have calamities, poisons, or specific requests who should uphold it; rather, all sentient beings [should do so].
All who are born [into this world] should receive and uphold it. Below, we shall compare the merit that one ought to uphold. △ Second, the comparative evaluation:
"O Akṣayamati, if there were someone... (up to) ...it could not be exhausted even in hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas."
This clarifies that upholding the name of a Bodhisattva is like consuming *vajra*; it cannot be compared to consuming other substances. To point directly:
first, taking the vast merit of a single person as the basis—sixty-two billion [Bodhisattvas] constitute a great field of merit; for the duration of one’s entire life, the time is extensive;
with the four requisites fully provided, the offerings are abundant; and by upholding their names with deep reverence, the degree of respect is immense. Thus it is illustrated.
These four matters serve as the basis for comparison. From "In your presence" (*tvayi*) onwards is the question; from "The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati" (*Akṣayamati*) onwards is the answer.

From "The Buddha said" (*bhagavān āha*) onwards, the text again singles out one person who invokes the name of Avalokiteśvara; this is the formal comparison itself. It then returns to citing the four great elements.
Although the number of recitations for the various Bodhisattvas is four times greater, their merit is exactly equal [to that of Avalokiteśvara]. Question:

Why is it that while the recitation of the various Bodhisattvas involves much effort, the resulting merit is comparatively small, whereas the recitation of Avalokiteśvara involves little effort, yet the resulting merit is comparatively great? Answer:

The various Bodhisattvas still remain within the fifty-four stages, whereas Avalokiteśvara already dwells in the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi). It is like the case of these two individuals.
If one person serves many ministers while another person devotes themselves exclusively to honoring their sovereign, the difference in the degree of the favor they receive can be clearly understood.
Furthermore, within the *Yuan-tong* (Perfect Penetration), he states of himself: "My single name is no different from those many names.
Since it was through my cultivation that I attained true perfect penetration, by this one knows that self and others are fundamentally equal.
...and so forth. △ Third, the concluding praise:
"The merit and benefit of the immeasurable and boundless blessings gained by Wujinyi (Akṣayamati) through upholding [the name of] Guanshiyin...
Even reciting the name once, the merit cannot be exhausted. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "If one scatters a single flower into the air... and so on until the end.
"Suffering. Its merit is inexhaustible. The *Yishu* (Explanatory Commentary) states: "Offering a single flower to a Buddha is comparable to reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara once.
The phrase "suffering ends" means that the two deaths are forever exhausted; it refers to reaching the state of Buddhahood.
Even so, the merit of scattering flowers remains inexhaustible. The reason the comparison is made using sixty-two billion [offerings] is to expand upon the six sense faculties.
...and so forth. The above constitutes the total of the fourteen fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), which are shared with all sentient beings in a single compassionate reliance.

The section on the names of those who ask and answer is completed. △ Second, the inquiry into the manifestations of the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*). This is divided into two parts. First, the inquiry into the bestowal of the three karmas (*trikarma*).
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One... [up to] ...what are the matters regarding the power of skillful means? Tiantai says:

The previous question asked by what causes and conditions he received his name; the Buddha answered that the three karmas of sentient beings manifest as the conditions (*mārga*) which serve as the object (*viṣaya*).
The Dharma-body and numinous wisdom are in profound resonance as the response; it is by virtue of these conditions of object and wisdom that [the name] is obtained.

Now, the question is asked: "How does one roam, and so forth? The Buddha answers by revealing the response through the three karmas manifested via the Universal Gate (Samantamukha), thereby answering the hidden potential.
"How does one roam" refers to the body; "how does one speak" refers to the mouth; and "expedient means" refers to the mind. These are the three karmas of the Sage.
Without deliberation, it universally responds to all; this is also called the inconceivable transformation of the three wheels. The *Yishu* states:

"When sentient beings invoke the Name, constantly maintain mindfulness, and perform prostrations, the three karmas manifest before them; hence it is said that the capacity [of the practitioner] is revealed.
The numinous wisdom of the Dharma-body is the true body formed by the union of the two aspects of initial and original enlightenment. It is through this wisdom that suffering is uprooted."

Therefore, it is called "mysterious response" (ming-ying). Now, to clarify: the Bodhisattva’s mind reflects upon the capacities [of beings], manifesting forms with the body and preaching the Dharma with the mouth, enabling sentient beings to have realization, knowledge, seeing, and hearing;
therefore, it is called "manifest response" (xian-ying). Furthermore, the specific characteristics of the three karmas practiced by sentient beings are not explicitly stated;
this is because their past goodness lies dormant within them, yet is able to evoke a resonance. Therefore, it is called "mysterious capacity" (ming-ji).
Furthermore, regarding the inquiry concerning the "mental action of skillful means": this is not the skillful means for grasping the principle prior to the Path;

rather, it is the skillful means for discerning the capacities [of beings] subsequent to realization. △ Second, answering his wondrous response, divided into two parts: first, answering the manifested body.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati (up to the point where he) immediately manifested a Buddha-body and preached the Dharma for him.
This answers all three questions. Tiantai says that the two characters "should" (*yīng*) answer the underlying intent.

This is because the mental ground observes the capacities of beings and perceives what is appropriate—namely, which body should be manifested and which Dharma should be preached. Manifesting a body is the bodily karma (*kāyakarman*). Preaching... [the Dharma is the verbal karma].
The Dharma is the vocal karma (*vākkarman*). Within this specific response, he manifests thirty-two bodies in total; nineteen of these preach the Dharma.
These are condensed into ten realms of existence (*daśadhātu*), yet two realms—the Bodhisattva realm and the hell realm—are missing. The Bodhisattva is simply his own original body.
How could it be that there is a deficiency in the text? The hells must indeed exist; it is merely that the wording is abbreviated.

Although they are not mentioned in the specific answers, they are fully contained within the general description. This refers to the passage stating that [the Buddha] "traverses various lands in various forms.
The thirty-two bodies are divided into eight categories: first, the holy body; second, the celestial body; third, the human body; fourth, the fourfold assembly; fifth, women; sixth, children...
Male. Seven or eight sections. Eight vajra-bodies. Regarding the Buddha-body first explained among the holy bodies:
it is either a *saṃbuddha* (response-body) or a *nirmāṇabuddha* (transformation-body). However, the holy person’s accommodation to beings possesses two meanings.

If [the body] suddenly appears at one time as a transformation, yet shares the same beginning and end as the response, it is called a "response" (*saṃbuddha*). Now, the *saṃbuddhabuddha* has two aspects: first, the supreme response; second, the...

The inferior response is for those of the *hīnayāna* capacity; the superior response is for those of the *vaipulya* and *pratyekabuddha* capacities. The inferior [response] is for the multitudes of the *pitaka* and *āgama*. A commentator says:

"The 'lands and sentient beings' refers to the two types of retribution—the environment and the inhabitants—within the trichiliocosm; this is a general statement regarding the capacity (*tūpa*). 'Should' (*yīng*) means 'to respond. 'By means of' (*yǐ yòng*) means 'by using.

This refers to the case where, within the lands of the trichiliocosm, there might be a single sentient being of *yuan-dun* (perfect and sudden) capacity who wishes not to traverse the gradual stages."

To attain Buddhahood directly beneath one’s feet means that this person is to be delivered by means of a Buddha-body; therefore, [the Buddha] immediately manifests that body and preaches the Dharma of the perfect fruition for them.

As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "If there are bodhisattvas who enter samādhi and advance in the cultivation of the untainted (anāsrava), such that their superior understanding becomes fully manifest, I manifest a Buddha-body and preach the Dharma for them. This refers to that very point.
To those who should be delivered by means of the body of a *pratyekabuddha*, he manifests the body of a *pratyekabuddha* and preaches the Dharma for them.
As with Mañjuśrī, for two trillion *kalpas* he acted as a *pratyekabuddha*, teaching and transforming sentient beings, manifesting his body to preach the Dharma.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If those in training [the *śaikṣas*] possess tranquil, pure, wondrously bright, and superior understanding that is fully perfected," and so forth. Thus, it is said:
To preach the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas—tranquil, wondrous, and luminous—is to manifest in the form of a Śrāvaka for those who are to be saved by a Śrāvaka body and to preach the Dharma for them.

At times he appears as a Śrāvaka of the *zàng* (Treasury) or *tōng* (Penetration) teachings; at times he appears as a Śrāvaka who transforms according to the five flavors. Thus, he conceals his inner realization while manifesting outwardly.
It also guides sentient beings. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "If those in training attain the emptiness of the Four Truths and enter cessation through the cultivation of the path," and so forth;

this refers to the teaching of the Four Truths for the Śrāvakas. This clarifies the manifestation of the bodies of the four noble ones; next, it clarifies the manifestation of the bodies of the six classes of ordinary beings.
To those who are to be saved by the body of a Brahmā King, he manifests as a Brahmā King and preaches the Dharma for them.
The *Yingluo jing* states: "Each of the four dhyānas has its own king; this term 'Brahmā' should refer to the summit of the first dhyāna."
There still remains the discourse on the dharma of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).

[The text] states that Avalokiteśvara attained the status of Lord of the Trichiliocosm by practicing the White-Colored Samādhi, neither grasping nor abandoning. Because he does not grasp, he is not reborn according to the stages of dhyāna;

because he does not abandon, he manifests as a Brahmā King and expounds the *Vairāgya-śāstra* (Treatise on Transcending Desire), using skillful means to lead toward the ultimate reality. The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says: "If there are sentient beings who desire..."
When the mind attains clear awakening and does not transgress against the dust of desire and so forth, this is the teaching on the dharma of detachment from desire that has been expounded.
To those who are to be delivered by the body of Śakra, he manifests in the form of Śakra and preaches the Dharma for them.
Because the Bodhisattva cultivates the white samādhi without grasping or rejecting, he expounds various supreme discourses, using skillful means to lead toward the ultimate reality.
As the Śūraṅgama Sūtra says: "If there are sentient beings who wish to become a celestial lord, presiding over and ruling all the heavens..."
That which is taught is the Dharma of the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths of action.
To those who should be delivered by means of the body of Īśvara, he manifests the body of Īśvara and preaches the Dharma for them.

In the Sanskrit language, this is called Vaśavartin; here it is translated as "Mastery over Others' Emanations" (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*). This refers to those who achieve their own pleasure by utilizing the creations of others;
they are the Māra kings. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states that most of them are bodhisattvas of inconceivable liberation (*acintyavimokṣa*).
Abiding in the red-colored samādhi, neither grasping nor rejecting, one should act as a Māra king, causing all māra realms to immediately enter the Buddha-realm.
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If sentient beings desire bodily mastery and so forth, then the method for traveling throughout the ten directions that is taught [applies].
Hereafter, every manifestation of a body is the Bodhisattva abiding in samādhi, by means of which—
The provisional leads to the ultimate; by this principle, other cases may be understood.
One should preach the Dharma for those who are to be saved by means of the body of Maheśvara (up to...).
*Loutan jing* names it Akaniṣṭha; the *Avataṃsaka* calls it Akaniṣṭha-bhūmi. The *Śāstra* says: "Ma..."
Śiva is called Maheśvara; he rides a white bull, has eight arms and three eyes, and is a general of the various devas.
Is it that [the deity] shares this same name, or does it refer directly to this very deva? Furthermore, the *Śāstra* states:
"Beyond the Śuddhāvāsa devas, there are Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage called Maheśvara, who act as lords of the trichiliocosm. According to this, [it would be the Bodhisattva].

This likely does not refer to that [specific case]. The *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* states: "If sentient beings desire bodily mastery, such as flying through the void, then this refers to the dharma of bodily mastery that has been taught."
For those who are to be saved through the form of a celestial great general (up to), he preaches the Dharma for them.
In the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, Saṃjñeya is designated as the Great General; it is also called Kumbhaka, which means "Child.
The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* states: "If there are sentient beings who desire to preside over spirits and deities, or to protect the land and its people..."
This is the teaching on the methods for protecting and saving the land.
To those who should be saved through the form of Vaiśravaṇa, he manifests in the body of Vaiśravaṇa and preaches the Dharma for them.
As stated in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*: "If there are sentient beings who desire to govern the world and protect its inhabitants," and so forth—this is what is being taught.
This is the Dharma for protecting sentient beings. However, in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the Four Heavenly Kings and their princes appear;
here, they are subsumed under Vaiśravaṇa, as he is one of the four kings. This concludes the explanation of the "Manifesting Wondrous Sound" chapter.
Above, the lords and commanders of the celestial vehicle were described; below, the kings and ministers of the human world will be described.
To those who are to be delivered by the body of a minor king (*kṣudra-rāja*), he manifests as a minor king and preaches the Dharma to them.
A "minor king" is a term used in contrast to a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*). The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* states:

"If there are sentient beings who delight in being human kings and the like, then the Dharma taught to them is the path of the ten wholesome actions. However, being a human king is not something that ordinary people naturally desire.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva also preaches the Dharma for those who desire to fulfill their vows;
that is, for those who wish to govern states and transform the people so that the Way and the Dharma may circulate—therefore, they too should seek [the Dharma].
To those who are to be saved by means of the body of a householder, he immediately manifests in the body of a householder and preaches the Dharma for them.
The interpretation is as explained in the preceding chapter; that is to say, he teaches the principles of how one’s clan and lineage are esteemed and honored by the world.
To those who are to be liberated by means of the body of a layperson (*gṛhapati*), he manifests in the form of a layperson and preaches the Dharma for them.
This refers to one who possesses virtue but holds no official rank, dwelling in the Way as his own abode; thus, the names and phrases he employs are the teachings of dwelling in purity.
To those who are to be saved by means of the body of a minister, he manifests the body of a minister and preaches the Dharma for them.

From the Three Ducal Ministers and the Chancellor down to the governors of provinces, prefectures, and counties— all are called ministers— and thus what is preached is the method for governing the realm and administering the states and districts.
To those who are to be saved through the form of a brāhmaṇa, he manifests in the body of a brāhmaṇa and preaches the Dharma for them.
Among the four castes of the Western Regions, this is one; they are called "Pure Conduct" (śrotriya) and also "Brahmacārin.

This refers to the arts of calculation and the methods of self-protection. "Arts of calculation" refers to divination by physiognomy and so forth; "self-protection" refers to medical arts for regulating and preserving the body and longevity.
Regarding those who delight in [the Dharma] and so forth, one should preach the Dharma to them—whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās.
This refers to the fourfold assembly of monastics and laypeople; thus, one should preach the five precepts, the ten precepts, and the two hundred and fifty precepts.
This is the method for [teaching] the five hundred precepts.
One should manifest in the form of a laywoman (*gṛhiṇī*), a householder (*gṛhapati*), or a high official (up to and including manifesting in the body of a woman) to preach the Dharma.

The *Yinzhi* (Record of Sounds and Meanings) states: "This differs slightly from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. In that [sūtra], first one manifests as a queen, and second, one manifests as a noble lady (*rājamahiṣī*)."
Third, she appears as a titled wife (*mingfu*); fourth, she appears as a great lady (*dajia*). Gushan says: "The 'lady of the state' refers to the consort of the Son of Heaven;

the 'state lady' (*guofuren*) is, for example, as in the *Lunyu*, where the wife of a lord of a state is called the 'lord’s lady' (*junfuren*). A 'titled wife' refers to one whose status is honored because of her husband.
A 'great lady' is, for example, Cao Shetou’s wife from Fufeng during the Later Han, who was [the daughter] of Ban Biao of the same commandery."
Her daughter was named Zhao, with the courtesy name Huìjī. Emperor Hè summoned her to the palace several times and commanded the Empress and the noble ladies to serve as her disciples;
she was titled Dàjiā (The Great Lady). Among these were the wives of high officials and ministers, corresponding to the *mìngfù* (ladies by rank) of that realm;
they are not called "present female rulers" or "lady marquises" because Miaoyin had manifested in a female body within the royal harem.
That he preached this sutra has already been recounted. Thus, what was taught concerns the internal governance of the self and the methods for cultivating the family and the state.
He preached the Dharma to those who were to be saved through the forms of young boys and girls, and so forth.
This refers to the two sons of King Wondrous Adornment, Śakra, and the youth from the *Avataṃsaka* who played at counting sand, and so forth.
Thus, it is as stated: their male organs were not impaired, nor did they seek to commit acts of violence or aggression. The above concludes the manifestation of males and females in the world.
Next, the eight classes of beings are manifested.
One should manifest [the assembly] from devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas (up to the various classes of beings) and preach the Dharma for them.
The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* opens its narrative with nine sections; these are the methods taught that excel beyond their peers.
To those who are to be liberated by means of the Vajrapāṇi deity, he manifests as the Vajrapāṇi deity and preaches the Dharma for them.
In the Sanskrit language, *vajra* means "diamond" (or "thunderbolt"); in the Sanskrit language, *pāṇi* means "hand.
Since "hand" carries the sense of "grasping," he is named accordingly as the "Vajra-grasper" (*Vajrapāṇi*). The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "In the past, there was a king..."

The first wife gave birth to a thousand sons; because he wished to test the sequence of those who would attain Buddhahood in the future, Krakucchanda Buddha drew the first tally, and so on until Ruci Tathāgata drew the thousandth. The second wife gave birth to two sons.
One vow was to request the Thousand Brothers to preach the Dharma on behalf of the Brahma King; the other vow was to serve as a Vajra deity to protect the Buddha-dharma of the Thousand Brothers.
It is for these reasons that this occurred. The explanation of the manifested bodies is hereby concluded. △ Second, the general response regarding the saving of sentient beings.
"Akṣayamati, this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara... travels through various lands to deliver sentient beings.
This concludes the summary and detailed answers to the questions posed above. Tiantai says: "The names are not uniform;
horizontally, they pervade the ten directions, and vertically, they encompass the three lands. Manifesting according to conditions, how could he be limited to thirty-two bodies? He relies upon..."
Transformation follows conditions; how could it be restricted to the Sahā world? By manifesting in various forms, it clarifies that the manifestation of the body is vast.
By traveling through all lands, it clarifies that the scope of transformation is vast. By delivering sentient beings, it clarifies that the benefit obtained is vast.

Although the words are concise compared to what precedes them, the meaning is more expansive than before. Those who understand the sound [of the teaching] say: the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states, "This is called the wondrous..."

The thirty-two pure manifestations for entering lands are all accomplished with mastery through the effortless, wondrous power of cultivation based on hearing and the permeation of hearing via samādhi.
According to the phrase "effortless, sovereign, wondrous purity," the nineteen instances of preaching the Dharma herein are all discussed in terms of the responsive resonance of sentient beings;
regarding the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-body, they are like reflections appearing in a mirror.
It is like the moon appearing in water; this is precisely what is meant by "harmonizing upward with the compassionate power of all Buddhas of the ten directions.

This concludes the second section on the two rounds of questions and answers. △ Second, the exhortation to offer sincere worship, divided into two parts. First, the Tathāgata’s exhortation to offer worship.
"Therefore, you all should with one mind... [and] all address him as the Bestower of Fearlessness.
The phrase "therefore" refers to the preceding two rounds of question and answer. In the previous answers to the questions, there was first a general statement followed by a specific one.
Because it is difficult for these sentient beings to escape their realms of suffering, there is a concern that the Bodhisattva’s compassion might not universally reach them.
Therefore, the text first states in general terms that those who undergo various sufferings and distress will all attain liberation by single-mindedly invoking the name.

This clarifies that the Bodhisattva’s compassionate mind is boundless, and thus it accords with the needs of sentient beings. The previous emphasis on "single-mindedly invoking the name" implies that through the Bodhisattva’s true body (*dharmakāya*), [the practice] is performed in secret harmony.
It is so. There is nothing to be sought; it can only be designated by name. In the subsequent answer to the question, the response proceeds from the specific to the general.

This is because the manifested body is the condition for the joy of sentient beings. The underlying intention is that since the Bodhisattva universally manifests clouds of bodies throughout the ten dharma-realms, his wondrous responsiveness does not exceed this.
Therefore, the final summary states: "He wanders through various lands in manifold forms."
This passage clarifies that the Bodhisattva’s compassionate mind is inexhaustible and that he is thus aligned with all Buddhas above.
Now, this further exhortation to offer single-minded worship arises because the Bodhisattva manifests his body and preaches the Dharma before all sentient beings;
thus, they see various forms and hear various sounds. Since these sights and sounds are perceived with such clarity, one ought to offer worship with a single mind.
This is cultivation. To first say "single-mindedly recite the name" is to know that there is a Bodhisattva who can be honored;

to later say "single-mindedly make offerings" is to see that there is a Bodhisattva who can be revered. With such single-mindedness and such reverence, if one does not regress over time, then one may enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* uses the fourteen fearlessnesses to provide salvation.
Regarding the seven calamities, responding to the two types of seeking, and escaping the three poisons and so forth—these constitute fearlessness (*abhaya*).
Now, following the thirty-two manifestations, it is further stated that "one can bestow fearlessness amidst terrors and urgent perils.

This summarizes the preceding two cycles of question and answer, for being freed from suffering and attaining happiness are both termed fearlessness. Now, while the Sahā world is said to be a place where fearlessness is bestowed, [the text continues:]
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, are all called 'Bestowers of Fearlessness.
This makes it even more evident that they are those who ought to be venerated. **II. Receiving the Mandate Without End.** This section is divided into six parts. **1. Receiving the Command.**
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying: [up to] “accept this precious necklace as a gift of Dharma.
This indicates that the recipient, responding to the occasion, offers what he prizes without attachment; having attained mastery over the Dharma, he performs the gift of Dharma.
The Buddha says, “You all should make offerings,” thereby manifesting his fearlessness. The recipient then says, “I shall now make offerings.”
If one nurtures them, those below will understand what they hold dear; thus, by seeing that which is most revered, one forgets [self-attachment] and attains fearlessness.
As for the mention of "various jewels," they are formed through their intermingling. The *Sūtra of the Necklaces* (*Yingluo jing*) states:

from the copper jewel of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) up to the *maṇi* jewel of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). The current reference to "jewel beads" allows us to infer the corresponding stages. Tiantai says:
The neck represents the principle of the single reality of the Middle Way. It is adorned with numerous non-attached dharma-gates, just as a jeweled necklace adorns the neck.
As for "understanding" (*jie*), it signifies that the Bodhisattva does not dwell in or cling to any of the practices, vows, or merits, up to and including Buddha-wisdom and *nirvāṇa*.
"Hundreds of thousands" signifies that within each stage (*bhūmi*) there are ten thousand merits.

On each stage, there is an increase [in merit]. Regarding the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*): it is giving in accordance with the Dharma; that is, because one is able to relinquish both Buddha-wisdom and *nirvāṇa*.
△ Second, non-acceptance.
At that time, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva was unwilling to accept it.
He untied the necklace from his neck; this was precisely what the Bodhisattva esteemed and granted. However, there are no three characters meaning "unwilling to accept.
How can one express an inexhaustible interpretation on behalf of the assembly while they themselves do not yet understand the intent of that "untying"? From [this point]...

Akṣayamati spoke out of compassion for us; the Buddha, moreover, out of compassion for Akṣayamati and compassion for the eight classes of beings and others, exhorted him to explain the meaning of the necklace. This person [Akṣayamati] understood it through analogy.
Thus, Avalokiteśvara’s refusal to accept it, Akṣayamati’s earnest request to accept it, and the World-Honored One’s exhortation to accept it—all serve to let the assembly know.
To explain a single point: whether it be a thousand Buddhas or ten thousand Buddhas, they desire only that people understand and realize [the truth]. △ Third, the request for compassion:
Ajita (Akṣayamati) again addressed Avalokiteśvara... [up to] "...out of compassion for us, please accept this necklace."
The three characters "out of compassion for us" constitute the basis for what may be accepted.

When the Buddha bestows [the gift] out of compassion for the assembly, and the Bodhisattva accepts it out of compassion for the assembly, then both are practicing the Dharma-gift. △ Fourth, the Buddha’s exhortation.
At that time, the Buddha told Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva... [omitted] ...therefore accept this necklace from humans, non-humans, and others.

The Direct Pointing says: "The reason the Buddha exhorted Avalokiteśvara to pity the multitudes and accept it was precisely for the sake of the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings who have not yet entered the wondrous practice;
thus he entrusted it to Avalokiteśvara’s great compassion to gather them in, so that they may attain [liberation] from beginning to end."

The ultimate. The fourfold assembly represents those who embody the original and the manifested aspects as the primary recorders; the eight classes of beings represent those who embody the original and the manifested aspects as the external protectors of the remaining stream.
From the beginning, the intention has been inexhaustible; reaching this point, the opening, revealing, awakening, and entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are complete.
△ Five: Acceptance.
At that moment, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, out of compassion for the fourfold assembly... [up to] ...offered one portion to the Stūpa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna.
This clarifies that the Bodhisattva accepted the command immediately; thus, out of pity for the multitude, he accepted the gift of the Dharma. (Note: *Yinzhi*)
It is said: "Obeying the Buddha’s command and taking pity on the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings" signifies receiving the gift of the Dharma;

it expresses the lower convergence with all sentient beings in their shared sorrowful longing. "Dividing the necklace to offer to the Buddha and the stūpa" signifies the upper convergence with the Buddhas of the three periods of time in their shared power of compassion.
Tiantai says: "Dividing a single necklace into two parts" symbolizes the two aspects of phenomena and principle.

Regarding "offering to two Buddhas": this refers to being about to attain the two fruits. In principle, one perfectly realizes the Dharma-body Buddha; in phenomena, one perfectly realizes the Reward-body Buddha.

Furthermore, it symbolizes that a single practice must necessarily possess two causes: in principle, the direct cause (*dharmatā-hetu*); in phenomena, the conditional and responsive causes (*pratyaya-hetu* and *nirvṛtti-hetu*).
Principle and phenomena are non-dual; thus it is said that the wondrous cause can accomplish the wondrous fruits of the Dharma-body and the Reward-body.

Why does this not discuss the Response-body? It is said: because one seeks the fruit by means of the cause, [the teaching] combines to represent the two bodies. Once the Dharma-body and the Reward-body are perfected, the application [of the Response-body] manifests spontaneously. △ Sixth, the summary.

From "Akṣayamati, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara... wanders through the Sahā world" [to the end], this summarizes the preceding inquiry to provide an answer suited to the capacity of the audience. Fundamentally, it is because the Bodhisattva has attained two kinds of excellence.

When the three kinds of wondrous functions are manifested, the thirty-two manifestations, the fourteen fearlessnesses, and the four inconceivables are all termed sovereign spiritual powers by which one wanders through the Sahā world. However, this text omits the four inconceivables;
yet Zhiyin states that they are contained within the concluding responses of the four sections. The first states: "By the power of majestic spirit..."
Sublime it is in this way. Next, it says: "Possessing such great majestic power and spiritual authority, he brings benefit to many. Third, it says:
"For this reason, the Sahā world is all named 'Bestower of Fearlessness'. Fourth, it says: "He possesses such sovereign spiritual power. Why is this so?
Because through both identical-body mantras and distinct-body mantras, he destroys stinginess and evokes [compassion]."
Seeking. Making offerings to the Buddha’s birth—these four inconceivable matters are all due to the majestic spiritual power of Great Sovereignty (*mahāvaśitā*).
Therefore, these four answers encompass everything without exception. The prose section is concluded. △ Second, the verse summary, divided into three parts.
First, a double verse summarizing the two questions.
At that time, Bodhisattva Akṣayamati questioned [the Buddha] with verses.
The *Yishu ji* (Record of Explanatory Notes) states: "The Master Shi (Kumārajīva) did not translate the verse text. Various masters all maintain that it exists in the Sanskrit original.
Venerable Jingxi said: "This too has not fathomed the profound intention of the Master Shi. The *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks) states: "The verses are..."
Translated by Jñānagupta. At the time when the Wise One appeared, this verse had not yet been circulated; therefore, it was not understood.

Jingxi also cited the passage "returning to be attached to one's original person" within his *Fuxingji* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning). Thus, we know that providing a detailed explanation is likewise without hindrance.
Recently, there was the Dharma Master Shishi of the Tianzhu Monastery, who divided the text into sections in response to the [Long Scroll].
The exchange of questions and answers was like the fitting of a seal and its impression; therefore, I shall provide an explanation based upon them.
World-Honored One, you who are endowed with wondrous marks, I now ask again: for what causes and conditions is that son of the Buddha named Avalokiteśvara?

This verse first praises the Buddha’s virtues. Because the World-Honored One is fully endowed with the ten thousand virtues and the marks and signs of excellence, it says, "endowed with wondrous marks.
The phrase "I now" [of the following verse] praises the two preceding questions; since those characters encompass both persons and dharmas, the latter two lines single out the name.
This verse corresponds to the prose section which asks: "By what causes and conditions is he named Avalokiteśvara? △ Second, the pair.
The second part, the response, is divided into two sections. First, the narrative by the sūtra compiler regarding the response:
"The Honored One with Perfectly Complete Marks" responded to Akṣayamati in verse.
Master Shi says: "These verses seem to be a patchwork composition; it would be more appropriate for the Tathāgata to have answered directly, or perhaps [this was] compiled by the sūtra compiler."

The one who rides upon this [vehicle] may then praise it in verse. Alternatively, one may dig out many [verses] and translate them into gāthās; whether they follow the prose word-for-word or are arranged in a loose manner, there is nothing improper about it.
△ Second, the actual versification of the Buddha’s response, divided into two parts: first, the addition of verses to generally praise the practices and vows.
"Listen to the practices of Avalokiteśvara, who skillfully responds to all places... (until) he makes this great, pure vow.
The *Yinzhi* commentary states: "As for 'Listen,' it is a command to listen attentively; the entire verse below summarizes the profound vows corresponding to the six realms of existence."
This means that noble conduct can respond to all directions. Although this is a supernormal power (*abhijñā*), it is also brought about by profound and vast vows.
These vows are deep because they have been cultivated over many eons; they cannot be conceived by the mind nor discussed by the mouth.
Next, the verse summarizes the aforementioned purity of the vows shared with all Buddhas: having made great vows over many eons, they are inconceivable.
This is because, through having served many Buddhas, one is free from defiled attachment. "In all directions" refers to the three worlds within lands as numerous as atoms.
"Skillfully responding" means that upon hearing an invocation within the ten dharma realms, one responds immediately. The four lines following "vast vows" [refer to the four immeasurables].
The phrasing appears somewhat disjointed; it should read: "May one give rise to great pure vows. "The profound vow is as deep as the ocean;
serving many thousands of billions of Buddhas throughout inconceivable kalpas. Because the vow is greatly pure, it is said to be "like the ocean"; this clarifies the *praṇidhāna* (vow).

Because of serving thousands of billions of Buddhas, the duration of the kalpas is difficult to conceive; this clarifies the *caryā* (practice). "Profound vow" refers to the four... [the four immeasurables].
Regarding the "vast vows," what is called "purity" means not seeking for oneself the provisional and limited blessings and rewards of the human or celestial realms.
II. A separate verse specifically clarifying the two answers, divided into two parts: A. A verse answering the name of Avalokiteśvara, further divided into two:
1. A general answer.
"I have briefly explained for you that hearing the name and seeing the body, as well as mindfulness, are not in vain; they are capable of extinguishing all suffering within the realms of existence.
Śīla said: "Briefly explained" means to state the essential points. Hearing the name refers to the vocal faculty; seeing the body refers to the physical faculty;
and mental mindfulness refers to the mental faculty. Hearing the name is a response through the unmanifest, while seeing the body is a response through the manifest.
"Should" (應) refers to all existences, namely the twenty-five states of existence (二十五有). "Hearing the name" (聞名) summarizes the preceding dialogue concerning the seven perils and two requests;
by once invoking the name, one's vows are fulfilled. "Seeing the body" (見身) summarizes the subsequent dialogue concerning the thirty-two manifestations;
by focusing one's attention, accomplishment is attained. The two characters "mindful thought" (心念) encompass the single-mindedness within both responses.
One should offer worship by reciting the name with single-minded concentration. However, if one recites the name without single-mindedness, then such practice is largely wasted;
as it is said, "To be absent for even a moment is the same as being dead. How then could one swiftly extinguish the sufferings of the various realms of existence?
Furthermore, regarding "all existences" (*sarvabhava*): if one refers to the twenty-five existences, it cannot encompass the capacities of all beings within the ten dharma-realms.

However, even among the four classes of noble ones, there are those whose prayers for deliverance are not fulfilled; this too is suffering. One should know that the suffering of all existences is, in fact, all-encompassing suffering.
II. Specific Response. This also has two parts. First, a verse on the addition of the seven calamities to the remainder, which is divided into twelve sections. Section One.
The verse describes the peril of fire:
"Even if one should harbor a malicious intent and push another into a great pit of blazing fire, by the power of mindfulness of Avalokiteśvara, that fiery pit is transformed into a pool.

The *Yinzhi* (Sound-Knowledge) commentary states: From this point downward, all verses briefly explain the application [of the mantra]. The fiery pit arises from the transformation of anger; it is through anger that people [create such calamities].
Harmful [beings]. Because the Sages employ compassion and patience, one should contemplate their spiritual power; thus, a pit of fire was transformed into a pond.

This is because they rescue others by means of the true emptiness inherent in the nature of fire. [△@△] This section says "even if" (*jashǐ*), while the subsequent passage speaks of "either drifting away or being harmed," and so forth.

None of these are substantially existent; they are not permanent entities. Even if such things were to exist, it would not be difficult for one to merely obtain the name of that Bodhisattva through mindfulness.
This is what is called the power of the mutual resonance between the path and its response. △ Second, the verse on the peril of water.
Or if drifting upon the vast ocean, amidst the perils of dragons, fish, and various ghosts, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, one cannot be submerged by the waves.
[Commentary: The vast ocean is produced by greed. Greed for wealth is like a dragon; greed for lust is like a fish; greed for killing is like a ghost.
By the power of a single thought of the Sage, the five desires are instantly stilled, so that the waves do not submerge [the vessel].

This is to rescue [beings] by means of the true emptiness of the water of nature (*dharmatā*). The *Yaojie* (Essential Explanation) states: "To speak of drifting and waves in relation to the water implies the inclusion of the wind-disaster.
From this point until the dispersal of lightning and hail, all are verses on external karma; in the long prose version, these constitute the fourteen fearlessnesses, whereas here they are in verse.

The literary style and the characteristics of the content differ. Furthermore, as for the addition of the supplementary verses, they specifically cite the fourteen fearlessnesses (*caturdaśa-vaiśāradya*) by way of a general outline, because [the Buddha] actually possesses all merits in their entirety.
△ Third, the difficulty regarding the addition of verses concerning Mount Sumeru.
Or, if one were on the peak of Mount Sumeru and were pushed over by someone, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, one would remain in the sky like the sun.
One's own arrogance and conceit exceed even Mount Sumeru; such a person of pride thinks, "Others may be arrogant toward me, yet I am superior.
This is what is meant by being "pushed over by someone. Because the Bodhisattva’s light of humility illuminates all things, by a single thought of the Sage’s power, one becomes as bright as the sun.
The sun abides in space. This means that one is rescued by the true awakening of the emptiness of intrinsic nature. △ Fourth, the verse on the difficulty of the Diamond [Mount]:
"If pursued by evil people and falling toward the Diamond Mountain, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, not even a single hair can be harmed."
Ignorance and evil pursue a person like falling onto a diamond mountain; there is no one who is not wounded.

Because the Bodhisattva has forever severed ignorance and craving, those who mindfully recite [his name] gain power such that even if they were to fall [into such a place], not a single hair could be harmed.
This, too, is the salvation through the true awakening of the emptiness of nature. The *Dàkuǎn* quotes the *Āgama*: "In the trichiliocosm..."
Furthermore, there is a Great Diamond Mountain that encircles the waters of the great ocean. Outside this Diamond Mountain, there is another second Great Diamond Mountain.
Between these two mountains, in a place profound and dark, lie the eight great hells—places where the majestic light of the sun and moon cannot reach.
△ Fifth, the verse on transcending the difficulty of hostile thieves.
Or if one encounters hostile bandits surrounding them, each brandishing a blade to inflict harm, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they all immediately give rise to a compassionate heart.
○ When enemies and bandits are entangled in the darkness of suspicion, this refers to each of them brandishing blades to inflict harm. The Bodhisattva regards enemies as kin;
there is not the slightest suspicion of harm. Therefore, those who gain power through such recollection all give rise to compassion and rescue them. △
Sixth, the verse on the perils of swords and staves:
Should one encounter the suffering of royal punishment and face execution at the end of one's life, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, the sword shall be shattered into pieces.
○ Royal punishment arises from the view of a self (satkāya-dṛṣṭi). Because this body is born, that death of the body follows; this is what is meant by facing [execution].

"Execution" refers to the end of life. Because the bodhisattva has eliminated and forgotten the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), those who possess the power of mindfulness cause the sword of that view of a self-body to be shattered into pieces.
△ Seventh, a verse summarizing the difficulty of shackles and fetters.
Or, if one is imprisoned and shackled, with hands and feet bound by cangues and fetters, through the power of contemplating Avalokiteśvara, one attains release and liberation.

(○) This is like being bound by the shackles of extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Giving rise to such extreme views as existence, non-existence, annihilationism, or eternalism constitutes being imprisoned by property, shackled by wife and children, and bound by the constraints of one's kinsmen. The Bodhisattva...
Extreme views are suddenly emptied; thus, those who hold the name attain liberation. △ Eighth: Adding Verses on the Difficulty of Curses and Poisons.
Regarding curses, incantations, and various poisons intended to harm the body: by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they shall return to the person who sent them.
Regarding spells, medicines, and the like: these are produced by wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). They harm others but ultimately bring harm upon oneself.

Since the Noble Ones (*ārya*) are free from wrong views, those who maintain mindfulness of them will not encounter poison or untimely calamities. As it is said in a sutra: There was a lay follower of pure faith who initially observed the five precepts.
Later, as he grew old and infirm, he forgot much of what he had learned. At that time, there was a person suffering from thirst in the mountains...
The brahmin begged for a drink from him. Because the man of the fields was busy with his work, he did not fulfill the request; the brahmin departed in resentment.
This brahmin was able to raise corpses and command ghosts; he summoned a murderous ghost and commanded it, saying, "He has insulted me; go and kill him.
There was an arhat in the mountains who knew of this and went to the man of the fields, telling him, "Tonight, light your lamps early and be diligent in the three..."

He took refuge for himself and recited the verse for guarding body and speech: "Do not commit transgressions with mouth or body. He maintained loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, whereby they were able to attain peace and security.
The host followed his instructions, and the ghost was unable to cause him harm. Because it could not harm him, the ghost became enraged and sought to kill the brahmin.
The Arhat rendered it tattered so that the ghost could not see it. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) quotes this, saying:
"This is precisely the meaning of 'returning to the original person' found in the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*. △ Ninth: A supplementary verse on the peril of the rākṣasa.
Or if one encounters evil rākṣasas, venomous dragons, various ghosts, and the like, when they call upon the power of Avalokiteśvara, none dare to harm them.
(This refers to the arising of all views and attachments. Because the Bodhisattva has eliminated and forgotten all views, those who call upon him gain this power to sever all views;
thus, the dragons and ghosts have no means of harming them. △ Tenth: A verse added regarding the peril of fierce beasts.
If one is surrounded by fierce beasts with terrifying sharp fangs and claws, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, one shall flee swiftly to boundless directions.
○ This is analogous to the grasping at precepts and prohibitions (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which acts as a fierce beast possessing sharp fangs and claws that are terrifying.

Because the Bodhisattva is free from attachment to such precepts and prohibitions, he enables those who recollect him to gain power, whereby they can seize and subdue fierce beasts such as oxen and dogs, and flee swiftly.
They flee to boundless regions. △ Eleven: An Added Verse on the Peril of Snakes and Scorpions.
"Vipers, snakes, and venomous scorpions, whose poisonous breath blazes like smoke and fire—when they recall the power of Avalokiteśvara, they turn back upon hearing his voice."
○ Vipers, snakes, and the like possess the evil of wrath and resentment; their poisonous breath is like the burning of fire and smoke, killing upon contact.
The Bodhisattva has no such toxic harm; therefore, those who bring him to mind gain power, and all malevolent insects naturally avoid them.
△ Twelfth: An added verse on the difficulty of rain and clouds.
When clouds gather like thunder, lightning flashes, hail falls, and great rains pour down, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they shall be dispersed and vanish in their very hour.
Flattery is like clouds covering the sun; arrogance is like the startling crash of thunder.
To envy the strengths of others and seek out their weaknesses is as swift as a flash of lightning, leaving not even a hair’s breadth of concealment.
They delight in harming the goodness of others, like hail that prematurely destroys things.
They utter mad words of praise or slander toward people, like pouring rain that falls upon things and soaks them. The Bodhisattva is free from these various evils;
therefore, the practitioner gains power, and whenever they encounter any harm, it dissipates instantly. Master Shi said: "The above verses describe the seven difficulties."
Together these constitute twelve, which do not transcend the six elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness. Mount Sumeru and the diamond [vajra] are earth;
clouds and rain are water; snakes, beasts, and curses belong to sentient beings and thus pertain to consciousness.

Through the revolving restoration of the Bodhisattva’s physical body, one’s petitions will surely be fulfilled. Furthermore, one must understand that all form and mind, as well as the environment and its inhabitants, are entirely...

This Bodhisattva possesses wondrous form and wondrous mind. Sentient beings, regarding this noble form and mind, spontaneously give rise to a sense of difficulty [in their own plight] and a sincere cry for salvation;
this is precisely Avalokiteśvara. Thus, when the conditions are met, the response is immediate. One should contemplate it through this principle:

what cause for concern is there that [the practitioner] would not be as effective as Avalokiteśvara in benefiting sentient beings? The section on the seven calamities and their subsequent resolutions is hereby concluded. △
The two verses address the three poisons and the two types of seeking.

Sentient beings are beset by calamities and constrained by immeasurable suffering that oppresses their bodies; yet through the wondrous power of Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom, he is able to rescue the world from its suffering.
While the preceding verse rescues one from external perils, this verse liberates one from internal karma. This is truly because sentient beings are [driven] by greed and anger.
These ten fetters (*saṃyojana*) cause beings within the three realms to falsely create and falsely experience [suffering].

The six classes of ordinary beings are entangled by coarse afflictions, while the four types of noble ones are obscured by subtle afflictions. Although the afflictions differ in their coarseness and subtlety, they are one and the same in how various heavy and light sufferings oppress them.
Thus it is said: "Immeasurable suffering oppresses the body. For all these various capacities, the Bodhisattva, by means of his wondrous...
By the power of wisdom and supernormal faculties, there is nothing within the three worlds that cannot be saved.
Thus, the sentient beings herein and the world itself all possess the meaning of the ten dharma realms. The verse response concerning the name of Avalokiteśvara is now complete.

△ Second, the verse response concerning the manifestation through the Universal Gate, divided into two parts. First, the actual verse on the manifestation, which is further divided into two. First, the transposed verse on the general [manifestation].

Answer: "Possessing the power of supernatural penetrations and extensively cultivating the skillful means of wisdom, there is no land throughout the worlds of the ten directions in which he does not manifest his body.
This verse provides a general answer to the prose section concerning how he travels through various lands in diverse forms, etc. It further points directly out: "Also..."
This extensively praises Avalokiteśvara’s supernatural powers, wisdom, and skillful means, all of which are fully perfected;

thus, he is able to universally respond to the capacities of sentient beings throughout the lands of the ten directions, manifesting the characteristics of his perfect practice as being equal to the realm of empty space.
